title: Gene therapy that led to boy’s death had limited efficacy
raw_text:
Results from the first human trial of an experimental gene-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), in which a young Chinese boy died, have been published1. Although the trial provides evidence that the treatment developed by HuidaGene, based in Shanghai, China, edited some target genes, the therapeutic benefit was limited and led to a catastrophic immune reaction in one participant. Researchers say there is an urgent need to establish safe dosages for these kinds of experimental treatment.
The trial gained attention when HuidaGene announced on 5 August that one participant, a boy, had died roughly a year earlier. Researchers criticized the company for waiting so long to publicly report the death — and the event put a spotlight on China’s fast-track clinical trials. On 27 August, HuidaGene told Nature that the firm wanted to “establish the clinical facts and undertake a comprehensive investigation” before communicating with the broader public. They said a manuscript detailing the boy’s death and post-mortem findings had been submitted to a journal in January, which has now been published in Cell.
The boy who died was one of four children to receive the experimental therapy for DMD, a progressive and ultimately fatal genetic disorder that mostly affects boys, causing difficulty in walking and gradual muscle weakening. Children with DMD have mutations in the DMD gene that affect their ability to produce dystrophin, a protein that strengthens muscle fibres. The therapy used an adeno-associated virus (AAV) to deliver a base editor — a form of CRISPR gene-editing technology — to muscles to correct the mutation. The boy who died and another boy received a high dose of the therapy in AAVs; two other boys were given a low dose.
Within 24 hours of receiving the therapy, the authors say that the boy who died experienced sudden, severe abdominal pain, followed by a fever that responded only partially to treatment. The team says his condition declined rapidly, and he developed discoloured skin due to a lack of oxygen in his blood, as well as a slow, irregular heartbeat. His heart eventually stopped, and doctors could not revive him. The authors report that an autopsy revealed that he died of acute respiratory distress syndrome, which was related to the treatment.
Ian Woodcock, a paediatric neurologist and researcher at Murdoch Children’s Research Institute in Melbourne, Australia, says the boy’s fast decline suggests it was a reaction to the dose he received. In general, a large dose of AAVs are required so the gene therapy reaches muscle cells across the body. But this increases the risk of severe immune reactions, including death, that have been reported in this and other gene therapy trials for DMD2,3. “Even though the AAV doesn't cause disease in humans, this amount of foreign invasion really triggers the immune system,” he says.
Animal studies
The authors report that they performed safety testing in cynomolgus macaques (Macaca fascicularis) before the trial in people. No negative side effects were observed with either a high or low dose, but the monkeys did have a weak, short-lived immune reaction following treatment. The authors acknowledge that the monkey experiments could not detect rare side effects, such as the severe immune reaction experienced by the boy who died, because they only tested the treatment in four animals.
When asked whether they should have run tests in more animals, co-author Hui Yang, co-founder of HuidaGene, said that increasing animal numbers alone could not guarantee prediction of an uncommon reaction in people, particularly because different species have different immune responses.
The boy who died was the second to receive the high dose, and only after safety data for the other high-dose recipient and the two low-dose recipients were reviewed by the trial’s safety review committee, the authors said. The exact dosage the boys received was based on their weight.
The team said that the boy who died received a higher dose than the other boy in the high-dose group because he had a higher body mass index (BMI). But that does not necessarily mean that he had more lean muscle, which is the target of the therapy. Yang says that the boy’s muscles might have been exposed to a higher dose than in the other boys, but it is still unclear whether that could have triggered the severe immune reaction. The authors suggest that dosing on the basis of body weight might not be appropriate.
Yang says the team tried to reduced the risk of severe immune responses by giving the boys immunosuppressants, testing both doses in animals and staggering each boy’s treatment following a safety review. But given the boy’s death, those measures were insufficient, he says. “We therefore need to re-examine the assumptions underlying dose selection, the role of body composition,” and the predictive value of preclinical studies, he adds. Stronger independent safety oversight and ways of reducing the effective dose also need to be developed, he adds. “The most important lesson is that severe systemic immune toxicity following AAV administration remains difficult to predict.”
Next-generation AAVs that are better at penetrating muscles could mean that lower doses can achieve the same editing effect, says Woodcock. Or the team might consider an alternative to AAVs, he adds.

title: Mysterious flickering brain signals could help to unlock secrets of consciousness
raw_text:
The reaction to neuroscientist Doris Tsao’s latest preprint, she says, has been “surreal”. Tsao, at the University of California, Berkeley, described the study on social media on 17 October. Ten days later, her summary has drawn more than two million views and 11,000 likes.
Posted on bioRxiv, the study1 probed the brains of macaques (Macaca mulatta) during a visual-perception experiment. Using only the monkeys’ neural activity, Tsao’s team managed to reconstruct with high fidelity not only images that the animals were consciously seeing, but also images that were in front of their eyes but escaped their awareness.
Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be
Previous studies in monkeys have detected neural activity in response to content they are not aware of, but only as weak signals. “It’s super surprising to find this strong signal that is not consciously perceived,” Tsao says. Even more unexpected to Tsao, the study showed that brain activity switched between patterns associated with conscious processing and those associated with unconscious processing several times per second.
The authors say that the findings, which have not yet been peer reviewed, could be a small step towards solving one of neuroscience’s biggest mysteries: how brains give rise to consciousness, or the subjective experience of being aware.
Scientists studying consciousness were intrigued by the research and praised its rigorous methods. But some pointed out that the social-media buzz might have been overblown. “It’s an interesting little firestorm of a paper,” says John Sakon, a cognitive neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles. “But some of the findings were not totally unexpected.”
Out of sight, out of mind?
Imagine someone looking through binoculars that show a different image to each eye. The person would perceive only one image at a time, rather than a mix of the two. This phenomenon, known as binocular rivalry, is important for the study of consciousness, because it enables researchers to study what happens in the brain when an image enters someone’s consciousness.
How does the brain control consciousness? This deep-brain structure
Exploring this paradigm with monkeys, Tsao and her team presented one image of a face to one eye of a monkey and, after a couple of seconds, introduced an image of a different face to the other eye. When this experiment is done in humans, people who are shown both images report seeing only the second. Researchers assume that the same thing happens with monkeys.
The scientists recorded activity in two brain regions that are known to be involved in facial recognition: the inferotemporal cortex and the prefrontal cortex.
Researchers first showed both faces to the monkey, one at a time, so that they could identify the distinct patterns of neural activity elicited by each image. Then they began the experiment by introducing the first image to one eye. When they introduced the second image to the monkey’s other eye, its brain activity quickly flickered between two neural patterns 15 times per second.

title: Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks
raw_text:
The future of psychedelics is looking bright, after some dark times. Just two years ago, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) rejected an application to use MDMA — the active ingredient in the party drug ecstasy — to treat post-traumatic stress disorder. With that refusal, the whole field seemed to stall. But now, billion-dollar investments and more clinical-trial data suggest that the field is forging ahead.
The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care
The FDA refusal “stimulated a lot of thought and conversation”, says Rachel Yehuda, a neuroscientist at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. “But it didn’t make people want to give up on these medicines. Everyone can see that loud and clear.”
In July, the drug giant Eli Lilly in Indianapolis, Indiana, announced plans to acquire AtaiBeckley, a psychedelic-medicine development firm in New York City, for up to US$3.8 billion. The company’s lead asset, BPL-003, targets treatment-resistant depression, a condition affecting millions of people around the world.
Eli Lilly’s bet is one of the largest so far. And it comes on the heels of other big investments, such as Illinois-based AbbVie’s $1.2 billion acquisition in 2025 of bretisilocin, a short-acting psychedelic being developed by Gilgamesh Pharmaceutical in New York City.
How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
Why such persistence in the pursuit of psychedelic therapies? Researchers partially credit increasingly clear guidance from regulators worldwide on how these treatments should be studied and used. Even in the United States, where regulatory teams in the FDA have been thinned by layoffs, psychedelics are still a priority. “Where there’s a governmental will, there’s a governmental way,” says Yehuda.
Many psychedelic-development programmes have now advanced to late stages. Findings include rapid and potentially lasting effects for anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Definium Therapeutics, based in New York City, released results in August and September from late-stage studies of its LSD-based pill, showing a significant reduction in symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder. Preliminary trials also hint at psychedelic benefits for conditions such as substance-use and eating disorders.
Meanwhile, researchers are zeroing in on specific properties of psychedelics, with the goal of engineering drugs that act for less time and with fewer hallucinations — tweaks that could make them more viable in the clinic.
Magic-mushroom compound blocks a severe side effect of chemotherapy, in mice
Still, scientists emphasize that there’s much more to be done. Further research is needed to understand, for example, the extent of possible mental and physical adverse effects and how long effects of various compounds need to last to have a therapeutic benefit.
Continued progress is not inevitable. The enthusiasm seen in the late 1990s and early 2000s, which led to the increased pace of discoveries, also happened in the 1950s and 1960s. However, it was stifled by the US government-led war on drugs, says Philippe Lucas, director of research at the non-profit organization Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies in San Jose, California. “So I always have that red flag in the back of my mind.”
Still, given the big recent investments, he says, the field “looks to have significant legs”.
Boom over bust?
The failed FDA approval of MDMA initially seemed to have “a really sobering effect on the field”, says Ekaterina Malievskaia, co-founder and chief executive of n1 bio, an autism biotechnology firm in Miami, Florida, and co-founder of Compass Pathways, a psychedelic-development company headquartered in London that is trying to earn US approval of a psilocybin treatment.
In 2024, the FDA voiced specific concerns about the MDMA therapy from Lykos Therapeutics, now Resilient Pharmaceuticals in Lake Forest, Illinois. One major issue was that participants and researchers could guess whether someone was on an active psychedelic treatment during the trials, a phenomenon known as functional unblinding. This July, the FDA finalized psychedelic-trial guidance that includes advice for reducing functional unblinding.
The agency also flagged the difficulty in disentangling MDMA’s effects from those of the accompanying psychotherapy during the trials. Both safety and efficacy probably depend on the therapeutic context, says Yehuda.
Lykos’s studies were “guinea pigs” for the industry, says Emma Wille, an analyst at business-intelligence provider Citeline in New York City. “Now, companies know more about what will make a good data-submission package.”
And many are moving forwards with applications. Resilient resubmitted a new-drug application this year. Meanwhile, Compass Pathways has announced positive results from two late-stage trials of a psilocybin therapy for treatment-resistant depression. “It does look as though it’s inevitable that they will get the license”, says Robin Carhart-Harris, a neuroscientist and psychopharmacologist at the University of California, San Francisco.
The US government seems to anticipate movement on psychedelics. An August report from the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration in Rockville, Maryland, urges states to prepare for possible FDA approval of psychedelic therapies by, among other recommendations, building the necessary health-system infrastructure to deliver such treatments.
How ecstasy and psilocybin are shaking up psychiatry
Although MDMA and psilocybin are likely to be the first psychedelics to be “pharmaceuticalized”, says Lucas, “dark horses are running in the same room”. Among the compounds getting attention as potential therapies are 5-MeO-DMT, the primary component of the poison excreted by the Sonoran Desert toad (Incilius alvarius), which can cause an almost complete dissolution of the sense of self, and ibogaine, which has psychedelic effects that can last for more than 24 hours and carries cardiovascular risks. “Ten years ago, many of us would have thought these would be the least likely to go through pharmaceutical development,” says Lucas.
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order in April that streamlines research into psychedelic compounds and increases the government’s financial investments. The order specifically highlights ibogaine. The chemical, found in a Central African shrub, is being studied as a treatment for substance-use disorders and PTSD. In October, the FDA announced a request for public input on the design of government-funded clinical trials of ibogaine.
Odette Hauke, a regulatory-affairs consultant based in Los Angeles, California, welcomed the move. There are many unresolved safety questions, she says. “It’s important that we’re approaching this cautiously.”

title: Functional architecture of the human insula - Nature
raw_text:
Abstract
The insular cortex has a central role in pain1,2, interoception3,4 and feelings5,6, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula7,8,9,10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal–posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral–posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior–polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

Extended data figures and tables
Extended Data Fig. 1 Multidimensional scaling of functional response profiles across insular cytoarchitectonic areas.
a, Three-dimensional multidimensional scaling (MDS) visualization of the functional similarity between the cytoarchitectonic areas of the human insula based on their electrically evoked response profiles (somatosensory, pain/temperature, visceral, and no response). Each point represents one cytoarchitectonic area, with distances between points reflecting dissimilarity in functional response profiles. The low stress value (<0.01) indicates a good representation of the original dissimilarities in three-dimensional MDS space. Areas are grouped according to the four functional regions identified by unsupervised k-means clustering (see Methods: Functional Clustering of Insular Areas).
Extended Data Fig. 2 Electrical stimulation parameters across response categories.
Distribution of stimulation current amplitudes (milliamperes, mA) for a) all responsive sites, b) all unresponsive sites, c) responsive sites excluding pain and temperature responses, and d) pain and temperature-responsive sites. The small bars between the larger bars represent the relatively few instances in which currents of x + 0.5 mA were used. Stimulation amplitudes were comparable across response categories, indicating that differences in subjective responses were unlikely to be explained by systematic differences in the stimulation current applied.
Extended Data Fig. 3 Transition between somatosensory and pain/thermal sensations follows granular architecture.
a, In four participants with oblique electrodes traversing the posterior insula, we observed a sharp change in the evoked experience when crossing the border from the ventral posterior dysgranular Region II (somatosensory responses) to the dorsal posterior granular Region I (pain and temperature responses). Notably, the few somatosensory responses observed in Region I (e.g., in participant 1) originated from area Id4 in the anterior insula, which consistently evoked sensory sensations localized to the oral cavity. Slight discrepancies between individual participant borders and the group-averaged cytoarchitectonic boundaries are expected, as the atlas represents the highest-probability location of borders, whereas individual participant anatomy may vary. Of note, electrodes localized close to the anterior insular pole remained unresponsive to stimulation.
Extended Data Fig. 4 Somatotopic organization of the insula assessed by somatosensory evoked potentials.
a) Somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) were recorded from 218 insular contacts in 37 participants from an Italian cohort following peripheral stimulation of the mandibular (blue), median (red) and tibial (salmon) nerves (see Methods: Somatosensory Evoked Potentials (SEPs)). Electrodes showing significant responses to peripheral nerve stimulation are displayed according to the stimulated nerve; grey electrodes indicate recording sites without a significant response. Significant responses to stimulation of all three body parts were observed only within granular Region I. b) Radar chart comparing the regional distribution of single-body-part responses between the peripheral nerve stimulation and direct cortical stimulation cohorts. The proportion of contacts showing single-body-part responses was highest in Region I in both cohorts (37/92 contacts, 40.22%, peripheral nerve stimulation; 95/215 contacts, 44.19%, direct cortical stimulation), followed by Region II (12/52 contacts, 23.08%; 38/194 contacts, 19.59%, respectively) and the anterior insula (11/74 contacts, 14.86%; 1/272 contacts, 0.37%, respectively). c) Comparison of anterior–posterior (Y) coordinates of single-body-part responses within Region I between the direct cortical stimulation and peripheral nerve stimulation cohorts. For direct cortical stimulation, n = 18 contacts for mouth, n = 43 contacts for arm and n = 21 contacts for leg responses; for peripheral nerve stimulation, n = 1 contact for trigeminal, n = 30 contacts for median and n = 6 contacts for tibial nerve responses. Boxplots show lower-extremity responses at more posterior locations, upper-extremity responses at intermediate locations and mouth-related responses at more anterior locations. Centre lines indicate medians (50th percentile), box bounds indicate the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5× the interquartile range; observations beyond the whiskers are plotted individually as outliers.
Extended Data Fig. 5 Beck Anxiety Inventory scores according to electrical stimulation responses.
a, Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) scores were assessed in participants undergoing electrical stimulation of Region III, where visceral and anxiety responses were evoked. Twenty-four participants were categorized into three groups based on their responses to intracranial electrical stimulation: Anxiety (stimulation evoked anxiety symptoms), Visceral (stimulation evoked visceral sensations without anxiety), and No Response (stimulation evoked no subjective symptoms). BAI scores are separated into cognitive and visceral/somatic components. The Anxiety group exhibited higher scores than the Visceral and No Response groups. Notably, four participants in the Anxiety group showed an asymmetry between cognitive and visceral/somatic scores (cognitive > visceral/somatic or visceral/somatic > cognitive), indicating differences in the relative contribution of the two symptom dimensions.
Extended Data Fig. 6 Anterior insular pole activation during the reversed salience task.
a, To assess whether activation of the anterior insular pole during salience detection and changes in action mode was independent of the required motor response, the task condition was reversed. In the original condition, participants responded to frequently presented city stimuli and withheld responses to infrequent target mountain stimuli. In the reversed condition, a subset of six participants (100 electrodes) withheld responses to frequent city stimuli and responded to infrequent mountain stimuli. The reversed task produced a comparable activation pattern, with predominant activation in and around Region IV.

Extended Data Fig. 9 Connectivity among insular Regions I–III.
Causal electrophysiological connectivity was assessed using the same cerebro-cerebral evoked potential (CCEP) analyses as in Fig. 4 (see Methods: CCEPs: Within-Insula Connectivity). Connectivity strength was quantified by the F1 feature, reflecting the early high-frequency, phase-locked response to stimulation. For each regional comparison, flat maps show electrode-level connectivity, with each recording electrode colour-coded by its mean F1 connectivity from all stimulation sites in the other region within the same participant. Participant-level plots show mean connectivity in both directions, with the x- and y-axes representing mean F1 connectivity strength in the two opposing directions, respectively. The identity line represents equal bidirectional connectivity, and deviations indicate directional asymmetry. Pair-level spectrotemporal contrasts show significant time–frequency clusters in which connectivity was stronger in one direction than the other. a–c) Connectivity between Regions III and I (n = 254 matched bidirectional CCEP pairs from 30 participants) showed no significant directional asymmetry in F1 connectivity at either the matched-pair (two-sided paired permutation test, 10,000 permutations, BH-FDR-adjusted P = 0.656) or participant level (PFDR = 0.7756), while spectrotemporal analysis revealed stronger late low-frequency connectivity from Region I toward Region III. d–f) Connectivity between Regions III and II (n = 144 matched bidirectional CCEP pairs from 30 participants) showed stronger F1 connectivity from Region III to Region II, significant at both the matched-pair (PFDR < 0.0001) and participant levels (PFDR = 0.0018). Conversely, spectrotemporal analysis revealed stronger late low-frequency connectivity from Region II toward Region III. g–i) Connectivity between Regions II and I (n = 186 matched bidirectional CCEP pairs from 26 participants) showed no significant directional asymmetry in F1 connectivity at either the matched-pair (PFDR = 0.4256) or participant level (PFDR = 0.7756). Cohen’s d effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals for these directional F1 connectivity comparisons are shown in Fig. 4k. Together, these analyses demonstrate that connectivity among Regions I–III depends on both direction and the temporal and spectral characteristics of the evoked response, with posterior Regions I and II showing a potential late low-frequency influence toward Region III.

title: Daily briefing: The Selfish Gene, 50 years on
raw_text:
Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.
What did biotech learn from Theranos?
Elizabeth Holmes and her failed blood-testing start-up, Theranos — subject of the new documentary You Can See Everything — left “a crater in the whole field of monitoring and diagnostics”, says bioengineer Paul Yager. But the field hasn’t given up on the promise of blood tests that are faster, more convenient and more accessible than current methods.
‘Hell chicken’ dino kept a strict diet
The newly described Infernogallus jamesi — or ‘hell chicken’ — is among the first non-bird dinosaurs thought to have exclusively eaten fruit. The species, about the size of a modern turkey, lived around 120 million years ago. Analysis of bones in an I. jamesi fossil revealed that it probably had a weak bite, strong lower-jaw muscles associated with gnashing and ridges across its beak — adaptations that closely resemble those of modern fruit-eating parrots. Researchers hypothesize that the dinosaur ate the ancient equivalent of fruits such as cherries and peaches.
Reference: Nature Communications paper
‘Cable bacteria’ make their own MOFs
For the first time, researchers have discovered living creatures that make their own MOFs — metal-organic frameworks — with exceptional conductivity. Chemists Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry last year for their work on synthetic MOFs. Candidatus Electrothrix gigas is relatively huge — up to 8 µm long — and appears to produce centimetre-long filaments of a nickel-based MOF that help it to access energy and electron sources in the sediment of the seafloor.
Chemistry World | 7 min read (free registration required)
Reference: Nature Communications paper
Features & opinion
50 years on, go beyond The Selfish Gene
The idea set out in Richard Dawkins’s 1976 book The Selfish Gene — that bodies are just genes’ way of making more of themselves — “seemed pretty harmless”, writes historian of science Nathaniel Comfort. Today, “the determinism baked into the ‘gene’s-eye view’ in the book troubles me, as does the passivity of the organism in Dawkins’s telling”. Comfort dives into modern efforts to synthesize ecology, evolution, genetics and developmental biology to create “a less gene-centred view” that “is more accurate — and infinitely more satisfying”.
Should I disclose my disability?
A new PhD student whose disability requires rest has found themselves in a lab where long hours are rampant, colleagues are burnt out and time off is a no-go. They ask: ‘should I risk disability stigma by disclosing to my principal investigator?’ Four researchers weigh in on how to proceed. “Regardless of what you decide about your PI, informal goodwill evaporates under pressure, while documented accommodations do not,” says management researcher Deepti Sharma.
Video: how to keep coral reefs afloat
As the El Niño weather event turns up the heat in oceans already warmed by climate change, scientists are turning to a suite of unorthodox methods to save temperature-sensitive corals. Underwater speakers that play the sounds of a healthy coral reef can encourage free-roaming larvae to settle in areas where adult corals are struggling, and a low-tech ‘one-star hotel’ helps to raise resilient youngsters.

title: How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
raw_text:
More than one billion people globally live with a mental-health condition. Collectively, these disorders are now the world’s leading cause of disability. Depression and anxiety alone cost the global economy an estimated US$1 trillion every year.
The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care
Conventional pharmacological approaches to improving mental health are falling short. However, two Nature News features this week report on innovations that indicate a shift is under way. One describes the personalization of psychiatric care; the other discusses developments in psychedelic medicine. Although neither effort will provide a complete solution for the mental-health crisis, both are bringing much-needed ingenuity to the field.
To ensure that these ideas translate into improvements in mental-health care, they must be pursued with rigour and in a way that ensures they have the widest possible reach. As psychedelic-development programmes move towards regulatory approval, the US Food and Drug Administration has rightly clarified what types of evidence and outcome it expects to see in trials (see go.nature.com/4bstrh2). Funders and regulators must now ensure that approaches that prove successful actually reach the people who need them. This will not be straightforward because many psychedelics and proposed personalized treatments are expensive. They are developed with small groups of people with a specific condition in mind and therefore do not benefit from economies of scale. At the same time, personalized treatments can be out of reach for people from low-income backgrounds, who are more likely than others to have a mental-health condition.
Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks
Under the current psychiatric model for mental-health conditions, two people with the same diagnosis of depression can have distinct symptoms, different underlying biology and divergent responses to the same treatments. That heterogeneity is reflected in clinical outcomes. A substantial proportion of people don’t respond to the first antidepressant drug that they try, and around 30% remain symptomatic after trying several treatments (C. Njenga et al. BMJ 386, e073823; 2024).
In practice, conditions are more complex than conventional diagnostic categories suggest. One reason for this is that classifications have relied on subjective reporting of symptoms. Now, precision psychiatry approaches aim to improve diagnosis and outcomes. The idea is to personalize treatments by cataloguing symptoms in detail and as objectively as possible, and identifying measurable biological indicators, or biomarkers. The expectation is that this can help to match people with more-effective treatments, and do so faster by shortening the process.
Methods include the use of genetic and blood-based biomarkers; measures of brain activity such as functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalograms; and ‘digital phenotyping’, in which smartphones and other sensors record sleep and movement, for instance. But these assessments have yet to consistently yield improvements for people with mental-health conditions, as one of the features reports. Some researchers say that another approach would be to gather as much data as possible on how people respond to specific treatments and which responses correlate with mental-health improvements. Those data can then be fed into artificial-intelligence models to predict how individuals might fare. It is unclear, however, whether the benefits of such tools would outweigh their costs.
Psychedelics: concerns and opportunities
As reported in the other feature, psychedelics might tap into the brain’s capacity to reorganize its connections and circuits, potentially disrupting rigid patterns and enabling psychological changes — even for some people for whom conventional treatments haven’t worked.
The ‘bible for psychiatry’ is getting a rewrite: your guide to the next DSM
Outcomes could be optimized by personalization. But, as with precision psychiatry more broadly, this approach comes with a duty to prioritize research into treatment responses across diverse populations. The use of psychedelics introduces additional concerns. Adequately trained health-care workers are needed to bolster the drug’s efficacy and safety, especially during potentially intense, unpredictable and lengthy psychedelic experiences.
Existing treatments for mental-health conditions, including psychotherapy and antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, can be extremely effective for some people. But their full therapeutic benefits can take time to emerge. The rapid relief provided by psychedelics could complement such therapies.
However, even the most sophisticated and effective treatment strategies will have limited impact if people can’t access them. That’s why funders and regulators must work out who is going to cover the cost of a brain scan (if they are found to be clinically useful) or pay for a hours-long session so people can take psychedelics safely. Someone will need to assess whether these approaches have enough benefits to offset the spiralling costs of mental-health care — and whether those benefits can be provided equitably.
US speeds up research into mind-altering drugs — including mysterious ‘ibogaine’
There are ways to reduce upfront costs as well as expand reach, for example, by using low-cost biomarkers and therapy sessions in which participants take psychedelic substances together in a supervised setting. Several studies have found that such group sessions can even enhance the therapeutic effects in some cases (A. L. Back et al. Psychedelic Med. 4, 209–221; 2026). Psychedelics with briefer hallucinogenic effects, currently under development, might be an alternative, too.
However, progress on diagnoses and treatments should be paired with innovation on another front: preventing people from developing a mental-health disorder in the first place. No medical breakthroughs can substitute for a society that supports good mental health — and more could be done to reduce the factors that contribute to mental illness, such as economic insecurity, sleep disruption, environmental pollution and social isolation.
The field’s willingness to consider how to reinvent psychiatry is welcome. Proponents of the ideas must now ensure that all who can benefit have access to these therapies and that the highest standards of quality and rigour are adhered to.

title: Preprint-centric publishing model gets major boost
raw_text:
Science funders and research organizations in Europe are joining forces to expand open-access publishing and make the peer-review process more transparent, with the aim of spurring change in scholarly communication.
By early November, the European Commission will roll out an expanded version of its Open Research Europe (ORE) platform, which uses a ‘publish, review, curate’ model. In this approach, preprints are posted, reviewed openly — with the identity of the reviewers and their reports made public — then flagged as ‘peer reviewed’ on the same platform.
Open-access journal eLife announces ‘preprint first’ publishing model
Joining the ORE are funders from 11 countries, including the German Research Foundation DFG and the Swiss National Science Foundation, as well as three major research organizations, including the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS). More than 2.5 million researchers will now receive full editorial services on the platform at no charge. Since its launch in 2021, ORE has published some 1,500 articles.
“This is a collective effort to build a more transparent, sustainable publishing system that serves the research community and society as a whole,” says Karla Anaya-Carlsson, who chairs the ORE Funders Group and is based in Stockholm.
A big burden?
Mario Malički, a metascientist at Stanford University in California, says that the platform simplifies publishing for researchers and reduces funders’ costs. But, he cautions, running something at that scale “becomes a major undertaking of who runs the checks, who curates it and makes the final decisions”.
The expanded project has a budget of €16 million (US$17.7 million) between now and 2030, 60% of which will be provided by the European Commission and the remainder coming from the other funders and research organizations. It will be governed by these bodies, and hosted and operated by CERN, Europe’s particle-physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland.
Independently of the expansion of ORE, a group of 40 funders, institutions, publishers and platforms announced on 28 October the creation of the Publish, Review, Curate Alliance to promote such open publishing initiatives. Members include the journal eLife, the preprint organization OpenRxiv and the archiving service Europe PubMed Central. Other members include funders such as the Howard Hughes Medical Institute and the Gates Foundation, and institutional libraries at Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and the University of Cambridge, UK.
Radical approach
eLife implemented the ‘publish, review, curate’ system in late 2022 and it caused controversy. Some saw the system as a threat to the reputation of the journal, saying that the possibility of rejecting manuscripts during the peer-review process is key to integrity and consistency. Others lauded the model as the future of research publishing.
Within two years of adopting this model, eLife lost its impact factor. Some bibliographic databases, including Web of Science, changed the way the journal was indexed. The finer details of how indexing services will respond to the expansion of ORE are not yet clear; ORE also has no impact factor, nor will it seek one.

title: These three red flags could unmask dodgy journals
raw_text:
Researchers have identified three warning signs that suggest journals might be engaging in suspicious publishing activities. Using these, they have found dozens of titles indexed in the leading scholarly database Scopus that could be problematic.
The three red flags are, for any given journal in a single year: a doubling of publication output; having more than 70% of published articles originating from a single country; and having at least 15% of articles flagged by the Problematic Paper Screener, a free online tool.
Using titles extracted from the freely available database OpenAlex, the researchers identified 3,753 journals that met at least one of these criteria. They cross-referenced these with journals indexed in Scopus and found that, of those, 5% had been delisted. The findings were published in a preprint1 on 20 October.
Exposing predatory journals: anonymous sleuthing account goes public
The researchers, and research-integrity specialists, say that the signals help to identify journals that merit further investigation — but do not prove that titles are problematic. They serve as “rudimentary flags”, says Achal Agrawal, a co-author of the preprint and freelance data scientist in Raipur, India. And they indicate the problems that databases face as poor publishing practices proliferate, he adds.
Rankings basis
Bibliometric databases such as Scopus are important in the global research ecosystem because they inform many rankings used to evaluate individual researchers and institutions. Inclusion in Scopus, run by the Dutch publisher Elsevier, typically indicates that a journal is reputable.
Scopus regularly reviews the journals it lists, using a tool to spot signs of suspicious activities that suggest titles are churning out low-quality research that doesn’t adhere to accepted scholarly standards. These include “changes in publication volume and journal scope, unusual patterns in authorship and author collaboration, anomalous citation behaviour, and indications that a journal has become vulnerable to questionable content”, a spokesperson for Elsevier told Nature.
For flagged journals, Scopus then conducts “a careful, individual assessment of all available information, including consideration of the journal’s own response”, the spokesperson added. It removes journals that do not meet certain metrics thresholds. Scopus delisted 156 journals last year, and 100 so far this year.
“No single signal, and no fixed threshold, determines the outcome,” Elsevier’s spokesperson said. “A signal is a prompt to investigate, and where needed the journal is put forward for re-evaluation” by Scopus’s content-selection board.
Hijacked journals are still a threat — here’s what publishers can do about them
Signs of trouble
The study reported that the roughly 3,500 journals that have not been delisted together contributed more than half a million papers in the years that they were flagged by at least one signal. Nearly 300 journals were flagged by two signals and 28 journals by all three.
Each signal warrants a further look into the journal, but on its own is not “a definite decision to delist”, says Anna Abalkina, a research-integrity sleuth and social scientist at the Free University of Berlin. “There could be a lot of reasons why a journal duplicates the volume of publication.” For example, that often happens for a new journal, or as part of a publisher’s business plan, she says. But Abalkina thinks that a journal with all three red flags suggests suspicious activity that is difficult to find legitimate justification for.
Álvaro Cabezas Clavijo, who studies research evaluation at the International University of La Rioja in Logroño, Spain, agrees that the three signs should be interpreted with care. For instance, for small journals, having a large proportion of papers from one country might not be “a mark of questionable practices”.

title: Is research funding now a lottery? Elite funder ERC swamped by applications
raw_text:
A 60% growth in applications to one of the world’s most prestigious research-grant programmes could result in an exceptionally low success rate, raising fears that quality scientific ideas will go unfunded. This rise is attributable, in part, to the ease of writing applications with artificial-intelligence tools.
When the best decision is no decision: the rise of randomization in grant funding
“The number is a bit scary,” says Maria Leptin, president of the European Research Council (ERC) in Brussels, noting it’s increasingly difficult for their staff and peer reviewers to tackle so many applications.
The ERC’s Starting Grant programme — which offers base funds of up to €1.5 million (US$1.7 million) over five years to early-career scientists — received 7,710 proposals for 2027 grants before the deadline on 14 October, up from 4,807 last year (see ‘Rising torrent’).
With up to 373 grants available, down from 421 last year because of funding constraints, that will mean a success rate of less than 5%, compared with 8.8% for the 2026 grant call. “It’s almost a lottery,” says Devang Mehta, a systems and synthetic biologist at the Catholic University of Leuven in Belgium who applied for a Starting Grant this year.
Submissions rocket
The ERC is the Europe Union’s elite funder of basic research with an annual budget of nearly €3 billion. It offers three grant categories — Starting, Consolidator and Advanced — for individual researchers at growing stages of seniority. All have seen significant increases in applications in recent years.
Europe as science superpower: what it will take to rival the US and China
Similar rises in research-grant applications are happening worldwide, says Lynn Kamerlin, a molecular biologist at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta who has studied grant success rates. An ideal success rate for grant programmes is about 20%, she says. Any lower and it becomes increasingly difficult to select the best research without subjective judging, meaning that a lot of good science will go unfunded, she adds. “People can’t tell the difference between the top 6, 8, 12%.”
She suggests that one solution is to have a panel select the top 20% of applications and then pick winners at random, as is being done by some funders. Anything below that threshold “is a lottery anyhow”, she says.
The rise in submissions has been attributed in part to AI making it simpler to write grant applications. “It’s just so much easier to generate text,” says Kamerlin. That’s putting huge pressure on the system, she says, because “it can spin absolute nonsense”, meaning that reviews of applications require greater scrutiny.

title: The grand plan to transform psychiatry — by personalizing mental-health care
raw_text:
You go to see a psychiatrist a decade from now. Alongside the usual questions about how you’re feeling, your work and your relationships, they look at biometric data from your phone about your sleep and speech patterns, examine the results of a blood test or a brain scan and even check your postcode to see whether your neighbourhood has high levels of pollution. An algorithm then compares that information with data from thousands of other people, determines which types of treatment have worked best for people similar to you and uses its findings to suggest a treatment regime.
How personalization and psychedelics are revitalizing psychiatry
That’s a vision of the future called precision psychiatry. And it’s a world away from most people’s experiences today. For all the progress that has been made across the medical sciences, psychiatry remains a frustratingly imprecise discipline. Doctors use someone’s symptoms and clinical history to make a diagnosis and prescribe treatments. But mental-health diagnoses are broad and can be vague — a particular therapy might transform one person’s life, but offer little help to someone else with apparently the same disorder.
As a result, people with mental-health conditions often find themselves cycling through treatments and doses, searching, mostly by trial and error, for one that works.
To improve things, psychiatrists want to divide broad diagnoses into more useful subgroups and match treatments to individuals using a data-driven approach. Some researchers are looking at genes and brain circuits; others are turning to data on speech, sleep or social circumstances. Psychiatrists working on The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), the discipline’s dominant classification system, are even considering how socio-economic, cultural and environmental factors might be incorporated in the future.
Why pharma firms are betting billions on psychedelic drugs despite setbacks
“I think precision psychiatry is certainly part of the future,” says Tom Insel, a psychiatrist and former director of the US National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), who now co-directs several mental-health-focused companies. “We’ll be able to say from the get-go, this patient needs this treatment and that’s where they’re going to do best.”
But some clinicians say that the personalized approach has yet to prove itself. Advances in genetics, brain imaging and biomarker research for psychiatry have failed to deliver on their promise before, and studies continue to reveal just how heterogeneous many psychiatric disorders are. “Psychiatry has this model that the white knight is going to ride over the hill and solve all our problems,” says Kenneth Kendler, a psychiatric geneticist at Virginia Commonwealth University in Richmond. “And we’ve been repeatedly disappointed.”
Classifying with precision
Personalized psychiatry is a catchy phrase, but it’s not a new idea.
Psychiatry has been trying to add precision to diagnosis and treatment for decades. In 1980, the third edition of the DSM introduced specific diagnostic criteria for many conditions. The aim was to boost reliability: a diagnosis of major depression or schizophrenia should mean roughly the same thing for everyone, even when issued by different psychiatrists.
But the DSM relies on symptoms to define conditions, and that proxy introduces complexities. The same symptoms appear in many conditions, and one person might have several diagnoses. Moreover, two people who have been diagnosed with the same condition can manifest it in quite different ways.
To meet DSM criteria for major depressive disorder, for example, a person must, in a two-week period, experience at least five symptoms out of a list of nine. The five must include a depressed mood or a loss of interest or pleasure; the remaining criteria include insomnia or excessive sleep, weight loss or gain, feelings of guilt or worthlessness and suicidal thoughts.
“It’s possible to have two people have the same diagnosis without a single required symptom in common,” says Vikram Patel, a psychiatrist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts.
By the late 2000s, researchers were increasingly questioning whether the approved disease categories were the best way to classify and treat people.
At the NIMH, Insel helped to develop the Research Domain Criteria initiative, which tried to go beyond categories and instead study and measure processes such as reward, fear and cognition, which cut across diagnostic boundaries. The idea encouraged researchers to study behaviours and brain functions that are shared across conditions. Although the programme has helped to shift research towards the underlying mechanisms of illness, it was never intended to replace the symptoms-based diagnostic system, and it does not provide a reliable way to select treatments for individuals.
Another approach to precision is to measure someone’s symptoms and behaviour with more rigour. A psychiatrist assessing psychosis, for example, listens to a person and judges qualities such as coherence, paranoia and grandiosity. That relies on human expertise, but also introduces human subjectivity.
Insel imagines a machine-learning system listening to the same person speaking and assigning more objective, reproducible measurements. “The paranoia score here is 6.1,” he suggests. “The coherence level is 2.2.”
John Torous, a psychiatrist at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Centre in Boston and at Harvard Medical School, works on a related approach known as digital phenotyping, in which information from smartphones and wearable sensors is used to study behaviour. The term emerged around a decade ago, when researchers proposed that sensors already carried around in smartphones could provide continuous measures of various behaviours, such as physical mobility and communication, that could inform diagnosis1.
Can GLP-1s heal the brain? Obesity drugs get a makeover for addiction and depression
Small studies have since found links between activity levels and depressive and manic symptoms in bipolar disorder2, and between location data and symptom severity in schizophrenia3.
The difficulty has been turning these data into something that is useful in the clinic. Medical education has not generally trained clinicians to interpret this information, Torous says, and researchers have not yet developed standards and protocols for using it. “So, we are in the early days in that sense.”
Artificial intelligence could make the difference, he suggests, because it can analyse a range of data streams and package them into useful clinical information.
The approach does come with concerns about privacy: personal data on location, movement, sleep and communication can hold intimate information and could even be used to identify individuals. Furthermore, a systematic review published this year4 found that digital-phenotyping studies showed wide variation in terms of the devices and analytical approaches they used. This could limit their reproducibility and potential for clinical translation.
Biological markers
Digging into biology more deeply could offer another route to precision. As genetics and neuroscience continue to advance, some researchers hope that the insights they provide will help to separate broad psychiatric syndromes into distinct diseases, with different underlying biological mechanisms and, eventually, different treatments.
This hasn’t happened yet, and some argue that it’s a futile exercise. Whereas biological insights helped researchers to divide diabetes into two separate types nearly a century ago, “we’ve never approached that in psychiatry”, says Kendler. Mental-health conditions could be “heterogeneous a long way down”.
Still, genetics has managed to produce one of psychiatry’s more promising potential biomarkers. By looking at the genomes of thousands of people with schizophrenia, in a type of study called genome-wide association, researchers have gleaned some idea about which gene variants confer risk.
For most health conditions, it is the combined small effects of many variants that add up to susceptibility. Geneticists call this collective estimate of risk a polygenic risk score. People towards the top of the polygenic-risk distribution for schizophrenia, says Kendler, can have around a tenfold increase in risk, although the size of the relative increase varies depending on the study. Published estimates5, for example, put risk at about six times higher for the top 1% than for everyone else. But the scores cannot predict who will develop a condition.
“Is it at such a stage now that I would get that score and immediately change what I’m doing diagnostically? No,” Kendler says.
The hidden links between mental disorders
In five or ten years, he says, it is conceivable that a score distinguishing schizophrenia from bipolar disorder could help in a difficult case in which the distinction would affect treatment.
Researchers have also investigated levels of hormones and metabolites as psychiatric biomarkers. But Kendler says that such measures have “almost always” proved to be non-specific. An average biological difference between groups is hard to translate into a specific test that can flag what is wrong with a particular person, or which treatment to offer.
Brain imaging offers another version of the same problem. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies have reported large numbers of associations between features of the brain and psychiatric symptoms, but many of these have been difficult to reproduce.
A 2022 analysis6 of around 50,000 people found that associations between behavioural or mental-health traits and differences in brain structure or function were generally much smaller than previous studies had suggested.
Helen Mayberg, a neurologist at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City, says that scans can still provide clinically useful information if researchers ask specific-enough questions.
Prozac use for childhood depression skewed by single flawed medical trial
She has spent decades mapping brain circuits involved in depression, focusing on a region of the cortex called the subcallosal cingulate. This is tucked beneath the corpus callosum, the dense bundle of fibres that connects the two sides of the brain.
In one study7, researchers used functional MRI to scan the brains of 122 people with depression. They then assigned the individuals at random to one of two treatment groups: the first received 12 weeks of cognitive behavioural therapy, and the other received antidepressant medication for the same period of time.
The researchers found that connectivity between the subcallosal cingulate and three other brain regions differed according to the outcome of the treatment. People for whom psychotherapy worked and medication didn’t typically showed one pattern, whereas people with the opposite responses showed another.
In other words, this pattern of connectivity had the potential to act as a biomarker that can help assign treatment. “A scan done at baseline could actually help you to make that decision,” Mayberg says.
But there is a considerable distance between a potential biomarker and a routine clinical test. Mayberg says she has been told repeatedly that “nobody’s ever going to do a scan to decide how to treat people”, because it is too costly and time-consuming.

title: How the pandemic changed trust in science — in four charts
raw_text:
Trust in science and researchers has fallen following the COVID-19 pandemic, the largest survey of public confidence in science shows. Led by the global biomedical funder Wellcome in London and published on 10 October, it explores how people feel about science and health — including vaccines, pandemic preparedness, clean energy and, for the first time, artificial intelligence (see ‘Trust in decline’).
“We should be paying attention to, and thinking about, what needs to be done to earn that trust,” says Philippa Michael, head of public initiatives at Wellcome, who led the project. This is the third survey of its kind conducted by Wellcome, following editions in 2018 and 2020.
The analysis points to a “mixed” picture that varies between countries and regions, says Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a specialist in science communication at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia (see ‘Regional differences’).
The study also shows a connection between science and people’s broader experiences, including their perceived financial security, says Michael (see ’Money matters‘).
“If people feel economically insecure, then they’re going to feel a greater distance between themselves and science and scientists,” says sociologist Gordon Gauchat, at Harvard Kennedy School in Cambridge, Massachusetts. This disconnect “is not about science’s efficacy or its ability to fix problems”, he adds.
The survey found that countries where people reported high confidence in hospitals and health-care clinics were “more likely to have greater trust in science”, notes Michael. Levels of trust were also high in respondents who were confident in accessing health-care services when needed. “It’s really essential that science is credible, relevant and beneficial to people in their lives,” Michael adds.

title: How to keep tabs on the tools in your lab
raw_text:
When Greg Bannard started her master’s degree in chemistry at the University of Calgary, Canada, she didn’t have an arsenal of tools available to her, so it became incredibly frustrating when equipment went missing. And, being the sort of scientist who’s picky about the kind of spatula that she uses, it could be extremely annoying when her favourite ones disappeared. After several instances of vanishing kit, she could no longer endure running around trying to find tools that had been misplaced.
This inspired her to create a portable pouch that fitted into her pocket of her laboratory coat. “It’s mostly things that I ended up finding myself reaching for,” says Bannard, who now works as an industrial designer, but still keeps the pouch as a keepsake of her time in research.
At the time, Bannard worked in a dye lab, studying the functionality of perylene diimide dyes for the active layers of solar cells. She packed a whole lot into the pouch: a diamond glass cutter, a carbide glass cutter, an ear curette used for working with tiny amounts of powdered dye, a test-tube holder, a pencil, a spatula, little scissors, a felt marker and an “army” of tweezers. “It was a busy lab and people needed to get their own work done,” she says. “The best way that I could get my work done was knowing where everything was.”
Public-speaking tips from the experts: what scientists can learn from comics, musicians and actors
Beyond Bannard’s frustration, missing equipment can disrupt crucial scientific research. Scientists often need particular tools to keep delicate experiments on track. Momoko Takahashi, a neurobiologist at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, knows this too well. She recalls panicking when she could not find a syringe during a time-sensitive procedure involving mouse neurons. “There’s an entire domino effect that starts if one particular moment fails,” she says. “If [the experiment] is not successful, I just wasted a bunch of animals’ lives and that makes me feel really guilty.”
Everyday acts of borrowing, accidental theft, mislabelling and sample moving can turn shared laboratories into crime scenes. The social-media platform Reddit is awash with scientists asking how to guard against ‘disappearing’ items and seeking solutions to track down their missing solutions. Nature spoke directly to researchers about how they protect their work, equipment and sanity without becoming the lab secret police. After all, much ‘stealing’ is done by accident or at least not with malicious intent.
Prevent it
Put systems in place. Scientists who spoke to Nature recounted that all kinds of equipment can disappear from the lab, from small items such as pens and pipettes, to larger and more expensive equipment such as centrifuges and computers. Many interviewees emphasized the importance of having systems in place, such as inventory lists, sign-out sheets and shared equipment guidelines, so that it’s much harder for things to vanish without a trace.
Takahashi highlights the importance of centralizing organization by having official, or unofficial, lab managers and having documentation to keep track of equipment. “A lab is a small business and it should be run like a small business,” she says, noting that she has fallen into a “pseudo lab-manager” position in every lab she’s been in. “Having organizational management implemented right off the bat is crucial to making sure that everything runs smoothly.”
Sandra Petrus-Reurer, a cell-therapy researcher at the University of Cambridge, UK, also stresses the importance of having a really good inventory from the start so people can track who has used specific samples. This way, if something goes missing, it’s easier to work out when and how it could have happened.
Have clear procedures and usage rules. Procedure is especially important when several researchers share equipment or space. According to a PhD student in Australia, who wishes to remain anonymous, shared fridge and freezer space, reagents and fume hoods cause the most conflict in her facilities. To reduce issues in these communal lab spaces, the university has a booking system for benches and hoods. Everyone has allocated trays in each fridge and freezer, each with its own managed inventory to keep track of items and sample movements.
Six tips for better spreadsheets
Some expensive machines or equipment might be funded by several labs, which can also create confusion and conflict, says George Chen, a neurologist at the Children’s Hospital Los Angeles, California. Displaying who can use the equipment can make a world of difference: something as simple as a poster that explains which materials are co-owned and can be shared between labs could be enough. “Be transparent and find systems in which it’s just immediately obvious to everyone what's going on,” he says.
Mark your territory. Making ownership unmistakable can help to mitigate issues. One of the first things Takahashi did when joining her current lab was to label everything. “I always tell the undergrads to initial it or write your name on it,” she says. In Bannard’s lab, each member had electrical tape of a specific colour, which they would wrap around their designated tools. Bannard’s, for instance, was green.
The Australian PhD student says that having clearly labelled reagents and pipettes helps to provide clarity about what some people can and cannot use. After being accused of nabbing another lab’s antibodies, her lab started putting custom stickers on anything that was their property. Indeed, labelling something with a name only the lab group can understand can also ward off sticky fingers. “My lab group once made up code names for our cell lines, as previously our cell cultures were going missing,” she said. The thinking was that potential ‘thieves’ would not know what the code names corresponded to. She says that her group’s cells stopped disappearing after they started adding code names.
You might also consider using hidden labels. A former neuroscientist at the University of Oxford, UK, who preferred not to be named so as not to reveal his lab’s method, had his own hack: “We would put some marker hidden on the inside of the hardware,” he said. “Labels can easily be removed or rubbed off if they’re visible, so by using hidden labels, we could prove that misplaced equipment was ours.”
Hidden and kept under lock and key. Takahashi recommends keeping equipment in cabinets or drawers rather than leaving it out in the open where it can easily be taken or picked up by mistake. People are less likely to rifle through drawers than they are to take things from the bench, she says, noting that she used to hide her prized forceps in her drawer before she went home.
And if you need an extra level of protection, the PhD student recommends getting a lockable box or container that only you, or your team, can access. Petrus-Reurer once bought a lockable fridge, both for extra space and for the appearance of limited access: “I never removed the key, but adding a bit of a physical barrier helped.”
Minimize it
Store separately. When equipment does go missing, there are ways to lessen the impact. Petrus-Reurer and Chen recommend keeping a second stock of everything, because commonly used items tend to run out faster than scientists can replenish them and if they get stolen or misplaced, it can further this nuisance. Chen personally keeps a secondary stash of tissue-culture plates and pipette tips in a hidden drawer. “They’re not expensive, but they just seem to always disappear from the cabinets before someone can reorder them.”
Bring your own tools. Despite best efforts, tools kept communally in the lab can still go missing. “In a well-stocked lab, stuff still happens,” says Bannard. You can plan accordingly, however. Like Bannard, Chen keeps some of his own personal instruments separate, making it clear that they belong to him so that others do not accidentally — or purposefully — nab them.

title: Nerve activity initiates autoimmune hair loss
raw_text:
- NEWS AND VIEWS
Nerve activity initiates autoimmune hair loss
“I’m as free as my hair,” proclaims the pop star Lady Gaga in her song ‘Hair’. Indeed, hair can be a statement of freedom and it informs our sense of self. Conversely, baldness (a condition called alopecia) can be considered an attack on the self, not only in a psychological sense, but also in a literal sense through autoimmunity, in which immune cells that usually ignore the body’s own tissues instead damage organs and cause problems such as hair loss. Writing in Nature, Cui et al.1 provide insights into autoimmune hair loss from their studies of mice.

Can plants defend coasts against storms?
Plants and other organisms can reduce the erosion of coasts by winds and waves. The physical structures of sand-dune and wetland plants, seagrasses, oysters and macroalgae can slow the flow of water and wind, capture sediment and modify soil. Over time, these organisms can also build land, store greenhouse gases, provide habitats for other species and beautify beaches and wetlands1. In some cases, they can be used as a nature-based solution in place of engineered structures. But coastal engineers and planners are often hesitant to incorporate them into construction projects, because their ability to perform in extreme conditions is unknown. Writing in Nature, Willemsen et al.2 determine the limits of coastal protection that salt-marsh plants can provide.

title: ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2 - Nature
raw_text:
Abstract
Patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain at high risk of relapse despite perioperative treatment1-3. NeoCOAST-2 (NCT05061550), a phase 2, randomised platform trial, tested novel perioperative treatments in patients with stage IIA–IIIB NSCLC. At primary analysis, combining standard chemotherapy plus durvalumab (anti-PD-L1 antibody) with oleclumab (Arm 1, n = 76), monalizumab (Arm 2, n = 72) or datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd; Arm 4, n = 54) resulted in pathological complete response (pCR) rates of 20.3%, 25.7%, and 35.2%, respectively4. Here, we present the first report of prespecified secondary endpoints of event-free survival (EFS) and circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) clearance, and exploratory analyses of associations between ctDNA dynamics and clinical outcomes. The 24-month EFS rates were 70.5%, 75.7% and 77.9% in Arms 1, 2 and 4, respectively. Using a tumour-agnostic assay, ctDNA clearance at neoadjuvant Cycle 3 Day 1 was highest in Arm 4 (50.9%, 54.5%, and 72.5% in each arm, respectively). ctDNA clearance correlated with prolonged EFS versus non-clearance (pooled hazard ratio (HR) 0.22; 95% CI = 0.11–0.45, P = 0.0000443). Patients with both ctDNA clearance and pCR had favourable EFS outcomes versus those with neither (EFS HR 0.10, 95% CI = 0.02–0.42, P = 0.002). These findings suggest combined assessment of ctDNA clearance and pCR may improve risk stratification, and that the numerically highest pCR4 and EFS rates with the Dato-DXd combination warrant further evaluation.

title: Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance - Nature
raw_text:
Abstract
For more than two millennia, Archimedean screws have been used for water pumping and, more recently, as turbines in hydroelectric power stations[1]. Their helical-blade structure, essential to their function, is also found in chiral molecules and nanostructures, where injected electric current has been proposed to generate torque-mediated rotation[2,3]. Here, we present a torque-driven molecular machine with a rotor actuated by electric current and conductance enhanced by its rotation. Suspending a helicene molecule between two electrode tips, we show that an applied voltage induces cyclic molecular motion with 100% directional preference that can be inverted by the voltage’s polarity. Above a voltage threshold, the current through the rotating molecule is significantly enhanced, and the enhancement onset is tuned by stretching or compressing the helical molecule. Such effects were absent in previous helical molecular junctions, likely due to structural and operational differences[4–6]. Calculations show that molecular rotation by current-induced forces explains both the observed cyclic motion and current enhancement. This mechanism predicts a transition from stepwise to continuous rotation at a threshold voltage, yielding a current increase as rotation allows adopting highly conducting configurations not accessible at rest. Our work introduces a prototype for a new class of torque-driven molecular machines with perfect rotor unidirectionality and significant current modulation.

title: De novo design of enantioselective artificial metalloenzyme photocatalysts - Nature
raw_text:
Abstract
The ability to create protein scaffolds that impart enantioselectivity to simple, readily available metal catalysts could redefine the landscape of asymmetric catalysis. Artificial metalloenzymes (ArMs), hybrid catalysts that combine a synthetic metal cofactor with a protein scaffold, offer a potential means to achieve this goal, but scaffold discovery has remained constrained by trial-and-error approaches and the functional limits of extant proteins.1–5 This challenge is acute for metal polypyridine photocatalysts, which are widely used in visible-light chemistry but have not enabled highly enantioselective photocatalysis within protein scaffolds. In this study, we show that generative protein design6–8 can create de novo scaffolds that selectively bind these photocatalysts and that directed evolution converts the resulting artificial metalloenzymes into efficient, highly enantioselective photocatalysts9. The evolved proteins support diverse light-driven reactions, high catalyst turnover and catalyst recycling, and can function with commercially available racemic metal complexes. Spectroscopic studies show that the protein environment extends the photocatalyst excited-state lifetime and organizes substrate near the cofactor, altering energy transfer and controlling stereoselectivity. These findings establish de novo protein design as a route to functional scaffolds for synthetic metal complexes that lack natural protein partners and provide a strategy for combining protein design and evolution to control non-natural catalytic chemistry.

title: The contribution of salt marshes to wave attenuation during extreme storms - Nature
raw_text:
Abstract
Salt marshes protect coastlines by attenuating wind waves with their elevated marsh platform and above-ground vegetation1. Confidence in the persistence of this service under a changing climate requires knowledge on how extreme storms damage the platform and vegetation; however, a comprehensive, quantified understanding of salt marsh–wave interactions under extreme events is lacking. A unique experiment was conducted by transferring intact salt marsh to one of the world’s largest wave flumes, and subsequently exposing it to increasingly higher waves that reach up to 2 m significant wave height. We show that marsh substrates can persist with negligible erosion, despite cumulative wave exposure. By contrast, the vegetation was progressively damaged during continued wave exposure, gradually reducing vegetation-related wave attenuation. Results emphasize that vegetation was most effective in attenuating waves at low-energy marsh coasts (up to 1 m), where attenuation exceeded 10% (up to 50%), whereas attenuation at high-energy marsh coasts (wave height > 1 m) does not exceed 10%. Our global assessment supports the differentiation between low- and high-energetic conditions resulting from the flume experiment. Our results suggest that the marsh platform remains stable under extreme wave events and that substantial wave attenuation by marsh vegetation is limited to low-energy marsh coasts.
