Privacy Policy
This policy was last updated on 21 October 2026.
This is the privacy policy (“policy”) for nature.com which is run and provided by Springer Nature Limited (we, us and our). Springer Nature Limited is located at The Campus, 4 Crinan Street, London N1 9XW. We can also be contacted at feedback@nature.com.
We will only use the personal data gathered over this website as set out in this policy. Below you will find information on how we use your personal data, for which purposes your personal data is used, with whom it is shared and what control and information rights you may have.
I. Summary of our processing activities
We publish scholarly journals, books, news and data. Some of this material is freely available; some of it is only available to subscribers. The following summary offers a quick overview of the data processing activities that are undertaken on our website. You will find more detailed information under the indicated sections below.
- When you view on-demand video on our websites, we may collect your viewing and usage information, and we may share information that identifies you as having viewed particular video content with service providers that enable video functionality, personalization, and usage analysis and third parties for advertising and marketing, as well as editorial purposes.
- When you visit our website for informational reasons without setting up an account, only limited personal data will be processed to provide you with the website itself (see III).
- If you are identified as belonging to a customer organisation then we collect information in order to be able to provide usage reporting to that customer.
- In case you register for one of our services, use the submission and peer review systems or subscribe to our newsletters, further personal data will be processed in the scope of such services (see IV and V).
- Furthermore, your personal data will be used to provide you with relevant advertising for our services and products (see VII) and for statistical analysis that helps us to improve our website (see VIII). Additionally, we improve your website experience with third party content (see IX).
- Your personal data may be disclosed to third parties (see X) that might be located outside your country of residence; potentially, different data protection standards may apply (see XI).
- We have implemented appropriate safeguards to secure your personal data (see XII) and retain your personal data only as long as necessary (see XIII).
- Under the legislation applicable to you, you may be entitled to exercise certain rights with regard to the processing of your personal data (see XIV).
II. Definitions
- Personal data: means any information relating to a natural person who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, or an online identifier.
- Processing: means any operation which is performed on personal data, such as collection, recording, organisation, structuring, storage, adaptation or any kind of disclosure or other use.
III. Informational use of the website
When you visit our website for informational reasons, i.e. without registering for any of our provided services listed under IV and without providing us with personal data in any other form, we may automatically collect additional information about you which will contain personal data only in limited cases and which is automatically recognised by our server, such as:
Examples might include:
- information about video content that you viewed
  
- your IP address; 
  
- your device type, name and IDs;
  
- the date and time of your requests;
  
- the content of your requests;
  
- information on your browser version;
  
- your screen resolution;
  
- information on your operating system, including language settings.
We use such information only to assist us in providing an effective service (e.g. to adapt our website to the needs of your device or to allow you to log in to our website), and to collect broad demographic information for anonymised, aggregated use.
If you are identified by IP or equivalent method as belonging to a customer organisation such as university or a company then we will also collect the identity of that organisation and use it to create usage reports which show the organisation how much of the content we publish is being read by their students, members or employees. This information does not contain anything related to a personal login unless (a) you are a nominated administrator for that organisation or (b) your organisation specifically requires it as a part of a usage-based access contract.
The personal data automatically collected is necessary for us to provide the website, Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. b GDPR, and for our legitimate interest to guarantee the website’s stability and security, Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. f GDPR.
IV. Registration for our services
Access to subscription content is provided via a variety of mechanisms such as IP site licenses, login via third party federated identity providers or by a personal account with us. Using the federated authentication method institutional selection data may be stored locally in your browser and shared with third party websites that you visit to ease the process of institutional authentication. If your access to our content is provided by an organisation or an institution like a university or a company then they choose the access method on your behalf. A personal account is required to purchase content directly from us, or to receive personal services like newsletters and alerts.
If you need to create a personal login with us then we will store and process the following:
 
- Information (such as your name, user name and email address) that is provided by registration;
  
- Information in connection with an account sign-in facility (e.g. log-in and password details);
  
- Communications sent by you (e.g. via e-mail or website communication forms)
The information that is necessary for the performance of the service is labelled accordingly. All further information is provided voluntarily.
We will process the personal data you provide to:
 
- Identify you at sign-in;
  
- Provide you with the services and information offered through the website or which you request;
  
- Administer your account;
  
- Communicate with you;
  
- (behavioural) Advertising and profiling;
  
- Facilitate attendance of a conference;
  
- Manage manuscript submissions;
  
- Provide access (where appropriate) to other Springer Nature group content if you so request
 
For this, the legal basis is Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. b GDPR. The use of your personal data for behavioural advertising and profiling is done with consent, Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a GDPR.
We use the personal data and contact data you provide by registration to inform you directly about our additional products and services. The use of your personal data for directly advertising related products and services is with consent, Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a GDPR.
You can object to the use of your personal data for direct marketing at any time. We will then refrain from any processing to the extent it is related to such purposes. You may opt-out of direct marketing via opt-out links in any marketing communication or via user profile pages on the website (where available). You can also inform us about your objection by contacting our customer service at https://support.nature.com/en/support/home.
Registration data is kept until such time as an account deletion request is made. If such a request is received we will erase your data within 30 days. Statutory storage obligations or the need for legal actions that may arise from misconduct within the services or payment problems can lead to a longer retention of your personal data. In this case, we will inform you accordingly.
V. Information about the specific uses that require registration/identification
1. Blogs
You can publicly comment on our blog where we post a variety of articles to inform you about our activities. When posting a comment your name or user name will be made public. To be able to comment on our blog you will have to register as described in IV.
In addition to the extent of processing described under IV, when you post a comment we will retain some of your personal data such as your IP address and name and other metadata such as time of posting. This is necessary to defend ourselves from possible liability claims that may arise from unlawful comments posted by you and reflects our legitimate interest with regard to the legal justification of this processing activity in Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. f GDPR.
We reserve the right to delete comments that are off-topic, spam, abusive, use excessive foul language, include ad hominem attacks or offend against legal regulations.
2. Web shop
For the use of our web shop you have to set up an account as described under IV. Your customer account retains your personal data for future purchases. You can delete the personal data as well as the account in your account’s settings. This processing is based on Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. b.
When purchasing a product that requires shipping we may share the delivery data with a Contractor to provide shipment tracking to you. Such a transfer will be based on data processing agreements in accordance with Article 28 of the GDPR. Therefore, our Contractors will only use your personal data to the extent necessary to perform their functions and will be contractually bound to process your personal data only on our behalf and in compliance with our requests.
By statutory law we are required to retain the provided financial data in relation to transactions (including address, payment and order information) for ten years. However, after 2 years we will restrict the processing of your personal data to comply with the statutory requirements and will not process the personal data any further. Regarding this, the retention of your personal data is based on Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. c GDPR.
3. Article alerts and newsletters
With your email address you can subscribe to our newsletters that provide you with the latest news about our products and services if you consent to receiving such newsletters. The legal basis for this processing is Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a GDPR. Your email address will be retained as long as you subscribe to our newsletters.
This service is provided by means of a double-opt-in. Thus, you will receive an email containing a link by which you can confirm that you are the owner of the email address and wish to be notified via our email service. When your subscription is not confirmed within 96 hours after the confirmation mail has been requested, the personal data you provided will not be processed for any purpose and it will be automatically erased.
You can unsubscribe from this service by opting out via the link provided in each newsletter.
You can sign up for newsletters and request to be contacted about our products and services via Facebook. For this purpose, we are using Facebook Lead Ads, a service of Meta Platforms Inc, 1 Hacker Way Menlo Park, California 94025, USA (“Meta”). Lead Ads makes it even easier for you to sign up to newsletters and request to be contacted as the form will already be pre-populated via Facebook with your data and you only need to submit the form. Of course, you have the opportunity to amend and review the data before submission. For more information on how lead ads works see here - https://www.facebook.com/business/ads/lead-ads.
The legal basis for this processing is Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a GDPR. Your email address will be retained as long as you subscribe to our newsletters or until you request the removal of your email address.
You can unsubscribe from newsletters by opting out via the link provided in each newsletter. If you inquired about a product or service and no longer wish to be contacted, you can email onlineservice@springernature.com, citing the name of the product or service, and request that your email address be removed.
4. Nature Conferences
Springer Nature America, Inc. (“SNAI”) [1 New York Plaza, Suite 4500, New York, NY 10004-1562, USA] and for China, Macmillan Information Consulting Services (Shanghai Co. Ltd) [10-11unit, 42 Floor, The Center, 989 Changle Road, XuHui District, 200031 Shanghai, CHINA], affiliates of Springer Nature Limited (together “Springer Nature entities”), collect personal data from attendees to Nature conferences to facilitate registration and plan for the events. This includes data categories such as: Identification data (which may include name, address, telephone number, email address), entity type (e.g. academic, government, industry), position titles, curriculum vitaes, professional license information, dietary requirements, gender, information for travel arrangements (i.e., passport data, date of birth) and payment information. We also request information relating to requirements for reasonable accommodation where physical assistance may be needed to attend. We may collect data through a third party vendor. Third party vendors act as a data processor on our behalf. The use of your personal data in relation to conference attendance is based on Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. b GDPR and Art. 9 sec. 2 lit. a GDPR with regard to all health-related information you share with us in order to enable us to provide the required physical assistance to you.
With the consent of attendees, we may use personal data, specifically identification data such as name and email address, to share information with attendees about future Nature conferences or other products, services and special offers. We’ll continue to send you information and store your data until you ask us to be removed. This notification service is based on your consent, Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a GDPR.
5. Manuscript submission and Peer Review
Our Submission and Peer Review System offers the services of peer review, content preparation and proofing, publication and dissemination of research. In order to use the aforementioned services you have to set up an initial account. Where optional paid services may be engaged, you will be prompted to set up an additional, or enhance an existing account.
With regard to the registration of an account and its subsequent use, we process the following information.
- Information that is provided by registration such as your name, user name and email address.
  
- Information in connection with an account sign-in facility, e.g. log-in and password details;
  
- Communications sent by you, e.g. via e-mail or website communication forms.
  
- Content files and covering letters provided by you
  
- Grants, funding, membership, institution, society, committee registration
  
- Billing or invoicing information
  
- Information received from societies we work with, e.g. address, name, email address
The information that is necessary for the performance of the service is labelled accordingly.
We will process the personal data you provide in order to:
- Identify you at sign-in;
  
- Administer your account;
  
- Provide you with the services and information offered through the Submission and Peer Review System or which you additionally request;
  
- Communicate with you;
  
- Process payments
 
- Provide information about a range of benefits to you, designed to recognise and celebrate your achievements within the research community.
 
- Provide information to you as an Author about other publishing opportunities, with the Springer Nature group, you can stop these communications at any time by clicking the link in each email or contacting customer services;
- Communicate with you in your capacity as a current or potential Peer Reviewer, Editorial Board Member, or external Editor to provide information about the journal (s) and content you have worked on; you can stop these communications to you as a Peer Reviewer, Editorial Board Member, or external Editor at any time by clicking the link in each email or contacting Customer Service at https://support.nature.com/en/support/home. Stopping these communications will not affect your status as Peer Reviewer, Editorial Board Member or external Editor with respect to the journal.
- Create a profile of your publication record based on publicly available data, such as published books and articles, citations and grants awarded. This information will not be used to determine article acceptance, nor will it be used for automated decision making (see section VI for more information on automated decision making). This information will be used to personalise communications and provide you with the latest news about our products and services;
- To ensure the accuracy of content attribution and the quality and integrity of the peer review process
- Ensure that our research is conducted with honesty, accountability, respect, and responsibility, contributing to the credibility and trustworthiness of scientific findings;
- Provide you with e-alerts
- Offer to transfer your submission to an alternative Springer Nature title if applicable
- Authorise and process Article Publication Charges (APCs)
As an author, we’ll highlight publishing opportunities in the form of recommendations via our Researcher Home website. We’ll use your publishing history to do this. You can opt out of these recommendations at any time by emailing personalisation@springernature.com.
For this, the legal basis is Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. b GDPR, and for our legitimate interest in optimizing our services, protecting research integrity and preventing fraud, Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. f GDPR.
We use Permutive cookie data to recommend relevant content to you based on your reading history. For this activity, the legal basis to process your data is Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a GDPR. This reflects your consent to non-essential cookies that help with communications and marketing. You can update or withdraw your consent by clicking Your Privacy Choices/Manage cookies in the page footer. You can also opt out of these recommendations at any time by selecting “Opt out of personalised recommendations".
Your personal account registration data is, in the absence of exceptions within the specific services mentioned, retained for as long as your account is used. Content and communications, associated with submissions, reviews or decisions made by an account holder as well as the submission history will be kept on file. Content and submission history may be engaged in relation to the services provided and in the interests of the integrity of published material. Such a decision will be made under the oversight of the Springer Nature Research Integrity Group. The need for legal actions within the services or payment problems can lead to a longer retention of your personal data.
In order to ensure the high quality of our journals and publications as well as the significance of the scientific research published, we have implemented a peer review procedure.
In order to find and contact suitable and qualified peer reviewers within the relevant research community, editorial team members may process some of your basic personal data (i.e. Email address, name and research interest) to register you for our Peer Review System. The legal basis for processing your personal data is our and the Publisher’s or the respective editor’s legitimate interest in finding and contacting suitable and qualified peer reviewers to ensure the high level of papers and articles published in our journals, Art. 6 (1) sent. 1 lit. f GDPR.
As a Peer Reviewer or external Editorial Board Member we will contact you from time to time about the journal(s) and content that you have worked on, Art. 6 (1) sent. 1 lit. f.
If you do not wish to be contacted any longer, you can contact us via our support portal. Please note that we may keep some of your personal data to recall your explicit wish to not be contacted for any peer review procedure in the future and thus, to prevent any future processing of your data in this regard. The legal basis for this is our and your legitimate interest in recalling your wish and preventing any future contacting, Article 6 (1) sent. 1 lit. f GDPR.
6. Research Intelligence
To use these services in parts or total you might have to set up an account as described under IV.  Your customer account retains your personal data for future purchases. You can delete the personal data as well as the account in your account’s settings. This processing is based on Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. b.
 
As an author; Nature Research Intelligence processes personal data collected by research data aggregators such as Dimensions, Crossref, OpenAlex and others in order to generate aggregated research overviews of different research fields and topics. This includes data categories such as: Identification data (which may include name, ORCID iD), affiliation and entity type (e.g. academic, government, industry). You can be part of these data collections because of your publication history with a scientific publisher (exceeding Springer Nature). The use of your personal data in relation to our generation of research overviews is based on our legitimate interest to develop our products and services that benefit the research community by providing them with research intelligence.  Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. f GDPR. 
Please refer to our more detailed and non-technical description of this processing on this webpage.
7. Customer service
If you contact us by either
- e-mail or physical mail
- telephone or fax
- Chat/messaging support
- through a website communication or submission form
we will process the personal data you provide to process and fulfil your request. For this, the legal basis is Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a and b GDPR.
To provide the requested service your data may be stored in a ticketing system and/or on a support platform to enable data access by the relevant customer support team member. Where appropriate the data will also be forwarded to a different team to fulfil the request (e.g. to update your data) or be used on physical data records, e.g. invoices. We may use generative AI to support us in providing the response or service requested; any output is subject to human oversight before being used.
We use Freshdesk (provided by Freshworks GmbH, Neue Grünstraße 17, 10179 Berlin, Germany) as a ticketing system to store and process your requests. Depending on the region you call from and team providing support we use different telephony solutions. For the most part, customers contacting customer service are directed to our level 1 teams at our Philippines-based data processor Straive (77 Robinson Road, # 13-00 Singapore 068896), if necessary, the service ticket is forwarded to a local level 2 Springer Nature Customer Service team or another relevant team at Springer Nature.
We do not process any sensitive data unless provided by you because you e.g. need support in coping with access issues due to a disability or reveal any protected characteristics during communication. For this, the legal basis is Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a GDPR.
We share anonymous, aggregated data within the business. We forward emails internally, or provide access to tickets for other teams to e.g. share positive feedback with a stakeholder, or for review by internal teams seeking to improve the products and services. For this the legal basis is Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. f GDPR and represents our legitimate interest to improve our service quality and provide tailored solutions to the customers.
We store your data until completion of the request and, if applicable, as long as required by statutory retention requirements (e.g. for 3 years after completion to prove adequate handling of service requests or subject access requests made under the GDPR).
8. Researcher Profiles
Springer Nature may process personal data collected by research data aggregators such as ORCID in order to validate or supplement the publication records we hold to support the Researcher Profiles on link.springer.com. This includes data categories such as: Identification data (which may include your name and ORCID ID), biographical data (field of study, keywords, country or region) affiliation data (e.g. employment and education or qualifications), and publication data (DOIs, Journal IDs). You can be part of these data collections because of your publication history Springer Nature.
A Researcher Profile may be automatically created for researchers that have a Springer Nature Account with a linked ORCID ID. When a researcher links their ORCID ID to their Springer Nature Account, they authorize Springer Nature to access information in their ORCID record set to Trusted parties. For more information on how ORCID processes personal data please see their privacy policy here.
The use of your personal data in relation to our generation of Researcher Profiles is based on our legitimate interest to develop products and services that benefit the research community by providing them with better discovery experiences of researchers and their attributed research. Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. f GDPR. If you don’t want Springer Nature to access this information, you can remove your ORCID ID from your SN Account. Please see the ‘Linked Accounts’ section in your Account settings: https://my-profile.springernature.com/linked-accounts
9. Nature Careers
9.1 Personal account
A personal account is required to purchase advertising directly from us, or to receive personal services like newsletters and alerts. If you need to create a personal login with us, then we will store and process the following:
 
- Information (such as your name, username, and email address) that is provided by registration.
 
- Information in connection with an account sign-in facility (e.g. log-in and password details).
 
- Communications sent by you (e.g. via e-mail or website communication forms).
The information that is necessary for the performance of the service is labelled accordingly. All further information is provided voluntarily.
We will process the personal data you provide to:
 
- Identify you at sign-in.
 
- Provide you with the services and information offered through the website or which you request. 
 
- Administer your account.
 
- Communicate with you.
 
- Deliver Advertising and profiling.
 
- Facilitate attendance to an event.
 
- Provide access (where appropriate) to other Springer Nature group content if you so request
For this, the legal basis is Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. b GDPR. The use of your personal data for behavioural advertising and profiling is done with your consent, Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a GDPR.
We may use your registered personal data to inform you directly about closely related products and services. This activity is based on our legitimate interest as a service provider, Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. f GDPR. You can object to the use of your personal data for this purpose at any time, via opt-out links in any such communication or via user profile pages on the website (where available). You can also inform us about your objection by contacting our Data Protection Office at dataprotection@springernature.com.
Registration data is kept until such time as an account deletion request is made. If such a request is received, we will erase your data within 30 days. Statutory storage obligations or the need for legal actions that may arise from misconduct within the services or payment problems can lead to a longer retention of your personal data. In this case, we will inform you accordingly.
Springer Nature Limited may contract 3rd parties to process data on our behalf, including Madgex Limited who will act as a Data Processor on our behalf.
9.2 Information about the specific uses that require registration on Nature Careers
1. Advertising eCommerce
For the use of our advertising eCommerce, you must set up an account as described under IV. Your customer account retains your personal data for future purchases. You can delete the personal data as well as the account in your account’s settings. This processing is based on Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. b.
By statutory law we are required to retain the provided financial data in relation to transactions (including address, payment, and order information) for ten years. However, after 2 years we will restrict the processing of your personal data to comply with the statutory requirements and will not process the personal data any further. Regarding this, the retention of your personal data is based on Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. c GDPR.
2. Newsletters
With your email address you can subscribe to our newsletters that provide you with the latest news about our products and services if you consent to receiving such newsletters. The legal basis for this processing is consent, Article 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. a GDPR. Your email address will be retained if you subscribe to our newsletters.
This service is provided by means of a double-opt-in. Thus, you will receive an email containing a link by which you can confirm that you are the owner of the email address and wish to be notified via our email service.
You can unsubscribe from this service by opting out via the link provided in each newsletter.
10. Nature Research Assistant
Nature Research Assistant is an AI-powered assistant that helps researchers understand scientific literature and prepare their own research outputs and requires an account as described in section IV.
We process the content you submit — research papers, documents you are working on (such as manuscripts and drafts), and your messages with the assistant — to provide AI-assisted features such as summaries, conversational answers, feedback on your documents, and recommendations of related literature. Third party large language models (LLMs), such as from OpenAI, are used only to generate responses and not to train them.
You  are responsible for  ensuring you are entitled to share content with us, including any personal data it  contains about others such as co-authors, as set out in our Terms  and Conditions.  
 
The legal basis for processing your content to provide the service is Art. 6 sec. 1 sent. 1 lit. b GDPR (performance of a contract).  
 
If you use the Microsoft Word add-in, the document you are working on is transmitted to and processed by the service, which you agree to by using the add-in.
 
11.Use of Email for Marketing & Communications.
We may collect and use your email address to send you marketing & communications related to our products, services, or events. This may occur when you provide your details through one of our platforms (e.g., event registration, product sign-up, or journal submission). We process your data based on either:
- Your explicit consent, where you have opted in to receive such communications; or
- Our legitimate interest, where we have an existing relationship with you and the content is relevant to your professional interests.
Your email address is securely transferred to our marketing platform (Braze) via encrypted channels and stored in secure cloud environments (Google Cloud Platform – including but not limited to Google BigQuery and Google Cloud Storage). Data is held for only as long as needed to facilitate our marketing campaigns, then deleted. If you choose to unsubscribe, we will retain only the minimal information necessary to ensure you are not contacted again.
You have the right to:
- Withdraw your consent at any time.
- Request deletion of your data.
- Object to processing based on legitimate interest.
You can withdraw consent, or object to processing at any time using the opt-out/unsubscribe link in our footer of any email sent. Alternatively, you can email us at customerservice@springernature.com for any of the above.
We may share your email address with trusted third-party service providers who support our marketing operations, including:
- Retool (internal tool interface),
- Google Cloud Platform (data storage and processing),
- Braze (email delivery platform).
These providers are contractually bound to protect your data and may only process it on our instructions.
12. Ask about this article
This service uses third-party AI functionality. If you use this service, any data you input will be processed by our partners Langfuse and OpenAI, who act as Data Processors on our behalf. This use of the data you input is done with your consent, Article 6 sec. 1 sein nt. 1 lit. a GDPR.
VI. Automated decision making
We do not use your personal data for automated decision making which produces legal effects concerning you or similarly significantly affects you; however we do use your personal data to offer you content and services which we believe may be of interest.
Use of AI based tools

This data is necessary for the usage report as it provides information on the usage and overall interest in a particular journal or group of journals or eBooks.
The legal basis is Art. 6 (1) 1 lit. f GDPR. We have a legitimate interest to assess and evaluate the use of our content to be able to improve our services. We will retain this data securely for ongoing internal analysis and future reference.

If the Licensee resides outside the EEA, the transfer is safeguarded by a Commission’s adequacy decision such as EU Standard Contractual Clauses. You can find further information about the aforementioned safeguards by contacting onlineservice@springernature.com.

Springer Nature is deeply committed to fostering a research community that supports and benefits from the talents of researchers from a wide range of backgrounds (see Inclusion at Springer Nature ). Within the scope of our information sharing activities set out above, your personal data may be transferred to other countries (including countries outside the EEA) which may have different data protection standards from your country of residence. Please note that data processed in a foreign country may be subject to foreign laws and accessible to foreign governments, courts, law enforcement, and regulatory agencies. In the case of a transfer outside of the EEA, this transfer is safeguarded by EU Model Clauses in accordance with Article 46 GDPR. XII. Security
We have reasonable state of the art security measures in place to protect against the loss, misuse and alteration of personal data under our control. For example, our security and privacy policies are periodically reviewed and enhanced as necessary and only authorised personnel have access to personal data. Whilst we cannot ensure or guarantee that loss, misuse or alteration of information will never occur, we use all reasonable efforts to prevent it.
You should bear in mind that submission of information over the internet is never entirely secure. We cannot guarantee the security of information you submit via our website whilst it is in transit over the internet and any such submission is at your own risk.
XIII. Data retention
We strive to keep our processing activities with respect to your personal data as limited as possible. In the absence of specific retention periods set out in this policy, your personal data will be retained only for as long as we need it to fulfil the purpose for which we have collected it and, if applicable, as long as required by statutory retention requirements.
XIV. Your rights
Under the legislation applicable to you, you may be entitled to exercise some or all of the following rights:
1. require (i) information as to whether your personal data is retained and (ii) access to and/or duplicates of your personal data retained, including the purposes of the processing, the categories of personal data concerned, and the data recipients as well as potential retention periods;

3. refuse to provide and – without impact to data processing activities that have taken place before such withdrawal – withdraw your consent to processing of your personal data at any time;

In this case, please provide us with information about your particular situation. After the assessment of the facts presented by you we will either stop processing your personal data or present you our compelling legitimate grounds for an ongoing processing;
5. take legal actions in relation to any potential breach of your rights regarding the processing of your personal data, as well as to lodge complaints before the competent data protection regulators;
6. require (i) to receive the personal data concerning you, which you have provided to us, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and (ii) to transmit those data to another controller without hindrance from our side; where technically feasible you shall have the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from us to another controller; and/or
7. not to be subject to any automated decision making, including profiling (automatic decisions based on data processing by automatic means, for the purpose of assessing several personal aspects) which produce legal effects on you or affects you with similar significance.
You may (i) exercise the rights referred to above or (ii) pose any questions or (iii) make any complaints regarding our data processing by contacting us using the contact details set out below.
XV. Contacting us
Please submit any questions, concerns or comments you have about this privacy policy or any requests concerning your personal data by email to our Group Data Protection Officer. You can contact our Group Data Protection Officer via our support portal.
The information you provide when contacting us via our support portal will be processed to handle your request and will be erased when your request is completed. Alternatively, we will restrict the processing of the respective information in accordance with statutory retention requirements.

title: Volume 658
raw_text:
Volume 658
- No. 8138 29 October 2026 Easy to swallow The cover shows an artist’s impression of Megacauda sungei, a predecessor to modern mammals that lived some 165 million years ago in what is now Inner Mongolia. This fossil animal is described in this issue by Zhe-Xi Luo, Chang-Fu Zhou, Thomas Martin and colleagues, where they reveal that Megacauda was semi-aquatic and could dig and swim like the modern platypus. But it is the remarkable preservation of Megacauda’s throat that makes this fossil particularly noteworthy. This allowed the researchers to infer that Megacauda had both a soft palate and constrictor muscles, providing rare evidence for a pharynx, the machinery that allows modern mammals (apart from monotremes such as the platypus) to suckle milk and to swallow liquids and food without them getting into the airway. This suggests these abilities evolved in a common ancestor of Megacauda long before mammals appeared on the planet.
- No. 8137 22 October 2026 Winging it Hiding from sight or using camouflage are excellent ways to try to avoid being caught while remaining still, but everything has to move at some point and evading predators while in motion is a trickier proposition. It has long been suggested that markings, such as a zebra’s stripes, can help to confuse would-be predators, but clear evidence for this is surprisingly lacking. In this week’s issue, Jolyon Troscianko and colleagues attempt to address this problem courtesy of butterflies. The team wanted to see if wing markings worked in combination with flight dynamics to help butterflies avoid being eaten by birds when in flight. The researchers approached the issue from multiple angles: first they filmed butterflies during take-off to capture their shape and wingbeat, finding that when combined with wing patterns, their apparent movement shifted backwards and sideways rather than forwards. They then did a phylogenetic analysis, which revealed this kind of effect is widespread among butterfly species. To verify this effect was a result of selection, they created a computer model for the evolution of wing patterns and found that it resulted in wing patterns similar to European butterfly species. Finally, they tested their ideas by having people try to catch virtual butterflies. As a result, the team affirmed that the combination of wing pattern and flight dynamics created an illusion of backwards motion that made it harder to apprehend the insects.
- No. 8136 15 October 2026 Walk this way. Some of the fundamental differences between humans and other apes lie in their skeletons. Evolutionary changes that shaped the human skeleton opened the way to key adaptations, such as walking upright on two legs and larger craniums that could accommodate bigger brains. But the genetic changes that gave rise to the human form are largely unknown. In this week’s issue, David Gokhman, Fumitaka Inoue and colleagues work to change that by mapping the gene-regulatory changes that helped drive the evolution of the human skeleton. Using cells found in cartilage called chondrocytes, the researchers generated a genome-wide atlas of human-specific changes in gene regulation and the genetic sequence variants that drive them. The researchers also shed light on the cost of the bipedal human skeleton: they found a marked suppression of glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis in humans, which could help to explain why humans are so susceptible to degenerative skeletal diseases. Nature Index
- No. 8135 8 October 2026 Cortical transfer Studying how the human brain develops and functions is challenging, not least because access to living human brain tissue is understandably limited. Human brain organoids, models generated from stem cells, have proved valuable in this respect by providing a way to study living neural cells. But these models still have limitations: they are typically not integrated with other brain structures and offer limited insight into circuit-level or behavioural consequences. In this week’s issue, Sergiu P. Pașca and colleagues present an experimental model designed to overcome some of these limitations. The researchers developed a genetic strategy to generate mice lacking most of the cerebral cortex and hippocampus, creating space into which they grafted a human cortical organoid, generating what they call a ‘xenocortical mouse’. The grafted organoids grew extensively, differentiated into a diverse range of human neural cell types and organized into neural circuits that integrated with the host brain. The researchers were also able to use the model to assess aspects of behaviour and examine the effects of neurological injury. The team suggests that this model could aid the study of human neurodevelopment, neurological and psychiatric disorders, and potentially therapeutic interventions. The work was conducted under extensive ethical oversight, and the team emphasizes the importance of developing appropriate guidance as the field considers the scientific, medical, social and ethical implications of such models. Spotlight
- No. 8134 1 October 2026 Family secrets The cover captures an aerial gathering of Natal long-fingered bats (Miniopterus natalensis). Bats are extraordinary creatures — they are the only mammal capable of powered flight, have remarkable disease resistance, use echolocation for navigation, hibernate and have longer than expected healthspans. But our knowledge of bat evolution and their remarkable adaptations is far from complete. In this week’s issue, Emma Teeling, Michael Hiller, Liliana Davalos, Sonja Vernes, David Ray and their Bat1K consortium colleagues present genomes for 103 bat species, representing all 21 bat families. Using these data, the researchers were able to redraw the bat phylogenetic tree, resolving some contested relationships among species as well as identifying the factors that originally caused the confusion. The team was also able to combine the genomic data with fossil data to probe the question of how long ago and where bats originated, estimating that they arose about 60 million to 65 million years ago in Europe. Use this page to explore the subject terms that have been assigned to articles published in Nature. The width of each bar shows the relative number of articles for each subject term. Articles are typically tagged with more than one subject term. Click on a subject to view the articles with that subject term assigned.
                        
                            
                                
                                    
                                    Physical sciences are those academic disciplines that aim to uncover the underlying laws of nature - often written in the language of mathematics. It is a collective term for areas of study including astronomy, chemistry, materials science and physics.
                            
                        
                        
                    
                
            
                
                    
                        
                            
                                
                                    
                                    Earth and environmental sciences cover all aspects of Earth and planetary sciences, and broadly encompasses solid Earth processes, surface and atmospheric dynamics, Earth system history, climate and climate change, marine and freshwater systems, and ecology. It also considers the interactions between humans and these systems.
                            
                        
                        
                    
                
            
                
                    
                        
                            
                                
                                    
                                    Biological sciences encompasses all the divisions of natural sciences examining various aspects of vital processes. The concept includes anatomy, physiology, cell biology, biochemistry and biophysics, and covers all organisms from microorganisms, animals to plants.
                            
                        
                        
                    
                
            
                
                    
                        
                            
                                
                                    
                                    The health sciences study all aspects of health, disease and healthcare. This field of study aims to develop knowledge, interventions and technology for use in healthcare to improve the treatment of patients.
                            
                        
                        
                    
                
            
                
                    
                        
                            
                                
                                    
                                    Scientific community and society encompasses research and material which directly concerns, or is relevant to, members of the community of scientists in particular or society at large.

title: Research Cross-Journal Editorial Team
raw_text:
Research Cross-Journal Editorial Team
The Research Cross-Journal Editorial Team comprises experienced, full-time in-house scientific editors who work across Nature and the Nature Research journals, managing manuscripts throughout the editorial process. Established in January 2024 as a counterpart to the Reviews Cross-Journal Editorial Team, the group brings together expertise spanning the life, chemical, physical and environmental sciences, as well as engineering.
Cross-Journal Editors join individual journal teams for defined periods, providing editorial continuity during staffing changes and fluctuations in workload. As fully embedded members of their host journal teams, they take ownership of manuscripts throughout the editorial process while working closely with editorial colleagues and consulting on decisions where appropriate. Like all in-house editors, they exercise independent editorial judgement and are responsible for the manuscripts they handle.
By working across journals within their areas of expertise, Cross-Journal Editors combine deep subject knowledge with broad editorial experience and the ability to adapt to different scientific communities, journal scopes and editorial approaches. This flexible model strengthens resilience across the nature research journals ecosystem, supports continuity during periods of change, and facilitates the sharing of editorial knowledge and best practices across journal teams.
The Research Cross-Journal Editorial Team is an editorial group and does not operate a manuscript transfer service, advise authors on submission strategies, or recommend alternative journals for consideration. Editorial responsibility remains with individual journals, each of which operates independently and makes its own editorial decisions. Authors seeking guidance on journal suitability should consult the scope and submission information provided on the relevant journal websites.
 
Head of Team | Prateek Dongare, PhD, Springer Nature, Heidelberg, Germany
  
Dr. Prateek Dongare is a chemist and materials scientist specializing in catalysis and solar energy research. He began his editorial career at Springer Nature in 2018 as an Associate Editor at Communications Chemistry, moving to Nature Communications in 2019, where he advanced to Team Manager and became Chief Editor in 2023.
 
At Nature Communications, Prateek established and led the energy materials team, championing areas such as catalysis, electrochemical energy storage, and energy harvesting. He played a key role in expanding the journal’s scope, team, and reach within these research communities. Alongside his leadership, he handled a broad portfolio of submissions spanning photo- and electrocatalysis, materials for solar fuels, and batteries, managing thousands of manuscripts across chemistry, materials, and energy-related fields.
 
Prateek also completed a secondment with the nature journals publishing team, where he conducted market research and data analysis to help assess opportunities for new journals, ultimately supporting the launch of two new nature research journals. In January 2024, he moved into his current role, establishing and leading the Research Cross-Journal Editorial Team, where he manages a team that works flexibly across Nature and Nature Research Journals. As part of his role, he also handles submissions across several Nature Research Journals and contributes to cross-journal editorial strategy, workflows, and talent development.
 
Prateek holds a PhD in Chemistry from Memorial University, Canada, and completed postdoctoral research at Uppsala University, Sweden, and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, USA. He remains active in the scientific community, regularly delivering editor-led workshops and talks at international conferences, advising researchers on publishing strategies, research communication, and navigating the editorial process.
 
E-mail: prateek.dongare#nature.com*
 
Life Sciences
 
Senior Editor: Michelle Badri, PhD, Springer Nature, New York, USA 
 
Michelle obtained her PhD at New York University where she was co-mentored by Richard Bonneau and Martin J. Blaser. As part of her graduate studies, she developed and benchmarked bioinformatic methods to model interactions at the host–microbiome interface. After her PhD she worked as a computational biologist in the pharmaceutical industry where she led data analysis for preclinical development of microbiome therapeutics. Michelle joined Nature Biotechnology in March 2024 as a Locum Associate Editor where she managed submissions in computational biology. Michelle joined the Research Cross-Journal Editorial team in December 2024.
 
E-mail: michelle.badri#us.nature.com*
Senior Editor: Michelle Korda, PhD, Springer Nature, London, UK
  
Michelle managed advanced therapy clinical trials at University College London (UCL) and ran a stratified medicine consortium and clinical trial for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis at Queen Mary University of London. Her expertise encompasses advanced-therapy clinical trials and in vivo and in vitro models for bone-defect healing. Michelle obtained a PhD in biomedical engineering from UCL in 2007, focusing on stem cells’ regenerative capabilities around revision hip implants. Michelle started her editorial career at Nature Biomedical Engineering as part of its launching team in May 2016. In her role, she managed a broad spectrum of submissions, with a focus on medical devices and tissue engineering. Michelle brings a wealth of experience and an understanding of cutting-edge biomedical research to her role. Michelle joined the Research Cross-Journal Editorial team in January 2024.
 
E-mail: michelle.korda#nature.com*
Associate Editor: Aparna Anantharaman, PhD, Springer Nature, Philadelphia, USA, ORCiD 
 
Aparna Anantharaman earned her Ph.D. in Bioscience at the International Center for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB), New Delhi, India, where she de novo designed, synthesized, and tested antibiotic peptides against pathogenic bacteria. She later moved to the United States, where she held multiple postdoctoral positions in gene regulation and RNA biology. She transitioned to research publishing in 2023, first as Managing Editor and then as Publisher for the npj Series. Aparna serves in a joint appointment with Nature Methods and the Research Cross-Journal team.
 
E-mail: aparna.anantharaman#us.nature.com*
Associate Editor: Cong Zhao, PhD, Springer Nature, Shanghai, China
 
Cong received her PhD from Johann Wolfgang Goethe-Universität in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, where she studied the role of histone demethylase in cardiovascular development and disease. After completing her PhD, she joined Elsevier as a scientific handling editor and an ecosystem managing editor, where she oversaw editorial workflows and coordinated article transfers across multiple journals and portfolios. Her broad research background spans molecular and cell biology, with expertise in epigenetics, signal transduction, autophagy, embryonic development, stem cells, and disease models. She is dedicated to advancing biomedical research by supporting the scientific community in the dissemination of high-quality science. Cong joined the Research Cross-Journal Editorial Team in September 2025.
 
E-mail: cong.zhao#nature.com*
 
Physical Sciences
 
Senior Editor: Bishwanath Gaire, PhD, Springer Nature, New Jersey, USA, ORCiD
 
Bishwanath has a Master of Science degree in plasma physics from Tribhuvan University. He obtained a PhD in physics from Kansas State University. His doctoral research was on laser induced molecular fragmentation using coincidence momentum imaging technique. He then continued research as a postdoctoral fellow at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in a team of international collaborators working on light-matter interaction using X-rays.
 
He joined Nature Communications in 2016 as an Associate Editor handling manuscripts in nuclear, atomic, molecular, optical and plasma physics. He joined the Research Cross-Journal Editorial team in March 2024 and is based in the Jersey City office.
 
E-mail: bishwanath.gaire#us.nature.com*
Associate Editor: Joel Cejas Sánchez, PhD, Springer Nature, Berlin, Germany 
 
Joel received his PhD in Chemistry from the University of Warsaw and the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, as part of a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Program. With an academic background in organic chemistry, polymers, and catalysis, his dissertation was focused on the immobilization of ruthenium complexes in macromolecular supports (such as dendrimers and Metal-Organic Frameworks) for the development of homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts. Joel joined the Research Cross-Journal Editorial team in May 2025.
 
E-mail: joel.cejassanchez#nature.com*
 
Associate Editor: Saunak Das, Dr. rer. nat., Springer Nature, Heidelberg, Germany, ORCiD 
 
Saunak Das studied chemistry at the Vellore Institute of Technology in India before completing his Dr. rer. nat. at the University of Jena, Germany, where he investigated noncovalent interactions in fullerenes for hybrid solar cells. He then continued his research as a postdoctoral fellow at the University of British Columbia, Canada, and later expanded his expertise in advanced optical and X-ray spectroscopy on self-assembled monolayers and molecular electronics during his postdoctoral work at Heidelberg University and as a visiting scientist at the BESSY II synchrotron in Berlin. Most recently, Saunak was a project leader at the Max Planck Institute for Solid State Research in Stuttgart, where he explored optoionic processes in carbon nitrides and, in collaboration with the Saliba group at the University of Stuttgart, investigated interfacial charge transfer processes in perovskite solar cells.
 
E-mail: saunak.das#nature.com*
 
Earth, Environment, and social sciences
 
Associate Editor: Camilla Brunello, PhD, Springer Nature, Berlin, Germany, ORCiD 
 
Camilla holds an academic background that encompasses evolutionary biology, earth science, and climate science. She earned her Ph.D. in Physical Geography and Geomorphology from the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, Italy. Following this, she held postdoctoral positions at the GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences and the Alfred Wegener Institute for Polar and Marine Research. Her research primarily focused on the water cycle's evolution over time. She delved into past hydroclimatic variability by studying the key factors affecting precipitation isotopes and the mechanisms that transfer climatic signals into geological records. Camilla joined the Research Cross-Journal Editorial team in April 2024.
 
E-mail: camilla.brunello#nature.com*
Associate Editor: Wen Liu, PhD, Springer Nature, Shanghai, China
 
Wen is an interdisciplinary social scientist with PhD training in environmental and resource economics. She earned her PhD in food and resource economics from the University of Florida, where her research focused on labour economics, immigration policy, and agricultural sustainability. Her work integrates econometric modelling and policy analysis to examine the socio-economic drivers of environmental technology adoption and labour market dynamics.
 
Wen also holds two master’s degrees: one in agricultural and resource economics from the University of Tennessee and another in soil and water science from China Agricultural University. She joined the Research Cross-Journal Editorial Team in February 2026.
 
E-mail: wen.liu#nature.com*
Associate Editor: Inge Wiekenkamp, PhD, Springer Nature, Berlin, Germany, ORCiD 
 
Inge received her PhD in hydrology from the University of Stuttgart, Germany, while carrying out her doctoral research at the Agrosphere Institute (IBG-3), Forschungszentrum Jülich, Germany. Her research focused on the impacts of deforestation on hydrological processes. Her work integrated environmental observations and modelling to advance understanding of water movement and ecosystem functioning in terrestrial systems. Afterwards, she worked at the GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences, focusing on ecosystem-atmosphere interactions in peatlands, using airborne eddy covariance data from drones and small aircrafts. Within the broad field of Earth system science, her research background encompasses (eco)hydrology, biogeosciences, atmospheric science, hydrogeophysics, and environmental modelling. Inge joined the Research Cross-Journal Editorial team in September 2026.
 
E-mail: inge.wiekenkamp#nature.com*
Associate Editor: Shuai Yang, PhD, Springer Nature, Beijing, China
 
Shuai has an academic background in biogeochemistry, climate change ecology, and hydrology. He obtained his Ph.D. degree from Peking University, China, where he investigated water-food-carbon interactions under climate change and anthropogenic activities. After completing his Ph.D., he worked at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, United States as a postdoctoral researcher. His work focused on methane cycling, carbon dynamics, and causal inference analysis. He joined the Cross-Journal Editorial team in November 2025.
 
E-mail: shuai.yang#nature.com*

Senior Technical Editor: Georgia Tsoukala, PhD, Springer Nature, London, UK
  
Georgia earned her Ph.D. in Pharmaceutical Chemistry from The School of Pharmacy, University of London (now UCL School of Pharmacy), where her research focused on designing and synthesizing carbohydrate-based compounds with potential anticancer properties. Following a brief period as a medicinal chemist at the drug discovery and development company Evotec (UK), she joined the Nature Publishing Group. In her role as a Technical Editor, Georgia contributed to semantic enrichment projects and the creation of chemical compound information pages. Her responsibilities have since expanded to include assisting editors in the preparation of figures containing chemical structures.

- Biography As Editor in Chief, Magdalena leads Nature’s magazine and research editorial teams. A geneticist by training, she has considerable editorial and publishing experience: having started in Nature Publishing Group in 2001, she was Chief Editor of Nature Reviews Genetics, Senior Editor for genetics and genomics at Nature, and Executive Editor for the Nature Partner Journals. Before joining Nature as Editor in Chief she was Editor in Chief of Nature Communications. She studied sex determination at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge, UK, and Notch signalling in the vertebrate gut epithelium at the ICRF Laboratories (CRUK today), London. She is passionate about mentorship, research integrity as well as open and equitable research practice. She is the editorial champion of diversity, equality and inclusion at Springer Nature. She serves on the advisory board of the University of Oxford Centre for Personalised Medicine and the board of directors for GESDA. She is a member of the Strategic Council for Research Excellence, Integrity, and Trust and the Scientific Advisory Council for the UK Blavatnik Awards for Young Scientists. title: Livelihood, education goals affect migration under climate change
raw_text:
Livelihood, education goals affect migration under climate change
Swati Mestri
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
Climate-driven hazards can push many to leave their homes in search of a livelihood elsewhere, but aspirations for the future may change where they decide to migrate, according to a new study led by researchers at Penn State. At the same time, income losses due to climate shocks, or extreme weather events like floods or droughts, may constrain migration options for vulnerable populations.
The interdisciplinary team spanning three continents adapted a migration flow model to see how computational agents representing individuals in the same environment but with different aspirations might navigate climate-driven migration decisions in Senegal.
The model, detailed in a study published in Global Environmental Change, revealed that accounting for the balance between short-term investments, like the cost of moving and paying for further education, and long-term opportunities, like potential income after earning a degree, significantly shifted geographic migration flows compared with those of agents operating without livelihood aspirations.
These nuanced migration decisions may not be restricted to people living in Senegal, the researchers said. Understanding how people migrate, they explained, could also help policymakers support these populations and build resilience.
Field research, the researchers said, has long emphasized that individuals do not simply respond to present conditions when making decisions to migrate but also consider their future expectations and desires. For this study, the team's model assigned agents to a livelihood in one of six representative categories, such as agriculture or trades, with income varying by time and location.
They simulated 25 years in two different climate shock scenarios: a multiyear drought and rising sea levels. They compared these scenarios with a reference scenario with a fixed climate state.
The team also compared these scenarios with simulations of the same environments in which the agents acted on long-term aspirations rather than just near-term livelihood opportunities. Over the simulated 25 years, the agents could make decisions about moving as they learned more information, like whether the soil could maintain a productive crop or whether a new vocational program was available within a more reasonable distance.
The team's findings show that accounting for those aspirations in the model yielded, on average across the climate shock scenarios, almost 50% more migrants than predicted in the simulations without aspirations, with migrants often moving to atypical destinations. The team also found that government efforts like investment in vocational training in rural areas can act as shock absorbers, helping mitigate some of the climate impact by creating opportunities that require migrating shorter distances and possibly increasing income potential in the future.
"Our findings demonstrate the value of integrating a livelihood aspirations framework with modeling tools to understand the long-term consequences of climate shocks on migration and economic outcomes," said Nicolas Choquette-Levy, assistant professor of climate risk and decision-making at Penn State and lead author of the paper. "These insights can inform targeted investments in improved access to education and mobility to build resilience to these shocks."
The team selected Senegal as the test bed for the modeling work because it is situated in the Sahel, a region facing major climate threats to agricultural livelihoods, and has what the researchers called a "culture of migration." Migration plays a significant role in the strategies of individuals and households to improve their families' circumstances and achieve a form of social mobility.
"This model offers a fresh approach to and understanding of migration dynamics in Senegal by combining three significant factors within a population characterized by its youth: social mobility, education and climate change," said Véronique Petit, deputy director of the Centre Population et Développement—Université Paris Cité and co-author of the paper.
The team previously built a basic model to simulate migration flows driven by climate shocks, but they needed to incorporate additional decision-making factors regarding whether, where and why people decided to migrate. The project started with in-person workshops to understand what influenced people to move.
Andrew Reid Bell, the Schleifer Family associate professor of sustainability at Cornell University and a paper co-author, explained that the workshops provided key information about how individuals viewed migration as a strategy for better education and economic stability. The team incorporated these data into the model by allowing the computational agents to consider economic opportunities as a migration driver, along with climate constraints.
Co-author Fabien Cottier, associate professor at Hiroshima University and lecturer at the University of Geneva, explained that agent-based models enable researchers to see how individual choices contribute to population-level changes. The team's model incorporated data from the Senegal census, other statistical models and the workshops to account for the heterogeneity of the population, Cottier said.
"We want to focus on the attributes that influence individual decision-making, like location, social connections, resources and risk aversion," said Choquette-Levy, also a faculty affiliate with the Institute of Energy and the Environment at Penn State. "We can see how the heterogeneity at the individual level bubbles up to the societal level. And we can look at those population-level trends and drill back down and see how they differ for demographic characteristics."
Alex de Sherbinin, director and senior research scientist for the Center for Integrated Earth System Information at Columbia Climate School and a paper co-author, said that wanting better education and economic opportunities leads more people to migrate, but climate shocks often limit the opportunity.
These limitations translated to atypical migrant destinations. Often, migration models predict movement from rural areas to urban ones, where there are more resources and opportunities for individual development. According to the researchers, the baseline scenario of migration in Senegal showed most agents moved from rural areas to urban areas, such as the capital city of Dakar. However, climate impacts shifted where people could move.
"Dakar is a coastal city, so sea level rise makes it a less desirable place to move or constrains its ability to support migrants," Choquette-Levy said. "On the other hand, drought in rural areas restricts people's financial capability to move or invest in things like a bigger farm. One of the few pathways that was left in the model was moving within the interior regions to attend one of the government-sponsored vocational schools."
These vocational schools can absorb some of the impact from climate shocks by offering opportunities for further education and aspiration fulfillment without the need to migrate as far. The researchers explained that the schools are designed to help the people who are at the greatest risk of climate-induced losses.
"Vocational training is seen as one way to anchor or retain young people in their society by enabling them to obtain a qualification and a job," Petit said. "It is also a strategy developed by migration governance stakeholders, who offer training in trades and agriculture to repatriated or returning migrants."
Through the agent-based model, the researchers found that migration and vocational training can help mitigate the consequences of climate shocks in terms of income potential. Understanding how such opportunities intersect with livelihood aspirations could help better predict climate migration and inform policy, Choquette-Levy noted.
"From a policy perspective, one message is that areas that haven't traditionally had to think about influxes of population might need to be more prepared for that as a function of future climate risks," Choquette-Levy said.
The researchers said they hope to extend this model to further understand policy scenarios and explore how formal and informal education may help build resilience against climate changes.

title: Sound-levitated particles reveal how static charge builds up
raw_text:
October 28, 2026 report
Sound-levitated particles reveal how static charge builds up
Sam Jarman
Author
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
When two objects touch and then separate, they can swap tiny amounts of electric charge, even if they are made from exactly the same material. This 'triboelectric effect' is the source of everyday static electricity, but it is still poorly understood in large samples of powder, where vast numbers of particles are constantly colliding with each other.
Through new research published in Physical Review E, Tom O'Hara and colleagues at the University of Bristol have investigated the effect using acoustic levitation: using sound waves to trigger repeated collisions between pairs of particles. Their experiment shows for the first time how charge builds up on repeatedly colliding particles, before leveling off at a set limit.
Many-particle mystery
Charge exchange through collisions plays a role in systems including windblown dust, clouds of volcanic ash and the powders handled in many industries. But because these systems involve so many collisions, it has been extremely difficult to follow how charge evolves on any single particle. As a result, researchers have long debated whether the charge on colliding particles keeps on growing or eventually approaches some maximum value.
Levitation with sound
To address this question, O'Hara's team built on earlier advances in trapping small objects in midair using carefully shaped sound waves. Their new platform, named "MultiLev," offers far more control, allowing the team to bring two tiny polystyrene balls together, make them collide, then pull them apart again.
To measure the charge on each particle, the researchers placed a pair of "Faraday cups" on either side of the collision point. These devices detect the charge on an object placed inside them. Crucially, the cups were designed to let sound waves pass straight through, so each particle could be returned to its own cup after every collision and have its charge measured, without disrupting the levitation.
After each individual collision, the team found that fairly random amounts of charge were transferred between the particles. But as the collisions mounted up, a clear pattern emerged: the particles gained steadily growing opposite charges, before this growth leveled off toward a maximum, rather than continuing indefinitely. This behavior closely matches the charging of a capacitor.
Uncovering the mechanism
For now, the precise process behind the charge exchange remains unclear. In future studies, O'Hara's team hopes that stronger acoustic traps could allow them to levitate denser materials and to move particles farther apart between collisions for cleaner measurements. They could enable them to vary how fast the particles collide and track exactly where on their surfaces they touch.
Ultimately, these improvements could deepen our understanding of how static builds up in natural systems like dust storms and volcanic plumes. They could also help to improve safety standards in industries that handle flammable powders, where a single static spark can be enough to trigger an explosion.

title: Machine learning simulations reveal how plastic transforms into hard carbon
raw_text:
In a new study published in Chemical Science, researchers from the University of Oxford's Department of Chemistry have used machine learning simulations to trace how a common polymer transforms into hard carbon, revealing the atomic-scale processes that give this technologically important material its disordered structure.
Hard carbon is an important anode material for sodium-ion batteries, which are attracting interest as economically viable alternatives to conventional lithium-ion batteries, owing to the high natural abundance and low cost of sodium. Unlike graphite, hard carbon contains curved, irregularly arranged carbon structures that resist transformation into ordered graphite, even at very high temperatures.
The origins of this unusual behavior have puzzled scientists for decades. In the 1950s, Franklin established the distinction between graphitizing and non-graphitizing carbons, showing that the choice of precursor plays a crucial role in determining the resulting carbon structure. However, precisely how hard carbon develops at the atomic scale has remained difficult to observe experimentally or simulate directly.
Tracing hard carbon's disordered structure
The Oxford team's study focused on polyvinylidene chloride (PVDC), a polymer that is a classic precursor of non-graphitizing carbon.
To investigate the thermal decomposition of this polymer, the researchers used machine learning-driven atomistic simulations, which combined the accuracy of quantum-mechanical calculations with the computational efficiency needed to study complex chemical structures. This allowed them to follow the movement of individual atoms and observe how chemical bonds break and form as the polymer is heated, providing a detailed microscopic picture of how hard carbon develops.
The simulations reveal that removal of hydrogen and chlorine atoms from the PVDC precursor generates highly reactive carbon sites that progressively form new carbon–carbon bonds. Over time, these bonds connect the remains of the polymer chains together into an extended network.
Crucially, unlike graphite, this network contains not only six-membered carbon rings but also five- and seven-membered rings that introduce curvature. Think of a classic soccer ball: five-sided pentagons allow its otherwise hexagonal surface to curve into a sphere. Similarly, the non-hexagonal motifs in hard carbon distort the carbon network, preventing it from forming the flat, ordered layers characteristic of graphite.
The study was led by Litong Wu, building on pilot studies conducted by former students Zitong Wu and Zakariya El-Machachi, under the supervision of professor Volker Deringer at Oxford's Department of Chemistry. Their approach demonstrates how machine-learned simulations can uncover chemical pathways in complex materials that would be prohibitively expensive to study using conventional quantum-mechanical methods.
Lead author Litong Wu said, "Working on this project felt like opening a book that no one had ever read before. Out of the chaos of atoms moving at high temperatures, neat and intuitive patterns start to appear. It was a real honor to revisit the work of Rosalind Franklin, someone I've long admired. I'm equally proud that our study shows what modern computational methods, combined with today's computing power, can make possible."
Deringer said, "I will just add to Litong's words how delighted I am to see multiple members of our group making this research possible: herself as a current DPhil student expertly leading the study; Zitong as a former MChem project student (whom I had first taught in her first year on the course); and Zak as a DPhil alum who helped build the foundations for this work."
Connecting precursor chemistry to battery performance
Beyond advancing our understanding of hard-carbon formation, the work promises future steps in connecting precursor chemistry to the structure and electrochemical properties of battery anodes. This prospect reflects the group's broader vision of "designing" amorphous functional materials with the help of machine learning-driven atomistic simulations.
The authors' research data are available openly as well, so that they can be readily used for further research.
