title: Engineered albumin helps a therapeutic protein last longer and cross mucosal barriers
raw_text:
Protein-based medicines have transformed the treatment of many diseases, but they often come with a limitation: they must be injected, sometimes repeatedly, because they are rapidly cleared from the bloodstream. For patients who depend on long-term or lifelong treatment, frequent injections place a considerable burden on everyday life.
Now, researchers from the University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital, together with international collaborators, have developed an approach to make a therapeutic protein last longer in the body while also opening the possibility of delivering it across mucosal surfaces without the use of needles. The work is published in Nature Communications.
Engineering the carrier to extend EPO's reach
The researchers used human erythropoietin (EPO), a hormone that stimulates the production of red blood cells and is widely used to treat anemia, as a relevant model therapeutic protein. By genetically fusing EPO to an engineered form of human albumin, they designed a long-acting molecule that remained biologically active and showed improved persistence in circulation.
The engineered EPO-albumin fusion protein could also be transported across mucosal barriers following noninvasive administration through the nose in humanized mice.
"This study shows how an understanding of the fundamental biology that regulates albumin homeostasis can be used to design engineered albumin-fused biologics with tailored transport properties," says Professor Jan Terje Andersen, who led the study at the University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital.
"Instead of only focusing on the therapeutic protein itself, we have engineered its carrier. By doing so, we can control how long the fusion protein stays in the circulation and, at the same time, improve its ability to cross selective biological barriers," he adds.
Harnessing albumin's natural recycling system
Albumin normally circulates for around three weeks because it binds to a receptor called the neonatal Fc receptor, or FcRn. Inside cells, FcRn rescues albumin from degradation and returns it to the circulation via a pH-dependent mechanism.
The researchers have previously reported on the characterization of an engineered human albumin variant (E505Q/T527M/K573P; QMP), which interacts more efficiently with human FcRn. Fusion to QMP limits antibody fragments from crossing the placenta during pregnancy.
In the new study, EPO was genetically fused to this engineered albumin to determine whether the natural recycling and transport functions of FcRn could be exploited to improve the properties of the therapeutic protein.
Longer persistence without losing therapeutic function
When administered intravenously to mice engineered to express human FcRn, EPO fused to engineered albumin showed a plasma half-life of 5.7 days, compared with 1.1 days when EPO was fused to normal human albumin—a more than fivefold improvement.
The engineered EPO-albumin fusion could be detected in the circulation for up to 27 days, whereas the corresponding fusion with normal albumin was no longer detectable after 10 days.
Extending its persistence did not compromise the therapeutic function of EPO. The engineered fusion bound the EPO receptor with similar strength to a commercially available long-acting EPO product and efficiently stimulated the production of red blood cells.
Following a single intravenous dose, both molecules initially increased red blood cell numbers. However, the effect of the commercial EPO product subsequently declined, whereas animals receiving the engineered EPO-albumin fusion maintained elevated levels for longer.
Crossing mucosal barriers while retaining activity
The researchers then asked whether engineered albumin could act as a molecular carrier to transport EPO across mucosal barriers, and five times more of the QMP-containing albumin EPO fusion was shown to reach the blood than the corresponding fusion containing normal albumin.
The protein remained functional after crossing the mucosal barrier, with a stronger and more prolonged increase in red blood cells measured compared with a commercially available EPO product used for comparison.
"The combination of long circulatory half-life and improved ability to cross mucosal barriers is particularly exciting. Protein medicines are normally injected because they do not readily cross the body's barriers. Our results show that we can use QMP and its receptor, FcRn, as a transport system. This could potentially contribute to protein-based medicines that can be given less frequently—and perhaps, for some applications, without needles," says Andersen.

title: Comets probably didn't seed life on Earth after all, new study suggests
raw_text:
The theory that comets delivered the molecular building blocks for life on Earth is a long-standing one, since comets are known to carry many of these molecules. However, a new study challenges this idea.
The researchers, led by the University of Cambridge, found the cometary delivery of these building blocks would be—at best—a 'one-off fluke,' and not the steady rain of prebiotic molecules that had been theorized.
Using computer modeling, the researchers determined that comets travel too fast and at too sharp an angle to Earth's atmosphere for the fragile organic molecules to survive: they would almost certainly vaporize on impact with the surface. However, the researchers also found that another planet in our system—Mars—could be a slightly more promising candidate for cometary delivery of prebiotic molecules, although this is still highly unlikely. The results are published in the journal Scientific Reports.
"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon- and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get out of jail free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said lead author Dr. Richard Anslow from Cambridge's Institute of Astronomy. "It's kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it's highly unlikely."
Testing the planet-hopping comet theory
In 2023, Anslow and several of his co-authors on the current paper theorized that in systems where planets orbit closely together, comets might slow down by 'bouncing' from one planet to the next, delivering organic molecules as they went.
Building on the earlier study, Anslow and his colleagues investigated whether such a scenario might be possible in our own solar system. "We're learning more and more all the time about how our solar system and the Earth formed, and pulling this together with lots of different advances in modeling, which allowed us to investigate this idea that has been around for close to a century," he said.
However, the new study shows just how rare that scenario is. The researchers used recent advances in comet impact simulations, comet-atmosphere interactions and dynamic modeling of the origin and evolution of comets to conduct their study. Taken together, the researchers found that while the successful delivery of prebiotic molecules cannot be ruled out completely, it would be extremely unlikely.
A narrow window for prebiotic chemistry
For their study, the researchers focused on hydrogen cyanide (HCN), an important prebiotic molecule that is regularly found on solar system comets. Their simulations showed that even in the rare event that HCN molecules survived impact with Earth, impacts delivering a useful concentration were extremely uncommon.
The number of comets hitting the Earth declined rapidly in our planet's first 500 million years, and there were, at most, a handful of opportunities in Earth's early history for HCN delivery on a comet. Even if HCN carried on a comet made it to the Earth's surface, it would not have stayed concentrated for long, meaning that any prebiotic chemistry would have needed to progress very quickly from impact, which the researchers say is highly unlikely.
"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can't rule out for certain that it happened that way. But it seems to be a really rare occurrence—at best, a one-off fluke."
So where did the molecular seeds of life on Earth come from? The researchers say there are several possibilities, including the synthesis of these molecules following the impact of asteroids, which hit the Earth far more frequently than comets. Or the chemical precursors formed from processes that occurred on Earth itself, without any outside interference.
Mars offers a less unlikely target
Although cometary delivery of HCN and other prebiotic molecules to Earth seems highly unlikely, the researchers found that one of our closest neighbors could be a better candidate. Since Mars is smaller than Earth, and currently has a much thinner atmosphere, comets would be much more likely to make it to the planet's surface during the period of the solar system's development when comets were far more frequent visitors.
"This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn't happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn't happen on either planet."
The researchers say their results could be useful when searching for life in other systems, especially when the successors to the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), such as the proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, come online. Identifying systems where 'bouncing' comets could exist could be one way that future astronomers could narrow their search.

title: Major Southern Hemisphere ocean layer shifts, raising questions about heat and carbon storage
raw_text:
The Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW)—a vast layer of fresh water spanning much of the Southern Hemisphere's ocean—has rapidly reversed its long-term trends in salinity and density, according to new research. The AAIW helps store carbon, supply oxygen and drive global ocean currents.
The AAIW plays a role in heat, freshwater and carbon redistribution around the planet.
The international research team says its findings, published in Nature Climate Change, show we may have underestimated the extent of deep-ocean warming and rising sea levels.
Freshwater loss drives an abrupt reversal
Led by associate professor Bishakhdatta Gayen (University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Science (IISc)) and Ph.D. student Kaushik Mishra (IISc), with co-author professor Alberto Naveira Garabato (University of Southampton (UK)), the paper describes how, from 1995 to 2015, the AAIW was kept healthy by the Antarctic summer ice melt. From 2016 to 2024, that trend abruptly reversed when reduced freshwater input led the layer to become saltier, denser and deeper.
It is the first direct observational evidence of this change in AAIW properties.
The team analyzed data from the global Argo program—a network of around 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans—as well as satellite and atmospheric data sets.
Associate professor Gayen said the last time the AAIW switched was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in the Antarctic.
"That transition took thousands of years, not two decades," associate professor Gayen said.
"The Antarctic region is the freshwater engine of oceans around the globe. Melting Antarctic sea ice influences circulation thousands of kilometers away. Until 2016, the seasonal summer melt was triple the Amazon River's entire annual flow of roughly 6,600 cubic km (1.7 quadrillion gallons).
"From 2016, Antarctic sea ice shrank to record lows. This abruptly choked off that critical seasonal surge and the meltwater delivery dropped to roughly double the Amazon's annual flow."
Carbon storage and warming projections at risk
He said oceans act as a 'climate buffer,' absorbing and redistributing most of the excess heat and a large share of human CO₂ emissions, storing them for decades to centuries and thereby slowing and moderating atmospheric warming and its immediate impacts.
"If the altered AAIW changes the way surface water is carried down into deeper layers, it could affect how much carbon the ocean locks away—although the magnitude and timing are uncertain," he said.
"This could be the tipping point for the Atlantic Ocean and the AAIW current, leading to larger, longer-lasting changes to the climate in the Southern Hemisphere."
Mishra said the abrupt reversal reveals a critical missing feedback loop.
"The ocean absorbs over 90% of all heat released into the environment by human activities, with most of that heat stored in the upper ocean. A weakened AAIW layer could push more excess heat deeper. That would mean existing models are underestimating deep-ocean warming and therefore miscalculating regional sea level rise and long-term ocean and land surface temperatures."
Changes could spread across ocean basins
Professor Naveira Garabato said the changes are an urgent reminder of how climate change is impacting almost every part of the Earth's surface.
"As this altered, saltier and denser water mass travels north, it moves across the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. Because this water layer forms part of the upper limb of the ocean's global 'overturning circulation,' a sustained shift could, over years to decades, feed into the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation—the deep-ocean current system often linked to climate stability in the North Atlantic.
"It could also ultimately influence atmospheric circulation, weather and storm track in the Southern Hemisphere. However, the impact can cascade globally."
Provided by University of Melbourne

title: DNA analysis identifies root-dwelling fungi as potential keystone species in forest microbial communities
raw_text:
Beneath the forest floor extends a vast ecosystem where a diverse array of microorganisms inhabit soil and root systems. Here, fungi and bacteria play pivotal roles in processes such as nutrient cycling and carbon sequestration. Within these microbial communities may exist a keystone species, which exerts a disproportionately large influence on the entire structure and function of such an ecosystem.
While scientists often associate a keystone species with conspicuous predators, pollinators and plants, there is also a belief that the myriad microorganisms inhabiting the soil include 'hidden' key species. These may be crucial to understanding the dynamics of a complex ecological community, but identifying them within microbial environments is particularly daunting, as experimentally assessing the impact of any one species is impossible in a system as vast as a forest.
Tracing microbial influence through DNA
Fortunately, recent developments in DNA analysis technology have made it possible to capture the diversity of forest microorganisms as large-scale data sets. A team of researchers at Kyoto University was inspired to use this data to identify the masterminds hiding beneath the forest floor. The study is published in Nature Communications.
"Even a single plant root measuring less than one millimeter in diameter harbors a diverse array of coexisting microorganisms," says first author Mikihito Noguchi. "By identifying a keystone species, we aim to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the formation and maintenance of the microbial communities that support forest ecosystems from below."
The team collected 1,270 root samples from a cool-temperate forest in Sugadaira, Nagano prefecture, and analyzed DNA data from fungi and bacteria residing there. With this, they represented the microbial communities as one landscape by modeling the compositions they tend to adopt. This allowed the researchers to develop a theoretical framework to identify species that may be capable of dramatically altering the structure of the landscape: a resulting algorithm was fed to a supercomputer. Finally, the scientists compared their data from Nagano to a large data set of forests in Europe to verify their findings across vast geographical distances.
Endophytes emerge as key fungal players
Their results point toward a group of fungi known as endophytes, which symbiotically inhabit plant tissue and may play a key role in reshaping the symbiotic relationships between plants and microorganisms in the roots and soil. Endophytes had previously received little attention for their effect on forest ecosystems, but this study has revealed that these hidden masterminds significantly influence the landscape structure of fungal communities.
Further, the novel methods developed in this study serve as a versatile framework for identifying the crucial microorganisms that underpin the dynamics of other complex microbiomes and have the potential for application in ecosystems far beyond the forest. In the future, these methods are expected to lead to management techniques that consider the ecosystem as a whole, including microbial communities.

title: Rubin Observatory reveals its first dwarf planet candidate in our solar system
raw_text:
Rubin Observatory reveals its first dwarf planet candidate in our solar system
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Scientists may add a new dwarf planet to the official roster of our solar system. The distant, icy body, provisionally dubbed 2026 ED138, orbits our system beyond Pluto. It was spotted earlier this month by a scientist combing through data from the Simonyi Survey Telescope at the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory.
Initial measurements place ED138 among the largest dwarf planet candidates ever discovered beyond Neptune; if confirmed, it would join the five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.
The results were presented at a press conference today by Matthew Holman, a senior astrophysicist at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, and by Mario Jurić, a University of Washington professor of astronomy and leader of Rubin's solar system team. Holman first spotted the candidate, and Jurić contributed additional observations.
"If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds," Holman said. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for 10 years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach."
"Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation," Jurić said. "It's the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope."
Tracing ED138 through a decade of images
On the evening of Oct. 13, Holman was running data collected by Rubin earlier in 2026 through a search code he developed with colleague Kevin Napier. The code is built to look at billions of detections of moving objects, compare them and find the detections that correspond to the same object. Using this method, Holman uncovered ED138, and he immediately noticed that its brightness and distance indicated that it is unusually large.
"My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman said. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."
To remove any doubt, Jurić searched through Rubin's catalogs and images and found 20 more observations, going back to March 2026. The team also spotted ED138 in archival images from other surveys going all the way back to 2016, allowing the team to trace more than 10 years of ED138's orbit.
Size estimates point to a dwarf planet
ED138 is currently at a distance of about 46 astronomical units (au), where 1 au is the average distance between Earth and the sun. For reference, dwarf planet Pluto orbits at an average distance of 40 au. This classifies ED138 as a trans-Neptunian object (TNO)—an object that orbits the sun at a distance greater than Neptune's.
Scientists study the size, composition and orbital trajectories of TNOs to understand how the solar system formed, how the giant planets migrated over time and how smaller objects have been scattered throughout this evolution.
Not all TNOs are considered dwarf planet candidates, with the distinction being in the size and shape of the object. To be a dwarf planet, an object needs to be massive enough for its own gravity to pull it into a round shape. Based on ED138's distance, brightness and estimated surface reflectivity, the team estimates that its size is between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (370 and 930 miles); icy bodies this large are expected to be round. Further observations are needed to measure its exact size and confirm its nature as a dwarf planet.
Finding a world hidden among stars
ED138 was found in a region of sky close to the plane of the Milky Way—a crowded area filled with millions of stars. To most telescopes, ED138 has been lost among the myriad background sources, which is likely why it was not discovered until now. Rubin Observatory's regular and continuous monitoring of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky, combined with powerful algorithms that sift through millions to billions of points of light to identify those corresponding to small moving objects, enabled the team to spot ED138 within the crowded field.
ED138 joins the rapidly growing sample of solar system objects discovered by Rubin since it began collecting early data in preparation for the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), which began in June 2026. In April, before LSST formally began, the Rubin solar system team announced observations of over 11,000 new asteroids, which included roughly 380 new TNOs.
At the time, the team called this large submission "the tip of the iceberg" and expressed their excitement for the discoveries to come once LSST began. With the discovery of ED138, those hopes are coming to fruition.
"Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth and precision," Jurić said. "And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and 'precover' objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system."

title: Metal-free magnetic sensor can be safely implanted for wireless monitoring
raw_text:
October 27, 2026 feature
Metal-free magnetic sensor can be safely implanted for wireless monitoring
Sam Jarman
Author
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Researchers in the U.S. and China have created a biocompatible, metal-free magnet that can be safely implanted and generate signals from deep inside the body. Led by Wubin Bai at the University of North Carolina, the team revealed how magnetism can emerge from the rearrangement of atoms in heated carbon nitride, which strengthens the coupling between unpaired electrons.
Published in Nature Materials, their research could lead to new types of wireless sensors that provide valuable medical data, without any need for potentially harmful radiation.
Implantable magnets
Magnetic fields are ideally suited to medical monitoring. With their ability to penetrate deep into living tissue and track the real-time movements of organs wirelessly, techniques including MRI are now routinely used to create detailed medical images without subjecting the body to ionizing radiation.
But as Bai explains, the approach has so far proven far less suitable for wearable or implantable sensors. "Conventional strong magnets usually contain metals that can corrode or remain in the body, while metal-free magnets have generally been too weak for reliable sensing through tissue," he says.
In metals such as iron, magnetism arises when the magnetic moments of unpaired electrons are locked into a strong, long-range alignment. While this behavior can also emerge in metal-free compounds, the coupling between their unpaired electrons is generally far weaker.
Ultimately, this means that the alignment is easily disrupted, leaving these materials only weakly magnetized once they are removed from an external magnetic field.
Rearranged atomic structure
Yet through their previous research, Bai's team uncovered an effect which appeared to upend this trend. When carbon nitride is heated to temperatures of several hundred degrees, they found that it produces a tiny amount of magnetically attracting residue. To investigate the effect, Bai's team studied the material using a combination of advanced analytical techniques.
The observations revealed that the heating had removed some nitrogen atoms from the compound, leaving behind sites which could host unpaired electrons. At the same time, the reshaping of the compound's atomic layout introduced a new type of bonding structure, creating pathways that enabled these electrons to couple together.
As a result, the alignment of their magnetic moments could persist even after the material was removed from an external magnetic field.
Flowerlike patch
Building on this discovery, Bai's team created their magnet from heat-treated graphitic carbon nitride: a semiconductor made from stacked 2D layers, best known for its use in absorbing visible light. "We combined this material with a biodegradable polymer and silk protein to make a soft patch that folds into a narrow delivery tube and opens like a flower on the cardiac surface," Bai describes.
Once the patch is in place, an array of magnetic sensors worn on the skin can register the rising and falling magnetic signal produced as the patch is shifted by each heartbeat. Crucially, the signal is detected completely wirelessly, so the implant needs no battery or wired connection.
When the team tested their system in pigs, it allowed them to calculate the proportion of blood pumped out of the heart's main pumping chamber with each heartbeat. Their estimates closely agreed with well-established ultrasound measurements. Over four weeks of continuous monitoring, the material proved compatible with the pigs' living tissues, before gradually breaking down into nontoxic molecules.
Routes to medical sensing
Altogether, their results show how a metal-free magnet can provide a medically viable signal from inside the body. While much more work will be needed before the technology can enter human trials, Bai's team is confident of its potential for medical monitoring. "This could eventually help doctors follow recovery after a heart attack or surgery more continuously, with a temporary implant that does not require a later operation for removal," Bai says.

title: Embedded enzymes help plastics break down faster in the deep sea
raw_text:
October 27, 2026 report
Embedded enzymes help plastics break down faster in the deep sea
Paul Arnold
Author
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Scientists have developed a way for certain types of compostable plastic to break down much faster in marine environments, from shallow coastal waters to the deep sea. The breakthrough comes from tiny enzymes embedded in the plastic that help degrade it from within.
As the name suggests, compostable plastics are a type of biodegradable plastic designed to decompose completely due to the action of microorganisms in a composting setting, such as an industrial composting facility. And although they degrade in compost, they can persist for a long time in cold marine environments.
Every year, millions of tons of plastic end up in the ocean, where they can remain for decades and threaten marine life and ecosystems. So to help tackle this problem, researchers led by Tadahisa Iwata at the University of Tokyo set out to make compostable plastics degrade rapidly in the sea without losing their strength during use.
They published details of their research in the journal Nature. A Research Briefing in the same edition also summarizes the work.
A neat way to tackle plastic pollution
The scientists took four types of compostable plastic (PBS, PBSA, PCL, and PBAT) and melted them down. Mixing enzymes into molten plastic is usually difficult because extreme heat destroys delicate proteins. However, the team solved this by using heat-stable, freeze-dried forms of Candida antarctica lipase B and Humicola insolens cutinase. They then shaped these materials into films and microbeads to simulate plastic waste and microplastics ready for testing in real-world settings.
To see whether they would degrade relatively quickly, the scientists deployed the samples in different marine locations, including shallow coastal waters and deep-sea floors. And they monitored them over periods ranging from one month to 18 months.
Promising findings beneath the waves
Overall, the results were promising, though they varied by polymer, enzyme and location. At 757 meters (2,483 feet) deep, films of three types of plastic containing 3% cutinase lost nearly all their mass within five months, while enzyme-free controls barely changed. Microbeads containing cutinase also showed signs of degradation at this depth.
Some materials proved tougher, like PBAT, which lost just over 12% under the same conditions. Even at extreme ocean depths of 5,503 meters (18,054 feet), the enzymes kept working to break down the plastic.
In shallow coastal waters, adding just 0.1% of an enzyme sped up the breakdown process.
As impressive as the science is, the researchers emphasize that tech solutions are only part of the answer. "Improved marine biodegradability alone does not guarantee overall environmental sustainability."

title: 121-million-year-old fossils suggest Longipteryx had no tail feathers
raw_text:
October 27, 2026 feature
121-million-year-old fossils suggest Longipteryx had no tail feathers
Sandee Oster
Author
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Around 121 million years ago, somewhere in modern northeastern China, an early bird took to the skies. If you drew its silhouette, you'd notice something was missing. Unlike any bird alive today, it had no tail feathers.
Longipteryx is one of the most abundant fossils from an early group of birds called enantiornithines. Yet scientists know surprisingly little about its plumage. A new study published in the Journal of Paleontology describes the feathers of two remarkably preserved fossils. They suggest Longipteryx flew unlike any living bird today.
"Even though modern birds are the closest analog we have to enantiornithines … in reality, they really are worlds apart in terms of lifestyle and potentially movement," said Alexander Clark, a paleontologist at the University of Chicago and the Field Museum and lead author of the study.
A bird with teeth
The enantiornithine group was one of the most diverse groups of birds to exist during the Mesozoic. According to the study, much of what we know about them comes from the Jehol Biota, a collection of fossils from northeastern China dating to between 121 million and 131 million years ago.
These fossils are famous for their extraordinary preservation, thanks in part to the ancient volcanic lake environment where they died, which preserved traces of skin, muscles and feathers.
"It's always great to see soft tissues preserved in fossil specimens," Clark marveled. "It's just such a treat."
Longipteryx is one of the few Jehol birds known from multiple specimens. It's easily recognizable by its long snout tipped with curved teeth and is similar in size to modern meadowlarks, the study authors wrote.
Despite this, earlier specimens often lacked well-preserved feathers.
A fluffy rear end
The two new Longipteryx specimens were collected by an amateur fossil collector in Jianchang County, who donated them to the Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature.
According to the study, almost the entire body, from head to ankle, was covered in dark traces of fluffy body feathers. Only the snouts and feet were left bare.
However, the study noted that the fossils' back ends showed only short tufts of fluff roughly 0.2 to 0.3 inches (4 to 8 millimeters) long. Of the 19 known Longipteryx fossils, none show tail feathers, suggesting this species may never have had them to begin with.
That makes Longipteryx different from its relatives, whose males often sported long ornamental tail streamers likely used to show off.
Modern birds can still fly without tail feathers, the study authors wrote, pointing to instances in which birds shed their tail feathers to escape predators, a process called shock-molting.
But a complete lack of tail feathers may have affected how they flew, Clark said. "Enantiornithines, like Longipteryx, lacked a tail fan of feathers, which, in modern birds, helps them brake and steer (among other things). So landing may have looked different."
They flew like nothing we know today
The new fossils also allowed the researchers the first proper glimpse of the shape and length of Longipteryx's wing feathers. According to the study, the inner flight feathers were just over half as long as the outer ones. This suggests Longipteryx had a wing, somewhat like those of modern warblers, finches and thrushes, which flap continuously or alternate between flapping and short glides.
But the bones tell another story. In birds, flight muscles attach to a ridge in the upper arm bone. In Longipteryx, that ridge is long and weak, much like in modern gliding birds such as vultures. Its half-moon-shaped shoulder joint also suggests it could not swing its wings as high as modern birds.
"Enantiornithines may have not been able to bring their wings all the way above their bodies (clapping the wrists), like birds can today," Clark said.
Together, the unique combination of features suggests that Longipteryx and its relatives may have flown in a way unlike anything today.
The researchers caution that the fossils capture only a small part of enantiornithine diversity. Even so, Clark is working to understand what the wing may have looked like when fully stretched out, which may explain exactly how these birds flew through the skies millions of years ago.
"Every new discovery we find in paleontology is another piece of the puzzle of how complex and wonderful life on this planet has been and is," Clark said.

title: Climate health harms outpace action, prompting calls for global health emergency
raw_text:
Climate health harms outpace action, prompting calls for global health emergency
Swati Mestri
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
The 2026 Report of The Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change finds that many of the health risks and harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement was introduced (2016–2025) than in the decade before it (2006–2015).
Clean energy investment, health system leadership, more health-protecting legislation and growing scientific evidence helped deliver real health gains, but not enough to offset the rapidly growing harm from fossil fuel–driven climate change.
The report's authors call for climate change to be formally recognized and addressed as a global health emergency, and for health to shape both climate policies and funding priorities to prevent climate change.
The 10th Lancet Countdown annual report, led by University College London (UCL) and produced in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO) and published in The Lancet, represents the work of 146 multidisciplinary researchers from more than 100 institutions across more than 30 countries.
Published ahead of the 31st U.N. Conference of the Parties (COP31), it tracks 54 indicators of the health impacts of climate change and the health effects of climate action, including four new indicators introduced this year covering the availability of water in land (indicator 1.2.2), health care sector greenhouse gas footprint assessments (indicator 3.5.2), climate-related health research funding (indicator 4.3.4) and legislative engagement with health and climate change (indicator 5.5).
New this year, the report includes an updated media engagement indicator (indicator 5.1) and now also attributes estimated heat-related deaths to human-caused climate change (indicator 1.1.5).
"A decade after the Paris Agreement, our findings are unambiguous: the health harms of climate change are growing faster than the world's response to them, and in many cases even accelerating," says professor Marina Romanello, executive director of The Lancet Countdown, based at University College London.
"Real progress has been made in clean energy, health system readiness and health-protective regulation, all of which are already delivering health benefits to local communities. However, progress has been too slow, too small, and isn't reaching those who need it most. That is why we are calling for climate change to be formally recognized as a global health emergency, with health placed at the center of every climate decision."
Many health harms accelerating faster than a decade ago
Heat was linked to an average of 540,800 estimated deaths per year between 2016 and 2023, 68% of them (369,900) caused by climate change, up from 55% (219,100) per year in 2006–2015. In 2023 alone, the hottest year in that period, heat was linked to a record 710,000 estimated deaths, exceeding those from malaria or HIV, with 71.5% of them driven by climate change. Altogether, climate change is estimated to have caused almost 3 million heat deaths between 2016 and 2023.
Heat also reduced people's capacity to work productively in 2025, costing the global economy an estimated $1.07 trillion in potential income (0.91% of global economic output), the third consecutive year that losses topped $1 trillion. Southeast Asia and Africa were hit hardest, with losses equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of GDP, respectively, compared with 0.2% in Europe and 1.5% in the Americas.
The agriculture and construction sectors, both largely outdoor and physically demanding, absorbed the biggest share of the losses (38% and 29%, respectively), because heat directly affects people's labor productivity and puts workers' health at risk. The impact is particularly pronounced in Africa, where agriculture accounts for 71% of heat-related potential income losses.
More than half the world's land (51.8%) was hit by extreme drought for at least a month in 2025, the second-worst year on record after 2023. Since 2016, the area affected by drought has grown more than 700% faster than it did in 2006–2015.
In addition, a new satellite analysis identifies growing extremes in water storage. Since 2003, 43% of the world's land has seen a long-term drop in water storage (getting drier) while a separate 37% has seen a long-term rise (getting wetter), together creating hydrological extremes affecting more than 80% of the world's land and threatening crops, food supplies and sanitation.
Very extreme rainfall is also becoming more common, reaching almost 17.2% of global land each year in 2016–2025, up from 14.8% the previous decade, and increasing the risk of floods, landslides and waterborne disease.
"These numbers point to a clear emergency," says Romanello. "The rate of increase in many climate-related health threats is accelerating, while heat deaths linked to climate change have reached a record high, and the economic toll is battering vulnerable sectors and communities the hardest.
"The risks become even more profound when you consider how different hazards interact and compound. At the same time, drought is spreading, and the world is swinging to water extremes, some drying out, while others are flooding. This isn't a gradual worsening; it's a step change that must be recognized as the global health emergency it is."
Despite gains, progress is falling short
Cleaner energy, more resilient health systems, more health-protecting legislation and growing scientific evidence have brought real health benefits to local communities since the 2016 Paris Agreement, but these gains are still too slow, insufficient and inconsistent to offset the growing risks.
Global investment in clean energy grew 7.2% in 2025, to a record $2.1 trillion, 82% more than the $1.16 trillion invested in fossil fuels. Such investment has helped renewable electricity grow from 5.5% of total generation in 2016 to 13.5% in 2023. Health gains are already evident, with cleaner air preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths a year in at least 77 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen since 2016.
However, rising overall energy demand and slow system change mean fossil fuels still supply over 80% of the world's energy, and climate-heating emissions reached a record high in 2024. Despite gains in some countries, fossil fuel air pollution still kills an estimated 2.73 million people a year worldwide.
Health systems are taking important early action: a quarter (56 of 194) of WHO member states now have a national plan for adapting health services to climate change, up from just 14 in 2015, and 47 have separately completed a vulnerability assessment to underpin plans.
Beyond planning, almost half of WHO member states reported already having a health surveillance system that incorporates climate information, and more than half (75 of 145 respondents) reported having at least one climate-informed health early warning system. The report finds that health early warning systems are slowing down the increase in deaths from extreme weather events in those places that have them.
Legal momentum is building as well. National laws referencing both climate change and health have risen roughly 50-fold since 2000, most of that since 2016. Funding for climate-related health research has also increased, up 655% between 2016 and 2024 from $42 million to $316 million, though almost all of it (84%) still goes to researchers in the world's wealthiest countries, leaving evidence gaps where the risks are often greatest.
"Ten years ago, we proposed that responding to climate change could offer the greatest health opportunity of the 21st century through adaptation efforts and rapid progress in phasing down fossil fuels and other emission sources," says professor Anthony Costello, co-chair of The Lancet Countdown.
"A decade on, we have proof that health-centered climate action works: cleaner air, more resilient health care and warning systems are protecting health and saving lives globally. But the pace and scale of emissions reduction remain entirely out of step with the pace and scale of the harm."
Fossil fuel expansion and funding gaps raise the risk
The report finds that progress on the transition away from fossil fuels is continuing to fall short. Fossil fuel production plans are increasingly misaligned with the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal, with the world's 100 largest oil and gas companies now planning to produce 150% more fossil fuels by 2040 than is compatible with keeping warming to 1.5°C, up from 138% in 2025.
Production plans persist despite rising fossil fuel costs, which are straining public finances. In response to energy price spikes, global net fossil fuel subsidies reached record levels in 2022–2024, and 10 countries spent more on them in 2024 than on their health systems. Net subsidies have doubled since 2016, with countries allocating a cumulative $6.20 trillion to them since the Paris Agreement was introduced.
Despite the critical need to move away from fossil fuels to protect health and lives, vested interests continue to obstruct progress. The report details how lobbying and disinformation by fossil fuel interests and their political allies continue to weaken support for climate action, despite growing scientific evidence linking climate change and health. The report also finds that national governments, international organizations and the private sector are now less engaged with health and climate change, reversing previous progress.
Adaptation funding is falling far short of what's needed: the health adaptation needs quantified so far by developing countries (as classified by UNFCCC) put the minimum cost at $3.3 billion a year, based on data from only 48 of the 79 countries that have completed these estimates. Yet only around a third of this declared need, $1.1 billion, was committed in 2024.
This substantial financing gap is reflected in countries' ability to translate adaptation priorities into action, with financing and staffing identified as the top barriers to implementation of Health National Adaptation Plans. Shrinking foreign aid budgets, including cuts to official development assistance, risk widening this gap and placing the heaviest burden on the most vulnerable countries.
A call to declare a global health emergency
A decade after the Paris Agreement, the report's authors are calling for climate change to be formally declared a global health emergency, for a new WHO instrument to enable a coordinated global response, and for governments to put health at the center of every climate decision, from emissions targets to climate funding. Priorities include urgent, fair cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, sustained investment in science, and climate finance for health delivered as grants rather than loans, so that countries can adapt without taking on more debt.
"This report is a stark warning that climate change is a health emergency. What's missing is not evidence, but the political will to act on it," said Helen Clark, former prime minister of New Zealand and chair of the board of The Lancet Countdown.
"Governments must double down on their climate action commitments and rebuild momentum for international cooperation. This must go hand in hand with rapid emissions reductions and significantly greater support for adaptation, particularly for the communities least responsible for climate change and most vulnerable to its impacts."

title: Bonobo females hunt more than males, decade-long study reveals
raw_text:
In humans, hunting is considered a man's endeavor. But in one of our closest living relatives, hunting is primarily women's business.
A 10-year study of wild bonobos reveals that hunting is predominantly carried out by females, regardless of whether they carry infants. They are just as skilled as males at the dangerous task of hunting monkeys in the tree canopy and are more likely than males to take down large terrestrial prey.
The study, led by researchers from the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior (MPI-AB), is the first to examine hunting behavior in two wild bonobo communities across a decade and thus overturns the species' reputation as largely nonhunting. The research is published in the journal Current Biology.
"Bonobos not only capture a wide variety of prey," says first author Dr. Gottfried Hohmann, "their communities also develop distinct hunting cultures."
The study's results also challenge narratives of gender differences in early humans. "Bonobos are a window into humanity's past," says senior author Barbara Fruth. "Thanks to these females, we can rethink the image we have formed of our hunter-gatherer ancestors."
An unlikely hunter
Bonobos are not known as great hunters. Among the great apes, it is the bonobo's closest relative—the chimpanzee—who is the famed hunter. Individuals can cooperate in highly coordinated attacks that take down large primates from treetops. These hunts are carried out by males working together, who then share the prey among themselves.
"In chimpanzees, hunting is the business of males because keeping the reward is related to dominance," says Fruth. "But what happens in a society where females enjoy high status?"
Bonobos are unique among great apes because females are dominant alongside males. This is evident after a kill when females are in possession of the prey and decide who gets to eat and when. Fruth and Hohmann wondered if these powerful females would invert the male bias in hunting typical of chimpanzee societies.
Hunting is dominance
After analyzing 415 prey captures from bonobos at the LuiKotale field site in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the pair discovered exactly that. Unlike in chimpanzees, bonobo hunting was female-biased.
Their team examined all successful prey captures seen in two habituated communities of bonobos over a decade. Because it is not always possible to see the original hunter, the team analyzed every recorded hunt in which the hunters could be identified, noting the hunters' sex and age and the prey captured.
Females were identified as hunters in 60% of the recorded hunts. "They were the initiators of the hunts," says co-author Dr. Mattia Bessone, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Konstanz and the MPI-AB who led the analysis. "They were not opportunistically stealing prey from males."
Females also hunted regardless of maternal state, overturning the idea that mothers avoid hunting to protect their infants. The prey posing the highest risk—arboreal monkeys such as red colobus—were hunted by males and females equally. For Hohmann, this was striking.
"Young females tear through the treetops to chase monkeys who fight back in defense. This is a seriously dangerous business," he says.
Age also shaped what females hunted. Younger females pursued primates in the treetops, while older females targeted large, ground-dwelling ungulates such as forest antelopes, taking these three times more often than males. Once the antelope is caught, the females also enjoy the privilege of keeping their sizable prize, and the authors say this power is the secret to their success.
"Catching prey is one thing but maintaining control of the carcass is another one," says Hohmann. "It's possible that males are not capturing large prey in order to avoid conflicts with females over meat."
Beyond 'man the hunter'
The results raise questions about hunting in the last common ancestor of humans, bonobos and chimpanzees who lived 5–7 million years ago. "Chimpanzee behavior alone may not provide a reliable picture of how this ancestor hunted," says Fruth.
The findings thus challenge a familiar narrative about human evolution: that hunting was primarily a male activity. If female bonobos can be the main hunters in a society where females hold high status, male-dominated hunting was not necessarily the only path available to our ancestors.
A dynamic culture
The team also compared hunting behavior between the two neighboring communities. Despite access to the same prey, the communities consistently differed in what they hunted. The first hunted mostly terrestrial mammals, whereas the second specialized in hunting monkeys. The findings suggest that bonobo hunting is shaped by local traditions, rather than simply by the availability of prey.
The team plans to investigate these differences further, exploring how hunting strategies vary between communities and how they change over time.

title: Scientists reveal the staggering number of bat deaths at wind turbines
raw_text:
Bat populations across the United States face numerous threats, and one of the biggest may be the number of collisions with wind turbines. According to the most comprehensive study of the problem to date, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, more than 18 million bats may have died at wind energy facilities between 1981 and 2024.
Many bats killed at wind farms collide with turbine blades, but it is not clear why this happens. They could be attracted by the noise, mistake the structures for trees, struggle to detect the blades or be drawn to them for other reasons. While previous research has tried to quantify these losses, earlier studies did not show how individual bat species were affected across the country.
Counting the casualties
In this research, a team led by Charles J. Labuzzetta at the U.S. Geological Survey combined 499 postconstruction monitoring (PCM) reports from 277 wind facilities surveyed between 1996 and 2024. Wind farm operators compiled these assessments to estimate how many bats were killed near turbines.
But these records alone did not reveal the full picture because search methods were different between wind farms, and researchers inevitably missed some fallen carcasses. For example, scavenging animals might quickly remove them, or tall grasses could hide the dead bats.
So the study authors developed a statistical approach that accounted for missing data and estimated how many bats of each species may have been killed across the country, including at wind farms that had not been monitored.
A staggering death toll
The findings make for grim reading. In total, the team estimates that 18.7 million bats from 10 species were killed by wind turbines across the contiguous United States between 1981 and 2024. The most affected species were hoary bats with 6.7 million deaths, eastern red bats with 5.8 million and silver-haired bats with 3.4 million. But there was even more bad news.
While the problem has existed for decades, it has escalated sharply in recent years. The estimated number of bat fatalities has risen as wind energy has expanded, exceeding 1.5 million deaths annually from 2021 onward.
However, even with the extensive nature of this research, the authors acknowledge that data constraints posed a challenge. "Despite using modern statistical methods, the state of data remained a limiting factor in our analysis."
In addition to the high number of bat deaths, the paper identifies factors that could help reduce fatalities. These include changes to turbine design and placing wind facilities in locations where bats face a lower risk of being killed. "Collectively, these results suggest that siting strategies to reduce bat fatalities are possible, but species-specific approaches could be beneficial."

title: Technician cracks 1,600-year-old mystery to replicate color-changing effect of Roman glass masterpiece
raw_text:
Technician cracks 1,600-year-old mystery to replicate color-changing effect of Roman glass masterpiece
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
The Lycurgus Cup, a world-renowned 4th-century A.D. artifact housed in the British Museum, is constructed of "dichroic" glass that shifts from jade green in reflected light to ruby red in transmitted light. This means that depending on where the light source is positioned, observers can see the cup displayed in two distinctive, contrasting colors.
It is one of only 40 surviving glass cage cups from the period and is one of the most complete. The Lycurgus Cup is the only one exhibiting this visual effect. Its colors, artistry and almost perfect condition have intrigued and confounded historians and glassmakers alike for centuries. Its exceptional colors and narrative, depicting a mythical Thracian king ensnared in vines because of his misdeeds, led to the artifact being recognized as one of the seven glass wonders of the world by an international panel of artists and conservators in 2022.
While no one knows exactly how its famous color-changing effect was created, experts believe the Romans achieved it by adding tiny amounts of gold and silver which, under the right conditions, formed layered nanoparticles thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand. Because these nanoparticles are smaller than the wavelengths of light, they absorb light strongly and display vibrant colors depending on their size and shape.
Many have tried to reproduce this dichroic effect with varying success, but establishing a consistent, repeatable recipe has long proved elusive.
After being challenged by project manager Christina Metcalfe to replicate it for the university's LightFest in 2025, experts from the University of Sheffield have successfully reproduced the effect observed in the famous artifact, finally solving the age-old mystery.
Recreating the Roman glass recipe
For University of Sheffield technician Dr. Lisa Hollands, replicating the effect was very much a labor of love.
"I knew that making a glass of this type was likely to be a complex task, as it is not just a case of adding nanoparticles to glass," said Hollands, from the University of Sheffield's School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering.
"I've studied and worked with glass for over 25 years, so I used the knowledge and experience I've gained, coupled with a modern scientific understanding of what I was trying to achieve.
"To start with, I worked with a leading Roman glass expert, professor Caroline Jackson, to research what was already known about glass of the time and developed a base glass using modern materials to mimic what the Romans might have used. Then came the more difficult part of trying to get small amounts of gold and silver into the glass in the right form.
"Although if the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they'd probably laugh and ask: 'Why does she not know how to make this?'"
After many painstaking experiments with different furnace types, starting materials and oxygen levels—and even the inclusion of sugar—Hollands finally hit upon a glass recipe that appeared opaque green in reflected light and red when a light was shone through it.
An ancient recipe becomes contemporary sculpture
The initial piece was exhibited at LightFest, an event held in Sheffield by the Molecular Photonic Breadboards project in partnership with the universities of Sheffield and Bristol. The project aims to design new materials that harness the power of light for sustainable technologies, vital to the U.K.'s economic success in areas like solar energy, quantum technologies and health care diagnostics.
Molecular Photonic Breadboards project manager Metcalfe said, "The next step was to commission a piece worthy of paying homage to its illustrious predecessor.
"We approached Elliot Walker, one of the U.K.'s finest glass artists and winner of season two of Netflix's 'Blown Away,' who accepted the challenge and was commissioned to create a contemporary sculpture using Hollands' recipe."
Walker said, "It is a very rare thing to have the opportunity to work with glass developed from ancient mixtures and recipes, and it is always a very exciting one.
"You can really get an idea of how the glassmakers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it's like shaking their hands."
This idea of a bridge between the intervening centuries, along with practical considerations, provided the inspiration for the final piece.
"I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass," Walker added.
"The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture, with the globe replaced by a cup."
A public debut and lasting applications
The piece will be unveiled to the public at the Millennium Gallery as part of the university's Festival of the Mind from Nov. 6 to 15, 2026. From there, it will be on display in perpetuity at the Turner Museum of Glass in the School of Chemical, Materials and Biological Engineering.
"We set out to create something tangible to help the public understand what is possible when these tiny nanoparticles are embedded in something," Metcalfe added.
"What Lisa and Elliot have managed to achieve has surpassed all our expectations. The incredible historic narrative really captures people's imaginations, and I like to think we've created something that people will marvel at for years to come."
While this specific glass will mainly have decorative applications, the scientific understanding gained will feed into new photonic materials and advanced glasses for radioactive waste management.

title: New converter could bridge light wavelength gap in quantum communications

October 27, 2026 feature
New converter could bridge light wavelength gap in quantum communications
Ingrid Fadelli
Author
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Quantum networks, systems that connect devices using quantum mechanical effects, could potentially allow users to share information more securely and efficiently. Building these networks typically entails linking stationary qubits, units of quantum information encoded in trapped ions or other physical systems, using photons (particles of light) transmitted through optical fibers.
One challenge when trying to realize quantum networks is that some physical systems that serve as qubits emit ultraviolet light, electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths ranging from approximately 100 to 400 nanometers. This is problematic because optical fibers, the thin light-guiding strands used to link quantum devices, are known to transmit light at these wavelengths poorly.
Researchers at the University of Science and Technology of China, Jinan Institute of Quantum Technology and other institutions recently developed a new converter that could help to bridge the gap between the ultraviolet light emitted by these systems and the light wavelengths transmitted with fewer losses through optical fibers. Their device, introduced in a paper published in Physical Review Letters, relies on thin-film lithium niobate, a crystalline material that enables interactions between light waves with different wavelengths, patterned into a structure that confines and directs light.
"Trapped-ion systems with dominant emission in the ultraviolet and blue spectral regions possess exceptional properties including long coherence times and high-fidelity control, making them one of the leading platforms for scalable quantum networks," Qiang Zhang, co-author of the paper, told Phys.org. "However, for those wavelength bands, fiber attenuation is severe."
One known approach to converting photons to telecommunications wavelengths that travel through optical fibers with low losses is quantum frequency conversion (QFC). This method entails changing the frequency of photons while preserving the quantum information they carry.
"Previous converters generally suffered from low efficiency and high noise, restricting entanglement distribution in this band to meter-scale distances," said Zhang. "To address this, we aimed to realize high-efficiency, low-noise QFC from the ultraviolet to the telecom band, thereby laying the foundation for the remote interconnection of trapped-ion nodes in scalable quantum networks."
A new approach for quantum frequency conversion
The converter developed by the authors operates in accordance with the principle of energy conservation. This principle states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, so the energy of interacting light must balance while it is converted.
"In our converter, driven by an intense 527 nm pump laser, an incoming 393 nm ultraviolet photon splits into a 1550 nm telecom photon and a 527 nm photon," explained Zhang. "This transformation must occur within a nonlinear medium, and its viability is governed by two critical metrics: conversion efficiency and pump-induced noise."
The researchers wanted to change the wavelength of light with high efficiency while introducing little noise (i.e., unwanted background light that could obscure useful signals). To do this, they developed a chip made of lithium niobate and patterned it into a waveguide that can confine and direct light.
"We successfully realized this frequency conversion within a periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide chip, overcoming the long-standing challenges of low efficiency and high noise," said Zhang.
The team fabricated hundreds of samples of their lithium niobate-based chip and then selected one of the best-performing examples. This chip was integrated into an optical setup that relied on lenses and other components to direct light through free space, into and out of the chip.
"After rigorously characterizing its efficiency and noise with a 393 nm laser, we interfaced the optimized QFC module with a ⁴⁰Ca⁺ trapped-ion system," said Zhang. "Operating at extremely low excitation rates, this integrated platform delivered an ultrahigh signal-to-noise ratio, ultimately enabling high-fidelity operations."
A step toward advancing quantum communications
In the tests run by the authors, their converter achieved an external photon-conversion efficiency of 28.8%, accounting for optical losses through the module, with a background noise rate of 35 counts per second. In their paper, the researchers also introduced a mathematical model that can predict how imperfections in the patterned polarization regions of a crystal reduce the efficiency of light conversion.
"We also revealed a new noise control mechanism for short-wavelength pumping by utilizing the differential-tuning behaviors of the difference-frequency generation and pump-induced nonlinear noise processes," said Zhang. "Regarding their implications, these mechanistic innovations are not only applicable to other QFC processes for diverse quantum systems, but they also hold significant potential to drive progress in classical and integrated nonlinear photonics."
In the future, the converter introduced by the authors could help to efficiently connect quantum devices that emit ultraviolet light over optical fibers, facilitating the realization of larger quantum networks. In addition, the team's approach for controlling noise could potentially be adapted and used to improve other technologies for converting and manipulating light.
"Future research will proceed along two primary avenues," added Zhang. "First, we plan to explore a broader range of applications based on our current 393 nm QFC interface. Second, we aim to extend our methodologies for efficiency enhancement and noise suppression to other quantum systems, such as ¹⁷¹Yb⁺, ⁸⁸Sr⁺ and ¹³⁸Ba⁺ ions, to further drive the interconnection of diverse physical nodes within quantum networks."

title: Decoding the loopy physics of hula hooping with high-tech earthquake sensors
raw_text:
Decoding the loopy physics of hula hooping with high-tech earthquake sensors
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Hula hooping may be literal child's play, but as it turns out, the physics behind the gym-class staple is so complicated that scientists have spent decades trying to understand how the hula hoop defies gravity.
Multiple scientific papers have been devoted to this minor mystery: How do one's hips and legs collude with friction and centrifugal forces to keep a simple toy spinning in midair? The still-unresolved question led a team of UC Berkeley-affiliated engineers to tackle the problem by using an innovative method to analyze motion-tracking data.
Their results, recently published in the journal Nonlinear Dynamics, challenge 20 years of conventional wisdom about hula hooping—and suggest a better way to model complex mechanical systems like the hula hoop's twirl, which could be useful in fields like physical rehabilitation and robotics.
The hoop's orbit and wobble are linked
Previous studies had concluded that two distinct sets of movements, one back-and-forth and the other a vertical bounce, separately controlled the hoop's orbit around the body and its up-down wobble. To reach these findings, these studies used a mathematical method called principal component analysis to distill a vast quantity of data into its clearest patterns. But the Berkeley team's analysis revealed that the orbit and wobble were inextricably connected—they couldn't be divided into two clean categories because one set of movements impacted the other.
Led by Oliver O'Reilly, a professor of mechanical engineering and vice provost for undergraduate education, the Berkeley researchers initially intended to build on previous studies by tracking the motion of the hoop itself with a specialized sensor that gathered 120 snapshots a second of rotational velocity, acceleration, gravitational force and magnetic fields.
When a principal component analysis of the additional data they'd gathered led them to starkly different findings than past teams, they changed tack and employed a nonlinear mathematical method to process their data, which revealed that the thigh, shin and feet bones work together to keep the hoop circling, while thigh movement is responsible for the toy's vertical wobble. Unlike previous studies, they showed that the hoop's rotation and wobble were fundamentally linked.
Earthquake sensors meet a spinning hoop
Upending the physics of hula hooping wasn't the study's primary goal. O'Reilly—who has previously dissected the physics of how shoelaces become untied and Star Wars' spherical droid BB-8 rolls—started by trying to pinpoint which body motions were essential for hula hooping.
His collaborators, structural engineering postdoctoral researcher Chrystal Chern and recent Berkeley Ph.D. Theresa Honein, now an assistant professor at the American University of Beirut, devised a way to rig high-tech sensors, the kind Chern normally used to track how model buildings would react to simulated earthquakes, to the hoop, right leg and foot. (The hips didn't get tracked, since the sensor would have hit the hoop.) Then Chern, an erstwhile gymnast, hooped as the sensors gathered a massive trove of data.
When they tried to replicate others' results with their data, the researchers found that the numbers didn't add up. Those previous studies had used principal component analysis, which relies on linear math—in which the relationships among variables are driven by addition and subtraction, and when mapped, become straight lines—to distill a morass of data into the strongest and most consistent patterns.
"We were really surprised," said O'Reilly. "The dominant results … show that the motion of the body did not influence the hula hoop at all and vice versa." But logically, that couldn't be the case.
Nonlinear math reveals the body's coordination
They checked their work repeatedly and realized it would make sense to try an approach called functional network analysis. This technique is based in nonlinear math, or the kind of math behind curved lines such as quadratics and exponential equations. Building on a fairly new method Honein had learned about from a researcher at Hamburg University of Technology, they analyzed the data once more. This time, the results made sense.
They determined that the hula hoop's orbit around Chern's waist was a joint project of the femur, or thigh bone; tibia, or shin bone; and the metatarsals, or the long bones of the midfoot. The femur and tibia twisted like faucet knobs, the tibia moved up and down as she bent and straightened her legs, and her metatarsals shifted as she rocked her weight from the inner to outer edge of her foot. The crucial role that the ankle and foot played surprised the researchers, O'Reilly said.
When hula hooping, the hoop doesn't stay perfectly parallel to the floor but tilts up and down; Chern's thigh bones were influencing that wobble as they rotated in their sockets. Because you can't move the femur like this without also twisting the tibia, you can't separate the actions that account for the hoop's rotation from those that drive its wobble.
From hula hoops to rehabilitation
While it centers on a 1950s toy, the research's implications are far from trivial. The findings could lead to better models of how people take steps with the aid of a walker, for example, which would help physical therapists focus on rehabilitating the most essential movements. This kind of motion analysis could also prove useful in prosthetic design or robotics, Honein added.
O'Reilly confessed to feeling a bit disappointed their project was over; bringing a hula hoop to work and drilling down on the complex math that made it whirl had been genuinely fun. O'Reilly's officemates had even picked up on a "spirit and spark" in the air of California Hall when the trio was meeting.
"This was just a wonderful collaboration that started out with curiosity and became far more interesting than we ever imagined," he said.

title: Scientists uncover new way to control magnetism and topology using light in atomically thin materials

Scientists uncover new way to control magnetism and topology using light in atomically thin materials
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Envision a material whose magnetic properties and electronic topology can be toggled by exposure to light, paving the way for future electronic devices that do not rely on traditional electrical switching, which wastes energy by producing heat.
Researchers at Monash University have predicted that this kind of switching is possible in the two-dimensional magnetic topological material MnBi₂Te₄, through a type of hybrid light–matter excitation they call magnetophononic polaritons. The study is published in ACS Nano.
"Controlling magnetism and topology with light has long been a challenge in topological quantum materials research. Our calculations show a way to achieve both at once, which could enable ultrafast on–off switching of topological states," said Dr. Enamul Haque, the study's first author, who carried out the work during his Ph.D. at Monash University.
Using first-principles calculations, the researchers show that magnetophononic polaritons allow light to change both magnetic order and electronic topology. Their calculations indicate that a strong terahertz pulse, 0.6 picoseconds long with a field of about 2 MV/cm, drives lattice vibrations that switch the magnetic coupling between the two layers of a MnBi₂Te₄ sheet 14 atomic layers thick from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic while the lattice is being driven (see image above).
In this state, the sheet changes from an ordinary insulator to a topological one, with protected conducting channels along its edges. The effect requires low temperatures, below about 20 to 25 kelvin, for the material to be magnetic.
In quantum materials, electrons, atomic vibrations and magnetic moments interact to produce collective excitations known as quasiparticles. Phonon polaritons are one such quasiparticle, formed when light couples to vibrations of the crystal lattice (phonons). They confine light into very small spaces, which makes them useful for nanophotonics. In MnBi₂Te₄, one of the polaritons compresses light to an effective wavelength of about 18 nanometers, compared with about 65 micrometers for light of the same energy in free space.
"What stands out in this result is that a single material can confine light tightly and also let that light control its magnetic and topological properties. Our next step is to work with experimental colleagues to test the prediction at low temperature using terahertz pulses," said professor Nikhil Medhekar, who supervised the research at Monash University.
Optically induced magnetic changes offer a route to ultrafast switching, and confined polaritons suit miniaturized photonic components. Combining both in one material points to devices in which light controls magnetic and topological electronic states, with potential uses in reconfigurable electronics, spintronics and nanophotonic switches.

Haque is currently a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the Polytechnic University of Cartagena (UPCT) in Spain, focusing on quantum materials, condensed matter physics, and light–matter interactions, with particular emphasis on magnetic and topological phenomena. Haque investigates how fundamental quantum interactions can be harnessed to control material properties and advance future quantum and electronic technologies.
