title: Study finds heat waves speed snowmelt substantially, but rivers respond unevenly
raw_text:
Study finds heat waves speed snowmelt substantially, but rivers respond unevenly
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
A new study by researchers at Montana State University has found that heat waves substantially accelerate the melting rate of mountain snowpack; however, the resulting water doesn't necessarily produce an immediate increase in streamflow.
The findings were published Oct. 1 in the paper "Heatwaves drive rapid snowmelt and disrupt streamflow in the western United States," in the journal Environmental Research Letters. The researchers analyzed data collected from 2001 through 2024 at 823 Snow Telemetry, often called SNOTEL, stations across the western United States. Operated by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Natural Resources Conservation Service, the network measures snowpack, precipitation, temperature and other environmental conditions.
"It's a very valuable data set, especially because it contains decades of observational records, providing statistically meaningful information," said Siwei He, assistant professor of civil engineering in MSU's Norm Asbjornson College of Engineering and co-author of the paper.
The researchers examined 24 years of snowpack and temperature observations, along with streamflow records from the U.S. Geological Survey. Previous studies focused primarily on individual heat waves or smaller regions. This analysis used data collected from actual observations to investigate how heat waves affect snowmelt rate and streamflow across the western United States.
"Our data is not from a model. Our data comes from real-world observations," said Haonan Guo, a third-year civil engineering doctoral student at MSU and the lead author of the paper.
For the purposes of this study, the researchers defined a heat wave as a period of three or more consecutive days with temperatures exceeding the 30-year historical average by more than twice the typical amount of temperature variation.
Faster snowmelt, but not always more streamflow
Of the 823 SNOTEL stations studied, at least 250 experienced a heat wave during the 24-year study period. At 98% of those affected stations, snow melted faster than the historical norm during heat waves. Across the observations, the likelihood of faster-than-normal snowmelt increased by roughly 80% during heat waves compared with normal conditions.
Of 168 headwater watersheds affected by heat waves, only 93—or around 55%—showed increased streamflow following heat waves. Faster melting, in other words, did not reliably produce an immediate surge in river flow.
"We thought that was very interesting," He said. "If you melt more snow, it's natural to expect more streamflow."
Guo calls that mismatch an "asymmetric response." He pointed out that the fractions of watershed area covered by snow and affected by heat waves play important roles, but he also hypothesized that some water may soak into the soil and release gradually, while some snowpack water may be lost to the atmosphere through evaporation. But those are possible pathways, not conclusions established by this study. The researchers have not yet determined the fate of water that did not appear as a measurable streamflow increase.
Disrupted timing and lingering melt
Mountain snowpack serves as a natural reservoir for water as snow accumulates during winter and gradually melts in spring and summer, supplying water for communities, agriculture and ecosystems. Heat waves can disrupt that seasonal timing, potentially leaving less snow available during the warmer months, Guo said.
"If the snow melts faster than the normal rates, it means we might not have enough snow in the spring and summer to release," Guo said, explaining that earlier melting could complicate irrigation and other water needs.
The researchers also found that the increased snowmelt persisted after the unusually warm weather ended. Snowmelt rates remained above normal for three to five days, with especially pronounced lingering effects in winter and spring. Guo likened this to a person recovering from a fever: Even after the fever subsides, its effects might not subside for several days. Similarly, snowpack does not return immediately to its previous melting behavior when the temperatures cool.
Tracing where the meltwater goes
Guo said the next challenge is to trace snowpack losses through different pathways using additional observations and models. That work could help explain why snowpack and river responses diverge and ultimately improve predictions about when mountain water becomes available downstream.
"Mountain snowpack is one of the West's most important natural resources, and this research demonstrates why understanding how it responds to a changing climate is so important," said Alison Harmon, vice president for research and development. "This is exactly the kind of work we want to see at MSU: Rigorous science that advances our understanding of complex systems while addressing questions with real consequences for agriculture, communities and ecosystems across Montana and the West."

title: Fishmeal alternative aims to protect marine wildlife from overfishing
raw_text:
Fishmeal alternative aims to protect marine wildlife from overfishing
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
Technology that transforms organic waste into animal feed could help ease an overreliance on fishmeal in aquaculture. University of Queensland researchers have developed a production process that converts organic waste into biogas to grow a high-protein alternative to fish feed.
Dr. Lars Puiman, from UQ's Australian Institute for Bioengineering and Nanotechnology, said aquaculture has become one of the world's fastest-growing food production sectors in recent decades.
"Fish farming industries have traditionally relied on fishmeal—a practice that harvests large quantities of small wild-caught fish including anchovy," Puiman said.
"This can lead to overfishing, depleting fish populations and draining the ocean's resources, as well as creating long emissions-intensive supply chains."
"With farmed seafood estimated to make up about 62% of all seafood produced globally by 2030, finding ways to make fish farming more sustainable is important to supporting efforts to reduce pressure on marine ecosystems impacted by overfishing.
"Australia's aquaculture industry is paving the way in becoming more sustainable.
"Our technology aims to support this, assisting ongoing efforts from the aquaculture industry to move away from fishmeal."
The fermentation technology, developed at the UQ Biosustainability Hub, uses carbon dioxide and methane naturally produced when organic waste is broken down by microorganisms in an oxygen-free environment.
Produced through a process called 'anaerobic digestion,' these gases are used in the process to grow protein-rich cells.
"Once harvested, the cells are processed into a high-protein ingredient called 'single-cell protein,' which is a nutritious supplement with similar properties to fishmeal, and has potential to act as a sustainable substitute," Puiman said.
A patent has been secured by the researchers for the biogas conversion production process.
Dr. James Heffernan, from UQ's Australian Institute for Bioengineering and Nanotechnology, said the process could expand to produce sustainable alternatives for other animal feeds and soil fertilizers.
"The process reuses carbon from organic waste to produce fish feed while helping to minimize the need for additional emissions," Heffernan said.
"Australia's agriculture industry is also a major part of the economy, and we can use the technology to easily convert gases generated by agricultural waste into an alternative fish feed."
Puiman said replacing fishmeal entirely remains a long-term goal, but studies have shown that microbial single-cell proteins can replace up to 75% of fishmeal in barramundi diets—a key sector of Australia's aquaculture industry.
The technology is currently under development, with researchers' next steps to trial the product at a pilot scale ahead of testing on aquaculture feeds.
"Ultimately we are working toward developing a cost-effective solution that has the potential to deliver environmental benefits," Heffernan said.

title: Dead tree branches rise and fall with changing humidity, laser scans reveal
raw_text:
Dead tree branches rise and fall with changing humidity, laser scans reveal
Swati Mestri
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
Dead tree branches are by no means static but move throughout the day. Geoinformatics researchers at Heidelberg University tracked these movements in a study conducted in cooperation with the Finnish Geospatial Research Institute (FGI).
With the help of an autonomously operating laser scanning system, the scientists mapped a specific forest plot at regular intervals. Using a specially developed tracking algorithm, they were able to quantify even small branch movements, which are driven by changes in humidity. Their approach opens up new opportunities for automated monitoring, which could make it possible to assess tree health based on characteristic movement patterns.
The work is published in the journal Agricultural and Forest Meteorology.
Tracking branch movements in the forest
Trees appear static at first sight but are constantly adapting to environmental influences and moving their branches in response. Systematic movement of dead tree branches had long been suspected but had not yet been quantitatively demonstrated under real forest conditions.
The 3D Geospatial Data Processing (3DGeo) research group at Heidelberg University's Institute of Geography, led by Dr. Bernhard Höfle, has now explored this question in international cooperation with the FGI. Using terrestrial laser scanning, the scientists succeeded in automatically measuring the suspected movement in detail every hour over several days and making it visible using the tracking algorithm.
Humidity bends dead branches
To explain what drives these movements, the scientists modeled the anatomical and mechanical properties of tree branches. They found that relative humidity is one of the key factors: As it changes, the branch wood absorbs or releases moisture, causing the wood to expand or contract.
"This change in length does not occur uniformly across the branch's cross section. Depending on the tree species, the upper and lower parts expand at differing rates. As a result, even dead branches can move significantly up or down as humidity fluctuates during the day," explains Vanessa Guthier, a research assistant with the 3DGeo research group. The analyses show that all branches studied—from 16 conifers and a deciduous tree in a boreal forest in Hyytiälä, Finland—followed a clear, systematic pattern of daily movement.
Guthier explains that the dead conifer branches moved downward during the day and upward at night, while the dead birch branch they studied exhibited the opposite pattern. The tips of the branches moved up to 43 centimeters (17 inches) in height within a few days.
Their movement was closely connected with what is called the wood equilibrium moisture content, which is calculated from relative humidity and air temperature. The branch movements occurred, on average, approximately three and a half hours after the changes in moisture content modeled by the scientists.
"Our results support the assumption that the daily movements of dead branches are primarily due to the hygroscopic properties of the wood, i.e., that they are caused by the absorption and release of moisture in wood," Guthier says.
Movement patterns could flag declining tree health
According to the Heidelberg geoinformatics experts, the precise quantification shows that the movement signatures of living and dead branches clearly differ from one another. Analyzing these patterns with the help of the tracking algorithm and the autonomous laser scanning system would ultimately make it possible to identify dead branches on several trees at the same time without physical contact.
"This research approach offers great opportunities for tree monitoring in forests and cities, enabling automated tracking of tree health and detecting a decline in tree vitality early on," Höfle emphasizes.

title: Why do people self-harm? The mind-body divide might hold some clues
raw_text:
In Finnish lore, the goddess Kivutar stashes away pain in a mountain for safekeeping. And yet she's also a healer, channeling it into rocks or boiling it down into a less potent form in a huge vat.
The complexity of pain—as well as the idea of changing one type into another—isn't just the stuff of myths. Nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a mental health condition that involves intentionally hurting the body to temporarily ease psychological distress. It affects as many as one in five adolescents worldwide, according to Northeastern psychology professor Iris Berent and her colleagues. But adults aren't immune, either.
The whole thing is puzzling, Berent told Northeastern Global News.
"How come the infliction of pain on the body alleviates psychological pain?" she asked. "It doesn't compute."
In an Oct. 22 Scientific Reports paper, Berent and colleagues Chelsea Boccagno and Jill Hooley propose some answers. They show an association between NSSI and the way people intuitively perceive the relationship between their mind and body.
Most people lean toward dualism, a psychological bias that makes them see their mind as separate from their body—despite the fact that science says otherwise. In contrast, physicalism is a view that assumes both are made of the same stuff and lines up better with the scientific perspective.
Berent's survey found that people with histories of more frequent self-injury leaned toward physicalism. While it can't prove that this belief causes NSSI or provide specific recommendations, the study gives clinicians a valuable window into the mind of someone who self-injures. Experts noted this could help specialists build rapport and trust, making it easier to identify triggers and reframe urges before they lead to harmful behaviors.
After all, NSSI can be a lonely battle.
Most people learn to avoid pain. Tear open a bag of microwaved popcorn instead of heeding the warning about scalding steam and—ouch!—the lesson sticks. That's an ancient evolutionary safeguard at work.
But for those engaging in NSSI, it's not that simple.
"Nonsuicidal self-injury is an attempt to manage emotions that feel unbearable, overwhelming or impossible to communicate," Shelli Qualtieri, founder of a therapy practice in Calgary, Canada, that specializes in counseling people struggling with self-harm, told Northeastern Global News.
Research points to shared brain circuitry between physical and psychological pain as a possible cause. Could the sting of the injury temporarily overwrite the emotional suffering underneath?
On one hand, it makes sense. Signals from the mind and body can be ambiguous, and getting physical and emotional wires crossed is familiar territory for many people. Ever felt "hangry"—a popular term for that extra "arrgh" that melts away with a slice of pizza?
The thing is, intuitive dualism keeps most people from interpreting physical and emotional pain as interchangeable. That's what makes it adaptive, Berent explained. This intuition allows you to take stock of what you're feeling and resolve the confusion.
"You stop to ask yourself, 'Is this my mind or body?'" Berent said, adding that you then "stand a better chance of detecting whether what you feel is psychological or physical."
Imagine you spot an engagement announcement from that ex who didn't believe in marriage—while wearing new shoes that are shredding the skin off your heel. The double whammy might add up to a supremely bad day, but you probably won't confuse the two sources of distress.
If you have a natural bent toward physicalism, however, these boundaries get blurred, Berent and her colleagues propose. Emotional pain in particular becomes hard to define, leaving you with the "ugh, something's amiss but I don't know what" sensation.
That unease opens the door to self-harm as a way to feel something concrete and give the experience a name, Berent explained.
"Not knowing what happens to us is probably worse than even feeling pain," she said.
The confusion doesn't just apply to psychological pain, either. People who self-injure tend to have trouble teasing other feelings apart from bodily signals, too. Seeing the mind and body as part and parcel of the same perceptual stew could explain why the border gets murky, leading to distress.
To put all these theories to the test, Berent and her colleagues recruited participants with and without a history of self-injury. They then used some futuristic thought experiments to see where everyone landed on the dualism scale.
Say there was a way to make an exact replica of your body and brain, they proposed. What traits would it have?
A card-carrying dualist wouldn't expect a replica to share their love for their dog, fondness for game shows or fear of spiders—all features of the ethereal mind. Physicalists, on the other hand, would imagine the entire bundle of characteristics getting forwarded along.
To make sure the physicalists weren't just saying "yes" to everything on autopilot, Berent and her colleagues added another scenario.
Consider the afterlife, they asked. With all physical trappings out of the picture, which traits would be retained?
A true physicalist would answer "none," whereas a dualist would implicitly contrast the two types of characteristics, saying those belonging to the psychic realm would persist into the great beyond.
Participants who reported recent self-injury tended to give the physicalist answers to both questions.
The team also found that the more physicalist someone who engaged in self-injury happened to be, the harder it was for them to explain what drove them to the behavior. The finding supports the idea that a struggle with naming and processing emotions in general sets the stage for NSSI, with challenges in identifying psychological pain as just one particular sticking point.
The connection offers a new lead in understanding why people self-harm.
Comprehending the possible mechanism behind the patient's struggle could allow clinicians to help patients separate bodily signals from emotions and label what they're feeling.
"This research reinforces the importance of treating the whole person rather than focusing on a single behavior," Qualtieri said.

title: U.S. moves to weaken methane limits on oil and gas producers
raw_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump announced Tuesday a sweeping rollback of rules that stop oil and gas producers from emitting methane, a greenhouse gas superpollutant.
Trump made the announcement at a rally in support of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who faces a tough battle for a U.S. Senate seat in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The regulations were put in place by Republican Trump's Democratic predecessor Joe Biden.
"Tonight, I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers $45 billion," Trump said at the rally in Lubbock, Texas.
To cheers from the crowd, Trump added that the move would "unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas." Texas is by far the country's leading fossil-fuel-producing state.
An Environmental Protection Agency statement earlier this month gave the same $45 billion figure in cost savings, without offering a detailed breakdown of the savings.
"Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work," said EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. "They can't do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens."
Trump is pushing ways of bringing down energy costs ahead of the midterms, amid voter anger over soaring oil costs caused by his war on Iran.
Polls show Republicans could lose control of Congress to the Democrats in next week's vote.
Methane, the main component of natural gas, is the second-largest cause of global warming behind carbon dioxide—responsible for about a third, or 0.5C, of total planetary heating since the preindustrial era.
A molecule of methane traps far more heat than carbon dioxide, but persists in the atmosphere for only seven to 12 years, whereas carbon dioxide can last for hundreds of years.
'Toothless'
The changes take aim at rules to curb methane emissions from oil and gas operations. Emissions occur at every stage, from extracting gas held underground to processing, transmission and distribution.
"Zeldin's EPA is giving oil and gas corporations exactly what they've long wanted: a toothless methane standard they can use to pretend they're well-regulated, all while they continue to knowingly leak and flare dangerous amounts of the heat-trapping gas," said Julia Kane, a researcher at oil and gas watchdog Fieldnotes.
The United States is the world's leading emitter of methane from its oil and gas sector, followed by Russia, according to the International Energy Agency.
The new changes include proposing to kill off the "Super Emitter Program," a provision that allows EPA-approved observers to report major leaks with a rate of over 100 kilograms (220 pounds) per hour.
Another will weaken regulation against so-called "marginal wells" that produce 15 barrels or less of oil equivalent a day.
Yet another will relax rules around the routine flaring of "associated gas."
In places like the Permian Basin where oil is the main product, the associated gas that comes up is considered a byproduct, with the cost of capture exceeding its market value, leading operators to often burn it off, or flare it.

title: Cyclone eases after lashing India coast, no deaths reported
raw_text:
Ferocious winds and torrential rain lashed India's southeastern coast after a cyclone made landfall on Wednesday, but officials said there were no initial reports of deaths and the storm later began to ease.
Cyclone Arnab hit southeastern Andhra Pradesh state as a "very severe cyclonic storm," with winds of 125–135 kilometers (77–84 miles) per hour and gusts reaching 150 kph (93 miles per hour) in the early hours of Wednesday, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.
Torrential rain was recorded—as much as 30 centimeters (nearly 12 inches) in parts of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states, IMD said, with the storm due to weaken into a "deep depression" throughout Wednesday afternoon.
Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Nara Chandrababu Naidu said there had been no reported deaths from the storm, congratulating government officers who had "worked tirelessly throughout the night."
Naidu "expressed satisfaction that no loss of life occurred due to the proactive measures taken," his office said in a statement.
"We are making every possible effort to minimize the impact of the cyclone... and restore normalcy at the earliest," Naidu added.
Around 50,000 people were told to move to safer areas in Andhra Pradesh and another 48,000 in neighboring Odisha.
"Our homes get flooded, and we have to stay in the water," said Rajeshwari, 65, who gave only one name and had been taken to a government-run shelter near Kakinada.
Overnight, gales battered trees and heavy rain lashed the port city of Kakinada, close to the heart of the storm, as powerful waves crashed ashore.
Residents on Wednesday emerged onto flooded streets to what appeared to be limited damage in the city.
'Safe indoors'
Emergency officials were also busy clearing uprooted trees and other debris from affected roads in the coastal region.
"Thank God, there was not as much damage this time," said businessman Hussain, 43, who uses one name.
"The sea is very rough, several trees have fallen, and sheds and billboards have been damaged."
Sadiq, 40, a Kakinada city resident, told AFP that the situation had become "very dangerous" on Tuesday night, but early warnings from authorities had helped people prepare.
"Many people locked their houses and moved to safer places," he said.
Cyclones, called hurricanes in the North Atlantic and typhoons in the Pacific, are a regular menace in the Bay of Bengal and northern Indian Ocean.
The storm season, however, has been turbocharged by the El Niño weather phenomenon that has contributed to unprecedented warming.
Neighboring Sri Lanka and Nepal had also issued warnings.
Nepal's disaster authority warned that the storm would move inland toward the Himalayas, bringing heavy rainfall and "a high risk of heavy snowfall, snowstorms and avalanches."
Nepal is still recovering from a catastrophic Aug. 26 flood triggered by a glacial mountain collapse, which killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.

title: MapInsights helps police trainees learn the territory
raw_text:
In early 2026, the University of Illinois Division of Public Safety was facing a challenge. It had 11 security guards it planned to convert to community service officers, which meant they would change from being based in one building to working a whole beat.
"Their jobs completely changed," said Lt. Ty Ledbetter, administrative lieutenant for the division, who also manages the community service officer program and officer training. Public Safety needed a way to get the officers up to speed, and quickly. Its solution was to call associate professor Yun Huang, who ultimately built the MapInsights program.
Huang, whose research focuses on human-AI collaboration and interactions, was already at work on interactive mapping software. She started working with Ledbetter and Jennifer Whiting from the university's Police Training Institute in March, and by May had created MapInsights, a web-based training platform that converts the memorization of a large real-world operating environment into structured, measurable practice.
For a public safety officer, knowing every building on a beat is essential. However, memorizing more than 1,000 buildings on the University of Illinois campus, which is divided into three beats on roughly a north-to-south basis, can be tedious and time-consuming.
Furthermore, the division's test of campus geography, on which trainees must score 80% or higher before moving to the next training module, was a clunky web form that didn't even save progress.
In contrast, MapInsights is highly reactive. MapInsights identifies each building by name but also by the number used by the campus Facilities & Services office. All maps are connected to the university's archaeological services, so if a building number changes in the system, it will change on the map.
When the assessment begins, all buildings are outlined in red. Each time a user clicks on a building and identifies it correctly, the red changes to green. Progress is savable, and the interface is reactive.
The design turns campus geography into a short practice loop: each round shrinks the map to one beat and either buildings or parking lots, shows a highlighted target, and offers a short list of names, then brings back only the misses until the officer can recognize those places with less help.
The system design was informed by cognitive psychology research. For example, it incorporates a sense-of-direction assessment framework to help measure the trainee's sense of direction, map reading, distance judgment, route memory, orientation in novel places and mental map formation. With that information, the training can adapt to each user's abilities and tendencies.
"This generation," Ledbetter said as he clicked through a practice exam, "this is exactly what they're used to doing."
MapInsights has become part of training for both sworn police officers and community officers in Public Safety. With some additional mapping, Ledbetter envisions possible training for campus SafeWalks escorts and even publicly available maps showing the best-lit or most accessible walking routes across campus.
"It's really affected the department as a whole," he said, calling Huang's work "phenomenal."
Meanwhile, Huang sees other applications of MapInsights. For example, it could allow new students to upload their course schedules, showing them the best and quickest routes to classes—or whether they even have enough time to get from one class to the next based on their schedule.
Huang has worked to design technology for public safety since 2010, including SafeRBot, a large language model that helps dispatch centers respond to nonemergency situations.
She potentially sees the two applications working together.
"We want to turn this research platform into something really practical that people can use," she said.
Huang's experience with MapInsights also reflects how AI is reshaping the role of experienced researchers.
"It's exciting to be back in the creator's seat," Huang said. "AI allows me to return to hands-on development while doing intense research and advising, combining the technical skills I've built over the years with a much deeper understanding of real-world problems. I can navigate between research and reality smoothly and see immediate impacts."

title: What students think about my teaching doesn’t matter. Am I wrong?
raw_text:
Nature reached out to other scientists to review your behaviour. Are you insensitive to the needs of your students or are you right to focus on challenging them?
Comments from the jury
“A teaching style that doesn’t seek universal popularity is usually manageable, because you work with students only for a limited time. However, leadership roles often also come with power, and with great power comes great responsibility. It is not wrong to use that authority when necessary, as long as it is exercised with fairness and care.” — Monalisa Mallick, quantum engineer at Friedrich Schiller University, Jena, Germany.
“The prof makes a fair point. But in their situation, I’d be sure to collect evidence of learning because if the students hate their professor and also don’t learn anything, it's not a good deal for anyone.” — Russ Altman, researcher in bioengineering, genetics, medicine and biomedical data science at Stanford University, California.
“It’s inevitable that you cannot be universally liked, but good leaders and teachers should still reflect on why people might feel negatively about them. A bit of self-criticism can go a long way. Dismissing criticism, instead of learning from it, I find worrying.” — Juliana Sanchez Alponti Millar, biologist at the University of York, UK.
“I strongly agree. Academic leadership should not be measured only by popularity, but also by fairness, clarity and the ability to help people grow beyond their comfort zones.” — Jay Jesús Molino Cornejo, physicist at UDELAS, Panama City.
“Totally fair! I also started out giving far too much of myself to students. Now I have firm boundaries on how much time I will spend on e-mails and preparation. It’s helped my workload and means that I don’t make my students’ feelings my own.” — Maggie Swift, conservation scientist at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Wildlife Health in Ithaca, New York.
The verdict
Feedback can be a valuable tool for self-reflection, but it’s a truth universally acknowledged — both in science and in life — that you really can’t please everyone. Most respondents seem to back Nguyen Chaplin’s conviction that she was better off putting her energy into teaching in line with her values.

Journal Metrics
DORA: The San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment
Springer Nature is a signatory of the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA). Because small numbers of highly cited articles can have outsized influence on certain citation measures like the 2-year Journal Impact Factor (JIF) (see below for definition), Springer Nature believes that these citation measures are not necessarily measures of journal quality, and that authors and readers should consider a range of metrics when evaluating journals to read and publish in.
Article metrics such as number of downloads, citations and online attention are available from each article page, and provide an overview of the attention received by a paper.
Citation Impact
- Journal Impact Factor: 56.1 (2025)
- 5-year Journal Impact Factor: 56.7 (2025)

Usage 2025
- Downloads: 205,603,435
- Altmetric mentions: 956,164
Definitions
The metric definitions below are shared by all Springer Nature journals.
Citation Impact
Journal Impact Factor
The Journal Impact Factor is defined as all citations to the journal in the current JCR year to items published in the previous two years, divided by the total number of scholarly items (these comprise articles, reviews, and proceedings papers) published in the journal in the previous two years. Though not a strict mathematical average, the Journal Impact Factor provides a functional approximation of the mean citation rate per citable item. A Journal Impact Factor of 1.0 means that, on average, the articles published one or two years ago have been cited one time. A Journal Impact Factor of 2.5 means that, on average, the articles published one or two years ago have been cited two and a half times. The citing works may be articles published in the same journal. However, most citing works are from different journals, proceedings, or books indexed in Web of Science Core Collection. (Source: Clarivate Analytics)
5-year Journal Impact Factor
The 5-year journal Impact Factor, available from 2007 onward, is the average number of times articles from the journal published in the past five years have been cited in the JCR year. It is calculated by dividing the number of citations in the JCR year by the total number of articles published in the five previous years. (Source: Clarivate Analytics)
Immediacy Index
The Immediacy Index is the average number of times an article is cited in the year it is published. The journal Immediacy Index indicates how quickly articles in a journal are cited. The aggregate Immediacy Index indicates how quickly articles in a subject category are cited. The Immediacy Index is calculated by dividing the number of citations to articles published in a given year by the number of articles published in that year. Because it is a per-article average, the Immediacy Index tends to discount the advantage of large journals over small ones. However, frequently issued journals may have an advantage because an article published early in the year has a better chance of being cited than one published later in the year. Many publications that publish infrequently or late in the year have low Immediacy Indexes. For comparing journals specializing in cutting-edge research, the immediacy index can provide a useful perspective. (Source: Clarivate Analytics)
Eigenfactor® Score
The Eigenfactor Score calculation is based on the number of times articles from the journal published in the past five years have been cited in the JCR year, but it also considers which journals have contributed these citations so that highly cited journals will influence the network more than lesser cited journals. References from one article in a journal to another article from the same journal are removed, so that Eigenfactor Scores are not influenced by journal self-citation. (Source: Clarivate Analytics)
Article Influence Score
The Article Influence Score determines the average influence of a journal's articles over the first five years after publication. It is calculated by multiplying the Eigenfactor Score by 0.01 and dividing by the number of articles in the journal, normalized as a fraction of all articles in all publications. This measure is roughly analogous to the 5-Year Journal Impact Factor in that it is a ratio of a journal’s citation influence to the size of the journal’s article contribution over a period of five years. (Source: Clarivate Analytics)
Speed
Submission to first editorial decision
This measures the median time in days from when the journal receives a manuscript submission to when the submission is either sent out for peer review or rejected.
Submission to acceptance
This measures the median time in days from when the journal receives a manuscript submission to when the submission is accepted. This includes all peer review and can also include time in revision.
Usage
Downloads
Downloads reflect the number of times full text or PDF versions of articles are accessed directly from the journal website and Springer Link. Downloads are defined as HTML, LookInside, PDF, and Epub clicks. Please note that this does not include article downloads from mirror databases such as PubMed Central. These download counts comply with the COUNTER5 standard. COUNTER5 is the fifth iteration of the “Code of Practice,” from Counter Metrics, which is a not-for-profit organization financially sustained by its global community of members, including libraries, consortia, publishers, aggregators, and technology providers.
Altmetric mentions
Total number of mentions (e.g. X, Facebook, Reddit, Blogs, News articles, Policy documents, and Faculty of 1000 reviews) for articles published in the specified timeframe, as provided by Altmetric.

title: New feed supplement addresses honey bee declines after blueberry pollination
raw_text:
New feed supplement addresses honey bee declines after blueberry pollination
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
Washington produces more blueberries than any other U.S. state, but farmers sometimes struggle to obtain honey bees to pollinate the plants and produce fruit. That's in part because beekeepers are reluctant to provide bees to blueberry farms, given that there have been increased—and mysterious—bee colony losses after blueberry pollination.
Researchers, however, may have found a solution: a feed that shows promise for boosting the size of bee colonies. "We don't know exactly why the losses happen, but fear has led some beekeepers to avoid blueberry pollination season entirely," said Lisa DeVetter, a professor of small fruit horticulture at Washington State University's Northwestern Washington Research and Extension Center. "We want to help beekeepers maintain the health of their colonies while also helping blueberry growers produce the best crop."
In a study published in the journal Entomological Communications, DeVetter and colleagues with a company called H4Bees found that feeding the pollinators a product called Nano-B-Feed resulted in increased honey bee colony size.
Larger colonies support blueberry pollination
"The colonies that received the special feed had a statistically significant increase in the number of bees over the control group," DeVetter said. "Increased population is often a strong characteristic of colony health."
Even though her specialty is small fruits, the importance of pollination in those crops has led DeVetter to study the beneficial insects so she can help growers.
"The industry wants to improve pollination, so that has led me to do a lot of research on the topic," DeVetter said. "Wild pollinators do contribute, but not enough in large commercial settings. Without renting honey bee colonies, berries are smaller and the yield and quality are reduced as well."
A supplement with a possible detoxifying role
The feed is a powdered supplement that is placed at a colony entrance for bees to consume. It's a combination of minerals and organic compounds mixed with powdered sugar. Each ingredient is listed as generally recognized as safe by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
"I've tested many other products to see if we can stimulate increased foraging or induce other colony growth indices," DeVetter said. "This is one of the few times when I've seen a positive response. And since we don't have to open up the hives to provide the supplement, it's less invasive and easier to provide to the bees."
Additional studies are needed to understand precisely how Nano-B-Feed works, but DeVetter and her H4Bees colleagues believe it may help bees detoxify pesticide and fungicide residues. Blueberry growers rely on fungicides to protect their crops from disease, DeVetter said, and bees can also pick up insecticides while foraging in nearby fields of other crops.
"You can't keep bees on one farm; they fly around," DeVetter said. "Detoxifying pesticides that bees encounter in crop fields adjacent to blueberries is likely to provide meaningful benefits. Pesticide exposure from blueberry fields during bloom is typically low because growers aim to minimize risks to bees."
Field trials expand across crops
H4Bees, an Israel-based company, developed the powder by testing different ingredient combinations and selecting those that had better performance.
"This involved nearly a decade of field trials and collaboration with researchers, growers and beekeepers," said Yuval Eshed, a co-author on the paper and chief technology officer at H4Bees.
"Our development work began in Israel, where the product is now used commercially across crops including apples, blueberries, cherries, plums, kiwifruit, almonds and seed-production crops such as onions, cotton and herbs."
Eshed added that the company is also testing its product on coffee in Vietnam, avocados and blueberries in Peru, and crops in several African countries.
DeVetter and H4Bees are in discussions about conducting a larger study, hopefully adding honey bee scientists, in the 2027 growing season. They hope to learn more about the product and how it can help blueberry producers and beekeepers.
More information
Lisa DeVetter et al., Feasibility and effects of a nano-scale feed supplement on honey bee colony performance during blueberry pollination, Entomological Communications (2026). DOI: 10.37486/2675-1305.ec08034

title: The way Earth's 'thermostat' works may have changed during Pangea era
raw_text:
The way Earth's 'thermostat' works may have changed during Pangea era
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Life arose on Earth at least 3.5 billion years ago, and our planet has remained habitable ever since—not too hot, not too cold. These life-sustaining conditions are possible in part thanks to a built-in, carbon cycle–based climate "thermostat" that controls the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
"There appears to be some kind of balance in what sustains the main greenhouse gas in Earth's atmosphere, keeping the climate at a pretty nice temperature, habitable for life over really long timescales," said R.J. Graham, a postdoctoral scholar in the University of Chicago's Department of the Geophysical Sciences.
The process that manages this balance, however, may not be an unchanging mechanism.
In a new study published in Nature Communications, Graham and colleagues from UChicago and the University of Southampton present evidence that this so-called climate thermostat may have operated in one mode for most of the past 480 million years, briefly—by geological standards—flipped modes during the age of Pangea, and then flipped back.
If the thermostat mechanism did in fact flip, the scientists said, that change could provide a new perspective on our planet's history and climate mechanisms, as well as the future of life on our planet as the sun brightens.
Thermostat controls
Carbon dioxide is the main long-term controller of Earth's greenhouse effect. Removing it from the atmosphere essentially turns on the air conditioning, and putting it back turns on the heat.
The feedback cycle relies on a process known as silicate weathering. CO₂ in the atmosphere combines with rainwater, turning it slightly acidic, which chemically breaks down rock. The dissolved minerals and carbon from the CO₂ wash into rivers and oceans, where they form carbonate rocks on the seafloor.
Over millions of years, those rocks get carried into Earth's interior through subduction, and carbon gets released by volcanoes as carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere, completing the cycle.
Silicate weathering speeds up to cool the planet and slows down to warm it. But scientists have long debated what exactly is driving the rate—temperature or rainfall? Does warmer rock simply react more quickly, or is weathering more affected by the amount of water washing over rock and through soil?
In the version of events where temperature is the main driver, weathering is primarily affected by heat. Chemical reactions occur faster in warmer conditions.
In the version where rainfall is the main factor, though, an absence of water can become a limiting factor. When water passing over rock becomes saturated with dissolved minerals, temperature doesn't matter; only more water will allow weathering to continue.
Scientists care about this distinction because the water-based thermostat is weaker. "It's less efficient," explained Graham, the study's first author. "Hotter temperatures increase rainfall, but the amount by which that speeds weathering is less than the amount by which you would directly increase the dissolution of rock just by turning the temperature up.
"So the hydrologic mechanism might be a less efficient thermostat, and it might allow for larger climate changes while maintaining that balance between the influx and outflux of the carbon," Graham explained.
The UChicago team, which included professor Dorian Abbot and assistant professor B. B. Cael, hypothesized that they could distinguish between the two "modes" by searching for signatures related to the position and distribution of landmasses.
To identify the signatures, the team analyzed 120 climate model simulations, all identical except for the layout of randomly generated continents, and calculated weathering rates under both the temperature and the hydrology assumptions. They then looked for correlations between weathering rates and landmass distribution.
They found that temperature-driven weathering depends on how much land sits in the tropics, where the land gets hotter but not necessarily wetter because extra rain evaporates with more sunlight.
Water-driven weathering, however, correlated with how consolidated or broken up the continents were. Scattered landmasses with more coastline regions allow for more runoff.
Patterns of the past
Because faster weathering cools the planet, the signatures of each mechanism should be reflected in the geologic record of global temperatures, so the team searched the past for those clues.
Comparing a 480-million-year reconstruction of Earth's temperatures against reconstructed maps of ancient continents, the researchers found signs that for the majority of that time, Earth's thermostat was running on the temperature-dominated mode, where weathering was primarily driven by heat.
Yet for roughly 100 million years, the pattern switched to the hydrology signature. This overlaps the period when most of Earth's land was combined into the supercontinent Pangea.
The researchers suggest Pangea's aridity may explain the shift: with less water moving through the soil, weathering was controlled primarily by water—or lack thereof—rather than temperature.
The scientists also said, however, that these results rely on simulations with idealized factors—no mountain ranges, rock type differences, plants, or other variables were considered. There are also different reconstructions of ancient geography, and volcanic carbon dioxide output was assumed to stay steady for the purpose of the modeling, though it may have increased as the supercontinent broke apart. Studying ancient soils from the Pangea era for the thermostat mode signatures could corroborate the hypothesis.
In addition to offering new insight into our planet's climate regulation, the possible dynamic nature of our thermostat could also inform our understanding of the "Goldilocks zone," the range of orbits around a star where a planet could have liquid water and might support life.
"The concept of a habitable zone is based on assumptions about the functionality of this CO₂ feedback," said Graham. "If your thermostat isn't as efficient as it could be, then it's plausible that it won't operate well enough to keep planets across the whole habitable zone habitable."
Publication details
R. J. Graham et al., Paleogeographic controls on Phanerozoic weathering rates and implications for climate regulation, Nature Communications (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77289-3
Journal information: Nature Communications
Provided by University of Chicago

title: National parenting support strategy could strengthen Australia's efforts to protect children
raw_text:
National parenting support strategy could strengthen Australia's efforts to protect children
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
Australia has no shortage of policies relating to children. In fact, these policies are often in the headlines. Billions of dollars are invested each year trying to improve outcomes for children and young people.
Yet we continue to see stubbornly high rates of child maltreatment and family violence, mental ill-health, school disengagement, youth offending and child protection system involvement.
The problem may not be that we are doing the wrong things. It may be that our policy architecture lacks the most important piece of the puzzle: parents.
Inconsistent support
For three decades, I have examined child maltreatment, child protection systems and family welfare.
Across these areas, one theme repeatedly emerges: we are remarkably willing to invest in systems that respond to problems, but much less willing to invest in parents—the people who have the greatest influence on children's lives.
Parenting is one of the strongest determinants of child well-being. Warm, responsive, consistent parenting is associated with better mental health, stronger educational outcomes, healthier relationships and lower risks of abuse, neglect, violence and offending.
But for all its importance, parenting remains largely invisible in policy.
Support for parents is fragmented, inconsistent and often only available once families reach a crisis point. We have pockets of excellent practice, but these don't add up to a coherent national parenting support system.
Imagine if we approached health this way. We would never expect better health outcomes if we only invested in hospitals and ambulances, and not primary care physicians and vaccination programs.
Yet when it comes to parenting, we often treat support as optional, episodic or targeted only to "problem" families.
Missed opportunities
One of the most significant findings from the Australian Child Maltreatment Study was not simply that child maltreatment is common. It was that many Australians experience multiple forms of harm.
Abuse, neglect, family violence, bullying and adversity rarely occur in isolation. Harms accumulate across childhood and often have lifelong consequences for health, education, employment and relationships.
These findings reinforce the fact that we can't rely solely on statutory child protection services to solve problems that often emerge long before a notification is made.
By the time a child comes to the attention of child protection authorities, opportunities for prevention may already have been missed. This is why many researchers and policy leaders have advocated for a public health approach to child well-being and safety.
Rather than focusing on responses after serious harm has occurred, public health approaches seek to reduce risk factors, strengthen protective factors and provide support across the whole population.
But to do this, we need to include parents.
Invisible parents
Parents go unmentioned across a broad range of policy areas.
In youth justice, debate often focuses on policing, detention, sentencing and community safety. Yet decades of research show many young people who enter youth justice systems have experienced significant adversity, including abuse, neglect, family violence and family disruption.
When governments discuss youth offending, parenting is often mentioned only in the language of responsibility for what has happened—not with a preventive lens.
If we genuinely want fewer young people entering justice systems, we must think ahead. That means supporting parents and caregivers long before problems emerge or become entrenched.
The same pattern appears in child sexual abuse prevention.
In the midst of last year's safety crisis in early childhood centers, we interviewed parents about their role.
They want to keep children safe, but many lack confidence, resources or opportunities to learn how to talk with their child about body safety and consent or recognize grooming or other signs of harm.
The same lesson emerges from contemporary debates about consent and respectful relationships education.
Across Australia, schools are being asked to deliver education on consent, respectful relationships, gender-based violence and online safety. Schools have a crucial role to play, but they can't do it alone.
Research with school leaders, parents and communities consistently points to the importance of school–family partnerships. Children develop attitudes about consent and respect through everyday interactions with parents, siblings and the broader community, not just at school.
When parents are engaged and supported, school-based violence prevention education becomes more powerful. When parents feel excluded, uncertain or ill-equipped to continue conversations at home, opportunities for learning are diminished.
What would better policy look like?
Social policies with a bigger role for parents would normalize parenting support as something for all families, not just those in crisis.
They would make evidence-based resources easy to access through trusted universal services such as maternity care, child health services and schools.
Effective policy should recognize that parenting challenges evolve over time. The support needed by a parent of a newborn differs from the support needed by parents navigating online harms or adolescent mental health difficulties, for example.
A modern parenting strategy would also promote diversity, seeking to support all manner of care arrangements and cultures.
Supporting parents isn't about blaming them or suggesting they alone determine children's outcomes. Children's well-being is also shaped by a range of things, from housing to poverty to education.
But because parenting is so important, it deserves more attention, not less.
If we are serious about doing better at protecting and raising children, parents are key. This means not treating parenting as an invisible private matter and recognizing it as essential social infrastructure.

title: Parts of Tibetan Plateau's frozen ground are gaining ice despite warming
raw_text:
High on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, the ground stays frozen, with only the top few meters melting each summer. Although the region is warming about twice as fast as the global average, a new study finds that more than a third of its permafrost, mainly in the central plateau, has gained ice since 2000. Stronger westerly winds bring more rain and snow, which seeps into the ground in summer and freezes again in winter.
The work was led by Li Dongfeng at Peking University's College of Environmental Sciences and Engineering, with colleagues from the Alfred Wegener Institute in Germany, Nanjing Normal University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, among others. It was published in Science Advances.
Roads, buildings and bridges on the plateau rest on frozen ground, and the plateau feeds rivers that supply water to about 2 billion people downstream. Most permafrost research asks how much warming will melt the ice. Far less is known about what happens when rainfall changes. This study begins to fill that gap and shows that ground ice can continue to grow even in a warmer climate.
Extra precipitation drives ice gains
Ice buried underground is hard to measure, so the team turned to boreholes—narrow holes drilled into the permafrost. In the field, they compared pairs of nearby holes, one drilled before 2000 and one after. The newer hole generally held more ice, mostly near the bottom of the layer that melts each summer.
The likely reason is water: Weather data show that yearly rain and snow in the westerly-influenced interior plateau rose by 60% after 2000. In summer, the extra water seeps into the bottom of the active layer and refreezes in the perennially subzero environment, adding to the existing ground ice over time and driving the anomalous ice increase.
To test this, the team ran a computer model of heat and water in the soil. In the simulation, when rain and snow were kept at constant levels while warming continued, the ice gains turned into losses; when temperature was held steady and rain dialed up, the ice grew. So, the conclusion was that a rapid increase in precipitation may outweigh temperature in driving ground ice evolution.
The research points out that changes in ground ice in the permafrost regions of the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau should be more closely observed, which could inform risk assessment and planning in major construction projects. Engineers and planners could use rainfall trends, not just temperature, to spot where frozen ground is likely to gain ice and shift, and allow for that movement in their designs. Ecological evaluations and climate adaptation policies could also benefit from closer observations.

title: Ants prioritize brain energy during starvation, echoing pattern seen in humans
raw_text:
The human brain accounts for roughly 2% of total body weight but uses approximately 20% of our body's energy. Relative to our body size, human brains are much larger than those of other mammals and take a lot of energy to keep humans going. The evolution of our unusually large "social brain" is thought to have given us advanced intelligence and enabled the formation of large, complex societies.
Research from Boston University now suggests that this brain metabolic functioning may not be unique to humans.
Researchers studied pavement ants and found that their brains account for about 5% of body weight while consuming roughly one-quarter of total body energy—almost the same energetic relationship seen in humans and other mammals. When ants were malnourished, their bodies dramatically reduced energy use while their brains continued operating at nearly full capacity.
The study results are published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The findings suggest that protecting the brain during times of stress may be a deeply conserved feature of evolution rather than a uniquely human adaptation. The research demonstrates that ant brains, like human brains, require a disproportionate amount of energy for workers to perform their social behaviors.
To learn more about this work, first author Dr. Zachary Coto, a member of BU's Traniello Lab, answered questions about this study looking at brain size and energy demands.
Why are you interested in brain evolution?
Understanding brain evolution in animals that live in complex societies has been a key research area for decades and has generated much controversy. How does social life influence brain size and the energetic cost of its functions? Our research integrates sociobiology and evolutionary neurobiology to focus on how social life influences brain evolution. Questions of brain size evolution must be addressed with integrated studies of the energetic cost of brain tissue, which is metabolically expensive.
Why study ant brains and what were you hoping to learn?
We have a limited understanding of how brains of any size and of any animal generate complex social behavior. Humans and ants provide an interesting comparison that is particularly compelling because ant brains are so small and both ants and humans are so social.
Human brains are unusually large relative to our body size, disproportionately larger than the brains of other mammals, and require a disproportionate amount of energy to maintain.
To explain this, researchers have proposed the "selfish brain" theory—the idea that when energy becomes scarce, the brain claims priority over other organs to preserve critical functions. Although previous studies hinted that this occurs in humans and other mammals by measuring size, directly measuring both brain metabolism and whole-body metabolism has proven difficult. We can measure all of these variables in ants.
Our research addresses fundamental questions about brain evolution by recording metabolic rates of ant brains by measuring whole-body metabolism. We wanted to determine whether the energy allocated to the brain is maintained while other systems are compromised during stress. When resources become scarce, worker ants may not regulate their physiology to survive low-energy conditions, but instead simply die.
What are your key research findings?
Several key findings indicate remarkably similar patterns of brain energy usage between ants and humans, despite the significant differences in body size, brain size and physiology. We found that worker ant brains are about 5% of their body weight but use approximately 25% of body energy, consistent with the mammalian pattern.
Additionally, we found that worker ant brain metabolic rates did not significantly decrease under physiological stress, despite declines in whole-body metabolic rates. The proportion of energy allocated to the brain nearly doubled, consistent with the pattern of energy prioritization observed in human brains.
When workers faced severe physiological limits, like starvation, we found that within only a few days of dying, they still maintained their brain physiology. We paired these brain metabolic measurements with behavioral tasks to determine if they could still process information relevant to significant social behaviors such as nestmate identification and colony defense, and found that workers performed comparably with those that had not been starved.
These results suggest that during starvation, workers maintain their brain physiology at the expense of other physiologically demanding systems, and they maintain adaptive social behaviors.
Furthermore, we scaled human and mammalian data to predict the brain energy use of an ant-sized mammal. The model accurately matched our ant species, showing that shrinking a brain doesn't change its basic energy requirements.
Our findings show that even miniature brains are expensive to run, and even in social insects that put the colony above the individual, prioritizing energy for brain processing remains essential.
How does this research correlate with humans?
The question of the uniqueness of our species is of enduring interest. Tool use, social learning, personality, consciousness, and even numerical ability and facial recognition have all been found in other species, including insects. Our "big brains" shape our individuality and creativity, allow us to navigate complex, dynamic and nuanced social relationships, and are critical to the cultural sophistication that defines us as human.
Our finding that ants allocate no less energy to operate their brains than humans is surprising. Our brains are complex relative to those of ants, but nevertheless share significant neurophysiological properties and thus offer insights into understanding the evolutionary neurobiology of the brain.

Curated collections on hot topics and conversations from across the chemistry community. All you need to get up to date – in-depth features, the latest news, research, comment and opinion.
- Energy storage and batteries In this collection, we explore energy storage and battery research, covering innovative battery chemistries, materials design, device fabrication techniques, solutions to transition to clean energy, and applications including electric vehicles, grid-scale energy storage, and portable electronics.

In this collection, experts in science and policy envision how India’s innovation ecosystem can empower its scientists by building research infrastructure, improving governance and translating discoveries into real‑world applications.
- 2025 in review Our favourite stories from 2025

In this collection, we look at the gender gap in health and drugs, how treatments for menopause are slowly changing and what we're finding out about period products.
- Solutions for India's sustainability challenge Experts in law, policy, science, finance and education explore the sustainability challenges facing India, and how chemistry can enable the country to meet its ambition of reaching net zero emissions.
- The future of analytical chemistry We're looking ahead to the future of analytical chemistry, from monitoring the planet from satellites, diagnosing cancer quickly and easily from small blood samples, to where the discipline itself is heading. And with a century and half passing since the Society of Public Analysts was founded, what does the future hold for this important role?
- Chemistry of the brain In this collection, we turn the spotlight inside our heads and focus on big questions of the brain. How do we remember things and feel pain? Are we any closer to a cure for Alzheimer’s? What is the chemistry of addiction? And how are researchers getting around the blood—brain barrier?
- Water and the environment In this collection, we explore the industrial use of water, water supply and its role in the environment, covering responsible mining, large-scale desalination and hydrogen production, drinking water and public health, the impact of climate change on oceans, and solutions for repairing polluted waterways and ecosystems.
- Chemical bonding In this collection, we explore the fundamental principles of chemical bonding, covering covalent, ionic, and metallic bonding, as well as molecular structure, intermolecular forces, and the role of chemical bonding in shaping the properties and behaviour of molecules.
- Antimicrobial resistance In this collection, we explore the critical issue of antimicrobial resistance, covering the latest research on antibiotic mechanisms, microbial evolution, resistance detection methods, and strategies for combating antimicrobial resistance in healthcare and the environment.
- AI and automation In this collection, we explore the latest developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and automation, covering technologies and applications such as machine learning, robotics, laboratory automation and data analysis, and their impact on chemistry research, the profession, and chemistry-using industries.
- Sustainability In this collection we explore sustainable solutions for addressing global challenges, covering interdisciplinary approaches to sustainability, including renewable energy sources, green chemistry, reducing waste and emissions, circular economy principles, and solutions for a low carbon and net ze
- Research culture In this collection we explore fostering a positive research culture and scientific practices, covering topics such as reproducibility, open science, diversity and inclusion, leadership and mentorship, career instability, discrimination, misconduct and the evolving landscape of research ethics and integrity.
- Nobel prize Who won the Nobel prize in chemistry? Discover the science that made them a Nobel laureate with news, interviews and features from Chemistry World
- Food science and cookery In this collection we explore the chemistry of cooking, food production, processing and storage including food analysis, safety and quality assurance, packaging and preservation, additives and flavour, agriculture and biotechnology and bio-based foods and meat alternatives.
- Plastics and polymers In this collection we explore advancements in plastics and polymers research, covering topics such as polymer synthesis, characterisation techniques, material properties, biodegradable polymers, plastic waste and recycling, and the impact of microplastics and PFAS on the environment and human health.
- Periodic table In this collection we explore the history and significance of the periodic table. We cover its origins and evolution, from Dmitri Mendeleev’s groundbreaking arrangement to the modern periodic table’s organisation, its influence and role in science and culture, the discovery of new elements and element scarcity.
