title: I’m sharing my @cancerwidower journey to bring a realistic understanding of research progress
raw_text:
Regular Chemistry World contributor Andy Extance is trying to help others after his late partner’s death
In 2021, checkpoint inhibitor and CAR-T immuno-oncology therapies were achieving remarkable outcomes for many cancer patients. As an ex-pharmaceutical industry chemist who had become a freelance science journalist, I’d spent years covering these advances. Then, in August, the news came: my partner, E, had cancer.
Just a month before I had an article published in the RSC’s Education in Chemistry explaining how new cancer treatments were helping people live longer. The key statistic had been that the proportion of patients surviving a decade after diagnosis had grown from one person in four 30 years ago to one in two today. But those statistics rang hollow when E tragically died in 2022.
Her journey, and mine before and since, have inspired me to set up an Instagram account called The Widowers Guide to the Science of Cancer (@cancerwidower). To help ensure E’s death isn’t wholly in vain, I share the basics of how cancer and treatments for it work, the gaps between expectation and reality, and advice based on my experience.
The decision hasn’t been easy, and not all my friends and family are happy about me sharing this so openly. But many people say it’s a great idea, and my experiences strongly suggest why.
A hard lesson
E’s death in 2022 inevitably left my life in turmoil. As I grieved and gradually rebuilt, writing was a reassuring constant.
Yet, when Chemistry World asked me to write about new cancer drugs, I felt that my previous stories had been too uncritical. Contrary to my expectations, none of the new immuno-oncology drugs were available to help E. In fact, most new cancer drugs target mutations that are not present in every patient and are usually only approved in certain types of cancer. And the flipside of the figures on cancer progress is that it is still massively widespread – it’s responsible for the death of someone in the UK every three minutes.
E was regularly screened – but the type of cancer she developed doesn’t have a standard screening test. I’ve angrily asked why. Siddhartha Mukherjee’s amazing biography of cancer, The Emperor of All Maladies, provided some of the answer: It’s very hard in many cases to get the balance between false positives and negatives right. That helps me realign my expectations – but the anger remains.
Redefining victory
All of which relates to the way many people discuss cancer research. Not least James Watson, who famously won the Nobel Prize for discovering the structure of DNA. In 2009, he said: ‘Beating cancer now is a realistic ambition because, at long last, we largely know its true genetic and chemical characteristics.’
Watson was wrong on many things, and I think he’s wrong on this too. Cancer is too complex to overcome completely. Instead, I agree more with Mukherjee, who just two years later wrote about a more modest ambition. ‘We might as well focus more on prolonging life than eliminating death’, he says. ‘This war on cancer may best be “won” by redefining victory.’
I now try to include a more grounded perspective in my cancer coverage. Meanwhile, I’m trying to convey the idea of focussing on prolonging life rather than eliminating death with The Widowers Guide to the Science of Cancer – as it’s another message I have personal experience of.
Had it not been for great medics providing surgery, chemotherapy, palliative and hospice support, E might have died within six months of her diagnosis. But we got an extra year after that, a precious one full of joyful moments. And that showed me that even in its harshest moments, cancer can sharpen our appreciation of life’s beauty and brevity.

title: A salmon-safe alternative to 6PPD & the first known example of naturally produced MOFs
raw_text:
In this episode, we discuss the difficulties in finding a safer replacement for a chemical in tyres that has been causing extensive salmon deaths in North American streams, along with the first known naturally synthesized MOFs with Phillip Broadwith and Patrick Walter.
This week’s headlines
Featured stories
Think about the last time you drove through the rain. While your tyres smashed through the puddles, a little bit of that tyre rubber got left behind, washed off of the road and into the drain with the rest of the stormwater.
That rubber contains a preservative called 6PPD, which has been used in tyres for around 60 years. It’s great at stopping rubber from degrading. But when it reacts and breaks down, it forms a byproduct called 6PPD-quinone, which is deadly to some species of salmon and other fish.
Virtually every tyre on the market contains 6PPD, and tyre chemistry is a delicate balance of multiple ingredients working together. So how do you replace this chemical without creating a new problem?
And for the first time, researchers have discovered a microorganism that makes metal–organic frameworks (MOFs). Cable bacteria are filamentous microorganisms that can move electrons over distances of several centimetres. It may not sound very far, but in reality this distance is about 10,000 times the width of the bacteria itself.
Facilitating this transport are naturally biosynthesized nickel-organic frameworks. It’s the first example of naturally synthesized MOFs known to us, and this it conducts electricity with a similar efficiency to some of the best synthetic polymers and MOFs currently used. How did we discover them, and can we learn something from this structure?
We would love to hear your feedback on this podcast, so if you have any questions or comments please get in touch.
Introduction and Chemistry News Roundup
Mariana Kneppers
A chemical that keeps tyres from cracking is also killing salmon when it washes into rivers. We discuss the difficulties in searching for a safer replacement for 6PPD. And researchers have identified a living organism that produces and uses metal organic frameworks at the bottom of the sea floor. How is it possible and what can we learn about it for our own design of materials?
I’m Mariana Kneppers, Chemistry World science media producer, and this is the Chemical Breakdown.
We’ll be diving deeper into these stories shortly, but first let’s take a look at this week’s news from the Chemistry World website.
A warning has been issued that England’s current student loan system could drive talented science graduates away from research, as many face the choice between pursuing lower-paid scientific careers or moving into higher-paying sectors to manage their debts. Critics argue that the growing financial burden risks undermining the UK’s future scientific workforce and widening inequalities in who can afford to stay in science.
Researchers in China have shown that covalent organic frameworks can be used to rearrange water molecules, increasing the efficiency of the reduction of nitrate to ammonia. This could both reduce the energy intensity of ammonia production and help to remediate water pollution.
Chemists have tracked the fleeting intermediates in the natural synthesis of penicillin using ultra-short X-ray pulses. The research could usher in improvements in ring-forming reactions on useful intermediates for the pharmaceutical industry or aid enzyme engineering.
And the annual Small World Microscopy Competition has announced its photography winners, but this year’s video champion was stripped of the title after judges discovered the entry had been created using AI-generated imagery. The incident has reignited debate over how scientific imaging contests can verify authenticity as AI tools become increasingly sophisticated.
You can find these stories and more online. Just visit chemistryworld.com for more of the latest news in the chemical sciences.
Think about the last time you drove through the rain. While your tyres smashed through the puddles, a little bit of that tyre rubber got left behind, washed off the road and into the drain with the rest of the storm water. That rubber contains a preservative called 6-PPD, which has been used in tyres for around 60 years. It’s great at stopping rubber from degrading, but when it reacts and breaks down, it forms a byproduct called 6-PPD-quinone, which is deadly to some species of salmon and other fish.
Virtually every tyre on the market contains 6-PPD, and tyre chemistry is a delicate balance of multiple ingredients working together. So how do you replace this chemical without creating a new problem?
Here to discuss today’s stories are business editor Phillip Broadwith and news editor Patrick Walter. Hello to you both.
Searching for a Safer Replacement for 6PPD
Phillip Broadwith
Hi Mariana. Hello.
Mariana Kneppers
Hi, thanks for being here. So Philip, how did this all start? When did we first realise that this was even an issue?
Phillip Broadwith
Well, people have been finding these strange deaths of salmon for about 20 years and they’ve been trying to work out what it was and it’s taken a lot of investigation and it wasn’t until about 2020 that we found out that it’s this particular tyre additive that’s causing the problem. There’s now moves to regulate that chemical in the US, in Canada, in the EU. And so we need a replacement.
Mariana Kneppers
Yeah, fair. And what is the role of 6PPD? On a chemical basis, how does that work?
Phillip Broadwith
Well, tyre rubber has carbon-carbon double bonds in it, alkenes. If those are exposed to ozone, they can be attacked by the ozone and degraded. That causes the rubber to crack, which means it doesn’t perform its job as a tyre. It loses grip, it can fail, and then you’ve got a big problem.
So what 6PPD does is preferentially react with the ozone at the surface of the tyre and stop it from degrading the rubber. But that means that the 6PPD also has to be able to move through the rubber of the tyre, because it’s just in all of the rubber, but it only acts at the surface.
And that’s one of the problems when you’re finding a replacement. You need something that reacts with the ozone and protects the rubber, but can also move through the solid matrix of the rubber of the tyre and diffuse around it. So it can’t just be covalently bonded to the tyre rubber. It needs to be mobile as well.
Mariana Kneppers
I see. This might be a really silly question, but how does it get to the surface of the tyre? Is that just kind of like it diffuses out towards where the ozone is?
Phillip Broadwith
Yeah, it’s just diffusion. So as the 6PPD at the surface is reacted, you get a concentration gradient and the stuff that’s deeper in the tyre moves out to the surface.
Mariana Kneppers
I see. Okay, so in 6PPD is kind of the chemical of concern here. Now, is it just 6PPD or are there other chemicals? Maybe is it the whole family of concern?
Phillip Broadwith
So the bit that reacts with the ozone is kind of in the middle of the molecule. It’s called a paraphenylenediamine. It’s an aromatic ring and it gets oxidised.
And then on the periphery of the molecule, attached to some amine groups, there are some alkyl groups. And there’s a whole variety of different variations of this family available, and some of them are used elsewhere in rubber, in aircraft tyres when you need a slightly different performance or for other rubber applications.
And it turns out that not all of those are anywhere near as toxic to fish. And part of the problem is we don’t really know how this toxicity works. We don’t know why it’s only toxic to this very specific species of salmon, coho salmon and a few other things like rainbow trout.
For other fish, it’s nowhere near as toxic. And some of the other PPDs definitely aren’t toxic to coho salmon or rainbow trout. But then we don’t know if the other members of this family are going to be toxic in different ways to different kinds of fish.
So there’s a lot of toxicology to do to understand this whole family of chemicals. Because the main front runners for replacing 6PPD are other PPDs, other paraphenylenediamines, and they’re set in the same, but with different alcohol groups on the side. So they retain a lot of the same properties.
They’re relatively easy replacements because they’re already in use in some places. So that would be probably the path of least resistance, if you like, as long as they’re not super toxic to fish, which they don’t appear to be toxic to the same kinds of fish, but we don’t know about other kinds of fish.
And in Europe particularly and Canada, there are moves to regulate the family of PPDs as a whole. So if they end up restricted, then that’s going to mean none of them are really suitable to be tyre additives.
Mariana Kneppers
Yeah, fair enough. Yeah, it’s a challenging situation because as you say, like this family of chemicals, we know that it works. You need a very specific kind of chemical for this very unique process to work.
But with chemistry and a lot of biochemistry in particular, one small change could make it safe for one thing, but toxic for a load of other things. Like it’s that really fine, nitty gritty balance that you only really know the results once you’ve kind of tested through all of the candidates, I guess.
I mean, is that the approach that they’re taking? Are they kind of just going through the family and just seeing one by one what works, what doesn’t?
Phillip Broadwith
So a lot of this work is being done by a group of companies in the US, a group of tyre manufacturers. And to start with, they’ve tested a load of possible alternatives to see if they work in the tyres, because that’s their priority. They want something that works and retains the performance of the tyres.
They’ve ruled out a whole load of compounds based on that. And they’ve now got left with about 40 compounds that they’re still looking at. Some are PPDs, some are not PPDs, completely different families of molecules and materials.
But they’re now taking the kind of most promising of those and looking in much more detail at the toxicology.
Patrick Walter
So Philip brings up a really interesting point there that is an issue that has been affecting industry on the whole. This concept of regrettable substitution.
So this is the idea that you identify a chemical that is a known problem, perhaps it’s toxic to animals, and you try to replace it with something else. Often the chemical is similar because you need that chemical to perform a certain role.
But what often happens is you replace it with one and then you find it causes different problems, somewhat similar. So one example could be bisphenol A. So BPA was replaced with BPS and this was found to cause other but similar toxicity issues in humans and animal models.
Mariana Kneppers
I see, fair enough. Yeah. That’s a really, really good point.
What about the 6PPD that already is in the environment? Is this like a situation like PFAS or these other forever chemicals where it’s in the environment, it’s stuck now? Or are there efforts being done to maybe try and like clean the rivers? Or I don’t know, how long does it actually last?
Phillip Broadwith
That’s one of the interesting things. When it’s in contact with the air, it doesn’t last very long at all. It’s broken down by ozone, it’s broken down by oxidation pretty quickly. And that’s one of the reasons it was assumed that it probably wasn’t a problem.
But as it turns out, when it gets into the river sediments, when it gets into an anaerobic environment where there’s no oxygen to break it down, it can last for much, much longer.
It’s not super persistent. We’re not talking like PFAS levels of lasting for hundreds of years, but it can definitely last for a much longer time. And as things get stirred up, it gets released back into the river, it gets oxidised back to the quinone.
And the quinone is so toxic at such tiny concentrations that it really doesn’t take very much to have a significant effect on these particular salmon and trout populations. And that’s why there’s an issue, because because it’s toxic at tiny concentrations and those concentrations are easily achievable under the conditions that it gets into the environment.
Mariana Kneppers
I see. Fair enough. And is this, I think this was mainly focused in America, right? America and Canada. But is this a problem elsewhere?
I mean, presumably these tyres, tyres around the world use 6PPD or something similar. So is this, are we seeing this in Europe? Are we seeing this in Asia?
Phillip Broadwith
There’s definitely moves to regulate it in Europe, and partly I think that’s down to where the populations of the fish that are particularly susceptible to this chemical are.
So we’ve seen it in the coho salmon, which is mostly in the northwestern US. It’s not so toxic to salmon that are present in Europe, but it is toxic to rainbow trout, which is why we’re seeing some moves for regulation in Europe as well, because there are rainbow trout populations there.
And in some ways, when we get to replacements, we don’t know what effects they might have on other fish that are elsewhere. So partly it’s focused on the areas where there are populations of the kind of fish that are most strongly affected by the chemical.
Mariana Kneppers
Sounds like people are trying to find a solution. Fingers crossed that they find one soon, but definitely developing stories. So we’ll have to keep our eyes on this one. So thanks so much, Philip.
Natural Metal Organic Frameworks in Cable Bacteria
Mariana Kneppers
For the first time, researchers have discovered a microorganism that makes metal organic frameworks or MOFs. Cable bacteria are filamentous microorganisms that can move electrons over distances of several centimetres. It may not sound very far, but in reality, this distance is about 10,000 times the width of the bacteria itself.
Facilitating this transportation are naturally biosynthesised nickel organic frameworks. It’s the first example of naturally synthesised MOFs known to us, and these MOFs conduct electricity with a similar efficiency to some of the best synthetic polymers and MOFs currently used.
How did we discover them, and can we learn something from this structure?
So Pat, give us some context here. How did the researchers come across this discovery in the 1st place? I mean, did we always know that this was out there or was this an accidental discovery?
Patrick Walter
Well, we’ve known about cable bacteria for some time now, but what hasn’t been known is what these incredibly long filaments are made out of.
I mean, these filaments are just one to two micrometres thick, but can be up to two, 3 centimetres long. That’s like 20,000 micrometres.
So while we were interested in these bacteria, while we knew what they were up to, what we didn’t know is we didn’t have a detailed idea of what these filaments were actually made out of. And it’s been quite a surprise to discover that they’re made out of MOFs.
Up until now, it was always thought that MOFs were a purely human invention. I mean, there’s a lot of interest around MOFs. Last year, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to three researchers for the discovery and development of MOFs.
Mariana Kneppers
Yeah, that’s such a good point. MOFs have been such a hot topic lately. You know, they’ve been a hot topic for a while, but particularly with the Nobel Prize last year.
Can you break down the MOFs that are being used in this context? What is the difference between, you know, the MOFs that we’re familiar with and we’re creating versus what we’re seeing with these bacteria?
Patrick Walter
I mean, there’s been a lot of interests around MOFs because they’re so versatile, so they’re composed of a metal iron and a linker, and you can swap these out to create all sorts of different structures. There’s thousands and thousands of different MOFs that have now been created.
Now what’s great about MOFs is this versatility, but they also have a huge surface area. So this interconnected network has a vast surface area, so people have been very interested in looking at them for storing things like gases, so capturing carbon dioxide for instance.
An often repeated fact is that a gram or so of a MOF might have the surface area around a football field.
So what is going on in this case? The bacteria are making MOFs from something similar, a similar process to what we use. In this case they’ve used nickel and dithiolene ligands and what they do is they’ve connected them up into these long kind of strings and that’s what’s acting as the wire.
Although they are doing something interesting and a little bit different in that they’re twining these MOFs into nanoribbons. So they’re making these great long structures of MOFs and these MOFs are also electrically conductive so that’s what’s important to them for surviving on the ocean floor.
Mariana Kneppers
So how are they using the MOFs? in this context.
Patrick Walter
So these bacteria live in a pretty harsh environment. They’re living on the sea floor. There’s no sunlight, not much energy, not much lives there. So where are they going to get their energy?
Well, they look to the sediment. So in this case, they worm their cables into the sediment. The cables are able to, they’re making use of chemical energy there. So they metabolise sulfides they find in the sediment.
And then what they do, as we’ve said, they’re highly electrically conductive, these cables, so they’re transferring the electrons from sulfides when they oxidise them, and they’re moving them up like power lines, directing the energy into the bacterial cells.
And from there, they use these electrons to power metabolic processes like glycolysis or respiration.
Mariana Kneppers
Oh, wow. So this would be like an example of chemosynthesis. Is that fair to say? Versus like normally things get energy from light, for example, and that’s where you get photosynthesis. But would this be an example of chemosynthesis?
Patrick Walter
Yes, I believe that is the correct word. So you got photosynthesis, so making use of light, chemosynthesis tapping into chemical energy.
Mariana Kneppers
Yeah, so cool. Wow.
So looking at the design of these morphs, it’s quite, as you say, really cool, almost like this power line structure that they’re using them. Is that similar to how we’ve been using morphs? Or I mean, is there something that we can learn from this?
Patrick Walter
It’s not really. There’s some similarities with 2D MOFs, but there’s a lot more interest, I think, right now in the chemistry community with three-dimensional MOFs.
But in this case, the bacteria are kind of layering up all these MOFs to create these nanoribbons. And that’s what’s interesting here.
There hasn’t been so much focus, I don’t think, on electrical conductivity in MOFs and what we’re seeing here is MOFs that have a similar electrical conductivity, like you said, to conductive, the best conductive polymers or even some metals.
And what’s quite interesting here, we mentioned that bacteria make use of nickel and dithiolene ligands. These kind of complexes already exist in other species of bacteria but they’re not all chained together into these big long structures.
So they’re just acting as a simple cofactor and they use them to transfer electrons between proteins in metabolic processes.
So this is a case of nature once again repurposing something. So it seems likely to me that in the past this nickel base complex was used purely as a cofactor for transporting electrons around and then it’s been repurposed.
So it’s evolution in action again. So just like bacteria, just like multicellular cells, they often take a motif, a process that works for one thing, but it can be adapted. It might not be very good at doing something else, but it’s okay enough to make a start and then it’s improved upon from there.
Mariana Kneppers
Yeah, really, really interesting.
Phillip Broadwith
Pat, you mentioned that these are nearly as conductive as some of the conductive polymers that we’ve seen. And if I remember rightly, there are conductive polymers that use similar kinds of chemical motifs, these kind of dithiolenes using sulphur-based chemicals to integrate it into the polymer.
So it’s kind of interesting that there’s that parallel that we’ve almost independently come to a similar arrangement of molecules to do a similar job, but without knowing that this has been going on for hundreds of years or hundreds of millions of years in bacteria.
Patrick Walter
So it’s almost like a convergent evolution, except we’re going through a different way. So science, it works, I think is the phrase often bandied about. And in this case, it’s found a very similar way to the same process.
Mariana Kneppers
Fair enough. Do we see any kind of applications for, I don’t know, has it gotten the wheels turning, I guess, in chemist minds of future BOF design?
Patrick Walter
Oh, definitely. I think the team working on this are now looking into concepts like sustainable and biologically grown electronics. So these structures would be really interesting for that.
And as I said, this kind of nano ribbon structure is unusual in MOF construction.
Phillip Broadwith
Yeah, I mean, I guess we’re going to have to find a way of replicating that. I mean, either you get the bacteria to grow it for you, right? Or you’ve got to find a chemical way, because so far when we’ve chemically made MOFs, it’s mostly as kind of crystals, it’s not as these long ribbon structures.
So it’s going to take some thinking to work out how we can make those on a bigger scale or just get the bacteria to grow them for us. But I don’t know how well they ferment.
Patrick Walter
I mean, it’s certainly quite an unusual structure for a MOF, but what I did think it was reminiscent of is proteins.
So bacteria found another way to produce a structure that’s similar to proteins that are used in long filaments, very reminiscent of actin, which acts as a skeleton for cells and helps them to do things like divide.
So really interesting that the bacteria have come up with another way of doing something that other bacteria have also found similar ways to do.
Mariana Kneppers
Yeah, it’s really interesting. I thought, yeah, that’s a really good point. It did remind me a bit of the actin filaments as well. And it’s almost like the way they’ve designed it feels very like almost like morph section. I don’t know if you can term that, but it’s just morphs on morphs on morphs.
Patrick Walter
It’s they’ve kind of literally no one has used that word before.
Mariana Kneppers
They’ll never use it again after this. But yeah, it’s amazing. It’s kind of looking at morphs in a different way that maybe we hadn’t thought of yet.
So yeah, really interested to see how this can be applied in the future. Well, thank you both so much.
Patrick Walter
Good stuff.
Chemistry History: Christopher Ingold
Mariana Kneppers
And finally, this week in chemistry history, Christopher Ingold was born on October 28th, 1893 in Ilford on the outskirts of London.
Ingold would go on to coin some of the vital chemistry concepts used in reaction mechanisms. In the early 20th century, organic chemistry was largely a science of recipes. Chemists knew what went in and what came out, but what the electrons were doing in between was anyone’s guess.
Ingold set out to change that.
At Leeds, Ingold became fascinated by the nature of chemical bonding and began developing ideas that would eventually clash with those of Robert Robinson, a professor at the University of Manchester.
In a 1922 paper, Robinson described reagents, borrowing terms from Arthur Lapworth, as either cationoid, meaning they behaved somewhat like a positive ion, and anionoid, meaning they behaved like a negative ion.
He began to think about reactions in terms of shifting electrons within molecules, and pioneered the use of the curly arrows we still use today as a symbol describing electron movement during a reaction.
Ingold, on the other hand, took these ideas much further, formalising, expanding, and categorising these ideas into the terminology we still use today, including examples like resonance and the inductive effect.
The terms cationoid and anionoid were replaced with electrophilic and nucleophilic to describe a reagent as electron attracting or repelling.
He also disagreed with Robinson on the sign to be attached to the substituent effects, designating electron-donating substituents as positive and electron-withdrawing substituents as negative, while Robinson’s convention was the opposite.
So chemists at the time thus had two similar versions of an electronic theory of organic chemistry characterised by different terminology and convention, and they had to decide which one to use to write up the results.
Ingold’s approach quickly became the favourite, perhaps due to his notoriously rapid rate of publication in the field.
Robinson, despite having moved from electronic theories towards biosynthesis, grew bitter over what he perceived to be a lack of credit. However, his curly arrow is still a staple of chemical notation to this day.
Ingold made a number of other contributions to the field across his career. Perhaps his most well-known was during his time at the University College of London.
Here, Ingold partnered with Edward Hughes to describe for the first time the two different forms of nucleophilic substitutions known as SN1 and SN2.
It’s one of the most common reactions in organic chemistry, and this work established a language for discussing the mechanism of organic reactions in solution and became widely accepted by the field.
Ingold was knighted in 1958 for his extensive contributions to the field, and he died in 1970.
He’s remembered as being a kind and courteous man. In the 1930s, he worked closely with Frederick George Donnan to help Jewish scientists and refugees escape Nazi Germany and resettle in Great Britain.
Today, UCL’s chemistry building bears his name as a reminder of his landmark work conducted at the university.

title: Learning the language of chemistry
raw_text:
Chemical structures embed vast amounts of information that needs translating for machines
Outside of my day-job at Chemistry World, I teach a couple of small-group tutorial classes of first-year chemistry undergraduates. With a new academic year just starting, I’m getting to know my new students, and one of the first things we cover is their familiarity with drawing and interpreting chemical structures.
Ensuring we have a firm grounding (and ideally a neat hand) in chemical notation is worth spending some time on, given the enormous amount of implicit information that can be embedded in even the simplest structural drawings. And like learning syntax and grammar rules in any other language, my students are expected to follow the conventions that have evolved over a couple of centuries of chemists communicating their ideas and conceptions of molecular complexity.

title: Covalent organic frameworks could clean up water pollution and generate ‘green’ ammonia
raw_text:
Supramolecular structures can break down nitrates to produce ammonia and close the fertiliser loop
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) can be used to rearrange water molecules, increasing the efficiency of the reduction of nitrate to ammonia, researchers in China have shown. This could both reduce the energy intensity of ammonia production and help to remediate water pollution.
The Haber–Bosch synthesis of ammonia, developed in the early 20th century, has helped enable Earth’s population to grow from around 1.6 billion in 1900 to 8.3 billion today. Global production is currently nearly 250 million tonnes per year, with 70% of this being used to produce fertiliser. More recently, ammonia has attracted interest as a carbon-free fuel.

title: Punitive student loans threaten the future of UK science
raw_text:
Science graduates face choice of leaving science sector for higher paid careers or becoming stuck in debt trap
Debate around the contentious plan 2 student loan system has garnered widespread attention over the last year: retrospective changes by successive governments have led to spiralling graduate debt and increasing cost-of-living pressures for the newest entrants into the workforce. A generation of students feels betrayed by the establishment and the hidden inequalities embedded into this flawed system are now becoming apparent.
Beneath the radar, the plan 2 loans’ predatory terms have quietly taken a disproportionate toll on the UK’s science graduates, with the most punitive features hitting this group hardest. More than 20% of the loan holders Chemistry World surveyed in a recent poll said they were considering cutting their losses: leaving the sector, moving abroad, or restricting their hours and responsibilities. More and more are simply choosing to cut their losses: leaving the sector, moving abroad or restricting their hours. This steady drain of talent from the UK scientific workforce is a worrying trend, and one that is only set to get worse as the next generation begins to make career choices, says Neil Walsh, pensions officer at the trade union Prospect. ‘There’s a complete undermining of science as a sector and where it gets really problematic is when that starts seeping through to secondary school students deciding where their career future lies.’

title: Multivariate MOFs make the case for embracing complexity
raw_text:
Frameworks built from multiple different metals and ligands are expanding the possibilities for materials that can do many things at once
Omar Yaghi is convinced that chemists should embrace complexity. ‘Right now, materials in general have one structure, one property, one operation,’ he says. ‘[Yet] it would be great if we could design materials… where several things are happening at once.’
This is surprising for a chemist who helped establish the field of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), a contribution recognised by last year’s Nobel prize in chemistry, which Yaghi shared with Susumu Kitagawa and Richard Robson. Yet in recent years, Yaghi has moved away from creating conventional MOFs built from a single type of linker and metal node. Instead, he and other chemists have found ways to incorporate multiple organic ligands and different metal building blocks within a single structure.
This new class of materials – known as multivariate- or MTV-MOFs – drastically expands the scope and capability of porous frameworks. ‘[Chemists] look at [MTV-MOFs] and they say “Oh my God, this is just in one structure? You have too many things happening”,’ says Yaghi. ‘A lot of people shy away from it [but] I think that [it’s] a big opportunity to transform our chemistry.’

title: Could a giant sunshade in space ‘solve global warming’? Scientists are taking the idea seriously
raw_text:
In August, entrepreneur Elon Musk suggested in a social-media post that Earth could be cooled by launching satellites into space to shade the planet from the Sun. These “sentient satellites”, he wrote, “can solve global warming for ~1B years”.
Climate engineering faces hostility — here’s how scientists say it might move forwards
It’s unclear whether Musk, the chief executive of aerospace firm SpaceX in Starbase, Texas, meant for this to be taken seriously. But some researchers are earnestly investigating space-based methods of reflecting sunlight away from Earth to cool the planet as temperatures rise to increasingly dangerous levels.
A non-profit organization called the Planetary Sunshade Institute in Los Angeles, California, published a report this month that researchers say is the most detailed analysis yet of such geoengineering methods. The report — which summarizes studies from a consortium of engineers and climate scientists, including some from leading space agencies such as NASA — estimates that it could become viable to begin building a ‘planetary sunshade’ in as few as 20–40 years. The timeline would depend on the rate at which heavy-lift rockets are developed that can haul millions of tonnes of material into deep space to create the sunshade. (SpaceX, which is not involved in the report, did not respond to a query from Nature about whether it is conducting research on this topic.)
A lot of people think this idea is “just fantasy”, says Chantal Cappelletti, a space-systems engineer at the University of Nottingham, UK, who is part of the consortium. But the falling cost of space launches have made the prospect seem more feasible, she says.
Not so science fiction
Blocking sunlight to cool the planet through solar geoengineering has long been controversial. Proposals have included releasing sunlight-reflecting particles into Earth’s atmosphere, which could affect the planet in poorly understood ways, such as disrupting precipitation and plant growth. Space-based approaches could come with unique risks, including the pollution unleashed from many thousands of rocket launches. Critics also say that focusing attention on geoengineering distracts from the urgent need to cut greenhouse-gas emissions to address climate change.
Controversial geoengineering projects to test Earth-cooling tech funded by UK agency
But solar geoengineering has received more attention from researchers as Earth looks set to hurtle past 1.5 °C of warming above the planet’s pre-industrial baseline temperature. The “accelerating climate crisis” is pushing the world towards solar geoengineering, says Morgan Goodwin, a climate activist and executive director of the Planetary Sunshade Institute.
The report is the group’s biggest project so far, funded by a £400,000 (US$530,000) grant from the UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), a body sponsored by the government to fund high-risk, high-reward research. That grant is part of a larger £56.8-million ARIA research programme on solar geoengineering.
Daniele Visioni, a climate scientist at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, says that he had previously dismissed space-based approaches as science fiction. But after attending an engineering workshop on such approaches earlier this year, he was persuaded that they deserve more attention. However, “I still wouldn’t put this as something feasible before the end of the century”, he says.

Job Details
The Department of Molecular and Human Genetics at Baylor College of Medicine invites applications for tenured and tenure-track faculty positions in computational genetics and experimental genetics and genomics. We welcome applications at the Assistant, Associate, or Full Professor level from established leaders and rising investigators whose work will define the next generation of genetic discovery and its translation to human health.
We seek Ph.D.- and/or M.D.-trained scientists with a record of rigorous, high-impact scholarship and the potential to establish and sustain an externally funded, independent research program. Successful candidates will contribute to a highly collaborative scientific community and participate in the education and mentorship of graduate students, postdoctoral fellows, residents, and other trainees. Research may address rare or common disease, fundamental genetic and genomic mechanisms, technology development, or other major questions in biology and medicine.
Computational Genetics
We seek computational investigators who develop or apply innovative quantitative approaches to important problems in genetics, genomics, and human health. Areas of interest include, but are not limited to:
- Artificial intelligence, machine learning, statistical genetics, algorithm development, and responsible genomic data science.
- Analysis of whole-genome, long-read, single-cell, spatial, multi-omic, proteomic, imaging, biobank, and electronic health record data.
- Variant interpretation; genotype-phenotype relationships; and population, comparative, structural, functional, and evolutionary genomics.
- Knowledge representation, causal and network modeling, data integration, visualization, and scalable software or cloud-enabled systems.
Experimental Genetics and Genomics
We seek experimental investigators who use innovative systems and technologies to elucidate biological mechanisms in health and disease and translate discovery toward diagnosis or therapy. Areas of interest include, but are not limited to:
- Genetic, epigenetic, nucleomic, RNA, protein, metabolic, cellular, developmental, or systems mechanisms in health and disease.
- Human genetics integrated with model organisms, organoids, patient-derived systems, induced pluripotent stem cells, transdifferentiated cells, and other innovative platforms.
- Functional genomics, single-cell and spatial biology, genome and epigenome engineering, synthetic biology, quantitative phenotyping, and technology development.
- Mechanism-driven therapeutic discovery, including gene, RNA, cell, small-molecule, and other precision approaches.
Candidates who connect computation and experiment, or who create platforms that enable such integration, are especially encouraged to apply.
About the Department of Molecular and Human Genetics and Baylor College of Medicine
The Department of Molecular and Human Genetics at Baylor College of Medicine has sustained national leadership in genetics research, reporting the highest number of NIH grants among genetics departments at U.S. medical schools and average annual NIH funding approaching $75 million over the past decade. The Department includes more than 70 primary research faculty whose work spans computational genetics, bioinformatics, functional genomics, genome structure and function, disease mechanisms, model systems, and therapeutic development.
The Department brings physicians, experimental scientists, quantitative researchers, clinical laboratories, and trainees into a shared genetics and genomics mission. Research programs span genome sequencing and interpretation, computational and integrative biomedicine, model-organism and precision disease modeling, neurogenetics, cancer, aging, developmental biology, metabolism, genome stability, multiomics diagnostics, gene and genome editing, and clinical investigation. Departmental programs participate in major NIH and industry consortia and support work from fundamental mechanism to diagnostic innovation, preclinical development, and clinical research.
Faculty benefit from a deeply integrated research environment that includes the Human Genome Sequencing Center; the Bioinformatics Research Laboratory; the Computational and Integrative Biomedical Research Center; Baylor Genetics; the Medical Genetics Multiomics Laboratory; the Undiagnosed Diseases Center; the Center for Precision Medicine Models; the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute; the Dan L Duncan Comprehensive Cancer Center; and major programs in neurogenetics, aging, cancer, skeletal biology, genome editing, rare disease, and clinical research.
The Department has exceptional capabilities in large-scale and clinical-grade genome sequencing, long-read sequencing, multi-omic analysis, software engineering, computational modeling, cross-species genetics, deeply phenotyped human cohorts, patient-derived systems, and mouse, Drosophila, yeast, bacterial, cellular, induced pluripotent stem cell, and organoid models. Its translational infrastructure supports diagnostic innovation, target discovery, preclinical studies, technology transfer, and clinical investigation.
Candidates will join a highly collaborative scientific community with potential partners across Baylor College of Medicine, Texas Children’s Hospital, the Texas Medical Center, Rice University, The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, and the University of Houston. The Department also supports outstanding Genetics and Genomics Ph.D. training, quantitative and interdisciplinary graduate programs, postdoctoral training, medical genetics residencies, and clinical laboratory fellowships.
Qualifications and Expectations
- A Ph.D., M.D., or equivalent doctoral degree.
- A record of original, rigorous, and important scholarship appropriate to career stage.
- A clear vision for an independent, externally funded research program.
- A collaborative approach and the ability to build productive bridges across disciplines, data types, model systems, and clinical domains.
- A commitment to excellence in mentorship and education.
- Professionalism and alignment with Baylor College of Medicine’s values of Respect, Integrity, Innovation, Teamwork, and Excellence.
Appointment and Support
Appointments will be made at the Assistant, Associate, or Full Professor level, commensurate with experience and accomplishments. Baylor College of Medicine and the Department offer competitive recruitment packages and resources to launch or expand an outstanding research program. Qualified candidates may also be eligible for recruitment support through the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas. Additional opportunities may emerge through the Dementia Prevention and Research Institute of Texas.
Application Instructions
Applicants should submit one PDF containing:
- A curriculum vitae.
- A two-page statement summarizing major accomplishments and the vision and priorities for the applicant’s future research program.
Email the application to mhgfacultyrecruits@bcm.edu. Applicants should arrange for three letters of reference to be sent directly by the recommenders to the same address. Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis until the positions are filled.
Learn more: bcm.edu/genetics
As part of the recruitment process, Baylor College of Medicine may conduct reference and background checks, including verification of credentials and degrees and review of professional-misconduct history.

title: Our publishing models
raw_text:
Our publishing models
As part of the ongoing changes in scientific publishing, which aim to increase the readership, reach and impact of published research, many journals are moving from the traditional, subscription-based publishing model to an Open Access (OA) model. Under a gold OA model, an article is made freely available online when published, rather than being behind a paywall. Payment for publication is made by the authors’ institutions or funding bodies, who pay an Article Processing Charge (APC) when the manuscript is accepted.
From January 2021, authors submitting primary research articles* to Nature are able to choose to publish their work either through the traditional subscription publishing route OR gold Open Access.
*Non-primary research articles (e.g. Reviews, Comments, News & Views) should not include original (previously unpublished) research findings and may only contain minimal new supporting data. These non-primary articles are not eligible for gold Open Access and can only be published using the traditional subscription-based publishing route.
Find out more about publishing in Nature.
Authors may need to take specific actions to achieve compliance with funder and institutional open access mandates. If your research is supported by a funder that requires immediate open access (e.g. according to Plan S principles or the NIH public access policy) then you should select the gold OA route, and we will direct you to the compliant route where possible. Because authors warrant under our subscription licensing terms that they haven’t committed to licensing any version of their article under a licence inconsistent with the terms of our agreement – including the applicable embargo period - publication under the subscription model isn’t suitable for authors whose funders require no embargo.

title: Editorial Values Statement
raw_text:
Editorial Values Statement
Editors of the Nature Portfolio believe in the transformational power of science and its potential to drive positive change in the world.
As members of the scientific community, we are committed to supporting the research enterprise by curating, enhancing and disseminating research that is rigorous, reproducible and impactful. We work to promote openness and transparency as well as the highest standards in research culture.
We provide an independent forum for reporting and discussing issues concerning research and the community, and we engage with researchers at all stages of their career to understand their needs and advocate for positive change.
We believe that science should represent everyone. As such, we recognize that it is our responsibility to work towards overcoming inequities and to foster a culture of diversity and inclusion in our communities.

Editorial policies
As part of Nature Portfolio, Nature follows common policies as detailed via the menu on the left that our authors and prospective authors must follow.
In particular, when you submit a manuscript to Nature its content must not significantly overlap with any other papers from you or your co-authors’ groups that are under consideration or in press at other journals, with the exception of conference abstracts. We do, however, support the posting of preprints.
If you submit a related manuscript to any other journals while the submission to Nature is under consideration, you must send us a copy of the related manuscript and details of its progress towards publication. Nature Portfolio journals take publication conduct seriously. We reserve the right to decline publication of a paper even after it has been accepted if it becomes apparent that there are serious problems with the scientific content or violations of our publishing policies.

title: Journalistic Principles
raw_text:
Journalistic Principles
Nature’s journalism: our principles and ethics
Besides the editorial teams that assess research manuscripts for potential publication, Nature maintains an editorially independent magazine section that seeks to inform scientists and the general public by providing news and analysis about important developments in science and science policy. Journalists employed by Nature work independently from the teams assessing primary research, and are also editorially independent of Nature’s publisher, Springer Nature.
Nature’s reporters and editors aim to work to the highest journalistic standards of fairness and objectivity, independence, accuracy and accountability, and integrity.
Fairness and objectivity. We treat sources and readers with decency and without favouritism. We do not shy away from reporting awkward facts, but we aim to do so objectively and in a way that does not violate readers’ trust. For example, we will always give subjects of a story the chance to respond to any criticism. At the same time, we aim to avoid bias and false equivalency; although equal time for differing opinions is common in politics, research is backed by evidence, and not all views are equally based in sound science. Opinion content that we publish will be clearly labelled as such.
Independence. We aim to avoid or mitigate conflicts of interest in all their forms, whether actual (where journalists’ financial or personal relationships could compromise their objectivity) or apparent (where they could give a reasonable outsider grounds to question the objectivity of a journalist). Where a journalist has an actual financial or personal conflict of interest, they will not be allowed to report a story or otherwise influence it. Any apparent conflicts of interest will be disclosed in the published article. Our reporters and editors do not accept financial or other benefits (including gifts, teaching fees, honoraria or speaking fees) if doing so would create a conflict of interest.
Accuracy and accountability. We do not in general send quotes, excerpts of articles or full articles to sources for checking before publication, to avoid undue influence on what we publish. There are rare exceptions to this, for example when an interviewee is in a vulnerable position or when we use quotes in translation. We always expect our journalists to assume full responsibility for the accuracy of what they report. All articles undergo a rigorous fact-checking process initiated by the reporting journalist and supervised by our editors and subeditors. We quote all sources for graphics and pictures, and grant anonymity to quoted sources only to protect them from retaliation or other severe anticipated harm. In these cases, stories will disclose why we granted anonymity. When an error in a published article is identified, we correct and acknowledge it in the location (online or print, or both) where the error appeared as soon as reasonably possible.
Integrity. We do not fabricate or plagiarize words, data or images, nor do we alter the truth of an image or video by substantially changing it. Our journalism is produced by humans. Artificial intelligence tools may be used to assist journalists’ research, but not to produce words or images for final articles.

title: History of Nature
raw_text:
History of Nature
A note on Nature’s archive
Nature’s archive comprises all the content published since the journal’s launch in 1869; it includes some images, articles and language that by twenty-first-century standards are offensive and harmful, including sexist, racist and other discriminatory content. This content does not represent Nature’s current values and would be unacceptable to publish today. We have not sought to suppress it because it is part of the scientific and historical record, and so should remain available for scholars now and in the future. Nature is committed to making the changes necessary to ensure that it learns from its past and creates a publication that champions science for everyone.
1860s
The first issue of Nature was published on 4 November 1869. Many earlier publishing adventures in science had failed dismally, but Nature’s eventual success grew out of the social and scientific conditions under which it was founded — driven by the vision of strong personalities, who forged ahead when the odds seemed against them. Nature, above all, has been a survivor. This it owes to Alexander Macmillan, who tolerated a loss-making venture for three decades; to Norman Lockyer, the first editor; and to a string of influential collaborators and contributors, including biologist Thomas Henry Huxley — one of the heavyweights of Victorian science and a staunch ally of Charles Darwin (he was known as ‘Darwin’s bulldog’).
Brothers Alexander and Daniel Macmillan founded their bookshop and publishing house in Cambridge, UK, in 1843. After Daniel’s death in 1857, Alexander opened a London branch at 23 Henrietta Street, Covent Garden. Macmillan’s headquarters were in Cambridge until 1863, when they moved to 16 Bedford Street in London. The academic standing of the Macmillans in Cambridge (their shop was at the heart of the university city) later helped Alexander to establish contacts with eminent men of science in London. He would host ‘tobacco parliaments’, at which science, art and hot topics of the day, such as Darwinism, would be discussed. This “talk, tobacco and tipple on Thursdays” group, as he described it, fostered friendships among the great scientific educators of the Victorian era, including Huxley and the physicist John Tyndall, who were eager to write for Macmillan. In 1859, Alexander launched Macmillan’s Magazine, the first shilling monthly in England, aiming to unify science, literature and the arts under one banner, with David Masson as the editor. Huxley’s article ‘Time & Life’ was published in the second issue.
Lockyer (pictured) was born in Rugby in Warwickshire on 17 May 1836. A clerk in the UK government’s War Office, he was a keen and talented young amateur astronomer — he was later to co-discover the element helium in the corona of the Sun, using a spectroscope. Lockyer frequently shared a train carriage to London with publisher John Ludlow and author Thomas Hughes, both friends of Macmillan, and they asked him to be the science editor of their proposed weekly, The Reader, which was to cover the arts, literature and science. The Reader, launched in 1863, was in many ways an early forerunner to Nature — 38 people who supplied reviews to The Reader later contributed to Nature. Unfortunately for Lockyer, the paper was commercially disorganized and its poor financial performance meant that — like many publications in the Victorian era — it lasted for only a few years. Image source: Life and Work of Sir Norman Lockyer by T. Mary Lockyer and Winifred L. Lockyer (Macmillan, 1928).
The exact time and place of Macmillan and Lockyer’s first meeting is not known, but the twin topics of science and publishing would have dominated their early conversations. With their shared interests and friends (including poet laureate Alfred Lord Tennyson), they soon became friends themselves, travelling to France together in 1867 after Lockyer’s second nervous breakdown (he had three, the first in 1864). Macmillan commissioned Lockyer to write a book about astronomy. Then, in 1868, he asked Lockyer to act as scientific adviser to his publishing house. This was lucky for Lockyer, because — despite his best efforts — The Reader had proved editorially and financially troublesome, and his career path at the War Office was uncertain.
Lockyer approached Macmillan in early 1869 with plans for a new scientific journal. Lockyer’s early career was at its zenith: he had co-discovered helium in 1868, which earned him election to the Royal Society the following year. Macmillan and Lockyer’s relationship was mutually beneficial: scientific publishing was prominent in Macmillan’s long-term publishing strategy and, if he were to undertake the risky venture of a new scientific journal, Lockyer was the man to take the helm. As botanist Joseph Hooker pointed out, the record of eminent men of science in publishing was “dismal”. However, Lockyer’s organizational and editorial skills on The Reader had attracted praise — for example, Hughes wrote to Huxley: “Lockyer ... knows the machinery ... has the science already in the right grooves, and is not above taking advice.” Competition loomed from the new science weeklies Popular Science Review and Scientific Opinion.
It’s not clear who proposed the title Nature, but a letter in July 1869 from Huxley to Lockyer reveals that Macmillan made the final decision: “Macmillan told me yesterday that he had nailed his colours to the mast — and was going in for ‘Nature’, pure and simple. I am inclined to think it is the best plan on the whole.” In a letter to Lockyer, the mathematician James Joseph Sylvester enthused wildly on the potential: “What a glorious title, Nature — a veritable stroke of genius to have hit upon. It is more than Cosmos, more than Universe. It includes the seen as well as the unseen, the possible as well as the actual. Nature and Nature’s God, mind and matter. I am lost in admiration of the effulgent blaze of ideas it calls forth.”
Early issues of Nature (pictured) included what today would be called a mission statement. “First, to place before the general public the grand results of scientific work and scientific discovery, and to urge the claims of science to a more general recognition in education and in daily life; and secondly, to aid scientific men themselves, by giving early information of all advances made in any branch of natural knowledge throughout the world.” The journal carries essentially the same message to this day. These bold assertions were not unique to Nature; the prospectuses of both Scientific Opinion and The Reader made similar rallying cries for men of science and lay people to have at their disposal a specialized organ for communicating science to scientists and the masses. You can access the first issue of Nature here.
1870s
“I am very anxious about Nature. I cannot help feeling that a very little more of something would make it a success.” Macmillan’s 1871 letter to Lockyer reveals that, although Lockyer boasted of 5,000 subscribers and 15,000 readers in 1870 (a circulation in reality not attained even by the end of the century), the future of the fledgling Nature was by no means secure. Macmillan gave it a competitive cover price — at fourpence, it was less than the sixpence charged by most weeklies. Science historian Roy Macleod has estimated that the four pages per issue given over to advertisements in 1869–70 would have accounted for only half the annual costs of producing the magazine, and that there were in fact probably fewer than 200 subscribers in Nature’s first year. At least the potential rival weekly Scientific Opinion had ceased publication in 1870, but Nature was not yet established as a preferred place of scientific communication.
Lockyer wrote 66 editorials from 1869 to 1919; others were composed by subeditors working with a band of more than 100 contributors. Besides scientific articles on topics such as the HMS Challenger oceanic exploration mission, transits of Venus and eclipse expeditions, Nature campaigned hard on issues such as research endowments, scientific reform, the rise of German science and teaching in schools as the education acts laboured through the British government. By 1878, Lockyer seemed to be satisfied that, through Nature, awareness of the right questions was on the rise as a result of the growing space given to such matters by the daily press: “Questions concerning scientific discovery, research and teaching, have now a much more direct interest to the public than they formerly possessed.”
The 1870s were a decade of scientific advances, and the pages of Nature celebrated many of the most important, such as the inventions of the typewriter and bathometer, and included notes on the telephone, duplex telegraphy and the application of electricity to lighting. But early Nature also had a less technical readership, as evidenced by correspondence featuring readers’ observations on “ingenuity in a pigeon” and “a carnivorous goose”, as well as discussion of simple and amusing experiments.
Nature’s contributors were usually eminent men of science, often from the upper echelons of Victorian society, but this did not preclude private squabbles from becoming public — indeed, Lockyer seems to have encouraged controversy in the pages of Nature. The year 1873 saw perhaps the most acrimonious exchange, between physicists Peter Guthrie Tait and John Tyndall. Tait’s critique of Tyndall’s pamphlet Principal Forbes and his Biographers led to bitter rivalries in the correspondence columns; these resurfaced with a review of Tyndall’s book The Forms of Water in Clouds and Rivers, Ice, and Glaciers, and spilled over into other journals, newspapers and pamphlets. It was a damaging affair, and Lockyer was privately chastised. Writing to T. H. Huxley, Tyndall bemoaned that: “My notions regarding him [Lockyer] have been too undisguised.” Writing about a different dispute, Joseph Hooker stated that: “My suspicions are strong against Lockyer, of whom I have heard much that I do not like.”
Nature’s early international flavour might well have influenced a host of foreign rivals that appeared in the 1870s and bore the same name. In France, La Nature (pictured) was first published in 1873. Then came the Norwegian Naturen in 1877, also the year in which the Italian La Natura was launched — this even echoed the banner of its English counterpart with “Giornale Illustrato di Cognizioni” (‘illustrated newspaper of cognitions’). There was a Belgian Natura printed in Ghent from 1883 to 1885, and the Dutch geillustreerd maandschrift (‘illustrated monthly book’) Die Natur was published from 1881 to 1894. Beyond Europe, the Mexican La Naturaleza started a second edition in 1887.
Throughout his life, Lockyer experienced nervous exhaustion and bouts of depression. In March 1877, he had his third breakdown, probably due to the pressures of his professional commitments and exacerbated by caring for his ill wife and son. Lockyer’s physician recommended to a Macmillan employee that he should spend some time abroad to recuperate. Alexander Macmillan obliged with a cheque and a note that: “The firm desires your acceptance of it with the love of all the members.” Again, we see Macmillan’s affection and solicitude in taking great care of his editor. Lockyer recovered, but his son Frank died in 1878, and Lockyer’s wife, Winifred, died the next year, leaving Lockyer to care for their seven remaining children.
The journal had been making a loss since the first issue, but only after almost ten years did Alexander Macmillan raise the price from fourpence to sixpence, expanding it to 28 pages. Lockyer opened “what is practically a New Series of Nature” with a bold editorial: “it is because Nature has become more and more widely recognised as the organ of science all the world over that at last we are compelled to enlarge it in order to find space for the stream of communications that week after week come pouring in upon us from all parts.” Picture shows Macmillan’s letter to Lockyer in 1869, detailing 24 pages at fourpence per issue as “quite high enough [a] price”.
1880s
Nature editorials in the 1880s expanded on the strongly political topics of the 1870s and were directed to the politicians of the day with increasing conviction. The 1880 Elementary Education Act made school attendance compulsory for all children in England and Wales up to the age of ten. A few months before it passed, Nature appealed to William Harcourt — who would become British home secretary that year — to make the teaching of science a priority in schools: “Those who have the true welfare of our country at heart will use every means to get education in science introduced into all our schools and colleges ... so that in future years rulers and people will be guided ... by the principles of scientific statesmanship.” Other editorials urged a scientific approach to management of the state.
The short letter of 28 October 1880 by Henry Faulds entitled ‘On the Skin-furrows of the Hand’ was perhaps one of the earliest significant and original contributions to science published in Nature: “When bloody finger-marks or impressions on clay, glass &c., exist, they may lead to the scientific identification of criminals.” Fingerprint patterns (pictured) were described scientifically in 1823, but Faulds was the first to detail how “skin-furrows” could be used in identification, ethnography, studies of heredity and medical–legal investigations — essentially sketching out the basis of what was to become forensic science. Just a month later, William Hershel (grandson of the discoverer of Uranus) published a letter in Nature claiming previous use of the identification technique in India: “I have been taking sign-manuals by means of finger-marks for now more than twenty years.” Argument raged between the two, with statistician Francis Galton weighing in, but Faulds’s letter clearly documents the advantages of having “a nature-copy of the for-ever-unchangeable finger-furrows of important criminals”.
The 1880s were a time of career milestones for Lockyer. In the late 1870s, he had been appointed head of the Solar Physics Observatory in South Kensington, London, a post that awarded him £500 in research expenses. Following this, in 1881, Lockyer was made a lecturer at the nearby Normal School of Science (later to become the Royal College of Science, and then part of Imperial College) and awarded a salary of £750 per year. He was made professor of astronomical physics in 1887. Friendships bloomed with notable figures from outside science, including Alfred Lord Tennyson. Tennyson, who was particularly interested in astronomy, later wrote a note to Lockyer: “In my anthropological spectrum, you are coloured like a first rate star of science.” In 1910, Lockyer wrote a book called Tennyson as a Student and Poet of Nature.
Early Nature carried a strong international flavour and covered science from around the globe. Following the cataclysmic eruption of the volcano Krakatau (pictured) in what is now Indonesia on 26–27 August 1883, Nature appealed to its worldwide audience to send observations that would be forwarded to the Royal Society Krakatoa Committee.
For most of the nineteenth century, there was very little in the way of a career structure in science in Britain. There were few universities, and therefore few professional posts to fill, and scholars concentrated on classic subjects, such as ancient Greek, rather than science. But by the late 1880s, enough had changed for Nature to proclaim that the scientific movement had at last been truly born, thanks to the part played by great scientific educators of the day such as John Tyndall (pictured). An editorial celebrating his achievements declared of the English people: “It has been no easy task to convince them that a new era — that of science — was dawning ... that our industrial position can only be maintained if armies of well-equipped followers are ready to seize the ground which the leaders win.”
1890s
In the 1890s, Nature saw many events that consolidated its position as an increasingly successful scientific publication. At last, it was breaking into profit. The journal pressed on with its editorial campaigns on education, following with utmost scrutiny the implementation of the British Technical Instruction Act and supporting a single University of London on the grounds that “a duplication of Universities in London would be a misfortune of the first magnitude, dividing resources and diverting energies into channels that would lead to many undesirable results”. Overall, the 1890s were to be celebrated: the journal had survived for 25 years and attracted high-quality submissions. These included work that foreshadowed the discovery of the electron and powered flight, and a four-page exclusive on X-rays. Lockyer’s influence grew and, although he lost favour with some scientists, a former laboratory assistant — and future editor — joined the team.
An article in the Nature issue of 23 July 1891, entitled ‘Experimental Researches on Mechanical Flight’, was supplied by US physicist Samuel P. Langley, based on an address he had given to the Paris Academy of Sciences earlier that month. More than ten years before the brothers Orville and Wilbur Wright made their famous flight — the first controlled, sustained flight in a powered, heavier-than-air craft — the author modestly provided experimental proof that wings or blades could generate sufficient lift by altering the angle of inclined planes over streams of air. Image shows an early aeroplane, courtesy of NASA.
In 1889, the Technical Instruction Act had come into force, setting out how science should be taught in schools. Nature kept a close eye on its implementation, lamenting in an editorial in February 1890 that — “great advance as it was on its predecessors — [it] fell a victim to the fears of one party and the lukewarmness of another”. Nature continued to address the politics of education: in the same article, it mocked the “so-called ‘educationists’ (a newly introduced word with an ominous ring to it)” for not tackling the core issue of how the few precious years of education should best be utilized. But an editorial in April 1890 gave praise to attempts to “link the instruction of the school to the life in the home”, and another on the education fees debate set out the journal’s stall in June 1891: “We want a free road kept open to the University.”
Richard Arman Gregory (pictured) joined Nature in 1893 as an assistant editor, after a brief stint as Lockyer’s assistant at his South Kensington laboratory. The early 1890s were the only time when Gregory was an active researcher: his work was mainly routine, measuring the positions and spectra of sunspots and solar prominences, and he does not appear as co-author on any published papers of original research during his time at South Kensington. Nevertheless, Gregory was a skilled astronomer and teacher, and he resigned from the laboratory in 1893 to pursue work as a journalist and lecturer; he had already taken the post of extension lecturer at the University of Oxford, which he occupied from 1890 to 1895. Lockyer saw in Gregory a man of sharp intellect, and duly recommended to Alexander Macmillan his appointment as assistant editor. Gregory later became an editor for Macmillan’s science books, and oversaw the publication of more than 200 titles until his retirement in 1938.
In November 1894, Nature celebrated its 25th anniversary with a splendid dinner at the Savoy Hotel in London, attended by George Macmillan, son of Alexander, and Frederick and Maurice Macmillan, sons of Daniel Macmillan. T. H. Huxley led the toasts: “Better to be an architect building a house under the dual control of a husband and wife ... than an editor.” Huxley also contributed to the anniversary issue, including a hint of self-mockery at his own choice of opening article in the very first issue, a translation of the rhapsody ‘Die Natur’ by Goethe, which he doubted would have been understood by “more than half-a-dozen of the readers”.
Archive sources reveal how, more than 25 years after its first issue, Nature was beginning to command a position as the preferred place for researchers to reveal their findings. William Crookes, an English physicist and chemist who had discovered the element thallium in 1861, sent an account of the spectrum of helium to Lockyer in 1895, soon after Scottish chemist William Ramsey had isolated the gas terrestrially (27 years after Lockyer had detected it in the Sun’s corona). Crookes’s letter reveals how Nature had a higher standing than its weekly competitor Chemical News, which Crookes had founded in 1859: “It will appear in the Chemical News on Friday, but my circulation is not to the same class of researchers as that of ‘Nature’, and having taken a great deal of trouble about it I want the results to get to the right people.”
Nature was at last attracting serious scientific papers. On 23 January 1896, the journal carried the first description of X-rays in English, in two lavish articles spread over four pages, including three photographs. The first article was written by the rays’ discoverer, Wilhelm Röntgen. The second is an early forerunner of today’s News & Views section — a brief commentary by a different author on the same subject, to add context to the discovery.
At the close of the nineteenth century — three decades after the journal’s launch — Macmillan’s ledgers finally showed that Nature was no longer making a loss. George Craik, Macmillan’s ‘chancellor of the exchequer’, wrote to Lockyer: “I am glad that your diligence and tenacity has been at last rewarded by money besides all the honour that Nature has brought you. We have waited many years.” The last line is particularly poignant, because Alexander Macmillan, the man who had founded and stood by the journal, had retired in the early 1890s; it is to him that Nature owes its position today. Lockyer — who was knighted in 1897 — made the magazine a success in scientific terms, but without the patience and deep pockets of the publisher, Nature would not exist.
1900s
The editorial ‘The New Century’ heralds an era in which electricity and the “space-annihilating power” of mechanics have made Earth a “tiny satellite”, whereby an idea can be spread “as soon as it has emerged from the brain of the Thinker”. Indeed, true powered flight and the basis for television would arrive during this decade. However, there was little in the way of real celebration in the new century’s editorials. Britain’s global power and influence were in decline, and its industrial power was waning by comparison with that of Germany and the United States. More resources for education, closer ties between science and industry, and the application of the scientific method to government were consistent themes of Nature’s prescribed medicine for the ills of the British Empire: “The attempts to put our house in order will be made on scientific lines.”
Lockyer resigned from the Royal College of Science in 1902, remarried in 1903 and was elected president of the British Association for the Advancement of Science the same year. In his inaugural address to the association, he pointed out that the Royal Navy had received £21.5 million for a five-year building programme in 1888. By contrast, British universities received £156,000 per year between them in the early 1900s — a paltry amount when compared with, for example, the equivalent of £169,000 allocated to the University of Berlin alone by the German government a decade earlier. Lockyer’s address, widely commented upon and quoted in speeches and in the press, was published as a pamphlet by Macmillan, titled On the Influence of Brain-Power on History. An editorial on similar lines in Nature noted: “It may be long in this slow-moving country before the influence of Brain-power on history is recognised as fully as the influence of Sea-power ... but undoubtedly it will be bad for our future if much more time is lost.”
Chemists William Ramsay (pictured) and Frederick Soddy reported in the 13 August 1903 issue of Nature that helium gas is produced by the radioactive decay of radium. Working at University College London, they had unknowingly discovered the spontaneous transmutation of elements, but candidly offered no explanation for the effect: “The spectrum [of helium] was apparently a new one, probably that of the emanation, but this has not yet been completely examined, and we hope to publish further details shortly.” The spectrum was that of a previously unrecognized isotope of helium, but it would be another ten years before Soddy coined the term ‘isotope’ in the pages of Nature. He would go on to win the 1921 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on radioactive elements and isotopes.
Following enthusiastic reviews of scientific lectures for women in previous decades, Nature continued with its then forward-looking attitude towards the role of women in science in a book review in 1904. Eleanor Anne Ormerod was an entomologist who applied her skills to agriculture and helped to found the field of economic entomology. The review of her biography throws much praise on her abilities, comparing her to pioneering astronomer Caroline Herschel and mathematician Mary Somerville, and hints that her work might have influenced London’s Linnean Society to open its doors to women — papers submitted by women were previously read to a male-only audience. Sadly, much as Ormerod’s achievements are lauded, the same cannot be said for the book, which Nature summarizes as “one the most glaring instances we have ever seen (and we have seen sufficiently bad ones before) of how not to edit a biography”.
By 1905, Nature had espoused the importance of science education and lobbied for the application of the scientific method to government for decades. The British Science Guild was launched to formalize such activities, and Lockyer was a principal instigator. The 12 October 1905 issue of Nature carried news of the first meeting of the guild, which would push for “making the scientific spirit a national characteristic which shall inspire progress and determine the policy in affairs of all kinds”. The organization was associated with no political party and its membership was open to men and women. Lockyer took the position of chair of the committees, because many members were Nature contributors and many others were close friends, including Joseph Hooker, geologist Archibald Geikie, Alfred Lord Tennyson and zoologist Ray Lankester. Lockyer’s wife, Mary, was honorary assistant treasurer.
The development of the telegraph in the previous century had been a revelation. Now, the race was on to transmit images.
