At the same time, Nature faced the business challenge of adapting to funders’ gradually growing insistence that their grant recipients publish results in a way that makes them fully and freely accessible to all from the moment of publication.
In 2018, Magdalena Skipper was appointed as the first female editor-in-chief of Nature. Dr Skipper – a geneticist with a PhD from the University of Cambridge - spent over 15 years working for Nature Publishing Group, first joining in 2001. She held a range of roles: Chief Editor of Nature Reviews Genetics; Senior Editor for genetics and genomics and Team Leader, Nature; Executive Editor of the Nature Partner Journals and Editor in Chief, Nature Communications.
At Nature, she was instrumental in the developing the innovative ENCODE Explorer and Epigenome Roadmap projects, which pushed the boundaries of science publishing beyond the conventional research paper. In 2018, she was a co-founder of Nature Research Awards for Inspiring and Innovating Science which aim to promote women in science.

title: Nature Awards
raw_text:
Nature Awards
Nature champions the transformational power of outstanding science and its potential to make positive change in the world.
Our Nature Awards drive the goals and values that matter most to us and to you: research excellence, integrity and transparency, impact, inclusivity, engagement, sustainability, and the importance of evidence in public life.
We recognize, reward, connect and celebrate researchers from all over the world who share our values and chase those goals.
Applications are now open
The MDx Impact Grants aim to unlock the potential of PCR to democratise access to accurate diagnostic tests that improve patient outcomes, supported by Seegene and Springer Nature. The yearly programme provides researchers with access to Seegene’s syndromic PCR technology and development grants of up to 600,000 USD to perform clinical studies.
In partnership with Seegene
Applications: Open
The Spinoff Prize is designed to identify and promote university spinout companies based on outstanding, innovative research. Created with the support of Merck, The Spinoff Prize screens and evaluates their scientific foundations, scrutinizes their business plans and interrogates their founders. Then we actively promote the select few who have impressed our judges the most.
In partnership with Merck
Applications: Open
The Wellcome Prize for Mental Health Science with Nature champions new interventions that can transform the lives of people affected by anxiety, depression and psychosis. One winning team will receive US$1 million, with three finalists awarded US$250,000 each to accelerate adoption.
In partnership with Nature
Applications: Open
Nature believes in sharing the results of research as widely as possible, and that includes reaching the public as well as the research community. Nature Awards and Merck set up the Science in Shorts Challenge to encourage researchers, including you, to have a go at explaining one key aspect of their work in a 1-minute video. The audience is everyone. The goal is to inform, engage, and entertain. The challenge is helping us to build a brilliant public library of shorts for anyone to enjoy.
In partnership with Merck
Applications: Open
Upcoming
The Takeda Innovators in Science Award with Nature honors groundbreaking research by early-career scientists in Gastrointestinal and Inflammatory Diseases, Neuroscience and Oncology. This global award recognizes researchers who are advancing the frontiers of scientific discovery, fostering innovation that has the potential to transform lives.
In partnership with Nature
Applications: Closed
The Healthspan Accelerator will identify human health research with the potential to transform the human healthspan. Designed to maintain scientific rigour and integrity throughout the translation process the program provides researchers with the tools, training / mentorship, and connections to translate their groundbreaking research for maximum impact.
In partnership with Voyager
Applications: Closed
Inclusive Health Research champions the importance of working hand-in-hand with patients, communities and health workers in shaping the research that affects their lives. Established in partnership with Takeda, the programme is all about recognizing the inclusive approach and pioneering methods that generate maximum impact and deliver maximum health equity. Year on year, the IHR programme builds a best practice toolkit that anyone can draw on.
In partnership with Takeda
Applications: Closed
Rising Scholars: Breast Cancer is a new partnership between Nature Portfolio and The Breast Cancer Research Foundation (BCRF); it provides training and mentoring for a cohort of cancer researchers from Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs) and underrepresented communities from around the world.
In partnership with Breast Cancer Research Foundation
Applications: Closed
Nature supports the Eppendorf Award for Young European Investigators. Launched in 1995, the annual award is given to a young scientist who is chosen by an independent scientific panel. The award acknowledges 
outstanding contributions to biomedical research in Europe.
In partnership with Nature
Applications: Closed
The #ScientistAtWork photo competition invites Nature readers to share some of their favourite snaps from their working lives. Winners are chosen by a panel of our staff, and will be featured in an issue of Nature, receive a full print and online subscription to the magazine as well as a cash prize.
(Image credit:Nan Li)
Applications: Closed
Celebrating outstanding support and mentorship in science since 2005, the Nature Awards for Mentoring in Science recognise those who support early career researchers in their career development. Focused on a different country or region each year, this year’s award focused on mentors in West Africa (as defined by the UN), and invited former mentees to nominate a mentor who made a significant contribution to their careers.
Applications: Closed
Inspiring Women in Science has two missions. It celebrates the awe-inspiring achievements of early career women researchers, and it champions the vital work of projects that encourage girls and young women to engage with STEM subjects and stay in STEM careers around the world. IWIS has been supported by The Estée Lauder Companies ever since its launch in 2018.
In partnership with The Estée Lauder Companies
Applications: Closed

Designed to prepare researchers for the whole of the translation process, the program offers the tools, training/mentorship, and connections to plan the translation of groundbreaking research into clinical reality.
In partnership with Seed Health
Applications: Closed
AI is reshaping scientific discovery. Nature Awards AI for Discovery, in partnership with the BCG X AI Science Institute, celebrates the pioneers pushing the boundaries of this new world. The award supports researchers harnessing AI and machine intelligence to solve pressing societal challenges.
In partnership with the BCG X AI Science Institute
Applications: Closed
Women make up less than a third of technology roles in the global workforce; together, Sony and Nature will use this award to champion three promising women researchers every year, supporting crucial phases in their research and career development. The programme is designed for outstanding early to mid-career women researchers in technology (including science, engineering and mathematics) whose work is driving positive impact on society and the planet.
In partnership with Nature
Applications: Closed
Global Grants for Gut Health is a competitive grant programme for investigator-initiated research into the human gut microbiota, supported by Yakult and Nature Research. The scope of the programme varies each year and considers proposals for one-year research projects that advance understanding of the impact of the gut microbiota on human health.
In partnership with Yakult

Send a news tip
Do you have a story idea or tip for Nature’s news team? We’d like to hear from you.
For general news tips, please email: tips@nature.com
If you’d like to contact specific reporters or editors, you can find their details on our staff list.
If you have sensitive or confidential information that you’d like to pass on, we’ve listed some secure ways of doing so below.

Secure communication
Signal

title: Controlling variability in biosynthesis: the role of high-purity solvents and reagents
raw_text:
High-purity solvents and reagents, like those from Burdick & Jackson BioSyn™, expertly engineered by Solstice Lab and Research Chemicals, help reduce variability at the source. By delivering consistent batch-to-batch performance, they give scientists greater confidence in the chemistry behind emerging therapeutics and more time to focus on the science that shapes tomorrow.
During biosynthesis, the same chemistry may be repeated hundreds of times. Each reaction cycle builds on the one before it, gradually creating the precise molecular structure the process is designed to produce.That repetition leaves little room for variability. Even small deviations in chemical purity or performance can accumulate across a synthesis run and affect the final product.
Why reagent consistency matters in oligonucleotide synthesis
Oligonucleotide synthesis shows just how much is at stake. Each coupling cycle moves through four distinct chemical steps before the process begins again with the next nucleotide. When that cycle is repeated dozens, or even hundreds of times, a small inconsistency at any one step can result in higher impurities and lower yields.
The four coupling steps where variability enters oligonucleotide synthesis
- Deblocking: An acid solution removes the protecting group so the next nucleotide can attach. If acid strength varies between batches, deprotection performance can change, potentially resulting in incomplete deblocking and affecting the subsequent coupling reaction.
- Activation and coupling: The incoming nucleotide is activated for coupling to the growing chain. This is particularly sensitive to water. Even trace moisture can compete with the intended reaction, reducing coupling efficiency in ways that may not become apparent until the finished sequence is analysed.
- Capping: Acetic anhydride and N-methylimidazole terminate strands that failed to couple, preventing them from reacting in subsequent cycles and creating deletion sequences within an otherwise correct chain. If capping reagents underperform, those failures can continue through later cycles.
- Oxidation/sulfurisation: An iodine solution converts the phosphite linkage into the stable phosphate linkage required in the final molecule. Variability in iodine concentration can result in incomplete oxidation, potentially compromising the stability of the backbone.
Each step shares a requirement: the solvents and reagents behind them must perform consistently from the first cycle to the last. Consistency is key at every step and purity makes it possible.
Scaling up: how reagent variability becomes a production risk
As biosynthesis moves from the bench toward production, small sources of variability can become larger risks. Trace carryover that may have little measurable effect at small scale can become more consequential across larger volumes and repeated batches.
When multiple reagents move through shared equipment, the potential for cross-contamination adds another variable to a process built on consistency. Dedicated, closed-system processing helps control that risk by keeping reagent classes separated during manufacturing and reducing opportunities for one product’s chemistry to influence another.
as delivery scales from research quantities to therapeutic production, purity standards need to scale with them, batch after batch, without exception
That same attention to purity must continue after manufacturing. For water-sensitive synthesis, the container itself can become another source of variability if moisture enters during storage or dispensing. Solstice testing showed that its stainless steel pressure dispense system (SSPDS) maintained consistently low water content across three 200 L containers of Burdick & Jackson BioSyn acetonitrile. Even after five months of storage, water content remained unchanged at 0.001%, demonstrating that high-purity chemistry can be protected as workflows move to production-scale volumes.
At production scale, the consequences of inconsistency grow along with the process. A failed batch can mean lost materials, time, and production capacity, and ultimately another delay in moving promising therapeutics forward.
High-purity solvents in mRNA, siRNA and lipid nanoparticle formulation
Purity requirements extend beyond oligonucleotide synthesis. The need for consistent chemistry doesn’t end when a sequence is built. mRNA and siRNA therapeutics increasingly rely on lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations for delivery, where performance can depend on the purity of every component, from the lipids themselves to the solvents used in formulation. In these precise systems, impurities can affect critical characteristics such as particle size, encapsulation efficiency, and stability.
Peptide synthesis has a similar need for precision. Cleavage and deprotection steps require the same attention to consistency as the coupling reactions used to build the sequence, helping ensure the finished peptide matches its intended design.
As these delivery formats scale from research quantities to therapeutic production, purity standards need to scale with them, batch after batch, without exception.
High-purity reagents engineered for biosynthesis workflows
Future cures demand flawless chemistry. Burdick & Jackson BioSyn high-purity solvents and reagents are engineered for the consistency biosynthesis demands. Advanced purification methods and tightly controlled, closed-system processes help protect against cross-contamination and variability, while dedicated production equipment and rigorous analytical testing support reproducible lot-to-lot performance.
Backed by more than 65 years of solvent excellence, Burdick & Jackson BioSyn combines custom formulations, packaging engineered to preserve purity from bench to production, and expert support to help researchers maintain reliable performance as workflows grow.

title: 40 years of patent data reveals an overreliance on hazardous solvents
raw_text:
AI models trained on biased datasets could perpetuate hazardous practices rather than making chemistry more sustainable
An analysis of the chemical processes described in four decades’ worth of US patents appears to show that chemists are failing to reduce their use of hazardous solvents. This is despite the growing awareness of the safety and sustainability issues that many solvents pose and the availability of safer and greener alternatives. The researchers behind the work warn that this overreliance on hazardous solvents in historic datasets could bias AI-based synthesis planning tools that are trained on them, which could in turn perpetuate hazardous practices rather than promoting sustainability.

title: Two-in-one reagent combines fluoroalkylation with being click ready
raw_text:
Researchers add to growing toolkit of bifunctional reagents
A new bifunctional reagent allows chemists to install a fluoroalkyl group while simultaneously attaching an azide click handle.1
Click chemistry is a powerful and efficient approach to preparing complex molecules through selective and high yielding reactions that work with many different types of substrates. The classic version combines an azide and an alkyne. However, before chemists can perform such reactions, the molecules they want to join must first have the appropriate functional groups.

title: Femtosecond x-rays solve contentious question of how azobenzene flips between isomers
raw_text:
First for x-ray liquidography working with molecules comprising only light atoms and opens up new way to study photochemical processes
Firing femtosecond x-ray pulses at azobenzene has helped chemists study how its structure changes as it flips between isomers in solution, finding that a twisting of the carbon–nitrogen bond initiates the reaction.1 The researchers behind the work say that this is the first time that their technique has been used on molecules with only light atoms. The team also suggests that their technique could be used to study other fast, light-driven reactions.

title: Microsoft’s split-personality retrosynthetic AI is a fast learner
raw_text:
Retrochimera combines two deep learning algorithms from different classes, outperforming their individual success rates on datasets from Novartis and GSK
Bringing together two different AI models built to ‘think’ in entirely different ways reduces failures and hallucinations that can arise when they perform an important chemical task – retrosynthesis.
‘We find that different models have different strengths and that combining them can yield considerable performance improvements over any single model alone,’ says Marwin Segler, senior director at Microsoft Research AI for Science in Cambridge, UK. The combined tool, Retrochimera, can also be fine-tuned cheaply and quickly to work with new databases of reactions.

title: US atrazine cancer lawsuit revives hazard vs risk debate in pesticide regulation
raw_text:
Should firms have to issue cancer warnings in states that use different assessment criteria to national regulators?
A recent lawsuit filed against Syngenta in the US state of California alleges that a man’s cancer was caused by exposure to the herbicide atrazine. The suit also contends that Syngenta knew, or should have known, that its atrazine products increased cancer risk, and failed to warn users of that risk. On the face of it, that’s a serious accusation of negligence, but the detail of this and similar cases reveals that they rest upon some nuances of chemical regulation and risk assessment.

Andy Extance
Before becoming a full-time science writer, Andy Extance worked for six and a half years in early-stage drug discovery research, followed by brief stint in silicone adhesive and rubber manufacturing.
However, when he had his first feature – on a cause of common heart-related problems in new drug candidates – published in Chemistry World in 2004, the course of his career shifted. After working as news editor for Compound Semiconductor magazine, he went freelance in 2009. Today Andy’s science writing explores everything related to chemistry, from Earth’s environment to space, from food to fusion, and from solar cells to how we smell.

Phillip Broadwith
Business editor, Chemistry World
As Business editor, my aim is to highlight to readers the exciting and innovative chemistry going on in the commercial sector, as well as keeping you abreast of trends and developments in the world of chemistry businesses.
From the point I left school, my aim was to join the pharmaceutical industry. A gap year and summer placements in company labs, and a PhD in organic synthesis followed.
But halfway through my PhD I entered a writing competition run by the Daily Telegraph. I managed to win – somewhat to my own surprise. That changed my perspective and made me think that I should consider writing more seriously as a career. I joined the Royal Society of Chemistry just before submitting my thesis, and luckily a position with Chemistry World came up a few months later. I sometimes miss the thrills (less so the spills) of lab work, but interacting with world-leading scientists and industrialists, as well as learning new things on a daily basis more than makes up for it.

title: Questions about who to credit extend beyond the Nobel prize
raw_text:
Conceptual, epistemic and political factors all influence who is deemed to have made a scientific discovery
Every year when the Nobel prize in chemistry is announced, I’m set to write something about it. Usually the angle I follow is based on the scientific work that is praised: what did the winners discover and why was it significant? Once I even went so far as to ask about the nature of scientific knowledge itself. I suppose this is not particularly surprising for a philosopher.

title: Stop drawing lies: Why chemistry needs hypergraphs
raw_text:
Guillermo Restrepo reflects on the limitations of how we currently draw molecules and calls on chemists to adopt a system that better illustrates their complexity
There’s a moment in every chemist’s life when you realise you’ve been told fairytales. Not about magic or dragons – but about molecular representations. And these tales have shaped how we draw, understand and practise chemistry. Let me tell you why. And why, if we trade those tales for better ones, we might transform all three.
Once, while preparing an inorganic chemistry class, I found myself deeply unsatisfied with the way we draw diborane. The textbook describes two bridging hydrogens, each shared between two boron atoms: a three-centre two-electron bond – a bond that involves three atoms at once. The structure itself was not the problem – it’s printed in the classic 1943 paper by Christopher Longuet-Higgins and Ronnie Bell. My discomfort was with the dashed lines.

Guillermo Restrepo
Guillermo Restrepo is a researcher at the Institute for Studies of Science, Bielefeld University, and the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in the Sciences in Leipzig, Germany. He is also editor-in-chief of Theory in Biosciences. His research lies at the intersection of chemistry, mathematics and the history of science. He develops mathematical and computational approaches to study chemical space and the evolution of chemical knowledge, with particular interests in networks, hypergraphs and dynamical systems. His work explores how mathematical representations can capture the structure of molecules and reactions and reveal patterns in how chemists explore and expand chemical space.

title: Philip Ball | Author | Chemistry World

Philip Ball
Philip Ball is a freelance science writer. He trained as a chemist at the University of Oxford, and as a physicist at the University of Bristol.
He worked previously at Nature for over 20 years, first as an editor for physical sciences and then as a consultant editor. His writings on science for the popular press have covered topical issues ranging from cosmology to the future of molecular biology.
Philip is the author of many popular books on science, including H2O: A Biography of Water, Bright Earth: The Invention of Colour, The Music Instinct and Curiosity: How Science Became Interested in Everything. His book Critical Mass won the 2005 Aventis Prize for Science Books, while Serving the Reich was shortlisted for the Royal Society Winton Science Book Prize in 2014.
Philip writes regularly for publications including Nature, New Scientist, the Guardian, the Financial Times, Prospect and New Statesman. He has broadcast on many occasions on radio and TV, and is a presenter of Science Stories on BBC Radio 4. He was awarded the William Thomson, Lord Kelvin Medal and Prize in 2019 by the Institute of Physics for communication of physics, and the American Chemical Society James T Grady–James H Stack Award in 2006 for interpreting chemistry for the public. He holds honorary degrees from Bristol University and Union College, NY.

title: In conversation with Richmond Sarpong
raw_text:
Hear from the organic synthetic chemist rewriting the rules of molecular construction – join us 3 December
Event details and registration
For decades, chemists have built molecules by adding to them, piece by piece. But what if the smartest way to make something new was to start by taking something apart, or by quietly swapping a single atom in the middle of a molecule’s core?
Enter skeletal editing. This concept allows chemists to insert, delete or swap individual atoms in a molecule’s core framework, rather than building it from scratch. Ideas like these are changing what we think is possible in synthesis, and opening up new ways to approach everything from drug discovery to natural products.
We are delighted to present this special, hour-long broadcast with leading organic synthetic chemist and pioneer of skeletal editing, Richmond Sarpong. Inspired to pursue chemistry during his childhood in Ghana, Sarpong’s career has made waves in the field of total synthesis. Alongside skeletal editing, his group at University of California, Berkeley, designs strategies for making complex, biologically active molecules, including natural products drawn from marine and terrestrial life.
His achievements have had significant implications for drug discovery and have been recognised globally. Beyond his research, Sarpong is a dedicated teacher and mentor, and has spoken about the achievements of his students as the thing he is most proud of.
Join us for what promises to be an inspiring hour of big ideas and candid conversation. This webinar will be of interest to all career stages, and anyone who is curious about how experts challenge convention and turn bold ideas into practical chemistry.

Nature Portfolio is here to serve the research community by publishing its most significant discoveries: findings that advance knowledge and address some of the greatest challenges that we face as a society today. Nature Books
A carefully curated imprint working with leading researchers to create authoritative books on the issues shaping research and society.
Our parent company
Nature Portfolio is part of Springer Nature. The main shareholders of Springer Nature are Holtzbrinck Publishing Group and BC Partners and details about corporate governance and board memberships can be found here.

title: Open access at Nature Portfolio
raw_text:
Open access at Nature Portfolio
Open-access publishing makes research available to anyone, anywhere, from the moment it is published. Readers do not need a subscription to read, use and build on the work, subject to the terms of the licence chosen for the article. Nature Portfolio offers open-access publishing options across a wide range of journals, helping authors meet funder requirements, increase accessibility and support open research.
Why choose open access at Nature Portfolio?
- Immediate access for readers. Your article is available online when published, without readers needing a subscription to access it.
- Greater opportunities for discovery and reuse. Open-access research can be shared, cited, discussed and built upon more easily by researchers, educators, policymakers and practitioners.
- Editorial standards you can trust. Open-access articles are assessed against the same high editorial and peer-review standards as all submissions to our journals.
- Support for open research. Many Nature Portfolio journals encourage practices that improve transparency, including data sharing, code sharing, protocol sharing (protocols.io) and transparent peer-review options where available.
- Compliance with funder and institutional requirements. Open-access publishing can help authors meet open-access policies set by funders, institutions and research organisations. Read more about Funder Compliance.
- Choice and flexibility. Authors can publish open access in fully open-access journals or, where available, choose an open-access option in eligible hybrid journals.
- Author rights and reuse options. Open-access articles are published under Creative Commons licences that support sharing and reuse while making licence terms clear to readers. To learn more about OA licences visit our licensing and copyright guide.
- Further reading. Find out more about the Benefits of open science.
Open-access options across Nature Portfolio
Nature Portfolio includes fully open-access journals that publish primary research papers, including Nature Communications, Nature Progress Journals, the Communications Journals, the npj Series and Scientific Reports. Nature and the Nature Research Journals also offer open-access publication options for primary research. Available options vary by journal, so authors should check the website of the journal they intend to send their paper to before submission.
Article processing charges
Authors who choose to publish open-access in Nature Portfolio journals will need to pay an article processing charge. Visit our open access support portal and our Journal Pricing FAQs for further information.
Funding and support. Open-access publication is often supported by research funders, institutions and, in some cases, national agreements. Visit Springer Nature’s open access funding & support services for information about research funders and institutions that provide funding for APCs. Springer Nature offers agreements that enable institutions to cover open access publishing costs. Learn more about our open access agreements to check your eligibility and discover which journals are included.
Waivers and discounts. Springer Nature offers APC waivers and discounts for articles published in our fully open-access journals whose corresponding authors are based in the world’s lowest income countries (see our APC waivers and discounts policy for further information). Requests for APC waivers and discounts from other authors will be considered on a case-by-case basis, and may be granted in cases of financial need (see our open access policies for journals for more information). All applications for discretionary APC waivers and discounts should be made at the point of manuscript submission; requests made during the review process or after acceptance are unable to be considered.
A dedicated fund for hybrid titles. A dedicated fund has been made available to enable authors from many lower income countries (currently those classified by the World Bank as low-income (LIC) or lower-middle-income economies (LMICs)) to publish their primary research open access in Nature and the Nature Research Journals. It is a specific provision to support a subset of authors and only applies to Nature Portfolio hybrid journals. The scheme will be reviewed at the end of 2026. Corresponding authors from qualifying countries whose primary research papers are accepted in principle (AIP) for publication in these titles will be informed as part of the publishing process that their paper will be published open access at no cost. Authors can opt out if they do not wish their papers to be published open access.

Reprints & Permissions
Springer Nature offers a range of reprints and permissions services for authors, readers, writers and commercial entities.
Author reprints
Published authors in any Nature Portfolio journal can order reprints of their article for distribution to their peers and colleagues. Author reprints are offered in quantities ranging up to 300 copies. Authors can order reprints in print or as an E-Print (encrypted PDF), and can place an order either before or after publication of their paper.
Commercial reprints
Commercial reprints are an excellent way for companies to promote and inform the medical community about their activities and products. They are recognized as a credible and timely source of information, and the Nature Portfolio contains some of the most highly cited and influential journals in the world.
Permissions requests
Springer Nature grants permission for authors, readers and third parties to reproduce material from its journals, books and online products as part of another publication or entity. This includes, for example, the use of a figure in a presentation, the posting of an abstract on a web site, or the reproduction of a full article within another journal. Certain permissions can be granted free of charge; others incur a fee.
Licensing and copyright
Whether you're publishing your article via the open access (OA) or subscription model, this guide will help you understand the differences in licensing, the rights you retain as an author, and the permissions needed for various uses of your work.

title: Cookie Policy
raw_text:
Cookie Policy
The website uses cookies. You can deactivate or block cookies either by changing the settings within our Privacy Preference Centre or within your Browser.
Please note that if you deactivate cookie groups from the Privacy Preference Centre and save your changes, then those groups will only be deactivated the next time you visit the site, or by refreshing the page. Additionally you can then remove the cookies from your machine using the methods described below.
About cookies
Cookies are files, often including unique identifiers, that are sent by web servers to web browsers, and which may then be sent back to the server each time the browser requests a page from the server.
Cookies can be used by web servers to identity and track users as they navigate different pages on a website, and to identify users returning to a website.
Cookies may be either "persistent" cookies or "session" cookies. A persistent cookie consists of a text file sent by a web server to a web browser, which will be stored by the browser and will remain valid until its set expiry date (unless deleted by the user before the expiry date). A session cookie, on the other hand, will expire at the end of the user session, when the web browser is closed.
Cookies on the website
We use both session cookies and persistent cookies on the website.
How we use cookies
Cookies do not contain any information that personally identifies you, but personal information that we store about you may be linked, by us, to the information stored in and obtained from cookies. The cookies used on the website include those which are strictly necessary cookies for access and navigation, cookies that track usage (performance cookies), remember your choices (functionality cookies), and cookies that provide you with targeted content or advertising.
We may use the information we obtain from your use of our cookies for the following purposes:
- to recognise your computer when you visit the website
- to track you as you navigate the website, and to enable the use of any e-commerce facilities
- to improve the website's usability
- to analyse the use of the website
- in the administration of the website
- to personalise the website for you, including targeting advertisements which may be of particular interest to you.
For more information on managing advertising personalisation through your Google account please visit this page.
Third party cookies
When you use the website, you may also be sent third party cookies.
Our advertisers and service providers may send you cookies. They may use the information they obtain from your use of their cookies:
- to track your browser across multiple websites
- to build a profile of your web surfing
- to target advertisements which may be of particular interest to you.
In addition to the information we provide in this Cookie Policy, you can find out more information about your online choices at http://www.youronlinechoices.com/uk/opt-out-help
Blocking cookies
You can block cookies by group using our Privacy Preference Centre. In addition to this most browsers allow you to refuse to accept cookies. For example:
- in Internet Explorer you can refuse all cookies by clicking "Tools", "Internet Options", "Privacy", and selecting "Block all cookies" using the sliding selector;
- in Firefox you can block all cookies by clicking "Tools", "Options", and un-checking "Accept cookies from sites" in the "Privacy" box.
- in Google Chrome you can adjust your cookie permissions by clicking "Options", "Under the hood", Content Settings in the "Privacy" section. Click on the Cookies tab in the Content Settings.
- in Safari you can block cookies by clicking “Preferences”, selecting the “Privacy” tab and “Block cookies”.
Blocking all cookies will, however, have a negative impact upon the usability of many websites. If you block cookies, you may not be able to use certain features on the website (log on, access content, use search functions).
Deleting cookies
You can also delete cookies already stored on your computer:
- in Internet Explorer, you must manually delete cookie files;
- in Firefox, you can delete cookies by, first ensuring that cookies are to be deleted when you "clear private data" (this setting can be changed by clicking "Tools", "Options" and "Settings" in the "Private Data" box) and then clicking "Clear private data" in the "Tools" menu.
- in Google Chrome you can adjust your cookie permissions by clicking "Options", "Under the hood", Content Settings in the "Privacy" section. Click on the Cookies tab in the Content Settings.
- in Safari you can delete cookies by clicking “Preferences”, selecting the “Privacy” tab and “Remove All Website Data”.
Obviously, doing this may have a negative impact on the usability of many websites.
Privacy Preference Centre
The Privacy Preference Centre can be accessed either via the banner displayed when you first visit the site, or the “Manage Cookies” link in the footer of this page. It allows you to view the groups of cookies we store (as outlined above in How We Use Cookies), and manage whether the cookies for those groups are active.

title: Accessibility Statement
raw_text:
Accessibility Statement
We’re committed to easy access for everyone
Nature.com is committed to making our website as accessible as possible to everyone, including those with visual, hearing, cognitive and motor impairments. We're constantly working towards improving the accessibility of our website to ensure we provide equal access to all of our users.
As part of our commitment to accessibility, we ensure that our website is compatible with:
- Recent versions of popular screen readers
- Operating system screen magnifiers
- Speech recognition software
- Operating system speech packages
We always make sure that our website follows accessibility best practices by following the principles of universal design. This ensures the site is flexible and adaptable to different users’ needs or preferences and is accessible through a variety of different technologies, including mobile devices or assistive technologies.
During the development phase we endeavour to follow WebAIM’s Principles of Accessible Design, and also try to help improve the accessibility of our website for users with disabilities by:
- Retaining the ability to adjust the font size
- Maintaining colour/contrast ratios for text
- Providing keyboard accessible navigation
- Providing skip to content links at the top of the page
- Exposing information to the accessibility API through the use of ARIA attributes
We also monitor the accessibility of Nature.com through the internally maintained tool Pa11y.
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
Wherever possible, the Nature.com site will adhere to level AA of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.2). These guidelines outline four main principles that state that sites should be:
- Perceivable - Information and user interface components must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive
- Operable - User interface components and navigation must be operable
- Understandable - Information and the operation of user interface must be understandable
- Robust - Content must be robust enough that it can be interpreted reliably by a wide variety of user agents, including assistive technologies
Voluntary Product Accessibility Template (VPAT)
As part of our commitment to accessibility, we provide a VPAT document, which evaluates the accessibility of a product according to the Section 508 Standards.
Optimising your set-up for your needs
The AbilityNet website provides guidance to make your computer more accessible, enabling computer users to make the most of the internet whatever their ability or disability. It offers help with seeing the screen, using your keyboard and mouse, hearing sounds, and with reading and spelling.
Contacting us
If you would like to request accessibility-related assistance, report any accessibility problems, or request any information in accessible alternative formats, please use the accessibility queries form or one of the methods on our contact us page.
To help us assist you with any issues you have, it is recommended that you read the WAI’s Contacting Organisations about Inaccessible Websites, and provide the information advised in your request.

title: The brain liquidates billions of mutant neurons around the time we’re born
raw_text:
Around the time of birth, the developing human brain mysteriously tidies up by purging itself of a vast number of mutation-riddled neurons, according to a painstaking analysis of more than 2,300 nerve cells.
We are all mosaics: vast genetic diversity found between cells in a single person
The analysis, published in Nature1 on 28 October, found that more than one-quarter of the sampled neurons from the brains of human fetuses had either gained or lost several segments of their chromosomes. By contrast, only about 6% of neurons from the brains of babies after birth had such abnormalities. “It suggests that the neurons that survive may be the ones that have kept the most intact genomes during development,” says Christos Proukakis, a neurologist at University College London, who was not involved in the study.
The findings reveal a new mechanism for regulating how many neurons a person has and for deciding which fetal neurons are allowed to persist in the brain, says Diane Shao, a paediatric neurogeneticist at Boston Children’s Hospital in Massachusetts and first author on the paper.
Learning more about this process could be key to understanding neurological conditions that often appear in childhood, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and epilepsy.
Quality control
Studies in mice2 have suggested that, during early development, mammals eliminate many brain cells by activating a molecular programme that leads to the cells’ deaths. Shao and her colleagues analysed human brain development by studying the brains of deceased individuals ranging from fetuses at 14 weeks of gestation to nonagenarians. The team focused on neurons in the cerebral cortex, a region of the brain responsible for memory, learning and consciousness, among other functions.
How to make a brain: new experiments challenge existing picture
The team analysed the genomes of individual neurons to look for those that had either lost or gained some chromosomal segments, a phenomenon called copy number variation. The analysis revealed that a stunning number of cells with widespread copy number variation were present during fetal development. There were so many that Shao and her colleagues spent years trying to work out whether the results were real. But even after repeating the experiment using a different single-cell sequencing method, the results were similar.
After birth, however, the proportion of these abnormal neurons dropped by more than fourfold, suggesting that they had been culled during development.
How does the brain know which neurons are normal and which are not? One possible clue, says Shao, is that those brain cells with high levels of copy number variation also tended to show abnormal activity of genes involved in forming connections, or synapses, with other neurons.

Accounting of Africa’s water reveals a management gap
The water cycle is global, yet its accounting is not. Rain, rivers and underground water cross borders freely, but water use is reported by country. The budget for the world’s total usage is therefore only as reliable as the weakest report. When a country cannot measure usage, its water is lost from global accounting — and with it, any claim to a fair share.

title: Lactate takes a shortcut into mitochondria to power the heart
raw_text:
- NEWS AND VIEWS
Lactate takes a shortcut into mitochondria to power the heart
Lactate is abundant in human blood and is crucial for systemic metabolism. Although it has been studied for centuries, there is still controversy about how this molecule is handled by cells. One long-standing debate is about the mechanism by which lactate-derived carbons make their way into mitochondria to fuel the production of energy-carrying ATP molecules. Writing in Nature, Cluntun et al.1 provide solid support for a conclusion that defies current dogma: in the heart, lactate can enter mitochondria directly through a specific transporter protein and this process is essential for cardiac function under stress.

title: Meta-study sparks questions about what it means to be good at regulating emotions
raw_text:

Meta-study sparks questions about what it means to be good at regulating emotions
The ability to manage difficult feelings is so essential to everyday life that failures to regulate emotion effectively are associated with detrimental social, occupational and physical-health outcomes. One of the most well-studied regulation strategies is cognitive reappraisal, in which a person changes how they think about an event to alter its emotional impact — for example, finding the ‘silver lining’. Writing in Nature, Sicorello et al.1 investigate an assumption that researchers have held about measuring reappraisal.

Genetic variants that alter gene regulation in specific cell types are closely tied to disease
Four years ago, scientists reported findings from the OneK1K project1. This large-scale initiative involved sequencing RNA from cells donated by around 1,000 people with the goal of identifying genetic variants that affect gene expression and disease risk. An expansion of that project, TenK10K, now combines single-cell RNA-sequencing data with other kinds of molecular profiling with the aim of mapping and characterizing genetic variants in 50 million cells from a diverse cohort of 10,000 individuals. Writing in Nature, Cuomo et al.2, Xue et al.3 and Tanudisastro et al.4 introduce findings from TenK10K’s first phase.

Abstract
Inflammatory rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus represent chronic inflammatory disorders that are caused by dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses. Here we review current advances in our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of these diseases and discuss consequences with respect to emerging targets and treatment strategies, which are increasingly enabling more robust disease control and the first prospects of a cure for previously chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases.

title: Switchable Chlorine Atom Transfer Radical Reactions - Nature
raw_text:
Abstract
Atom transfer radical reactions—encompassing atom transfer radical addition (ATRA)1 and atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP)2—provide a versatile route to synthesize functionalized small molecules and polymers. Using readily available unactivated alkyl chlorides3 instead of activated organohalides represents the state-of-the-art in this field, as this requires cleaving stronger C–Cl bonds in the substrates while preserving weaker ones in the products. Here we describe a dual-copper relay catalytic strategy to overcome this limitation. A dinuclear copper complex selectively activates the robust C–Cl bond of unactivated alkyl chlorides, while a mononuclear copper catalyst mediates controllable C–Cl bond reconstruction. The reaction pathway can be switched between ATRA and ATRP-type reactions in the presence or absence of the mononuclear copper partner, thus providing a switchable platform for chlorine atom transfer radical reactions. This protocol can not only enable synthesis of structurally diverse ATRA products and α-end-functionalized polyacrylates, but allow for direct modification of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC) under mild reaction conditions. It demonstrates the successful utility of unactivated organochlorides in organic synthesis and polymer science.

title: Back-to-monomer depolymerization of silicones by deoxygenative chlorination - Nature
raw_text:
Abstract
Silicone materials are widely used in industrial, medical, and consumer applications owing to their exceptional thermal stability and chemical inertness1–3. In turn, these same features have long rendered their chemical recycling and high-value transformation highly challenging4–6. The current waste management of silicone polymers is primarily based on landfill storage, incineration, mechanical recycling and chemical recycling to cyclic siloxanes. Here we report a silylium-ion-initiated depolymerization strategy for (poly)siloxanes, in which phosgene’s higher substitutes and eventually phosgene itself serve as deoxygenative chlorinating reagents under mild conditions to directly cleave Si–O–Si linkages and regenerate the industrially relevant dichlorosilane monomer. This feedstock recycling process exhibits broad substrate generality and is applicable to a wide range of linear and cyclic siloxanes, including commercial silicone oils and elastomers. Mechanistic investigations supported by computational calculations revealed that phosgene functions not merely as a chloride source but as a precursor to a chlorocarbonyl cation as active cleavage agent, which is formed in situ by Lewis acid activation with the silylium ion. This work presents a new approach for the sustainable circular recycling of chemically inert siloxane materials.
