title: Slow-motion electron camera reveals light-driven quantum jumps in graphene
raw_text:
Slow-motion electron camera reveals light-driven quantum jumps in graphene
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Using a new slow-motion electron camera, physicists from Regensburg, Marburg and Jülich revealed how intense electric fields drive electrons in graphene, causing them to jump across energy gaps in a seemingly paradoxical manner. This was made possible by a novel combination of laser technology and electron microscopy.
The electrons' behavior is roughly equivalent to riding an elevator where the floor indicator suddenly jumps from "1," "2," and "3" to "20." You never passed through the 17 floors in between, yet you arrive on the 20th floor. What sounds like an impossible leap is actually possible in the quantum world. Such processes are called Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions. It has long been suspected that these transitions could play an increasingly important role in high-speed semiconductor electronics.
A research team from the University of Regensburg, Philipps-Universität Marburg and the Forschungszentrum Jülich has succeeded in visualizing the ultrafast dynamics of such transitions in the material graphene. The team reports on this achievement in its latest study, published in the journal Nature.
The researchers observed how electrons are accelerated by the electric field of a light pulse and switch between energy bands as they move. In semiconductors and related materials, electrons can only occupy certain energy ranges, known as bands, which are separated by a forbidden energy gap. Typically, electrons remain firmly trapped in their respective bands. However, during a Landau-Zener-Majorana transition, electrons appear to overcome this forbidden zone with ease.
A slow-motion camera for electrons
In order to observe such extremely fast processes, the team developed a novel combination of laser technology and electron microscopy. "If you want to know who has won a race, you have to watch all participants," explains Vincent Eggers, first author of the study. "Likewise, we must observe as many electrons as possible at one time to catch those that undergo a quantum mechanical transition while moving." This is made possible by a so-called photoemission momentum microscope. Unlike a conventional microscope, it does not show magnified images of objects. Instead, it records the energies and states of motion of the electrons and uses them to create a map of their distribution.
The special challenge was to combine electron spectroscopy with strong, extremely fast oscillating light fields that set the electrons in motion in a targeted manner. "Our team worked on this experiment for many years. Now, we can track electrons moving across the entire energy landscape of a solid in real time," says Rupert Huber.
His cooperation partner Ulrich Höfer—one of the pioneers of ultrafast electron spectroscopy—adds, "Being able to observe such a fundamental quantum mechanical process during our first measurement campaign was a very special moment for us—it was also made possible by the samples we used."
The measurements were based on tailor-made, atomically thin carbon layers of the highest purity, which were produced at Forschungszentrum Jülich. "These precision experiments require material that is nearly perfect at the atomic level. This ensures that impurities do not obscure the delicate quantum dynamics of the electrons. Another important factor for the study was the use of 'rotated' graphene, a specialty from Jülich, which allows the quantum dynamics to emerge particularly clearly," emphasizes Stefan Tautz from Forschungszentrum Jülich.
The slow-motion images revealed a surprising result: Under the influence of the strong light fields, the electrons overcome the band gap with a tunneling probability of up to 100%. Landau-Zener-Majorana transitions can occur with a high probability even if the energy states involved are clearly separated from each other. The decisive factor is how fast the electrons approach the band gap. In this respect, these dynamic transitions differ fundamentally from standard quantum mechanical tunneling through a spatial energy barrier.
A panoramic view of the quantum world
The new method can be used to investigate not only fundamental quantum mechanical transitions, but also the processes that limit the targeted control of the electrons. The measurements on graphene already show how interactions with the crystal lattice disrupt the initially orderly movement of the electrons. Such findings are particularly important for the development of future technologies in which electrons are no longer controlled only by electrical voltages, but directly by the extremely fast oscillations of light.
Or as Giacomo Inzani from the University of Regensburg sums it up: "Our experiment opens a panoramic window into the quantum world. Now, we can follow in real time how electrons move through the energy landscape of a material. And this is just the beginning. Our method can be applied to many other quantum materials, opening up completely new possibilities for controlling their electronic properties selectively with light."

title: 2024 solar storm triggered ultrarelativistic electrons inside Earth's 'impenetrable barrier'
raw_text:
2024 solar storm triggered ultrarelativistic electrons inside Earth's 'impenetrable barrier'
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
The Earth is surrounded by an invisible barrier that was thought to prevent highly energetic electrons from reaching closer to our planet. But in 2024, Japan's Arase space probe detected these electrons well inside the barrier. Now, research led by Nagoya University has found evidence that the electrons were accelerated locally rather than infiltrating from outer radiation belts.
The Earth's magnetic field traps energetic charged particles, namely protons and electrons, in two donut-shaped belts called the Van Allen radiation belts. These particles can potentially damage hardware and electronics in spacecraft flying through the belts.
At the inner edge of the second Van Allen belt, at roughly 3 Earth radii from Earth's center, electrons with extremely high energies seem to hit an invisible, impenetrable wall.
This barrier was first discovered in 2014, and its source is not completely understood. One possibility is a phenomenon known as "plasmaspheric hiss": low-frequency radio waves in the Earth's magnetosphere that produce static noise when played through a speaker. Human-made very-low-frequency radio transmissions, used to communicate with undersea submarines, may also help shape this boundary by scattering radiation-belt electrons into Earth's atmosphere.
A superstorm tests the barrier
Under typical conditions, this region of space is devoid of extremely fast-moving electrons. But space weather can be as precarious as what we experience on the planet.
In May 2024, high solar activity unleashed a geomagnetic "superstorm" on Earth. The aurora borealis, or northern lights, appeared in night skies in Hokkaido and in places as far south as Hyogo prefecture.
During and after this superstorm, the Japanese radiation space probe Arase, operated by JAXA, collected data from within the impenetrable barrier.
And sure enough, it recorded a large flux of high-energy electrons moving close to the speed of light. Some electrons had energies exceeding three megaelectronvolts—high enough to go through some satellite shields. The so-called impenetrable barrier seemed to have been broken.
The researchers looked for possible explanations.
"One of the key questions was how these highly energetic electrons appeared inside the barrier," said Yoshizumi Miyoshi, a professor at the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University and the lead author of this study. "Were they transported inward from the outer radiation belt, or were they accelerated locally within this region?"
Evidence points to local acceleration
The first clue came from analyzing electron phase space density (PSD), a quantity that describes how electrons are distributed according to their energies and motion. Using measurements collected during multiple Arase orbits, the researchers examined how PSD varied with distance from Earth while accounting for changes in the electrons' motion.
They found that a distinct local peak in PSD developed near the usual barrier boundary and became stronger over time. Such a growing peak provides evidence that electrons were gaining energy locally, rather than merely being transported inward from the outer radiation belt.
But what gave them this boost? Arase also detected intense electromagnetic waves that repeatedly swept upward in frequency.
"When converted into audio, it sounds like a bird song," Miyoshi said. These chirping waves, called "chorus waves," are natural, low-frequency electromagnetic waves that ripple through the Earth's magnetic field. These waves can transfer energy to electrons when their oscillations match the electrons' spiraling motion around magnetic field lines.
Depleted plasma sustained conditions for acceleration
Their effect was particularly pronounced in May 2024 because the storm had dramatically eroded Earth's plasmasphere, a region filled with relatively cool charged particles. Its outer boundary retreated unusually close to Earth, leaving the region around the previously impenetrable barrier much less densely populated with plasma. This allowed hotter electrons to reach farther inward and generate chorus waves.
Additionally, the depleted plasma density did not recover quickly. "Typically, the plasmasphere recovers on a timescale of about two days," Miyoshi said. "During the May 2024 superstorm, however, it took approximately 4.3 to 4.7 days for the plasma density to recover to more than half of its pre-storm level in the observed region."
This unusually slow recovery allowed the low-density plasma conditions to persist for several days, potentially providing favorable conditions for chorus-wave activity and the continued acceleration of energetic electrons inside the previously impenetrable barrier.
Radiation risks in seemingly protected regions
Miyoshi said these findings, published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters, demonstrate that even regions of near-Earth space previously considered relatively protected from extremely energetic electrons can experience substantial radiation enhancements during severe space weather events.
"This discovery highlights the need to understand and predict how energetic electrons behave under extreme space weather conditions," Miyoshi said. "Such knowledge is important for assessing radiation risks to spacecraft and improving future space weather predictions."
The findings also provide new insights into how the Earth's magnetosphere responds to extreme solar activity, emphasizing the importance of continuous observations of the near-Earth space environment.

title: Against all expectations, researchers control the magnetic core of a single atom
raw_text:
Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have succeeded in controlling the magnetism in the nucleus of a single atom with radio waves. This came as a surprise: until now, physicists believed that this nuclear spin could not be manipulated directly. The discovery could open up new possibilities for storing and reading quantum information. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications.
In metals such as iron and nickel, every atom is slightly magnetic. But inside the atom, different magnetic "compass needles," known in quantum mechanics as spins, are also at work. "By far the strongest magnetism comes from the electrons," says lead researcher Sander Otte. "But in some atoms, the nucleus also carries a spin. That spin is much weaker, but it is also much better shielded from the outside world."
Otte's group studies spins using a converted scanning tunneling microscope. This enables electrical signals to be directed with extreme precision at a single atom. In the past, the researchers mainly focused on the electron spin, which is the easiest to read out. The nuclear spin appeared only indirectly, through the so-called hyperfine interaction. This causes the spins of the nucleus and the electron to become slightly entangled.
Control against expectations
In their latest experiment, main author Hester Vennema and her colleagues sent two different signals to an atom simultaneously: one targeting the electron and one targeting the nucleus. This allowed them to study the influence of each signal independently. To their surprise, they found that they could flip the nuclear spin even when the two spins were largely disentangled.
That result came unexpectedly. "According to our simple understanding, this should not really happen," says Otte. "The nuclear spin should not be sensitive at all to the electrical signals from a scanning tunneling microscope."
Guitar strings
For this research, the team refined an established measurement technique known as double magnetic resonance for use on a single atom. This enabled them to address the magnetism of the atomic nucleus and that of an orbiting electron independently.
In magnetic resonance, the orientation of a spin is altered using a wave signal. According to quantum mechanics, only a limited number of such rotations are possible. As a result, the signal must have exactly the right frequency.
"You can compare it to the strings of a guitar," Vennema explains. "Each possible spin rotation is like a string with its own note. You have to play precisely the right note to make a particular string vibrate. The 'notes' of a nuclear spin are a hundred to a thousand times lower than those of an electron spin."
Secure quantum information
The nuclear spin of atoms is of particular interest for applications in which quantum information needs to be stored securely. The ability to control nuclear spins could provide new opportunities for storing and reading out quantum information. For now, however, the research mainly raises new questions about the mechanism driving the nuclear spin.
"Back to the drawing board, then," says Otte. "That is really how science works. There is always something new left to figure out."

title: Portable device accurately and rapidly detects PFAS in water
raw_text:
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are synthetic chemicals known for their exceptional resistance to degradation, earning them the nickname "forever chemicals." These persistent substances can accumulate in water, soil and living organisms, raising concerns about their potential impacts on human health and the environment.
Detecting PFAS contamination is a critical first step toward addressing these risks. However, conventional PFAS analysis typically requires collecting environmental samples and transporting them to specialized laboratories equipped with advanced mass spectrometry instruments. Although highly sensitive and accurate, these methods can be costly and time-consuming.
Researchers from the Micro/Bio/Nanofluidics Unit at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have created a reliable, easy-to-mass-produce platform that enables regulators and other environmental actors to detect PFAS on the spot without the need for an external lab.
"Our goal is to develop a sensitive, low-cost technology that can eventually be used outside specialized laboratories," says Dr. Mark Sullivan. "We have demonstrated that it works for PFOA and PFOS, and the same platform could potentially be adapted to detect other PFAS compounds."
The new device is described in Biosensors and Bioelectronics.
Catching PFAS with synthetic antibodies and electrical currents
The researchers have designed a new class of molecularly imprinted polymers, or MIPs, that are tailored to fit PFAS. The materials are formed around the target molecule—in this case, PFAS—creating a binding site. The target molecule is then washed away, leaving behind a material that recognizes and captures the target again, like a lock that is shaped for a key. This is also why MIPs are often called 'synthetic antibodies.'
Their device detects PFAS by measuring changes in electrical current as target molecules bind to a sensor coated with PFAS-specific MIPs. The greater the change in electrical current, the higher the PFAS concentration is in the water sample. Because the measurement requires no additional chemical reagents, this approach could provide a simpler, lower-cost solution for portable, onsite water monitoring.
The platform is compact, low-cost and designed for easy manufacturing. For the prototype, the researchers screen-printed 100 disposable electrodes onto repurposed fabric in a few hours. These were then coated with PFAS-specific MIPs and connected to commercially available potentiostats, which measure electrical signals and can plug directly into a smartphone or laptop.
Furthermore, the MIP manufacturing method is modular, meaning the target molecule can be replaced with any member of the PFAS family; for this prototype, the researchers chose the two most common PFAS chemicals with documented health risks: PFOS and PFOA.
Strengthening the global environmental immune defense against forever chemicals
PFAS have proven to be an insidious problem for the environment and health due to two key factors: their exceptional resistance to heat, water, oil and environmental degradation, which makes them both useful and extremely difficult to break down; and their diversity, with the PFAS family encompassing more than 10,000 similar chemicals, of which 50–150 members are regulated across the globe.
The team's MIP platform's modularity makes it relatively simple to adapt it to different PFAS molecules and, more importantly, lowers the barrier to addressing PFAS contamination going forward. Dr. Perrine Lasserre continues:
"It shows that it's possible to make a detection system that empowers local agencies or even families to make an informed decision about whether and how to address potential PFAS contamination—such as alerting municipal authorities to contamination at specific sites, or whether to invest in a water filter. Whatever we can achieve with this system is going to be beneficial."
"Accurate and accessible detection is an important step toward addressing PFAS contamination," says professor Amy Shen.
"Our study demonstrates how synthetic molecular recognition can be combined with low-cost electrochemical devices to detect extremely small concentrations of these persistent chemicals. While further development and field validation are needed, we see considerable potential for making environmental monitoring more accessible and widely available."

title: How evolutionary biology became an unwilling ally of the manosphere
raw_text:
How evolutionary biology became an unwilling ally of the manosphere
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
From steroid use to "bone smashing", the "looksmaxxing" movement is only the latest example of the manosphere's toxic hold on young people.
Less obvious is the role ecologists have unwittingly played in its rise. Contemporary male supremacist arguments routinely borrow from evolutionary biology and behavioral ecology, and that should give ecologists pause.
As a professor of environmental science at the Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières (UQTR), I study, among other things, how these sciences and philosophy have shaped one another over the centuries. My co-author, a master's student, researches the distribution of chemical elements in aquatic ecosystems and the social and political implications of advances in environmental science.
Biology as a justification for sexism
Before the internet, men's rights and anti-feminist movements rarely invoked biology. They relied mainly on psychological and sociological arguments to justify keeping men above women in the social hierarchy.
Today, members of the manosphere ground their ideology primarily in biology.
This shift gives them a rhetorical advantage: they can claim that their fatalism and misogyny simply reflect the natural order. Their grievances then appear to rest on facts while feminist demands are dismissed as ideology.
The alpha male through the years
The concept of the alpha male is the most glaring example of the manosphere's appropriation of what's known as behavioral ecology.
The term was first used nearly a century ago in a study of social hierarchy in mice. It gained popularity in the 1980s through the work of scholars David L. Mech on wolves and Frans de Waal on chimpanzees.
While this research made no misogynistic arguments, it did show a certain gender bias. Alpha males received more attention than alpha females, who were mentioned mainly in the context of reproduction; alpha males were described in a much wider range of roles.
Since then, the concept of the alpha male (unlike that of the alpha female) has spread widely in public discourse and it has taken on particular significance within the manosphere, where it now refers to a virile, confident man who attracts many women effortlessly.
Yet the definition of an alpha male is hotly debated in behavioral ecology. De Waal himself sought to refute the popular belief that aggression is what defines a dominant male's status, emphasizing instead the importance of empathy.
Unfortunately, this correction has done nothing to alter the manosphere's discourse, which cherry-picks its references. It would be unfair to blame Mech and de Waal for bringing the "alpha male" into manosphere ideology; still, the way their research was presented made the term easier to appropriate.
The manosphere's modern ally
Evolutionary psychology, which aims to explain human behavior through the principles of evolutionary biology, is a field that has drawn heavy criticism within academia.
The manosphere is particularly fond of evolutionary psychology, which seeks to link evolutionary mechanisms directly to human behavior. It's much easier to cite a study claiming that evolution drives women to marry high-earning men than to try to explain women's personalities by studying animal behavior.
What should worry ecologists is this: just as the manosphere borrows from evolutionary psychologists, evolutionary psychologists borrow from ecologists.
The "sexy son hypothesis", proposed by ecologists Patrick J. Weatherhead and Raleigh J. Robertson in 1979, holds that a female's ideal mate is one whose genes will give her sons the best chances of reproductive success. According to this hypothesis, females should therefore favor a male's attractiveness over his other traits.
The hypothesis has since been taken up in numerous evolutionary psychology articles, which have in turn been cited on incel forums.
This is why ecologists need to be more careful than in the past. An entire field of psychology is combing through the ecological literature, seeking to link evolutionary theories to the complexities of the human mind, regardless of the intentions of the scientists who developed them.
Our aim is not to cast aspersions on evolutionary biology or behavioral ecology, but to make researchers and the public aware of the repercussions this research can have in the current political climate. Today, people use science not only to define their environment but also to define themselves. That is why ecologists must choose their words carefully and interpret their findings with caution.

title: The hydrogen atom: The raw material of the universe barely exists on Earth—now we've made it in a flask
raw_text:
The hydrogen atom: The raw material of the universe barely exists on Earth—now we've made it in a flask
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
What do you see when you look up at the night sky? While everyone may have a different answer, the truth is that almost everything out there is hydrogen. The first element in the periodic table is by far the most abundant substance in the cosmos. It's the fuel of stars and the raw material from which the heavier elements were forged over billions of years. Even the sun is, at its core, a furnace for fusing hydrogen atoms together.
Despite this abundance, the hydrogen atom has been almost completely inaccessible in the chemistry lab for over a century. It's a strange irony; physicists have explored the hydrogen atom for as long as modern science has existed.
In fact, the hydrogen atom is the most studied and well-understood system in the history of physics. Take Niels Bohr's famous model of atomic structure—it was built on the hydrogen atom. Erwin Schrödinger solved his famous quantum wave equation for it first. And when Paul Dirac merged quantum mechanics, the theory of particles and atoms, with Albert Einstein's special relativity, it revealed a lot of the fine structure of the element.
For synthetic chemists, who build chemical compounds and molecules, it has been almost out of reach—until now.
To be clear, I'm not talking about the hydrogen molecule that comes in a gas canister, which consists of two hydrogen atoms bound together. And I'm not talking about the hydrogen ion (which has an extra electron) or the proton (a particle which makes up the atomic nucleus of the hydrogen atom). What I am talking about is the lone, simple hydrogen atom: a single electron orbiting a single proton.
This single, unpaired electron makes it what chemists call a radical: the most fundamental reactive species in all of chemistry. Until recently, generating it required conditions so extreme that it was simply not a tool synthetic chemists could use.
How we got here
In 1912, Irving Langmuir, an American chemist at General Electric who would win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1932, became the first scientist to temporarily make atomic hydrogen. He did this by heating molecular hydrogen over a tungsten filament to above 1,700°C, splitting hydrogen gas into individual hydrogen atoms. When these atoms combine at a cooler metal surface, they release enormous amounts of energy, producing temperatures of 3,400°C to 4,000°C.
In fact, this heat proved sufficient to weld tungsten, the most heat-resistant of all metals. For decades, this method was one of the most potent industrial welding processes.
And progress continued. In 1922, James Franck, a German-American physicist who would later win the Nobel Prize in Physics, discovered that mercury atoms exposed to ultraviolet light at 254 nanometers could absorb that energy and then transfer it to hydrogen molecules, breaking them apart into atoms.
This process, called mercury photosensitization, was based on fundamental physics, however. It wasn't intended to be used to do chemistry. And while it worked, it required toxic mercury vapor, the use of which is heavily regulated, and specialized ultraviolet lamps.
The first chemist to recognize that hydrogen atoms might be genuinely useful as synthetic reagents (artificial substances that can cause, control or assist chemical reactions) was Robert Crabtree at Yale University. In a 1991 paper in the Journal of the American Chemical Society, he demonstrated that Franck's mercury photosensitization could be adapted.
The hydrogen atoms that were created in the process could be used to break double carbon bonds (where two carbon atoms are bound together by four bonding electrons instead of two) in organic compounds such as olefins, which are a building block of plastics. This was important work, as it showed that the hydrogen atom could be successfully used to do chemistry, such as discovering new drugs.
But his method still required toxic mercury vapor and a specialized UV lamp. Critically, it also failed to work in liquid solutions, requiring vapor instead. Synthetic chemistry, however, is done in solutions (it's easier to mix components in a liquid). So even after Crabtree, the hydrogen atom remained out of reach to synthetic chemists.
A flask and a lamp
My laboratory at University College London set out to close that gap. I wanted to know if it was possible to create atomic hydrogen at room temperature, in a liquid solution, using ordinary laboratory equipment. Surprisingly, after all these years, the answer appears to be yes. We've now published our results in the Journal of the American Chemical Society.
I began this work alone in my laboratory. But I was lucky that Nils Flodén, a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Colloids and Interfaces in Potsdam, Germany, soon joined me as a collaborator.
Our method uses two inexpensive, commercially available chemicals: hydrazine (a molecule consisting of two nitrogen atoms and four hydrogen atoms) and thiophenol (consisting of a mix of carbon, hydrogen and sulfur). When mixed together and exposed to near-ultraviolet light from a standard LED lamp, these generate atomic hydrogen at only 30°C. The result amazed me. We used no toxic mercury vapor, no extreme temperatures. All we needed was a flask, a lamp and two reagents available from any chemical supplier.
When hydrazine and thiophenol are mixed, they form an intermediate substance that absorbs near-ultraviolet light. This triggers an electron to move places, producing a short-lived, highly unstable species that rapidly falls apart, releasing a hydrogen atom in the process.
But our goal was not creating a fleeting hydrogen atom that quickly disappears—we wanted to use it to do chemistry. And we discovered that the hydrogen atom we'd created was free to react with organic molecules in ways that are crucial in many chemical experiments, such as adding it onto double bonds of carbon to form less reactive (more stable) single bonds, and removing halogens (such as fluorine, iodine and chlorine).
The precise nature of the unstable intermediate is still being investigated, but our current evidence points toward a species physicists call a Rydberg radical, in which an electron occupies an unusually large and diffuse orbit around the molecule before the whole thing breaks apart. In fact, our hypothesis is inspired by the work of Nobel laureate Gerhard Herzberg on something called a Rydberg radical of ammonia (ammonium radical), which was published in 1981.
How do we know we have made a hydrogen atom? We used something called EPR spin-trapping, consisting of a chemical net that can ultimately catch short-lived radicals that we can identify by their magnetic fingerprint. And this revealed that hydrogen atoms had formed at the end.
When we used a version of hydrazine where the hydrogen atoms were replaced by the heavier isotope deuterium (a hydrogen atom with a neutron added to its nucleus), we caught deuterium atoms instead, exactly as predicted. This EPR spectroscopy was performed with Alberto Collauto at Imperial College London.
A molecular stopwatch called a radical clock further supported the mechanism. Every experiment pointed in the same direction.
What can you do with it?
Having atomic hydrogen available as a practical reagent in a liquid solution could open possibilities that were not there before. The most immediate application is hydrogenation: adding hydrogen atoms across a carbon-carbon double bond to break it up. This is one of the most important reactions in pharmaceutical manufacturing, used to make drugs ranging from cholesterol treatments to antivirals.
Currently, most industrial hydrogenation requires metals such as palladium, rhodium or iridium to act as catalysts, often under high-pressure hydrogen gas. But there's a limited global supply of such metals, making them expensive and strictly regulated in drug products.
Our hydrogen atom method requires none of them. It is metal-free, operates at atmospheric pressure and close to room temperature. But could it actually be used in drug manufacturing? We managed to use our method, without disturbing other chemical groups, to reduce double bonds in a derivative of fluoxetine (an SSRI), in terpenoids (compounds found in fragrances and flavors) and in an amino acid. This can help make drugs more stable in the body and less reactive.
We also demonstrated hydrodehalogenation: the selective removal of halogen atoms from organic molecules. This is often done in medicinal chemistry for fine-tuning drug candidates.
As for other applications, atomic hydrogen is already used industrially for cleaning semiconductor surfaces in microchip manufacturing, where it removes naturally occurring oxide layers that reduce device performance. Those processes currently require plasma equipment and ultra-high vacuum conditions.
Whether our mild solution could eventually offer an alternative is currently unknown. But for the first time, it is an actual alternative worth exploring.
A long obsession
How did I come up with the idea in the first place? It grew from two parallel interests. I have long been fascinated by hydrogen as a clean fuel and the challenge of storing it conveniently. After all, hydrogen has been the fuel of the universe for 13 billion years.
At the same time, I was working on developing new synthetic methods in organic chemistry. About half a decade ago, it struck me that, despite decades of exploration, the reactive hydrogen atom itself has remained almost entirely unexplored as a synthetic tool. Finding a practical way to generate it could be useful for hydrogen storage and beyond. This was the starting point.
This was ultimately a dream project. The more I thought about it, the harder it was to let it go. At some point, it practically consumed me.
It's been a long journey for me. In 2010, as a student from a small village in northern India, I had the opportunity to travel to Berlin and work in the lab of Hans Ulrich Reissig of Freie Universität Berlin, the first research laboratory I had ever set foot in. The paper is dedicated to him on the occasion of his 77th birthday. It was where I first understood, with absolute certainty, that chemistry was my calling.
It may have taken a century to bring atomic hydrogen into the synthetic chemist's laboratory, but we hope it will prove to be worth the wait.

title: Discovering Vasari beyond the page
raw_text:
Discovering Vasari beyond the page
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
Most students of Renaissance art encounter Giorgio Vasari through a book. His Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, first published in 1550 and expanded in a second edition in 1568, is often considered the first major work of art history, shaping how generations have understood artists such as Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci and Raphael. For centuries, Vasari's reputation has rested largely on his role as the artistic biographer of the Renaissance.
Less familiar, however, is Vasari's own work as a painter and architect. While his biographies helped to immortalize many of the Renaissance's greatest artists, their accomplishments ultimately eclipsed those of their chronicler, despite Vasari's influential career and the prestigious commissions he received throughout Italy. Among his most notable projects is the Salone dei Cinquecento (Hall of the Five Hundred) in Florence's Palazzo Vecchio, which Vasari and his workshop renovated and decorated for Duke Cosimo I de' Medici.
Sally Cornelison, professor of art history in the College of Arts and Sciences and director of Syracuse University's Florence Graduate Program in Italian Renaissance Art, is bringing greater attention to aspects of Vasari's legacy beyond his literary achievements. Through years of archival research, travel across Italy and an intensive study of Vasari's work in his hometown of Arezzo, Cornelison is looking beyond the pages of Lives to examine his work as a painter, architect and builder of local identity.
Her latest book, Vasari and the Sacred Image, investigates how art, religion, civic pride and personal ambition intersected in one of the most important churches in Arezzo, the Pieve di Santa Maria, where Vasari was baptized in 1511 and buried in 1574. Her scholarship reveals a more complete picture of a Renaissance figure whose artistic accomplishments have long been obscured by his literary fame in a town that often falls off the Renaissance radar.
Rediscovering Vasari
Cornelison's journey into the world of Vasari began in 2012, when she curated an exhibition at the Spencer Museum of Art in Lawrence, Kansas, while a professor at the University of Kansas. What started as an effort to authenticate a small painting attributed to the circle of Vasari evolved into a much larger scholarly journey. As she uncovered new materials and archival sources, she became increasingly fascinated by the artist and the many aspects of his career that had received limited attention from historians.
"I found so much material in the process of working on that exhibition," Cornelison says. "I got the Vasari bug."
All of that research culminated in her new book, in which Cornelison examines a group of altars and altarpieces that Vasari designed for the medieval basilica of the Pieve but that were removed or destroyed during a late 19th-century renovation. By analyzing these works and reconstructing how they originally functioned individually and collectively within the Pieve, she reveals how Vasari transformed the church into an integrated artistic and devotional environment.
Cornelison studied paintings, drawings and archival records to better understand Vasari's approach to sacred art. Her research revealed an artist who carefully conceived images in relation to their surroundings and audiences, creating works that were part of larger narratives about faith, identity and place. She argues that these achievements deserve greater recognition than they have traditionally received.
"He has a long-standing reputation as a bad artist that isn't deserved," Cornelison says. "He was an excellent draftsman, and his drawings are really spectacular. It's just a hard label to shake, the idea that he isn't worth looking at as an artist and that it's really the Lives of the Artists that matters. I think there's more value in his art than he's been given credit for."
Stepping inside Vasari's world
But the book wasn't the end of the journey. Drawing on years of research, travel and firsthand documentation, Cornelison found a new way to bring Vasari's world to life. She translated her scholarship into a digital humanities project, creating immersive experiences that invite audiences beyond academia to explore Vasari and Renaissance art.
The idea emerged while she was developing a class project that would require students to create StoryMaps, an interactive digital platform that combines maps, images, text and multimedia storytelling. Wanting to learn the technology herself before teaching it, she created a StoryMap focused on Vasari and Arezzo. What began as an experiment quickly became a passion project, allowing her to translate years of research into an accessible, visually engaging format that invites users to explore the artist's hometown and artistic legacy.
"It started as just playing around with the tool, and I became completely obsessed," says Cornelison. "I cranked out the Vasari and Arezzo StoryMap in about two and a half weeks over the summer."
She has since expanded the initiative with additional projects, including a second StoryMap exploring Vasari's refectory (dining hall) paintings, and is planning future projects focused on Vasari's writings and other research topics.
Bringing history to life for students
The project also reflects Cornelison's commitment to teaching and student collaboration. Among those who contributed to Vasari and the Sacred Image was Sarah Ritchey, a Syracuse University School of Architecture alumna who later completed the Florence Graduate Program in Italian Renaissance Art that Cornelison directs. Ritchey produced the altar reconstructions featured in the book, helping readers visualize how Vasari's chapels and altars originally appeared before later renovations dramatically altered the church's interior. These reconstructions became an important component of the publication, demonstrating how faculty research and student expertise can work together to shed new light on centuries-old works of art.
Vasari is already an important figure in the history of Italian Renaissance art because of his famous biographies, and Cornelison's expertise brings his world to life for students both within and outside the classroom. In her graduate-level Proseminar in Italian Renaissance Art (HOA 623), students enrolled in SU's main campus and Florence art history graduate programs engage with Vasari's literary and artistic works.
In addition, she has taken Florence graduate students to Arezzo on multiple occasions to explore the city where Vasari was born and baptized, began building the artistic legacy that would influence generations, and was ultimately laid to rest at the foot of the high altar he designed for the Pieve.
For students, there is no substitute for experiencing these places in person. For Cornelison, that hands-on engagement is at the heart of both her research and teaching. Through Vasari and the Sacred Image, she has helped to broaden scholarly understanding of Vasari's artistic and architectural achievements. In the classroom and on site in Italy, she brings that same research to students, combining archival discovery, immersive learning and firsthand exploration to make the Renaissance come alive.

title: The Advanced Placement gender gap is narrowing but not across all subjects
raw_text:
The Advanced Placement gender gap is narrowing but not across all subjects
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
The gender balance among the top scorers on Advanced Placement exams tends to track the gender balance among students taking those tests, according to a new study led by the University of Georgia.
That gender gap is currently wide.
Across more than two decades of exam data, the researchers found participation in AP tests was often split along gender lines. Girls dominated the languages, humanities and arts, while boys took more STEM (or science, technology, engineering and math) subjects.
In many subjects, the more evenly split the AP test takers were, the narrower the gender gaps among students earning top scores became, the study found.
"Gender stereotypes about ability, like persistent beliefs that boys are naturally better at mathematics, physics, computing or similar STEM courses, or that girls are better at arts, can influence both students' choices on which class to take and how well they do in that class," said Kadir Bahar, corresponding author of the study and an associate professor in the Mary Frances Early College of Education. "Students are more likely to enter and persist in a field when they feel that people like them belong in it."
AP classes are offered in high schools across the country. They are designed by the College Board to match the rigor of college courses and can count toward college credits if students score well on the AP exams at the end of term.
Gender gaps narrowed significantly in some subjects, grew in others
The researchers analyzed more than 70 million AP exam results, covering about 40 million students between 1997 and 2020.
Out of 45 subjects, boys outnumbered girls in many science and math-centered subjects, especially physics and computer science, the study found. For example, the researchers found that for every one girl taking the AP Computer Science A exam, more than four boys were taking the exam.
Girls outnumbered boys in studio art exams by almost three to one, and in English literature exams by almost two to one.
"Think about it: You are going to an AP physics course, and there is only one girl for every three boys. That might give a girl a sense that physics is a boys' room. That subject belongs to them," Bahar said. That feeling may make girls question whether they should take a course, even if it interests them.
The researchers found that male overrepresentation has decreased in many of those STEM-related courses—calculus, computer science and chemistry, for instance—over the years.
AP Calculus AB exam participation, for example, stayed close to evenly split between boys and girls while the gap in Calculus BC narrowed. Statistics also evened out, and German and Latin were roughly balanced throughout.
That was not the case for algebra-based Physics 1, though. It remained male-dominated, and the gap widened. In the years the exam was offered (2015 through 2020), three of every five students who took it were boys.
Studio art continued to skew more female, and that gap also grew. Roughly seven out of every 10 students taking those exams were girls.
"We aren't sure exactly what changed," Bahar said. "But there were nevertheless encouraging signs of change. Gender gaps narrowed significantly in several subjects."
Participation in AP tests and exam scores could be linked
Across many AP subjects, gender representation among exam takers was strongly associated with gender representation among students earning a top score of 5. However, the relationship varied substantially by subject.
In some subjects that maintained a sizable gap in participation, the gender that made up the majority of students also earned the highest scores. But in several subjects where girls were most of the test takers, such as biology, environmental science and world history, boys still outnumbered girls among top scorers.
The gaps remained striking in some subjects. Across the study period, boys were represented among top scorers at roughly four times the rate of girls in Physics 1 and nearly six times the rate in Computer Science A.
"Participation and top achievement are related," Bahar said. "Getting more girls into computer science may help narrow those excellence gaps." Physics was a notable exception, though. There, changes in participation did not track changes among top scorers.
Simply increasing participation by one gender won't necessarily close gaps among top scorers, the researchers said.
"Gendered expectations can accumulate over many years," Bahar said. "Parents may perceive sons as more mathematically capable and daughters as more verbally capable. Teachers may unintentionally enforce such expectations, and peer norms can make certain subjects appear more or less socially appropriate for boys or girls."
Making all students feel comfortable trying different subjects is key, the researchers said.
"Equity doesn't mean forcing equal numbers of boys and girls into every subject," Bahar said. "But it means ensuring that gender is not creating unnecessary barriers to opportunity, participation, support or high achievement."
The study was published in the Journal of Educational Psychology and was coauthored by Yasemin Sipahi, a doctoral student in the Department of Educational Psychology, as well as Eter Mjavanadze, Erdogan Kaya and Ummugulsum Aydin.

title: NASA systems engineering team details Habitable Worlds Observatory mission architecture
raw_text:
NASA systems engineering team details Habitable Worlds Observatory mission architecture
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
Finding an Earth-like world beyond the solar system is the holy grail of exoplanet research, and the field has seen remarkable technological advances in detecting and studying exoplanets since the first confirmed exoplanet around a sun-like star was discovered in 1995. These advances include ground- and space-based telescopes, notably the James Webb Space Telescope. Although astronomers have already directly imaged some exoplanets, directly imaging Earth-like planets around sun-like stars remains a major technological challenge, primarily because these planets are extremely faint compared with their host stars and appear very close to them in the sky.
But a proposed mission called the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) could advance progress toward not only observing but directly imaging Earth-like exoplanets. While HWO has been in the works for about 10 years now, it's still not slated to launch until sometime in the 2040s. In the meantime, researchers are developing new engineering concepts for this highly anticipated telescope. These concepts were discussed in a June 2026 study published in the Journal of Astronomical Telescopes, Instruments, and Systems and hold the potential to continue HWO's development well in advance of its launch.
For the study, the researchers introduced engineering concepts called Exploratory Analytic Cases (EACs) designed to balance the demands of the science goals with the engineering needs. The purpose of this study was to discuss the first three of five EACs regarding HWO's architecture design, focusing on telescope type, size and whether an on- or off-axis design is needed.
The telescope size includes the mirror diameter in meters, and the type of telescope includes the mirror and aperture design, with the study focusing on inscribed, circumscribed, round and outer diameter. For example, inscribed includes the inner baseline measurement while circumscribed includes the measured outer region that holds a set of mirrors. A round mirror is how it sounds, while an outer diameter mirror denotes the maximum edge-to-edge measurement.
The difference between on-axis and off-axis design is that the former has all of the components within the field of view of incoming light, obstructing a portion of the view, while the latter has all of its components outside the field of view, resulting in an unobstructed view.
For the EACs, the researchers designed EAC1 as having a 6-m inscribed / 7.2-m circumscribed, off-axis design; EAC2 with a 6-m round, off-axis design; and EAC3 having an 8-m outer diameter, on-axis design. In the end, the researchers favored the off-axis design to allow greater light-gathering operations, along with focusing on a larger aperture size to enable greater light-collecting area.
Another design consideration the researchers recommended was temperature properties, which influence light-collecting and overall telescope operations. This is especially relevant to the coronagraph instrument (CI), which blocks out the star's glare, enabling the direct imaging of orbiting exoplanets.
The study notes, "The SET [Systems Engineering Team], composed of team members across NASA centers and JPL, successfully completed design architectures for EACs 1 to 3 and developed end-to-end modeling for EAC1. This team was established to support design explorations and formulating technology requirements. Using model-driven practices based on JWST heritage and enhanced by Roman experience, the team developed several tools to perform parametric design studies and trades. In parallel, the models were shared with industry partners to support their technology maturation efforts and independent architecture studies."
As noted, HWO isn't slated to launch until the 2040s, but its science goals remain unchanged as it is also slated to replace the James Webb Space Telescope as the primary space telescope. The primary goal of HWO will be to directly image Earth-like exoplanets, and the designs and objectives outlined today will influence these science goals and the telescope operations in determining whether Earth is the only habitable planet and whether we're alone in the universe.

title: Refugees' experiences of loss shape their business ambitions
raw_text:
Refugees' experiences of loss shape their business ambitions
Swati Mestri
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
The severity of the losses refugees experience can shape the kinds of businesses they build in a new country, according to a qualitative study by Tilburg University researcher Kurian George and colleagues.
Among the refugee entrepreneurs they interviewed, accounts of more severe losses accompanied a focus on businesses within familiar communities, while accounts of less severe losses often accompanied ambitions to grow beyond those communities.
For the study, Kurian George and his colleagues interviewed 62 refugee entrepreneurs from 17 countries who had resettled in the northeastern United States. They also visited 46 businesses. The researchers wanted to understand how experiences during forced migration shape the business opportunities refugees recognize and the businesses they build.
The findings are published in the Journal of Business Venturing.
Refugees often lose much more than their homes or jobs during forced migration. Family ties, professional networks, and familiarity with social and cultural norms may also be lost. The researchers call this profound disruption" wholesale disruption." Before refugees can recognize business opportunities, they often first need to make sense of their new environment.
"We call this 'community remapping'," says George. "It means discovering where you belong, which networks and resources are available, and what opportunities you can pursue."
Different experiences, different businesses
The researchers identified two broad pathways, linked to the severity of losses experienced during forced migration.
Refugees who reported less severe losses were more likely to see the wider host-country community as accessible. They built relationships across different groups, viewed obstacles as manageable, and recognized a broader range of business opportunities. Their businesses were more likely to serve customers beyond their own ethnic community and pursue growth.
Those who reported more severe and prolonged losses, including violence, detention, family separation, or extended periods in refugee camps, were more likely to find trust and support within their own ethnic or refugee communities. Their businesses often served these familiar communities, prioritizing stability over growth.
The two pathways should not be read as a divide between success and failure. Businesses rooted in familiar communities can meet overlooked needs, preserve cultural connections, and provide stability. "Our findings suggest that refugees' experiences shape not only the challenges they face, but also the business opportunities they recognize and pursue," George explains.
More than business training
The findings have implications for organizations and policymakers supporting refugee entrepreneurship, George says. "Supporting refugee entrepreneurs is about more than business training or financial assistance. Helping them build trusted relationships and connect with local networks can be just as important."
The research also challenges the idea that refugee entrepreneurs act only out of necessity. Participants actively explored opportunities and built new relationships. What mattered was not simply whether resources existed, but whether entrepreneurs saw them as accessible and relevant to their businesses.
More information
Todd W. Moss et al., Who are my people and what can I do? Community remapping for entrepreneurial venturing after forced migration, Journal of Business Venturing (2027). DOI: 10.1016/j.jbusvent.2026.106654

title: Urban street trees lose much of their capacity to cool during droughts
raw_text:
Urban street trees lose much of their capacity to cool during droughts
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
The combination of heat waves and drought markedly reduces the capacity of street trees to cool the air in Mediterranean cities. The lack of soil moisture severely restricts plant transpiration, reducing the thermal relief provided by these trees during extreme heat events.
This is demonstrated by a study published in Urban Climate and conducted by the Institute of Environmental Science and Technology at the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (ICTA-UAB), Spain. The study analyzes the behavior of street trees in dense streets of Barcelona during intense heat episodes. The goal was to determine how soil moisture and plant canopy interact to mitigate urban heat.
Under ideal soil moisture conditions, plant transpiration reduces air temperatures by an average of 1.2 °C to 1.7 °C from midday to midafternoon. It reduces heat stress experienced by pedestrians—measured with the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI)—by up to 3.2 °C and decreases mean radiant temperature (that perceived by pedestrians from solar and asphalt radiation) by up to 12.3 °C in areas most exposed to the sun.
However, when extreme heat coincides with drought periods, the lack of water forces trees to close their stomata to prevent dehydration, severely impairing or eliminating evaporative air cooling.
When soil is dry, shade from tree crowns plays a key role in providing refuge from the heat. Despite the loss of evaporative air cooling, foliage blocks direct solar radiation, preventing overheating of asphalt and facades and shielding pedestrians beneath the trees from direct sun exposure. This shading retains between 71% and 97% of its protective cooling effect on pedestrian thermal comfort.
Thus, the study determines that urban greening strategies must adapt to the new climatic reality of the Mediterranean. To maximize tree effectiveness, the authors recommend prioritizing evergreen species and/or drought-tolerant deciduous species that sustain canopy structure during summer months. They also recommend ensuring strategic irrigation during heat peaks for deciduous species that retain their foliage in summer, as well as preserving soil moisture in tree pits and pervious soil.
According to the authors, "One of the main challenges facing the city is ensuring that trees maintain sufficient foliage during drought periods, and especially during heat waves, which is precisely when shade is needed the most."
More information

title: Launch of global seed platform to tackle native seed bottleneck holding back nature restoration
raw_text:
Launch of global seed platform to tackle native seed bottleneck holding back nature restoration
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
On Oct. 13, the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (RBG Kew) launched the Seed Portal for Online Data (SeedPOD), a new open-access platform designed to tackle bottlenecks affecting global ecological restoration, by making native seed collections and the knowledge needed to grow them easier to discover.
Efforts to restore degraded ecosystems and build resilience in the face of a changing climate face a fundamental challenge: getting the right seed to the right place, along with the information needed to grow it successfully. Recent research led by scientists at Kew's Millennium Seed Bank (MSB) at Kew Wakehurst, Sussex, has highlighted the limited availability of suitable native seed as a persistent challenge for restoration.
This challenge is set against ambitious international restoration targets as, under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), countries have committed to ensuring at least 30% of degraded terrestrial, inland water, coastal and marine ecosystems are under effective restoration by 2030.
Seed banks around the world conserve vast collections of genetically diverse wild seeds. Kew's Millennium Seed Bank alone holds more than 2.5 billion seeds from over 40,000 wild plant species. But finding information about what seeds exist, where they came from, whether they are available and viable, and how to successfully germinate them often requires searching across multiple institutions, scientific literature and disconnected databases.
What's more, smaller seed banks and seed custodians may lack the funding or technical infrastructure to make their collections visible online at all.
SeedPOD has been developed by Kew's scientists to bring this information together, helping restoration practitioners, researchers, land managers and communities find native seed that meets their needs and understand how to propagate it successfully.
Getting the right seeds to the right places
Successful ecological restoration depends on more than simply finding seeds of the correct species. Seeds from different wild populations of the same species can carry different traits and respond differently to environmental conditions. Understanding where seeds originated, their genetic diversity and the conditions in which they can successfully establish can be critical when selecting material for restoration. Kew scientists also highlight the importance of population-level differences, including local climate, site conditions and genetic variation, when sourcing seeds for restoration.
Identifying appropriate material can currently involve searching across multiple organizations and sources to establish what seeds exist, whether they can be accessed and how to turn them into viable plants.
Making existing collections easier to discover could help practitioners rebuilding degraded habitats introduce genetic diversity into available seed sources, reduce reliance on a narrow pool of commercially available material and reveal important taxonomic or geographic gaps in collections.
SeedPOD allows participating seed custodians to make their collections discoverable in one place, including:
- Where wild seeds were collected and whether they are available and viable, helping inform sourcing decisions
- How seeds have successfully been germinated, including conditions, dormancy and storage behavior
- Standardized information about plant species and their traits, making collections held by different institutions easier to find and compare
Elinor Breman, senior research leader for seed conservation at RBG Kew, says, "Countries around the world have committed to restoring degraded ecosystems on an unprecedented scale, but delivering on those ambitions ultimately depends on having the right native seeds, from appropriate and diverse sources, and knowing how to grow them successfully.
"Seed banks hold an extraordinary resource and decades of knowledge, but much of that information is scattered between institutions or can be difficult to access. SeedPOD will help unlock those collections and that expertise so they can be put to use where they are needed."
Opening up seed collections worldwide
SeedPOD has also been designed to make it easier for smaller seed banks and seed custodians to be involved, many of which lack the resources or technical infrastructure to make their collections easily discoverable online. Some native seed networks currently rely on channels including WhatsApp and Facebook to connect people looking for seeds with potential suppliers, with no centralized way to access information on what material is available.
Cacilda Manhiça, national coordinator of the Wild Seeds Program at Instituto de Investigação Agrária de Moçambique (IIAM), says, "Working with native seeds has shown me how much valuable plant diversity exists in Mozambique, and how important it is to make these resources accessible to those working to conserve and restore our ecosystems. For me, SeedPOD is an exciting opportunity to share IIAM's seed collections beyond our borders, connect with others doing similar work and contribute to a global effort to protect and restore native plant diversity."
SeedPOD therefore provides people with a free platform through which they can make their collections discoverable without having to build and maintain their own digital infrastructure.
The platform is available in multiple languages and has been designed to work in low-bandwidth environments, widening access for organizations with different levels of technical capacity. It is also intended to connect with complementary biodiversity resources rather than becoming another standalone source of data.
As more organizations contribute, SeedPOD will build connections between seed custodians, growers, researchers and conservation practitioners, while enabling knowledge and data to be shared and reused more effectively across the international native seed community.

title: Japan's genome-editing law sets a global ethics challenge
raw_text:
Japan's genome-editing law sets a global ethics challenge
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
A Hiroshima University researcher contends that Japan's newly enacted law regulating human genome-edited embryos and germ cells marks a significant advance in the governance of reproductive genome editing. Tsutomu Sawai, professor at Hiroshima University's Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, praises the new law for defining prohibited activities and penalties for violation but also stresses the need for stronger international coordination to prevent the prohibitions from being circumvented by individuals seeking procedures abroad.
The correspondence article was published in the journal Nature Medicine.
The law, enacted on July 17, 2026, imposes penalties on prohibited reproductive uses of genome-edited human embryos and germ cells, also known as heritable human genome editing. The prohibitions and penalties take effect on July 24, 2027—one year after the law's promulgation.
While the reproductive use of heritable human genome editing had previously been disallowed in Japan, there were no legal penalties for transferring genome-edited embryos or germ cells into a uterus. While the law prohibits the reproductive use of heritable human genome editing outright, it permits basic research on heritable human genome editing under binding ministerial oversight.
"This is an important step by Japan," said Sawai. "Japan is already a leader in regenerative medicine, and it is expected to also be a leader in the ethics of such therapies."
Therapies based on genome editing are still permitted
The correspondence notes that Japan's law carefully distinguishes between forms of genome editing that affect future generations and those that do not. Therefore, it does not affect the development of somatic gene-editing therapies, whose effects remain confined to the treated individual.
This distinction is important as gene-editing medicine advances rapidly. Treatments for conditions such as sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia have already been approved for patients. These therapies are unaffected by the new law and should continue to be developed through normal scientific and regulatory pathways.
International coordination is crucial
The correspondence agrees with the prohibitions, since the long-term consequences of the edits cannot be verified across multiple generations, and future children, who are most affected by these interventions, cannot consent to them in advance. However, it also warns that national prohibitions are likely insufficient and need international coordination, since people in Japan could seek heritable genome-editing procedures in countries with weaker regulations.
"No country can address heritable genome editing alone," said Sawai. "National laws are necessary, but they must be complemented by international frameworks and cooperation. The decisions we make today will affect generations that cannot speak for themselves."
At the same time, the correspondence notes that prohibitions today do not necessarily imply prohibition forever. Future developments in science, safety and ethical understanding may justify reassessment of the law and its underlying ethical assumptions.

title: Nature-inspired additive could help protect living cells during freezing and thawing
raw_text:
Nature-inspired additive could help protect living cells during freezing and thawing
Swati Mestri
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
In Australia, around 2,000 people are on the waiting list to receive an organ transplant, but thanks to new research being undertaken at the University of New England (UNE), this number could someday be significantly reduced.
Ph.D. student Michael Foster is working alongside supervisor Dr. Brendan Wilkinson and colleagues from UNE, RMIT University and the University of Ottawa to develop an additive, otherwise known as a cryoprotectant, that could reduce damage when freezing living biological material for future use.
The study is published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry B.
"If we can develop new molecules and technologies that allow organs to remain viable for much longer periods, this could fundamentally change transplant medicine," says Foster.
"Better preservation technologies could give clinicians more time to find the right recipient and transport organs over greater distances, and in the longer term could help move toward organ banking."
Freezing living biological material for storage and later use is called cryopreservation and is almost identical to putting food in the freezer at home, but with a far greater challenge. Rather than simply preserving quality, the cells or tissues need to remain alive and functional after they are thawed.
To reduce damage, cryoprotectants such as dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) are added.
While DMSO is widely used and extremely effective, it can be toxic and incompatible with some cell types, so Foster is looking toward nature to design an alternative.
"Nature provides some remarkable examples of organisms surviving extreme cold and other stresses like dehydration," says Foster.
"These organisms accumulate molecules like sugars and amino acids that help protect their cells under these conditions. Trehalose is one well-known example, while amino acids such as proline are also associated with natural stress protection."
While using nature as inspiration for cryopreservation is not new, Foster's approach is unique in that he is modifying these naturally protective molecules to create a single compound with several complementary cryoprotective properties.
If successful, this new approach could lead to significant applications beyond human health.
"Cryopreservation can be used to store sperm, eggs, embryos, tissues and other genetic material from threatened species," says Foster. "These frozen collections can act as genetic banks that may support breeding programs and help preserve genetic diversity."
While the research is still in the early stages and clinical applications are a long way off, the work will be a critical building block in the long-term effort to improve fertility treatment, organ transplantation and biodiversity conservation.
"Better cryoprotectants are only one part of the challenge," he says. "Improvements in freezing and thawing technologies, delivery of cryoprotectants into complex tissues and organs, biological testing, engineering and eventually clinical or regulatory translation will all be important.
"Whether or not these particular molecules ultimately find direct applications, the work can help identify properties and design strategies that may be useful to pursue."

title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky—this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
raw_text:
Earwax is both slippery and sticky—this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects? It's earwax.
The medical term for earwax is cerumen, based on keros, the Greek word for beeswax. People have been pondering earwax since ancient times. Ancient hygiene kits including picks and spoons to remove earwax have been found in archaeological sites worldwide.
Even today, it remains a perpetual question: To remove or not to remove your earwax? The answer: Don't do it. The general medical belief is that ears are self-cleaning, and earwax brings benefits such as lubricating the ear canal, fighting infection and acting like a sticky net to trap debris before it reaches the eardrum. By poking in there you can accidentally make matters worse, pushing wax deeper or scratching your delicate ear canal.
Cerumen impaction—or blocked earwax—affects about a fifth of the American population, leading to 12 million patient visits per year. Blockages are worsened by daily activities such as wearing earbuds or hearing aids.
Another common problem with ears is wedged debris. For children, much of this is self-inflicted, in the form of items such as Legos or erasers. But for many adults who have something stuck in their ear, the debris is insects, such as ants, beetles, flies or cockroaches.
While rare for the average person, insects in the ear occurred with such frequency over the years that physicians began to wonder whether earwax evolved as a natural barrier for insects. But how would such a barrier work?
To answer this question, my Ph.D. student David Ancalle led experiments with earwax and insects. We teamed up with Yuhang Hu and her student Donjing He, experts in the behavior of soft solids such as hydrogels. As mechanical engineers, we wanted to focus on the physics rather than the chemistry of earwax.
Our research, published in the journal Soft Matter, shows that earwax can, in fact, stop insects without the use of dangerous chemicals.
Watching ants encounter earwax
To do experiments, we needed voluminous amounts of earwax.
Initially we obtained earwax from deceased mammals such as pigs, sheep and rabbits. Eventually we turned to our friends and family. A person has only a grain of rice's worth of earwax in each ear. Due to a mutation in a single gene, East Asians have dry, flaky earwax, while people of African or European descent have wet, squishy earwax.
To simulate an ant climbing into an ear canal, we used a glass beaker with its rim coated in earwax. Ants, like many insects, are climbing specialists, capable of traveling across many kinds of surfaces. To climb rough surfaces, ants have spikes on their feet, like mountain climbers do, that help them grasp onto ridges and cracks. For smooth surfaces, ants unfurl wet suction cups, which can support 60 times their body weight on smooth glass.
Watching ants trying to climb earwax showed us how strange a substance it really is. Rough earwax slowed them down, but with their claws they made progress.
But as soon as ants tried to climb smooth earwax, they fell immediately.
From these experiments, we concluded that earwax had anti-stick properties when in contact with the insects' feet.
We next conducted experiments with ants crawling through an earwax-coated tunnel, more similar in size to a human ear canal. As the ants attempted to travel through the tunnel, earwax stuck to them. Once coated, they groomed furiously, unwilling to walk until they had removed as much as possible. Even after several minutes of effort, the ants still had earwax sticking to hard-to-reach places.
So, earwax is a paradoxical material: It is simultaneously slippery, thanks to the lipids it contains, but also sticky. Similar to many materials—including ketchup, paint and shampoo—it thins out when it is physically deformed, what physicists call shear-thinning.
Figuring out earwax's physical properties
The dual qualities of earwax have to do with its unique composition. Earwax is made up of flakes of skin cells held together with a binder. This blend forms a kind of sponge with microscopic holes. When a body overproduces earwax, it heaps up in boulders that ants can easily climb over.
When the substance is smooth, however, ants rely on their wet suction cups. The holes in the earwax absorb the drops produced by the ants, preventing them from attaching. Absorbency makes earwax fundamentally different from commonly used forms of pest control.
In your local store, you will find sticky surfaces such as flypaper or chemicals that kill the insects. Some researchers look to nature to find bio-friendly alternatives to using chemicals; for example, plants have properties that prevent insects from climbing.
From this study, we learned that the ear is also a model for insect repellency. Earwax is made of natural materials but has a structure that prevents ants from sticking to it.
The porosity of earwax also gives it unique properties. We showed it can absorb twice its weight in water yet still cling to the walls of the ear. This water-absorbing ability may help prevent water from accumulating on the delicate eardrum and fend off infections such as swimmer's ear.
Scientists don't yet understand the complex relationship between earwax, water and bacteria. Some studies show that earwax kills bacteria, but other studies find that earwax harbors bacteria.
Our experiments showed that earwax is most challenging to insects when similar to the thin layer of earwax maintained by a healthy human body. Wax would accumulate more in human ears if not for two self-cleaning mechanisms. The skin in the ear canal grows outward like a conveyor belt. Over 8–10 weeks, this process—called epithelial migration—pushes the oldest earwax out of the ear.
Simultaneously, earwax dries over time, transforming from a gooey state to a brittle one that readily cracks. Every time you talk or chew, your ear canal deforms, and physicians found that this movement helps to dislodge the drier, older earwax.
As a test of our concept, a member of our team, chemical engineer Rafeen Rahaman, designed an artificial earwax based on the physical structure rather than the chemistry of the earwax. Ants struggled when they touched it, just like when they interacted with natural earwax.
Harvesting natural earwax and making artificial earwax using our recipe are not cheap. We don't foresee our methods replacing insect repellents produced at a large scale. But perhaps the concept might inspire new ways to prevent earwax from coating our earbuds or lead to the manufacture of insect control methods using safe formulations.
