title: Indonesia's El Niño–driven peat fires are choking the region—and releasing centuries of stored carbon
raw_text:
Indonesia's El Niño–driven peat fires are choking the region—and releasing centuries of stored carbon
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
Right now, people in parts of Indonesia are inhaling what may be the most polluted atmosphere on Earth. As the historically large 2026 El Niño intensifies, parts of Southeast Asia have been plunged into an air quality crisis of catastrophic proportions.
Smoke from fires has driven concentrations of dangerous and tiny particulate matter, known as PM2.5, to extreme levels—creating a public health emergency threatening millions of lives.
The World Health Organization (WHO) stipulates a maximum breathable "safe limit" of 15 micrograms per cubic meter of PM2.5 across a 24-hour average. In haze-affected parts of Indonesia, this year's concentrations have routinely exceeded 500 micrograms, and even 1,000 in places—that's more than 65 times the WHO maximum.
This is not the kind of polluted air you might find on a smoggy day in most parts of the world—it is a toxic atmosphere considered by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to be "hazardous." The delayed effects of breathing such air include increased risk of heart attack, stroke and a host of respiratory illnesses.
The roots of the crisis
The catalyst for this year's crisis is a collision between meteorological events and decades of changes to Indonesia's landscape. The historically intense El Niño has brought a punishing dry spell across the archipelago, leaving the landscape parched.
But the weather is only the match; land management practices provide the fuel.
Historically, lowland tropical forests growing on peat soils were naturally resistant to fire because of their moist conditions. However, deforestation for agriculture, forest fragmentation and peatland drainage have drastically altered the landscape and increased its flammability.
The effects can extend beyond the areas directly cleared or drained: even untouched forest close to degraded areas will have lost some of its natural fire resistance. The El Niño–driven drought has supercharged these changes, making it easier for fires to take hold and spread.
The hidden cost of peat fires
Fire is widely used across the region to help prepare land for agriculture, clear low-lying vegetation or to burn household waste. Yet, when fires are set during a drought, they can ignite the drained peatland soil and escape into the surrounding landscape.
A peat fire does not simply flame and pass; it also smolders downward into the ground, sometimes burning for weeks or months. An alarming consequence of peat fires is the release of ancient carbon—organic matter that has been safely locked away for hundreds of years. This carbon generally won't be reabsorbed by future forest growth, as the land has been repurposed for agriculture. It is a permanent transfer of carbon from land into the air.
This year alone, Indonesia's fires have released an estimated 175 million metric tons of carbon, equivalent to three-quarters of the country's annual fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions and exceeding the combined annual fossil-fuel and industrial CO₂ emissions of the U.K. and France.
The scale of the 2026 fire and haze marks a setback after some years of progress. There has been a promising downward trend in regional fire activity, due in part to improved fire management and efforts at "rewetting" peatlands to make them less flammable.
The severity of the current El Niño has interrupted this good work. Satellite analysis indicates more than 120,000 fire hotspot detections across Indonesia so far—fewer than in 2015 (another El Niño year), but seven times as many as in 2025.
The human and economic cost of the resulting haze is staggering, and many will likely perish from the effects of the toxic smoke. The haze has also drifted beyond Indonesia, at times blanketing neighboring Malaysia, Brunei, southern Thailand and Singapore.
The health effects of wildfire smoke extend around the world. Globally, exposure contributes to a million or more premature deaths each year, including almost one in 10 deaths of children under 5.
From detection to prevention
Worryingly, the number of fires in Indonesia could be underestimated as satellites are less effective at detecting the lower temperatures of smoldering peat fires. New technologies designed to better detect these fires could help authorities identify them sooner and respond more quickly, provided the data can be rapidly delivered to those who need it.
But better detection and fire suppression can only do so much. In many areas, the key action is to restore drained peatlands so they are less vulnerable to fire in the first place. A new national peatland and mangrove management agency is being established with this remit.
For now, the immediate prognosis remains bleak. It is hard to extinguish underground peat fires once they have taken hold, and the 2026 El Niño is projected to intensify until the end of the year. The immediate crisis will eventually end, but reducing the risk of future disasters will require Indonesia to restore and protect its peatlands with renewed vigor.

title: When consumers search 'cyclospora,' bagged salad sales take the hit
raw_text:
When consumers search 'cyclospora,' bagged salad sales take the hit
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
This year, the U.S. saw its highest annual count of confirmed Cyclospora cases, roughly 20,000, according to the CDC. New research published in Risk Analysis examines outbreaks from 2018 to 2022 and finds that the retail losses associated with these events vary with how much public attention the outbreak draws.
The study, conducted by researchers at The Ohio State University and the University of Florida, found that weekly bagged salad purchases were 3.89% lower on average during outbreak and recall periods, for an estimated retail loss of roughly $374 million.
Cyclospora cayetanensis, the parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, can survive standard chlorine washes at processing plants and live in soil or water for months. Symptoms of the infection include watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, bloating and loss of appetite. Most cases resolve on their own, but people with weakened immune systems can develop severe or prolonged illness, and, in rare cases, even die.
Large outbreaks were relatively rare before 2018. In 2018, reported outbreaks were linked to 1,165 illnesses nationwide, across both multistate events and smaller local clusters. Since then, annual outbreaks have sickened thousands of people and posed a substantial financial risk to the produce sector.
The study examined six large multistate outbreaks, four of which were linked to salad products. At the time of the analysis, these six accounted for 2,157 illnesses, or 65% of the 3,344 outbreak-associated cyclosporiasis cases reported to the National Outbreak Reporting System between 2018 and 2022.
To examine how consumers responded, researchers analyzed household purchasing data and Google search activity for "Cyclospora" across 210 media markets. Search volume served as a proxy for public attention to news coverage, public health notices and social media.
The study found that retailers did not meaningfully restrict supply during outbreaks or recall periods, suggesting that food safety concerns, not empty shelves, were the more likely explanation for the decline in purchases. Purchases were lower in outbreak-affected states, and also in states with no reported outbreak that shared a media market with an affected state.
The size of the decline varied with what people searched for. Searches for "Cyclospora" were linked to the steepest declines, while general salad-related searches were linked to much smaller ones.
The 2018 and 2020 outbreaks were associated with the largest retail losses, at $79 million and nearly $190 million, respectively. The 2020 salad outbreak was the largest single event in the study, at 771 illnesses, but search volume ran higher during the 2018 outbreaks. The authors note that the COVID-19 pandemic dominated media attention in 2020, which may have muted consumer response to that outbreak.
"What people read online shows up in what they put in their carts," said Xuerui Yang, a study author and former Ph.D. student at The Ohio State University, now a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences. "Balanced risk communication and consistent monitoring of search activity during high-stakes outbreaks can help anticipate where demand losses will concentrate."

title: Armored amphibian lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago, fossils suggest
raw_text:
Scientists report fossil evidence of the first fully marine amphibian in a study from the University of California, Davis; Peking University; and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. The amphibian is an armored, giant salamander–sized, bottom-dwelling ocean creature that the researchers named Gerrothorax maritimus.
The research, published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution, is based on the analysis of two nearly complete skeletons that date to the Late Triassic period nearly 237 million years ago. The fossils were discovered in an area of China's Guizhou province that was once covered by ocean and located hundreds of miles from large landmasses.
"This area is part of an ecosystem that we've been looking at and trying to reconstruct," said study corresponding author Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis. "We've been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian and it's a sort of very unusual member of the lineage."
Of the over 8,000 species of modern amphibians, none have been known to live in fully marine environments, and fewer than 2% exhibit some degree of salt tolerance. This is odd given that other four-limbed animals—including mammals, reptiles and birds—all have species capable of surviving without food or water from land. Additionally, no evidence of a fully marine amphibian exists in the fossil record.
Until now.
What did Gerrothorax maritimus look like?
Thanks to the pristine nature of the skeleton specimens, the researchers could reconstruct how Gerrothorax maritimus looked and lived in its ocean environment.
Notably, the amphibian had a flattened body that was covered in bony armor, a potential defense mechanism against predators like ichthyosaurs. The animal was almost 3 feet (0.9 meters) long with a disk-shaped body.
"If you think about today's amphibians, this animal is unusual because it's big," Motani said. "It's probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what's different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky."
Based on Gerrothorax maritimus' bony armor and the shape of its skull, the researchers hypothesize that the creature was a bottom-dwelling suction feeder.
"They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in," said Motani, who noted the feeding style is similar to the wobbegong, a modern, bottom-dwelling carpet shark.
Why can't today's amphibians live in salt water?
Today's amphibians are unable to live in marine environments due to their salt-intolerant skin.
"That skin is permeable, and that allows the animals to use it for multiple purposes," said Motani. "They use it for respiration and water intake, so amphibians don't drink or breathe through the mouth because they can do both through the skin."
This function of amphibian biology requires them to live in or near freshwater environments. While some modern species such as the crab-eating frog exhibit degrees of salt tolerance, they lose weight in brackish waters and need to recover in fresh water.
The researchers propose that Gerrothorax maritimus circumvented this limitation thanks to its bony armor and more fishlike biology. The armor would have prevented water absorption through its skin, requiring the amphibian to drink salt water with its mouth, which it would absorb through its digestive tract. The creature's gills, which are present in the Gerrothorax genus, would have allowed it to filter out the salt.
How did researchers determine Gerrothorax maritimus lived in the ocean?
In addition to the fossils being found in deep-sea sediments, Motani said the fact that the specimens were nearly complete skeletons led the researchers to believe Gerrothorax maritimus was ocean-dwelling.
"Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom," said Motani. "But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived."
Additionally, the researchers conducted geochemical analyses of the fossils, which revealed that the proportion of strontium isotopes in the fossils closely resembled those that would be seen in the oceans of the Late Triassic.

title: People may have preexisting immunity to bird flu
raw_text:
How immune are people to bird flu viruses? To find out, Canadian virologists analyzed blood samples that 24 health care workers at Université de Montréal's teaching hospital, the CHUM, gave before and after getting their annual flu shot.
They then assessed the ability of antibodies in that blood to recognize various strains of influenza virus, including several of the highly contagious and widespread H5 variety found in North America and Asia.
The result? Before vaccination, most participants already had antibodies against the viruses, the researchers found. In some cases, these antibodies were able to neutralize the viruses and eliminate cells displaying viral proteins on their surface.
The finding is published this month in the Journal of Virology.
"Raises important questions"
"What particularly surprised us was that in several participants this cross-reactivity was already present before vaccination," said the study's first author, Katrina Dionne, a UdeM doctoral student supervised by UdeM immunologist Andrés Finzi.
"This raises important questions about how our previous exposure to influenza viruses may influence our response to new avian influenza viruses," said Dionne.
Preexisting immunity may result from previous exposure to different influenza viruses or from vaccinations received over the years, Dionne and Finzi believe, suggesting that each person's immune history helps shape their ability to recognize new related viruses.
Some caution advised
The study also shows that, in some people, seasonal vaccination against the H1N1 and H3N2 strains induces antibodies that are capable of recognizing H5Nx viruses. However, the researchers did not observe a marked increase in this cross-reactivity following vaccination.
Hence it's unclear whether the seasonal flu shot protects against H5N1 or other emerging avian influenza viruses, the researchers say. So it's important that vaccines be developed that specifically target these viruses when future outbreaks occur, they add.
"This study gives us a better understanding of the extent of immunity already present in the population against certain avian influenza viruses," said Finzi, a researcher in the immunopathology research lab of the CHUM's research center, the CRCHUM.
"This knowledge could contribute to the development of vaccination strategies offering broader protection against future emerging influenza viruses," he said.

title: One extra quantum dot helps balance speed and stability in spin qubits
raw_text:
Quantum computers need qubits that can be controlled both quickly and reliably. Yet making semiconductor spin qubits faster often makes them more sensitive to electrical noise, creating a difficult trade-off.
Researchers at the University of Osaka and their collaborators have now demonstrated a way to loosen this constraint by adding one extra quantum dot, allowing speed and noise resistance to be tuned more independently after the device has been made.
The research is published in the journal npj Quantum Information.
An extra dot reshapes electron energies
Quantum dots are tiny regions in a semiconductor that can confine individual electrons. In conventional flopping-mode spin qubits, two quantum dots are used to move an electron between locations, enabling fast electrical control of its spin. However, the same conditions that increase operating speed can also make the qubit more vulnerable to small voltage fluctuations.
The researchers added a third, auxiliary quantum dot whose energy could be adjusted electrically. By tuning this extra dot, they reshaped the electron's orbital energy structure, a strategy they call orbital band engineering. This created a broader operating region that was less sensitive to voltage noise while preserving the strong coupling needed for fast spin control.
The team achieved operating frequencies above 100 MHz, reaching 271 ± 20 MHz under another tuning condition.
Feedback improves gate fidelity
They also combined the device design with machine learning–based feedback that continuously corrected slow shifts in qubit frequency. This extended the estimated dephasing time from about 52 nanoseconds to 580 nanoseconds. Randomized benchmarking showed a 4-nanosecond gate fidelity of 99.56% with feedback, rising to 99.72% with additional pulse optimization.
"In GaAs quantum dots, magnetic noise makes fast electrical control particularly important, while electrical control also makes voltage noise relevant," says Takafumi Fujita. "By adding an auxiliary quantum dot, we introduced an extra degree of freedom for tuning the qubit frequency and could explore operating regions that are less sensitive to electrical noise."
The approach could provide a useful design principle for correcting device-to-device variations after manufacturing, a key challenge when scaling semiconductor quantum computers to very large numbers of qubits. The researchers expect that the concept could also be applied to silicon- and germanium-based spin qubits.

title: Expanding hemp could boost Kentucky water quality and ecological diversity
raw_text:
Hemp has long been pitched to Kentucky farmers as a way to diversify their income. Research now suggests it could diversify the landscape itself, with measurable benefits for the state's water and wildlife.
Tyler Mark, Ph.D., an agricultural economist in the University of Kentucky Martin-Gatton College of Agriculture, Food and Environment (CAFE), co-authored the paper published in Applied Economic Perspectives and Policy alongside researchers at Mississippi State University and Central State University.
The study examined what happens to Kentucky's environment when hemp constitutes a larger share of the state's farmland. The team found that more hemp means more crop diversity, which is linked to cleaner water and a wider variety of birds.
Kentucky is one of the nation's leading hemp-producing states. According to the USDA 2026 National Hemp Report, Kentucky farmers planted 4,800 acres (1,940 hectares) of industrial hemp in 2025. Now, much of the conversation around the crop has centered on markets and prices, particularly as growers in a state with deep tobacco roots look for new options. The researchers wanted to look at a less-discussed side of the equation.
"Profitability, while important, is only part of the story," Mark said. "Hemp can also impact the environment. If hemp acres are going to expand, then we also need to understand and quantify these impacts."
Landscapes planted with diverse crops tend to offer more varied habitat for wildlife and can reduce the nutrient runoff that degrades streams and lakes. When a new crop like hemp enters rotations alongside corn, soybeans, hay and tobacco, it adds to that mix.
To measure the effect, the researchers took a two-pronged approach using county-level data from across the commonwealth.
First, they ran a series of simulations in which hemp planting increased from 1% to 10% of Kentucky's total agricultural land. In every scenario, crop diversity rose steadily as hemp acreage expanded. Next, the researchers used statistical models that follow counties over time to estimate how changes in crop diversity relate to environmental conditions.
Second, to assess water quality, the authors looked at water clarity, dissolved oxygen and phosphorus levels. For wildlife, they looked at bird diversity, a common indicator of overall habitat health. Economists call these "nonmarket" benefits. No one is directly paid for them, but everyone downstream benefits.
By linking the two steps, the team could estimate how much a hemp-driven bump in crop diversity would shift those environmental measures.
There's a catch, though. The study found the ecological payoff depends on scale. A handful of small hemp plots scattered across the state may help individual farmers' bottom lines without making much of a difference for water or wildlife. The broader benefits occur only when hemp, and the biological diversity it brings, reaches a large enough share of the landscape.
That finding carries implications for policy. Programs aimed at small-scale farmers tend to focus on helping them turn a profit, which the authors note is a worthy goal on its own. But if policymakers also want hemp to deliver environmental returns, the researchers say practical, proactive measures will be needed to bring more smallholders into hemp production so their combined acreage adds up to real change on the land.
"Hemp has the potential to be another crop Kentucky producers can add to their crop rotation once regulatory clarity allows the market to mature," Mark said. "This would give Kentucky producers another crop, one with benefits beyond profitability."

title: 27 exoplanet targets for the world's first private space telescope
raw_text:
The Lazuli Space Telescope will be the first private space telescope. It's the brainchild of Eric Schmidt, Google's former CEO. It will have a 3-meter mirror (9.8 feet), larger than Hubble's 2.4-meter mirror (7.9 feet), and will be launched by 2029.
Lazuli will have three instruments: a wide-field optical imager, an integral field spectrograph and the ExtraSolar Coronagraph (ESC).
New research proposes a list of targets for the ESC. It's titled "The first selection of optimal targets for the Lazuli ExtraSolar Coronagraph's reflected starlight exoplanet campaign" and is available at arXiv.org. The authors are Logan Pearce from the Department of Astronomy at the University of Michigan and Ewan Douglas from the Steward Observatory at the University of Arizona.
"Direct detection and characterization of exoplanet atmospheres via reflected starlight enables probes of composition of mature exoplanet systems (since flux is decoupled from age) at closer separations than via thermal emission (due to observations in visible wavelengths), and even probes of biosignatures," the authors write.
The telescope's ESC will be especially important in this context. Characterizing exoplanet atmospheres in mature exoplanet systems with reflected starlight means the observations will not depend on an exoplanet's leftover heat from formation.
As planets age, they emit less leftover heat and become dimmer. By using reflected starlight, the ESC will bypass that effect. It will also allow observations at closer separations than an infrared telescope, meaning it can observe planets closer to their stars, because planets closer to their stars reflect more light. (That's a simplified picture that ignores some details.)
"To date all exoplanets have been imaged through their self-luminous thermal emission, but direct, spatially resolved imaging of planets via reflected starlight is on the near horizon," the authors write.
"Reflected light imaging enables detection and characterization of planets decoupled from age (since reflected starlight luminosity does not decrease with age), and the smaller resolution limits provided by imaging shorter wavelengths (∼0.5–2μm), where the star luminosity peaks, allow access to closer-in planets compared to thermal emission."
The researchers present a list of 27 targets for observations with the ESC, and all of them are giant exoplanets. "Our target list spans ages and temperatures of planets not probed before by direct imaging," the authors write, adding that some of them will also be accessible to the ELT's METIS thermal imager and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope's coronagraphic instrument. The targets will benefit from synergies created by multiple observations, and that will "provide comprehensive atmosphere characterization."
While observations with the ESC will be valuable and open a new pathway to observing potential biosignatures, there are some constraints, particularly the required exposure times. "The high contrasts involved in reflected light detection (𝒪 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁹) and subsequent long exposure times (10s–100s of hours) make uninformed searches challenging for a 3m class observatory," the authors explain.
"Campaign efficiency can be dramatically improved by targeting known planets and leveraging well-constrained orbital priors in order to prioritize targets and time observations for the maximum likelihood of detection."
The list of targets is based on exoplanets with well-known orbits, since that will make the best use of observing time.
Those interested in exoplanets may recognize some of the 27 giant exoplanets on the list:
- 55 Cancri d, notable for being a Jupiter analog.
- HD 181433 d, notable because it follows a highly eccentric orbit and is part of an exoplanet family that also features an ultrashort-period super-Earth.
- β Pic b, notable because it was one of the first exoplanets to be directly imaged and also interacts with a well-known debris disk.
A private space telescope is something not seen before. It remains to be seen how effective it will be. It also remains to be seen what private ownership might mean—whether it makes the telescope more efficient, introduces unanticipated problems or both.
Ultimately, it's all about the contribution it makes to exoplanet science.
"Our target list expands direct imaging of gas giant planets into regimes colder than previously imaged, probing mature exoplanet systems, with some overlap with Roman CGI and ELT-METIS imaging, providing more comprehensive atmosphere characterization through synergies with those platform capabilities," the authors conclude.

title: Both selfishness and generosity distort how we see our impact, but the selfish view is more contagious
raw_text:
People can sometimes make decisions that benefit them but are less advantageous for someone else. In these scenarios, they might convince themselves that their choice causes little harm to others or that an alternative would not make much of a difference. The same can happen in reverse, as people who act generously may overstate how much good the outcomes of their choices did for others.
Researchers at the University of Zurich recently carried out a study investigating the possibility that people could use this ambiguity, particularly when the outcomes of a decision are uncertain, to portray their actions more favorably. Their findings, published in Nature Human Behaviour, suggest that when outcomes are uncertain, people's interpretations can favor what they want to do, regardless of whether their choices prioritize themselves or others.
"In public and private discourse, actions often come with a moral label: taking the train is 'better' than flying, paying extra for fair-trade products is 'better' than buying the cheapest option," Marius C. Vollberg, first author of the paper, told Phys.org.
"What struck me is that people often describe the consequences of their actions with great confidence, even though the exact consequences are usually unknown. Someone who flew may claim it made no difference; someone who took the train may claim it did a lot of good."
The team's study originated when Vollberg met his co-author Jörg Gross at a conference held by the Swiss Center for Affective Sciences. At the event, Gross presented work on the idea of "moral wiggle room," which suggests that people can use their ignorance of social consequences to act selfishly.
"At the time, the debates about whether to stay on or leave a certain social media platform were everywhere, and, as with so many debates, it seemed like neither side evaluated the consequences objectively," said Vollberg. "Most research had focused on distortions that excuse selfishness. But I was curious whether the prosocial side distorts too, in what direction, and what these distortions do to the people exposed to them."
Testing people's choices when outcomes are uncertain
As part of their new study, Vollberg and Gross carried out nine online experiments involving 8,769 participants, most of whom were living in the U.S. The main task that participants completed was built around one simple choice.
People could choose between a selfish option and one that benefited another at a cost to themselves. If they made the selfish decision, they received seven points and another participant received between one and three points. If they selected the prosocial one, they received five points, while the other received between three and five points.
"So, their own payoff was certain, but the other person's was only known as a range," explained Vollberg. "After choosing, participants estimated what the other person had received, and what they would have received under the other option, with a bonus for accurate guesses. The key feature of this design is that systematic deviations from the middle of the range can be interpreted as a distortion."
The researchers carried out several variants of this online experiment. Collectively, these versions allowed them not only to document distortions in the participants' estimates but also to shed some light on the psychological processes behind the observed patterns.
"We tested whether distortions appear before a choice is made, whether they persist when people are assigned a choice rather than making it freely, and whether people distort in the same way when they themselves are on the receiving end of an uncertain payoff," said Vollberg.
"In further experiments, we showed the distorted estimates to observers, who rated how trustworthy the chooser seemed, and to new participants, who saw a previous participant's estimates before making their own choice. That last step let us measure whether distortions influence other people."
Vollberg and Gross found that both selfish and prosocial choosers tended to describe the outcome of their decision in ways that made them look better. People who made the selfish choice inflated its benefit to the other person while downplaying the benefit of the alternative, making the two options seem more similar and their choice appear less costly to others.
On the other hand, people who made the prosocial choice tended to exaggerate how much better their decision was for the other person. In some cases, they also inflated their prediction of what the other person would have received under the choice they had rejected, making their relative sacrifice seem larger.
"You might think that we are just documenting how people justify the choices they already made," said Vollberg. "However, the distortions also appeared before people chose, and under forced choice they tracked what people would have chosen freely rather than what they were forced to choose."
The researchers also found that when the uncertain payoff was that of the participants, rather than someone else's, their choices did not reflect the distortions they had reported for others. This hints at a double standard. In a separate experiment, the observed distortion patterns appeared to make choosers appear more trustworthy to observers who were told the participants' estimates were the true outcomes of the experiment.
"Only the selfish-serving distortion was contagious: people who saw it adopted it and chose the selfish option more often, whereas the prosocial-serving distortion did not sway others," said Vollberg. "Fewer than one in 10 participants produced the selfish-serving pattern. But if that pattern spreads more readily than the prosocial one, a small minority can shift how a whole group behaves."
Possible implications for understanding people's behavior
This study offers insights that could guide behavioral science interventions. For instance, the team's findings suggest that disagreements about climate action, consumption, foreign aid or social welfare may arise not only from different values but also from people's interpretations of an issue's consequences.
"These disagreements could arise not only in how people value different outcomes, but in what they interpret the outcome to be," said Vollberg. "As our experiments are deliberately abstract and our participants were mostly U.S.-based, how exactly these distortions play out in specific domains and other cultures remains to be seen. One of the key open questions is why only the selfish-serving distortion spreads."
One possible explanation for why selfish-serving distortion spreads is that people find it easier to accept explanations that support what they already want to do than those encouraging them to change their behavior. For instance, an explanation such as "taking a flight has no impact" does not require a listener to change their behavior. This could be easier to accept than "your donation does a lot of good," which implicitly suggests that donating is the right thing to do. This hypothesis could be tested in future studies.
"From this perspective, it is less about how convincing each kind of distortion is than about what it would cost to follow it," added Vollberg.
"Beyond that, we would like to test distortions and their contagion in applied settings such as consumption and charitable giving, with more diverse samples, and to look at social judgments beyond trustworthiness. Critically, understanding why the asymmetry exists is also what would tell us where to intervene."

title: Plants may switch between reproductive strategies more easily than thought
raw_text:
When it comes to reproduction, plants have options. Some can fertilize themselves, while others rely on pollen from genetically different plants. Many populations even contain a mixture of both strategies. But scientists have long debated whether this mixed approach is truly stable or simply a temporary stage on the way from one reproductive strategy to another.
A new study led by Dr. Tamar Friedlander, Dr. Amit Jangid and professor Ohad Noy Feldheim from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem suggests that the answer may be more complicated than previously thought. Researchers identified a previously undescribed state in which plants capable of self-fertilization and plants that require a partner can coexist over long periods, even though the proportions of each group may fluctuate dramatically.
The trade-offs of self-fertilization
For flowering plants, the choice between self-fertilization and cross-fertilization comes with important trade-offs.
Self-fertilization can be useful when potential mates or pollinators are scarce. A plant does not have to depend on pollen arriving from another individual to reproduce. However, repeatedly reproducing with itself can increase the likelihood that harmful genetic mutations will affect its offspring, a phenomenon known as "inbreeding depression."
Many plants avoid this problem through a genetic mechanism called self-incompatibility, which essentially allows a plant to recognize and reject its own pollen. The system promotes reproduction between genetically different individuals and helps maintain diversity within a population. Self-incompatibility is found in about 40% of plant families and occurs in agriculturally important groups that include wild tomatoes, potatoes, apples, pears, citrus fruits and coffee.
But these systems are not foolproof. Various genetic changes can disrupt the self-incompatibility mechanism, allowing some plants to become self-compatible and fertilize themselves. As a result, populations can contain both self-compatible and self-incompatible plants.
Coexistence without a fixed balance
The question is what happens next.
Until now, one influential idea has been that such mixed populations are largely transitional. Eventually, one reproductive strategy should take over. Alternatively, it was proposed that mixed populations could exist in fixed and stable proportions. Friedlander and her colleagues used computer simulations of evolving plant populations to test whether these assumptions necessarily hold.
They found three possible outcomes. A population could become entirely self-compatible, entirely self-incompatible or remain in a mixed state containing both types.
It was the third outcome that surprised the researchers.
Rather than settling into a stable balance, the proportions of self-compatible and self-incompatible plants could rise and fall considerably over time. Yet despite these fluctuations, neither strategy disappeared. The researchers describe this as a "volatile mixed mode," a population that is constantly changing but nonetheless remains mixed over very long periods.
"What surprised us was that instability does not necessarily mean that a population is on its way to one final state," the researchers said. "In our model, self-compatible and self-incompatible plants can coexist for a very long time while their proportions continually change, even in the absence of fluctuations in external conditions. It suggests that what may look like a temporary or unstable situation in nature could actually be a persistent evolutionary state."
The researchers examined two major forces that can influence which reproductive strategy succeeds. One was the genetic cost of self-fertilization, or how severely offspring are affected by inbreeding. The second involved the tolerance of the molecular recognition system plants use to determine which pollen they accept.
By changing these conditions in their simulations, the team was able to map when each of the three reproductive states was likely to emerge.
Pollen shortages can favor cross-fertilization
The study, published in PRX Life, also produced a counterintuitive result concerning pollen shortages.
A shortage of pollen, which can occur when pollinators are scarce or when plants move into new environments, might be expected to favor self-fertilization. After all, a plant that can reproduce by itself has an apparent advantage when external pollen is difficult to find.
However, the researchers' model showed that pollen limitation could actually expand the conditions under which self-incompatibility is maintained. The reasoning behind this is that pollen limitation puts different selection pressures on the evolution of male and female parts of the self-incompatibility system. When these are taken into account, the outcome was more complex than the simple assumption that fewer pollinators should automatically favor self-fertilization.
The findings may also challenge the idea that the evolutionary shift from self-incompatibility to self-fertilization is necessarily a one-way street. Under many of the conditions tested in the model, populations could potentially move in either direction between reproductive strategies. Under certain conditions, a population that had shifted toward self-fertilization could therefore return to a system favoring cross-fertilization.
Testing the model in wild populations
The researchers stress that the study is theoretical. Mixed populations containing self-compatible and self-incompatible plants have already been observed in nature, but long-term studies tracking how the proportions of the two groups change are still lacking. Such field studies will be necessary to determine whether the long-lasting fluctuating state predicted by the model occurs in real populations.
Understanding these dynamics could become increasingly important as plants face changing environmental conditions. Climate change, shifting habitats and declining pollinator populations may all alter the pressures that determine how plants reproduce.
By showing that reproductive strategies do not always settle neatly into one state or another, the study offers a new way of thinking about how plant populations adapt and persist.
Rather than evolution always pushing a population toward a single reproductive solution, sometimes the lasting solution may be to keep changing.

title: Perseverance offers clues to protect crews from ultrafine Mars dust
raw_text:
Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA's Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including particles small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and could inform spacesuit and habitat design, dust-removal procedures and crew health standards for future NASA missions to Mars.
"NASA has a long history of turning challenges into workable solutions and of finding creative ways to use the data that we have to answer questions beyond what it was originally collected for," said Lindsay Hays, acting director of the Planetary Science Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "Dust has been a surface-exploration challenge since the Apollo program. Perseverance is giving our engineers and flight surgeons measurements they can use to improve our existing designs well before the first American astronauts arrive on Mars."
Lunar dust scratched visors, degraded outer spacesuit layers and damaged their seals during NASA's Apollo missions, and some crew members reported symptoms similar to hay fever.
Rounded by wind-driven collisions with other particles, dust grains on Mars are less abrasive than those on the moon. They also are enriched in sulfur, chlorine and iron and contain more silica than lunar dust. Regional and global dust storms on Mars can keep the grains recirculating throughout the atmosphere as well.
The rover carries a set of five samples of spacesuit material. The swatches, each three-quarters of an inch (20 millimeters) square, are part of a calibration target used to test the settings of SHERLOC (Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman and Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals), an instrument on Perseverance's robotic arm.
The calibration target for another instrument that provided the dust measurements, called PIXL (Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry), carries a sample of Teflon and of basaltic glass.
Because Teflon contains no elements that PIXL can directly detect, whatever elemental signals the X-ray spectrometer picks up from that sample come from dust resting on it.
The team also analyzed swatches of Teflon and Vectran, two materials used in spacesuits, on SHERLOC's calibration target. NASA sent the swatches to Mars to study how spacesuit materials hold up on the planet's surface.
"Perseverance's main job is to search for signs of ancient microbial life, but the mission was also designed to help prepare for human explorers. That effort includes technology demonstrations like MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment) and Ingenuity, as well as the spacesuit samples," said Katie Stack Morgan, Perseverance's project scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.
Fine, ultrafine
While earlier measurements on Mars resolved dust particles down to about 3 micrometers across, PIXL detected two categories of even smaller particles: fine particles measuring less than 2.5 micrometers (a human hair is about 70 micrometers wide) and ultrafine particles around 100 nanometers (about 700 times thinner than a human hair). Particles on PIXL's Teflon target and SHERLOC's Vectran swatch averaged about 2 micrometers. On PIXL's basaltic glass and SHERLOC's Teflon swatch, dust particle sizes ranged down to about 100 to 300 nanometers.
Static electricity appears to determine which size dust particles stick to which surface. Dust grains become charged as they collide in the air, and different materials on the calibration target attract grains of different sizes. The finest particles stayed attached through years of driving and drilling. Organic polymers like SHERLOC's Teflon spacesuit sample are common in the outer layers of spacesuits, and the results show they readily collect fine dust.
The study also found that some materials hold less dust than others, which could guide future choices of materials and protective coatings for spacesuits and habitats. Designs such as suitports, which let astronauts enter a suit attached to the outside of a habitat, and dual-chamber airlocks could reduce how much dust gets inside astronauts' living quarters.
"The existence of Mars dust at these ultrafine sizes has been predicted for a long time, and PIXL gave us the chance to measure it directly on Mars," said Scott VanBommel, a Perseverance scientist at Washington University in St. Louis and the paper's lead author. "The larger clumps, the Martian dust bunnies, get shaken off over time. But the smallest particles stay behind, and those are the ones that pose the greatest challenge for human support systems."
Chemically, the dust matches the iron- and sulfur-rich composition that earlier missions measured. The PIXL instrument also found the dust to be enriched in phosphorus and detected signs of calcium sulfate.
Protecting crews
On Earth, airborne particles, or particulate matter, below 2.5 micrometers (that is, fine particles) are tied to a range of negative health effects because they can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Studies have shown that ultrafine particles (those no larger than 100 nanometers) can travel from the nasal cavity to the brain along the olfactory nerve.
Martian dust is composed predominantly of silicate minerals and carries chemically reactive compounds, including perchlorates that can disrupt thyroid function and reactive iron that induces cellular damage. Scientists believe that the health risks of Mars dust depend on the quantity of dust and length of exposure.
The PIXL results are the first on-site measurements of fine and ultrafine particles on Mars, and this research can inform broader efforts to refine indoor dust-exposure limits for astronauts, develop safe habits and establish ways to remove dust while exploring Mars.
NASA is already working on solutions to extraterrestrial dust hazards, using ground test facilities and lunar missions as proving grounds for future Mars explorers. In March 2025, the agency tested an Electrodynamic Dust Shield, which used electric fields to clear lunar regolith from glass and thermal radiator surfaces on the moon. Developed at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, it landed on the moon aboard Firefly Aerospace's Blue Ghost Mission 1.
At NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, engineers at the Lunar Development and Test Facility use vacuum chambers and lunar regolith simulant to test spacesuit components, mechanisms and a Handheld Lunar Electrostatic Dust Mitigation tool ahead of Artemis missions to the lunar surface.
Provided by NASA

title: Q&A: Why does the right side of the brain control the left side of the body?
raw_text:
Dr. Martin Wessendorf is a neuroscientist and an associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota. His work focuses on how the brainstem controls the function of neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang also researches the brain, focusing on cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases.
They are the authors of a new article in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy that explores several brain circuits in four-limbed animals that are cross-wired (meaning one side of the brain connects with the opposite side of the body). It proposes a novel hypothesis about how they might have evolved.
If you've studied neuroanatomy, you might have wondered about the brain's cross-wiring and its evolutionary history. We'll go over different pathways and then propose our hypothesis on why most of these contralateral (midline-crossing) pathways evolved.
How information gets from the eyes into the brain
The story begins with sensory input from the eyes. Because the lens of the eye reverses the image on the retina, what the eye sees to the right of us forms an image on the left side of the retina and vice versa. The optic nerve carries this information to the optic chiasm, where the nerve fibers responsible for the right visual field are separated out and directed to the left half of the brain. This process is mirrored for the left visual field. Our visual inputs target, among other things, an ancient structure called the optic tectum.
The optic tectum (which in mammals is called the superior colliculus) is a structure in the midbrain that generates rapid responses to what we see. Information from each visual field is mapped to the opposite side of the optic tectum. In its deeper layers, physical sensations (somatosensory information) are mapped as well. The optic tectum is present in all vertebrate species and, as a result, appears to be among the oldest neuroanatomical structures in vertebrates.
How information about the body gets to the brain
We address two neural pathways that mediate physical sensations in most of the body. Both cross the midline of the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord), and both appear to be present in all tetrapod species (the animals with four limbs, including mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians).
The dorsal column pathway mediates light touch, vibration and body position. As the name suggests, it transmits sensations from the limbs and body by ascending the dorsal column in the spinal cord. It then connects to another neuron and crosses the midline in the brainstem, which is located just above the spinal cord. Although fishes don't have this pathway, it has been observed in amphibians, birds, mammals and reptiles—demonstrating a highly conserved presence in tetrapods.
Meanwhile, the spinothalamic tract pathway carries information about pain, itch and some forms of touch from the body to the brain. Besides carrying different types of sensation, this tract differs from the dorsal column pathway by crossing the midline in the spinal cord itself. After this, it ascends and conveys its sensory information from the body to the thalamus: the part of the brain that sits just above the midbrain and processes much of the information about movement and sensation. A contralaterally organized spinothalamic tract has been found in birds, mammals, reptiles and even in some cartilaginous fishes: sharks and rays.
How information gets from the brain to the body
We also looked at three contralaterally organized pathways that control skeletal muscle.
First is the tectospinal pathway. The optic tectum receives visual input, but it also receives auditory and somatosensory inputs, which are mapped in registration with the visual inputs to the contralateral tectum. If you're about to enter a crosswalk and from the corner of your eye see an oncoming car, you turn toward it. This is one example of how the tectospinal pathway mediates responses to visual stimuli. It can mediate similar responses to auditory and tactile stimuli.
The motor component of this pathway originates from the deepest layers of the optic tectum and projects its axons to the contralateral spinal cord. This pathway is present in most tetrapods and some cartilaginous fishes.
The rubrospinal pathway is thought to facilitate limb control in animals. This pathway, large in most mammals, originates in the red nucleus of the midbrain before it projects to the contralateral spinal cord. It has been reported to exist in tetrapods and some cartilaginous fishes.
The corticospinal pathway, which in humans allows for our fine motor control, is a special case. While all vertebrates have a telencephalon—the front part of the brain making up most of its mass in humans—only in mammals does it contain a six-layered cerebral cortex. The six-layered cortex is responsible for higher-order functions like integration of different sensations with memory, motor control and language. The corticospinal tract can modulate either somatosensory input or, in the case of primates and a few other species, motor output.
In most mammals, the corticospinal pathway travels from the cerebral cortex of the brain, projects to the part of the spinal cord where sensations enter and modulates somatosensory input. In primates (including humans) and some other dexterous species, this pathway projects to the part of our spinal cord that controls our muscles and allows, for instance, fine control of the fingers.
Thus, depending on the species, the corticospinal pathway can be either a motor pathway or a pathway that modulates somatosensation. In both cases, the corticospinal tract crosses the brain midline. This suggests that we humans obtained our fine motor control by co-opting a circuit whose ancestral function was somatosensory control.
Evolution, the visionary engineer
All things considered, we propose that evolutionarily ancient visual pathways biased our central nervous systems toward being organized contralaterally—at least in tetrapods. Given that all living vertebrates have both an optic chiasm and a contralaterally organized optic tectum, we think that Cambrian-era jawless fishes that lived roughly 538 to 486 million years ago had both an optic chiasm and an optic tectum. It may be possible to test this hypothesis by examining fossilized remains of their skulls.
Since evolution is conservative in its innovations—it often retains and builds upon existing structures, pathways and mechanisms rather than inventing new ones—the organization of the visual system (and in particular, the optic tectum) may have defined the organizational principles required of the sensory and motor pathways that evolved later. We propose that contralateral organization didn't necessarily evolve as an adaptation, but because evolution is an engineer that builds with the foundation and materials it has at hand.
Provided by Frontiers

title: Q&A: Is AI making it harder to learn? What a former executive wants every student to know
raw_text:
When Miriam Friedel started working at Capital One in 2020, generative AI was still largely a research curiosity. By the time she left the company as vice president of machine learning engineering in 2026, AI tools were writing code, building applications and reshaping how people work.
We spoke to Friedel, who recently joined the University of Virginia School of Data Science faculty, about the realities of navigating school and work in the age of AI. In this interview, Friedel lays out the AI skills employers are looking for, explains how data science has changed and describes how this technology can be used to augment, but not replace, learning.
In the midst of the AI boom, is learning data science still relevant?
The hardest part of data science is understanding the right problem to solve. If you have a massive data set, AI can help you with some of the data exploration and modeling, but it can't tell you if you are solving the right problem in the first place. You need to understand why we are doing what we're doing. What are we trying to accomplish? How is this going to impact actual humans? Data science also requires a ton of business context, which isn't often available in a form that can be effectively used by AI.
What we teach at the School of Data Science is foundational to understanding how AI works. Loss functions, linear regression, gradient descent—these are the building blocks on the way to understanding transformers, the architecture on which LLMs are built. Ensuring that our students really understand the technical underpinnings of this technology is going to make them more able to use it with both technical rigor and skepticism.
Why is skepticism important as we integrate AI into our work and learning?
Blindly relying on LLMs can be problematic because they're so sycophantic. They often just tell you what you want to hear, and that's actually really bad for making impactful decisions. You need another human who's going to push back and make sure you are solving the right problem for the right reasons.
Generative AI systems produce output based on data they've seen before, and it could be complete garbage. The underlying model is saying, "This is my prediction. Here is what the user wants based on what they are asking and what I've seen."
LLMs do this on a more complex scale. Not understanding the nature of this technology can lead people to blindly trust what is coming out. You need to have a healthy skepticism about what you are seeing.
Part of that comes from your own knowledge and experience, and part of that comes from a more foundational understanding of data and how these models and systems work. We are working hard to instill this understanding in our students.
How can students use AI in a way that doesn't negatively affect their learning?
One thing that has been a big shift for me coming from industry is how to use AI when you have years (or even decades) of expertise versus when you're learning something for the first time. Many companies have associates using AI on things they are already experts on, so they have a good sense of how to gauge the output, and it can be a real accelerator. For students learning foundational concepts for the first time, they haven't yet built up the knowledge of how to best leverage AI.
If you're a student using AI, it should be for things that you can verify the answer to. If students are just putting things into Claude or ChatGPT and assuming the answer it gives is truthful without having any way to validate it, that's not a good use of AI and it can short-circuit your own learning process.
Being able to think through hard problems and get frustrated and push through—that's how you learn, and that's how you innovate. New things are created because some things are hard.
Use AI to refresh things in your mind that you know. If you've never built a linear regression in Python or R and you're trying to learn how it works and what the outputs are, AI can be incredibly helpful in getting you started and getting you unstuck, but you should do the hard thinking. Use AI like a TA, like a sparring partner, but you have to actually do the work. If it turns into, "I'm just going to have Claude tell me what to do," it's replacing your learning.
How is the AI boom changing the way data scientists work?
Claude Code really raised the bar in terms of the quality of the code that an LLM can generate. It can also help with things that can feel like drudgery or are not central to your learning process. Lately, I've been using it to help generate plots to share with my students. I can never remember plotting syntax, and AI helps free up my time to think through more foundational concepts I want to teach so I'm not getting bogged down in making a plot look exactly how I want it to.
At Capital One, we liked to try to automate everything but the creative thinking and problem-solving. Use these tools to free you up from the tasks that are repetitive and don't require a lot of human input. This gives us time to think about more complex and interesting problems.
What do employers mean when they say they want candidates with AI skills?
I usually like to answer this question by telling students what employers are not looking for. Typing a prompt into ChatGPT, waiting a few minutes and cutting and pasting the answer without review is not a skill.
Employers are looking for people who have the discernment to know both when an AI is an accelerator for pushing innovation and when it is getting things wrong. When I left Capital One, if you were committing code that was being written by an agent, you were saying, "I, the human, am responsible for what this code is doing."
When there is risk involved, they are looking for people who are going to have good judgment and can own that risk. This requires knowledge of coding best practices and systems design, and the ability to identify when things can fail. Having a deep understanding of technical fundamentals is going to make you much better at using AI effectively.
If you're a data scientist, employers want to know how you can effectively leverage AI to build pipelines or speed up the model development process. This might look like an agent that builds a model with certain knowledge or guardrails you have put in place.
If you are a researcher, employers are looking for someone who deeply understands the architecture of LLMs and how you might be able to contribute to the frontier.
If you're an engineer, employers are asking if you can build systems that leverage an LLM as one part of a broader ecosystem. They want to know that you can use AI tooling to both write code and build agents, and that you can properly test the generated code and be sure it's doing what you think it's doing.
Across the board, if you can build an app that uses AI or write a skill for repetitive tasks, you will be at an advantage.
What was your biggest challenge working in industry?
The hardest problems that I had to deal with as an executive were not technological challenges; they were figuring out the right problem to solve, executing on it and working with other humans. Technical skills matter, but effective communication and a willingness to solve problems are paramount.
That meant dealing with disappointment (both mine and others'), giving and receiving difficult feedback and managing conflicting viewpoints. Sometimes you need to make decisions for your team that might upset someone.
If you are interested in leadership, it is important to ask yourself, "Can I work hard to solve hard problems, and can I deal with other humans in a way that is fair and gracious?"

title: Greenhouse gas levels hit new record highs in 2025: UN
raw_text:
Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to new record highs in 2025, locking in climate impacts that will persist for centuries to come, the United Nations said Tuesday.
Levels of the three main greenhouse gases—the climate-warming carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide—all rose to unprecedented figures in 2025, the U.N.'s weather and climate agency said.
The World Meteorological Organization said the rise would lead to more long-term temperature increases for the planet.
The WMO's 22nd annual Greenhouse Gas Bulletin comes ahead of the COP31 U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, running from Nov. 9 to 20.
"Another year, another new record," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
"Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies.
"The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) has a very long lifetime and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries."
El Niño effect
The bulletin looks at greenhouse gas concentrations—the amount of those gases in the atmosphere—rather than new annual emissions amounts as the world burns more coal, oil and gas.
In 2025, carbon dioxide concentrations were at 426.8 parts per million (ppm), methane at 1,948 parts per billion, and nitrous oxide at 339.1 parts per billion.
That takes them respectively to 153%, 267% and 126% of the preindustrial levels witnessed before 1750.
Of the three major greenhouse gases, CO₂ accounts for about 66% of the warming effect on the climate.
Around half of the total CO₂ emitted each year remains in the atmosphere; the rest is absorbed by the land and oceans.
From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO₂ rose by 2.8 ppm—smaller than the record surge from 2023 to 2024 of 3.6 ppm.
WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova said this reflected the "recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Niño," the naturally occurring, climate-warming weather phenomenon.
"However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning."
It is also above the average growth rate over the past decade of 2.6 ppm—a figure that stood at 0.8 ppm in the 1960s.
Monitoring station data show that CO₂ levels have continued rising in 2026.
"Every additional part per million matters because it traps additional heat," Barrett told reporters.
"In effect, we are supercharging the ocean and the atmosphere. That means that heat waves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for."
Growing concerns over H₂, SF₆
Methane accounts for about 16% of the warming effect on the climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, though it has a much shorter lifetime than CO₂.
Around a third of methane emitted into the atmosphere comes from natural sources like wetlands, with the rest from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, landfills and biomass burning.
The bulletin said that as countries shift their energy systems toward decarbonization, more attention should be paid to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H₂) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆).
Used primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution, SF₆ has been rising steadily over the past three decades.
"Why should we be concerned? Because SF₆ has an atmospheric lifetime of up to 3,200 years. Its global warming potential is more than 24,000 times that of CO₂," Barrett told reporters.
Why H₂ levels have increased over the past decade is unknown, but it has begun to be used as an energy storage medium.

title: Greenhouse gases hit record highs, yet again
raw_text:
Levels of carbon dioxide (CO₂) and other major greenhouse gases in the atmosphere reached unprecedented highs in 2025, locking in more long-term warming for the planet, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
The WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin reported that the globally averaged surface concentration of CO₂ in 2025 was 426.8 parts per million, or 153% of the 1750 preindustrial baseline. Concentrations of methane and nitrous oxide—the second and third most important long-lived greenhouse gases related to human activities—also rose to record highs.
"Another year, another new record. Greenhouse gases are trapping an unprecedented amount of heat in the atmosphere, providing energy for more extreme weather and associated risks to our economies and societies. The past 11 years have been the warmest on record and this trend is set to continue. CO₂ has a very long lifetime and so will affect the global climate not just for years but for decades and even centuries," said WMO Deputy Secretary-General Ko Barrett.
WMO releases the bulletin, one of its flagship annual publications, to provide authoritative scientific information for negotiators at the U.N. climate conference. The COP 31 meeting in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9–20 is seeking to turn climate commitments into concrete actions.
CO₂ growth rates tripled
The bulletin reports on greenhouse gas concentrations—namely the amount of gas that accumulates in the atmosphere—and not new annual emissions. About half of the total CO₂ emitted each year remains in the atmosphere, and the rest is absorbed by Earth's land ecosystems and oceans.
When the bulletin was first published in 2004, the annual average level of CO₂ measured by WMO's Global Atmosphere Watch network of monitoring stations was 377.5 ppm.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Annual Greenhouse Gas Index shows that from 1990 to 2025, radiative forcing—the warming effect on our climate—by long-lived greenhouse gases increased by 56%, with CO₂ accounting for about 81% of this increase.
Growth rates of CO₂ have tripled since the 1960s, accelerating from an annual average increase of 0.8 ppm to 2.4 ppm in the decade from 2011 to 2020. From 2024 to 2025, the global average concentration of CO₂ rose by 2.8 ppm—above the decadal average but slightly less than the exceptional surge of 2023/2024.
"The more modest growth rate from 2024 to 2025 reflects recovery of the land carbon sinks and reduced fire carbon emissions in 2025 after the strong 2023/2024 El Niño, which reduced the efficiency of the biosphere through more drought, drier vegetation and more wildfires," said WMO senior scientific officer Oksana Tarasova.
"However, a 2.8 ppm annual increase is still a substantial addition of carbon to the atmosphere from fossil fuel burning. We can expect to see a further increase in concentrations in 2026 because of fossil fuel burning and the development of a powerful El Niño which will impact land carbon sinks as it did in 2023/2024. The risks of reduced CO₂ uptake by the ocean are also increasing in our changing climate," said Tarasova.
Methane and nitrous oxide
Methane accounts for about 16% of the warming effect on our climate by long-lived greenhouse gases, but it has a much shorter lifetime than CO₂. Approximately 35% of methane is emitted into the atmosphere by natural sources (for example, wetlands), which are sensitive to climate as well, and about 65% comes from anthropogenic sources such as cattle, rice farming, fossil fuel exploitation, landfills and biomass burning.
The globally averaged methane concentration in 2025 was 1,948 parts per billion (ppb)—or 267% of the 1750 level.
Nitrous oxide is the third most important long-lived greenhouse gas and comes from both natural sources and human activities such as biomass burning, fertilizer use and various industrial processes.
The globally averaged concentration of N₂O reached 339.1 ppb in 2025, 126% of the 1750 level.
Smart transition to clean energy
WMO's Global Atmosphere Watch network monitors carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and other long-lived gases of potential concern.
As countries respond and take steps to transform their energy systems toward decarbonization, careful attention should be given to two potent but less abundant trace gases closely related to electricity production and distribution: molecular hydrogen (H₂) and sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆).
SF₆ has been rising steadily over the past three decades in proportion to increased global electrification, since SF₆ is used primarily as a spark suppressant in electricity distribution.
It has an atmospheric lifetime of more than 1,000 years and the highest 100-year global warming potential, approximately 24,300 times that of CO₂. The increase in SF₆ in 2025 was a record high.
Hydrogen concentration increased by 5.3% between 2010 and 2024. Hydrogen is being used as an energy storage medium for hard-to-decarbonize sectors such as steelmaking, shipping and long-duration energy storage, as well as for renewable energy sources and as an energy source for transportation.
Yet its leakage into the atmosphere from production facilities, pipelines, storage tanks and fuel cells poses a growing concern. Hydrogen is not a greenhouse gas, but it influences atmospheric chemistry and so has a strong indirect effect on warming.
SF₆ represents the challenge of irreversible, long-lived greenhouse gas accumulation from industrial processes, while H₂ illustrates the subtle but potentially significant indirect climate effects of a gas used as an energy carrier. Both H₂ leakage and SF₆ persistence represent potential threats that could undermine the climate benefits of the energy transition. Careful monitoring of the composition of Earth's atmosphere is essential to detect, understand and prevent unintended consequences of these changes.
WMO, through its Global Atmosphere Watch program, coordinates global observations of both gases and supports a stable and internationally recognized calibration scale for atmospheric SF₆ and H₂ measurements. The robust WMO-GAW framework allows for joint data use across different programs around the world, enabling researchers to confidently track changes in atmospheric SF₆ and H₂ concentrations and investigate changes in their sources and sinks.

title: Can gravitational fields break and reconnect? Einstein's equations suggest they can
raw_text:
More than a century after Einstein first devised the equations that describe gravity, physicists are still finding new ways of interpreting them. Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, recently found a new way of looking at Einstein's equations that reveals a striking analogy with "magnetic reconnection" in plasmas, which occurs when magnetic field lines break and reconnect, powering explosive phenomena such as solar flares.
Their work shows that something similar can happen to gravity: Under the right conditions, gravitational field structures can also break and reconnect—a process they call "gravitational reconnection." When they do, energy moves out of the gravitational field and into matter.
The findings, published in Physical Review D, could help physicists better understand some of the universe's most extreme events, including the collision of black holes. In these environments, gravity is so powerful that space-time becomes highly distorted, making its behavior extraordinarily difficult to calculate. The researchers' approach offers a way to identify fundamental rules governing how gravitational fields behave, potentially revealing insights that conventional computer simulations alone cannot provide.
From magnetic lines to gravitational sheets
To understand how gravitational reconnection works, it helps to start with a more familiar phenomenon: magnetic reconnection. Most people have seen a picture of magnetic field lines: the arcs of iron filings around a bar magnet, or the loops that erupt from the surface of the sun. In a plasma, those lines get dragged around, stretched and twisted. Sometimes the stress becomes too great.
"Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration," Comisso said. "When they break and reconnect, they release energy." This is the process behind solar flares, and one of the most important energy-release mechanisms in all of astrophysics. "It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events."
Gravity, the researchers argue, can do something similar. But the geometry is different because Einstein's space-time has four dimensions rather than three, which describe space alone.
"Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field 'sheets' rather than field lines," explained Comisso. "Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a 'sheet.'"
So instead of magnetic field lines that stretch, reconnect and release energy, the gravitational field takes the form of sheets that move, reconnect and release energy. These sheets are mathematical structures rather than physical objects, but their reconnection describes a process through which energy can be transferred from the gravitational field into matter.
Hidden constraints in Einstein's equations
The discovery emerged from an unconventional way of looking at Einstein's equations, building on earlier research into the fundamental rules governing how space-time evolves.
Comisso and Asenjo's paper, "Reconnection of Gravitational Fields," builds on an earlier paper published in Physical Review Letters with Maricarmen A. Winkler. That research identified a set of previously unrecognized rules constraining how space-time is allowed to bend, stretch and evolve.
"Einstein's equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent," said Asenjo. "By revealing these hidden new properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves."
In their latest paper, Comisso and Asenjo show how gravitational field connections can change when the ideal conditions that preserve them break down—a process they call gravitational reconnection.
"Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them," Comisso said. "You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior."
That rewriting is the heart of the work. Over the past few years, physicists have developed a new formulation of Einstein's equations—mathematically equivalent to the originals but expressed in different variables. Written that way, the equations of gravity start to look a great deal like the equations that govern plasmas: gases that make up the sun, fuel fusion experiments and fill much of the space between stars.
Comisso has spent his career studying plasmas. Recognizing the resemblance, he and his colleagues brought plasma physics methods to bear on gravity.
"It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time," Comisso said. "Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints."
Toward predictions for merging black holes
That matters because of how this kind of physics is usually done. When astrophysicists want to know what happens when two black holes collide, they run enormous supercomputer simulations: pick a set of starting conditions, let the computer grind forward and watch what emerges.
The results are used to predict the shape of the gravitational-wave signal that detectors such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), an observatory designed to detect ripples in space-time from events like colliding black holes, are designed to measure.
For now, gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical discovery. The next challenge is to investigate how the process might unfold in specific astrophysical settings, such as merging black holes, and whether it produces measurable effects. Comisso hopes the approach will eventually help researchers predict how much energy such events release and what signatures they might leave in gravitational waves.
Provided by Columbia University
