title: A 60-year search is over: Chemists isolate long-elusive molecules with boron-oxygen triple bonds
raw_text:
In a new publication in the journal Nature Chemistry, chemists in professor Holger Braunschweig's team at the University of Würzburg, supported by computational work from the team of professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University in India, detail their discovery of a method for preparing and isolating a range of surprisingly stable oxoboranes—a challenge that has stood for over 60 years.
Oxoboranes: Stumping the best minds in chemistry
The element boron does not like to form triple bonds—this challenge has motivated Würzburg chemist Braunschweig to make molecules with boron-containing triple bonds for over 15 years.
In 2012, his team reported the first molecule with a boron-boron triple bond, and in 2025 they reported the first neutral molecule with a boron-carbon triple bond. In the first row of the periodic table's p-block, just one challenge remained: organic oxoboranes, compounds with boron-oxygen triple bonds.
Since at least the early 1960s, oxoboranes have been the target of decades of synthetic attempts from a wide range of inorganic and organic chemists around the world. They have been trapped and detected under extreme conditions, their existence has been inferred from chemical reactions and a number of derivatives have been made—but isolation of stable examples remained elusive.
Creating the right conditions for serendipity
When Würzburg chemistry doctoral students Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl combined a molecule called a diboracumulene with different ketones—standard reagents in organic chemistry—they independently noted that the reactions had led to unusual orange or yellow solids. "The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were on to something," says Lubczyk.
It was a great surprise that, out of many other seemingly more likely outcomes, and despite decades of attempts to prepare these compounds, the elusive oxoboranes would be the main products of these reactions. "Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them," says Braunschweig.
Three oxoboranes were prepared, showing that the method could lead to many new oxoboranes in the future. The team is now trying to see just how far the method can be pushed to prepare other elusive molecules across the periodic table.

title: Amber fossils reveal how ancient Australian landmass helped seed Southeast Asia's tropical forests
raw_text:
A landmass that broke away from northwestern Australia about 150 million years ago and drifted north for the next 100 million years helped lay the foundations for Southeast Asia's extraordinarily diverse tropical forests, new research has revealed.
An international study of more than 3,000 fossil specimens preserved in amber in Myanmar has uncovered a diverse plant community dating back about 99 million years, providing a remarkable window into the ancient flora carried north by the West Burma Block before it collided with Southeast Asia about 50 million years ago.
Curtin University co-author and professor Byron Lamont said the findings, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, revealed a remarkable connection between Australia's geological past and the origins of one of the world's richest tropical plant regions.
"It's an amazing story of a landmass breaking away from northwestern Australia, drifting north across the ancient oceans for millions of years and eventually becoming part of Southeast Asia," Lamont said.
"Along the way, it carried a rich tropical flora that evolved in relative isolation near the equator for tens of millions of years. When the landmass eventually joined Southeast Asia, it helped provide the foundations for the extraordinary plant diversity the region is renowned for today.
"We identified at least 392 morphological types of flowering plants in the amber, alongside an array of ferns, conifers and other ancient plant groups.
"These fossils give us a rare glimpse of that ancient world and help explain the deep evolutionary roots of Southeast Asia's tropical forests."
Lamont said the diversity is among the highest recorded for a single fossil plant assemblage from the early to mid-Cretaceous period, when dinosaurs still roamed the Earth.
"Preserved in exceptional three-dimensional detail, the fossils include flowers, fruits, leaves and seeds that offer evidence of a flourishing tropical plant community 100 million years ago," Lamont said.
"Because the West Burma Block drifted north while remaining close to the equator for tens of millions of years, this prolonged tropical environment provided a refuge in which ancient plant lineages could survive and diversify.
"The findings challenge the long-held view that Southeast Asia's diverse flowering-plant ecosystems largely originated much more recently, showing that flowering plants had already diversified extensively in equatorial environments during the Cretaceous period."
Provided by Curtin University

title: Digital tools and 3D printing emerge as key themes in circular economy research
raw_text:
A review of the research literature spanning the years 2020 to 2026 has found that digital technologies, additive manufacturing and resource recovery are major themes in the transition toward a sustainable, circular economy. The work, published in the International Journal of Services and Operations Management, highlights the need for more cooperation between businesses and other stakeholders and for better governmental policies to ease the transition.
Traditionally, industry has extracted resources and manufactured products. Consumers use these products, and when they are finished with them, they are dumped into the waste stream. The notion of the circular economy replaces that model to minimize resource use and reduce waste. Strategies such as reuse, repair, recycling and upcycling, and remanufacturing are all in development and used to varying degrees to reduce the demand for raw materials and limit environmental harm.
The study analyzed research from 372 journals covering operations, production, logistics and supply chain management. The team found that information technology and additive manufacturing are being used to reduce material waste. The review also identified regeneration and resource recovery as important approaches.
Fundamentally, the transition to a circular economy will improve efficiency, lower costs, open new markets and create jobs. However, its adoption will depend on coordinated action and putting policies in place that support sustainable practices across industry and its supply chains. Currently, financial and operational constraints mean companies need tailored strategies and workforce training to help with the transition.

title: New election forecast updates predictions every 10 minutes
raw_text:
From Alaska to Texas, the battle for control of the U.S. Senate is unfolding across 35 races. And a new Northwestern University election model is tracking them all—every 10 minutes.
Called NowCasting, the new system uses data from political prediction markets to calculate the probability of a Republican victory in each race as well as the likelihood that the party will retain control of the Senate.
Every 10 minutes, the model runs 1 million hypothetical midterm elections—simulating 35 million individual Senate race outcomes in the process. Its algorithm places particular emphasis on market activity from the preceding hour. Using this method, NowCasting can see immediate responses to singular news events.
As of noon on Tuesday (Oct. 27), NowCasting projects the Republican Party has a 23.2% chance of maintaining control of the Senate. Users can explore state-by-state predictions and overall trends on an interactive, color-coded map.
"Politics can change quickly, and I wanted to develop a system that can keep pace," said Northwestern's Thomas Miller, who developed the forecast platform. "By combining the collective expectations of thousands of traders with sophisticated statistical modeling, we can capture how the political landscape shifts in real time. We're not just looking at individual races. We're connecting the dots across the country to understand the bigger picture in the battle for Senate control."
Miller is the faculty director of the master's in data science program in Northwestern's School of Professional Studies.
NowCasting is the latest model in a string of election forecasts for Miller. During the 2020 U.S. presidential election, he developed The Virtual Tout, a prediction system that used political betting markets to simulate 1 million hypothetical elections every hour. His final forecast predicted 294 Electoral College votes for Joe Biden, just 12 votes shy of Biden's actual total of 306.
Miller introduced prediction surveys in January 2021 to track Georgia's two Senate runoff elections. His model correctly predicted wins for Democratic Sens. Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock.
Returning to the presidential race in 2024, Miller's Virtual Tout correctly predicted President Donald Trump's victory. His model favored Trump even as several other prominent forecasts—such as FiveThirtyEight, The Economist and Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin—narrowly favored Vice President Kamala Harris.
Now, Miller has taken his model a step further.
Although Miller's previous models relied on PredictIt, NowCasting draws on two major platforms: Kalshi and Polymarket. It also incorporates statistical models used in finance and economics to identify underlying trends and relationships among the 35 Senate races. The new model updates every 10 minutes—six times more frequently than his original hourly system.
But the biggest change is how Miller interprets the data. While his earlier models focused on forecasting election outcomes, NowCasting aims to capture what prediction markets signal right now. Instead of treating prediction market prices as probabilities, the system analyzes and calibrates the data to generate its own estimates of each candidate's likelihood of winning.
"Prediction markets provide event contract prices, not probabilities," Miller said. "NowCasting takes that information and uses statistical modeling to generate probabilities that reflect what the markets are telling us right now."

title: Halloween meets history in many ghostly tourism attractions. Is this a problem?
raw_text:
Halloween, the fall holiday and $13.5 billion industry, lurks around the corner.
But what's behind the more than 11,000 acres of pumpkin patches (4,450 hectares) across Canada and $3.9 billion in consumer spending on candy alone?
Halloween has ancient origins in the pre-Christian religion and practices of the Celts. It was customary to honor the transitions between the seasons and harvest, acknowledge the thin veil between different planes of existence and also to commemorate the dead.
Modern-day commercialization has shifted how people experience Halloween, but the spirits of the dead continue to play a significant role in the occasion and the time of year.
The day's appeal and its marketability extend beyond a one-day "holiday." Many people are drawn to carefully curated encounters, seeking thrilling yet sanitized experiences that allow them to engage with the macabre and mortality from a safe distance.
Consequently, Halloween's commercial success in commodifying dread and the monstrous can be analyzed alongside broader "dark tourism"—an umbrella term that explores tourism involvement with sites of death, disaster and a difficult heritage.
Anthropologist Philip Stone notes that a range of motivations exist for promoting engagement with death, disaster and the macabre: for example, political reasons or remembrance, education, entertainment or economic gain.
So how should we think about worldwide Halloween-related attractions that not only seek to entertain but also promote interpretation and engagement with sites marketed as scary, which often have genuinely dark pasts?
Prisons, forts
For example, a tourism attraction at Eastern State Penitentiary—a former prison in Philadelphia—markets itself as a Halloween festival of epic proportions. The onetime prison was an 11-acre (4.5-hectare) institution that was the first jail in the United States to introduce the practice of solitary confinement in the late 1800s.
In the late '90s, the property switched gears, launched "Terror Behind the Walls" as an annual haunted house and then rebranded as "Halloween Nights."
The facility notes that proceeds from Halloween Nights benefit a mission to preserve the site and advance "public understanding of the criminal justice system and its impact on the lives of those affected by it [and] to inspire a more just future," including through public education and exhibits.
Another example is Fort Henry in Kingston, Ontario.
Although Fort Henry was never a battlefield site, it was the site of an 1838 execution. It was also used as a prison for combatants captured during the 1837–38 Rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada and again during World War I and World War II for "civilian enemy aliens."
Today, coffin rides and a monster shooting range are part of the heritage sites tourist attraction called Fort Fright, which simulates a haunted attraction and experience throughout the month of October leading up to Halloween. Historical educational programming exists through the year.
These types of attractions are examples of fright tourism, when people seek scares and thrills for pleasure at a destination that may have a sinister history or is promoted as having one.
Other forts have also offered similar experiences timed to Halloween.
Urban ghost stories
Urban ghost stories also continue to spark interest, both at Halloween and at other times.
The Lost Souls of Gastown Tour, a performance-theater experience in Vancouver, is one example. Visitors participating in the tour immerse themselves in the city's stories of crime, disaster, historical figures and hidden urban spaces.
Victoria Ghost Walking Tours offers a tour touching on "horrible deeds" and other eerie experiences for folks on Vancouver Island, as do tour operators in other cities.
Important questions raised
Why do people seek fear if it's associated with danger? Why do tourists travel for entertainment or fun to places with tragic or apparently haunted pasts, sometimes associated with horrible, disturbing or traumatic events?
Although fear is fundamentally a warning mechanism that alerts us to potential danger, it also generates the release of adrenaline. In settings where people perceive themselves to be safe, this tension between threat and security can become an appealing experience.
Stone analyzes dark tourism along a spectrum. The "darkest" end of the spectrum is characterized by experiences pertaining to education and authentic sites where death and suffering happened. The "lighter" end is "heritage-centric," with an entertainment orientation perceived as inauthentic and more associated with tourism.
Many Halloween-themed sites and experiences are arguably situated on the lighter end of the dark tourism spectrum and marketed as entertainment. As mentioned, some are linked to real experiences or engage with stories or sites associated with death, social control, crime and disaster.
Ethical boundaries?
Researchers studying dark tourism in prison museums have noted that people's interactions in these spaces demonstrate that "not all dark experiences are equally 'dark' to all visitors." This means that sites cannot dictate how their curated experiences will be received.
This suggests it's important to pay close attention to the ethical boundaries between interpretation and entertainment.
When these boundaries are blurred, the dignity of victims can be compromised while the educational and commemorative value of historic sites may be diminished. This raises important questions about the responsibilities of tourism providers when presenting difficult and often painful histories, and, as Stone also examines, their relationship to political ideology.
Some argue the boundary between a tourism attraction and the site of a traumatic past can become nuanced—for example, when former prisons, as attraction sites, provide educational resources for visitors.
All attractions situated along the dark tourism spectrum, whether they lean toward the "lighter" or "darker" end, must carefully navigate the line between respectful engagement and exploitation. This is particularly relevant for Halloween tourism experiences that draw upon stories or sites that intersect with crime, death or tragedy.
When attractions encourage visitors to engage with local history, they should not glorify perpetrators, sensationalize violence or trivialize suffering.
In these cases, exhibit operators should prioritize historically grounded narratives that provide context, acknowledge victims and encourage reflection. This may be a daunting challenge.

title: Brambles are a problem weed in South Africa, but researchers are closer to finding a natural enemy to manage them
raw_text:
Invasive alien brambles have been spreading across South Africa since the early 1900s, having come from North America and Europe. All brambles fall within the genus Rubus. Their common names in South Africa are braam (Afrikaans), ijingijolo (isiZulu) and monoko-metsi (seSotho).
Over the decades, these plants have crept into tree plantations, pastures and native grasslands. Dense, thorny thickets now choke open spaces and impede livestock and wildlife movement. They restrict access to water, smother young trees used for timber, interfere with plantation management and disrupt roadsides.
They have become one of the most widespread and damaging weeds, though it's hard to estimate how much land they cover because satellite imagery doesn't capture them in grasslands and they "hide" under forest canopy.
Beyond ruining hiking experiences and doing agricultural damage, these infestations also displace native vegetation and negatively affect specialist flower visitors like butterflies.
People have tried to manage invasive brambles, yet traditional chemical and mechanical controls don't work. This is due to the sheer scale of the invasions, costs that are too high for low-value land, rugged terrain that limits access and the plant's ability to resprout from rootstocks or re-emerge from bird-dispersed seeds.
Consequently, there is an urgent need for additional management tools. Biological control (biocontrol) has been considered in South Africa, but never tried.
My research focuses on biological control of weeds, which works by introducing specialized natural enemies from the plant's native range (where they came from originally) to suppress its growth or reproduction. Before any natural enemy is released, it undergoes rigorous testing in quarantine to make sure it only damages the weed. By using tested, host-specific natural enemies that cannot survive on any other host, biocontrol aims to restore ecosystems with minimal disturbance. Biocontrol offers a proven safety record that far outweighs the hazards of traditional control methods.
The first step is to be sure what the weed is, where it came from, what its natural enemies are and how much of a problem it is.
Recently our research team published the results of a study into brambles in South Africa to start answering these questions. Until recently, the most damaging brambles in this country were treated as a single species, Rubus cuneifolius Pursh. Research has since separated the dominant invasive species into three taxa. Our study concludes that biological control of Rubus sect. Cuneifolii and two forms of R. sect. Arguti is feasible and may be a suitable option to manage the impact of the weed in South Africa.
Identifying the enemy
Establishing a clear identity for the target plant is essential to finding natural enemies. This requirement has been a major stumbling block to bramble biocontrol.
In the past, invasion biologists and botanists lacked clarity on which species the brambles in South Africa belonged to, and which ones were driving invasions. This was complicated by the tendency of brambles to hybridize, both across invasive species and between invasive and native species. (South Africa has several native brambles that need to be protected.)
Overcoming the identification hurdle and others became the aim of research carried out at the Agricultural Research Council and at the Centre for Biological Control, attached to Rhodes University, from 2018 on.
At the same time, a world-leading Czech batologist (a person who studies brambles), Michal Sochor, was conducting studies to untangle South Africa's bramble diversity, in collaboration with John Manning of the South African National Biodiversity Institute. This work revealed a complex mix of 18 pure taxa and 12 hybrid lines of Rubus in South Africa.
It separated the dominant invasive species, previously identified as Rubus cuneifolius, into three taxa (an upright form and two sprawling forms).
We then evaluated 91 highly affected forestry, grassland and roadside sites to map Rubus spp. distributions, genetic structures and morphological (shape) traits.
These revealed that the upright form (Rubus sect. Cuneifolii) was the most widespread invader in the grassland biome, dominating 42 of the 69 accessible sites. In KwaZulu-Natal province, it heavily invades open grasslands and timber plantations as a single, genetically uniform clone. No hybridization was recorded.
The sprawling forms (R. sect. Arguti) were recorded at 26 sites, mainly along roadsides and in disturbed habitats across three provinces (KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga and Limpopo). These plants were genetically divided into five distinct genotypes showing clear geographic clustering.
Cost-benefit analysis
Anyone spending time outdoors in South Africa is likely familiar with wild brambles, having enjoyed picking and eating their fruit, often without knowing which species they were. Foraging from wild populations even supports small cottage industries, such as making jam and preserves, brewing small batches of gin and selling whole berries in local farm stands.
To ensure future management strategies avoid potential conflicts of interest, our research included a socioeconomic study of the economic value of these Rubus species.
This confirmed that alien brambles generate positive private value through wild berry harvesting, dietary supplementation and small-scale processing. But our research found that environmental and management costs outweigh these local benefits. The cost to government of clearing the weeds was 13.5 times greater than the recorded financial benefits (which were all in one province, the Free State).
Wild harvesting proved to be a "nice to have" rather than a vital part of local livelihoods or daily nutrition.
Decisive control measures are therefore needed.
Next, find enemies
Biocontrol should provide a helpful tool in the management of invasive Rubus in South Africa, as it has in several other countries.
Thanks to a much clearer understanding of where Rubus fits into the plant world, what seemed like an intractable challenge in the 1980s and 1990s is becoming a manageable research project. This is because we can now determine the plants' exact origin to ensure that the right or most closely associated natural enemies are collected and considered for further testing.
The next steps are to track down populations of Rubus in the U.S. which closely match those in South Africa, survey them for natural enemies (preferably an insect that damages the stem or leaf) and select one or more of these for host-specificity trials.
It is entirely realistic that an effective biocontrol agent could be released within the next decade for South Africa's invasive North American brambles, hopefully reducing their vigor and competitiveness while paving the way for cost-effective integrated management.

title: Researchers produce urea in the field using system powered by biobatteries and solar energy
raw_text:
The CONFETI project, coordinated by the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona (UAB), has concluded three years of research with the commissioning of a pilot system capable of producing urea, a nitrogen fertilizer widely used in agriculture, directly in the field using renewable energy. This fertilizer is produced from carbon dioxide (CO₂) and nitrates in an electrochemical reactor powered by energy from biobatteries and solar panels.
The experimental installation, located in an agricultural setting in Viladecans, also incorporates a photochemical reactor that produces ammonia, a key compound used in urea production, using sunlight.
Bringing this system into operation is one of the main milestones of the project, which has taken the technologies it developed into the field to explore alternatives to conventional nitrogen fertilizer production processes. The prototype has continued to operate throughout the summer and following recent periods of heavy rainfall, while the consortium continues to study its performance under real-world conditions.
"The main challenge has been moving the device from the laboratory to an agricultural setting. It has been one of the most difficult tasks," explains Gonzalo Guirado, a professor in the UAB's Department of Chemistry and project coordinator. "Thanks to the team's efforts, it has been possible to validate the devices and their components in the laboratory and bring them here for testing in a real-world setting," he adds.
Sustainable technologies
The CONFETI system combines three complementary technological developments. The first is an electrochemical reactor that produces urea from CO₂ and nitrates. The reaction produces this fertilizer through a process that offers an alternative to conventional industrial methods, which are energy-intensive and have a high environmental impact.
One of the system's distinctive features is that the reactor is powered by a combination of biobatteries and solar panels. The biobatteries use microbial activity and organic matter present in the soil to generate electricity. An electronic system manages this energy together with the energy from the solar panels to power the electrochemical reactor. Both energy generation systems are operating at the pilot installation and constitute the second development.
The third is a photochemical reactor that converts nitrates in water into ammonia, using sunlight and a photocatalyst. The process also allows this material to be separated and recovered for reuse. The technology is designed to make use of nitrates that crops do not absorb, with the aim of recovering them and reusing them as fertilizers.
The challenge of moving from the laboratory to the field
Integrating the different devices into an installation in an agricultural setting has been one of the project's main challenges. Unlike laboratory tests, the pilot system is exposed to weather conditions and the specific characteristics of its surroundings, allowing its operation to be studied under conditions closer to those of a future application.
The trials are helping to characterize the different components and the integrated system, and to identify the technical issues that will need to be addressed in subsequent stages of development.
"What we want to demonstrate with CONFETI is that there is another way to produce fertilizers, using pollutants such as CO₂ and nitrates and converting them into value-added products with green energy," says Guirado. "In addition, our technology allows fertilizers to be produced sustainably at the very place where they will be used, and supplied on demand, so that they do not need to be stored."
This vision raises the possibility of developing local fertilizer production systems in the future that make use of resources available in agricultural settings. Further research is now needed to assess the technical, environmental and economic viability of commercial application.

title: Researchers discover why some frogs have escaped the current amphibian mass extinction
raw_text:
Amphibians are the most threatened vertebrates on Earth, with 41% of species facing extinction. In the highlands of Central and South America, a killer fungus has wiped out much of the once-abundant amphibian diversity. Yet in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, an isolated mountain range in northern Colombia, amphibians still thrive. The mountain range is home to a remarkable amphibian community of at least 48 species, including 25 found nowhere else on the planet.
New research led by Ghent University and Trier University shows that the threat is dangerously close. Their study is published in the journal Current Biology.
After screening more than 2,000 frogs, toads and salamanders, researchers found no evidence of the deadly fungus in the region. Yet only about 20 kilometers (12 miles) away, they detected a highly virulent variant of the disease.
Warm and dry lowlands probably act as a natural barrier that has kept the fungus out so far. But the study shows that some of the region's unique amphibian species are highly vulnerable to infection. Arrival of the fungus is thus expected to lead to massive loss of amphibian communities as witnessed elsewhere.
The findings offer a rare opportunity to protect an intact amphibian community before a devastating disease outbreak occurs. Researchers warn that contaminated equipment, materials or transported amphibians could carry the fungus past the natural barrier.
Preventing introduction must therefore be a conservation priority. The authors call for strict biosecurity, continued disease surveillance and urgent protection of particularly vulnerable species.

title: Yeast paired with electricity can convert CO₂ into a chemical used in biodegradable plastics
raw_text:
Yeast paired with electricity can convert CO₂ into a chemical used in biodegradable plastics
Swati Mestri
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
To limit further climate change, researchers are exploring technologies that can convert atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) into useful products. In collaboration with BOKU University in Vienna (Austria), researchers at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) have demonstrated that electrochemical and microbial processes can be combined to capture CO₂ and produce itaconic acid, a bio-based chemical used in industry. According to the researchers, this new process demonstrates how CO₂ emissions can be converted into sustainable bio-based products, with the potential to produce a wider range of valuable chemicals by using different microorganisms.
Itaconic acid is a bio-based organic acid used to manufacture biodegradable plastics, textiles, adhesives and resins. It is considered a promising sustainable alternative to petroleum-based chemicals. Worldwide, around 70,000 t (77,000 short tons) of itaconic acid are produced annually, and production is increasing.
"On an industrial scale, itaconic acid is produced biotechnologically from sugar using a fungus. We have now developed a process that uses CO₂ instead of sugar as a starting material so that we can put emissions to productive use," explains Falk Harnisch, an electrobiotechnologist at the UFZ and last author of the study.
The work is published in the journal Angewandte Chemie International Edition.
From carbon dioxide to yeast fuel
In collaboration with researchers from BOKU University in Vienna, the UFZ team has developed a method that combines electrochemical and microbial processes in a single bioreactor. But how exactly does this electrobioreactor work? And how did the researchers come up with the idea of combining the use of CO₂ with the production of itaconic acid in the first place?
A previous study by BOKU University showed that itaconic acid can be produced biotechnologically from methanol, a type of alcohol. Because microorganisms can metabolize a wide range of substances, the team led by Harnisch tested a chemically similar substance that can be produced relatively easily from CO₂.
"Electricity, ideally from renewable sources, can be used to convert CO₂ into formate, which is chemically related to methanol because both contain just one carbon atom. We therefore wanted to investigate whether the yeast could also use formate as an energy source for itaconic acid production," says Dr. Paniz Izadi, a researcher on Harnisch's UFZ team and first author of the study.
Reconciling competing reactor conditions
The design of the electrobioreactor in which electrochemical and microbial processes take place simultaneously presented a number of challenges. The electrochemical conversion of CO₂ into formate works best at elevated temperatures and an alkaline pH in the presence of as few other chemical substances as possible. The genetically engineered yeast strain Komagataella phaffii, which is used in the bioreactor, requires entirely different conditions: temperatures of around 30°C (86°F), a neutral pH and a nutrient-rich medium.
"In order to ensure that both the electrochemical and microbial processes took place and operated as efficiently as possible, we had to find a compromise between their different requirements in the electrobioreactor," explains Dr. Simone Bachleitner, senior scientist at the Institute of Microbiology and Microbial Biotechnology at BOKU University.
A working process with lower yields
The experiment was successful, and the yeast produced itaconic acid from CO₂ using electrochemically produced formate as an energy source. "We successfully combined electrochemical and microbial processes in our bioreactor. A self-contained process chain offers major practical advantages because it eliminates the need to transport intermediate products between separate facilities. Although the yield of itaconic acid was lower than when sugar or methanol was used, our study clearly demonstrates that CO₂ can be converted into complex and valuable biochemicals," says Harnisch.
The researchers hope that their new process will provide a model for practical applications and contribute to the development of industrial-scale facilities. The researchers now plan to optimize the processes in the electrobioreactor and investigate their suitability for other microorganisms and bio-based products.

title: Elementary school homework could be reinforcing educational inequality, study suggests
raw_text:
Elementary school homework could be reinforcing educational inequality, study suggests
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
Homework set by elementary schools could be reinforcing educational inequalities by rewarding families who have more time and resources to spend helping their children, new research from the University of Manchester suggests.
The study argues that homework is not simply an educational activity carried out by children at home. It also requires parents to invest their time, knowledge and resources, potentially giving some children an advantage over others. Researchers found that parents can face very different demands on their time, particularly when they are balancing homework with work, childcare and other family responsibilities. The study is published in the British Journal of Sociology of Education.
Yet schools may treat parents' ability and willingness to spend time on homework as a measure of how well they are supporting their children's education. The researchers argue that this can create a 'deficit' view of parents, in which families who have less time or fewer resources are perceived as less engaged with their children's education.
When homework becomes a parental responsibility
Homework is often presented as a way for children to practice what they have learned at school. But the researchers argue that it also creates expectations about how parents should use their time, examining the process through which homework is set by a teacher, completed by a child with parental involvement, and then returned to the teacher.
This creates an opportunity for parents to invest time in producing work that can subsequently be recognized and rewarded within the education system. The researchers use the sociological theories of Pierre Bourdieu to argue that this investment can become a form of cultural capital—the time and knowledge available to families can be converted into educational advantage.
Not all parents have the same amount of time
The study highlights the very different circumstances in which parents are expected to support homework. One parent, referred to as Emma in the paper, describes trying to help her children despite working until 8 p.m. She says that doing homework late at night can be extremely difficult and argues that homework should be regarded as a 'bonus' if parents are able to do it, rather than something automatically expected of every family.
Emma also describes the experience as potentially 'shaming' for parents who do not understand the homework themselves. The researchers argue that this illustrates how apparently neutral expectations about parental engagement can have very different consequences depending on families' circumstances.
A parent with flexible working hours, financial resources and confidence with schoolwork may be able to provide substantial support, while a parent working long or irregular hours may have much less time available, even if they are equally committed to their child's education.
Are parents being judged on how they spend their time?
A central argument of the paper is that schools can develop implicit ideas about the 'proper' use of parents' time. The researchers describe these expectations as part of the educational field's 'doxa'—beliefs that become so taken for granted that they appear natural or unquestionable.
This can mean that spending time on educational activities is treated as evidence of being a good or committed parent, while parents who cannot or do not engage in the expected ways may be judged as lacking commitment. The researchers argue that this can obscure the structural reasons why parents have different amounts of time available.
The 'colonization' of family life
The paper builds on previous research describing homework as a 'colonization of the home by school.' The researchers argue that homework does not simply extend learning beyond the classroom; it can also give schools an influence over how families are expected to spend their time together.
This is illustrated by the views of one teacher, Higgins, who describes homework as an opportunity for parents and children to spend time together. She also argues that parents have a responsibility to prioritize their children's education and suggests that schools sometimes have to compensate when parents are not sufficiently involved.
The researchers argue that this illustrates a tension between two very different understandings of homework. For teachers, it can be seen as an opportunity to support learning and strengthen parent-child relationships, while for some parents it can represent an additional demand on already limited time and a judgment about whether they are using that time 'properly.'
A hidden advantage for families with more resources
The study also highlights an apparent contradiction in how parental involvement can operate. Families with greater financial resources may be able to overcome a lack of time by outsourcing educational work, for example through private tutoring. This means that having limited time does not necessarily prevent more affluent parents from ensuring their children receive substantial educational support.
Families with fewer financial resources may instead have to choose between spending their own limited time on homework and other demands such as paid work, child care and household responsibilities. The researchers argue that inequality is therefore not simply about how much parents care about their children's education, but also about who has the resources to turn that commitment into educational advantage.
Why simply removing homework may not be enough
The researchers argue that eliminating homework would be desirable as a school-directed parental engagement practice, but caution that this would not automatically remove inequalities. Other forms of parental engagement could emerge to take its place and continue to reward families with greater resources.
Instead, the authors argue that schools need to examine the assumptions underlying parental engagement and develop practices that recognize the different circumstances in which families live. They call for schools, teachers and researchers to better understand families' experiences and to develop approaches that legitimize non-dominant experiences, rather than treating them as evidence of parental failure.
Making the invisible visible
The research uses a detailed case involving a parent, a teacher and the first author, who was herself a parent at the school. The authors argue that this unusual perspective allowed them to examine how different people could experience the same homework practice in very different ways.
The first author describes a moment when she realized that homework was being used not only to develop children's academic skills but also as a way of encouraging a particular form of parental behavior. The researchers describe this as a moment in which something that had previously appeared natural became visible as a social practice shaped by power and class.
They argue that recognizing these hidden assumptions is an important step toward challenging educational inequalities.
What the experts say
"We need to be careful about assuming that a parent who spends more time helping with homework is necessarily more committed to their child's education," said Dr. Emilia Howker. "Some parents simply have more time and resources available to them. When schools reward that investment, we risk turning differences in family circumstances into differences in children's educational opportunities."
"If homework rewards families who have the most time, knowledge and money to invest, then it can end up reinforcing the very inequalities that education is supposed to overcome. Simply removing homework may not solve the problem, because other forms of parental involvement can create similar advantages. The bigger challenge is to rethink what we expect from parents in the first place," said professor Laura Black.
More information

title: Supersonic waves could explain the strange orbits of hot Jupiters and Neptunes

Supersonic waves could explain the strange orbits of hot Jupiters and Neptunes
Sam Jarman
Author
Lisa Lock
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Using advanced new simulations, a team of astronomers in the U.S. has developed a promising new theory for how giant, gaseous exoplanets migrate into stiflingly close orbits around their host stars. Led by J. J. Zanazzi at The Pennsylvania State University, the team showed how both massive "hot Jupiters" and smaller, Neptune-sized planets could migrate from distant, elliptical orbits as they release energy via dramatic shock waves in their outer atmospheres. Their results have been published in The Astrophysical Journal.
Pileup, ridge, and desert
Hot Jupiters are a class of exoplanets with masses comparable to the largest planet in our own solar system, but which orbit extremely close to their host stars—imparting them with temperatures that can exceed some 2,000 Kelvin. Not only are their orbital periods extremely short, they also cluster within a window between three and five days: a phenomenon dubbed the "hot Jupiter pileup."
Similar clustering can also be seen in smaller gas giants, with masses between those of Neptune and Saturn, known as the "Neptune ridge." Yet unlike hot Jupiters, these planets are strikingly scarce on orbits shorter than about three days, creating a stark observational gap named the "Neptune desert."
For astronomers, these features offer clues about the dramatic histories of these exoplanets. To explain their formation, it is widely proposed that they began their lives in highly elliptical orbits, far farther out in their stellar systems. As tidal forces from their host stars drained the energy from their orbits, they would have then migrated inward, eventually reaching stable, circular orbits with strikingly similar lengths.
But for their orbits to change shape in this way, the planets themselves must have absorbed vast amounts of orbital energy. "What always bugged me is although all this energy is thought to pass through the planet—enough to completely blow off most of the planet's mass—few have ventured to understand what process causes this to occur," Zanazzi says.
Surface gravity waves
To investigate, the team examined detailed simulations of giant migrating exoplanets, carried out by co-author Morgan MacLeod at Harvard University. At its closest approach on an elliptical orbit, a planet will experience intense gravitational forces from its host star. As a result, planetary-scale oscillations called "surface gravity waves" appeared in the simulations, which ran horizontally across the planet's surface.
In the thin outer atmosphere, where the density drops sharply, MacLeod's simulations showed that these waves could move faster than the speed of sound within the gas. At this point, the supersonic flow breaks into a shock wave, which is an abrupt jump in pressure and density that rapidly converts the wave's energy into heat. Since this energy is drawn from the planet's orbit, each shock changes its orbital path into a lower-energy, more circular shape. In some cases, the heat also imparted the energy needed for gas to escape from the planet.
Eviscerated planets
In the simulations, the ultimate fate of each planet hinged on how deep the shock emerged within the atmosphere. "We found that shallow shocks were able to retain the mass of a gas giant, while deep shocks blew off the gaseous envelopes for these planets, leaving behind barren giant-planet cores," Zanazzi explains.
The team suggested that this violent latter case could be responsible for the dense, rocky exoplanets with masses tens of times larger than Earth's mass which are often found at extremely small orbital distances from their host stars. "We also predict that the process that blows off these planetary envelopes should be observable, and are currently working out what telescopes are capable of detecting these luminous events," Zanazzi adds.
Explaining the desert
In the team's model, a planet's fate depended on how quickly its orbit was stretched. Usually this happens slowly—once a planet strays close enough to its star, surface gravity wave shocks begin to circularize its orbit, halting any further stretching. This leaves both hot Jupiters and smaller gas giants stabilized at a safe distance, explaining both the hot Jupiter pileup and the Neptune ridge that astronomers observe.
But if its orbit is stretched more rapidly, a planet can plunge too close to its star before the shocks take effect, stripping its gas with every pass. This offers a new explanation for the Neptune desert, whose edge closely matches the distance where this stripping begins. It would also explain why the rare exoplanets found inside the Neptune desert are unusually dense: likely due to the mass they shed during their migration.
The team suggests that hot Jupiters on these closer orbits could have been dragged farther inward later by tides raised on their host stars. "Whether our predictions hold up after folks gather more observations will tell us if our ideas hold up or not," Zanazzi says.

title: Climate change amplified 2024 European floods more than rainfall, models show
raw_text:
Climate change amplified 2024 European floods more than rainfall, models show
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
In September 2024, Storm Boris brought extreme precipitation and severe flooding to large parts of Central and Eastern Europe. Poland, Czechia and Austria were particularly affected. In some areas, several hundred millimeters of rain fell within a few days, and numerous rivers burst their banks.
Earlier attribution studies had shown that global warming intensified precipitation during Storm Boris. These studies compare the observed event with a counterfactual scenario that largely excludes human influence on the climate. However, such analyses generally stop at the meteorological event itself and focus on questions such as how much extreme precipitation has intensified. The effects of these changes on flood hazards therefore often remain unclear.
Tracing rainfall into flood peaks
"In our study, we have taken this a step further. Using hydrological models, we investigated how changes in precipitation amounts caused by climate change affect the magnitude of flooding," says lead author Peter Miersch from the UFZ. Although it is known that an increase in precipitation does not necessarily lead to a proportional increase in flood magnitude, the size of this effect for individual events and the extent to which it can be attributed to anthropogenic climate change have so far remained unclear.
To investigate this, the researchers combined climate simulations with two different hydrological models in order to trace how rainfall in a catchment generates runoff and ultimately leads to flooding. The differences were substantial. Without anthropogenic climate change, precipitation during Storm Boris would have been around 6%–9% lower depending on the climate model, but flood peaks would have been 14%–22% lower on average.
The study is published in the journal Science Advances.
Saturated soil amplifies runoff
The reason for this disproportionate increase lies in how catchments respond to additional rainfall. "The soil can initially absorb some of the rain during a heavy rainfall event. But eventually the soil becomes saturated, and every additional millimeter of rain flows directly into the river," explains Miersch. Once the soil is saturated, additional rainfall leads to a particularly sharp increase in runoff.
To assess the robustness of the results, the researchers combined two different climate models with two hydrological models, one of which uses machine learning. Despite the different methodological approaches, the same basic pattern emerged in all combinations: flood peaks increased considerably more than precipitation.
Flood protection thresholds under pressure
This effect is particularly relevant where flood protection measures are designed for specific flood thresholds. "If climate change increases extreme precipitation by 10%, it does not mean flooding will increase by only 10%. It could also be 20%. If flood levels exceed the thresholds for which flood protection measures are designed, extensive damage can occur very quickly," says co-author Dr. Jakob Zscheischler, a climate researcher at the UFZ and professor of data analytics in hydro sciences at TUD Dresden University of Technology.
Assessments of flood risk and flood protection that consider only changes in extreme precipitation may therefore lead to an underestimation of the increase in flood hazard.
Isolating climate change's contribution
However, the researchers deliberately limited the scope of the study to isolate how much anthropogenic climate change altered a specific event under otherwise identical conditions. The study does not establish whether climate change makes weather patterns similar to those during Storm Boris more or less likely. Changes in land use or water management were also not taken into account. Put simply, the researchers compared the same present-day landscape under different climatic conditions.
The results therefore show that changes in flood hazards associated with climate change cannot be assessed solely based on changes in precipitation. When assessing future risks and developing adaptation strategies, it is therefore important to consider the entire process from the weather event to river discharge.

title: A spider named for Stephen Colbert has a genome about 50% larger than ours
raw_text:
A spider named for Stephen Colbert has a genome about 50% larger than ours
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Many spiders reach their maximum size about this time of year, having spent the summer eating, which helps explain their starring role in Halloween decorations. Researchers at the University of California, Davis, have found that one particular trapdoor spider, Aptostichus stephencolberti, which is about the size of a quarter, is big in another way: It has an outsized genome.
Given comedian Stephen Colbert's pompous pundit persona in the former Comedy Central show "The Colbert Report," it seems fitting that a spider named for him would have a genome roughly 50% larger than the human genome.
"At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it's not the largest genome among the spiders, but it's significant," said corresponding author Jason Bond, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology. Bond said the spider is the first member of its family to have its genome sequenced. The study was published in the Journal of Heredity.
Where it lurks
Along Northern California's coastal dunes, beachgoers often, and unknowingly, come into contact with Colbert's spider namesake, which hides in burrows. While it lacks Colbert's developed sense of irony, the trapdoor spider has a flawless sense of timing. Females spend their entire lives underground in silk-lined burrows sealed by a hinged, camouflaged door. They wait for vibrations, emerging quickly to catch prey that wander too close. Its venom is not dangerous to humans. Of the more than 50,000 known spider species, only 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to people, Bond said.
Its genome
The spider's genome is also complex, with 52 chromosomes compared to 23 in humans. Much of that size, 77%, comes from repetitive sequences, copied many times throughout the genome, rather than additional genes. All spiders, including this one, lack telomere repeats—the protection for the ends of chromosomes. This loss may explain the faster rate of chromosome evolution in spiders than we see in vertebrates.
"It lends itself to broadening our understanding of spider genome composition and consequently how genomes have evolved across the animal tree of life," Bond said.
Why Stephen Colbert?
In 2008, Colbert learned that Bond had named a trapdoor spider after rock musician Neil Young and developed a bit of spider envy. He used his segment, "Who's Not Honoring Me Now?" on "The Colbert Report" to demand a spider be named after him. Bond obliged.
At risk of losing their homes if we lose our beaches
The genomic research is part of the California Conservation Genomics project.
Because trapdoor spiders rarely travel far and their coastal dune habitat is fragmented, genomic data can help researchers identify distinct populations that may warrant protection.
"We Californians love our beaches and trapdoor spiders share them with us," Bond said. "We're hoping to understand how things like climate change, fire and urbanization might be impacting the genetic diversity of species."
Aptostichus stephencolberti (the "t" in Colbert is silent) lives only in coastal dunes in Central California, from the San Francisco Bay to Monterey. Rising sea levels threaten this narrow habitat.
"They're going to be incredibly sensitive to sea-level rise, but they're also very sensitive to invasive species," Bond said.
Untapped treasure
Spider genomes like this one might also help researchers discover compounds in venom that might have medical or agricultural applications. Some venom-derived compounds have potential as painkillers, while others may help control pests, Bond said.
"We don't really know what's out there in terms of untapped natural product diversity for venoms," he said.

title: Why hugs become memorable
raw_text:
Why hugs become memorable
Sadie Harley
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
A large-scale survey of adults in the U.K. shows that hugs are commonly remembered for comfort, support and understanding, according to a study published in PLOS One by Anna Lena Dueren of the University of Bristol, U.K., and colleagues. Notably, individual differences in empathy, attachment patterns in relationships, body perception and everyday hugging experiences were also related to the likelihood of remembering a hug for its positive emotional effect.
Hugs are an important form of social touch and have been associated with positive outcomes such as reduced stress and improved mood. Yet relatively little is known about the individual differences that affect how people remember hugs. In particular, it has been unclear whether empathy, body image, attachment patterns in close relationships or everyday hugging experiences influence the emotional value placed on hugs.
To fill this knowledge gap, Dueren and colleagues investigated whether hugs are generally remembered as emotionally salient experiences and whether individual differences are related to emotions linked to hugging.
Hug memories linked to individual traits
The researchers analyzed data from a survey of 15,049 healthy adults who were recruited in the U.K. through promotion on public broadcasting programs and other media. Overall, nearly 70% of participants remembered hugs for their positive emotional impact.
Specifically, the results showed that difficulty knowing how to hug and disliking hugging were negatively related to remembering a hug for its positive emotional value. The opposite pattern was observed for individuals who are more likely to greet family and friends by hugging. The researchers also found that higher scores on cognitive and emotional empathy measures were related to a higher likelihood of remembering a hug.
People who tend to display a higher level of independence in relationships were less likely to remember a hug for its positive emotional value compared with individuals who tend to experience distress when facing separation. Participants with higher scores on the body-perception scale, which focuses on the connection between body awareness and touch, were more likely to remember a hug.
Cultural limits and questions about context
According to the authors, the findings may not generalize to people who live in societies with different attitudes toward physical contact and interpersonal distance. In addition, 75% of the study participants were women, and the study design does not allow for firm conclusions on causal relationships between traits, hugging experiences and the formation of hug memories.
Despite these limitations, the study provides an important overview of psychological factors that shape the meaning of social touch and extends current theoretical work by linking emotional touch to the formation of autobiographical memories.
The authors add, "We hope our findings will help explain why hugs are perceived differently from person to person. A next step would be to further investigate how personality, previous experiences and the context in which a hug occurs shape its perception. Ultimately, this could help us better understand when and for whom hugging provides comfort and social support."

title: Eaton Fire may have exposed nearly 7 million people to elevated lead levels
raw_text:
Eaton Fire may have exposed nearly 7 million people to elevated lead levels
Swati Mestri
Scientific Editor
Robert Egan
Senior Editor
Caltech scientists have published the first detailed analysis of the atmospheric particles in the smoke plume from the Eaton Fire that devastated much of the town of Altadena in Southern California's San Gabriel Valley and the surrounding areas in January 2025.
The results confirm the very different chemical nature of the smoke produced by an urban fire compared with the plume from a typical wildfire. In the early stages of the fire, when many structures and vehicles were burning, the concentration of toxic metals in the atmosphere spiked dramatically.
This chemical signature, which was measured by an advanced air-monitoring station located downwind of the fire, then evolved as the blaze moved from urban areas up into the mountains above Altadena, part of the Angeles National Forest.
The scientists found that compared with wildfire smoke, the urban plume was enriched more than 50-fold in lead, sevenfold in chlorine and bromine, and threefold in arsenic. In fact, based on the data, they estimate that at the peak of the Eaton Fire's structural burning, nearly 7 million people in the Los Angeles metropolitan area were exposed to 24-hour lead concentrations 80 times higher than typical values.
These results are among the first to characterize the air that residents may be breathing during urban fires and could inform models used to determine emergency response to future urban fires.
A paper describing the work was published on Oct. 28 in the journal Science Advances. The lead author of the study is Haroula Baliaka (Ph.D. '27).
"Urban fire plumes are chemically distinct from those of wildfires. Now that we have these observational data about how they differ, we can go back and adjust our models to more accurately estimate how smoke might affect people," Baliaka says. "Smoke travels; it's not just about the burn area. What does a plume mean for people who are miles away from a fire but receive the smoke? We evacuate for fire, but we don't evacuate for smoke exposure."
Baliaka worked with former Caltech graduate student and co-author Ryan Ward (Ph.D. '25) to set up an air-monitoring station in the city of Pico Rivera, located roughly 11 miles (18 kilometers) south of Altadena, that gathered data on the smoke plume throughout the Eaton Fire. The station consists of a suite of four advanced analytical instruments that operate nearly 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, collecting data about the chemistry and physical properties of aerosols.
Aerosols are the tiny particulate matter suspended in the air that we commonly hear about in air quality reports (though those typically only report on PM₂.₅—particles that are 2.5 microns or smaller in diameter).
Colocated at an air quality monitoring station operated by the South Coast Air Quality Management District, the station is one of 12 around the country that make up the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork (ASCENT). ASCENT is managed by Nga Lee (Sally) Ng (Ph.D. '07), Caltech's Elizabeth W. Gilloon Professor of Environmental Science and Engineering and Chemical Engineering and a corresponding author of the new paper.
"ASCENT has the unique capability to measure the chemical components and the size of these different particles in real time," Ng says. "ASCENT is the first network in the U.S. to utilize these modern technologies for continuous aerosol measurements." All ASCENT data are now available to the public through both a long-term archive and near-real-time tools on the network's database.
The standard method for sampling aerosols is to collect a sample on a particle filter over a 24-hour period, every few days, and then to analyze the filters weeks or months later. However, with such a routine, it is impossible to capture concentration spikes that come and go rapidly—within hours, for example.
Because ASCENT stations run continuously, the scientists were able to observe the changing chemical nature of the Eaton Fire smoke plume as the fire itself moved up the San Gabriel Mountains, away from developed areas, and transitioned from an urban fire into a wildfire.
In the study, the scientists compared data obtained during two different fires that had been measured by ASCENT stations. The Pico Rivera site provided measurements from the Eaton Fire, and another ASCENT site at Rubidoux, California, gathered data on the so-called Airport Fire, which burned 24,000 acres (9,700 hectares) of vegetation in Southern California's Riverside County, located to the east of the San Gabriel Valley, in September 2024.
Filling a critical gap
"Essentially, this comparison between the two fires indicates how different and chemically distinct an urban fire is," Baliaka explains. That might seem intuitive, given that houses, buildings and everything within them, as well as vehicles, burn in an urban fire, but there has been a lack of data about the chemicals in smoke from urban fires. In fact, a 2022 report by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, titled "The Chemistry of Fires at the Wildland–Urban Interface," underscored the need for data on urban fire smoke plumes.
And as demonstrated by recent blazes in Los Angeles—as well as in Northern California (the Camp Fire), Colorado (the Marshall Fire), Hawaii (the Lahaina Fire) and, this August, in Spokane, Washington—fires increasingly involve elements of urban burning at this wildland–urban interface, the zone where development meets vegetation.
As the researchers pored over the ASCENT data from the Eaton and Airport fires, they noted an important relationship between the concentrations of two specific chemical elements, potassium and lead. Potassium is an essential nutrient that plants naturally take up from the soil. When vegetation and wood burn, some of that potassium is released into smoke, and so, unsurprisingly, the fire plumes from both the wildland and the urban fire showed elevated levels of potassium.
But in the Eaton Fire, which began on the evening of Jan. 7, lead concentrations spiked across eastern Los Angeles and the San Gabriel Valley on Jan. 8 and 9. The highest lead values were measured directly downwind of Altadena. The ratio of potassium to lead was at its lowest level (around 5:1, indicating the presence of five times more potassium than lead in the fire plume) on those days. As the fire moved into the mountains, the ratio increased toward wildfire-like values (a ratio of about 50:1 by Jan. 11, and then climbing into the hundreds by Jan. 12).
"What was really amazing is that we were able to capture that movement toward a more traditional wildfire signature within a single fire," Baliaka says.
For context, the scientists note that since the early 1980s, when leaded gasoline was being phased out in Los Angeles, typical concentrations of lead in the Los Angeles Basin have declined by more than two orders of magnitude, or by about 99%. So while the spike in lead values is dramatic compared with current baselines, it was in line with what was normal before the 1980s.
But they also point out that scientists do not yet know the health effects of the kind of short-duration, high-concentration exposure to toxic chemicals that millions of Angelenos experienced during the Los Angeles fires. "Unfortunately, Californians get exposed to fires all the time. What do all of these short-term but elevated air toxins, not just lead, mean for our health?" says Baliaka. "We need to start figuring that out."
Updating models for fire response
A goal for the scientists moving forward is to use the data to update models that predict air quality and the amount of pollutants expected to be released into the atmosphere as a result of both urban fires and wildfires. Such models are critical in emergency fire response for predicting where toxic smoke plumes will travel and in helping determine what actions should be taken for public safety.
Richard Flagan, Caltech's Irma and Ross McCollum-William H. Corcoran Professor of Chemical Engineering and Environmental Science and Engineering, says that the response to the Eaton Fire and to contamination of the debris left in its wake was predicated on the firestorm being a wildfire event. "But the Eaton Fire was an extreme urban fire event," he says.
"Perhaps it is time to reconsider fire codes to address the possibility of urban firestorms in densely populated urban areas, and consider the downwind health impacts and excess mortality as the important impacts of such events."
The researchers acknowledge that the strong signature of lead might be unique to the Eaton Fire, given the large number of older homes and structures that burned in Altadena, but they hope that the results provide a baseline for comparison with future urban fires.
Ng emphasizes that there is a need for additional real-time continuous aerosol-monitoring stations around the country to develop a comprehensive understanding of fires at the wildland–urban interface. "The existing monitoring stations provide a vital foundation, and ASCENT shows how we can build on it to modernize this country's air quality measurement infrastructure," she says.
"With ASCENT, we are not only seeing how much particulate matter is in the air but what it is made of, and we can watch it as the event unfolds. This kind of information is very useful for tracking the atmospheric chemical evolution of fire smoke, and it helps emergency managers and public health officials better understand what communities are being exposed to in real time."

title: US adults say craft and sustained commitment, not fame, separate creators from influencers
raw_text:
US adults say craft and sustained commitment, not fame, separate creators from influencers
Gaby Clark
Scientific Editor
Andrew Zinin
Chief Editor
The creator economy is a growing global industry that Goldman Sachs Research reports could be worth $480 billion by 2027. But what is a creator, and what is the difference between a creator and an influencer, a celebrity or everyone else who posts online?
The main differentiator between a creator and an influencer? Nearly 84% of U.S. adults surveyed define creators by their craft and their long-term dedication to it, which sets them apart from influencers, celebrities and everyday social media users.
That was one of the key findings unveiled by Syracuse University's Center for the Creator Economy (CCE) during the second annual 'CUSE Creator Con, which brought together creators, industry executives and thinkers. The two-day event featured a kickoff celebration Thursday, Oct. 22, and several sessions the following day that explored various aspects of the creator economy.
"'Creator' has become one of the most important words in media and one of the least defined," says Ryan Schram, executive director of the CCE. "This research gives the industry a definition grounded in what audiences, creators and the professionals who work with them told us. Their answer is clear: being a creator is about craft and commitment."
In its inaugural long-form research study, the CCE defined a creator as "an independent studio: a 360 enterprise that collapses whole industries into one person ... sharing knowledge with the audiences they build and carrying the expectations once placed on celebrities and institutions. They are defined by a love of the craft, a sustained commitment to it over time and an authenticity that earns trust and keeps audiences coming back ... ."
During the "Signature Research Unveil" panel at Creator Con, Carrie Welch, the CCE's launch director, shared one of the research's more surprising takeaways about how creators and influencers relate.
"There are creators who also influence, but there was a growing trend in our research that while creators can be influencers, influencers cannot be creators," says Welch. "There's an art and a craft attached to the creator that is not present for the people we spoke with for the influencer. The influencer was read as transactional: someone you employ for a marketing tactic. The creator is an artist: someone you want to formulate a long-term relationship with as a student of the craft."
Among the other findings:
- 75.5% of respondents see creators as a distinct professional role
- 66.7% see a difference between a creator and an influencer
- 87.2% see a difference between a creator and a celebrity
- 69.7% accept creators running their channels purely as a business
- 64.7% say changing content to chase sponsors compromises integrity
Want to grow an audience? Authenticity matters
Matty Weisholtz '27, a content creator and president of 'Cuse Creative Studios, has turned what started as a hobby into a growing personal brand. She was among the 40 creators and industry professionals who provided insights that helped the CCE define a creator.
Since landing her first brand collaboration with Valentino, Weisholtz has pitched and partnered with brands on her own, creating between five and 10 brand partnership videos each week.
"Authenticity is everything. I'm able to accept bigger campaigns because my engagement rate is so high and because people genuinely interact with my content and like to view it," says Weisholtz, a marketing management major in the Whitman School of Management who served as a student panelist during the "Signature Research Unveil" session.
One of the most important breakthroughs came when she realized she could build her own brand algorithm because she knew "what my audience likes, because my audience is a bunch of me's."
From that point, Weisholtz vowed to always produce authentic content.
"Authenticity came up in every interview we conducted," Welch says. "Authenticity is the special sauce that runs through the creator economy. If you're not authentic, you're not making really good content. You're becoming an ad and selling something."
Defining a creator to protect the future of the industry
The research was built on a census-matched national survey of 989 U.S. adults conducted via Prolific in October, along with initial findings from 40 in-depth interviews with creators and creator economy industry professionals.
Welch handled the qualitative research, including interviewing Weisholtz and Malik Evans, a growth adviser with Meta, while professor Nick Bowman, who oversees doctoral and master's programs in mass communications and media studies in the S.I. Newhouse School of Public Communications, handled the quantitative research.
Welch, Bowman, Evans and Weisholtz discussed the key takeaways during the panel conversation. Welch says the resulting definitions are vitally important to the future of the industry and will affect creators at every level, from those with millions of followers to those just getting started.
"These definitions need to constantly be redefined and updated, and this research is evolving," Welch says. "We're not just teaching our students how to be influencers. There are real business implications. If being a creator is the modern version of an entrepreneur, there are laws and regulatory problems we have to solve. The infrastructure isn't there yet. In trying to define what a creator is, we're hoping to protect this group of people."
What's next
Welch says the CCE is already working on its next flash research report, examining how creators influence holiday shopping, including whether consumers prefer to create gift wish lists or follow their favorite shopping influencer on social media.
