title: Sauerkraut at Every Meal? These Fermentation Fanatics Tried That Long Before MAHA
raw_text:
Waking early, I put a small jar of my sauerkraut into my messenger bag, hop on my bicycle, ride to Seattle's King Street Station, and board a train heading to the Portland Fermentation Festival, the yearly gathering affectionately nicknamed “Stinkfest.”
Usually the sheer existence of a festival like this is enough to get people revved up to come together and talk about their favorite ferments, but in an interesting twist, fermented foods are enjoying a popularity boost from a different crowd. The MAHA movement, and particularly the Donald Trump cabinet, are big into fermented food, eating meat, usually steak, with fermented sides like kimchi or sauerkraut at every meal.
I've come to Portland, Oregon, wondering if there was going to be any overlap in the Venn diagram between festival attendees and the MAHA steak-and-ferment crowd. I mentioned this to my cousin-in-law Erick, who's been part of the Portland food scene for years, and he laughed out loud.
“It'll be more like a Venn dumbbell,” he said, making a pair of thumb-and-forefinger circles and tracing a line in the air between them. “No overlap, but food will be the bridge.”
Still, I was curious. I’d check.
The festival is almost exactly what the fermentation-friendly might hope to find. Right inside the main door next to the check-in desk is a bacterial petting zoo—pure festival charm—and a table where attendees can drop off their own ferments to share. Further on, lining every wall of the main room, are exhibitors who have paid a grand total of 25 bucks for a table, handing out free samples of fermented foods.
The space quickly fills up–several hundred people flow through over the course of the evening–and it appears that there's both a line in front of each exhibitor and perhaps a more organic continuous line with people flowing clockwise from one exhibitor to the next. People are notably excited and happy. There's a kid walking around with a tray of handmade pickle pins he's giving people to wear and there's a collective gasp when 20 or 30 minutes in, Dillon T. Pickle, the mascot of the Portland Pickles West Coast League baseball team, walks into the room. At one point, a big baby crawls across most of the main floor, unhindered and happy.
In the middle of it all is festival co-organizer, journalist, and cookbook author Liz Crain. She explains that the Fest, now in its 14th installment, was started in 2009 by friends who love to ferment. There were members of a little company called Picklopolis and a club called The Kraut Collective, and, with some help from author and fermentation rockstar Sandor Katz, they launched a Portland tradition.
When I ask how the festival has evolved since its first year, she gets a little philosophical.
“Keep Portland Weird. People get excited,” she says in a tone where several punctuation options would be in the spirit of the festival. “People lined up on the sidewalk all the way around the building for the first one. I poured hard cider that I made from a tree in my backyard.”
“There's nothing for sale, and that gives it a potluck-y party style. Most big festivals have consumers and purveyors, but without those distinctions here, it makes conversations a bit deeper, a bit more personal,” she says. “There's no gatekeeping, no secret recipes. It's always been wacky and fun.”
She isn't sure how much MAHA crossover I'll encounter, but she has an openness to it.
“RFK is certainly infatuated with sauerkraut and steak. There's some good to be found in the overall MAHA tenets, but so much of it has been muddied by the anti-vax stance and ludicrous conspiracy theories,” she says, though she believes it's important to “look closely and critically at pesticides and favor less-processed foods.”
“But a diet that's based solely on meat, particularly beef, animal fats, and sauerkraut … well that's not a very diverse diet,” she says. “Let's just say I wouldn't want to sit next to that person on a plane or be stuck in an elevator with them.”
I pick up on these ideas with Chris Curtin, a fermentation microbiology researcher at Oregon State University.
“Historically, everything has shown that narrowing the scope of your diet misses some things. They don't turn out to be the best in the long run,” he says. An Australian living in the US for the last decade, he can clearly see the way trends are moving and notes that registered dietitians have consistently put fermented foods at the top of their superfood lists for the past decade.
Curtin describes his work as caring about what happens when we mess around with microbes to see what happens to the raw material. As he puts it, "I'm interested in tinkering if it involves microbe wrangling." He also gets the festival's popularity among those who ferment.
“Fermenting is such a readily accessible scientific experiment that you can do in your kitchen. People go, find foods they like and want to make in their own kitchens. It's accessible and tactile.”
This plays out at the festival as I begin to sample the merchandise. The first thing I taste is an “orange whey Julius” that includes whey and OJ and is pleasingly reminiscent of the Orange Julius I'd get as a treat as a kid at the Mall of New Hampshire.
Next to that is Nat West's booth with Peruvian corn beer called chicha. West has run a cider company, dabbled in politics, driven a TriMet city bus in Portland, and now runs the Vancouver, Washington, farmers’ market. In a chicha, the fermentation starts by the brewer chewing ground field corn. At the festival, attendees are drinking what West has chewed. As people in line joke about drinking this guy's spit, or at least the byproducts of it, West interjects, “nobody's died yet!”
“The ptyalin enzymes in the saliva kickstart the starch-to-sugar process,” he explains as I take a sip and gaze longingly at the draft beer in the hands of someone who's wandered into the show from the Hotlips pizza next door.
Further along, Portland's Jorinji Miso has a double booth with samples of miso soup with bonito flakes along with koji (rice fermented with Aspergillus oryzae spores) and amazake, a koji-based drink.
The couple who run Maypop Wine Co. have their hands full at the Fest. The company’s cofounder Vince Kelsea explains that they make “anything but pinot” in the Willamette Valley—a lush north-south valley in Oregon renowned for its pinot noir. Making unfiltered, low-intervention wines like Maypop in a region famous for its pinot sounds like they're making things hard for themselves, but the attendees maintain a several-deep line at the booth all night long.
In one corner is Kiyomi Hasagewa, a third-generation Japanese bean purveyor. She’s sharing tastes of a 15-year-old miso she dehydrated and ground so she could bring it from Hokkaido to the festival. She sprinkles it over the rice and tops it with a wedge of sun-dried daikon which her elderly mother fermented in a mashed pumpkin paste. It is easily the most interesting bite in the room.
Back in the entry hall are my personal favorites, the ferments that attendees have brought to share. Liz Crain has brought along plum and dandelion wines, pickle brine, a blackberry-blueberry-lemon water kefir, and a monster jar of sour dills. I note with pride that the jar of sauerkraut I brought is next to Liz’s pickles, near-empty. Nearby is another giant jar of “fermented carrot coins, cherry bomb, garlic, ginger, horseradish,” which I anticipate as a pleasant assault on my senses, but it's really just pleasant. A garlic blast for sure, but one with all of the harsh edges smoothed by time and beneficial bacteria into something lovely.
Also at the community table are Portland occupational therapist Eva Ortega and her fermentation buddy Letti Kittel who drove down from Seattle.
“I've only made unsuccessful ferments so far,” says Ortega, undeterred. “I'm here to learn.”
Kittel says she's been nerding out on fermenting for about a year and has brought a kombucha starter with its bacteria-and-yeast scoby for others to bring home and try. And while both of them have no comment about the MAHA connection, Ortega puts some of Kittel's starter in a little jar and drops it into her purse.
I'm expecting another round of “no comment” when the MAHA diet comes up with three other fermenting friends, Megan Andricos, Josh Monifi, and Desiré Demarest, but Andricos, aka DJ Sappho, followed a similar diet 20 years ago in what they call their “fermented-pickled food and protein phase,” which consisted of “mostly kimchi and meat.”
They're off that diet now, but they liked being on it. “Kimchi evens out my gut biome. I felt better. Not superhuman, but better.”
Also on the community table is something called “Higgins Kraut,” made with Napa cabbage, carrots, garlic, and ginger, which, with a lovely melding of flavors, won my personal Best-in-Show award.
Turns out it's made by one of the show’s other founders, George Winborn, who was involved for the first 10 years. He'd been farming in Dallas when he moved to Portland, to a place that had no yard and nowhere to farm.
“Doing the Fest helped scratch the itch,” he says. He's now getting Wellspring Farm in Gresham, Oregon, off the ground and noted how the festival has become a bit more commercial, a bit less homemade. But all that's relative, considering we're standing here over our jars of sauerkraut, and the exhibitors are very small businesses, if they're businesses at all.
“I still love the DIY and starter tables,” he says. “It reminds you that everyone can do this.”
Update, Wednesday October 28 at 3:30 pm: The original version of this story misquoted one sentence attributed to Liz Crain. When asked about the enduring popularity of the festival, she said “Keep Portland Weird,” which is an unofficial motto of the city that speaks to its countercultural enthusiasm. The story was updated to correct that quote.

title: Apple AirPods Max 2 Are $100 Off Right Now. Let the Rationalizing Begin
raw_text:
Apple makes some of the best headphones on the market. I almost never want to pay full price for them, though. Here at WIRED, we spend a lot of time testing Apple gear and tracking prices, so we know when it’s a smart time to buy and when it’s best to wait.
Right now, Apple AirPods Max 2 are $100 off on Amazon. If you prefer wireless earbuds, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 are also $49 off. We’ve seen both products go for a bit less, and they are likely to drop further for Black Friday. But if you've been eyeing Apple's headphones for a while and need them sooner than late November, now is a good time to buy.
For more of our Apple recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Apple Watches, iPhones, and iPads.
Apple AirPods Max 2 for $449 ($100 Off)
The AirPods Max 2 are the best-sounding headphones for Apple loyalists. I have been testing them for about three months now, and they have become my favorite headphones for travel. They unfortunately can’t prevent airplane ear, but their plush over-ear cuffs feel way more comfortable than cramming buds into my ear canals for hours on end. The headphones deliver up to 1.5 times more automated noise-canceling (ANC) performance than the previous version, support lossless audio, and can be plugged in via USB-C for ultralow latency audio.
This sale applies to all five colorways (midnight, blue, orange, purple, and starlight). I’ve seen the AirPods Max 2 go for cheaper, but $449 is still a good deal. If you already own the OGs, I wouldn’t upgrade, but if you need a new pair, think these over.
Apple AirPods Pro 3 for $200 ($49 Off)
This isn’t the best deal I’ve seen on the flagship AirPods Pro 3, so if you can hold out until Black Friday, I’d wait. But if you need a new pair of earbuds now and own an iPhone, these are my favorite, and $49 off is still better than full price.
When I'm out and about, working out, or want the convenience of removing an earbud to hear something—though transparency mode often makes that unnecessary—I reach for my AirPods Pro 3. They are my go-to for runs because their silicone ear tips stay in place even when I start to sweat. They may not be as new as AirPods 5, but they are better, with three times more ANC and built-in heart rate sensing for workouts. That's in addition to Apple's adaptive EQ and hearing aid features. Battery life is around eight hours with ANC enabled and up to 24 hours with the charging case. You get five sizes of ear tips to tailor the fit.

Mumbai, the capital city of Maharashtra state, was formerly known as Bombay. Now, it is also considered the financial and commercial capital of the country. The mega city has strong historical links, wonderful British architecture, museums, shrines, beaches and the Hindi film industry which is also known as Bollywood. The seven islands which form the metropolis were earlier home to fishing communities. For centuries, the islands were being controlled by the successive indigenous empires before being ceded to the Portuguese and later to the East India Company of Great Britain. During the mid-18th century, Bombay was reshaped with the construction of major roads and railways and subsequently it transformed into a major seaport on the Arabian Sea as we see it today. The city was renamed Mumbai in 1996. The happening city carries a vibrant and cosmopolitan culture. Be it Bollywood or Victorian-era buildings, Asia's largest slum in Dharavi or the lunchbox delivery and return system of the famous dabbawalas, every aspect of Mumbai boasts a unique identity.

Delhi, the capital of India, is also considered the heart of the nation. The massive metropolitan city lies in a triangle formed by the river Yamuna in the east and spurs from the Aravali range in the west and south. The city, a largest and busiest commercial hub in northern India, is also the largest centre of small industries. The IT sector, handloom, fashion, textile and electronic industry contribute a lot to Delhi's economy. The capital has a strong historical background too. It was ruled by some of the most powerful emperors. And thus, it radiates with its syncretic culture. The history of the city is as old as the epic Mahabharata. It was known as Indraprastha, where Pandavas used to live. In due course, eight more cities came alive adjacent to Indraprastha - Lal Kot, Siri, Dinpanah, Quila Rai Pithora, Ferozabad, Jahanpanah, Tughlakabad and Shahjahanabad. The city is divided into two parts - Old Delhi and New Delhi. New Delhi, also called Lutyens' Delhi, bears a striking contrast to Old Delhi with respect to architecture, building materials and layout. However, modern Delhi itself dates back to over a century when the British shifted their capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

- Chennai-bound flights are 23.9% cheaper when booked a month ahead than a day before departure, while Ahmedabad flyers face a 60.6% fare gap and Bengaluru sees just 5% On the morning of 28 October 2026, advertised fares into Chennai showed that booking 30 days ahead cost 23.9 per cent less than booking the day before, measured across seven routes. That gap is 10.2 percentage points better than the national network figure of 13.7 per cent. The cheapest point across those seven routes was 60 days before departure, and every one of the seven routes was cheaper at 30 days than the day before.
- Want cheaper flight tickets? Fares are lower on 53 of 54 domestic routes when booked 30 days ahead, while waiting until the last day carries a 15.9% premium On the morning of 28 October 2026, fare data across 54 tracked domestic routes showed that booking a flight 30 days before departure costs 13.7 per cent less than booking the day before. Fifty-three of the 54 routes followed this pattern. The fare-time index also showed that waiting until the last day carries a premium of 15.9 per cent over the cheapest point in the booking window.
- Booking Hyderabad flights 30 days ahead cuts fares 29% across 7 routes, beating network savings of 13.7% by 15.4 percentage points Fares into Hyderabad reward early bookers more sharply than the broader domestic network does, according to data captured on the morning of 28 October 2026. Across all seven routes studied, a ticket bought 30 days before departure carried an index score of 70.9 against the day-before benchmark of 100, a gap 15.4 percentage points better than the equivalent network figure. The steepest penalty for waiting falls on the Kolkata to Hyderabad route.
- Ahmedabad-Pune flyers pay 120.5% more when booking a day before departure than when booking 30 days ahead, while Bengaluru-Chennai fares rise by just 2.9% On the morning of 16 September 2026, fares across 54 domestic routes showed a stark divide in how much last-minute booking costs. On Ahmedabad to Pune, waiting until the day before departure meant paying 120.5 per cent more than a ticket bought 30 days ahead. On Bengaluru to Chennai, that same wait added just 2.9 per cent. The gap between the two extremes is wide enough to matter for anyone planning travel.
- TOI-DPA Airfare Index: A flight price tracker that will help you plan trips better The TOI-DPA Airline Price Index monitors daily fluctuations in domestic airfares across India, illuminating trends in inflation, demand, and pricing strategies for various routes. Additionally, the Fare Timing Index reveals how ticket prices adjust over time related to booking. Factors such as departure times and specific days of the week play a critical role in determining fare costs, leading to valuable insights into airline pricing dynamics.
- Flight fare analysis findings: Booking early can save you big, last-minute flights cost 25% more on average; get cheaper fares by planning 30 days in advance A ticket bought the day before departure costs about 25% more than the same journey booked 30 days ahead. On all 54 metro routes tracked, not one is cheaper to book late. The penalty runs from 3% on Bengaluru to Chennai to 121% on Ahmedabad to Pune. Thirty days out is the floor. Booking two or three months ahead is slightly dearer than booking one.
- Flying to Kolkata for Durga Puja? Be ready to pay 71% more on Oct 16 The median one-way fare into Kolkata for October 16, when Durga Puja begins, is Rs 14,117. The same routes cost Rs 8,259 for a departure next week. Kolkata is the only one of eight big metros where mid-October fares are running above mid-November fares. The increase applies only to flights coming into the city. Seats going out of Kolkata on the same day are priced normally.

title: Agartala News: Latest Headlines, Breaking Updates & Live News Today - Times of India
raw_text:
A social media content creator and mobile shop owner in Tripura was arrested for allegedly raping a tribal woman. He reportedly lured her to Agartala with the promise of an iPhone, then took her to a hotel and assaulted her. The accused also allegedly stole her phone and threatened her before her escape and subsequent complaint.
Tripura government mandates 50% of Group C and D employees work from home, effective immediately, following Prime Minister Modi's fuel conservation appeal. Departments must create weekly rosters, ensuring alternate attendance. Remote staff must remain reachable for urgent tasks. This directive excludes essential services personnel and applies to PSUs and local bodies.
Tripura convened a key meeting on carbon sequestration and climate finance. Government departments and organizations explored strategies for green economy initiatives. Experts discussed accessing climate funds for community development and livelihood enhancement. The state aims to monetize its high carbon sequestration potential. Preparations are underway for India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme.
A 70-year-old grandfather, Pranballabh Das, has been sent to 14-day judicial custody in Agartala on charges of raping and murdering his 16-year-old granddaughter. Police registered a case based on a complaint from the victim's father, with preliminary findings indicating multiple instances of sexual exploitation. The post-mortem report is awaited to further the investigation into the murder.

title: Ajmer News: Latest Ajmer News Headlines & Live Updates from Ajmer - Times of India
raw_text:
A 14-year-old student in Ajmer attempted suicide after facing teasing from classmates about her height. Rescued by passers-by, she was treated and discharged. The girl reportedly told police she was distressed by the body-shaming, but her parents opted to address the issue with the school instead of filing a complaint.
In a shocking incident in Ajmer, a woman has been arrested for allegedly killing her 3-year-old daughter by throwing her into Ana Sagar Lake. Anjali Singh, who had left her husband in Varanasi to live with another man, initially misled the police. However, CCTV footage revealed inconsistencies in her statements, leading to her confession.
Four men were arrested by police for making obscene remarks at an Israeli woman tourist in Kishangarh. The incident occurred when the woman recorded a video at a local dumping yard, a tourist spot. Following the woman's social media post, police initiated an investigation and formed a special team for identification. Officials used technical and intelligence inputs to trace the suspects.
Heavy rainfall in Ajmer, Rajasthan, led to the Boraj dam wall collapsing, flooding streets and homes. Residents were rescued, and the road was closed. While the water level is now decreasing, the IMD forecasts more rain. Simultaneously, rising Yamuna levels have flooded parts of the NCR, including Noida and Delhi, exceeding the danger mark at the Signature Bridge.

title: Amaravati News: Latest Amaravati News, Amaravati news Headlines & Live News - Times of India
raw_text:
Tensions heightened outside the Tirupati Municipal Corporation office as Vasu Yadav faced challenges while trying to file his nomination. After his papers were reportedly snatched by an unknown individual, police assigned for protection failed to prevent a second obstruction by a crowd. Tirupati MP Dr. M Gurumoorthy voiced displeasure over police inefficiency, suggesting possible ruling party interference to impede opposition candidates in the electoral process.
YSRCP has raised concerns regarding police interference during nominations for municipal polls in Pulivendula. Party members claimed they faced lathi-charges, tear gas, and were obstructed from filing nominations. YSRCP MP YS Avinash Reddy alleged that TDP supporters gathered openly while his party faced violence. The police reportedly failed to act against alleged TDP misconduct during the nomination process.
Cyclone Arnab made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast, causing widespread disruption due to heavy rain and strong winds. Numerous trees were uprooted, and electricity supply was severely disrupted across affected areas. Emergency teams worked to clear roads while police conducted rescues of stranded individuals in flooded areas. The Indian Meteorological Department warned about potential storm surges affecting low-lying coastal regions.
Violent confrontations broke out between TDP and YSRCP activists in Kadapa during the nominations filing phase. Police had to intervene in Pulivendula when YSRCP supporters tried to rush the nominations centre. Clashes also occurred in places like Mydukur and Rayachoti, resulting in injuries among party workers. Several YSRCP leaders were placed under house arrest due to these escalating tensions.

title: Amritsar News, Latest Amritsar News Headlines & Live Updates - Times of India
raw_text:
The Indian Overseas Congress chapters are rallying support for the November 1 Delhi Chalo event, with leaders from around the globe coming to India to participate. This significant rally aims to champion electoral integrity and address pressing issues surrounding democracy. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge and Rahul Gandhi are actively encouraging citizens from all walks of life to join, reflecting the deep commitment of overseas Congress supporters to India's political future.
In a series of operations, seven people were apprehended by Amritsar Rural Police for their roles in arms and drug trafficking. Among them was a soldier on leave, allegedly engaged in smuggling. Police recovered an impressive haul, including 14 pistols and 20.130kg of heroin. Ongoing investigations seek to establish ties with a foreign handler and clarify the supply chain's intended targets, working to dismantle this criminal network.
A drone originating from Pakistan met its end in a parking lot near the Attari international border after carrying illegal contraband. The incident occurred post the flag-lowering ceremony while several tourists were in the vicinity. Border Security Force officials successfully seized a Zigana pistol and around 500 grams of heroin from the wreckage. It’s suspected that electronic jammers may have disrupted the drone’s operation, and investigations are actively underway.
Teerath Singh was shot dead outside a gurdwara in Cheete Kalan village while his friend sustained injuries. Both men were returning from paying respects at the gurdwara when the suspected assailants opened fire. Preliminary investigations indicate the murder was connected to an old land dispute rather than political rivalry. Police have identified four suspects and filed an FIR, but no arrests have been made yet.

title: Cuttack News: Latest Headlines, Breaking News & Updates Today - Times of India
raw_text:
Fire breaks out in ICU at Cuttack hospital
While Cuttack gears up for a T20I, the village of Nuagarh has boycotted cricket for over two decades. This decision stems from the tragic drowning of 13 local cricketers in 2004 while en route to a tournament final. A memorial stands as a stark reminder of the loss that continues to shape the village's relationship with the sport.
A 30-year-old woman was allegedly gang-raped by at least six men late Tuesday night. The accused intercepted her car and assaulted her male colleague before the assault. The victim approached police early Wednesday, and a case was immediately registered. Police are examining the car and crime scene for evidence. Efforts are underway to identify and arrest all individuals involved in the crime.
Eight people, including a woman and two children, were stranded for nearly two hours after a swing malfunctioned at Bali Jatra in Cuttack. They were rescued safely with the help of a hydraulic lift by Odisha Fire Service personnel. All rescued individuals were taken to the hospital for medical examination.

Nisha and her boyfriend Pappu have been arrested for the tragic murder of her husband Anshul in Khoda Colony. Pappu shot him twice inside their rented home using a locally made firearm, which is now in police custody.
On October 26, a woman named Priya allegedly conspired with her gym trainer lover to stab her husband. CCTVs captured Priya leaving their home in Ghaziabad shortly before the attack occurred. The attack was brutal, happening while Shashank was asleep next to their young daughter. Shashank was immediately rushed to the intensive care unit after suffering severe injuries. Both Priya and her accomplice have been arrested and face multiple charges.
Many parks in Noida and Ghaziabad are facing alarming issues related to insufficient lighting and inadequate security measures. Residents are increasingly hesitant to enjoy these public spaces after sundown, as broken streetlights diminish safety and invite undesirable activities. Despite notifying the relevant authorities regarding these pressing concerns, timely improvements are desperately needed to restore community trust and ensure public safety in these areas.

After enduring severe heart valve leakage, retired engineer from Uzbekistan, Israilov Jakhongir, sought a less invasive solution. He underwent a transcatheter mitral valve-in-ring replacement at Paras Health, steering clear of high-risk open-heart surgery. Following the procedure, Jakhongir felt an impressive recovery and was soon discharged, expressing heartfelt appreciation for regaining his health.

Severe flash floods in Parsi Parlo, Arunachal Pradesh, have caused extensive damage. Incessant monsoon rains swelled rivers, inundating the remote border town during early hours. Affected areas remain inaccessible due to collapsed roads and bridges.

A Vande Bharat Express has recently crossed both the world's highest Chenab Bridge and India's first cable-stayed Anji Bridge. The maximum permissible speed in the Katra-Banihal rail section has been raised to 100 kmph after safety checks. This increase is expected to significantly reduce the travel time between Katra and Banihal. The section is part of the Udhampur-Srinagar-Baramulla Railway Link project.
India's most-wanted terrorist Hafiz Saeed is reportedly in Pakistan, the NIA informed a Jammu court. The agency secured a second non-bailable warrant against the LeT founder for terror funding. This warrant relates to a case involving weapons and funds supplied to terror groups. The investigation uncovered a terror network and led to several arrests. Saeed is accused of operating from Pakistan and directing terrorists in Kashmir.
Development is underway for a viewing deck and museum adjacent to the iconic Chenab railway bridge in Jammu and Kashmir. This museum will delve into the engineering feats and construction hurdles experienced during the bridge's creation. With the aim of enriching the tourist experience, visitors will appreciate both the bridge's impressive scale and the breathtaking natural scenery surrounding it.
A National Conference spokesperson's historical poverty remarks ignited a political controversy. Opposition parties condemned the statement, demanding an apology from the legislator. The Bharatiya Janata Party accused the party of insulting women and distorting history. The National Conference defended the statement, referencing historical accounts of hardship. The controversy highlights differing interpretations of Kashmir's past and present conditions.

2 million followers, just 33 votes: Poor poll result shocks Jodhpur astro-influencer
Omprakash Bishnoi, a popular astrologer and influencer, contested the sarpanch election in Jodhpur's Indon Ki Dhani-II. Despite his significant social media presence, he received only 33 votes from 1,600 eligible voters. Bishnoi had over two million followers across various platforms, which did not translate into electoral support. His role as president of a local cow shelter was also not enough to sway voters.

raw_text:
Situated on the banks of Gomti, Lucknow, the capital of UP, is known for its multicultural aura. Famous for its history, heritage, cuisine and Chikan art, it's India's 14th-most populous city.
Population3,764,619
Area in Sq Km2,528
HeritageCity of NawabTourist Attraction
Lucknow city has many fascinating heritage sites that include beautiful Mughal-era monuments, palaces, parks, some of the oldest markets and British-era residencies.
CuisineFood TourBurp!
Lucknow offers a wide array of dishes. Famous for its street foods, even tourists eat like a local here. Don't forget to taste Awadhi dishes & Bilai ki Gilori.
MangoesDussehriMalihabad
Lucknow's Malihabad, the land of Dussehri mangoes, is often called the 'mango capital' of India. These orchards have some of the oldest mango trees.
Check out the latest news in Lucknow on The Times of India with a wide range of topics including Lucknow’s politics, crime, sports, fashion, culture, civic bodies, Lucknow’s traffic and weather updates, new trends, education and civic issues of Lucknow. From the regular hustle-bustle in the capital city of Uttar Pradesh to the gastronomical delights in old alleyways of Nawab-era markets. From latest political developments to entertainment-related events or even traffic jams. We cover it all in detail and you can check it all in just one click. Lucknow is the eleventh most populous city and the twelfth most populous urban agglomeration of India. The city stands at an elevation of approximately 123 metres (404 feet) above sea level. Lucknow district covers an area of 2,528 square kilometres. Lucknow, the 'golden city of the east’ retains an old world charm that fascinates one and all. Regarded as one of the finest cities of the country, Lucknow emanates a culture that combines emotional warmth, a high degree of sophistication, courtesy and a love for gracious living. This sublime cultural richness famous as ‘Lucknowi Tehzeeb’ blends the cultures of two communities living side by side for centuries and sharing similar interests. Known for its refinement in speech, entertainment and manners, Lucknow is also called the ‘City of Adab‘. Infact, it is here that one can experience hospitality in the true sense of the term. It continues to be an important centre of governance, administration, education, commerce, aerospace, finance, pharmaceuticals, technology, design, culture, tourism, music and poetry.

title: Law Firm Linked to Elon Musk Started an ‘Election Integrity’ Organization
raw_text:
The law firm that helped set up Elon Musk’s America PAC has created a new, nationwide “election integrity” organization aligned with Donald Trump’s false claims of election fraud, WIRED has learned.
The organization, a nonprofit called the Association of State and Local Election Officials, was established by a lawyer then at Lex Politica, the Musk-linked law firm founded by Chris Gober, who was chief counsel for America PAC in 2024 and is now running in Texas for a spot in the House of Representatives.
The board of directors, according to the nonprofit’s registration filing in Texas, boasts Florida secretary of state Cord Byrd, current and former state election officials in Georgia, a Michigan state representative, and the president of Cleta Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, a Trump administration-aligned election denial group. Byrd announced his involvement with the group—which he said won’t begin until after the election—alongside Florida governor Ron DeSantis in September, as the pair touted its mission, which aims to bring what they call “election integrity” policies down to the state and local level nationwide.
It’s not clear if Musk is involved in the organization. Until now, Musk has simply been a funder of Republican candidates and causes, and a benefactor of government contracts. Musk’s financial involvement in the midterm elections has been extensive: Musk’s America PAC is financing a sprawling canvassing operation aimed at helping Republican candidates get out the vote in November, and Musk is the single largest donor to Republican candidates this election cycle, spending more than $445 million, targeting Senate races key to maintaining a Republican majority. Since July, Musk has spent nearly as much money—$276 million—to boost Republican candidates as he did during the entire 2024 presidential election cycle. These elections are crucial for Musk. If Democrats win majorities in the House and Senate, Musk and his companies could be the subject of congressional investigations.
The link between a law firm that has worked with Musk and officials involved in purported “election integrity” activities is not surprising. For years, Musk has pushed the racist great replacement theory, which posits that minorities are systematically replacing white people in the US and in Western countries around the world. Election denialism—rooted in the unfounded theory of widespread voting by undocumented immigrants—is part of that racist theory of demographic societal change.
Musk has continually pushed election conspiracies that align with Trump’s false claims of election fraud, and this year, he’s doubled down. Musk has been a major disseminator of election misinformation this cycle, and recently boosted the false story that Texas US senate candidate James Talarico had been committed to a psychiatric facility in Ohio. America PAC has also spread inaccurate information about mail-in ballots.
The Association of State and Local Election Officials was first registered on June 17 by Michael Garcar as a nonprofit in Texas. At the time, Garcar was an attorney at Lex Politica, which was expanded after its lead lawyer, Gober, helped launch Musk’s America PAC. Gober has represented Musk’s and America PAC’s political interests in court cases in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.
On July 20, the Association of State and Local Election Officials was granted tax-exempt status by the IRS, according to an agency letter addressed to the organization at its Washington, DC, address. That address—a box in a UPS Store on Pennsylvania Avenue—is the same as the one Garcar listed on the organization’s Texas filing and belongs to Lex Politica, according to a US Supreme Court filing from one of the firm’s attorneys, Erin Hawley, wife of Senator Josh Hawley. The nonprofit’s Texas registration was first unearthed by True North Research, a progressive research group.
Garcar has since left Lex Politica and now works for Five Rings Law Group. The firm lists just two partners—both Lex Politica alums—and former Koch Industries lawyer Jenny Kim. Before launching Five Rings, Kim worked for Gober.
Garcar, Kim, and Gober did not respond to questions about Lex Politica’s ties to the Association of State and Local Election Officials.
At a September 24 press conference about the organization, Byrd and DeSantis announced their partnership with the nonprofit and said the Association of State and Local Election Officials will use Florida’s hard-line voting and election rules as a “blueprint” to enact similar policies across the country.
Byrd said the organization would “have state chapters to support, educate, and train local and state election officials on election integrity, because that’s something that the other side has been very good at.”
“They’re the ones going in and certifying and training people who run our elections, and not doing it in a way that we think comports with the law and voter trust,” Byrd said. The association “will be a national organization to promote election integrity, principles, and federal law and policy,” he added.
Under Byrd and DeSantis’ leadership, Florida has enacted rules and laws that voting rights advocates have criticized, including passing a state version of the federal SAVE Act that requires proof of citizenship at polling locations and prohibits the use of student IDs to vote beginning in 2027. “I’m very excited to head up that initiative and take what we’ve done in Florida as the blueprint, as the model for the nation, take it nationwide,” Byrd said in September.
The offices of Byrd and DeSantis did not respond to questions about their involvement with the organization.
The organization’s board is also staffed by Sharon Bemis, the president of Mitchell’s Election Integrity Network, the country’s most prominent election denial organization; Julie Adams, an election denier who is both a member of the Fulton County Board of Elections in Georgia and a regional coordinator for the Election Integrity Network; Janice Johnston, who recently left the MAGA-dominated Georgia State Election Board; and Michigan state house representative Ann Bollin, who has coordinated with the Election Integrity Network.
The organization’s board members did not respond to questions for this story, though Johnston and Bollin have both previously denied being election deniers. The organization’s Texas registration contains no information about its work, and the group does not appear to have a web presence.
But the presence of Johnston and Adams on the board is telling.
In Georgia, Adams has made a name for herself by pushing Trump’s conspiracies about widespread election fraud and has sued multiple times for access to voting records with the help of the Republican National Committee. She has refused to certify results without being allowed to inspect voting records.
Johnston recently left Georgia’s State Election Board for what she said were “family and personal responsibility” reasons, and her time there was marked by turmoil, partisanship, and legal battles based on false fraud claims. Under her direction, the election board pursued specious investigations of Fulton County, supported mass voter purges championed by election denial activists, and worked to effectively eliminate voting machines.
Adams and Johnston have long targeted Fulton County for supposed fraud, and gleefully celebrated when, in January, the FBI raided an elections warehouse there, seizing tens of thousands of ballots from the 2020 election. Johnston was one of the unnamed witnesses in the FBI affidavit that preceded the raid, providing information about alleged double-counted ballots to the agency that had already been investigated and proven to have had no effect on the outcome of the 2020 election.
The Justice Department briefly fought in court to keep her name hidden from public view, but described a witness in the affidavit as “a Republican-appointed member” of the State Election Board who previously “was an obstetrician,” which identified Johnston. As the raid was being carried out, Johnston went live on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast from an SUV parked nearby.
When asked about Johnston’s presence on the board of the new Musk-linked election denial organization, Sara Tindall Ghazal, the lone Democrat on the Georgia State Election Board and Johnston’s former colleague, replied, “lol.”
“I mean this quite seriously, ‘lol.’ That’s my comment,” she tells WIRED.
And while Musk has quietly increased his political funding of Republicans, he has taken a bit of a step back from publicly discussing or posting about US politics and elections—with the exception of Talarico. His most recent post about voting is from September, when he responded to a question from Senator Mike Lee, a Republican from Utah. “Who benefits from noncitizen voting?” Lee asked on X.
“Democrats, which is why they push for open borders and noncitizen voting!” Musk responded. “Incentives explain behavior.”

title: An AI Breakthrough Has Made Decades of Computer Science Research ‘Irrelevant’
raw_text:
Linköping University professor Peter Jonsson is set to have his work presented in two weeks’ time at one of the most prestigious conferences in theoretical computer science. As of Monday, much of that work is “dead,” he says, after AI showed that a 27-year-old hypothesis underpinning it is wrong.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic claimed this week to have disproved the exponential time hypothesis (ETH). Vast swaths of theoretical computer science research on complexity and algorithm design have been built on the premise that the effort it takes to solve certain problems increases exponentially with the size of the problem.
Jonsson expects his predicament will be “very common” at the IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, where his work will be presented by one of his coauthors. “People will start the talks: ‘ETH is false, half of my paper does not work,’” he says. It’s a vexing problem, Jonsson says, “but at the same time, we learn a lot from it. And this is what science is about.”
Researchers haven’t independently verified, let alone had time to fully understand, the AI-produced proofs, which both firms have published on GitHub in both natural language and its machine-checkable Lean format. OpenAI has asked the UC Santa Barbara computer scientists who originally proposed the hypothesis, plus an MIT academic who has refuted a version of ETH, to rally researchers to unpack the proofs. So far, this effort includes a Google form asking for volunteers and feedback, and a commitment from OpenAI to fund a conference on the topic.
UC Santa Barbara professor Daniel Lokshtanov plans to join the effort, as he estimates the result—if confirmed—will render him “galactically wrong” and make around 50 of his published papers either “pointless” or in need of a revisit.
“It’s just a giant bomb dropped into the middle of the field,” he says. “It’s really cool and terrible at the same time.”
Thore Husfeldt, head of the algorithms research group at the IT University of Copenhagen, had spent most of this year thinking about one single problem in his subfield. “As far as I can tell, it’s now all irrelevant,” he tells WIRED. Having first formulated a version of the hypothesis now disproved by OpenAI, he has been writing calculations on his blackboard to figure out what other parts of his work might have become obsolete due to the “once-in-a-generation result.” Unlike the ennui that has gripped math researchers who have faced similarly field-upending proofs generated by AI models, though, Husfeldt expressed enthusiasm about the new results.
The finding is “fantastic,” he says. “Being a mathematician is a lot like stumbling about in a completely dark room,” he explains. “It's like somebody just illuminated an entire subfield in floodlights of knowledge, and now we just run around like overexcited bunnies and look at all the nooks and crannies that we can suddenly explore. So it’s a super exciting time.”
For centuries, science has advanced through making hypotheses and proving them wrong. It also isn’t unusual for an academic to be scooped or have their work otherwise undercut by another research group. But AI has accelerated this, obliterating whole research programs and spooking researchers in specific fields of math and science who wonder where they stand now that machines can outperform them.
“The last few months have been really tough. It's a lot of doom and gloom, because every week, or every second week, the results announced by AI just annihilate the ongoing research projects of many people,” Husfeldt says. “That is psychologically taxing for many people,” he says, adding that his department has considered hiring an occupational psychologist because “some people are really depressed and really sad.”
Researchers have also been overwhelmed by the volume of content now being produced, thanks to AI, including slop-level results. Midway through the interview, Husfeldt receives what he suspects to be an AI-generated 17-page paper on the consequences of the ETH result from a random Gmail account. He won’t read it: “Reading math is a very big investment of cognitive time,” he says.
OpenAI has directly contributed to this; earlier this month, it dumped 722 manuscripts on 400 problems on GitHub, to the annoyance of academics, who complain this makes it difficult to digest the results. Adding to the frustration were several documents that contained errors, reflecting what some mathematicians saw as a hasty rollout designed to juice the company’s planned initial public offering rather than moving the field forward. This time around, OpenAI’s 60-odd-page paper on ETH seems to be written better than the companies’ past publications, academics tell WIRED.
They are now scrambling to unpack the paper and find what other results they can quickly deduce from it.
If ETH is false and it doesn’t, in fact, take exponentially more time to solve problems as they become more complex, that’s “exciting,” says Victor Lagerkvist, an associate professor at Linköping. He plans to return to problems he had previously given up on under the assumption ETH was accurate.
OpenAI’s finding could also have impacts on the cryptography that underpins web security, which is based on the assumption that certain mathematical problems take an impractically long time to solve. While this particular result doesn’t directly affect cryptography, “it should definitely scare some cryptosystem designers,” says Lokshtanov.
That’s why continued human and AI-assisted work in theoretical computer science is important, Husfeldt adds: “We want the open scientific process to identify our misunderstandings about computation, in particular because lots of modern digital infrastructure is built on assumptions about computation.”
As for Linköping’s Jonsson, he plans to revisit both his own and others’ papers that hinge on ETH being true, and believes his conference paper may eventually be salvageable through another method. He’s excited to look into the details of OpenAI’s proof and see what he can learn from it and apply it to new problems. Even though it undoes the assumptions underpinning his work, having a verdict for ETH is something he could only “dream of” before, he says. “These are exciting times,” he adds. “Most people would never experience anything like this in their career.”
“I don’t care if it's a human-written proof, or it's written by AI, or if an alien transmitted this proof to us. If it’s true, then we must simply use it in the future.’’

title: A Hacker Targeted High-Stakes Poker Players With Malware That Exposed Their Cards
raw_text:
In a fitting sign of the times, the hacker’s carefully laid plans were foiled by an AI agent.
It was September 25, 2026, and Alex, a professional online poker player, was using his Claude AI agent to review some play statistics. (Alex only agreed to speak with WIRED under a pseudonym to avoid any risk of reprisals from threat actors.) After Alex’s SQL database crashed and needed to be reset, the Claude agent noticed something suspicious: A program called MeshAgent was operating in the background, where it seemed to be capable of capturing Alex’s screen and even controlling his entire machine.
Thanks to the Claude agent’s report, Alex could see the program had been installed on April 24, and not by Alex himself. Alex says the agent identified 11 time-stamped events when the program had been capturing his screen based on graphic errors it caused during screen sharing instances. During all 11, Alex had been playing a session on ACR, also called Americas Cardroom, a major worldwide online poker operator.
He checked his hand histories and quickly found the most troubling info yet: The same opponent, playing under the handle OxOO, was at his table for 10 of those 11 sessions.
The handle was familiar. Alex and several friends in the high-stakes community had shared suspicions about this player’s behavior in the past. Alex checked the player’s win rate stats via a public tracking site; they were astronomically higher than the best players in the world, a statistical impossibility given the sample of hands played. In Alex’s view, it was glaringly obvious that this player was cheating.
An investigation by Alex and other members of the high-stakes community in subsequent days confirmed his fears—and then some. Alex was one of hundreds of players allegedly targeted with this type of malware by the same reported threat actor across a period of multiple years. Alex, who was the first to discover MeshAgent on his computer, claims he was “only” ripped off for around $30,000, a relatively moderate sum for the level he plays at; many of his peers weren’t so lucky.
With millions of dollars allegedly stolen across the biggest sites on the internet, the poker world is searching for answers about how the scheme was allowed to continue so long, whether major sites took the risk seriously after it was reported, and whether online poker itself has been irreversibly compromised.
Poker has never been short on cheating controversies; online poker especially so. The “superuser” method, in which a cheater gains unauthorized access to their opponents’ cards and can therefore act with perfect information against them, was one of the first to show up online.
Two major sites in online poker’s early days, Absolute Poker and Ultimate Bet, served as cautionary tales in the mid-2000s. In separate instances, superuser cheaters were able to gain insider access to the websites and bilk players for millions of dollars. (Much of the loot was refunded to players following an investigation.) Those high-profile incidents led to tightened security measures from many top poker sites.
Another minor superuser incident took place in 2013, when a Finnish high-stakes player said his laptop had been stolen from his hotel room during a European Poker Tour tournament in Barcelona. When the laptop was recovered, it had been infected with malware that allowed a hacker to view his screen remotely. And maybe the most famous superuser scandal of all took place on the live felt: In a story that made it all the way to SportsCenter, a player named Mike Postle was accused of stealing over $250,000 from livestreamed games at Stones Gambling Hall in 2018 and 2019 with the aid of what observers believed to be an alleged accomplice with access to live card data who fed information to Postle’s phone. (Postle denied the accusations, alleging it was “fake news.”)
Outside one relatively small (and quickly remedied) incident in 2023, though, the online poker world had gone years without a confirmed superuser incident—until now. And some of what’s known about this latest attempt signals a savvier threat actor than in previous scandals, plus a degree of patience not typically seen in attacks like these.
“Traditionally, when you see these types of financially motivated threat actors, they will get access to a system and then as soon as they’re on it, they’ll do a scope of what they have access to and then they’ll hit everyone all at once and dump all the wallets,” says WolfSec, a cybersecurity professional who consults with many high-stakes poker players on security measures. He was first to break the news of the MeshAgent scam on September 29, on his X account. (WolfSec agreed to speak to WIRED under the condition his real name not be used out of fears of reprisals from hackers; WIRED independently confirmed his credentials as a cybersecurity expert.)
But this hacker didn’t do any of that, despite many of these players having large cryptocurrency holdings and other investments accessible on their machines. The attacker seemed instead to be performing advanced reconnaissance. In fact, WolfSec believes the same threat actor was attempting to attack players’ machines as early as 2022 using a more basic technique; because no known funds were stolen at the time, no other action was taken once the players wiped the malware from their computers.
It appears, though, that the hacker was simply biding his time and improving his methods in preparation for an eventual strike.
Instead of targeting individual players directly, this more recent attack involved third-party software programs called IntuitiveTables and Jurojin. These programs allow professionals to play dozens of online poker hands at once. Using these popular “multi-table” tools, players can switch between live games with a keystroke, place bets or make plays with hot keys, and other actions that make it easier to play at several virtual tables at the same time. The hacker compromised both applications, WolfSec says, pushing malicious software to over a thousand estimated users.
In the case of Jurojin, the attacker gained access to the developer’s own system for software updates and was able to deliver the remote-access agent to existing users through normal, automatic updates.
The developer of Intuitive Tables was running Jurojin on their test computer, and that machine got the remote-access agent as part of Jurojin’s compromised software update. Using the agent, the attacker added malicious code to the Intuitive Tables application before the developer signed the security certificate for an updated build of the app. That version carrying the malicious code was posted to the Intuitive Tables website as a public download, and everyone who installed that version of the app unknowingly also installed a backdoor on their computer.
In both instances, the malicious code was delivered through a standard update channel or an official release, so neither the users nor their antivirus apps detected anything amiss.
The modified version of Intuitive Tables behaved exactly like the clean version, with one exception: It also checked players’ files for their usernames.
“If you were on a hard-coded list that was stored on the attacker’s infrastructure, which [the malware] reached out to and downloaded and compared your username to, then it acted as a malicious program and downloaded additional malicious files,” WolfSec says. “If you weren’t on that list, then it became the normal program and didn’t do anything malicious at all.”
The list appears to have been populated primarily with regular high-stakes players across several sites. All of the players on the list appear to have had the MeshAgent program installed covertly on their machines. The hacker was ready to pounce.
In early 2025, a couple of new players began frequenting high-stakes games—one on ACR (using the handle “JackKlompus”) and another major global site called CoinPoker (handle: “Europe”). Strangely, despite not being familiar to other regulars in these games, the players refused to identify themselves in table chats, a common request that’s typically granted by new players in high-stakes poker. The new opponents were also winning with improbable frequency. (Later, once the pros started sharing information about their games, it was pieced together that these players were the same person.)
Mike, a professional poker player who spoke to WIRED using a pseudonym due to fear of reprisals from hackers, played on both sites at the time and was at tables with the player using these handles. Mike says at first he wondered if the mystery player’s success was somehow explainable. Maybe they were doing something new that Mike and his fellow pros just hadn’t figured out.
“You could kind of excuse it” at first, Mike says. “Maybe this guy is really, really good or something.”
As the number of winning hands grew, though, Mike and several high-stakes friends became more suspicious. They initially suspected that the player was using real-time assistance via game-theory-based engines that outperform the best human players. Real-time assistance is banned across major sites, but is difficult to police perfectly and is something pros are regularly watching out for. Mike mostly stopped playing at tables with the mystery player, as a precaution.
Like WolfSec, Mike reflects on a relative level of skill and discipline employed by this player during those 2025 sessions, especially compared to other known cheaters in poker history. The account generally used standard bet sizes and played normal hand ranges. Its session-by-session play never raised too many eyebrows; only the account’s win rate over time drew scrutiny.
But in June 2026, Mike played a two-hour heads-up (one-on-one) session on a different site, ClubWPT Gold, which he’d later determine—following reviews with the website’s security team—came against the same player from the 2025 sessions. The player used a different handle to evade detection, so Mike didn’t see a reason to be extra cautious. The opponent simply steamrolled Mike, making every correct decision even in seemingly impossible spots—almost like he could see Mike’s cards. “It was very blatant,” Mike says.
Immediately after the session, Mike messaged several friends in the high-stakes world to say he thought he’d been cheated.
Turns out he was right. When word of the hack broke publicly on WolfSec’s X account, ClubWPT Gold investigated. The site banned the account Mike had played against and refunded him for his losses, says Randy Lundy, head of customer operations for ClubWPT Gold.
This alleged cheater’s presence in online circles was an open secret across the community by this point. In fact, Mario Mosböck, a poker ambassador for CoinPoker who was authorized to speak about the company’s response to the hack, says the site began investigating this player as early as 2025, banning them and refunding over $100,000 in allegedly stolen funds to affected players. (Mosböck says the return of funds was delayed several months because the alleged cheater appealed the confiscation to regulators.) The player’s simple win rate and play style statistics appeared to be evidence of malfeasance, even if the site couldn’t definitively determine how the cheating was happening.
How, then, was the same alleged cheater allowed to keep ripping off players like Alex and Mike on multiple other supposedly reputable sites more than a year later?
“They confirmed multiple times that they looked at my report, but for whatever reason they didn't act on it,” says Patrick Howard, a professional poker player and founder of the coaching company Mobius Poker.
The “they” he’s referring to is GGPoker, arguably the most well-known site in the world for non-US players. Howard says he submitted a report to the site in early September 2026, weeks before the MeshAgent hack became public, highlighting the alleged cheater’s unusual play and urging the site to investigate.
“I found multiple three- to four-standard-deviation outliers,” Howard says, and that was across a limited hand history sample sent to him by friends and clients. He sent his findings to the GGPoker team but received no response. He got a reply only after WolfSec’s public reveal of the hack on X, with the site telling him there “wasn’t conclusive evidence” to act at the time of his complaint.
Various online poker sites handled the incident differently. Players have largely praised CoinPoker for proactively banning the player based on win rate and play tendencies alone, which are accepted as definitive indicators of cheating at stakes this high and with samples this large; while ClubWPT Gold only seems to have been impacted later in the scheme, that site also appears to have acted decisively upon discovering it.
But the hacker remained active on GGPoker and ACR until late September, allegedly stealing between $1.5 million and $4 million, based on the estimates of the sources WIRED spoke to for this story.
“Players are frustrated, because they had been reporting this for a year,” says John Andress, head of game integrity for A5 Labs, a cybersecurity platform that provides anti-cheating services to ClubWPT Gold and other brands. “A few of the platforms just completely ignored them.”
This was despite signs that many feel were all too obvious.
CoinPoker says the player’s alleged true identity was known early in this process, after the company conducted a webcam security interview with them in February 2025. The name the player gave matched the handle the player later used on GGPoker, which requires players to use their real name as their handle instead of a pseudonym for certain high-stakes games. (WIRED is not naming the player because they have not been charged with any crime. The player did not respond to multiple requests for comment on this story). The CoinPoker spokesman says their team reached out to ACR with their findings as well and received no response. (Requests for comment from WIRED to ACR and GGPoker received no reply.)
To its credit, GGPoker acknowledged the incident and announced several fixes in an October 15 blog post, including banning third-party tools and adding win-rate anomaly detection. The site also says it traced the accused attacker’s funds to a Coinbase account and has asked the crypto company to restrict the account and preserve its records; it says it also provided the wallet addresses to industry watchdogs and law enforcement.
But ACR is going the opposite direction: On October 18, it emailed players claiming its security team found no compromised game outcomes or wrongdoing and will not issue any refunds—despite, in the same email, announcing a new feature to stop remote-viewing tools from capturing the images of the cards in players’ hands.
Other entities have taken concrete action: Both Jurojin and IntuitiveTables (via its Discord channel) released tools to help users detect whether the MeshAgent hack had affected their machines. AceGuardian, a research group that’s part of A5 Labs, put out an open-source “superuser detection” tool designed for use on any poker site. WolfSec says he submitted a complaint to the the Internet Crime Complaint Center, the cybercrime arm of the FBI, and has been working with players on improving machine security. The FBI, when reached for comment by WIRED, would not confirm receipt nor any details of this complaint.
But these efforts will be so successful only if the sites treat these incidents with more scrutiny and don’t just spring into action in the aftermath of major attacks.
“Ultimately, the sites have to ban the players,” Howard says. “I think they dropped the ball here.”

title: Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
raw_text:
A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.
The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.
“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”
The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.
The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)
Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.
Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.
“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”
According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.
“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

title: The ‘Pain in the Ass’ Math That Could Save Vibe Coding From Itself
raw_text:
Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.
For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.
Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and which publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.
“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse, because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”
&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.
And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.
The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.
The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it’s unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user error and hardware breakdowns.
Will Wilson, who runs the bug-hunting AI software startup Antithesis, calls formal verification “a trap” for math nerds like himself. Antithesis spent millions of dollars to formally verify some of its cybersecurity defenses, a process Wilson describes as a “pain in the ass.” Yet the startup still uncovered additional errors using its own tool, and Antithesis has also found bugs in software that several of its customers had formally verified. “It can give you some assurance, but only robust exhaustive testing can prove your assurance is true,” Wilson says.
Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc.
Core Security
Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.
Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.
But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.
Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.
Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.
Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.
Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.
Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face, he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”
Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.
But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.
