title: Liquid Glass Finally Makes Sense on the iPhone Duo
raw_text:
Apple rarely admits a mistake. But when it unveiled new versions of its operating systems this summer, it came close.
“With all major design updates, there’s a natural process where we take a bold leap forward, and then we continue to iterate,” said Apple's human interface designer, Shubham Kedia, during a predictably sleek keynote video. “Our team really appreciates your feedback, and we considered it deeply as we refined the new design.”
Not quite “Sorry, everyone, we messed up,” but for Apple, practically an apology tour. The subject was Liquid Glass, Apple’s most divisive interface design since at least iOS 7. Apple's Vision Pro mixed-reality headset (which itself flopped) inspired the translucent design language, and the company brought it to millions of other Apple devices.
The result was a mess—at odds with Steve Jobs’ famous line, “Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.” Liquid Glass started obsessed with gloss and effects, despite promises it would bring your content to the foreground. Yet Apple’s own press release showed interfaces with illegible text. Worse, users found constant reflections and flickering color shifts distracting, and a lack of clarity across devices hurt accessibility.
But iOS 27, alongside updates to Apple's other software platforms, signaled a shift in priorities after Kedia’s mea culpa. Kedia spoke of reincorporating design cornerstones in what was, if not quite a U-turn, then at least a rediscovery of a core principle: how it works. Instantly, interface elements across Apple devices gained greater clarity and structure, making it easier to tell apps' components from content. The most obvious change, though, was a slider.
Thinking Differently
Apple said it tuned Liquid Glass to diffuse complex content more effectively, keeping elements legible when above imagery and text. But it also acknowledged that not everyone wants the same thing—some users might prefer a more tinted look, and others “would like Liquid Glass to be even more clear.” You can now decide for yourself with the Liquid Design slider in Settings. For a company known for being opinionated, such bet-hedging was surprising but not unwelcome. Choice isn’t a bad thing, and now users had more of it.
“I immediately pushed that slider all the way to the most tinted setting, and pretty much all the legibility issues vanished,” Ben Rice McCarthy, an indie developer behind popular apps like Obscura and Indigo, tells WIRED. McCarthy has long criticized Liquid Glass. Now? Not so much.
“Liquid Glass introduced a lot of issues without adequate solutions, but this year’s operating systems solved or improved a lot of them,” McCarthy says. “There’s the adaptiveness of the interface. Buttons can grow into menus. Controls merge and divide like cells as you transition between views. Toolbars can expand and contract smoothly as the view changes size.”
Flexibility matters when resizing windows across any device. But while announcing its updates, Apple also dropped major hints that all but confirmed new hardware—it showed iPhone apps running on an iPad or a Mac could resize to a suspiciously specific shape that matched the rumored inner display dimensions of Apple’s upcoming folding phone.
Designed to Flow
When Apple showed off the iPhone Duo, everything clicked. Its passport-shaped display bucks the trend of iPhones and their rivals growing taller over the years. The Duo is wider and almost squat, and when opened, it naturally defaults to landscape, echoing the iPad Mini display.
Apple being Apple, it wanted to avoid the jarring jolt between displays that’s often evident on rival foldables, so it made content appear to move seamlessly from one screen to the other. That begins with the hardware. As Molly Anderson, Apple's vice president of Industrial Design, said at the September keynote: “To achieve this continuity, we designed iPhone Duo around a consistent aspect ratio that is the same across both displays.” But it’s the software—rooted in Liquid Glass—that sells the illusion.
The most arresting element is a fancy animation, which various folks in the Android space are now busy being “inspired” by. It reinforces the idea of a flowing interface. Meanwhile, Liquid Glass freed Apple from being prescriptive about where essential controls live. On the Duo, they sit at the side. When the phone’s closed, that frees up space for content. When it’s open, the controls stay in a consistent spot, so you never have to hunt for them. Reorient the device, and everything settles into the most appropriate place.
That’s form following function, not function being subservient to form. This device and its flexible interface don’t strictly need the Liquid Glass design language, but the two feel made for each other. Liquid Glass finally makes sense on the iPhone Duo—and with Apple’s other refinements, it’s starting to make sense elsewhere, too.
Clarity of Purpose
How much of this is happenstance is hard to say. Given Apple’s lead times, pure coincidence seems unlikely. And even if Liquid Glass wasn’t made with the Duo in mind, it adapts to it.
Liquid Glass feels more considered. It’s increasingly tuned for individual devices rather than governed by a “universal” aesthetic forced onto them all. The result is operating systems that feel solid rather than fragile, with interfaces less likely to fight content for your attention. On Macs and iPads, the Liquid Glass revamp now looks more like a love letter to Aqua—Apple's water-themed interface introduced in 2000. On the iPhone, it’s usable again. On the Duo, it’s a delight.
That’s not to say it’s perfect. “There’s some weirdness that hasn’t been fully resolved, and there needs to be a consistency to all these materials or the metaphors break down,” McCarthy says. “But overall, Liquid Glass is vastly improved.”
And it’s worth remembering that while the Duo is new, Liquid Glass is relatively young, too. As developer Steve Troughton-Smith wrote, “For some iPhone apps, even with keen developers, it will take six months to a year of work to properly support iPhone Duo. A lot of developers are still trying to finish the Liquid Glass transition they started last year.”
A useful reminder that transitions take time. But at least now, Apple’s vision looks clear.

title: These Kindle Accessories Made Me Love My E-Reader Even More
raw_text:
Your Kindle doesn't have to be just a plain e-reader. The right Kindle accessories can transform the simple device into something that showcases your personality, makes it easier to read, or all of the above. Personally, I'm always looking for a way to hold up one less device in front of my face; I'm holding my phone enough already, thank you very much.
If you're shopping around for new Kindle accessories, I've got you covered as a fellow reader and owner of every single current Kindle model. I've tried everything from clear cases you can fill with stickers to ones with built-in straps, and have tested straps you can add to your e-reader without needing a case. Stickers? Charms? Got ’em. Hate holding your Kindle up to read? The Kindle holders and page-turning remotes are for you. This guide will give you ideas on how to improve your own reading time or gift your favorite reader.
As new Kindle models are rolling out that aren't the same size as the old, it's important to double-check what size and generation Kindle accessory you're getting. Most accessories in this guide were tested on the 2024 generation, unless otherwise noted.
Updated October 2026: I've added notes on the new Kindle Page Turn Case and Kindle Click, plus cases and grips from Bondi.
My Favorite Kindle Accessories
Kindle Cases and Covers
An easy must-have for any Kindle reader is a case or cover to protect your e-reader. Here are some of my favorites that I've tried on my various Kindles.
All of these were tested on 2024 models of the Kindle, usually the 7-inch Paperwhite or Colorsoft. The new 2026 generation has some slight size differences, so if you're shopping for accessories for a newer Kindle, double-check if there's a version for the model you have.
Kindle Straps and Grips
Looking for an easier way to hold your Kindle? Add these straps and grips right onto the Kindle or the case.
Kindle Holders
Hate holding up your Kindle? Or struggle with chronic pain that makes holding it feel terrible? These holders will literally take the weight out of your hands.
A Page Turner Made for Kindle
Page turners have been the latest item to have as an e-reader user, but while Kobo launched a remote last year, Kindle had yet to have one—until now.
Kindle announced the release of the Kindle Click, its first Bluetooth page-turning remote, in early October, and it's finally available to buy. It's a huge improvement over third-party devices that required you to have one part of the device on your Kindle so it could tap and turn the page for you, and a remote in your hand. The worst part was not just that it blocked some of the screen, but that you had to track the battery life of two separate pieces.
The Kindle Click solves these complaints, and while it launched on the same date as the new Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft, it's backward compatible with Kindle models from 2024. It's easy to set up: Just go into your device settings, click on Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and then Bluetooth devices to sync your Kindle Click. I tried it with both a 2024 Kindle and a 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, and both devices were able to find the Click almost instantly and start working.
The Click has two buttons on the main body that move forward and backward and will move around a page you're on, too (but won't select a book for you; it'll just move through your library or homepage). There are also two buttons on the right side that let you adjust screen brightness, which is a fantastic convenience. There's also an included lanyard to attach it to your wrist. It's great to pair with a Kindle stand of any kind so you can prop up your Kindle and turn the page without lifting a finger.
Some Charger Options
If you're getting a new Kindle, you might not be thrilled to discover you need to provide your own charging block to charge it. And if you haven't already switched over your home's collection of wall chargers to USB-C, you'll be especially frustrated when you open the box and find only a USB-C cord. If you're in the market for a new wall charger to pair with your Kindle, these are a couple of our favorites.
Looking to charge on the go? You shouldn't need to with a Kindle's long battery life. But in case you're a serial battery drainer, you can try these portable power banks we love. If neither of these suit you, check out our complete guide to the Best Power Banks.
Kindle Adornments
While everything else in this guide serves a protective or convenience purpose, this section features items with a singular purpose: fun. Here are a few I've liked adding to my Kindle.
Kindle Bags and Sleeves
Looking for a bag to tote your Kindle around? These carriers have you covered with a specific size and special pockets designed to safely store your device. Sure, you could throw your Kindle in any old bag, but these will keep it secure and prevent scratches from your keys. If you'd rather use the bag you have but want a separate sleeve to keep it safe, we've got ideas for that too.
Still Need a Kindle?
If you're reading this guide and actually are still in need of a Kindle, we've got an entire guide to the best Kindles to buy and why. The newest models are (for the most part) the smartest buy, unless the older 2024 models are on sale.
FAQs
Can These Accessories Work With Other E-Readers, Like Kobo?
Some of them can! You'll have to check descriptions for certain items (like cases or things that have to perfectly fit the device) since other devices like Kobo and Nook don't have the same dimensions as a Kindle, but flexible straps, generic tablet holders, and decorative items like charms and stickers would easily work with any other e-reader you own.

title: I Did Push-Ups With Snap’s Chunky AR Glasses
raw_text:
I hadn’t expected to be doing augmented reality push-ups in the middle of the mall. Yet there I was, wearing bulky Snap Specs while facing the ground.
The Lens (what Snap calls apps on its augmented reality headset) is called Thirty Ups. It is in Halloween mode now, so when I look down, a virtual cartoon Jack-o’-lantern sits right next to where I’m supposed to start working out. I’m not trying to get jacked right now, but my goal is to see if these gigantic smart glasses will fall off when I’m staring straight down and moving up and down.
I get into position and start my workout. When I go down and back up, a little virtual circle on the ground below me starts counting up. I don’t get to 30 push-ups. I’m surrounded by people, many of whom are now staring at me, and it feels too hot outside to keep going without feeling gross. I get in 12 reps before giving up. The glasses only count 11 because it tells me I “skipped” one. Great.
The nearby Snap representative is thrilled. “You’re the first person who’s tried that one,” he says. I’m also pleasantly surprised. These glasses seem huge, but they stayed on my face just fine.
Snap announced its Specs in June. They cost $2,195 and will start to ship in the coming weeks. It took a few months for Snap to share what actual features would be available on the glasses
WIRED’s Julian Chokkattu and I both tried out Snap’s Specs last week. He got a dedicated demo with the company. I was offered one, too, but instead I happened to stumble upon the Specs First Look demo at the Westfield Century City shopping center in Los Angeles. The space has been here for just a couple of weeks.
It was a warm Sunday afternoon, and a steady stream of people came through the mall’s demo zone. Snap reps handed out Specs to anyone curious enough to register and hang out. Kids were running around, and the glasses looked especially large on their faces. When people left the demo, they got a free cup of ice cream with a small, Specs-shaped chocolate cookie.
The Specs had a dozen or so Lenses available for testing. Aside from the push-ups, the Specs let you finger paint in midair, see navigation directions overlaid on the real world, or engage with the physical environment by drawing on a notepad or analyzing text in a print book. They also have some sporty features, like one that allegedly helps with golf and another through a partnership with the NBA that guides you through shooting hoops.
You may have noticed that the glasses look pretty chunky. That’s true, but I was pleasantly surprised by how lightweight they felt and how well they stayed put. (The glasses come in two sizes, so if the small is too tight, try the larger model.) Another surprise was how well the virtual digital elements held up in bright light. I made a point of walking into direct sunlight to test out the screen. With the brightness turned all the way up, the onscreen elements were still visible. The glasses had automatically switched into “sunglasses mode” and dimmed to block the sun. The Snap rep said the lenses protect the eyes from UV rays at all times.
The problem, though, is that Snap is really trying to make the case that these glasses—or at least future, smaller iterations—are the holy grail of consumer tech. But I still don’t care to wear them in public. Walking around with the AR elements on can be distracting. Even if you turn it all off, the waveguides on the lenses still have a rainbow shimmer in your vision as you move. I wouldn’t want to wear these while driving or even walking when I really need to see where I'm going. At one point in the demo, I had to dodge a kid wearing a pair of Specs who was wildly swinging punches at something on the screen only he could see.
Most of the device features are controlled with your hands, like pinching two fingers together to open a lens or move something around. You can play Beat Saber-esque games by moving your hands around. But the controls can be finicky, and I found myself clawing at the air repeatedly to move or open something. Chokkattu tried writing in Google Docs—a demo showing the Specs as a computer you can work with anywhere—but the connected Bluetooth keyboard had a severe input lag, making typing a chore.
It also feels odd that some Specs features really just feel like advertising. A Harry Potter spell-casting experience is a fun idea, but really it just comes across as an ad for the upcoming HBO show. The Specs also have a shopping feature which lets you browse stores online. It’s a reminder that one day your augmented vision will be bombarded with pop-up ads.
I have a hard time imagining who these glasses are for. Given the price, it’s clearly aimed at developers and early adopters. But I tried the developer version of the Specs in 2024. The new glasses are much more comfortable and slightly less chonky, but the software hasn't changed much since then. Snap has shown off the same finger painting demo every time I’ve tried them, and every time it works until it doesn’t. The Specs are interesting but lack a killer feature, and Meta and Xreal both have more polished mixed-reality glasses that cost less. That’s going to make Specs a hard sell.
“We see consumer adoption as a process—the hardware, software, available experiences and price all need to develop together,” a Snap representative wrote in a statement to WIRED. “Specs bring computing into the world without pulling you out of it.”
For now, Snap’s most compelling pitch might be the free ice cream.

An array of brilliant colors is what you want from an RGB television, and on that front, the Hisense UR8 RGB MiniLED delivers. After having reviewed a number of the top RGB TVs, including the flagship Hisense UR9 RGB MiniLED and offerings from Samsung and LG, I can report that this UR8 is solidly good. title: My Favorite Kitchen Composter Just Got $150 Cheaper
raw_text:
There’s a new Reencle composter in town, and of all the features I thought I might miss from the trailblazing original Reencle Prime, I didn't think it would be the auto-close lid.
The overly sensitive opening sensor annoyed me at first, but I ended up not giving the Prime’s lid another thought during my nearly 1.5 years of use. In hindsight, this is a testament to its convenience. It even has a setting for it to auto-open. Walk over to the receptacle, it opens; dump your scraps in, it closes. Buttons and lids remain clean and untouched by dirty, slimy hands.
Reencle’s brand-new, lower-cost unit, the Essential, is pretty much the same as the Prime (which is still available), with a few small tweaks—updated looks, a larger shovel, and a lid you have to manually close and a button you have to press to open. The button and lid already dirty after only three weeks, but my family consistently forgets to push the lid closed, having grown used to the auto-close lids of both our trash can and our old Prime. At least a few days a week, I will be caught off guard by a constant beeping—the Essential letting us know its lid is still open.
Aside from that, the Essential delivers the same user-friendly, close-to-compost-producing experience as its older sibling, but for $150 less.
Compost in Progress
You may have heard of kitchen composters before, whether the Lomi, FoodCycler, or the original Reencle Prime. It’s a compelling fantasy: Food scraps go in the bin, and out comes ready-to-use compost.
Unfortunately, for all of these machines, it’s just that: a fantasy. Many of them (like Lomi and FoodCycler) simply grind and dry the scraps to create a material that looks kind of like dirt. Sure, it’s odorless and shelf-stable, but if you want to use it in your garden, you’ll need to mix it into potting soil at a very low ratio—like 1:10, or even 1:20 if you’re processing a lot of meat and dairy.
Reencle, meanwhile, actually uses thermophilic bacteria (including Bacillus and Actinomycetes) to break down the waste, resulting in a biologically active material that, while not ready-to-use compost, is at least part of the way there. There are a couple of other machines that also do this, and I’ve tried them, but they’re bulkier, pricier, and louder than Reencle—don’t discount the noise-polluting effects of an audible fan running 24/7, especially if you live in a small space. (Reencle’s large-capacity Gravity model was—and remains—the only food recycler/composter I’ve ever tested that was truly silent at all times.)

title: Pornhub Stars Want to Teach You How to Make Dinner
raw_text:
Porn star Sweetie Fox is known for all kinds of gamer cosplay. She’s performed as a sex-hungry vault dweller from Fallout, as Lara Croft “The Dick Rider.” On Pornhub, one of the several platforms where she uploads content, her character videos do massive numbers. (One of her more popular vids netted 12 million views).
But Fox is also a miner—the term for someone who plays Minecraft—and in September, she posted a video of herself playing the game fully clothed. In less than a month, it has surpassed 1 million views on the site.
It’s the kind of content Pornhub is betting its future on. Starting this month, the adult entertainment site is inviting performers to earn new viewers from gaming, cooking, podcasting—or basically anything that doesn’t involve sex.
Ever wanted to learn what “physics-informed neural networks” are from Zara Dar, or what Jenna Starr likes to cook for dinner? (Steak and potatoes, by the way.) According to insights from the company, interest in safe-for-work content is blowing up on the platform. Podcast and gaming categories rose triple digits in 2025—podcasts alone spiked 327 percent—as did searches for “SFW,” which were up 114 percent.
Alex Kekesi, vice president of brand and community at Pornhub, believes these categories are gaining traction because viewers want to get to know performers beyond their adult roles. Nonexplicit content—which Kekesi says isn’t intended to replace X-rated videos on the site but rather complement creators’ existing content libraries—will be featured across video pages, search results, recommendations, and Pornhub’s various categories, in addition to Shorties, its scrollable vertical video feed.
By investing more in SFW content, Pornhub also wants to give creators the opportunity to grow their audiences and gain visibility in regions where the platform has decided to restrict access to the NSFW offerings on its site in response to age-verification laws in those localities.
Mounting censorship across the industry has forced adult creators to get more creative when it comes to protecting their livelihoods. Currently, 27 states (and counting) have adopted a form of online ID checks, which require users to upload an ID or other personal documentation to verify that they are not a minor before viewing sexually explicit content. Sixteen states, almost all of them with majority Republican legislatures, have likewise adopted resolutions declaring porn a public health crisis, with some, like Alabama, passing “porn tax” legislation on adult sites that operate within its jurisdiction. Free-speech advocates argue that age-verification laws, which have also been enacted in the UK, are making the internet less safe.
Since 2021, after passing up a PhD in neuroscience to work as an adult performer full-time, Isla Moon claims that she’s been banned from over 250 TikTok accounts. The instability of the industry has forced her to take SFW content seriously, and she is always on the hunt for creative solutions to make her income “more stable,” she says.
On TikTok, where the 25-year-old creator has nearly 2 million followers, she specializes in outdoor content—fishing, camping, “anything outside,” she says. Her adult videos sometimes play on the same themes with more of an uninhibited twist (as in “Busty Redhead Isla Moon Makes Horny Snow Angels”). In the past few years, due to the rising suppression creators are up against, she’s had to mix things up in terms of what she records while also strategically figuring out the best platforms to post on.
“Scary is the one word that comes to mind, honestly, because the platforms are getting very restrictive. I blew up on TikTok. It was my thing,” she tells WIRED, noting how her videos don’t get the same reach anymore. “Before you could you post stuff in a bikini, but now any cleavage is a no go.” Videos like that on Moon’s TikTok rarely exceed the five-digit view count, while others that feature her covered up breeze into six-figures. The push into more nature girlie content is “definitely a response to external pressures,” she says.
According to TiKTok’s community guidelines, nudity, “sexual activity,” and “sexually suggestive acts or significant body exposure involving youth” are prohibited. Similarly, the app bans “sexualized framing,” meaning “content that focuses on clothed intimate body parts through camera angles, editing, body positioning, or other methods and techniques” won’t get surfaced. “The creator’s intent matters, which we infer by looking at context,” the policy notes. Suggestive content is also age-restricted and sometimes not eligible for inclusion in the For You feed.
Moon, who cycles between OnlyFans, Fansly, YouTube, Facebook, TikTok, and Snapchat, raking in an estimated $700,000 a month, is already seeing results on Pornhub. One of her SFW longform videos, which she started posting in October, is getting three times more views than it did on YouTube. “Isla Moon Survives 24 Hours ALONE in a -20 Snowstorm” is the fifth most watched video on her Pornhub page, with 261,000 views, compared to 86,000 on YouTube, where it was uploaded in January 2025. She says because people expect adult content “on Pornhub and platforms like that, the conversion I’m seeing is a lot better.”
Previously, Pornhub blocked access to the platform in 23 US states in protest of state-mandated age-verification laws, but with SFW content now accessible in many of those previously restricted regions, only four states—Indiana, Mississippi, Tennessee, and Texas—remain blocked. Given that complying with age-verification laws has caused traffic to flatline on the platform, the pivot to SFW content is also a way for Pornhub to get more eyes back on the site. Nearly 80 percent of Pornhub’s UK viewership has disappeared since the Online Safety Act went into effect.
Pornhub, which has more than 130 million worldwide daily visitors, has the potential to be an alternative for creators who regularly deal with problems of shadow banning or deplatforming on social media. In July, YouTube mass terminated dozens of ASMR accounts for violating its policy against “sexually gratifying” content, 404 Media reported, before restoring most of the channels following backlash and review of its automated enforcement, including Nananightray, ItsBunniiASMR, and RoseASMR, who had more than 330,000 subscribers.
OnlyFans, which has tried to shed its reputation as a porn site by carving out lanes for all sorts of PG creators, including comedians and fashion designers, made a similar move in 2025 when it expanded further into SFW content exclusively for entrepreneurs. Last October, the UK-based platform invited lingerie executive and ex-SuicideGirl Rachael McCrary to post business classes focused on pitching investors and brand building.
“Pornhub is and always will be a porn site that supports sex workers,” Kekesi says. “But that doesn’t mean porn is the only content that belongs here.”

title: Macmillan Staff Say the Publisher Threw a Party for a Workplace AI Assistant That Was Later Killed
raw_text:
As staff at the Lower Manhattan headquarters of Macmillan Publishers headed into work one morning in January 2024, they filed past something strange on the walls—flyers welcoming a new member of the team named “NOA.” The cafeteria was festooned with purple balloons and banners, according to several workers present, and with NOA’s name in light-up marquee letters. A plate full of doughnuts spelled out “NOA IS HERE.”
NOA was an acronym for No Ordinary Assistant, which many of Macmillan’s human assistants found “offensive,” multiple employees tell WIRED. In an email to staff, NOA was introduced as an AI chatbot developed by the German software company Chaptr, which is “backed” by Holtzbrinck, Macmillan’s parent company.
The email also assured employees NOA was “a safe environment where you can input proprietary information without the risk of sharing that data with any third party.” Ostensibly, this means NOA was a closed-loop enterprise tool that did not retain or share data for model training.
Macmillan staffers say they were warned during training sessions that NOA could hallucinate and would always need to be fact-checked by humans. Still, employees say, they were encouraged to use NOA for composing emails, drafting copy, doing marketing research, and generating ideas. Multiple staffers say they were told to “only” paste a “percentage” of authors’ manuscripts into NOA. Employees could also adjust NOA’s speaking tone, with options including “lighthearted,” “spartan,” pessimistic,” “sarcastic,” and “regretful.”
One Macmillan employee remembers a Chaptr representative reassuring workers during an early in-person training session that Chaptr understood publishers were dealing with something very important—content. “And here I thought we were publishing literature,” the employee says.
Later in 2024, Macmillan employees were encouraged to use NOA to generate their goals for performance reviews. “We built a specialized prompt to have NOA write goals for you!” one email read.
Several Macmillan employees say NOA was unhelpful and unreliable. “It was terrible, and no one used it,” one says. WIRED spoke with multiple publishing employees for this article, including some who have since left their employers. WIRED is not naming these employees, nor the authors we interviewed, because they are concerned about professional repercussions.
In October 2025, Macmillan staff learned via a company-wide email that Chaptr would be sunsetting NOA. Since then, workers say, leadership has been attempting to integrate Google Gemini into the publishing process. Some staffers subsequently experimented with using Gemini to evaluate submission letters from literary agents, but the Gemini-generated evaluations were “useless,” according to one editor.
In response to WIRED’s request for comment, Kelly Collins, vice president of communications and community at Macmillan, says the publishing house uses Gemini for its “business” but “there has not been any directive from Macmillan leadership to use Gemini for any part of the publishing process, including to evaluate submission letters from agents.” She also says “the points shared do not accurately reflect how NOA was rolled out and communicated” but did not provide further elaboration when WIRED asked which aspects were inaccurate.
Collins notes that the company “takes a thoughtful approach to AI, focused on employee awareness and education while always keeping people front and center.”
Macmillan is usually cited as the smallest of the Big Five US book publishers based on the number of books sold each year. Its imprint Farrar, Straus and Giroux publishes literary fiction heavyweights like Sally Rooney, Yiyun Li, and Ben Lerner while Tor Books is a home for science fiction and fantasy authors John Scalzi, Martha Wells, and Nnedi Okorafor.
Since I first reported on the creep of AI in the publishing world, I’ve heard from staff at all of the Big Five who claim that executives are pushing them to use AI tools, even as Hachette, Macmillan, and Penguin Random House Verlagsgruppe (its German-language division) are suing some of the leading AI companies for copyright infringement.
At the same time, multiple bestselling Big Five authors say they’ve gone to “war” with their publishers over AI and are considering abandoning traditional publishing altogether.
At Penguin Random House (PRH), the largest of the Big Five after the 2013 merger between Penguin Books and Random House, several workers say they’ve been encouraged to use ChatGPT Enterprise in AI learning sessions, even though PRH’s German division is suing OpenAI for copyright infringement.
In February, representatives from Hay House—a new-age self-help publisher acquired by Penguin Random House in 2023—presented a slide deck to some PRH employees about how ChatGPT Enterprise had become a “core productivity, creativity, and collaboration tool” since they adopted it a year prior. One of the four return-on-investment pillars in the deck was “Creativity,” including “idea generation, content development, and storytelling innovations.”
Despite encouragement from the C-suite, all of the PRH workers WIRED spoke with say they’re avoiding ChatGPT whenever possible. “It makes it harder for us to do our jobs,” one employee says. Other staff say their managers have explicitly asked them not to use AI for creative tasks like publicity copy and cover design, which has caused some confusion.
“Penguin Random House approaches AI as we would any significant new technology,” says Claire von Schilling, executive vice president and director of corporate communications and social responsibility for the publisher, via email. “We are exploring ways it may appropriately support our work, guided by clear principles and safeguards, including protecting the intellectual property of our authors and the company and preserving the essential role of human creativity and judgment in publishing.”
Von Schilling also says that PRH’s “publishing groups and imprints have discretion to determine whether and how AI tools may be appropriate for particular workflows, including areas such as marketing, publicity, and design.”
Meanwhile, several bestselling Big Five authors say their relationships with publishers have suffered over the past year due to AI use. Combined, the Big Five authors WIRED spoke with have sold more than 30 million copies. One bestselling author says they received marketing copy that included AI-hallucinated quotes from their book, but the publisher insisted they were not AI-generated. “I was gaslit on all of it,” the author says. During a recent round of contract negotiations, another bestselling author says they could not get a single Big Five publisher to promise no AI would be used in any way on their books.
“It’s undermining the necessary sense of trust that has to exist between writers and publishers,” one author says.
“It’s also frustrating to watch publishers get these massive settlements [from] AI companies and then embrace AI to do their work,” another author says. “It feels like they’re feeding at both sides of the trough.”
Authors say cost-cutting layoffs at the Big Five have contributed to deteriorating conditions for their editors and forced some to embrace AI for survival. “We’re seeing editors not reading the material at all and using Claude to create marketing language that barely has any relation to the book,” one author says. Other authors and agents say they’ve been asked by editors to write their own plans for revisions “because the editors don’t have time to do it themselves.”
All of the authors I spoke with say they want publishers to communicate when and how they’re using AI. “The bare minimum we're asking for is disclosure,” one author says. Another wishes the Big Five “would get together and come up with a set of principles around AI that they intend to adhere to.” But some bestselling authors say their publishers’ use of AI is forcing them to consider publishing future books on their own.
“What are authors even doing with traditional publishers anymore if they’re going to outsource everything to a machine?” one bestselling author says. “Why can't an author do that themselves?”
Following WIRED's previous reporting, several high-profile authors condemned the adoption of AI tools in publishing. “I have never looked down on other publishing models (zine girly from way back) & every day, self pub looking ever more possible for future work,” Mo Ryan wrote on Bluesky. Her most recent book, Burn It Down: Power, Complicity, and a Call for Change in Hollywood, was published by HarperCollins.
John Scalzi, the sci-fi novelist who signed a 10-book deal with Macmillan’s Tor Publishing Group in 2024, wrote, “I would be EXTREMELY annoyed to discover my PR is ‘AI’-generated, and as someone bombarded with dozens of ‘AI’-generated emails daily, I assure you the stink of ‘AI’ is immediately noticable [sic] and immediately dismissible. Publishers are not doing their new books any favors in using it.”
Bestselling authors who have already accumulated huge readerships say they don’t need the institutional support of a Big Five publisher to sell copies. Brandon Sanderson, for instance, publishes some of his fantasy novels through Tor Books, an imprint of Macmillan, but raised more than $15 million in 24 hours from his readers on Kickstarter to publish four books on his own in 2022.
“Publishers have always seen authors as a bit of a nuisance, and now there’s a desire to make us obsolete,” says one bestselling Big Five author. “What’s fascinating to me is that in the process of trying to make authors obsolete by using AI, the publishers are rendering themselves obsolete.”

title: Grok Says Its AI-Generated Version of ‘The Odyssey’ Is ‘Not Historically Accurate’
raw_text:
You don’t hear the defenders of so-called Western civilization talk much about The Odyssey these days.
Maybe that’s because their rabid denunciations of Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of Homer’s epic were buried in an avalanche of money. The July blockbuster has grossed nearly $1.8 billion worldwide, silencing the right-wingers who predicted a massive flop due to diverse casting and deviations from the source material.
Perhaps the loudest of these preemptive critics was Elon Musk. The world’s richest man spared no vitriol for what he considered a desecration of the ancient Greek narrative; four days after its release, he vowed to produce a superior version. “Before this year ends,” Musk wrote on X, “Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”
A little more than three months later—long after the discourse moved on—the public finally has a first glimpse of what we might call the Grodyssey, an Odyssey rendered through prompts fed into xAI’s video and image generation model. Rather than a “full-length movie,” it’s a seven-minute “episode” of an apparently ongoing series, depicting how Odysseus, king of Ithaca, resists a call to war against Troy but is ultimately compelled by an oath of loyalty to sail there with his army.
“Odyssey with Grok Imagine,” Musk announced Friday on X when sharing the clip, produced by AI entertainment company Wonder Studios X. The subdued post received just 18,000 likes, notably less engagement than other recent posts in which Musk cast doubt on the results of Brazil’s elections, complained about pronouns, and disparaged “legacy news.”
Grok’s introductory episode bears many hallmarks of AI slop. The movements of faces don’t match the dialog, which is further undercut by stilted and unnatural delivery. Besides Odysseus, none of the principal characters are introduced by name, and the pacing issues are laughable: The Ithacans arrive on the shores of Troy immediately after leaving their homeland, for example. Even the blue checks on X were harsh in their assessment. “Someone actually watched this and still decided to post it?” wrote one user. “Fire that person.”
But Musk’s stated goal wasn’t to deliver a better-looking or more narratively cohesive version of The Odyssey. He and his culture war comrades dubiously claimed that they were against Nolan’s casting of Black and trans actors, the Americanized English spoken by the characters they played, and various designs of ships and armor in the film because they were “historically inaccurate.” Hence Musk’s guarantee of a “historically accurate” corrective.
So, did Grok Imagine succeed on that front? Asking Grok for a self-evaluation yields an interesting answer. “No,” the chatbot says when queried about whether this Odyssey snippet is historically accurate. “Grok Imagine’s Episode 1 (and the broader promised series) is an adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey, not a historically accurate reconstruction of real events.”
The AI model further notes that the characters have no basis in the historical record, and that the poem is dominated by “myth” and “invention” rather than confirmed events. “Homeric society mixes possible Bronze Age elements (palace-centered kingdoms, certain warrior practices) with later Iron Age features,” it also states. “Many details are anachronistic or literary.”
In laying out the reasons that the episode “does not meet a strict historical standard,” Grok points out that the characters speak modern English with British accents, “not Homeric Greek or any reconstructed Bronze Age language.” Visually, it says, the production reflects “modern cinematic tropes and AI training data,” not “primary archaeological evidence.” (The bot cites the appearance of cavalry in a battle scene as an error when compared with standard reconstructions of the period.) Grok concludes that “the Odyssey itself is not a historical document, and the production makes no serious attempt at archaeological or linguistic fidelity beyond a general ‘ancient Greek epic’ aesthetic.”
Of course, the creative license that comes with adapting a millennia-old legend swarming with gods, witches, magic, and monsters was understood by just about everyone but Musk and a handful of cranks insisting that Nolan had contradicted some fundamentally true account of heroic adventure. Even Grok can tell you that its master’s fit of pique led him to promise the impossible—as he so often does.

title: The 9 Best TV Shows to Stream This Month
raw_text:
October is serving up plenty of reasons to stay in and stream. This month’s lineup of our must-watch TV shows includes a high-stakes divorce between the ultrawealthy, a thriller about the real-world dangers of online radicalization, and a rebooted Marvel hero searching for his identity in an increasingly AI-driven world.
There’s also a return to the Land of Ooo, a dystopian culinary bloodbath based on the graphic novels cocreated by Anthony Bourdain, and enough psychological horror and monstrous mayhem to get you in the Halloween spirit.
As always, we’re not just chasing the biggest names or the shows everyone is already talking about, like Netflix’s excellent East of Eden. These picks reflect the kinds of stories WIRED covers every day, from technology and science to politics and culture, and the sometimes unsettling ways they intersect.
Whether you’re in the mood for a mind-bending sci-fi adventure, a quirky supernatural mystery, or a good old-fashioned scare, these are the TV shows worth making time for this month.
War
At a time when billionaire tech titans seem to dominate the headlines on a daily basis, War offers a fascinating, albeit fictional, glimpse into what happens when one of their personal lives spectacularly implodes. The HBO legal thriller follows the explosive divorce of tech mogul Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) and international film star Carla Duval (Sienna Miller), whose bitter split becomes a high-stakes battle over money, power, and reputation. If you like your legal dramas populated by spectacularly messy rich people, this one’s for you.
Tip Toe
Before he became a three-time Emmy winner for hosting The Traitors, Alan Cumming earned three Emmy nominations for his work on The Good Wife. Now, he’s trading his castle in the Scottish Highlands for a neighborhood where the real traitors might be living next door.
In Tip Toe, Russell T. Davies’ chilling new thriller, Cumming and David Morrissey play longtime Manchester neighbors whose relationship takes a deadly turn as online radicalization, toxic social media algorithms, and rising anti-LGBTQ+ prejudice poison their community. It’s a disturbing reminder that sometimes the most dangerous people aren’t strangers lurking in the shadows, but the ones we share a wall with.
Adventure Time: Side Quests
If June’s Adventure Time: Side Quests premiere left you craving more trips to the Land of Ooo, good news: Finn the Human and Jake the Dog are back for another round of monster battles, magical mishaps, and general cartoon weirdness. The companion series to Pendleton Ward’s Emmy-, Peabody-, and Annie-winning original Adventure Time deliberately recaptures the spirit of the show’s earliest days. Season 2 promises more of the absurdist humor and unexpected heart that made Adventure Time a cult favorite in the first place.
Get Jiro
In a dystopian Los Angeles, where celebrity chefs hold all the power and scoring a restaurant reservation can be a matter of life and death, dining out is a cutthroat business. Get Jiro follows a sushi chef who finds himself caught in a brutal war between rival food factions before setting out to serve up some revenge of his own. Based on the graphic novels cocreated by the late Anthony Bourdain, this dystopian satire serves up a twisted blend of food culture, violence, and dark humor.
Carrie
Between multiple big-screen adaptations, a sequel, and even a stage production, there’s certainly no shortage of Carrie retellings. That hasn’t stopped Stephen King superfan Mike Flanagan from putting his own spin on the master of horror’s first novel.
The horror maestro behind The Haunting of Hill House and Midnight Mass returns with an eight-episode series that revisits the story of a bullied teenage girl whose telekinetic powers turn a high school nightmare into something far more terrifying. Given Flanagan’s knack for finding the heartbreak and humanity lurking beneath even the genre’s bloodiest moments, his fresh take on King’s classic promises to deliver more than just a prom night gone horribly wrong.
Small Prophets
If you’re still mourning the end of Detectorists (you should be, and if you’ve never seen it, it’s streaming on Acorn TV), here’s a new reason to get excited about Mackenzie Crook. The writer-director returns with Small Prophets, a quirky comedy-drama-fantasy about Michael Sleep (Pearce Quigley), a man still reeling from his girlfriend Clea’s disappearance seven years earlier. Desperate for answers, Michael dabbles in alchemy, conjuring miniature spirits with the power to see into the future, hoping they can tell him whether Clea will ever come home. Expect the offbeat charm and gentle humanity that made Detectorists such a gem, with a little supernatural mystery stirred into the mix.
Below
What’s lurking beneath the surface? In Below, a six-episode miniseries, a mysterious sea creature begins terrorizing a coastal town—threatening not just the lives of its residents but a way of life that’s already slipping away. As the danger grows, fisherman Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett) must fight to protect his family and his community from a threat that may be as destructive as the forces already reshaping their quaint little corner of the world. If you like your creature features with a bit of small-town drama and a fight for survival, this one’s worth diving into.
VisionQuest
Marvel’s resident synthezoid is back—and this time, he’s got an existential crisis to work through. In VisionQuest, Paul Bettany returns as a rebooted Vision, on the run from those who want to turn him into a weapon and searching for answers about who, or what, he really is. That journey takes him deep into his own programming, where AI personas including Jarvis, Friday, Edith, and even Ultron force him to confront some very human questions about consciousness, identity, and what makes us who we are. For a franchise increasingly fascinated by the line between artificial intelligence and humanity, VisionQuest could be one of Marvel’s more intriguing detours.
Crystal Lake
Before Jason Voorhees became one of pop culture’s most infamous movie villains, there was his mother, Pamela Voorhees. In Crystal Lake, the Friday the 13th prequel, Mrs. Voorhees is played by newly minted Emmy winner Linda Cardellini, fresh off her win for DTF St. Louis.
The eight-episode first season takes viewers back to the 1970s, following Jason’s drowning, when Pamela finds herself caught up in a mystery that casts a shadow over the town. More psychological thriller than straightforward slasher series, the show taps into the era’s paranoia, institutional mistrust, and women’s liberation, offering a fresh perspective on the franchise’s bloody mythology. Consider it a trip to Camp Crystal Lake before the legend was fully formed. And with an October 15 premiere date, it’s arriving just in time for Halloween.

title: The 9 Best Movies to Stream This Month
raw_text:
October has rolled around, and that means only one thing: Spooky season is here! And what better way to celebrate Halloween than with some of the finest fright fests of the last 50 years?
We’re bringing you a more retro-tinged selection of the best films on streaming this month, but the mix of crowd-pleasers and cult classics offers something for horror fans of all tastes. For instance, David Cronenberg’s grotesque revamp of The Fly, buzzing onto Hulu, and Ken Russell’s Altered States materializing on The Criterion Channel, both bring uniquely visceral takes on body horror to your screens, while sleeper hit Under the Skin on Netflix offers slow-burn sci-fi scares, and Midsommar on Prime Video takes to the hills for a sun-drenched approach to folk horror.
If you fancy something a bit newer, fear not. Well, fear lots actually—Zach Cregger’s shockingly original horror debut Barbarian smashes its way onto Hulu, while Netflix brings the final chapter in the sumptuously scary Mononoke trilogy, an anime extravaganza that looks like nothing else. Plus, there’s even one post-credits stinger of an entry that’s too scary to mention here …
Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.
Barbarian
When Tess (Georgina Campbell) finds her Airbnb in a sketchy neighborhood double booked with Keith (Bill Skarsgård), you’ll probably think you know where Barbarian is headed. You don't—and you should brace yourself for everything that follows. Written and directed by Zach Cregger (in a seismic departure from his early comedy background), Barbarian constantly flips the script, regularly subverting viewer expectations of horror movie clichés at every turn.
Smartly written, brilliantly shot, and psychologically disturbing on multiple levels, Barbarian is a genuinely terrifying entry in the modern horror canon. If you’ve discovered Cregger’s work from the Academy Award–winning Weapons or his recent horror-comedy reboot of Resident Evil, this is where he first made his mark on the silver screen.
Under the Skin
Under the Skin almost defies explanation. Scarlett Johansson plays an alien in human form, roaming Glasgow and the Scottish Highlands, luring isolated and lonely men to their doom, drowning them in an inexplicable oily abyss that seems to exist in a null space. All the while, she’s observed by a motorcyclist, trailing her from victim to victim.
No names are given, no purpose explained (not even to the cast; director Jonathan Glazer shot many of the alien’s initial encounters with humans using hidden cameras, only explaining and asking for their involvement afterward), but it’s far better to watch this blind and make your own mind up. Be warned, though—Johansson’s performance is truly unearthly, and in conjunction with Glazer’s bizarre imagery and a soundscape that maddeningly claws at your nerves, this is a deeply unsettling slice of sci-fi.
Midsommar
This acclaimed indie horror movie stars Florence Pugh as Dani, an American student struggling to deal with a family tragedy, who joins her boyfriend Christian (Jack Reynor) and his friends on a trip to Sweden. The vacation sounds like the perfect escape—nine days of communing with nature at a festival held only once every 90 years; a true once-in-a-lifetime experience. The problem? The festival is a front for a pagan cult, and things get rapidly, wildly out of hand.
Midsommar is a deeply effective and distressing folk horror film, with none other than Jordan Peele, director of the smash hit Get Out, declaring it has "the most atrociously disturbing imagery I've ever seen on film." Perfect date night material for Halloween season, then.
Train to Busan
South Korean cinema seems to love combining the end of the world and trains. Bong Joon Ho’s Snowpiercer got things on track in 2013, but director Yeon Sang-ho really left the station with this 2016 zombie horror masterpiece.
Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) starts his journey on the express train from Seoul to Busan just wanting to drop daughter Su-an off with her mother. Unfortunately, the last passenger to board might be a teensy bit infected with the zombie plague that’s kicking off outside, turning the ride into the express train to hell. The tight confines allow for some incredibly inventive action choreography, while genre fans are treated to a revolting twist on the undead themselves, a misshapen, juddering, ravenous horde that moves like a liquid mass of corpses.
Like all the best zombie films, though, it’s the social commentary that really elevates Train to Busan, with its exploration of class and status standing alongside Romero’s work at his peak. A decade on from release, this is still one of the freshest takes on zombies you’re likely to find—look up animated prequel Seoul Station and stand-alone sequel Peninsula if it leaves you wanting another bite.
Altered States
A bit of a deep cut, but director Ken Russell’s 1980 outing will really mess with your head. No, really—this tale of psychological horror and transformational terror is loosely based on real-world tests of the effects of psychoactive drugs and sensory deprivation on the human brain. The film sees researcher Eddie Jessup (William Hurt) subjecting himself to highly questionable experiments with hallucinogenics and isolation in an effort to tap into other states of being. Unfortunately, he’s wildly successful, not only opening his mind to genetic memories and shared consciousnesses, but seeing his physical body horrifyingly warp and devolve beyond recognition with each trip.
And what a trip—Russell masterfully creates a sense of psychedelic overload with a pioneering use of bizarre imagery and sound, the film shifting with each of Jessup’s transformations until you feel you’ve taken mind-altering substances yourself. An uncomfortably weird experience, Altered States will stay on your mind long after the credits roll.
Colossal
Anne Hathaway is literally a monster—at least she is in this darkly comedic crossover between kaiju flick and character study. After her life in New York falls apart, Gloria (Hathaway) moves back home to New Hampshire. At the same time, a giant monster starts rampaging across Seoul, destroying buildings and causing mass panic. Yet these two incompatible events aren't unrelated, as Gloria starts to realize that she can somehow control the beast from half a world away—but her heavy drinking and constant bad decisions may get in the way of saving the world. Director Nacho Vigalondo lovingly pastiches the likes of Godzilla, Gamera, and King Kong in this quirky film festival favorite.
Mononoke The Movie III: The Curse of the Serpent
A nameless Medicine Seller (Hiroshi Kamiya in Japanese, Crispin Freeman in English) traveling Edo period Japan may seem a humble figure, but his strange tinctures and concoctions make him one of the few capable of tackling mononoke—powerful spirits corrupting places and people alike. This trilogy-capping third movie takes the enigmatic traveler back to the cursed Imperial Palace visited in predecessors Phantom in the Rain and Ashes of Rage, seeking to uncover once and for all why it seems to attract so many dangerous monsters.
A master class in tension and otherworldly horror, Mononoke maintains its stunning visual approach of kaleidoscopic watercolors swirling on parchment, making for one of the most sumptuous and visually striking pieces of animation you’ll ever see. It’s worth noting that there is some real-world controversy over a returning voice actor embroiled in a scandal in Japan, so this might be a rare case where the English dub is the better option.
The Fly
Despite being a remake, David Cronenberg’s quintessential slice of 1980s body horror has almost completely supplanted the 1958 original in the public consciousness (although the original stars Vincent Price and is definitely still worth checking out on Prime Video).
This wholesale reimagining twists expectations away from mad science clichés—it almost feels like a superhero origin movie to start, with scientist Seth Brundle (Jeff Goldblum) accidentally splicing his genes with a fly during a teleportation experiment, and emerging with enhanced physical prowess in every respect. But with great power comes great personality shifts, wiry black hairs growing along his back, and the need to vomit acid onto his food before eating. And, as animal instincts take over, the self-proclaimed “Brundlefly” starts looking at science reporter Ronnie Quaife (Geena Davis) very differently.
The groundbreaking effects work that marked Brundle’s slow metamorphosis into a repulsive hybrid monster won the film the Oscar for Best Makeup, but its ability to pack in some genuine emotion alongside the scares make it easy to see why this is the de facto iteration of The Fly.
The Social Network
Oh, you think this isn’t horror? Ask yourself: What could possibly be scarier than the deleterious impact social media has had on the human condition? Director David Fincher and writer Aaron Sorkin’s biopic telling of the rise, and rise, and rise of Facebook, is the kind of film you watch through your fingers, too.
There’s an almost predatory hunger in Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg, as he goes from a Harvard student whose hotness-ranking website was popular enough to crash the college’s whole network to a Silicon Valley darling attracting unheard-of sums of investment and power. Like most “based on a true story” horror films, it’s not entirely historically accurate and, true to genre norms, there’s a not-as-good sequel, with Sorkin returning to write and direct the newly released The Social Reckoning, but if you’ve been paying attention to reality the past few decades, this will definitely chill you to the bone.

title: Marvel Has Assigned 42 Hours of Homework Before ‘Avengers: Doomsday’
raw_text:
Marvel and Disney+ have issued a stacked watch list for fans ahead of the cinema release of Avengers: Doomsday on December 18.
The Marvel Cinematic Universe can be complex terrain to navigate. Its 38 movies and 25 series to date span varying superhero plot lines, crossovers, and multiverse action, with the latest Avengers release likely to spare no less lore and real fan knowledge.
Marvel released an official “Countdown to Doomsday” playlist with Disney+, featuring 15 official selections to help fans catch up on all the action before watching the new movie. Among the selections, fans will get refreshers on origin stories, team-ups, and key multiversal information gearing them up to the Doomsday storyline.
The studio also launched the Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday Official Podcast, available on Disney+, YouTube, and audio platforms. The podcast features weekly recaps of the MCU’s Infinity Saga.
Devoted fans were quick to spot that two X-Men entries predate the MCU entirely, presumably because Patrick Stewart, James Marsden, Ian McKellen, and Alan Cumming are all rumored to be coming back for Doomsday. The Marvels from 2023, interestingly, did not make the cut.
The official movie watch list will require 42 hours to get through, which is roughly under three hours a week if you spread it out evenly before the new movie drops in December. Disney+ releasing a homework list for its own film is a great bit of subscriber farming. It converts the hype ahead of the theatrical release into watching content on a streaming service that has to, in the meantime, justify its monthly cost.
Every title below streams on Disney+, which is available in many markets around the globe. Some titles are also available on other streamers, and most are available to rent or buy digitally through Amazon Prime Video or Apple TV.
What to Watch Before Avengers: Doomsday
Captain America: The First Avenger (2011)
Loki, both seasons (2021 to 2023)
Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings (2021)
Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021)
Black Panther: Wakanda Forever (2022)
Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022)
Captain America: Brave New World (2025)
The Fantastic Four: First Steps (2025)
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.
