title: Grok Deepfaked This UK Politician—Now She’s Taking Elon Musk’s xAI To Court
raw_text:
Grok Deepfaked This UK Politician—Now She’s Taking Elon Musk’s xAI To Court
This interview includes references to sexual assault and child sex abuse.
WIRED’s Rosie Swash speaks with UK politician Jess Asato about tackling Elon Musk’s xAI after being subject to deepfaking via Grok, xAI’s chatbot. Jess and Rosie also delve into the ‘AI kill switch’ proposal, the specifics of Jess’ court case and the harsh reality of being deepfaked on the internet in 2026.
Released on 10/28/2026
I wanted to take you back to the beginning of this year,
January 2026.
There was widespread reporting of Grok,
xAI's chatbot, being used to create sexualized images
of children and women
and those images being circulated on X.
How aware were you at this point of the phenomenon
of deepfakes being used in this way?
Very aware.
And actually had been working, you know,
with survivors who had experienced deepfakes
for quite a number of years, you know,
ever since the advent of AI, you know,
has been happening to women.
And the developing risks of children both
being, you know, put into child sexual abuse material,
but also children using nudification tools
on other children, thereby criminalizing themselves
because these tools are so easy to access, often free.
So I was already very alive to the huge harms
being created by AI deepfakes of both women and children
before Grok ever happened.
It was a known harm, which is why many of the tools
from, you know, other companies had already taken,
you know, steps to stop them from being used
to create this kind of content.
And, you know, there are a number of tools
where, you know, you type in
nudify or take the clothes off this person,
and the tool refused to do that.
So into that environment came Grok.
Was there a particularly egregious example
and incident prior to Grok when you became aware
of deepfakes that really stuck with you?
Yeah, I think it was probably listening
to the experiences of Jodie, who was deepfaked,
and it was such an affront to her
that somebody would do this.
And then she found out it was actually a friend.
Such a betrayal of trust.
These things destroy not just the individual involved,
but often families and everyone around them too.
For people who don't know, who exactly was Jodie?
This is a constituent of yours
or someone who came forward to you specifically?
No, no, no.
She's a very well-known campaigner on this issue.
That's not her real name.
Before, what happened was that victims had to prove
that there was no consent,
and now it's up to the perpetrators to prove
that there was no consent to create these images.
I know it sounds obvious,
but what exactly is nudification?
Well, it is where you ask an AI tool to take the image
or video of a real person
and, you know, using generative AI to make that person
either nude or engaging in pornographic acts
or making a part of them nude.
This is something that,
because of the huge development of AI
and the, you know, real photorealistic nature of it,
it has become increasingly hard to see this as,
you know, a fake image.
It can often look incredibly, incredibly real.
So what was it particularly about the Grok scandal
earlier this year that made you want
to raise this in the House of Commons?
It was the fact that we already knew
that you could stop this from happening
by designing the AI tool to reject the ability to do this,
that it actually says that the tool should
accept asks for the creation of adult sexual content,
even that which has dark or violent themes.
And the fact was that this was completely avoidable,
and that's why I spoke out,
but also because I just spent a year and a half
campaigning to get a ban on nudification apps,
and here was an all-purpose AI tool
becoming a nudification app.
And it just felt to me as though, you know,
we were making strides in the UK,
and then the world's richest man
and his product decided to turn the clock back.
So what exactly did you stand up and say?
What I did was I talked about the need
for the government to accelerate their ban
on nudification apps, which they did.
So the Secretary of State, Liz Kendall, said
that she was going to bring that ban into law
through the Crime and Policing Bill, which she did.
But I also said that it was very important
that we went further than that
because, of course, Grok itself
is not a sole-purpose nudification tool.
It has a general use,
and therefore we needed to bring all AI chatbots
under the auspices of the Online Safety Act.
And we're now waiting until
that legislation comes into effect.
There's got to be a consultation, I understand,
before it does.
So technically another Grok could happen in this period,
but in the future, there would be much stronger measures
that we could take against tools like Grok
creating nudification content.
So that's a really positive outcome
of your interjection in Parliament,
but what else happened as a result of you standing up?
Well, one of the things that happened was
that I posted on social saying that, you know,
Elon Musk should stop
and stop Grok from being able to do this.
And then, of course, I became a victim of,
you know, the same trend.
So, @Grok, put this woman in a bikini.
And, you know, most of the images, you know,
were sort of pornified, I would say.
So they weren't nude images,
but they were me with, you know, inflated boobs in a bikini.
Then people tried to, you know, make it funny, I guess,
by putting, you know, swastika on me
or hammer and sickles, depending friend,
or making me pregnant with quintuplets
and putting me in a kitchen,
because, of course, that's the only use for women,
is birthing and making dinner.
But the kind of really disturbing one was a video of me
being surrounded by a group of men,
chloroformed over my mouth,
and then I fall backwards onto a chair,
and then my skirts are lifted up.
So no nudity,
but clearly the next frame is meant to be a sexual assault.
So, you know, it was really,
really distressing and disturbing.
That was the point at which friend said,
You probably need to reach out to a lawyer,
because each of these things we reported to X,
and, you know, none of them contravened
their terms and conditions.
We just keep getting those sort of repeat emails
coming back,
We've looked into this and there's nothing to see here.
So I did engage a lawyer who sent a letter to X
to ask for these to be removed, and they were,
but it was at that point that he said,
Actually, I think you might actually have a case.
We think that xAI have broken the law.
I mean, I think it's brilliant that you did that,
and I can see the through line of your legal training
and how practically you tackle things.
But when you were just telling me that,
it really turned my stomach.
I had a very physical reaction to you describing
what they did, and I just wanted to sort of find out more
about how it felt.
I mean, I'm really impressed by how you handled it
and the sort of default to action,
but it must have been really awful.
It was awful.
You know, this is done to demean,
to degrade, and to push women out of online spaces.
From my perspective, I tend to use
bad or difficult things that happen as a way
of thinking about how do we change this for the future.
My old boss was an amazing woman called Tessa Jowell,
and she used to say to me, if anything went wrong,
she would say, How do we change this negative energy
into something positive?
How do we work our way out this into a place
where we actually feel that we've learned from it?
And so I guess, you know, she instilled in me
that sort of sense that when something bad happens,
you've got a choice.
You can wallow in it, you can try and forget about it,
or you can use it as a catalyst for change.
And so I was quite trepidatious about the idea
of taking on a legal action,
not least because of the person who is at the top of xAI,
now SpaceX AI.
He's the world's richest man.
But also because I didn't want myself
to necessarily be the story.
Many, many women, you know, had things that were created
of them through both Grok,
but also other nudification tools that are much, much worse.
Having said that, I knew that if there was the opportunity
to say that actually they'd broken the law,
there was an important point of principle
on behalf of all of the women and the children
whose images were manipulated and misused by Grok,
who would never, ever be able to bring a legal case.
And so I decided that, you know, I wanted to do this
because I wanted to be able to show
that no one is bigger than the law.
It doesn't matter how rich you are
or how powerful you are
or how big a reach you have
in terms of your social media presence
or who your friends might be
at the top of various governments.
If you break the law in our country,
you need to feel the force of that.
And as an ex-lawyer and now as a legislator,
it is important that, you know,
we uphold our law where it has been broken.
And so it's also about giving control back, I think,
to us as individuals, but also as a society.
So many of these digital changes have been done
without our consent, our say, you know,
and I think there's a feeling
that there's a sort of runaway train that we're all on,
whether we want to be or not,
because we all need to use online spaces
for our work, for connection.
And so my view is that we should be expecting companies
to respect our law or at least make new laws
to bring them more into line
with what society really needs.
You said there that you gave it some thought.
In that moment of trying to decide how to respond,
what are you weighing up?
Who are you talking to?
Are you going back and talking to your team
or your family to work out how you should respond,
knowing that it may invite further speculation
and further attention?
My family mostly.
So my husband in particular.
It's one thing, you know, being a politician
and arguing your case to change the law
on behalf of women and children;
it's another having your own legal case.
And so I was worried about the impact
that that might have on my family and my children.
I'll be honest, because I have been, you know,
at the heart of pile-ons on X before.
I also know that this can bring danger to politicians.
And so I worried about the fact that, you know,
I am obviously engaging and making the defendant
somebody who has got this very wide reach on social media.
However, I don't like bullies,
and I very strongly believe
that it's important to fight on the field that you've got.
And this was an opportunity I felt to make a difference.
So I weighed that up and thought that it was worth,
you know, having that kind of attention spotlight
and potential danger
because there is a bigger issue here
that we need to get right.
When you say you don't like bullies,
are you talking about the, let's face it, men
who used Grok in this way in the first place,
or are you talking about Elon Musk?
I'm talking about, yeah, the men who used this
as a form of trying to push women out of the online space.
And actually it was quite clear in quite a lot
of the comments that, you know, they were saying,
Well, if you don't like this, then get off the platform.
Either that or, you know,
If this is too hot for you, get out of the kitchen,
which I always find quite funny
because they put me in a kitchen.
It's a bit like,
Do you want me in the kitchen or out of it?
And I think it's really interesting
when you look at X in terms of its demographics in the UK.
It's highly weighted towards men.
So women are already, you know, voting with their feet
in relation to this particular platform.
And I think some of that's down to the fact
that there is just so much misogyny and abuse on it.
So I'm assuming, correct me if I'm wrong,
that the other side of the response to going public
and deciding to continue with being public on this issue
and to fight it in court
is that other women have come forward to you.
Did you have other women coming forward
talking to you about your decision to make this legal?
Absolutely.
And actually that has been one of the,
I guess the heartening things
has both been people coming forward and saying,
Thank you, because this has now given me the license
to actually accept that what happened to me,
you know, wasn't my fault.
It's not my shame.
And so, in a way, what I'm hoping is
that this has helped some victims to process
what has happened to them
and understand that this was not right.
It's not right.
I've also had emails from parents where they've said
that this has happened to their daughter.
It's been done by boys at school.
I've had teachers saying that
boys have made pornographic AI imagery of them.
And it is actually quite rife.
And it's something where we've just sort of let it happen
and wash over us and accept that somehow
this is now a part of the society we live in.
So yes, quite a number of people have come forward.
Obviously, not all of their experiences
have been through Grok.
And I think one of the things is that often,
you know, when you see these films or images,
you don't know what platform they've been created on.
I mean, the only reason why I knew it was Grok
was because it was integrated with X,
and you could see the commands that had been given
by the users.
But much of the time, I think when this content is created,
most victims don't know by who or on what platform.
And so there's really very little
that they can do about it.
And I think it's that sort of sense of helplessness
that, you know, you have been violated.
And that is the word that comes up so frequently
from victims of this particular issue.
And it's not just that it's nudified.
Of course, much of my content wasn't.
It's the lack of consent.
And lots of people say,
Oh, but you know, it's just, it's fake,
you know, it's fake, right?
It's just a laugh.
But what people don't understand is
that it is hyperrealistic and it's your face.
It is piece of you, a piece of your soul.
It's not just pixels on the internet.
It is a person.
And because obviously I've worked for a long time
in violence against women and girls
and, you know, spoken to many victims of sexual assault
and to children who've been victims of child sexual abuse.
It is the lack of consent that is so disturbing.
And it can leave people with PTSD and quite deep trauma.
And there have been a number of people I've met
who have said that the world seems less safe to them
because this has happened to them.
I mean, I think you've already touched on it,
but what is the biggest myth around deepfakes
that you would wish to dispel, that you now,
through experience and through the people
that you've spoken to, wish to dispel?
That it comes without any harm.
That it's just a laugh.
That it's just a laugh.
There is clear harm.
And even when it's not done to demean or degrade,
so even if it's done sometimes by friends,
the fact is that you haven't consented to that happen.
There is something about the human psyche,
which is that when you see yourself
so realistically created in a different situation
or scenario, that's not something you would have done,
I think it's quite discombobulating.
I think your brain can't quite process it
because your brain knows it's not true,
but it looks very true.
And I think psychologically,
we still don't really understand
how this content is going to change the way
that we think about our world,
how we know what is true and what isn't true.
Now, of course, you can do fantastic things
with generative AI.
And all I'm calling for
is that we respect people's consent.
And that's why one of the things I've been working on
since this happened is to look at whether we could create
a system of consent to be manipulated by AI.
Could we create a greater right over our likeness online
so that there's a new social norm, which is that,
No, you can't, you know,
copy and paste that picture into an AI chatbot
and do whatever you want with it.
That's not yours.
It's not your data.
It's their data,
and you're breaching the law if you do that.
And I think were we to do that,
would have a wide range of applications.
It wouldn't just be in this space
of the sexualization of women and children,
but also with political disinformation.
We are so close to a moment where somebody produces a,
you know, hyperrealistic video
of a politician saying something that they didn't,
and then that leading to real-world harm.
And so we've got to find a new social norm
that says, you know, unless for public figures
it's parody or satire, absolutely got to protect that.
But in all other instances, your picture, your voice,
and your moving image is your personal data,
and it's not for anyone else to use.
So that's interesting
because you're touching there on new social norms
and the possibility of new laws
to keep up with this technology,
but your lawsuit is specifically under a data law.
Talk to me about that versus a law
around consensual imagery or deepfakes particularly.
Yeah.
So my case is brought under existing law, the GDPR,
the data protection law,
and it contends that Grok misused my data
without my consent.
It didn't have consent to process my data,
the data being my face, my likeness.
But also under privacy laws
that I had a reasonable expectation of privacy.
And that particularly the video of me
being prepared for sexual assault, you know,
reaches a criminal threshold,
and that nobody should be expected
to be on the receiving end of a product.
Let's remember this is actually a product
that has been designed by software engineers and developers,
and that actually products should not lead
to an invasion of privacy
and the harm that I then experienced as a result of that,
including distress and, you know,
a sense that I was being harassed by, you know,
this particular creation of this particular video.
So it rests on good, solid legal grounds,
and we await the defense from SpaceX AI.
So that was going to be my next question.
I don't know how much you can say legally.
I'm not sure how you're bound,
but what part of the process are you in?
What happens next?
What's the timeline for a resolution to this case?
So like with a lot of legal cases,
it's very, very hard to pin down a timeline.
But my understanding is that we should be receiving
the response and the defense from SpaceX AI,
you know, in the near future,
but we don't have a deadline
or a particular time that I can put on it.
After that, my understanding is the case
will then be looked at,
and, you know, if there is a case to answer,
then it will go to a court hearing.
But once again, no idea when that might be.
And I think there's lots of legal things
that I don't understand that need to be worked out
in the meantime as well
between my lawyers and their lawyers.
And have you ever had any acknowledgment on X itself
from Elon Musk or anyone at X about this case?
Has he ever spoken publicly about it?
No.
Would you expect him to?
I don't think so.
They clearly want to challenge this case,
and so the best place to do that, I think, is in the courts
and to leave it to see whether the merits of the case,
you know, come through.
You were in New York to address-
That's right. Yeah.
Address city council about your case.
You didn't get to speak to anyone directly at SpaceX,
is that right?
No.
I mean, despite being subpoenaed, they didn't turn up.
So four of the other frontier AI companies
did attend under subpoena.
SpaceX AI didn't,
but they eventually did get their hearing
with SpaceX in the city council.
So, you know, they have now had their opportunity
to put questions and indeed did raise my case
with them, I understand.
Is it a little enraging to attend a hearing like that,
a company that you're suing who don't bother turning up?
I think it's quite rude to the elected members
of New York City Council
that you are a business who operates in New York.
And indeed I was told that
they were just four subway stops from City Hall.
So I had traveled, you know, quite a long way from England
to be there, and they couldn't be bothered to turn up,
which, yeah, it felt arrogant and a bit of a snub,
but they've now got there, so that's a good thing.
Since you made the decision to take this to courts,
there has been a number of proposals in Parliament,
notably that there was a proposal
for a kill switch bill at one point.
Now, I believe it's dead or it's not going very well.
Is that right?
So yes, there have been proposals put forth
for a kill switch.
My understanding is that the government rejected that.
There continues to be sort of strong calls for,
you know, regulation of particularly superintelligent AI.
We've heard various theories,
whether it's 2%, 10%, 20% risk of human extinction
from this sort of race to superintelligence, recursive AI.
And we wouldn't allow those margins of risk
in any other sphere.
We would not allow it in bridge building
or airplane making, you know.
They didn't even allow it
when they were testing the nuclear bomb
in the Trinity testings.
It feels to me as though so much of this decision-taking
is outside of democratic structures.
It's not with the public.
It is being done by some incredibly,
exceptionally wealthy companies
and organizations who say that
they have the interests of the planet at heart,
but each time actually, you know,
they're asked about whether that is the future of humanity
or, you know, whether they think
that these risks could kill humanity,
there's a sort of shrugging of the shoulders and, you know,
We'll just keep going because we want to make money,
I guess.
Well, part of the problem,
it has been reported in the British press
that there are members of Parliament,
some of whom are working on committees
to deal with technology,
who still don't really understand what AI is.
And clearly you're not one of them
because you are a sort of early adopter
of the dangers of this issue.
But do you feel, working across parties,
that you're still having to explain technology
and its dangers and possibilities
to people who are making laws
or should be making laws to protect the public from AI?
Well, look, I don't think that's only the case about AI.
We are humans, after all,
and we have to deal with every single subject
that exists under the sun.
We have to get our heads around things
that we've never heard of before.
A bit like being a journalist, actually.
Yeah, that's true.
But you don't have to then make laws and decisions.
So, you know, I don't want to be unfair to my colleagues.
You know, you may be a specialist in housing policy,
and you then need to get your head around AI.
But I would say that this is the most important issue
in front of anybody in Parliament or politics at the moment,
and therefore everyone needs to get their head around AI.
You know, I'm not a technology expert.
My background is in social policy, women and children.
But because we did quite a lot of work
on the Online Safety Act
when I was working for a children's charity,
we campaigned to get the age verification ban
for children in pornography into the OSA.
And indeed, you know, created quite a strong piece
of legislation in respect of that.
You know, we had to get our heads around,

title: Folklore Expert Answers Ghost Story Questions
raw_text:
Folklore Expert Answers Ghost Story Questions
Released on 10/27/2026
I'm Professor Tok Thompson, professor of anthropology
at the University of Southern California.
Let's answer some questions from the internet.
This is Ghost Story Support.
[thumping upbeat music]
First up, I wonder if you know
what the oldest recorded ghost story is?
I would really like to know.
So we know that from the earliest writings,
especially back to ancient Babylonian times, Sumer, Ur,
some of the earliest stories people were writing down
were stories about ghosts.
So maybe 3,500 years ago, we have inscriptions
of what seemed to be even an exorcism ritual.
So not only did they have ghosts,
but they already had ritual specialists
that figured out how to get rid of ghosts.
Again, we know that as soon as writing pops up,
we've already got ghost stories,
and these are some of our earliest writings.
From Anna, @lesaenni, What counts as a ghost?
Ghosts aren't a scientific concept.
We've never established them as a scientific reality.
So how do you define something
that science doesn't even acknowledge existing?
The definition I like to use is that a ghost
is a spirit of a dead person who appears to the living.
So this weeds out a lot of things
that might be other spirits or other demons or ghouls
or things that might not be the spirit of a dead person.
On the other hand, it opens up a lot of possibilities.
One example is what if the dead person
appears to you in a dream?
Is that still a ghost?
Some people might say yes, some people might say no.
So again, these are sort of handy definitions,
and we like to see how far we can stretch these.
From @imranzomg.
How come we don't have ghosts now
that are, like, '90s dudes with backwards caps and [beeps]?
I've been studying those for a while,
and one of the places we really find millennial ghosts
is in the internet.
It's in the cyber world.
We have all these stories of haunted servers.
Minecraft has one of the most famous
supposed ghost stories on the internet.
So there are a tremendous amount of new ghost stories
and especially this idea of the cyber world.
Maybe this is where our afterlife is.
We have souls maybe trapped on a computer game
or on a server.
So I have all these sort of stories I've collected
of people getting text messages from the beyond
of their good friends.
The online ghosts are all the people
that spend all their social time
and their social communications online.
So when they die, this is where they haunt.
@urnonshowbizgf.
Why do people believe in ghosts?
I like to always offer the possibility
that, well, one, maybe they're real,
or other suggestions might be something like
this helps us deal with death.
If you believe in ghosts,
you probably believe in some sort of an afterlife.
Ghost stories are also a way of establishing ethics
as something more than just transactional.
The idea that you can be haunted
by your ethical failures if you make them.
There was a great scientific experiment a few years ago.
They had these students come in and do a test.
The only catch was that they could easily cheat on the test.
And the psychologist said,
Okay, you know, please don't cheat.
But they kept track of how many students did.
And one group, they also said that,
Oh, by the way, this room is supposed to be haunted.
The group that felt their room was haunted
were far less likely to cheat at the test.
Next question.
@ClearShakes.
One fun theory I've heard
why ghost stories became so big in the Victorian era
is that that's when home gas lighting became prevalent.
Everyone's getting carbon monoxide poisoning
and hallucinating.
It's possible.
We know that people did
when they're trying to contact the spirit world.
They do try to become intoxicated
with various drugs or gases or whatnot.
The Oracle at Delphi in ancient Greece,
we know that gases were coming out,
and that had something to do
with the participants' experience being gassed.
But there's some other reasons
that ghosts became really big during the Victorian era.
One of the biggest ones was that, you know,
this is after the Reformation.
You have the Protestant
versus the Catholic groups in Europe.
And in the Protestant groups,
you weren't supposed to believe in ghosts suddenly.
That was supposed to be an old Catholic superstition
that, you know, the Reformation was supposed to get rid of.
And one of the big problems is that people
kept seeing a lot of ghosts in the Victorian era.
What we have is this really interesting rise
of spiritualism, of seances,
of scientific inquiries into ghosts.
So maybe ghosts weren't supernatural;
maybe they were natural, you know,
maybe science could prove ghosts exist, you know?
Maybe electricity had something to do with ghosts,
like Frankenstein, or maybe X-rays.
Maybe we could take photographs of the spirit world.
So there was a heavy blend
of sort of Eastern mysticism and science.
The other thing I think I could mention too
is the idea of the Gothic novel,
which was huge during the Victorian era.
And that's really talking about the fall of the aristocracy.
Charles Dickens wrote a lot about ghosts.
So this is a big deal in the Victorian era,
and they're becoming a big deal today as well
for different reasons.
@TakeThatDarwin.
Okay, I realize it's customary, if not mandatory,
for Christians to believe in demons and Satan,
but how did ghosts get in there?
When Christianity started off, one of its main core tenets
is that ghosts weren't supposed to happen.
You know, once you die,
eventually you're gonna go to the Day of Judgment.
So a lot of people were worshiping ancestors
and deifying ancestors,
and Christianity was saying, No, this doesn't happen.
Ghosts aren't real.
So this lasts for about 500 years.
And then [laughs] when it spreads into Northern Europe,
the Germanic peoples were very, very much into their ghosts.
And Pope Gregory I said, Look, you don't have to change
what people do.
You just have to Christianize it.
So by the time we get to the Middle Ages,
the church has shifted position.
If you see a ghost, you can go to your priest,
and you can say, Hey, priest, I saw a ghost.
And then the priest would say, Ah, yes, you know,
that's your grandfather, and he's stuck in purgatory,
and he needs help to bring him up the ranks of purgatory.
He needs me to pray for him.
Therefore, you need to pay me to pray for him.
So this idea of the sale of indulgences,
which is a big moneymaker for the church,
depended on ghosts now.
When Martin Luther started off the Reformation
with his complaints against the church,
the number one thing was the sale of indulgences.
And very connected to that, ghosts.
Martin Luther said, Look, Christians
aren't supposed to believe in ghosts.
The church shouldn't believe in ghosts.
You know, what are you doing believing in ghosts?
This ultimately led to the Protestant Reformation.
And so now you had the Catholic Church
that still believed in ghosts and exorcisms,
and the Protestant groups
largely denied the existence of ghosts.
That starts to change in the American experience
around the late 1880s
when you have these sort of newer religious movements,
the Third Great Awakening as it's sometimes called.
Southern Pentecostals, the so-called holy rollers,
actually tended to view the world
as comprised of demons, of devils,
and the devil's a very active force.
So this comes close,
but the idea now is going back to this older idea
that, oh no, there are no such things as ghosts.
It's only demons or devils trying to trick you.
Okay, Styling1998, Spirited Away.
What spirits in the movie are based off of real spirits
in Japanese folklore and Shintoism?
Not many.
Spirited Away which is a beautiful movie
about the spirit realm.
I think it really captures the look and feel
of traditional Japanese folklore.
The idea of the spirit world
is not that far away from the human world.
You can easily sort of wander into it by accident.
The idea that people can help out
spirits in the spirit world,
and sometimes people are necessary to help out spirits.
All of this is very, very traditional.
The actual figures, the actual characters themselves,
not so much based on actual Japanese folklore.
A friend of mine who's a scholar on Japanese folklore,
and he calls this the folkloresque.
You're making something really feel like folklore,
even if it's really not based on traditional folklore.
Another question coming in from EngineeringNo8660.
What cultures do you think
have the most ghost/spirit rich history?
A lot of surveys have indicated
that by far the majority of Taiwan believes in ghosts,
probably 90%, 95% of the population.
Which is to say, if you're in Taiwan
and you don't believe in ghosts,
you're kinda weird; you're kind of strange.
It's worked into the calendar.
You have Ghost Month in Taiwan.
You have the big celebrations for the ghosts.
In Japan, very similarly, this is the Obon Festival.
It's a bit like American Christmas.
Maybe you get days off;
you're supposed to go home with the family.
But the other thing is, it's not just your living family;
it's your ancestors.
Traditional families would set places out
and invite the ancestors to come in and enjoy a meal
and to return and greet their living relatives.
You have your wanted ghosts, like ancestor spirits,
and your unwanted ghosts,
the ones that tend to haunt us or cause trouble.
These work a little bit differently
from conflations of Buddhism and other traditions,
but we have several different types of ghosts.
Very often these ghosts are corporeal,
so you don't notice they're ghosts at first.
Ghosts are a little bit more alive
and fleshed out in a lot of East Asian traditions.
You can even have sex with a ghost and have ghost babies.
And so some people that are remarkable people,
people might say, Oh, yeah,
he's got a bit of ghost in him.
This idea that being close to the spirit world
and close to the ghost world
is also maybe what makes some people so very special.
This becomes a much bigger sort of cultural concern
in places like Taiwan and Japan
than we might see in places like America.
@NoctivagantPod, Are poltergeist and ghosts the same thing?
And if not, what's the difference?
How can you tell?
Poltergeist is a German word
that means literally noisy ghost.
The idea of the poltergeist experience
is when things are, you know, flying off the walls;
objects are moving.
So they're creating a lot of noise.
These are noisy ghosts.
But some people that believe in poltergeists and ghosts
would maintain that these are not ghosts,
that this is something else involved,
that they're not really ghosts; it's probably telekinesis.
@DJFreshUK.
Okay, well then how come
no one ever sees ghosts of animals?
The main reason that people don't see many ghosts
of animals in, say, America today,
it's largely an Abrahamic and largely Christian nation
where we have this idea that only people have souls.
A ghost is sort of your soul.
On the other hand, in societies that are non-Abrahamic,
Japan, you have animal ghosts.
Look at India; you have animal ghosts.
And if you look at Native American folklore,
you have a ton of animal ghosts.
And that goes to this fundamental thoughts,
very different thoughts about the soul.
And for Native American societies,
you know, does a bear have a soul?
Does a wolf have a soul?
Yeah, of course.
And so therefore, if you kill an animal
or even harvest plants, Native American tradition,
you have to, you know, say thank you.
You have to sort of say grace.
You have to pray for its spiritual journey.
You have to give it some sort of funerary ritual
or else, you know, something might go wrong,
and it might come back and haunt you.
This idea of being haunted by ghosts
really shaped a lot of Native American spiritual traditions.
@grace6569, Why do ghost stories
always talk about the lady in white?
Why not the lady in turquoise or the lady in burgundy?
Well, a lot of ghosts show up in night
and I think maybe white actually shows up better
in the middle of the night.
So it's a very sort of compelling imagery
if you see, you know,
the lady in white in the middle of the night.
We also find in many cultures,
especially sort of patrilineal and patriarchal cultures,
the idea of the failed bride becoming a ghost,
like the woman who never quite gets married,
abandoned at the altar and commits suicide,
this sort of thing.
And of course we represent unmarried women by wearing white.
So there's some very particular things about ladies in white
that have a long, long trajectory in European culture.
@dioscuri, I wonder if part of the reason
people tell ghost stories is that it's comforting to think
that horrible human suffering
leaves a spiritual scar in a place, rather than nature
and geography being utterly indifferent to human affairs.
I like to say that history is written by the victors,
but ghost stories are written by the victims.
One great example is called Duffy's Cut.
This was a valley in the East Coast.
Irish American laborers came in to work on a railroad.
They all died.
The local town said it was a cholera epidemic.
They buried them.
End of story, except for the next 100-plus years,
people kept seeing ghosts in this valley.
And so these stories kept going on
and going on and going on.
Finally, just a few years ago, people dug up the graves,
and they found out these people
hadn't died of cholera at all.
They'd been murdered.
So yeah, ghost stories do represent the sordid history,
the backside of history.
@thetoughestbean, Lincoln, and especially his wife,
believed in occultism.
I think they held a seance at the White House.
They held many.
This is sort of public knowledge.
It was mentioned in the newspapers.
They would've called it not occultism;
they would've called it spiritualism.
So this is kind of remarkable by today's standards.
Many, many people were believing
that the spirit world maybe was not so far away
and that the dead could actually be probably
pretty easily contacted.
So, yes, Lincoln and his wife
had several seances in the White House,
and this was completely acceptable during that time period.
@MIDNIGHTER, Why is the American South
so haunted all the time?
Like, why can't they just chill out for a sec?
Ghost stories come out very often of ethical failures.
So is the South still haunted by its slaveholding past?
Yes.
Okay.
I_Like_Languages.
A lot of Americans are obsessed with paranormal
and haunted locations.
Is it the same in Europe?
What's Europe's relationship with the paranormal?
Europe's a big place, got a lot of different countries.
So there's actually a lot of sort of differences
in the different European traditions as well.
A good friend of mine actually did a recent survey
over in Iceland, trying to figure out, you know,
what level of Icelanders believed in ghosts.
And it was somewhere around the 60%,
60% to 65% of Icelanders.
This is pretty much like we see in the United States.
Very, very similar results,
depending on what survey you look at.
On the other hand, you can look at some countries in Europe
that don't have a lot of ghosts.
France does not report a lot of ghosts.
What France does report is a lot of saintly apparitions,
Marian apparitions where they see Mother Mary.
So are these ghosts?
They wouldn't say they're ghosts in France.
It's like, Oh, no, this is religion.
These are saints.
Because some people might not like that word, ghost.
Like, Oh, no, I don't believe in ghosts.
Anything strange ever happened to you?
Oh, my dead husband appeared to me one night.
That was lovely.
This sort of thing happens all the time.
So surveys can be very, very difficult
at figuring out what people actually really believe.
What I will say is we can see
that people report on these surveys
very, very differently in different European countries.
@AdamBroud, Why are houses
the ones that are always haunted?
Can other living spaces be haunted?
Can I buy a haunted tent?
Go on a little camping trip with my new ghost buddy?
Adventure in the woods,
and come back home to my little spooky pal
in our little spooky place?
Can I do that?
Please.
Yeah, the haunted house shows up a lot.
We live in houses sorta like we live in our bodies.
There's a lot of metaphors that sort of, you know,
associate your house and your body.
So maybe this is where we spend a lot of our time.
So this idea that, you know,
as your spirit leaves your body, [laughs] still lingers,
and very often it still lingers in the house.
It also brings back this idea
that these are sort of domestic ghosts, right?
If ghosts are often ethical failings,
then these are domestic failings, maybe abusive families
or, you know, family murders, stuff like this.
Okay. Reptilian_Overlord20.
I am so tired of the horror trope
of kids who talk to ghosts.
This pops up around the world, interestingly enough.
This could go back to these ideas
that maybe kids are more susceptible to ghostly influence.
Maybe they don't have a hearty adult soul, in a sense.
Some people say,
Well, kids just haven't learned not to see them.
As adults, maybe we learn to shut them out,
but kids haven't learned that yet.
And then, of course, there's also the idea
of kids having a very active imagination.
So kids talking to ghosts is a very, very common motif,
and I think it brings in a lot of different thoughts
about childhood and about, again,
the relationship between kids and the dead.
@cloakbrand, What is Dia de los Muertos about?
Do you celebrate this holiday with your family?
Yes, you celebrate this holiday with your family, ideally.
This is a very, very well-beloved festival
in Hispanic communities
that was brought into the Catholic calendar.
So now it's been moved slightly
to overlap with the Catholic days
of All Souls' Day and All Saints' Day.
So long ago, this is probably developed to move Samhain,
the Celtic Halloween, into the Christian fold.
So this is why those days are right at Samhain,
at the beginning of winter.
And then when they came to the Americas,
they put the Days of the Dead from Central America
on this same calendar.
So right now in, like, Los Angeles,
we have a lot of Hispanic traditions for Days of the Dead,
going on at the same time we have Halloween celebrations.
So modern America, Halloween is very often about spooks
and being scared,
and the Days of the Dead for Hispanic culture
is very, very much about the wanted dead.
There's this idea that, you know, you can keep coming back.
You set up a little altar, an ofrenda,
and very often with pictures of loved ones,
maybe things that they enjoyed,
and a lot of interesting symbolism like marigolds,
which had long been a symbol of the return of the dead
in ancient Aztec and Mayan culture.
So Days of the Dead is this wonderful blend
of these different motifs
from pre-colonial indigenous traditions
and also very, very contemporary in today's society.
There's a phrase that often goes with it:
That which is remembered lives.
So your afterlife depends on the people remembering you,
and that's what Days of the Dead is all about.
This is everything I got for today.
Hope you learned something,
and thank you for watching Ghost Support.
[groovy upbeat music]
Starring: Tok Thompson

What Was It Like Interviewing Nathan Fielder?
What was WIRED Global Editorial Director Katie Drummond's takeaway from her interview with Nathan Fielder? Read the full interview.
Released on 10/24/2026
Transcript
It was great.
I love interviewing anyone,
whether it's, you know, confrontational or just curious.
And he was lovely.
We are both Canadian
and we both have a very deadpan sense of humor.
And so I think that maybe made it a little easier for me,
but look, I think there is a lot of commentary online
about him and his personas
and whether he's playing a character all the time
and who he really is,
which is interesting when you juxtapose it
with a film about Elizabeth Holmes.
I think he's just, like, a smart, thoughtful guy
who makes great stuff. That was my takeaway.

Maharashtra MLC polls: Congress candidate Abhijit Wanjarri wins Nagpur graduates' constituency with 67,231 votes
Abhijit Wanjarri, a Congress candidate, emerged victorious in the Nagpur Division Legislative Council elections. He secured a total of 67,231 votes through the first and second preference counts. His nearest rival, Sudhakar Kohale of the BJP, received 63,960 votes. The election process included over 41 hours of vote counting that followed the polling on October 23. The Election Commission finalized the entire process by October 31.

A Muslim youth named Yusuf was allegedly assaulted and removed from a garba event in Nalasopara. The incident arose after he wiped off a tilak that had been applied to him at the entrance. Organisers stated that the tilak was intended to prevent incidents of love jihad, although its application sparked controversy. BJP corporator Jayprakash Singh later distanced himself from the practice and the assailants.
A 22-year-old gym trainer has been arrested for allegedly raping a woman under the pretext of marriage. The complainant claims his mobile phone contains obscene videos of 80 women that were sold online. Investigators are examining the phone to verify these allegations and have received two complaints thus far. Local political leaders are demanding a thorough investigation into the increasing number of victims.
A 56-year-old woman was killed by a garbage truck at the Turbhe railway station intersection. The driver was assaulted by a mob at the scene before being rescued by police officers. This incident revealed ongoing concerns regarding the dangerous intersection near Turbhe Store. Over the past decade, 23 fatalities and numerous injuries have occurred at this site.
Two men were arrested for allegedly attacking the secretary of a housing society in Adai village. The assault occurred following a dispute about a non-functional elevator late at night. The attack was captured on CCTV, showing the severity of the incident. The victim, Vaibhav Ramchandra Patil, sustained multiple injuries and is currently hospitalized. The accused were remanded in police custody as investigations continue into the case.

title: Thane News, Latest Thane News Headlines & Live Updates, Breaking Thane News - Times of India
raw_text:
Thane municipal corporation has suspended acting chief fire officer Jhalke due to alleged negligence in safety measures. The negligence was observed at Datta Mandir Ghat and Ahilyadevi Ghat during idol immersion. Additional action has been taken against two other officials alongside show-cause notices to two junior staff members. Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde was reportedly informed about the inadequate safety equipment.
Recently, the Enforcement Directorate initiated an FIR following the discovery of unauthorized entry into a Thane flat associated with money laundering activities connected to Iqbal Kaskar and Dawood Ibrahim. The agency found the official seal had been unlawfully lifted by those claiming ownership. Acquired through coercion in 2015, Kaskar’s flat has now been repossessed by the ED, which has formally notified the court about the situation.
Severe water shortages are affecting residents across 27 villages of Kalyan-Dombivli Municipal Corporation, with the Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation implementing a 36-hour weekly water supply halt. This comes amid already low supply levels, which are at about half of the sanctioned quota. KDMC officials are concerned and plan to petition the MIDC to reconsider the additional water restrictions.
Vishwrajsinh, an employee at Timba post office, recorded a video expressing despair over harassment related to his marriage. He claimed that domestic violence laws were being misused against him and his family without proper evidence. He alleged that this situation led to unbearable mental and emotional pressure, culminating in his decision to end his life. Vishwrajsinh communicated his desire for changes to the law to prevent others from suffering similarly.

Sarah Groves, a British national, was murdered in 2013, leading to de Wit's arrest by police.

As cyclone Arnab approaches the Andhra Pradesh coast, schools in coastal districts have been closed for safety. The government has prohibited sea fishing operations and canceled over 50 trains due to impending severe weather. Heavy rainfall and strong winds are expected to escalate as the cyclone makes landfall on October 28. Currently, flight operations remain normal, with no cancellations reported.
Seven individuals lost their lives in a devastating explosion involving a vehicle at a road construction site. The incident occurred when a Mahindra Bolero Camper vehicle caught fire due to mishandling during fuel transfer. Local reports indicate that a spark led to the blaze, which ultimately ignited an LPG cylinder. Authorities are investigating the precise cause of the explosion and its aftermath.
Following cyclone Arnab, a low-pressure area has developed over the south Andaman Sea. This system may bring heavy rainfall to parts of Andhra Pradesh in early November. Rainfall could further damage the standing crops in coastal regions of the state. The IMD predicts heavy rains in various districts like Vizianagaram and Visakhapatnam during November 2 and 3.
On October 16, a disturbing case unfolded as retired IRS officer P Anand Kumar was abducted amid a financial dispute. While on his way to the airport, an armed gang overwhelmed him in his car. Responding rapidly to the situation, police launched a rescue mission, utilizing CCTV and mobile tracking.

Amid a rise in fire-related incidents across cities, this page tracks the blazes, rescue operations, safety lapses, investigations and policy responses shaping urban safety. From building violations and emergency preparedness to lessons learned from major fires, follow the stories that reveal how prepared your city really is.
- 'Allowed 2 Bangladeshis to use his home for money': Hotel owner Lavkesh Bajaj under scanner for international human trafficking Delhi Police is investigating Lovkesh Bajaj, linked to a deadly Hauz Rani fire, for suspected involvement in an international human trafficking racket. He allegedly used medical tourism as a front to smuggle foreigners into India, having previously been arrested for facilitating forged documents for a Bangladeshi family.
- TOI ground report from Hauz Rani Hauz Rani grapples with the aftermath of a fatal fire, highlighting the pervasive danger of tangled overhead wires and inadequate infrastructure. Residents voice concerns about authorities only acting after tragedies, leaving them to rely on themselves in emergencies. The constant threat of electrical hazards is a grim reality locals have learned to endure.
- TOI ground report from Malviya Nagar Signs are disappearing in Malviya Nagar as properties linked to arrested hotel owner Lavkesh Bajaj face scrutiny after a fire killed 21. Residents allege unchecked expansion and ignored safety concerns, with one hotel reportedly growing from two-and-a-half to five floors without approval. Bajaj allegedly admitted to illegal expansion, stating 'Delhi mein sab chalta hai'.
- TOI ground report from Malviya Nagar A family's journey to be with an ailing patriarch tragically ended in a devastating fire at a Delhi hotel, claiming the lives of eight members. The Aggarwal family, including three generations, perished in the blaze. Their abandoned Mercedes outside the gutted building stands as a silent testament to the unimaginable loss.
- Death traps behind glass facades: Delhi hotel hubs exposed to fire risk Affordable hospitality hubs in Delhi, like Mahipalpur and Paharganj, are rife with fire safety violations, including sealed windows and inadequate firefighting equipment. These conditions mirror those that led to a fatal blaze in Hauz Rani, raising concerns about potential catastrophes due to poor ventilation, narrow access, and delayed emergency responses.
- Delhi hotel fire: Owner Lovkesh Bajaj's earlier arrest over Indian IDs for Bangladeshis under lens The owner of a Malviya Nagar hotel where a fire killed 21 people was previously arrested in 2025 for allegedly facilitating the illegal stay of Bangladeshi nationals. Lovkesh Bajaj admitted to knowingly allowing individuals to use his address for fraudulent Indian identity documents in exchange for money. Police are now investigating his role in the deadly hotel fire.

Health experts emphasize that in the event of a fire, the real enemy is often the smoke, not the flames. Inhalation of toxic substances such as carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide can become fatal in moments, as they cause a lack of oxygen and serious lung injury due to extreme heat.

title: David French
raw_text:
Deport Immigrants? Oh Yes. But Not This Guy.
Suddenly, Empathy Isn’t So Toxic
By David French
I’m a new kid on the block in Opinion. I joined in January 2023, and while I write on a wide range of topics, a common theme is that I like to explore the story behind the story. What are the reasons for American polarization and dysfunction? Why do so many Americans feel lonely and anxious? Why is religious affiliation in such sharp decline? I’m just as likely to write about faith, friendship, marriage and parenting as I am to write about the war in Ukraine or the latest developments in American constitutional law. I also write quite a bit about religion in America, with a particular focus on the health of the evangelical church.
I took a long and winding road to journalism. I was born in Alabama, grew up in a small town in Kentucky, attended Lipscomb University in Nashville, and graduated from Harvard Law School. I was a commercial litigator for a number of years, and then ultimately switched to constitutional law. In 1999, I took a brief detour from my litigation career and served as a lecturer at Cornell Law School.
In 2006, I obtained an age waiver from the Army and joined the JAG Corps as an Army lawyer. After dragging my old body through basic training, I volunteered to deploy to Iraq and served with the 3rd Armored Cavalry Regiment in Diyala Province during the height of the Surge in 2007. I was awarded a Bronze Star.
During my litigation career, I worked for both commercial and public interest law firms and was a former president of the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression. I spent most of my career defending free speech, religious freedom and due process in courtrooms across the country.
After 21 years of legal practice, I changed careers. In 2015, I joined National Review as a senior writer, but left in 2019 to help start The Dispatch, a conservative media company. I also became a contributing writer for The Atlantic. In 2023, I joined The Times.
If there were a Nerd Olympics, I might take the gold medal. If you want recommendations on sci-fi or fantasy books or movies — or the definitive rankings of Star Wars movies — please ask. I’d be happy to answer, at length.
My most recent book, “Divided We Fall: America’s Secession Threat and How to Restore Our Nation,” outlined the dangers of polarization and the need to engage with people who have opposing viewpoints. I’m an evangelical conservative who believes strongly in a classical liberal, pluralistic vision of American democracy, in which people with deep religious, cultural, and moral differences can live and work together and enjoy equal legal protection and shared cultural tolerance. In both my personal and professional life I strive to live up to the high ideals of Micah 6:8 — to act justly, to love kindness, and to walk humbly before God.
I live in Tennessee.
I’m an opinion writer, but I’m not a polemicist. My goals are to treat opposing arguments fairly, to make sure that my facts are correct, that my analysis is sound, and to be transparent about gaps in my knowledge or limitations in my understanding. I believe in admitting mistakes and telling readers when I change my mind, and why. I think personal and professional transparency is important. If we ask readers to trust us, then they deserve to know us.
I follow the Times’s Ethical Journalism Handbook. I disclose potential conflicts of interest, and when I’m in doubt about any potential ethical question, I seek guidance from my editors in much the same way that a lawyer with ethical concerns seeks guidance from the bar association.

title: Submit Your Crossword Puzzles to The New York Times
raw_text:
Supported by
Submit Your Crossword Puzzles to The New York Times
The New York Times looks for intelligent, literate, entertaining and well-crafted crosswords that appeal to the broad range of Times solvers.
Puzzle Submission Guidelines
Submissions are open.
A New York Times crossword will be a collaboration between you and our staff of editors, who will seek to preserve your voice while making the puzzle as enjoyable as possible for solvers. This page of guidelines is a living document and reflects our current best practices on crossword construction.
A summary of what we look for:
- Lively fill, with words, phrases and names that solvers know or can infer from the crossings.
- Original, on-target clues, pitched at the puzzle’s intended difficulty level, including a variety of cultural reference points.
- No more than three puzzles pending at a time.
- What we could use more of: Thursday and Sunday puzzles that don’t involve a rebus.
Submission Guidelines
Themes
Themes should be fresh, interesting, narrowly defined and consistently applied throughout the puzzle. For example, if the theme includes a particular kind of pun, then all the puns should be of that kind. Themes and theme entries should be accessible to everyone. We generally prefer puzzles with playful themes rather than straightforward subjects.
Fill
Constructors should emphasize lively words, well-known names and fresh phrases. Common words that lend themselves to interesting and imaginative cluing angles are encouraged.
Diversity in cultural references — for age, gender, ethnicity, etc. — is desired.
Avoid offensive language. Be mindful of words that might impact solvers negatively. Non-English words are allowed, so long as they are familiar or inferable to people who don’t speak the language.
Avoid uncommon abbreviations and partial phrases longer than five letters (“So ___” for BE IT would be permissible, while “So ___” for IT GOES would not.)
Keep crosswordese to a minimum — that is, answers that appear far more in crosswords than in real life (ERNE, ASTA, ARETE, YSER, etc.). Difficult words are fine — especially for the harder daily puzzles that run late in the week — if the words are interesting bits of knowledge or useful additions to the vocabulary. However, never let two obscure words or names cross.
Clues
Clues should reflect the difficulty of the puzzle. Our difficulty scale increases through the week, with the easiest puzzles on Monday and hardest on Saturday. Sunday puzzles should reflect midweek difficulty levels.
Clues should be fresh, colorful and precise. Try to be original, and inject humor where possible. Themeless clues should be more difficult and require imaginative thinking. Show us your wit and wordplay!
For example, for the answer STRAP:
Monday clue: “Subway rider’s handhold”
Wednesday clue: “Part of a bike helmet”
Saturday clue: “What might keep a watch on you”
Constructor Tools and Tips
There are many options for making a crossword puzzle, including the good, old-fashioned graph-paper-and-pencil method, though several software programs exist as well. For a full list of these programs, as well as tips from New York Times constructors and editors on the puzzle making process, see our series on How to Make a Crossword Puzzle.
Technical Specs
Basic Rules
While we encourage new and creative crossword themes, there are a few hard rules (broken with extreme rarity) when it comes to constructing New York Times crosswords. These include:
- Crosswords must have black square symmetry, which typically comes in the form of 180-degree rotational symmetry;
- Crosswords must have all-over interlock;
- Crosswords must not have unchecked squares (i.e., all letters must be found in both Across and Down answers);
- All answers must be at least 3 letters long;
- Black squares should be used in moderation.
Maximum Word Count
78 words for a 15×15 (72 for a themeless); 140 for a 21×21. Maximums may be exceeded slightly at the editor’s discretion, if the theme warrants.
Rights
Times puzzles must never have been published anywhere before, either in print or electronically. The Times buys all rights, including first rights.
Submission Rules
Due to the volume of submissions:
- Please limit yourself to no more than three puzzles in the queue at once.
- We count collaborations as half for each byline.
- If your collaborator has never been published by the Times, the puzzle will not count toward your total.
Formatting
All crossword constructing programs have settings to create PDFs in the proper submission format, as follows:
- Clues should be double-spaced on the left, answer words in a corresponding column on the far right.
- Down clues need not begin on a new page.
- Include a filled-in answer grid with numbers.
- Include your name, address and email address on the grid page.
Please label your files LastName_PuzzleTitle for ease of editor review. Puzzle titles can be the theme revealers for daily themed puzzles or marquee entries for themeless puzzles.
An example is shown below, which you can download as a pdf.
If you need more help, take a look at our resource guide.

Mini to Maestro, Part 1: Crosswords for Beginners
Get started solving the Mini, Monday and Tuesday puzzles.
This is Part 1 of a three-part series on learning to solve crossword puzzles. Be sure to check out Part 2 and Part 3.
Here’s a not-so-well-kept secret for you: Everyone can solve the New York Times Crossword.
If you’re already rolling your eyes, take it from us: Jackie Frere, community engagement manager, and Isaac Aronow, associate editor of Gameplay. Jackie was someone who had tried the Monday crossword once, failed, got embarrassed and gave up completely. Isaac has been solving for a while but fell out of practice at the start of the pandemic. We challenged ourselves to see if we could start fresh and complete a Saturday New York Times Crossword in the matter of weeks. Spoiler alert: We did.
In case you didn’t know, the daily New York Times Crossword has a difficulty curve as the week goes on. Monday is the easiest puzzle, and then Tuesday is a little harder, climbing up to Saturday, which is the hardest day of the week. Sunday puzzles are sometimes asserted to be the most difficult puzzle of the week, but much of that difficulty comes from the larger size of Sunday puzzles, rather than the clues, the answers or the themes.
The Mini doesn’t have a difficulty curve like the daily crossword, so how tricky it is depends more on the individual puzzle you do, rather than the day of the week it runs on. Minis rarely include advanced solving elements like a rebus (more on those later) but will often include intermediate solving elements that are common in midweek puzzles. If you’re comfortable solving minis, we suggest that you’ll be comfortable solving daily crosswords up to Wednesday.
It takes time, practice and a little help from the Games team, but you too can solve a Monday puzzle and, eventually, a Saturday crossword. Let us show you how.
Start with the Mini
If you haven’t heard of the Mini, it’s a five-by-five daily crossword created by Joel Fagliano, a senior puzzle editor. It’s free, it includes pop culture clues, and it can most likely be solved in a matter of minutes — or seconds, the more you play.
Dip your toe in the crossword water by solving the Mini every day. You’ll gather a feel for how the tools work on the app or the web, and you’ll start to gain confidence in your solving skills.
Let’s solve the Mini from Feb. 8, 2022, together:
Jackie likes to fill in answers she knows and work her way around a grid. Remember that everyone approaches crossword puzzles differently.
Once you’ve gotten the hang of completing the Mini for about a week or so, it’s time to try a Monday puzzle.
Diving into the daily
Opening up the daily crossword can be daunting, especially if it’s your first time solving. Don’t be scared! Contrary to popular belief, the crossword is not a competition over how much trivia one knows. Yes, random facts and knowledge will come in handy when you’re filling out the crossword grid, but believe in yourself.
When attacking the grid head-on, take a few tries to figure out your style of solving. Jackie likes to go around the grid and fill in what she knows. Then she’ll continue to go back through and see if her memory has been prompted by any letters that were filled in or if an answer has “just come” to her the second or third time around. Isaac likes to start with easier clue types, like fill-in-the-blanks or abbreviations.
Rachel Fabi, a Wordplay columnist, takes a different approach. “I start every puzzle the same way: I start in the northwest and work my way through,” she said. “So it’ll be going back and forth between across and downs in the corner and then building off of what you have, until you have the whole thing.”
Have you gotten as far as you can? Try using autocheck to make sure your answers are correct. Do you need to adjust anything? Go ahead. If you’re still stuck, check out Wordplay, your new best friend. Wordplay is a daily column written by Games editors that explains tricky clues, answers and more about the New York Times Crossword. That one word Rachel, Deb Amlen or Caitlin Lovinger provides there may be the key you need to unlock the rest of your puzzle. And they’re great at explaining what certain crossword clues are asking you to do, or how they might trick you.
Now that you have some tools under your belt, let’s solve the Monday from March 21, 2022 together:
Your first crossword puzzle can be daunting, but let’s go through it together. Have some fun! Jackie went through all of the Across clues quickly and filled in what she knew off the top of her head.
Take some time to get comfortable with solving Monday puzzles, and don’t be afraid to use the tools we mentioned above. “The more you solve, the better you get and the quicker you are with these things — but just trust yourself; you’re going to get further than you think you will,” Sam Ezersky, a digital puzzles editor, said. “And when you keep coming back to these Monday puzzles, you’re going to continue to make more progress.”
For extra homework, read Deb’s guide on “How to Solve the New York Times Crossword.” It’s filled with tips, tricks and definitions of crossword lingo. We didn’t say this would be easy!
Here are five Mondays Rachel Fabi, Wordplay columnist, recommends:
So you’re ready for Tuesday
Honestly, Tuesdays aren’t that much harder than Mondays. A big lesson to learn is to make your solving experience your own. Some hard-core puzzlers may consider using autocheck or Google to be cheating, but at the end of the day, you should solve the puzzle in the way that’s most comfortable for you. Google a word or answer if you don’t know it. You might learn something new and use that piece of information in a future puzzle.
The beauty of a crossword puzzle is that you won’t know all the answers. That’s the fun part! It’s a learning game. But you will be surprised by how much you do know. And if you’re stuck, don’t be afraid to take a break. “You have to set it down and come back to it,” Sam said. “I will boldly say that every time you set this thing down and you come back to it an hour later, you are absolutely going to see something that you didn’t see prior.”
Another tip to help you crack open a puzzle is knowing a few things about clues. First, clues and their answers must always match. A plural clue will have a plural answer, a clue in another language will have an answer in the same language, the parts of speech will always be the same and the tenses will match. As well, clues with initials or abbreviations in them will always have initialed or abbreviated answers, so the answer to “J. Lo’s former partner” will be AROD, and not ALEX RODRIGUEZ, but there’s an exception for abbreviations used for the sake of brevity — U.S., V.I.P. or M.L.B., for example.
And by now, you may have noticed that Mondays and Tuesdays always contain a theme. It’s possible to solve the daily without figuring out the theme, but Rachel suggests always identifying the theme if possible. “It’s so much more satisfying when you figure it out early and then use that to predict what’s coming,” she said. The theme can give you an extra hint if you haven’t figured out other long answers in the grid.
We’ll expand more on the concept of themes and themeless puzzles in part 2. But first, try solving Tuesdays until you feel ready for another challenge.
