title: Which NFL win total projections are too low, too high or just right?
raw_text:
Week 1 for the 2026 NFL season is looming. In just over two weeks, on Sept. 9, a Super Bowl rematch between the champion Seattle Seahawks and runner-up New England Patriots kicks things off.
Does either team have what it takes to return to the big game at Los Angeles’ SoFi Stadium on Feb. 14?
Regular-season team win projections from The Athletic’s Austin Mock say they both have a chance. Mock’s model, which calculates an expected win total for every team, predicts the Seahawks to earn 10.8 wins in 2026 and the Patriots 10.3. Do our NFL beat writers think the projections for those teams are too high, too low or just right?
Read below for analysis of all 32 NFL teams and check out Mock’s full NFC and AFC projections as well.
Arizona Cardinals
Projected wins: 4.4
Verdict: Just right
Here’s the thing: The Cardinals should be more competitive than people expect. This team — with Trey McBride, Jeremiyah Love, Michael Wilson and Marvin Harrison Jr. — has offensive potential. QB Jacoby Brissett has been solid. First-year coach Mike LaFleur has been impressive. It’s just … everything else. Will the line — which has already lost rookie guard Chase Bisontis with a knee injury — hold up? Can the defense stop anybody? If everything goes right, six wins, even with a difficult schedule, would not be shocking. But that’s probably wishful thinking. — Doug Haller
Atlanta Falcons
Projected wins: 7.1
Verdict: Too high
It’s been a tough summer for the Falcons. One quarterback, Michael Penix Jr., was only cleared for full practice availability this week. The other quarterback, Tua Tagovailoa, has not looked great. Last year’s No. 15 pick, edge Jalon Walker, was lost for the season due to an ACL tear. Last year’s No. 26 pick, edge rusher James Pearce Jr., was suspended for the first eight games after violating the personal conduct policy. There are new sheriffs in town — president of football Matt Ryan, general manager Ian Cunningham and head coach Kevin Stefanski — but it’s going to take them a while to clean up these streets. — Josh Kendall
Baltimore Ravens
Projected wins: 10.9
Verdict: Just right
There’s a lot of volatility with the Ravens this year because of the new coaching staff. However, this we do know: Jesse Minter has had a really good defense just about everywhere he’s been and Lamar Jackson has been the league MVP in the first year of his last two offensive coordinators. The Ravens, at least now, are pretty healthy and have a forgiving schedule to start the season. A number of factors point to a Baltimore bounce-back. — Jeff Zrebiec
Buffalo Bills
Projected wins: 10.7
Verdict: Just right
There is one simple and undeniable fact in Buffalo: As long as quarterback Josh Allen is healthy enough to play for the entire season — which he has every year since 2019 — it’s hard to envision the wheels totally falling off. The difference this year is there are a lot more variables. By firing Sean McDermott and promoting Joe Brady to head coach, the Bills believe they have raised their ceiling. But with a rookie head coach figuring it out on the fly, the floor may be much lower. They have a brand-new defensive scheme and a first-time NFL defensive coordinator in Jim Leonhard, another variable. That’s why 10.7 wins feels on the nose, as you could easily make the argument for slightly higher or lower. — Joe Buscaglia
Carolina Panthers
Projected wins: 6.7
Verdict: Too low
I picked the Panthers to go 9-8 when schedules were released in May. But since then they’ve lost outside linebacker Nic Scourton for the season and right tackle Taylor Moton for a chunk of it, meaning the Panthers will enter Week 1 with new starters at both tackle spots, including rookie Monroe Freeling. That said, the defense will be better with the additions of Jaelan Phillips and Devin Lloyd and the Panthers play in the NFC South. So while 6.7 might be a tad low, there’s a real chance an eight-win team claims the division again. — Joseph Person
Chicago Bears
Projected wins: 9.6
Verdict: Just right
Injuries in camp may have tempered fans from making Super Bowl plans, with safety Coby Bryant out four to six months and the Bears still lacking clarity on nickel corner Kyler Gordon. They are probably another playoff appearance away from being in the upper echelon of Super Bowl contenders. The Ben Johnson-Caleb Williams duo with this offensive line and skill players has raised the floor in Chicago. Winning fewer than eight games seems unlikely. The defensive questions — from health to pass rush — lower the ceiling, though. — Kevin Fishbain
Cincinnati Bengals
Projected wins: 10.3
Verdict: Too low
The Bengals are currently favored in 15 of 17 games. In the last 16 games Joe Burrow started as a favorite, the Bengals are 13-3. Their defense looks dramatically more reliable with quality veterans now plastered across the roster. The hedge here is on Burrow’s health and that’s always a notable variable. They also paid $6 million to Joe Flacco to mitigate it. It’s hard to imagine a full season of Burrow complemented by a steady defense falling below 11 wins. — Paul Dehner Jr.
Cleveland Browns
Projected wins: 5.3
Verdict: Too high
For the Browns, 2026 is all about continuing to develop and evaluate a talented young corps. The quarterback play will almost certainly be dreadful, and the brand-new offensive line will need time to catch up. There’s little proven depth at any spot and six of the first nine games are on the road. The defense is still strong, but the focus is rightly on the future and the real goal should be a top-three draft pick. — Zac Jackson
Dallas Cowboys
Projected wins: 9.2
Verdict: Just right
If Dallas stays healthy, this should be a 10-win team competing for an NFC East title with the Philadelphia Eagles. The offense is loaded and the defense is showing signs that it could be significantly better in Christian Parker’s first season as defensive coordinator. But the offense would take a notable step back if franchise QB Dak Prescott or leading rusher Javonte Williams suffered a significant injury. That group probably has to be elite for Dallas to top the nine-win mark. — Jon Machota
Denver Broncos
Projected wins: 9.1
Verdict: Too low
The Broncos aren’t going 11-2 in one-score games like they did last season. History says regression in close games is coming, making it hard to envision them winning 14 games again. But the Broncos may be even deeper defensively than the units that led the NFL in sacks in each of the past two seasons. Offensively, they added Jaylen Waddle to bring a new element to the passing game, and new play-caller Davis Webb should help Bo Nix take a step forward in Year 3. There is too much talent on this well-coached roster to see Denver losing eight times this season. — Nick Kosmider
Detroit Lions
Projected wins: 10.2
Verdict: Just right
The Lions should greatly benefit from a schedule that ranks as the fourth easiest in the league, per Mock’s model. While there are major questions in the secondary and the offense will be without starting center Cade Mays until October, the Lions believe they’re better equipped to handle unexpected challenges this year. They have a new offensive coordinator in Drew Petzing, a younger and more athletic offensive line, a deeper defensive line rotation and return one of the league’s most talented rosters. Detroit’s projected win total of 10.2 wins is tied for the fourth-most in the NFC and leads the NFC North. Some things need to come together, and this division is one of the most competitive in football, but it’s certainly on the table for this group. — Colton Pouncy
Green Bay Packers
Projected wins: 9.7
Verdict: Just right
Until the Packers’ group of unproven edge rushers proves me wrong, I don’t think it’ll be able to adequately withstand the absence of Micah Parsons — however long that may be. Can Jordan Love will this team to a couple shootout wins? Sure, but there are also several questions along the offensive line that could prevent the Packers from getting over the No. 7 seed hump. Sustained health for tight end Tucker Kraft, right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele and Parsons later in the season will be paramount. — Matt Schneidman
Houston Texans
Projected wins: 9.8
Verdict: Too low
The way C.J. Stroud wilted in the playoffs last winter leaves a bad taste, but the Texans remain in good shape and could match last year’s 12-5 record. As crazy as it sounds, their already dominant defense should be even better this year thanks to additions in free agency and the draft. An overhaul of the offensive line, key additions at running back (David Montgomery) and tight end (Foster Moreau and Marlin Klein) check off key needs. The table is set. Houston just needs Stroud to take care of the football and facilitate. If Year 2 in Nick Caley’s system can produce the necessary growth, Stroud and the Texans should again contend for the AFC South title and have a shot at a deep playoff run. — Mike Jones
Indianapolis Colts
Projected wins: 8.2
Verdict: Just right
Part of me wants to stamp the Colts as a 10-win team, especially after they started 8-2 last year with a healthy Daniel Jones. But the other part of me knows Jones — who looks great amid his right Achilles rehab — has a lengthy injury history. He hasn’t played a full season since 2022, which makes me hesitant to bank on him in 2026. But even beyond Jones, the Colts’ revamped defense doesn’t have enough juice at pass rusher for me to think they can climb out of the cycle of mediocrity they’ve been in amid a five-year playoff drought. — James Boyd
Jacksonville Jaguars
Projected wins: 9.0
Verdict: Too low
The Jaguars have a brutal schedule and lost Devin Lloyd and Travis Etienne in free agency, so the projected regression is understandable. But the energy in Jacksonville is incredible this summer, and it’s more than reasonable to expect Trevor Lawrence and the offense to make another jump. Remember, the Jags won 13 games last season without scratching the surface with Brian Thomas Jr. and Travis Hunter — their last two first-round picks — so the Jags can get a lot more explosive with that pair. — Jeff Howe
Kansas City Chiefs
Projected wins: 9.6
Verdict: Just right
I’ve had the Chiefs somewhere around 11 wins for a while, but their razor-thin depth at offensive line and wide receiver also lowers the potential floor here. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes should be back in Week 1 from his December knee surgery, though, and Kansas City won’t go 1-9 again in one-score games as it did in 2025. The Chiefs competing for an AFC West title somewhere around 10-7 seems like a reasonable expectation to me. — Jesse Newell
Las Vegas Raiders
Projected wins: 6.2
Verdict: Just right
The Raiders will be better this year, because how could they not be? But that doesn’t mean they’ll make a huge leap in wins after going 3-14 last season. Playing in the AFC West is hard enough already, and Las Vegas also drew the NFC West and AFC East as cross-division matchups this year. It has nine games against playoff teams from last year as a result. Beating the other last-place AFC teams from last year seems reasonable, as do wins against some other lesser opponents. But exceeding six wins will be a difficult feat. — Sam Warren
Los Angeles Chargers
Projected wins: 9.4
Verdict: Too low
Jim Harbaugh has won 11 games in each of his first two seasons as Chargers coach. That included 2025, when he lost both starting tackles and was forced to play almost 30 different offensive line combinations because of injuries. Harbaugh has set a pretty clear floor in Los Angeles. The offense will be markedly improved with new coordinator Mike McDaniel calling plays. Even with a very tough schedule, I think the Chargers will get to double-digit wins. Harbaugh has earned that benefit of the doubt. — Daniel Popper
Los Angeles Rams
Projected wins: 11.6
Verdict: Just right
The Rams have been Super Bowl favorites nearly everywhere since the blockbuster trade to acquire Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett followed up another blockbuster to land All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie. It makes sense, then, that they’d have the top projected wins number in a model like this. The team does have risk in its depth at quarterback, offensive line and wide receiver, and it has to show improvement on special teams. The NFC West is also a gauntlet. But this team won 12 games a year ago and then added McDuffie, Garrett and cornerback Jaylen Watson while bringing back every other starter. This seems like the right target. — Nate Atkins
Miami Dolphins
Projected wins: 4.5
Verdict: Too low
I can absolutely see a world in which the Dolphins win three games and “earn” the No. 1 pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. No team in history has ever been more burdened by dead cap, so winning more than four games with those constraints should feel like a coup for new coach Jeff Hafley. But I think it’s doable. The offensive line might kick … butt, and Hafley is a good enough defensive mind to coax a better than expected year out of the defense. If quarterback Malik Willis plays as well as he did last year in Green Bay, sure, put the Dolphins down for a five-win season. — Jim Ayello
Minnesota Vikings
Projected wins: 8.7
Verdict: Just right
You can make reasonable arguments on both sides of this one. On the positive end, the Vikings present upside. Quarterback Kyler Murray’s floor should far exceed the play from 2025, and his dual-threat ability could further unlock advantages. Additionally, the Vikings revamped their run game with the hiring of assistant head coach Frank Smith (and promotion of offensive line coach Keith Carter). Increase the offensive output, and Minnesota could vie for the NFC North. A negative view is valid, too. The Vikings’ defense is banking heavily on defensive coordinator Brian Flores, the scheme’s ability to create chaos and a bevy of young players at all spots. Take a step back defensively — and suffer injuries on the offensive line or at quarterback — and the Vikings could find themselves in a rough spot. — Alec Lewis
New England Patriots
Projected wins: 10.3
Verdict: Just right
Plenty of betting markets list 9.5 as the Patriots’ win total, a number that has seemed too low all offseason. The offense was already one of the best in the league and, at least on paper, got significantly better with the additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. With a tougher schedule, the Patriots probably won’t match last season’s 14 wins. But I’ve waffled between predicting 10 or 11 wins this season. — Chad Graff
New Orleans Saints
Projected wins: 7.8
Verdict: Just right
Could I see the Saints surprising some folks and pulling off 10 wins? Sure! But does 8-9 or 9-8 feel more like it? Probably. New Orleans could be staring at 0-2 after opening the season with road games at Detroit and Baltimore. Stealing a win against either team could go a long way in the Saints surpassing the eight-win mark — and in the NFC South, eight victories might win the division (and it will if these projections stand firm). — Larry Holder
New York Giants
Projected wins: 7.1
Verdict: Just right
This may seem like a disappointment in John Harbaugh’s first season, but there needs to be an understanding of the situation the Super Bowl champion coach inherited. The Giants have won seven games combined over the past two seasons. Second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart’s play is the variable that could swing the win total dramatically in either direction. But with some growing pains expected and a defense that features questions around a potentially dominant pass rush, seven wins feels right. — Dan Duggan
New York Jets
Projected wins: 5.6
Verdict: Just right
It’s hard to argue with this projection. The Jets won three games last season and arguably opened the season with more talent (on paper, at least) on defense. By midseason, they had traded away two of their best players and had one of the worst defensive seasons in team history. They worked to raise the floor of the defense by adding veterans Demario Davis, Minkah Fitzpatrick, David Onyemata and talented young players like T’Vondre Sweat and rookie David Bailey. But the ceiling still isn’t especially high and they’ll be riding the Geno Smith roller coaster on offense. Five-to-seven wins sounds like the right range. — Zack Rosenblatt
Philadelphia Eagles
Projected wins: 10.4
Verdict: Just right
The Eagles won at least 11 games in each of the past four seasons. Their defense should be one of the best in the NFL, raising Philadelphia’s floor and making another double-digit win season a strong possibility. The ceiling will be determined by the offense, which is undergoing the most dramatic scheme change in the six seasons of the Nick Sirianni-Jalen Hurts partnership. If the offense adjusts quickly and the running game is reinvigorated with a healthy offensive line and Saquon Barkley in the new system, this will hit the over — and perhaps even easily. If the Eagles experience growing pains and the passing game cannot evolve while the A.J. Brown trade leaves a void, then pushing beyond this total could be more challenging than in previous seasons. — Zach Berman
Pittsburgh Steelers
Projected wins: 8.4
Verdict: Too low
It feels like every year at this time, oddsmakers are predicting the Steelers’ first losing season since 2003 — and every year, they find a way to get to nine or 10 wins. The roster is improved and so too should be the play callers (defensive coordinator Patrick Graham and head coach Mike McCarthy). But the schedule is also tougher and the Steelers can’t count on both MVP-candidate QBs in their division being injured again. Ultimately, three factors will determine how McCarthy’s first season unfolds: How close to dominant can the young offensive line be after years of early-round investment? Can Graham get the NFL’s highest-paid defense to play up to its collective cap hit? And more than anything, can Aaron Rodgers deliver vintage moments at clutch times? I’d put the over/under at 8.7, rounding up to a nine-win season. — Mike DeFabo
San Francisco 49ers
Projected wins: 10.2
Verdict: Just right
The 49ers made a couple of nice pickups this offseason in Mike Evans and Osa Odighizuwa, and De’Zhaun Stribling and the rookie class have been showing out at training camp and in the preseason games. And while we liked the initial over-under of 9.5 wins, we can’t get too much higher than 10 because injuries just won’t stop. The 49ers were ravaged by injuries last season, and this camp has been no different. Nick Bosa and Mykel Williams still haven’t practiced and running backs have had a revolving door to the trainer’s room, while the loss of receiver Ricky Pearsall was cushioned by the availability of old friend Deebo Samuel. The pass rush is still a big question, while on the other side of the trenches, left guard is a four-man battle of not very exciting options. That’s not ideal when you face the Seahawks and Rams twice each. — Vic Tafur
Seattle Seahawks
Projected wins: 10.8
Verdict: Just right
The Seahawks won 14 games last season, capped it off with a Super Bowl victory and are returning a large portion of their roster. Assuming good health, they should be a contender again but 10.8 wins — third-highest in the NFL — feels like it’s just right, teetering on being too high. Will Sam Darnold’s revival continue now that the league has a year of tape on him in Seattle? How will the offense adjust without Klint Kubiak and Kenneth Walker III? The schedule does no favors, either. The Seahawks play in a tough NFC West, with four games against the Rams and 49ers. They also play a first-place schedule, which includes both teams (Patriots and Broncos) that made the AFC Championship Game last season, plus the Eagles and the Bears, among other tough opponents. — Saad Yousuf
Tampa Bay Buccaneers
Projected wins: 8.0
Verdict: Too low
The Bucs are capable of winning more games than they did one year ago, when they were 8-9 in a season when everything that could have gone wrong did. The Bucs won 10 games two years ago and are capable of a similar win total in 2026, especially considering the mediocre state of the NFC South. For them to exceed eight wins, they will need impact from rookie edge rusher Rueben Bain Jr., effective game planning and play calling from new offensive coordinator Zac Robinson, and better health. Having a motivated and slightly perturbed Baker Mayfield won’t hurt. — Dan Pompei
Tennessee Titans
Projected wins: 5.8
Verdict: Just right
If the Titans can round that up to six wins, they’ll match their combined total for the 2024 and 2025 seasons. So yes, they can be pretty bad this season and still demonstrate progress. That’s how rough it has been, and how certain a fifth straight losing season for the franchise appears to be. If Robert Saleh can bring a certain level of stability, and defense, and the Titans can get in the six- to seven-win range and see clear growth from 2025 No. 1 pick Cam Ward, it would be the best Titans season since Mike Vrabel and A.J. Brown were doing their thing together in Nashville. If it’s another fall of vying for the No. 1 draft pick, and Ward doesn’t take a significant step forward, that’s certainly not how owner Amy Adams Strunk wants to open her new stadium in 2027. — Joe Rexrode
Washington Commanders
Projected wins: 7.6
Verdict: Too high
It’s amazing how one or two people can influence a season. Before losing Pro Bowl left tackle Laremy Tunsil, I would’ve pegged the Commanders as a potential nine- or 10-win team. They bolstered their receiving corps with the addition of Stefon Diggs, invested heavily in their defensive line and changed their systems to create more balance on offense and become more multiple on defense. But this team will go where quarterback Jayden Daniels goes, and Daniels may not be able to go far behind this line. There is no plug-and-play replacement for one of the game’s best pass-blocking tackles. Combined with the injury concerns of center Nick Allegretti, the up-and-down play of left guard Chris Paul and the line’s general lack of depth, Daniels could be running from pressure more than he’s running the Commanders’ new offense. — Nicki Jhabvala

title: Dream dominate Valkyries to force Game 7 in 2026 WNBA Finals: Live updates, reaction
raw_text:
live
Updated
Dream dominate Valkyries to force Game 7 in 2026 WNBA Finals: Live updates, reaction
Dream win to force Game 7 in 2026 WNBA Finals – Reaction
The Atlanta Dream have forced a Game 7 in the 2026 WNBA Finals, defeating the Golden State Valkyries 80-69 in a Game 6 matinee affair at State Farm Arena.
Allisha Gray and Rhyne Howard combined for 45 points in Atlanta's Game 6 win while Angel Reese added 15 points, 14 rebounds, six assists and two made 3s. Overall, Atlanta shot 13-of-30 from deep compared to just 7-of-27 by Golden State. Gabby Williams put forth a valiant effort for the Valkyries though, dropping 26 points in the loss.
Game 7 is set for Saturday night at 8 p.m. ET in San Francisco.
- Sound off with your thoughts in the game chat or email us: live@theathletic.com
Gray: We have another gear
Allisha Gray spoke after scoring 23 points for the Atlanta Dream in Game 6:
💬 "I was locked in, defensively. When I play well defensively my offense also gets flowing. I did not want to go home.
"We celebrated each other today. But it's not done, we still have to win one more.
"We played well tonight, but we still have another gear for Game 7."
Game of two halves from Williams
Gabby Williams had just 4 points at the end of the first half, but she came out firing in the second. The 30-year-old ended the game on 26!
Here is the view inside State Farm Arena just moments after the Dream won Game 6 to force a winner-take-all Game 7 on Saturday night in San Francisco.
THE @ATLANTADREAM FORCE A GAME 7 🅰️
The Dream defeat the Valkyries in Game 6, 80-69. This will be the first Game 7 in WNBA Finals history!
Allisha Gray: 23 PTS | 6 REB | 5 3PM | 3 AST | 3 BLK | 2 STL
Rhyne Howard: 21 PTS | 4 3PM | 4 REB | 4 AST
Angel Reese: 15 PTS | 14 REB | 6… pic.twitter.com/dHuBhetRiy
Reese: We grabbed our opportunity
Atlanta Dream star Angel Reese spoke on the court after her side forced a Game 7 in the WNBA finals:
💬 "Every time we've thrown the first punch we've won the game, so we wanted to come out strong early.
"I'm so proud of Allisha [Gray] and Rhyne [Howard]. We wouldn't have won without them today.
"Championship mentality. We just needed an opportunity and we grabbed it today."
Atlanta almost pulled an Atlanta, but they hold on to force a Game 7.
Everybody out!
Y'all don't gotta go home but you can't stay here.
Naz Hillmon leading the postgame huddle in the middle of the court as the crowd chants "Dream in 7"
Dream hang on, win 80-69 to force Game 7. Also, everyone here has 69 minutes to vacate the arena.
FULL TIME: We're heading to Game 7!
Dream 80, Valkyries 69 - Final
What a win for Atlanta at the State Farm Arena. That electric first quarter really set the pace for the Dream, and they have forced a Game 7 in the WNBA finals. 23 points on the day for Allisha Gray, 20 for Rhyne Howard, and even two fabled Angel Reese three-pointers!
As for Golden State, the pressure is on them now as they host the series decider. They made too many mistakes today and passed up on too many easy opportunities, and despite the best efforts of Gabby Williams, they could not complete the comeback.
Dream 80, Valkyries 69 - Q4 0:56.0
What a moment there for Allisha Gray, she sinks another three-pointer to calm Atlanta's nerves.
Amihere was out of the rotation the last couple of games, but she's been excellent in Game 6, a plus-14 in a game the Valkyries trail by 11.
Dream burned their challenge and now can't overturn this phantom sixth foul on Rhyne Howard.
Dream 77, Valkyries 69 - Q4 1:15
Surely not?! Another two points from a Gabby Williams layup and subsequent free throw and the Dream's lead is down to just 8.
Also, they lost the challenge. Ls all around.
Dream 77, Valkyries 64 - Q4 1:56
Don't love this challenge by the Dream. Looks like Reese may have hooked Amihere's arm. Even if Atlanta wins it, it's Golden State ball, and the Valkyries can try to shoot a 3 rather than have Amihere shooting free throws.
Dream 75, Valkyries 64 - Q4 2:36
Remember when I said too little, too late... Well the deficit is now 11. Amihere just missed a free throw though. Add that to the one Williams missed earlier in the quarter, and they could be even closer.
The one thing Atlanta can't do is foul Golden State 90 feet from the basket when the Valkyries are in the bonus. Also, they just did that.
Dream 74, Valkyries 61 - Q4 3:32
It's Gabby Williams again, another three-pointer! She has scored the Valkyries' last ten points and they have got the deficit down to 13. Still too little, too late, though.
A little tangle between Howard and Williams on the ground after Howard fouled Williams' layup attempt. Just holding your breath that nobody gets hurt before Saturday.

title: 2026 Elections Live Updates: Tensions Rise in Alaska Senate Race as Governor Calls for Peltola Campaign Investigation
raw_text:
Midterm Elections Live Updates: Calls for Investigation Ratchet Up Tension in Alaska Senate Race
Republicans are trying to defend vulnerable seats in traditional strongholds including Alaska, where the Democrat’s campaign for Senate faces scrutiny after a New York Times report.
Latest
The head of the House Oversight Committee on Thursday joined Alaska’s governor in calling for an investigation into Democrats’ effort to recruit candidates to draw votes from the state’s Republican incumbent senator. The announcement, by Representative James Comer, Republican of Kentucky, heaped extra attention on a race that could help determine control of the Senate in next week’s midterm elections.
The emergence of the Democrats’ attempts to stack the ballot — a common and generally legal tactic in politics — put Republicans on offense in Alaska, one of several unlikely battlegrounds where the party has spent weeks in a defensive posture because of voter discontent and President Trump’s sagging approval ratings.
The race between Senator Dan S. Sullivan and his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, is one of several competitive Senate contests in conservative strongholds, including South Carolina, where Mr. Trump continued his tour of reliably red regions on Thursday. Mr. Trump, who carried the state by 18 percentage points in 2024, held a rally in support of Senator Darline Graham, who is running even with Dr. Annie Andrews, her Democratic challenger, according to recent New York Times/Siena polling.
In the Alaska race, Republicans had complained for months about the participation of a candidate who shared a first and last name with the incumbent, but the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that no law allowed it to rule on the motives of a candidate. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the Peltola campaign was involved in recruiting the long-shot challenger Dan J. Sullivan in a bid to siphon support from the incumbent.
The report elicited an angry response from Mr. Trump and fellow Republicans — although the ballot-stacking effort was hardly the first to occur on either side of the aisle. On Thursday, Mr. Comer, the head of the House Oversight Committee, formally requested interviews with Elisa Rios, the former campaign manager and longtime aide of Ms. Peltola who was fired amid a staff shake-up in August, and the Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz. That request came hours after Gov. Mike Dunleavy of Alaska, a Republican, suggested that the Democrats’ efforts could warrant criminal charges or civil penalties.
Back on the campaign trail, Mr. Trump and former President Barack Obama will be joined Friday by a third president. Former President Bill Clinton is scheduled to campaign in Mississippi, where Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for Senate, has mounted a strong challenge in a state that last elected a Democrat to the chamber in 1982.
Here’s what else we’re covering:
- Early voting: As of Thursday afternoon, more than 40 million Americans had either gone to vote or mailed in their ballot, according to data collected by the University of Florida’s Election Lab, which tracks early voting.
- Obama on the trail: The closing days of the campaign have seen the return of a Trump foil, Mr. Obama, who is also visiting competitive states. As Mr. Trump bragged in Ohio on Wednesday night about his ability to pass cognitive tests, Mr. Obama assailed him in Atlanta over rising prices and what he described as rampant corruption.
- No show of support: After Representative Haley Stevens lost Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in August, she pledged to campaign with him. But the election is now days away, and the two have not appeared together. Read more ›
The State of Texas is suing elections officials in its largest county over allegations of racially discriminatory election advertisements. The attorney general’s office announced the lawsuit on Thursday, accusing the Harris County Clerk’s Office of targeting its Facebook advertisements to nonwhite voting groups.
Harris County is home to Houston, the state’s largest city and one that votes reliably blue. Ken Paxton, the attorney general, is locked in a tight Senate race with James Talarico. There have been questions over whether Paxton, who has backed voter fraud claims and sued over the 2020 elections results, would challenge the results were he to lose. County officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Paxton’s office said recused himself from the suit because he is on the ballot.
President Trump attacked Black and Jewish supporters of Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan, as “crazy,” stoking tensions between the two communities in Michigan, leaning into a strategy to pit ethnic groups against each other ahead of the midterms.
“If you’re Black or if you’re Jewish, and if you vote for Abdul, you’re crazy, OK? You’re crazy. You’re crazy anyway,” Trump said to applause from at a rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina.
Trump used a similar strategy to some success in 2024 with Jewish Democrats and Arab Americans as he accused Jews who vote for Democrats of hating their religion and Israel, later asserting that “if I don’t win this election,” then “the Jewish people would have a lot to do with a loss.” After his victory, Trump said that Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat and the highest-ranking elected Jewish official in the United States, was “not Jewish anymore” and “a Palestinian, as far as I’m concerned.”
More last-minute ads keep getting booked, and over $1 billion is now slated to air over the final week of the election, according to AdImpact data. Republicans have a slight advantage over that final week by about $34 million in spending. The most expensive races? The Senate races in Ohio and Michigan.
Ken Paxton delivered a roughly five-minute version of his stump speech about an hour before Vice President Vance was scheduled to speak in Texas. Several of Paxton’s usual lines did not elicit much of a response, but he roused the crowd by urging them forward in their opposition to the Democrats. “I’m going to ask you to do exactly what President Trump did after Butler, Pennsylvania, and that is fight, fight, fight to save Texas and America,” Paxton said.
At a venue in Rock Hill, S.C., President Trump rallying support for Senator Darline Graham, who is in a surprisingly tight race against her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician. Republican officials who spoke earlier in the day made similar pleas: Vote Republican on the whole ticket for conservatives and support Graham, even if she wasn’t your first choice.
Graham veered from her typically tame delivery during her speech, describing Andrews as “crazy” while using an expletive. The crowd roared. Trump is now praising Graham while lambasting polls as unreliable.
Trump will no longer travel to Kansas on Saturday for a campaign rally, a person familiar with the plans said. It is unclear why the president is no longer traveling to the state. He is holding a rally in Florida on Friday and in Iowa on Sunday, and officials say he will hold more than 20 telerallies before Tuesday.
Don Huffines, the hard line Republican state comptroller, delivered a harsh warning to the audience at Vance’s event in Weatherford, Texas. “Right now is not going well,” he said of the election. “You need to know that, and you need to be scared, and you need to be concerned,” he said. He said Republicans needed to vote even “if you’re mad at a Republican,” saying he had to “hold my nose” and vote for Republicans he didn’t like in the past, and those in the crowd needed to so the same.
I’m in Weatherford, Texas, where Vice President JD Vance is holding a rally in a construction company warehouse in a deep-red area west of Fort Worth. A short time ago, Ken Paxton, who was expected to speak, waved to the crowd lined up outside and went inside. His potential successor as attorney general, Mayes Middleton, the Republican nominee for the post, spoke early in the event and frequently attacked James Talarico, Paxton’s Democratic opponent — but only mentioned Paxton in passing.
The Trump political operation is doing its first spending in the Kansas Senate race, showing how concerned Republicans are about Senator Roger Marshall’s race. The Trump group No Going Back PAC has reserved about $1.5 million in ads for the race for the final week, joining some other Republican groups that are trying to make sure Marshall doesn’t lose.
Representative James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who leads the House Oversight Committee, is requesting testimony from two Democratic operatives tied to Alaska’s highly competitive Senate race. The committee announced Thursday that he had sent letters to Elisa Rios, the former campaign manager for Mary Peltola, Alaska’s Democratic Senate nominee, and Jerid Kurtz, a Democratic strategist who worked for the campaign.
Vice President JD Vance said that the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska, Mary Peltola, had committed a “moral failing,” regarding a New York Times report that operatives tied to her recruited a candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Senator Dan Sullivan, in an effort to siphon votes from him.
“I think we should certainly look into whether she committed election fraud,” Vance said before traveling to Texas to rally support for Ken Paxton, the Republican running for Senate there. “She is trying to steal a Senate seat from the voters of Alaska, and it’s disgraceful,” Vance added later.
President Trump continued to rant on Thursday about Democrats’ effort to stack the ballot in the Alaska Senate race, a common tactic in politics and generally considered legal. He called the situation “terrible.”
“It’s very unfair,” he told reporters before departing Washington for a campaign rally in South Carolina. “It’s very confusing and meant to be. It’s a fraud.”
The downtown streets of Mason, Mich., yield to vast stretches of open fields, where developers want to build a $1 billion data center a few miles from the farm that Bryan Droscha’s family has owned for more than a century.
He fears that construction could pollute the groundwater and air that his cattle and maple syrup operation, as well as the deer that he hunts, depend on. It’s why, he said, he supports a national pause on new data centers proposed by William Lawrence, the Democratic candidate in his purple congressional district.
But Mr. Droscha, 64, said he wasn’t sure if Mr. Lawrence could deliver on his promises, especially without a Democrat in the White House and with control of Congress unclear. So, he said, he would likely vote again for the familiar candidate, Representative Tom Barrett, a Republican seeking re-election.
“You can say it 100 times a day, every day, but is it going to happen?” Mr. Droscha said last week, before feeding hay to his cows. “That’s the distrust I have.”
The anger toward the data center boom rippling through rural America permeates the front lawns, council meetings and daily conversations in Mason, a mid-Michigan county seat of about 8,300 people where residents view the potential 400-acre project as a serious threat to their groundwater, property values, environment and quality of life.
Their shared backlash has upended local politics, driving emotionally charged public meetings where residents asserted that city officials did not speak openly about the developers’ plans. In exquisite timing, it has also collided with a marquee federal contest, the most expensive House race of the midterms and one that could change the balance of power in Congress.
Even as Mr. Lawrence and Mr. Barrett both oppose the construction of a data center near Mason, their contrasting remedies have managed to divide the community at the rare time neighbors are uniting across party lines.
“It’s the biggest issue for City of Mason voters, absolutely,” said Meg Short, 41, who works in real estate, adding that she wasn’t ready to return the ballot she had marked for Mr. Lawrence and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate. “It’s been hard to choose on the state level who I want to represent me.”
Mr. Lawrence, a progressive who has positioned himself as an anti-corporate outsider, has made reining in tech giants through federal intervention a central pillar of his campaign. On the Republican side, Mr. Barrett has called for repealing state tax incentives for developers but opposes federal action, saying that zoning decisions should remain entirely in local hands.
Some voters around Mason said that Mr. Lawrence’s engagement with the anti-data center community had appealed to them. Zachary Bartels, 48, a conservative who lives about a third of a mile from the proposed data center site, recalled Mr. Lawrence receiving thunderous applause after a speech against data centers in a city council meeting last month.
“He just earned — not even necessarily our vote — but the right to be in the room by being in the room so many times,” said Mr. Bartels, a pastor who has also spoken in recent municipal meetings.
Mr. Bartels said he was undecided about who would receive his vote, even though he had helped elect Mr. Barrett and President Trump. But, Mr. Bartels added, neither House candidate had offered a detailed enough plan on how they could help Mason from Congress.
“I’m kind of going both ways,” he said.
Much like Mr. Bartels, other voters said they were torn. They said they didn’t trust local officials to stop the project. But they were also hesitant to embrace federal regulation or to trust that the progressive candidate, Mr. Lawrence, could make meaningful changes.
They have seen how quickly the nationwide data center surge has suffused Michigan: Favorable tax laws, a cool climate, vast acreages and easy access to water for cooling have made it among the more preferred destinations for artificial intelligence nationwide.
Huge projects have advanced elsewhere in the state, including a $16 billion campus backed by OpenAI and Oracle in Saline Township. Mason-area residents seized on the project’s approval as proof that local governments lacked the legal and financial power to resist big corporations and that state laws favored tech giants over small towns.
The issue flared in Mason late last year, when city officials considered a new zoning ordinance addressing a potential data center. It passed this year, with officials saying they established guardrails, but residents said they were far too weak. The ordinance was later repealed.
Residents also forced a recall vote for a long-serving city councilwoman on the Nov. 3 ballot and began trying to unseat the mayor.
The discussion intensified in August when local landowners working with an Ohio-based developer petitioned the state to annex 400 acres of farmland into the City of Mason to secure municipal water and sewer for a data center, something many residents learned through public-records requests.
City officials have said the data center would bring tax revenues. The Trump administration has also said that the buildup of A.I. infrastructure is necessary to win technological supremacy over China.
A representative for the developer, Comino Development, and the property owners’ lawyer did not respond to requests for comment.
At a city council meeting last week, about 200 residents toting signs, shirts and hats declaring “No Data Centers in Mason” packed City Hall, many of them there to offer public comments before the council voted on a plan for a proposed zoning rewrite. (They ultimately rejected it.)
One resident, Doug DeLind, a sculptor who lives next to the proposed site, took the bold step of suggesting candidates they could support. Partisan divisions surfaced.
When Mr. DeLind said he endorsed Dr. El-Sayed, who has called for a ban on superintelligent A.I. and a cabinet-level agency to regulate the fast-developing industry, someone in the crowd said, “Terrorism.”
“Not terrorism,” Mr. DeLind replied, joining residents recoiling at the baseless accusation leveled at Dr. El-Sayed throughout his campaign that he had ties to terrorist groups.
When Mr. DeLind mentioned Mr. Lawrence’s name, someone said, “Socialist!”
“He is,” Mr. DeLind shot back, drawing applause. “I’m glad we got that out there.”
Mr. Lawrence has let his membership in the Democratic Socialists of America lapse, but still identifies as a progressive. Even with his left-wing platform, he said the issue had given him an opening to talk to conservative voters.
“There are some people that are voting with me on this issue for sure, including people who have been Republican voters in the past who see me standing alongside them,” Mr. Lawrence said in an interview.
For his part, Mr. Barrett said that he did not believe he was losing voters on the data center issue, adding that Mr. Lawrence’s proposal for a federal moratorium was unrealistic.
“Are you going to get enough votes in the U.S. Senate to do that?” he said in an interview. “And then, is President Trump going to sign it, knowing that he’s on record opposing these restrictions?”
Mayor Russell Whipple of Mason, a nonpartisan official, disputed residents’ accusations that he had withheld information about his conversations with data center developers. He said that residents’ fears about the dangers of such a center were exaggerated, adding that the city would establish standards for noise, as well as air and water quality.
But he said he expected the midterms to be “a little more blue” in his city because of Mr. Lawrence’s visibility.
“I had an old newspaperman tell me 30 years ago: He said, ‘In small town elections, the most signs wins,’” Mr. Whipple said. “There’s more Will Lawrence than Tom Barrett signs.”
Eric Pratt, a Republican congressional candidate in Minnesota, uses his campaign website to push the “Pratt Playbook,” a three-point plan to reduce prices, increase accountability and emphasize “common sense.”
But, at least for a brief while, his online pitch to voters also included an unusual passage. “The President is not popular,” it read, “so all messaging should be focused on local politics and needs.”
The odd sentence was a sign that artificial intelligence tools had been used to write parts of his website. A staffer had apparently asked an A.I. chatbot to steer clear of President Trump in its writing. (Mr. Pratt said in a statement posted to Facebook that the passage was “an internal note” and that his campaign had used A.I. tools to “clean up the wording.”)
It was one example among hundreds identified by The New York Times in which candidate biographies and position papers were apparently written with A.I. tools.
A.I. has increasingly seeped into all parts of the nation’s electoral process, rewriting the playbook for how politicians connect with voters. Money-strapped campaigns, eager for shortcuts, have rapidly adopted several A.I. tools, even though many of the candidates have not spoken publicly about their use.
“If it improves the quality of campaign information” for voters seeking information about candidates, “that can be a good thing,” said Lisa Argyle, an associate professor of political science at Purdue University, who studies generative A.I. and political communication. The problem arises when candidates begin prompting A.I. “without really reflecting in a meaningful way on their own views and what they want to do as a representative.”
Chatbots, like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, are capable of writing glistening prose almost instantly, after being provided with a set of simple instructions, called prompts. When producing their own text, they have a tendency to drift toward the most likely writing styles — and often the most predictable or clichéd.
To identify campaign sites produced with A.I., The Times downloaded text from the websites of 695 candidates running for House and Senate. That content was then analyzed by two A.I.-text detectors: Pangram and GPTZero. Both services can make errors and can be fooled if writers significantly rework A.I. generated text. But a 2025 study from the University of Chicago found that with the most common types of online writing, Pangram was accurate more than 99 percent of the time, with GPTZero not far behind.
The detectors found there was high likelihood that 291 candidate websites were written with A.I. tools. One hundred fifty had pages flagged as generated by A.I., while the detectors found the remaining sites were a mix of human and A.I. writing.
The A.I. detectors work by detecting subtle linguistic patterns like character frequency, word order and rhythm — all signs that are often imperceptible to humans and difficult for politicians to replicate by accident. That makes the tools less likely to falsely identify mere clichéd writing, which is common in campaign writing, as A.I.-made.
Many passages across the websites used telltale signs of A.I. writing. The systems, trained on billions of passages of text from across the internet, tend to repeat phrases and writing styles that were eventually identified by A.I. watchdogs.
“The cost of living isn’t just ‘high’,” Stephanie Vargas, a Republican House candidate in California, said on her platform page, which was flagged as A.I.-written by detectors. “It’s being driven up by government spending.”
That kind of passage — a phrase that includes the words “isn’t just,” followed by a phrase beginning with “it’s” — was repeated across dozens of campaign websites flagged as having A.I. text, including these:
- From Ray Pooley, a Democratic House candidate in Michigan: “True strength isn’t just a mighty military. It’s the wisdom to know when to use it.”
- From Patrick Halpin, a Democratic House candidate in New York: “Long Island’s environment isn’t just something we enjoy. It’s what makes this a great place to live.”
The tools identified each of those websites as having been heavily if not entirely written by A.I. tools.
“A.I. has allowed me to be able to run a campaign effectively,” said Dale Pabst, the campaign manager for Mr. Halpin, who is running against Andrew Garbarino, a well-funded Republican incumbent. “It allows us to compete with another campaign that has a 20-time financial advantage over us.” He said that he pulled together Mr. Halpin’s platform webpage in a few days using A.I. tools, instead of a couple of weeks.
The other campaigns did not respond to requests for comment.
While more than 30 states have laws requiring disclosures around A.I.-generated content in campaign ads, such regulations tend to focus on deceptive replicas of candidates, known as “deepfakes.” There are no laws requiring A.I.-written text to be disclosed.
Political operatives have adopted A.I. in a variety of ways this year, seeing the tools as useful for the difficult and monotonous work of campaigning, at least behind the scenes. That includes managing voter databases, writing campaign messages and processing feedback from voters through door-knocking operations nationwide.
Some candidates have also relied on A.I. to help guide their campaigns, turning to chatbots as a cheap form of campaign manager.
But the integration of A.I. in campaigns also threatens to send conflicting messages to voters, especially as lawmakers push for more A.I. regulations and fight plans for enormous data centers that make A.I. possible.
Many of the campaigns flagged for having A.I. text were congressional races with limited funds and long-shot odds. But some had far more resources.
The A.I. detectors found that the online biography for Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate in Texas, was heavily written by A.I. His race is one of the most expensive nonpresidential races in U.S. history, with ad spending surpassing $500 million.
“Ken Paxton is a fearless conservative, a relentless fighter, and a true defender of Texas values,” the site said. Pangram assessed the sentence as “100 percent A.I.,” indicating it was fully written by an A.I. model.
A representative Mr. Paxton’s campaign declined to comment.
The campaign website of James Talarico, Mr. Paxton’s Democratic opponent, was also tested for A.I. writing. It received a score of “100 percent human.”
They are both from storied New Hampshire families (one best known for governing, the other for its famous Manchester restaurant). They are both veterans of Washington. They are both kind of policy nerds.
On Wednesday night, Representative Chris Pappas, a Democrat, and former Senator John E. Sununu, a Republican, clashed in a tense debate at the WMUR television studio in Manchester, fighting over Social Security and the cause of the high cost of living, and seeking to yoke each other to unpopular figures in their respective parties.
Mr. Pappas and Mr. Sununu are running for a seat currently held by the retiring Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat. Both parties view the race as crucial to their hopes of retaking the chamber. Mr. Pappas, who leads in polling, seized opportunities to attack Mr. Sununu and present him as beholden to President Trump — perhaps reflecting a degree of discomfort that Mr. Sununu has been able to keep the race competitive by presenting himself as independent of the unpopular president.
Here are five takeaways from the night.
Neither candidate is new to voters.
Sometimes, a political candidate bursts onto the scene out of nowhere. That is not the story of New Hampshire in 2026.
The Senate race pits Mr. Pappas, an understated, four-term Democrat who has spent much of his adult life in elected office, against Mr. Sununu, a former congressman and one-term senator who won this same seat in 2002 before losing it in 2008. Mr. Sununu is the son and brother of former New Hampshire governors. Mr. Pappas’s family is best known for its popular restaurant, the Puritan Backroom in Manchester.
Mr. Pappas, 46, sought to present himself as a “new generation of leadership.” Mr. Sununu, 62, insisted he could shake things up in Washington after being first elected to Congress 30 years ago.
And each nevertheless accused the other of representing the status quo.
“Chris Pappas talked about all the things he wants to do and wants to accomplish, but he’s been there for eight years, and he hasn’t gotten the job done,” Mr. Sununu said.
“This election is about Team New Hampshire versus Team Trump,” Mr. Pappas said. “Fact is, John Sununu was our senator before and, if he was as effective and as independent as he says he was, then he’d probably still be our senator today. But voters had another idea.”
Both bragged about challenging their own party …
Mr. Sununu’s candidacy depends on his ability to convince voters in New Hampshire — a state that has never really warmed to Mr. Trump — that he is independent of a president who endorsed him early in the race.
So he rattled of a list of his differences with the president: the trade war with Canada, the war in Iran, the $1.8 billion fund Mr. Trump proposed for victims of “weaponization” by the Department of Justice and his now-scuttled plan to televise a military execution.
“When Donald Trump leaves office in two years,” Mr. Sununu asked, “where does the country go?”
What was more surprising, perhaps, was how frequently Mr. Pappas made a point of spelling out his differences with national Democrats like former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.
“I called out Joe Biden when he was president because he let things get out of control on the southern border, and it created a crisis,” Mr. Pappas said. “And I’ve taken on my own party on immigration, and I’ve gotten a lot of flak for it.”
… and working with the other side.
It’s an era of deeply tribal politics, but things are split in New Hampshire. Republicans have total control over state government, while Democrats hold each seat in the federal delegation.
That might be why, in a somewhat retro twist, both candidates were eager to talk about how frequently they reach across the aisle.
Mr. Pappas talked about his support for one bipartisan measure after another: a ban on stock trading by members of Congress, a measure that would provide heating assistance to low-income people, immigration measures and more.
Mr. Sununu said that he had worked with Democrats plenty, and he praised Senator Susan Collins of Maine — another Republican who likes to talk up bipartisanship — as a “model.”
“I even wrote bipartisan legislation with Hillary Clinton to improve auto safety and protect kids,” he said.
Sununu climbed in his Wayback Machine.
Mrs. Clinton wasn’t the only reference Mr. Sununu made that seemed, well, dated.
He talked about demanding changes to the Patriot Act during the presidency of George W. Bush. He said he was the first Republican to call for the firing of Alberto Gonzales, Mr. Bush’s attorney general.
He grew visibly annoyed as he parsed an attack by Mr. Pappas over legislation privatizing Social Security during his term in the Senate.
“That wasn’t my bill, Chris,” Mr. Sununu said. “OK, you can’t ascribe every crazy bill ever introduced in Congress to me. That’s dishonest.”
He also chafed when Mr. Pappas said his net worth had grown to an “estimated” $35 million after he left the Senate.
“Goodness knows, I’m not worth $35 million,” he said, before accusing Mr. Pappas of being unable to read a financial disclosure form, the federally required filings that publish broad ranges for public officials’ assets. “Now, I blame that on the time he spent at Harvard.” (Mr. Sununu attended M.I.T.)
Pappas demurred on impeachment.
Some Democrats are hungry for candidates who want to punish Mr. Trump for what they see as the excesses of his second term — but that’s not the audience Mr. Pappas was playing to.
Asked about the prospect of impeaching Mr. Trump if the Democrats gained a majority in Congress, Mr. Pappas called instead for “focused hearings” and “oversight.”
“We need to stay focused on how we can solve problems, make lives better for Granite Staters and lower costs,” Mr. Pappas said.
Mr. Sununu nevertheless accused him of being too liberal for New Hampshire. He said Mr. Pappas voted too often with former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and knocked him for campaigning alongside former Vice President Kamala Harris and Gov. Gavin Newsom of California.
“I don’t know what Chris’s infatuation is with California, but it’s not New Hampshire, and it’s not a good model for our state,” Mr. Sununu said.
Mr. Pappas reminded him that Ms. Harris won New Hampshire in 2024, and that Mr. Trump had not.
“Here in New Hampshire,” he said, “we welcome out-of-town guests.”
Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan, who lost to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in a bitter Democratic primary for Senate in August, has grown increasingly critical of him as the election draws near, injecting unusual intraparty tensions into the final days of a pivotal midterm contest.
While Ms. Stevens reiterated Wednesday night that she plans to vote for Dr. El-Sayed, she did so through seemingly gritted teeth in a televised interview just hours after her fiancé said that he would be voting for former Representative Mike Rogers, Dr. El-Sayed’s Republican rival. She also called on Dr. El-Sayed to denounce an ad from an outside group that she has argued amounts to “fear-mongering about Israel,” and to take down an ad from his campaign featuring Tucker Carlson.
“Of course, I’m voting for our Democratic nominee for Senate,” Ms. Stevens said on CNN. “I’m voting for the Democratic ticket. But I want to encourage this campaign to shut out the hate and to call it out and to make people who are in my coalition, right — make them feel comfortable about coming to the polls.”
Ms. Stevens’s remarks are an unwelcome development for Dr. El-Sayed in a high-stakes race. It is rare for the loser of a primary who has endorsed the winner to be publicly critical this close to the general election.
It’s not the first time it has happened in this year’s midterms. In Texas, Senator John Cornyn has missed few opportunities to needle Ken Paxton, who beat him for the Republican nomination in May. Mr. Cornyn, however, has not made as many cable news appearances as Ms. Stevens.
Ms. Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, said on CNN that she is representing Jewish Michiganders who supported her and are angry about advertising that they view as antisemitic. The campaign of Dr. El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel, has said it was “not affiliated in any way” with the ad that has come under scrutiny. But Ms. Stevens said that does not go far enough.
“He can disavow these ads, and he can reassure these undecided voters who are still out,” she said.
A spokeswoman for Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign declined to comment on Ms. Stevens’s remarks.
Dr. El-Sayed, speaking to reporters earlier Wednesday, dismissed concerns that Ms. Stevens’s fiancé was backing Mr. Rogers over concerns about Dr. El-Sayed’s Israel policy.
“I’m building a movement to take on the challenges that Donald Trump is facing,” Dr. El-Sayed said. “If folks have issues that are more important to them than that, that’s fine — that’s their choice.”
The public criticism from Ms. Stevens made clear that there has been little private reconciliation between the primary rivals despite her vow to vote for him. While Ms. Stevens couched her public remarks as constructive criticism, she has been more critical of Dr. El-Sayed in private, according to a person who has spoken with her, leaving some allies wondering if she would in fact vote for him.
She said in a text message on Wednesday that she would not appear with Dr. El-Sayed in the campaign’s final week. “I am not campaigning with Abdul,” she wrote.
Ms. Stevens’s criticism of Dr. El-Sayed had been building.
On Sunday, in another CNN interview, she said, “I can’t say that I agree with everything that’s gone on.” She questioned Dr. El-Sayed’s efforts to appeal to Black voters and suggested that he was too focused on foreign policy.
On Wednesday, Ms. Stevens’s fiancé, Jason Turkish, a Jewish Democrat, said he planned to vote for Mr. Rogers, and joined him at an event with the Republican Jewish Coalition in the evening.
“I watched Haley graciously concede an election, and open her arms and her heart to Abdul on Aug. 5, the day after the primary, and I prayed that he would moderate, and he hasn’t,” Mr. Turkish said in an interview.
Mr. Turkish said he was frustrated after Dr. El-Sayed declined to answer a question at an October debate about whether Iran or Israel was a greater threat to the United States. And Mr. Turkish expressed disappointment that the day after the primary, Dr. El-Sayed was joined by another Democratic primary contender, Mallory McMorrow, who finished a distant third after dropping out weeks before the primary, rather than Ms. Stevens at a celebratory news conference in Detroit.
Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign said that its leadership remains in frequent contact with Ms. Stevens and that the congresswoman had campaigned on his behalf at a mid-October Democratic event in Oakland County, which she had carried in the primary. It also said Dr. El-Sayed had brought on several staff members from Ms. Stevens’s campaign after the primary.
Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign said it had also asked Ms. Stevens to campaign alongside him. It did not respond to a question about why that had not happened recently.
“The Abdul campaign is grateful for Congresswoman Stevens’s immediate and sustained support,” Roxie Richner, a spokeswoman for Dr. El-Sayed, said in a statement.
Ms. Stevens’s tepid support — and the awkward dynamic between the two Democrats — is one of the most public points of tension among Democrats in Michigan, who remain far more divided than party leaders had hoped to be going into the election next Tuesday.
Opinion polls show that Dr. El-Sayed and Mr. Rogers are running neck-and-neck in Michigan, a traditional battleground state where a Republican has not won a Senate race in more than three decades. The battle between Dr. El-Sayed and Mr. Rogers could play a critical role in the national fight for Senate control.
Israel remains a dividing line for some Democrats in the state, and Jewish voters say they are torn about whether to support Dr. El-Sayed, who has called Israel’s government “evil.” Dr. El-Sayed is also trying to overcome tensions between Black and Arab American voters in the Detroit area.
Dr. El-Sayed and Ms. Stevens clashed regularly over Israel during the primary race, with Dr. El-Sayed assailing Ms. Stevens over support she received from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a lobbying group. AIPAC is now backing Mr. Rogers.
Lonnie Scott, a Democratic consultant in Michigan, said Ms. Stevens’s recent commentary was not “helpful” and that “Haley should be a team player.” But, he said, Dr. El-Sayed “should be doing more outreach.”
“I don’t place blame on one over the other,” Mr. Scott said.
Representative Debbie Dingell, a Michigan Democrat who stayed publicly neutral in the primary, defended Ms. Stevens.
“I’m sick and tired of people blaming Haley,” Ms. Dingell said.
An earlier version of this article misidentified the Republican who has not made as many cable news appearances as Ms. Stevens. It is Mr. Cornyn, not Mr. Paxton.

Alaska’s governor on Wednesday night said he was ordering an investigation into whether Mary Peltola’s campaign for Senate should face criminal charges or civil penalties over its role in recruiting candidates to draw votes from the state’s Republican incumbent.
The announcement by Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, followed a New York Times report detailing the Peltola campaign’s involvement in recruiting a retiree named Dan J. Sullivan to enter the race against Senator Dan S. Sullivan.
“Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” he said in a post on X. “Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.”
Earlier in the day, President Trump demanded that Ms. Peltola, a Democrat, be removed from the ballot and prosecuted without explaining what crime, if any, was committed.
“They said they didn’t do it, and they did do it, and they got caught,” Mr. Trump told reporters on his way to a rally in Ohio, describing the Democratic effort as “voter fraud at the highest level.”
The secret plan involved senior advisers to both the Peltola campaign and the top campaign committee supporting Senate Democrats. The retiree, who is from a small Alaskan fishing village, was recruited because he shared the Republican incumbent’s first and last name.
Both Sullivans will appear on the ballot on Tuesday alongside Ms. Peltola and a fourth candidate, Gerald Heikes. Mr. Trump called for Daniel J. Sullivan’s removal from the ballot.
Mr. Trump wasn’t the only Republican to object to the plan. But proving that a crime was committed is likely to be difficult. State leaders had tried earlier this year to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, but the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that nothing in state law nor in the U.S. Constitution allowed it to rule on the motives of a candidate.
And the Peltola campaign is hardly the first political committee on either side of the aisle to engage in ballot-stacking.
Many Democrats defended the plan by pointing out how commonplace such actions are. Republicans have employed them in a variety of states, including Alaska.
Some Democrats even said that the intricate plot was a welcome sign that the party was fighting tooth and nail to oppose Mr. Trump’s agenda in what they viewed as an existential election.
Lauren French, a spokeswoman for the Senate Majority PAC, a Democratic group aligned with Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader, posted a series of examples of G.O.P. chicanery on X. Her posts included the instance of a super PAC with Republican ties spending hundreds of thousands of dollars in Alaska to prop up Democratic and Green Party candidates in this year’s Senate primary.
In 2024, the Alaska Republican Party participated in a lawsuit arguing to keep on the ballot a Democratic candidate for the U.S. House who was a federal inmate campaigning from a prison in New York.
Also sharing examples was Chris Meagher, a veteran Democratic strategist who served in the Biden administration.
“The reality is that while it’s maybe an interesting story, this sort of thing is not really new,” he wrote on X.
Ms. Peltola herself appeared to brush off the news at a rally on Wednesday, saying it was “just another distraction.”
A spokesman for Senator Sullivan said in a statement that Ms. Peltola and her campaign “have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along.”
Before The Times published its article, the Trump administration had already filed a lawsuit calling for the Alaska Senate race not to be certified if Senator Sullivan lost. That suit did not, however, allege specific illegal activity. And in a Fox News interview on Wednesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche seemed to concede that laws may not have been broken. “It should be!” he exclaimed when asked if the Democratic plot was illegal.
The lawsuit, filed by the Justice Department last week at Mr. Trump’s direction, is unusual because it preemptively demands an investigation only if the incumbent senator loses. It accuses Daniel J. Sulivan, who has said he voted for Democrats in the last three presidential races and for Ms. Peltola in her 2022 and 2024 congressional campaigns, of trying to “dupe Alaska’s voters into believing that he is Senator Sullivan.”
Chief Judge Sharon Gleason of U.S. District Court in Alaska agreed to a motion by the Alaska elections division to move quickly, giving the Justice Department until Thursday afternoon to respond to a motion to dismiss the case.
She also noted in her rulings that the administration waited to sue until “after Alaskans had already begun casting their ballots for the November 2026 election — and nearly four months after the Alaska Supreme Court directed the Division of Elections to include Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot.”
The Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have asked to join the case, noting that the state election office tried to block Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot before state courts overruled them.
The Trump administration initially opposed that request, but on Wednesday afternoon it lifted its objection, “given a change in circumstances.” The administration cited the Times article detailing what federal lawyers called a “sprawling conspiracy to recruit and prop up a sham candidate for the purpose of deceiving Alaskan voters.”
Scott Kendall, a lawyer in Anchorage who has worked for Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican, and former Gov. Bill Walker, an independent, said the Democratic effort to influence the ballot might amount to a “dirty trick,” but one with a long history in American politics.
“Go back to J.F.K. There’s a long history of this kind of chicanery,” he said, noting that in John F. Kennedy’s first campaign for Congress, his father’s political operation was accused of paying a man to run against a better-known candidate with the same name, splitting the vote in a crowded Democratic primary.
Mr. Kendall, the architect of Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system, said the system could mitigate potential confusion because Republican voters who rank both Sullivans on their ballot are likely to see their vote go eventually to the incumbent senator.
One Alaska Republican not known to embrace the theatrics of the Trump administration also reacted with anger to the news of the Democratic plan.
“While some may try to write this off as just how politics works now, ballot-stacking should have no place in our electoral process,” Ms. Murkowski, a moderate Republican who endorsed Ms. Peltola in her previous campaigns but is supporting Senator Sullivan this year, said in a statement. “Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign — what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception.”
Dan Watson contributed reporting.

title: How Lula Came Back
raw_text:
How Lula Came Back
Maps show where Brazil’s progressive president surged ahead to win re-election.
In a dramatic reversal from the first round of voting, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil was re-elected on Sunday, besting his conservative rival and defying a right-wing wave that has swept through Latin America.
In just three weeks, Mr. Lula found more than 10 million new votes. He gained ground nearly everywhere, attracting vast new support in major cities like São Paulo and in his strongholds across the northeast, according to official results.
Election results by municipality
After a chaotic Election Day, Mr. Lula’s right-wing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, said that he would not accept the results and called for the election to be annulled.
Mr. Bolsonaro led by two percent in the first round of voting, and few pollsters expected Mr. Lula to turn things around. Many candidates who were eliminated endorsed Mr. Bolsonaro, and analysts expected he would pick up most of their votes.
But Mr. Lula reversed what had been a conservative shift, the results show. He reestablished his dominance in small towns. He made gains in working-class suburbs around some of the country’s biggest cities. He appeared to be helped by a broad, unexpected increase in turnout.
Mr. Lula was ahead by about 3.6 percentage points, a wider margin than his victory over Mr. Bolsonaro’s father in 2022. A map of the results shows almost every part of Brazil shifted to the left since the first round of voting:
Shift in margin between first and second round
The results suggested that Mr. Lula managed to overcome weaknesses with working-class voters that gave Mr. Bolsonaro the upper hand in the first round. His administration announced a series of economic measures in recent weeks, including more cash allowances for poor families, a ban on online betting, a program to help families get out of debt, and tax amnesties for small businesses.
In the second round, Mr. Lula amassed an additional 4.6 million votes in São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro, compared with only 1.9 million additional votes for Mr. Bolsonaro. Nearly 40 percent of Brazil’s population lives in these three states, home to some of the country’s biggest cities.
Shift in margin in Brazil’s most populous region
Brazil’s northeast region, Mr. Lula’s birthplace and home to many of the country’s poorest residents, has long been a left-wing stronghold. This region has heavily benefited from Mr. Lula’s social assistance programs.
Shift in margin in the northeast region
Mr. Lula’s rebound in the second round followed a pivot in his campaign strategy to reconnect with low-income and working-class voters, including strong online mobilization that relied heavily on informal messaging through influencers and online communities. A WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” surged from 50,000 to nearly 11 million followers after the first round.
Although the Brazilian economy grew modestly and unemployment fell over the past four years, household debt and a cost-of-living crisis left many working-class families feeling squeezed.
