title: Tracking the Early Vote in the 2026 Midterm Elections
raw_text:
Tracking the Early Vote in the 2026 Midterm Elections
A majority of voters now cast their ballots ahead of Election Day, and we are tracking the returns in key Senate battleground states.
The New York Times is tracking early voting in key Senate battleground states. More than half of all voters now cast their ballots ahead of Election Day, usually in person at a polling location, or by mail. The shift to an “election month” means there are some early indications of overall turnout and hints at enthusiasm among key subgroups.
But there are limits to what early voting can tell us. Each state has its own rules, and those rules can change from election to election. Some states record voters’ age, race or party registration, while others provide almost no demographic data.
We will present as clear a picture as possible of what the data can tell us in each of these battleground states, and how it compares to the general elections in those states in 2022 and 2024. Those elections serve as useful but imperfect comparisons: 2024 may be more similar in process, but 2022, the most recent midterm election, is expected to be closer in overall turnout.
We will continually update these trackers between now and Election Day, with states added as they begin reporting information.
Most of the recent polls in Texas show James Talarico, a state representative, running even with or ahead of Ken Paxton, the state’s Republican attorney general. Mr. Paxton, running with President Trump’s endorsement, trounced the incumbent, Senator John Cornyn, in a primary runoff earlier this year.
Still, a Democratic victory would be no small feat in a state that Mr. Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024.
Millions of Texas voters have cast their ballots since early in-person voting began in the state on Oct. 19, though it’s still fairly early. Like several other Southern states, a large majority of Texans — 68 percent in 2022, and 80 percent in 2024 — cast their ballots before Election Day, making early votes more representative of the final totals than they might be in other states.
While Texas does not include information on voters’ race or party registration, it does report its election results by vote method — in 2022 and 2024, early in-person voting was slightly more Democratic than the state as a whole.
The state’s turnout more closely resembles a presidential year than a midterm thus far, with turnout in the state’s Hispanic areas running particularly high — through the end of Saturday, majority-Hispanic areas were running at around 90 percent of their 2024 pace, compared to 82 percent statewide. (Midterms often see a much starker decrease in turnout.)
In order to retake the majority in the Senate, Democrats need a net gain of four seats, while holding their current ones. Georgia, a battleground state won by Joseph R. Biden in 2020 and President Trump in 2024, is one of the Senate seats they need to defend, and polls show Senator Jon Ossoff, the incumbent Democrat, with an advantage over Representative Mike Collins.
As recent elections in Georgia have demonstrated, however, early voting patterns can be unpredictable. In 2022, a Democratic advantage in the advance vote was enough to overcome a wide Republican lead on Election Day. Two years later, Republicans narrowly won early in-person votes, carrying the state even as their Election Day margin shrank.
The share of Georgia’s early in-person votes increased substantially in 2024, a similar pattern to other states that year. If that holds true this year, advance turnout could surpass the 2022 midterms. (The early in-person voting period is one day shorter this year than it was in 2022.)
Georgia is one of a handful of states that records voters’ race, and advance turnout by race has been relatively consistent between cycles. Around 30 percent of registered voters in the state are Black, and turnout among this strongly Democratic-leaning subgroup is key. Thus far, the share of Black voters is slightly ahead of 2022 and 2024.
Even these comparisons can be unwise, however. In 2022, Election Day saw a slightly smaller share of Black voters, while the inverse was true in 2024.
While voters in Georgia do not register with a political party, which makes it harder to discern the partisan makeup of the early vote, the state does record voters’ participation in party primaries. This vote history can be helpful for determining the breakdown of the electorate, though votes in a party primary, like party registration, can be a poor predictor of the final result.
Polls have indicated that Democrats are best positioned to flip a Senate seat in North Carolina, where Roy Cooper, the former Democratic governor, has consistently led Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee.
North Carolina was the first state to send mail-in ballots to voters, and began early in-person voting on Oct. 15. The state’s mail ballots tend to be disproportionately Democratic, and fairly unrepresentative — making up around 5 percent of all votes cast in recent cycles — while early in-person voting has surged in popularity, rising from 53 percent of the state’s votes in 2022 to 74 percent in 2024.
While Democrats had a large advantage in the Senate race in votes cast before Election Day in 2022, Donald Trump narrowly won the advance vote in the 2024 presidential race, as early in-person voting surged.
In the end, changes in the advance vote made little difference — Republicans won both races by virtually identical margins.
While mail ballot returns lag 2022, in which voting patterns may have still been influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic, overall turnout in North Carolina is meaningfully higher thus far.
Registered Democrats are currently making up a larger share of the vote in North Carolina than they did at this point in either 2022 or 2024, though in both years, the Democratic share of the early electorate decreased somewhat as Election Day neared.
A key demographic to watch is Black voters, who make up around 20 percent of registered voters in the state. (Like Georgia, North Carolina is one of a handful of states that includes race in its voter files.)
The share of Black voters spiked as in-person early voting began this year — a similar pattern to Georgia — and is currently outpacing 2022 and 2024.
Alaska has become an unlikely political epicenter this cycle. Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, is facing an unusually strong challenge from Mary Peltola, the only Alaskan Democrat elected to Congress since 2008, who narrowly lost her House seat two years ago. Ms. Peltola placed first in the state’s August primary, in which the top four vote-getters advanced to the general election regardless of party affiliation.
Most Alaskans cast their ballots on Election Day, though which party benefits from each voting method tends to vary. In general, Democrats tend to fare better with mail-in votes, and Republicans with Election Day votes. But the pattern varies significantly between urban and rural communities. (Many of Alaska’s rural areas are Democratic-leaning, an increasing rarity in modern politics.)
Roughly two-thirds of Alaskans are not registered with either major party, making the breakdown of votes by party registration less useful than in other states. Success for any statewide candidate depends on their ability to appeal to this swath of unaffiliated voters.
The full picture of results this year may not be known for weeks afterward, especially if the contest heads to ranked-choice tabulation, which would take place on Nov. 18. Why the delay? Alaska, a sprawling rural state, allows absentee ballots to be counted if they are postmarked on Election Day and received up to 15 days afterward. In many cases, these ballots are flown in from isolated, otherwise inaccessible localities.
In Iowa, where Senator Joni Ernst is retiring, Republicans are trying to hold her seat in a state President Trump won by wide margins in each of his three presidential campaigns. Recent polls have shown Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican, in a tight race with Josh Turek, a state representative.
Early in-person voting began on Oct. 14, though the majority of Iowa voters cast their ballots on Election Day, making trends in the early vote less informative. Still, the pattern of support across vote methods is a familiar one: Democrats tend to fare better in advance votes, while Republicans surge on Election Day. In 2024, as the share of early votes in the state increased, the Democratic advantage among those votes shrunk substantially, a trend mirrored by several other states that cycle.
(Unlike some other states, Iowa combines its mail and in-person absentee votes, and reports them as one method.)
At the moment, the votes cast in Iowa are predominantly made up of registered Democrats, with a slightly higher share than was seen at this point in 2024. Just a fraction of the state’s voters have cast a ballot, though, and it’s unclear which direction it might go from here — the partisan makeup of Iowa’s early votes got slightly bluer over time in 2022, and redder in 2024.
In Michigan, the Democratic Party’s left wing faces a rare test in a key battleground state, as Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, takes on Mike Rogers, a former Republican congressman who was his party’s nominee for Senate in 2024.
Michigan does not have party registration, and not every county reports its results by vote method. In the counties that do report that way, Democrats fared worse in 2024 with in-person votes, and far better with mail ballots. For instance, Mr. Rogers won Kent County’s Election Day and early in-person votes two years ago but could not overcome his Democratic opponent’s advantage among mail ballots.
Still, early in-person voting is new to the state, and there is not enough historical data to accurately predict the partisan breakdowns. In 2024, a mandatory nine-day early in-person voting period took effect in Michigan and made up 21 percent of all votes cast in the state that year.
If that were to hold this year, the share of votes cast on Election Day in Michigan could shrink substantially from the last midterm cycle, with the state’s early vote landscape looking much different from 2022.
Statewide early in-person voting began in Michigan on Oct. 24.
In Maine, Democrats are seeking to block Senator Susan Collins, a moderate Republican, from winning a sixth term. Maine has one of the highest turnout rates in the nation, and in-person voting began in the state this week.
Most Maine voters wait until Election Day to cast their ballots, though the share of in-person absentee votes surged in 2024. If that trend were to continue, higher rates of early in-person voting could lead to higher early turnout in the state than in 2022, which is what has happened so far.
Maine reports its results by municipality and does not break them down by vote method, making it impossible to know exactly how the absentee vote has broken in previous cycles. Still, Maine’s early votes are much more Democratic by party registration than the state as a whole. The share of registered Republicans who have voted is lower than at this point in 2022 and 2024.
President Trump won Nebraska three times in a row by double digits, but the Senate race between Pete Ricketts, the Trump-endorsed incumbent, and Dan Osborn, his independent challenger, has remained close in pre-election polling. Mr. Osborn, who is backed by the state’s Democratic Party, also ran for Senate in 2024, and he outperformed Kamala Harris in the state, losing to Deb Fischer by less than seven percentage points in a state Mr. Trump won by 20 points.
Registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats nearly two to one in Nebraska, though the partisan makeup of the early vote at this stage of the election has been more evenly distributed in recent cycles, and this year is no exception.
In both 2022 and 2024, Republicans held an advantage in the final early vote tallies. These numbers, however, ignore the substantial and growing share of unaffiliated voters in the state. And a majority of Nebraskans in both years eschewed early voting in favor of casting ballots in person on Election Day.
Polls show a surprisingly close race in Kansas, which Donald Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024. Senator Roger Marshall, the incumbent Republican, is fielding a strong challenge from Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor. Kansas, reliably Republican for decades, has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932.
While Republicans far outnumber Democrats by party registration in the state, registered Democrats are leading in advance votes cast thus far. These totals aren’t necessarily representative, though — Johnson County, a Democratic-leaning county and the largest in the state, tends to make up around 25 percent of the state’s total votes, but constitutes around half of all advance votes cast thus far.
Like other states, early in-person voting has increased since 2022, though a large share of Kansans cast their ballots on Election Day. Kansas does not report its results by vote method, making it difficult to infer the precise benefits each party receives from early ballots.
In Ohio, two decades-long fixtures of state politics — Senator Jon Husted, a Republican appointed to fill Vice President JD Vance’s old Senate seat, and Sherrod Brown, a former senator who lost his bid for a fourth term in 2024 — will face off in an erstwhile battleground state that has trended sharply toward Republicans over the last decade. The state’s early voting period kicked off on Oct. 6.
Ohio does not have party registration, and statewide turnout comparisons to the last midterm cycle are difficult. Ohio’s election system is decentralized, with elections governed by individual county boards of elections — while each county is required to produce a daily absentee report, this data was not standardized until 2023, leading to discrepancies among counties.
Though early in-person votes increased in the state in 2024, Ohio provides just one early voting site per county, which may hinder advance turnout. Much of the story will be told on Election Day, when the majority of the state’s votes are cast. As in other states, the share of early in-person votes increased in 2024.
Additionally, not all Ohio counties supply data on results by vote method. In 2024, the state’s mail ballots tended to favor Democrats in counties where that information was available, and Election Day votes tended to favor Republicans. (The composition of early in-person votes varied widely across counties.)

title: Polymarket and Kalshi Turn Midterm Elections Into a Multimillion Dollar Market
raw_text:
He Bet $1.5 Million on the Midterms. Will He Win Big?
Betting markets like Polymarket and Kalshi have transformed America’s democracy into a new kind of casino.
Practically everyone has an opinion on the midterm elections. David Bensoussan has one, too — and more than $1.5 million on the line.
Mr. Bensoussan, known online as Scottilicious, is a Polymarket sharp — an online trader who has made more than $1.7 million in profit on prediction markets. Websites like Polymarket and Kalshi allow anyone to place wagers on nearly anything, from the outcome of sports games to who will win “Traitors.”
Mr. Bensoussan, 49, has won mostly by predicting the outcome of elections. He uses a homespun method that combines polling, economic data and personal reads of voter enthusiasm with something more inexplicable: a sixth sense, an intuition or something closer to vibes.
He has now turned to this year’s midterm elections, where he has placed wagers worth over $1.5 million in over a dozen races. He’s predicting the outcome of everything from the Senate race in Alaska (he’s bet $113,000 on Mary Peltola, the Democrat) to whether the Republicans will control the House and Senate (he’s wagered $119,000 that they won’t).
In total, Mr. Bensoussan stands to win more than $340,000 after Nov. 3 if his bets prove correct. If Republicans perform better than expected, he could lose hundreds of thousands of dollars. But he has attempted to hedge that risk by placing his largest wagers only when the odds are high, usually a 75 percent chance or more.
“It’s not my primary line of business,” he said in an interview from Los Angeles, where he spends his days running a real estate portfolio. “But this one is by far the most interesting.”
A wave of bettors have flooded prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket this year with millions of dollars — and dreams of making a fortune on American democracy.
The frantic activity is transforming elections into a new kind of casino, crowning millionaires who can correctly predict who will win Senate races, control the House and even become president. Many more will lose their money after finding themselves on the wrong side of a bet.
Prediction markets let people wager on whether something will happen or not — like whether Democrats will control the House of Representatives next year. In early October, the odds for that outcome on Polymarket hovered around 90 percent, meaning a wager of $100 would result in $9.50 in profit if Democrats took control of the House. A long-shot $100 bet on Republicans controlling the House would haul in $864 if correct.
Nearly every national election around the world is shadowed by a bustling prediction market. The websites were credited with correctly predicting the presidential race in 2024 by favoring Donald J. Trump, even though polls had given the edge to Kamala Harris. But bettors incorrectly predicted the winner in Brazil’s recent presidential election, giving Flávio Bolsonaro an 81 percent chance of winning on Polymarket. He lost.
The companies’ popularity has also raised concerns about whether they violate state gambling laws and are being manipulated by those with insider information. Anti-gambling groups say the sites prey on addiction.
Both Kalshi and Polymarket said in statements that they are financial trading tools, distinct from gambling. Both said they monitor for insider trading and report it to the authorities and stressed that they are becoming accurate indicators for predicting elections.
In the United States, midterm prediction market trading has topped $221 million, compared with $92 million during the 2024 election, according to a report from the Anti-Corruption Data Collective, a Washington research group.
All that activity translates into odds that have become national talking points, supplanting polls in the eyes of many as the most reliable predictor of what will happen on Election Day.
Few races have drawn more attention than the Texas Senate race, a close contest between James Talarico, the Democratic candidate, and Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee and the state’s attorney general. Texas has not elected a Democratic senator in three decades.
Polls show that Mr. Talarico has a narrow lead over Mr. Paxton. Prediction markets show more confidence: Mr. Talarico has about a 65 percent chance of winning, according to Polymarket and Kalshi. More than $39 million has been wagered on the race, according to the Anti-Corruption Data Collective.
Mr. Bensoussan has put his money on Mr. Talarico, betting $114,000 through a combination of bets on Polymarket and Kalshi.
Those odds shifted briefly in Mr. Paxton’s favor in early October after a conspiracy theory circulated about Mr. Talarico’s well-being — a claim denied by the candidate, but not before it became national news.
Bettors have said those kinds of fluctuations are a strength of prediction markets over polling, which can be slow to adapt. Researchers at Vanderbilt University found that polling during the 2024 presidential race remained remarkably steady while prediction markets correctly predicted a win for Mr. Trump sooner.
To Polymarket sharps like Mr. Bensoussan, seeing the odds shift slightly in Mr. Paxton’s favor over an online conspiracy theory showed that there was still a lot of amateur interest in the race — what sharps call “dumb money” — reacting to a minor issue unlikely to shift the outcome.
The bets were “ideologically driven” by supporters of Mr. Paxton, he said, and are “informed by people thinking they can make 10 times their money by supporting their candidate.”
Though some bettors use sophisticated models and advanced methods to guide their decisions, Mr. Bensoussan puts weight on the vague sense of enthusiasm that voters feel toward candidates. He doesn’t have file folders stuffed with analysis or spreadsheets tracking each poll and economic metric. He keeps it in his head, refined through conversations with family, friends or his risk analyst, a member of his betting operation whom Mr. Bensoussan pays to avoid getting carried away with emotional bets.
That is the strategy Mr. Bensoussan has used since 2024. He had traveled to France to visit his father, who was dying, and began searching for a distraction. As a former Ph.D. student in political science, he decided on election betting. He discovered a knack for processing reams of information about politics and voters in his head.
He does not have a perfect track record. That year, he lost $52,000 after betting that Mr. Trump would not win every swing state — he did — and lost $36,000 after predicting that Ms. Harris would win the popular vote — she didn’t. But he earned more than he lost, pocketing more than $350,000 that year with bets in dozens of other contests.
Overall, he has won more than $3.15 million, and lost $1.05 million.
“We do a good amount of research, but I’m not always right, obviously,” he said. “You can’t be in this in this business without losing money from time to time.”
Mr. Bensoussan’s efforts to find an edge can border on the extreme. He traveled to Portugal last year to talk with more than 100 voters on the streets of Lisbon and Porto about the country’s presidential election, helping him earn about $80,000 in profit. To gain an edge in South Korea’s election last year, he hired freelance analysts in the country.
Many bettors have gravitated to election wagers on prediction markets because elections draw interest from across the nation — and sometimes the world — for an extended period of time. That allows millions of dollars to accumulate, giving people like Mr. Bensoussan the chance to place larger bets in more active markets.
Because voters feel as if they have a personal stake in elections, amateurs and partisans frequently enter the markets with risky bets fueled by dreams more than shrewd calculations.
“Everyone thinks they know everything about politics, right?” said Alex Keeney, a journalist turned trader who now runs Eventual, a news site aimed at bettors. Mr. Keeney made an excursion this year to Portland, Maine, to speak with voters about the Senate race there.
“Markets are a good tool for figuring out who actually knows what they’re talking about,” he added.
Just over a week before Election Day, Mr. Bensoussan traveled to New York City to defend his bets at a packed prediction market conference, called NEXTPredict. About 2,000 attendees filled conference rooms to hear from traders like Mr. Bensoussan, a new kind of celebrity.
Inside the conference, fortune cookies were handed out with ads tucked inside: “Your opinion on the future could be worth a fortune.” Outside, a truck with a large screen blared a protest: “GAMBLING IS NOT INVESTING.”
Mr. Bensoussan shared the stage with Matt Weiss, 28, a conservative-leaning bettor with nearly $220,000 on a prediction that the Republican Party will keep control of the Senate. Kalshi predicts they have a 36 percent chance of doing so, but if he’s right, he could earn around $133,700.
“Prediction markets offer a casino way to make returns on some fundamental analysis,” Mr. Weiss said in an interview.
Like Mr. Bensoussan, Mr. Weiss has a deep interest in American politics. His biggest bet also aligns with his political views: He suggested a wave of Republican super PAC funding will soon flood airwaves, closing polling gaps in key states like Texas.
“It’s impossible to not bet with your heart in some way,” he said.
Most of Mr. Bensoussan’s midterm bets are for Democrats — he identifies as a left-of-center independent. His biggest wager is more than $662,000 that Democrats will control the House.
Mr. Bensoussan hopes his hedging will bring him out on top, clearing $2 million in profit this year. After that, he plans to turn his attention to next year’s slate of global elections, including in France.
He would like to retire after earning about $10 million in profit. Or maybe, he said, closer to $50 million.
Stuart A. Thompson writes for The Times about online influence, including the people, places and institutions that shape the information we all consume.
Lauren McCarthy is a business reporter for The Times.

Searching for Jobs, Gen Z Feels Like It’s Staring Into ‘the Void’
Hundreds of applications later, even being rejected by an actual human being counts as a victory.
A 22-year-old with an undergraduate degree in biology has applied for 511 jobs and counting. She was recently rejected from a role at Whole Foods after being “interviewed” by a chatbot named Sage.
A 23-year-old applying for administrative jobs in Texas keeps being asked to videotape himself, alone in his apartment, answering questions about his qualifications.
A 23-year-old in Kansas started applying for jobs at fast-food joints and at movie theaters after failing to find work as a paralegal. He answered the phone for one job interview and realized he was speaking to an A.I. agent.
The New York Times recently asked members of Gen Z to write to us about what it feels like to be searching for a job right now. They described a process that is lonely, opaque and impersonal, in which it is hard to tell whether one is being rejected by a hiring manager or an A.I. screener.
The problem is not just that hiring has slowed across the labor market, or that the specter of A.I. is threatening entry-level positions, they said. It was that they could not get a real, live human being to speak to them. Ever. About anything.
The same language came up over and over in their responses: They felt as if they were throwing their applications into “the void.” Some of them opted for slightly different terminology — a “black hole” or an “abyss” — but they painted a similar picture of the application process as a swirling vortex where aspirations and cover letters vanish, unlikely to be retrieved.
“We’re here yelling, ‘I will take the job, I’ll take any job you give me!’” said Grace Dunning, 24, who lives in Seattle. After graduating last year with a degree in neuroscience from the University of Washington, she struggled to find work for six months.
Most rejections came in the form of silence. “It starts to feel like you are talking to someone who is not even listening,” Dunning said.
“I felt very alone.”
“I barely hear back.”
“I feel like my applications are getting sent into a void.”
“I get weeded out before I can even be seen by a real person.”
“There’s no way to talk to anyone, you’re just floating in space.”
“No real person is looking at my cover letter or résumé.”
“It feels like you’re talking to a machine.”
Ghost Jobs and One-Way Interviews
It’s not that everyone is jobless. The unemployment rate for recent college graduates is 5.7 percent. Yet many of these recent graduates are making lattes or bagging groceries — not the type of work they expected to be doing with their costly degrees. They aren’t sure that things are going to get better, either. The number of 18- to 29-year-old Americans who believe they will be better off than their parents is in sharp decline.
These young job-seekers are constantly hearing about past bad job markets from family members who are eager to offer suggestions. (Have they tried networking?) Yet they can’t help bristling when they hear people suggest that their generation is lazy. They want anyone delivering a well-meaning lecture to know that the process of getting rejected from hundreds of jobs is eerier than it was for previous generations.
“You can’t do the classic, ‘Give them a firm handshake and say you’re ready to start on Monday,’” said Imani Stone-Thompson, 29, who lives in Rochester, N.Y. “That hasn’t worked for a really long time.”
She echoed what many people said: There are no phone numbers to call, no publicly accessible hiring managers to charm with a personalized email. Instead, there is what feels like a wall of tech that needs to be pierced in order to reach a human being.
Stone-Thompson said she applied to nearly a thousand jobs after graduating with dual master’s degrees in brain sciences last year. While living with family and working part time in a makeup store, she applied to science-related roles through LinkedIn, then messaged people who worked at each company asking if they could speak with her about the position. (No dice.) She even put the old-school wisdom to the test by showing up to potential employers in person with a hard copy of her résumé. She was told to apply online.
“If you never receive any feedback, any comment, any response to anything that you do, it feels very empty and hollow,” she said.
Stone-Thompson eventually landed a role doing data management for a research foundation that she enjoys. But others are not so lucky. In a recent survey by the hiring platform Greenhouse, 38 percent of Gen Z applicants said they were often or almost always rejected from jobs without a conversation with anyone at the company.
Today’s job-seekers typically submit applications through online job boards where they can see the number of people who have already applied — an immediate source of discouragement. They worry about wasting time applying to so-called ghost jobs, the term they use for roles that are already filled or do not exist. Such listings are so common that several state legislatures are considering bills that would crack down on them.
These applicants are painfully aware that, by some estimates, as many as 90 percent of companies use artificial intelligence in the hiring process. They assume that most of their résumés are being fed into applicant-tracking systems, a type of software that scans job-seekers’ credentials and determines whom to advance in the hiring process, potentially to an actual person.
Lydia Crim, 29, said she spent hours on an application for an executive assistant job in April that required her to write several detailed responses. She got a rejection email from the company about two minutes after hitting submit.
“No human actually rejected me,” said Crim, who lives in western New York and works in higher-education administration. The result has been a breakdown of trust in the hiring process, she said: “It feels like something I’m coming and doing in good faith, and then these companies are putting up a wall that I can’t clear.”
Some job-seekers have responded with A.I. strategies of their own. Many write the first draft of their résumés themselves, then ask a chatbot to sprinkle in keywords from the job description. Others direct chatbots to compose their cover letters whole cloth. (Ethical or not, it may be a shrewd move: Research suggests that A.I. résumé screeners rate applications written by A.I. more highly than ones written by humans.)
And then there are the interviews.
Job-seekers described occasionally sitting down for video interviews with A.I. avatars complete with blank stares and too-shiny foreheads. They said they were especially sick of one-way video interviews in which applicants tape themselves answering questions for a hiring manager (or an A.I. system) to assess on their own time.
Jasmine DeGuzman, a 25-year-old in Orlando, Fla., finds these self-tape interviews a little bit depressing. An onscreen timer counts down while the applicant answers. “If you’re talking with an actual person, you can get a feel for, ‘Do they like me? Do they like what I’m saying?’” DeGuzman said. Instead, “you’re just talking to a camera in your bedroom.”
Growing up, DeGuzman, who uses they and them pronouns, had been told over and over that studying computer science was a path to a secure career. But after two years of searching, they have not been able to secure a job in a field that has been upended by A.I. coding tools.
Eventually they enrolled in a Ph.D. program, hoping to boost their credentials. The job-application process had begun to feel like a referendum on their life choices, they said.
“You just feel like the entire system has somehow flipped in the time that you’ve been in school,” DeGuzman said, “so everything has felt like a lie.”
“It feels like a game that’s rigged against you.”
“It just feels impossible to know what I’m supposed to actually do.”
“It doesn’t necessarily feel like there’s a safe path, or a safe industry.”
“A college degree doesn’t mean anything anymore.”
“It is a little embarrassing to be working a retail job as a college graduate.”
“It’s just hard to want to go out, party, celebrate.”
“I’ve had to reset my expectations.”
“I put the work in, but it’s just not enough anymore.”
“Could someone please just give me a chance?”
‘A Lot of Nihilism’
An unsatisfying experience on the job market appears to be deepening Gen Z’s sense of alienation from the political establishment. With the midterm elections approaching, these young voters are feeling ignored, destabilized and financially squeezed — a recipe for disaffection.
There is a disconnect between how politicians talk about the economy and how young people are actually experiencing it, said Daniel Erby, 23, who lives in Austin, Texas.
“The president will say something like, ‘The stock market and the American economy has never been more active, never been healthier,’” he said, “but everybody I know is broke and unemployed.”
After graduating with a degree in English from Texas State, Erby applied to hundreds of roles as a desk clerk or office assistant, he said. When none of them worked out, he got fed up and applied to every Starbucks in the city. (Only one got back to him, and he was hired as a barista.) But Austin has been too expensive for him and his girlfriend, and they are planning to move back in with family in Houston.
With the midterms approaching, Erby, who said he was not registered with either political party, sees his peers either gravitating toward the extremes of the political spectrum or choosing to sit the election out entirely. “It breeds a lot of nihilism in people, it breeds this vicious idea that nothing matters and so who cares, just burn it all down,” he said.
Rachel Janfaza, the founder of the Up and Up, a research and media firm focused on Gen Z, consistently hears in her focus groups with young people that they do not see the federal government providing solutions to their economic challenges.
That translates to a sense of frustration with the party in power, which, she said, could show up on Election Day. “Instead, it’s pretty much anti-authority, anti-establishment, anti-anyone who is currently in charge,” she said.
James Hernández, 23, who lives in Minneapolis, spent months looking for a job in public health — a task made more challenging by the president’s cuts to funding for the National Institutes of Health, he said. While Republicans insisted the economy was in good shape, Hernández was being asked about his hobbies by an A.I. recruiter.
This summer, after months of radio silence, he finally got what seemed like a golden opportunity: a video interview with two real people for a role at a utility company. But shortly after Hernández joined the call and began making his pitch, the recruiter onscreen closed his eyes and leaned back in his chair.
He seemed to have fallen asleep mid-interview.
“At that point, just give me the A.I.,” said Hernández, who did not end up getting the offer.

Meghalaya earthquake: 3.0 magnitude tremor hits East Garo Hills at shallow depth of 5km
On Monday morning, an earthquake measuring 3.0 on the Richter scale occurred in East Garo Hills, Meghalaya. The National Centre for Seismology reported this tremor at 6.38 am, with a depth of 5 km. The epicentre was identified at latitude 25.602 north and longitude 90.695 east. Previously, on October 18, a similar magnitude earthquake hit Kamjong district in Manipur.

title: Operation Sindoor- Get Latest Updates on India’s Strikes on Terror Camps in Pakistan and PoK
raw_text:

- Operation Sindoor
In a significant military operation codenamed 'Operation Sindoor,' the Indian armed forces conducted precision missile strikes on nine terrorist targets across Pakistan and Pakistan-Occupied Kashmir (PoK) early Wednesday. The strikes targeted key terrorist installations, including Jaish-e-Mohammad's stronghold in Bahawalpur and Lashkar-e-Taiba's base in Muridke.
The military action came two weeks after the Pahalgam terror attack that claimed 26 civilian lives. Prime Minister Modi had earlier granted the armed forces "complete operational freedom" to respond to the attack during a high-level meeting with top defense officials on April 29.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has criticised the West for its support of military regimes in Pakistan, asserting that this backing has significantly undermined democracy in the country. He highlighted Europe's focus on its own energy needs, questioning the expectation that other nations should suffer due to Europe's actions regarding Russian oil.
During his visit to Germany, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar firmly stated that India will not yield to nuclear threats from Pakistan and will only engage bilaterally. This declaration follows India's response to the Pahalgam terror attack with Operation Sindoor, emphasizing India's zero tolerance for terrorism.

Colonel Sofia Qureshi presented video evidence showing the destruction of various terror camps, including the Muridke facility where 2008 Mumbai attack perpetrators David Headley and Ajmal Kasab had trained. Other targeted locations included: 
- Sarjal camp in Sialkot

Top 10 museums and why they should be on your bucket list
Ranked ninth among the World’s 100 Best Museums, the Bihar Museum in Patna stands as a testament to Bihar’s rich cultural narrative. Since its inauguration in 2015, it artfully showcases historical artefacts that educate and inspire visitors. With features like a dedicated Children's Gallery and manicured lawns, the museum promises a modern and engaging experience, further highlighting India's unique contributions to global culture.
Which Indian city is known as the “City of Lakes”?
Udaipur and Bhopal are both referred to as the 'City of Lakes'. Udaipur is famous for its royal heritage and historic lakes, while Bhopal is known for its expansive water bodies. Lake Pichola and Fateh Sagar Lake are significant attractions in Udaipur. In contrast, Upper Lake and Lower Lake are central to Bhopal's identity. Both cities showcase unique landscapes influenced by their lakes and cultural significance.
Which city is known as the Silk City of India??
Known as the Silk City, Bhagalpur has a storied tradition in silk manufacturing. Its tussar silk stands out for its exquisite feel and natural shades. Dedicated weavers uphold traditional techniques that have survived centuries, yet they grapple with competition from lower-cost solutions and modern fabrics. Initiatives by the government seek to nourish and protect this crucial facet of Bhagalpur's heritage.
Bihar’s Falgu River appears to disappear beneath miles of sand; the ancient legend of Sita’s curse and why the river can never come to the surface
The Falgu River in Gaya, Bihar, has a legend about a curse from Goddess Sita that affects its water flow. It's super important during Pitra Paksha but is mostly dry, with just sand. Researchers are working on projects to bring the river back to life, which is crucial for many devotees who rely on it for their religious rituals.
Why today’s leisure traveller is looking beyond traditional staycations
Travelers today prefer vacations that focus on personalized and unique experiences instead of traditional itineraries. More individuals desire to engage in hobbies or skills during their holidays that enhance their everyday lives. Technology enables travelers to curate breaks that reflect their personal interests effortlessly. Families are now choosing destinations that accommodate the diverse preferences of each member during their trips.
5 things to spot in and around Delhi’s Jantar Mantar that most visitors walk right past
Constructed in 1724 by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II, Jantar Mantar presents an impressive collection of unusual astronomical instruments. The Samrat Yantra and Jai Prakash Yantra demonstrate a remarkable proficiency in geometry aimed at celestial studies. Many tourists mistakenly regard them as artistic sculptures rather than active scientific devices. Additionally, the adjacent Agrasen ki Baoli offers a contrasting architectural ambience.
Why do hotel towels have those horizontal stripes near the edges? The real reason behind that familiar design.
Horizontal stripes on hotel towels not only contribute to a sleek and polished appearance but also signify their durability and quality. These stripes facilitate easier folding for housekeeping, ensuring an immaculate presentation in every room. While some believe the stripes enhance hygiene, true cleanliness relies more on meticulous washing practices.
From hotel Wi-Fi to hidden cameras: 7 simple ways to check if your hotel room is safe
When you journey away from home, securing your temporary accommodations is essential. Before settling in, always check the internet connections and inspect the room for any hidden surveillance devices. Be mindful of smart devices to maintain your privacy by not linking personal accounts. A little preparation on your devices can safeguard against theft or loss, ensuring a comfortable and secure travel experience.
Why do hotels choose white sheets? The psychology and history behind the hospitality standard
Have you ever wondered why most hotels opt for plain white sheets instead of colourful ones? While it might seem like a simple design choice, there's actually more to it. White sheets not only look clean and aesthetic, but they also demonstrate that the linens are thoroughly washed and sanitized, which is crucial for guest comfort and hygiene.
Inside Mukti Bhawan, the unique death hotel of Varanasi where people check in to die; "sabko ek din yahin aana hai"; but you can stay only for 15 days because of this shocking reason
Mukti Bhawan, situated in the heart of Varanasi, serves as a haven for those approaching the end of their journey. This serene retreat encourages individuals to accept their final days with spiritual grace. Guests are permitted to stay for a strict fifteen-day period, during which their ultimate aim is to attain liberation through death in this revered city. Recognized globally, the establishment's mission is truly unique.
Tamil Nadu’s 10,000 forgotten mansions: Built with Italian marble, Belgian glass and Burmese teak by wealthy Chettiars, these grand homes were abandoned for decades, now some are finding a new life
Chettinad's grand mansions, built by wealthy merchants, now attract global travelers. These once-abandoned homes are being restored into unique heritage hotels. Visitors can experience the region's history by staying in these architectural marvels. The Chettiar community's prosperity declined, leaving many mansions neglected. Restored properties offer a glimpse into Chettinad's rich cultural and architectural past.
Sri Lankan cricket legend Kumar Sangakkara spent years restoring a historic villa built more than 100 years ago, blending old-world architecture with modern design; the heritage property is now ready for a new chapter
Cricket icon Kumar Sangakkara and his wife have beautifully restored a historic villa within Galle Fort, blending 120 years of Sri Lankan history with a modern touch. The restoration process highlights weathered walls and rich layers of patina, giving the home a distinct character. Now a four-bedroom residence, it features lush courtyard gardens and a rooftop pool, allowing visitors to experience the captivating heritage of Galle Fort.

- Steve Jobs said it wouldn't work, but with Apple's first touchscreen MacBook now here, John Ternus says you've gotta touch it to believe it In 2010, Steve Jobs called touchscreen laptops ergonomically terrible, and Apple spent the next 16 years agreeing with him. The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display ends that run, and its OLED panel is what made touch possible. Jobs would probably still complain about tired arms. He would also likely recognise the move, because his no was usually aimed at ideas Apple couldn’t yet do well.
- It only takes one rumour: How a small trigger can lead to a deadly stampede On October 17, a tragic stampede in Kolkata claimed 19 lives during the Durga Puja celebrations. The incident was caused by overcrowding, panic, and a misleading announcement about structural failure. Experts emphasize the importance of effective crowd management to prevent similar tragedies in the future. Investigators are examining various factors contributing to the disaster, including narrow exits and inadequate safety measures.
- Employment documents every employee should preserve and why they matter Employees should maintain a personal employment archive throughout their working life. It should cover not only documents received at joining and exit, but also statutory declarations, nominations and social-security records created during employment. Every monthly salary or wage slip should be downloaded and stored outside the employer’s portal. It usually provides a month-by-month record of basic pay, allowances, attendance or paid days, overtime, statutory contributions, tax deductions and net payment.
- From Hitler’s rise to farmers’ misery in India: How the Great Depression changed lives far beyond America The October 1929 stock market crash in the United States ignited a global economic disaster that resulted in widespread unemployment and business closures. In Germany and India, the crisis led to heightened political unrest and movements for independence. Falling agricultural prices devastated Indian farmers, pushing them closer to revolution against British oppression. Meanwhile, Britain faced significant industrial downturns and job losses, highlighting the urgent need for international economic collaboration.
- MLC election results: BJP wins big, but Congress and Samajwadi Party send a message from Nagpur, Varanasi While the BJP-led NDA won big in the MLC elections across four states, it suffered setbacks in two politically significant constituencies: Nagpur and Varanasi where the Congress and SP held their ground.
- World Psoriasis Day: Is psoriasis contagious? Expert explains symptoms, health risks and new treatment Psoriasis is an autoimmune disorder characterized by red and scaly skin patches, which are not infectious. Patients may experience joint discomfort known as psoriatic arthritis. There are numerous treatment avenues available, such as topical applications, light therapy, and innovative biological treatments. Raising awareness about psoriasis being non-contagious is crucial for alleviating stigma and promoting understanding. A dermatologist's guidance can empower individuals to manage their symptoms effectively.
- Gurdas Maan backs Daler Mehndi, REACTS on singers stepping back from playback singing, remix trend: ‘Artists are human too’ - EXCLUSIVE Gurdas Maan offers a thoughtful perspective on the evolving landscape of the music industry throughout the decades. He highlights the crucial elements of melody and deep emotion that resonate more than fleeting viral trends in today’s music scene. Maan also champions the spirit of collaboration among artists, composers, and filmmakers, urging young talents to remain grounded in their cultural roots as they navigate their careers.
- Tihar has seen escapes since 1965: How Delhi’s prisons are trying to keep inmates from breaking out Recent jailbreaks highlight vulnerabilities in prison security across various facilities, particularly in Delhi and Tamil Nadu. With over 20,000 inmates in Delhi’s prisons, experts emphasize the need for stringent security measures. Multiple layers of security, including extensive CCTV, are currently in place to prevent escapes. Historical cases reveal patterns in escape attempts and motivations among inmates.
- 'Better late than never': Why did F1 leave India, and why is it back on the agenda? Tax disputes ended the Indian Grand Prix after three races. Thirteen years later, the government has put Formula 1 back on its agenda, with a task force examining the challenges that led to the sport’s exit, including taxation, import duties and commercial arrangements. As India targets a possible 2028 return, the big question is whether it can put the right framework in place for F1 to return - and stay.
- They lost a daughter, me a son. We want compensation: Mother turns around a day after Gaighata rape-murder accused was killed in ‘encounter’ After a 17-year-old girl was raped and murdered, Prahlad Das was accused and killed in a police encounter. His mother, Rekha Das, initially accepted the outcome but later expressed doubts about the police's version of events. She questioned how her son could snatch a gun when his hands were tied. Rekha and Prahlad's father, Ramprasad, argued for a legal trial instead of extrajudicial killing.
- Pregnant woman carried on a sling across river as village remains cut off in Madhya Pradesh’s Dindori A pregnant woman from Kalgi Tola faced challenges reaching medical assistance during labor due to poor road connectivity. Her family carried her across the Silgi river before walking 3.5 km to an ambulance. After being transported to the healthcare center, she safely delivered a healthy baby. Residents have long requested the construction of a bridge to improve access, especially during monsoon season.
- Bhima river levels plummet near Pune, villagers use tanker water for last rites The Bhima river flowing through Pune has dried up, affecting the livelihoods of local residents. Villagers from Vitthalwadi are concerned about how to manage available water for drinking and irrigation. Despite the release of water from Bhama Askhed dam, it has not yet reached their area. There is ongoing worry about the coming months and the sustainability of farms and livestock.
- Mumbai’s power needs put Jaitapur nuclear project back in focus Mumbai's energy demands are increasing, prompting renewed interest in the Jaitapur nuclear power project. This proposed project has the potential to generate significant electricity, yet faces numerous hurdles before becoming operational. Concerns from local residents regarding environmental and safety issues must be addressed transparently. The project could also reduce dependence on imported fuels by promoting indigenous nuclear technology.
- Indian-American candidates in 2026 US midterms: Key races, profiles, latest polling & what's at stake From Ro Khanna's re-election bid in Silicon Valley to Vivek Ramaswamy's gubernatorial contest in Ohio, Indian-American politicians are competing in some of the most closely watched congressional, statewide and mayoral electionson November 3.
- Festive season sales are not always bargains: Avoid these 10 money mistakes Festive sales are designed to make every purchase feel like a bargain, and the fear of missing out can lead to buying far more than planned. Set a spending limit before the sales begin and list what is genuinely needed. A budget does not take the joy out of the season, but it ensures that the spending is decided by you rather than by the sale.
- Brahmaputra-Kaveri link: India’s river-interlinking dream explained, and the roadblocks ahead India is working on an initiative to interlink rivers, particularly focusing on the connection between Brahmaputra and Kaveri. This proposal aims to address water scarcity in southern states, which often experience erratic rainfall. Several challenges exist, including interstate disputes, environmental concerns, and the need for technical feasibility. The Godavari-Kaveri link is critical in this proposal, but agreement among states remains complex.
- Pakistan's gas mess: LPG prices soar, imported LNG piles up and the debt bill keeps growing
- Not blind but not the same: Kids still bear brunt of carbide guns Senu, a 12-year-old boy from Madhya Pradesh, faced severe vision impairment due to a carbide gun injury. His father incurred significant medical expenses while seeking treatment, but they have received no government compensation. Many children in the region experience similar issues affecting their education and future opportunities. The long-term consequences of these injuries may hinder their eligibility for certain academic programs and jobs.
- Worship before work: Just to make it out unharmed Employees at Kidwai Bhawan express concern over the building's safety as they encounter daily hazards. Visible deterioration includes cracked concrete, falling debris, and damaged ceilings, posing risks to their safety. Complaints regarding these issues have been reported, yet comprehensive repairs remain unaddressed. The NDMC chairman stated that the concerns will be investigated, and action will be taken afterward. Workers continue to fear for their safety while authorities investigate the matter.
- ‘Gondhal’ director Santosh Davakhar on India’s Oscar entry, Diwali release in 7 languages and more: ''Ramayana' would give our film more room' - Exclusive Director Santosh Davakhar is preparing for the release of his film 'Gondhal' on November 13. This psychological thriller represents Maharashtra's cultural heritage and is India's official entry for the Academy Awards. The film will be released in seven languages to reach a wider audience while retaining cultural authenticity. Davakhar emphasizes the importance of strong storytelling and audience support for the growth of Marathi cinema.
- Delhi man stabbed in sleep as daughter watches; wife, gym trainer arrested A Delhi government employee named Shashank Kanthariya was attacked in his home by his wife Priya and her lover. Priya, who left for the gym in the early morning, allowed Singh, her gym trainer, to enter the home. Singh then stabbed Kanthariya multiple times while he slept next to their daughter. After neighbors intervened, Singh was apprehended and both suspects were arrested.
- Goat takes the pyre as murder accused fakes death to dodge trial: How he tried to claim Rs 10 lakh insurance Raju, a murder accused, staged his death with the help of two practitioners and a fake certificate. His wife claimed an insurance payout of Rs 10 lakh while he evaded authorities. The elaborate plan involved using a goat in a cremation ceremony to pretend he was dead. After nearly 18 months, police tracked Raju down through his family contacts.
- 600 bags of cement, 27 years on the run: How SIR rolls led police to fugitive A cold case involving embezzlement of cement culminated in the arrest of a 54-year-old fugitive. Abdul Sattar Mohammad Habib Qureshi evaded law enforcement for nearly three decades after committing the crime. He was traced from Gujarat to Maharashtra through meticulous investigation of voter registries and vehicle data. Law enforcement utilized technical surveillance to confirm his identity before apprehending him in Nagpur.
- The world's climate bill is mounting. But who should really foot the cost? Developing nations are grappling with soaring costs from climate catastrophes, as seen recently in Nepal's pronounced losses. Commerce minister Piyush Goyal underscored the historical emissions from developed countries at a conference, urging wealthy nations to provide necessary support to those financially strained by disasters. Furthermore, the EU's new carbon regulations present additional hurdles for Indian manufacturers. Climate justice must involve an understanding of historical accountability alongside present capabilities.
- The AI social paradox: Better at communicating, worse at connecting? Artificial intelligence increasingly influences our daily conversations, providing quick responses and clarifications. While many appreciate its role in easing social interactions, a growing dependency raises concerns about the erosion of personal communication skills and genuine connections. Moreover, the subtleties and emotions that characterize human interaction could potentially be diminished, raising important debates regarding the implications of AI on our relationships.
- A proposal is more about power than love. Rashmika Mandanna proposing to Vijay Deverakonda 100 times doesn’t make her a doormat.
- Is Jagan Reddy's 'regret' message a calculated alliance pitch for Congress? YSRCP leader YS Jagan Mohan Reddy has publicly acknowledged his mistake of backing the BJP-led NDA government's law to appoint the CEC. Jagan, who was decimated in the 2024 assembly elections, is gearing up to navigate the complicated political landscape as the 2029 elections approach. Speculation abounds regarding a possible alliance with the Congress, creating formidable challenges, especially given the BJP's strong ties with Chandrababu Naidu.
- Gold prices have plunged: Should you buy yellow metal this Diwali? If we look at gold from one Diwali to the next and it has rewarded patient buyers. On the MCX, gold has risen from Rs 50,986 per 10 gm in November 2020 to about Rs 1,45,800 now. That is almost 3 times the price. It has fallen in only one of the seven Diwali-to-Diwali periods (down 6.7% in 2021). The best run was last year, when it jumped 66.5%.

Top News Audio Briefing - 26 Oct 2026, 11 AM 1- Good morning and welcome to the Times of India's Top News Audio Briefing, bringing you the latest headlines from India and around the world.
2- We're here to keep you informed on the most important developments shaping our day.
3- Starting in India, the Election Commission has declined to disclose details of the software it used to identify errors and anomalies in voter rolls during the Special Intensive Revision. They cite 'commercial confidence, trade secrets, and intellectual property' as reasons for exemption under the RTI Act.
4- This decision came in response to an RTI plea from a social activist in Telangana, who sought information on the software, application, algorithm, or AI platform used for identifying inconsistencies in electoral rolls. The EC stated no new software was developed or procured for the SIR exercise.
5- An official further clarified that software and algorithm details are conventionally not shared under RTI requests, drawing parallels to EVM manufacturers who have also refused to share source codes. The EC also said the information sought was a 'clarification' not covered by the RTI Act.
6- In other political news, the BJP has filed a police complaint in Patna against Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge. This follows his remarks about Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a program marking Bihar’s first chief minister’s birth anniversary.
7- Kharge had stated that the Congress would send those involved in SIR irregularities to jail, to which he retorted 'Modi ka baap bhi jayega' when an audience member shouted about the Prime Minister. The complainant is demanding an apology within 24 hours.
8- Moving to the Middle East, reports indicate a clash between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and IDF chief of staff General Eyal Zamir over a possible military operation.
9- The disagreement reportedly centers on a potential strike on Iran, coming just a day before Israel's polls. Zamir reportedly sought further discussions and written legal authorization from Netanyahu before proceeding, with unnamed sources expressing concern about the issue being used for political gain.
10- Netanyahu, however, dismissed these allegations as 'nonsense' and has previously stated he instructed the IDF and Mossad to work towards toppling the Iranian regime. This comes amidst heightened political tensions and US President Donald Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu.
11- Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is planning to store crude oil in Singapore from the second half of 2027. This move aims to bolster energy supply security in the region.
12- The kingdom intends to use Singapore's Jurong Rock Caverns, a strategic decision after oil supplies to Asia were severely choked in the Strait of Hormuz due to the US-Iran war. This arrangement will bring supplies closer to key Asian markets.
13- Saudi Aramco already stores crude oil in Japan and South Korea, where local governments have priority access during shortages. Singapore's energy minister stated the arrangement would strengthen Saudi Arabia's crude oil supply chain in Southeast Asia.
14- Turning to technology, Google CEO Sundar Pichai has admitted that the company is forgoing short-term Google Cloud revenues.
15- This is due to a strategic decision to prioritize its limited computing capacity towards developing advanced AI models, rather than fully accommodating rising demand from cloud customers. Pichai described access to computing power for Google DeepMind as 'non-negotiable'.
16- He emphasized that developing frontier AI models gives Google an early view of new AI abilities and helps prepare products for future uses, despite the current shortage of chips, servers, and data-center space across the industry.
17- Shifting to Europe, thousands have protested in Prague, the Czech Republic capital, against the government's plans to overhaul public television and radio funding.
18- Critics warn that replacing licence fees with direct state budget funding could undermine media independence and expose broadcasters to political pressure. The bill, backed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis's coalition, received initial approval in the lower house after being unexpectedly moved onto the agenda.

Toi BUDGET
About the Show
There are over 5 million South Asians in the United States - one of the most influential and fastest-growing communities in the world. Yet, their stories are often simplified, filtered, or left untold. Diaspora Dialogues by TOITM changes that.
Hosted by Sujatha Padmanabhan, the series explores what it truly means to build a life between cultures, through honest conversations on identity, ambition, creativity, and belonging. No scripts. No posturing. Just real stories from people shaping the world around them.
Testimonials
"The South Asian diaspora has built extraordinary things across the world. What has been missing is a platform worthy of their stories. That changes now."
Satyan Gajwani
Episodes
Why Des Mattered: Anirudh Pisharody on Never Have I Ever | Diaspora Dialogues by TOI
He played Des on Never Have I Ever — the smart, confident South Asian guy who changed what a Brown leading man could look like on American TV. Sujatha Padmanabhan sits down with Anirudh Pisharody to talk about the role that turned him into an unexpected internet boyfriend, why fans connected so deeply with Des, and what it meant to finally see a South Asian man written as both intelligent and desirable.
Watch Now
They Changed My Name to 'Roger' | Raj Mathai on the Future of News
He was told his name was too "difficult" for American television. For nearly four years, Raj Mathai became "Roger." In this episode of Diaspora Dialogues, Sujatha Padmanabhan sits down with Raj Mathai — the first Indian sportscaster in the United States and a 12-time Emmy Award-winning journalist — for a conversation about identity, credibility, and the future of journalism.

Saurabh Netravalkar went from India's U19 setup to bowling the USA to a historic World Cup win over Pakistan while working full-time as an Oracle engineer. On this episode of Diaspora Dialogues by TOI, Saurabh joins Sujatha Padmanabhan to unpack the journey that made him one of the faces of America's cricketing rise.

Neil Soni and Amrapali Soni Ryan are the siblings behind Laxmi House of Spices - the family business that brought Indian food to American kitchens. On this episode of Diaspora Dialogues by TOI™, they join Sujatha Padmanabhan to trace how their parents' search for familiar Indian ingredients grew into a brand serving millions of households across North America.
Watch Now
How to Scale a South Indian Restaurant Chain: The Chipotle Model | Jay Jayaraman on Diaspora Dialogues by TOI
How do you scale a South Indian restaurant chain without losing authenticity? Jay Jayaraman, founder of the Mylapore brand, reveals how he applied software engineering principles to revolutionize restaurant operations in the USA. From Chennai to California, Vidya's journey is one of the most inspiring Indian American stories on the internet. In this episode, she opens up about the moments that shaped her sound, her viral mashups, and what it really means to be a brown girl chasing a dream in the West.

At a time when America saw chai as a sugary latte, Ani and Ayan Sanyal decided to change the story. Why is Indian food always expected to be affordable? Chef Vijay Kumar has been asking that question for years, and Semma is his answer. THE TIMES OF INDIA | Oct 28, 2026, 23:18:43 IST
SUMMARY
Jio Platforms’ stock market debut was closely watched after its record-breaking initial public offering attracted bids worth billions of dollars and more than one crore applications. The $3.2 billion issue received subscriptions worth 22.19 times the shares on offer, with qualified institutional buyers subscribing to their reserved portion 70.55 times. 
The retail investor portion was subscribed 2.72 times, while non-institutional investors subscribed 14 times their reserved quota. Ahead of the listing, the grey-market premium indicated potential gains of about 22%, although the actual listing price will become clear only when trading begins. The company, valued at up to $108.3 billion, has more than 530 million customers and is backed by Meta and Google. 
Track the latest developments as Jio Platforms makes its market debut on Wednesday, October 28.
23:18 (IST) Oct 28
Ambani family’s next generation in focus after Jio Platforms’ blockbuster stock market debut
23:15 (IST) Oct 28
Reliance Group becomes biggest conglomerate by market valuation thanks to strong debut of Jio Platforms
The strong listing of Jio Platforms Ltd made the Reliance Group the biggest conglomerate by market valuation on Wednesday, overtaking the Tata Group.
Shares of Jio Platforms, the Reliance Industries-backed digital services company, made a blockbuster debut on Wednesday. The stock started trading at Rs 1,358, registering a jump of 21.36 per cent from the issue price of Rs 1,119, on both the BSE and NSE.
The shares ended at Rs 1,417.35, surging 26.66 per cent from the issue price on the BSE. During the day, the stock zoomed 27.23 per cent to hit the day's high of Rs 1,423.80.
On the NSE, the stock climbed 26.67 per cent to end at Rs 1,417.50. During intraday trade, it surged 27.24 per cent to Rs 1,423.90.
The company's market valuation stood at Rs 13 lakh crore.
18:20 (IST) Oct 28
Reliance Jio debuts today: Jio becomes 2nd most valuable Indian firm by market cap
Jio Platforms Ltd on Wednesday became the second most valuable Indian company by market valuation following an impressive debut on the Dalal Street.
The Reliance Industries-backed digital services company began trading at Rs 1,358, up 21.36 per cent from the issue price of Rs 1,119, on both the BSE and NSE.
The company's shares ended at Rs 1,417.35, up 26.66 per cent from the issue price on the BSE. On the NSE, the stock climbed 26.67 per cent to end at Rs 1,417.50.
The company commanded a market valuation of Rs 13,05,241.98 crore on the BSE. Jio Platforms is only behind Reliance Industries in the domestic market cap ranking. RIL commands a market valuation of Rs 15,67,744.61 crore.
The top five in market capitalisation (mcap) ranking are Reliance Industries with a valuation of Rs 15.67 lakh crore, Jio Platforms Rs 13.05 lakh crore, Bharti Airtel Rs 12.16 lakh crore, HDFC Bank Rs 10.58 lakh crore and ICICI Bank Rs 9.86 lakh crore.
The combined market valuation of both Jio Platforms and Reliance Industries is Rs 28.72 lakh crore.
Jio Platforms' Rs 30,213 crore initial public offering closed with bids for 22.19 times the shares on offer, as total demand across the public issue and anchor investor placement crossed Rs 7.4 lakh crore and applications approached a world-beating 1.39 crore.
The IPO was entirely a fresh issue of 27 crore shares and was priced at Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119 a share. Last week on Wednesday, the opening day of the IPO, Jio Platforms Ltd's offering was fully subscribed within 100 minutes, making it the fastest-subscribed mega public issue in India.
Jio Platforms, in which Reliance owns a 66.4 per cent stake, launched its IPO on October 21. The offering ended on October 23.
18:03 (IST) Oct 28
Jio stock price: Sensex drops 352 points on selling in Reliance, IT stocks; Jio Platforms makes stellar debut
Benchmark stock index Sensex fell by 352 points and Nifty closed below 22,700, dragged down by selling in IT shares and blue-chip Reliance Industries amid rising crude oil prices and caution ahead of the US Federal Reserve's policy decision.
The 30-share BSE Sensex opened lower and tanked 995 points to the day’s low of 72,603.57 in morning deals. The barometer later recovered some of the losses to settle at 73,246.03, down by 352.64 points, or 0.48 per cent.
The 50-share NSE Nifty dropped 50.90 points, or 0.22 per cent, to close at 22,698.85. Broader indices, however, advanced on select buying by investors. The BSE SmallCap Select index climbed 0.85 per cent and the MidCap Select index by 0.66 per cent.
Meanwhile, shares of Jio Platforms, the Reliance Industries-backed digital services company, made a blockbuster debut on Wednesday.
The stock ended nearly 27 per cent higher against the issue price of Rs 1,119, becoming the second most valuable domestic firm after Reliance Industries by market capitalisation. Jio Platforms commanded a market valuation of Rs 13 lakh crore.
From the 30 Sensex firms, Reliance Industries dropped 3.46 per cent, Infosys 3.34 per cent, Tech Mahindra 1.83 per cent, Tata Consultancy Services 1.68 per cent, Bharti Airtel 1.42 per cent and Tata Steel 1.37 per cent.
Larsen & Toubro jumped nearly 4 per cent after the engineering major reported a 32.5 per cent rise in consolidated net profit to Rs 5,202.10 crore for the quarter ended September 2026, driven by higher revenue.
Trent, State Bank of India, Axis Bank and InterGlobe Aviation were also the winners from the blue-chip pack.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, jumped 0.99 per cent to USD 114.5 per barrel.
17:03 (IST) Oct 28
Ambani family visits Siddhivinayak temple after Jio Platforms' IPO listing
The Ambani family visited Mumbai’s Shri Siddhivinayak Temple on Wednesday to seek the blessings of Lord Siddhivinayak following the Jio Platforms IPO listing ceremony, continuing their tradition of turning to the deity ahead of major milestones.
The family arrived at the temple under heavy security cover to express gratitude for the public listing of Jio.
The temple visit followed an emotional moment at the listing ceremony, where Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani was seen wiping tears from his eyes as his children, Anant Ambani and Isha Ambani, addressed the gathering.
Speaking at the Jio Platforms IPO listing ceremony, Isha Ambani, Executive Director of Reliance Retail Ventures, recalled a family conversation about Reliance's first public offering in 1977, when her father was 20 years old.
“A few evenings ago, at our dinner table, my father, Shri Mukesh Ambani, was remembering his days in 1977. He was 20 years old, working on Reliance's first public offering. My grandfather, Shri Dhirubhai Ambani, had decided to take Reliance to the people,” she said.
Isha also highlighted Jio's financial performance over the past decade, stating, “This year, Jio earned about USD 15.5 billion in revenue and about USD 8 billion in real earnings. Very few companies anywhere in the world have done this. That too in only 10 years. But behind every number is a customer. And to every customer, Jio aapne banaya. You welcomed it.”
She also praised her brother Akash Ambani, Chairman of Reliance Jio, for his commitment to building the platform. “Akash, for the last 13 years on this journey, I don't think you've come home a single night before midnight. I could not be prouder to be your sister,” she added.

Jio stock price: Jio Platforms shares rise 4.35% on BSE, trade 26.64% above issue price
Jio Platforms Ltd shares were trading at Rs 1,417.10 on the BSE, up Rs 59.10 or 4.35% against the opening price. The stock was trading Rs 298.10, or 26.64%, above its issue price.

Jio stock price: After blockbuster listing, Akash Ambani turns focus to AI and India’s digital future
In an email to employees, Akash Ambani said that Jio must now take the lead in the next phase of technological change, making advanced technologies accessible and affordable to people across the country. "From ubiquitous connectivity to digital services, from cloud to artificial intelligence, we must once again lead the next wave of technological transformation - making the world's most advanced technologies affordable, accessible and meaningful for every Indian," he wrote.
He said the listing brings "greater responsibility, higher expectations and an even bigger opportunity to shape India's digital future".

Jio Platforms listing: Akash Ambani says IPO 'response surpassed our imagination'
Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm, said the response to the IPO had exceeded the company’s expectations. The offering received demand worth more than Rs 7.5 lakh crore and over 1.3 crore applications.
“The response surpassed our imagination, breaking records in every investor category. We were fully subscribed for India's largest IPO within 95 minutes of launch, the fastest ever India has seen,” he said.

Shares of Jio Platforms, the country’s largest-ever public offering, made their stock market debut, listing at Rs 1,359 on the BSE and NSE, a 21.36% premium over the IPO price of Rs 1,119 per share.
