title: NBA trade rumor: Miami Heat are ‘actively monitoring’ $119 million Dallas Mavericks veteran to pair with Giannis Antetokounmpo
raw_text:
ESPN’s Shams Charania said Oct. 28 on The Pat McAfee Show the Miami Heat will monitor Dallas Mavericks guard Kyrie Irving, 34, who earns $39.5 million. Miami is 0-4 and, per Charania, has one first-round pick left to trade after paying three first-round picks and a swap for 
Giannis Antetokounmpo
. Dallas, 2-2, has shown no interest in a deal. The trade deadline is Feb. 11.
Kyrie Irving is on the Miami Heat’s radar. ESPN’s Shams Charania said Wednesday on The Pat McAfee Show the Heat will be “monitoring Kyrie Irving,” and added several other teams are doing the same. Miami is 0-4 to open the 2026-27 season, with the fourth loss coming against Dallas, 113-109 on Oct. 26. Heavy’s Joey Haverford sees point guard as a major flaw next to Giannis Antetokounmpo.
The sticking point is the price. Charania doubts Miami has enough to get a deal done, and BasketNews reports Dallas has shown no interest in trading its 34-year-old guard. The Mavericks are 2-2 with 19-year-old Cooper Flagg, and the Feb. 11 trade deadline is more than three months away. Irving missed the entire 2025-26 season with a torn ACL and has played three games since.
What Shams Charania said about Kyrie Irving and the Heat
Kyrie Irving. Image via: Jeff Haynes/NBAE via Getty Images
Charania put the Heat’s problem in terms of inventory. His question for Miami was “what can you give?” Antetokounmpo already cost three first-round picks, a swap and other assets, and Charania believes only one first-round pick is eligible to move. 
His sense on whether that buys Irving: “probably not.” He expects the price to run higher.
Irving earns $39.5 million this season and has a $42.4 million player option for 2027-28, per Bleacher Report. He signed a three-year, $119 million deal with Dallas. Miami entered Wednesday’s game against the Atlanta Hawks without a win.
How Miami could build a package for Irving
Davion Mitchell, Miami’s current starting point guard, goes to Dallas as the younger option, Andrew Wiggins matches the salary, and Pelle Larsson or Nikola Jovic supplies a prospect the Mavericks might want. Haverford rates Mitchell as the lesser return in upside, which is why a prospect has to be in the deal. It is Heavy’s proposal, not a reported offer.
His case for Miami is relationships and nerve. Giannis Antetokounmpo, Klay Thompson and Bam Adebayo have known Irving for years, and Pat Riley has a record of striking at the right time. Haverford sees a Kyrie, Giannis and Bam trio as a threat in any series.
Dallas is the bigger variable. Irving does not fit the timeline of a Flagg-led roster, per Bleacher Report, and Dallas could listen to offers if it falls out of the Western Conference playoff picture. Heavy adds many pundits expect him to be moved by the deadline.
Kyrie Irving’s stats and NBA résumé
Cleveland drafted Irving first overall in 2011. He won Rookie of the Year in 2011-12 and the NBA title in 2016, and he is a nine-time All-Star. His three All-NBA nods came in 2015 (Third Team), 2019 (Second Team) and 2021 (Third Team). He has scored 18,490 points over 782 games, with a career high of 60, and he has hit 1,884 threes at 39.3 percent. Basketball-Reference had him listed as questionable with a knee issue for Wednesday’s game against the Thunder.

title: Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan announced in late 2025 that they are shifting their donations, just weeks later Meta CEO gifted state of California $50 million to fund abatement, demolition and ...
raw_text:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan pledged a donation of $50 million to Sacramento State University. The gift from Zuckerberg and Chan was aimed to fund abatement, demolition and initial construction of a new downtown campus, Fortune reports. The donation came just weeks after the couple announced a major shift in the focus of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI), directing most of its philanthropic efforts toward biomedical AI research and scientific discovery. The move signals a broader strategy that mirrors Zuckerberg's aggressive push into AI both at Meta and through the family's charitable ventures. California Governor Gavin Newsom announced the gift on January 28 and tied it to a redevelopment of three vacant state office buildings on Sacramento’s Capitol Mall. The money, from Zuckerberg and Meta, will make room for new student housing alongside academic space, including state-of-the-art STEM labs and an AI center.
Zuckerberg also said that the investments will help strengthen communities and support the upcoming generation of leaders and innovators. Newsom added that this gift from the couple will enable the school keep building its pipeline of tech talent, and that students need to be able to afford to live where they study.
Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan gave $50 million for Sacramento redevelopment
Earlier this year, California Governor Gavin Newsom unveiled a $50 million gift from Zuckerberg and Meta tied to the redevelopment of three vacant state office buildings on Sacramento's Capitol Mall. As reported by Fortune, the funding made by Meta CEO and his wife will help support the abatement, demolition and initial construction work for a new downtown campus of Sacramento State University. The project is also said to include student housing, STEM-focused academic facilities along with a dedicated AI centre.
Newsom further added that the investment would also lead to encourage the students for technology-related careers and will also take care of the housing needs at the same time. The donation made by Zuckerberg and Chan also comes at a time when California is debating over the proposed billionaire tax. The state is proposing to impose one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires which has led to the exit of many high-profile and wealthy residents from the state. The report noted that Zuckerberg has not publicly commented on the proposal and continues to invest heavily in California through both business and philanthropic initiatives.
The philanthropic shift
The gift comes after Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, announced late last year that they would move most of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI) toward AI-powered biomedical research. The initiative launched in 2015 with a pledge to give away 99 percent of the couple’s fortune. It has since moved away from its original focus on education and social justice, though the couple say they will continue to make other local donations.
Biohub, a growing network of biomedical research institutes, is the centrepiece. The couple say it aims to cure or prevent all disease. At an event at the Biohub Imaging Institute in Redwood City in November, reported by the Associated Press, Zuckerberg said the Biohub model has been the most impactful thing they have done and that it will be the main focus of their philanthropy going forward.
The refocus has had a cost. CZI recently laid off 70 staff, mostly at its Redwood City headquarters in San Mateo County. Fortune argues that the Sacramento AI center follows the same playbook, funding infrastructure for training AI talent, similar to Biohub’s shared research tools, rather than one-off scholarships or small, incremental gifts.
California’s 5% tax on billionaires
The donation also arrives as California considers a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires’ wealth. Fortune notes that several prominent billionaires, including Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel and Craft Ventures’ David Sacks, have already moved their permanent residences out of state to avoid it. Zuckerberg has made no public statement about the tax and is instead putting more money into California. He owns a compound of 11 properties in Palo Alto’s Crescent Park neighbourhood, valued at more than $110 million, and Meta has a 57-acre headquarters campus nearby, plus more than 400,000 square feet of office space in Menlo Park.
Meta's AI ambitions
Fortune sees a common thread between Zuckerberg’s business and his giving. Meta has committed to spending between $115 billion and $135 billion on building “superintelligent” agents for feeds, ads and commerce, and the Sacramento gift helps build the talent pipeline for such jobs. Biohub, meanwhile, is focused on “frontier AI” and “frontier biology,” using large-scale models for virtual cells, immune reprogramming and disease prediction. In a November blog post, Zuckerberg and Chan wrote that they are very excited about the decade ahead and expect challenges as well as progress toward some of humanity’s long-term dreams.

title: Sam Altman is 'unhappy' with most MBA students; that he calls his 'chronic disappointment'; says: They always want to go do the thing that ...
raw_text:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has criticised what he sees as the tendency of many MBA graduates to pursue yesterday’s trends instead of embracing new opportunities created by artificial intelligence, calling it his ‘chronic disappointment’ with business school students. According to a report by Fortune, speaking during an interview with Stanford Graduate School of Business, Altman said AI is set to transform large parts of the job market, but argued that the disruption will also create unprecedented opportunities for ambitious workers and entrepreneurs willing to think differently. "It's totally true that huge numbers of tasks that people do today will be done better, cheaper, and faster by AI - and completely differently," Altman said, adding that wide swaths of existing jobs could eventually be handled by AI technologies. The transition, however, is likely to take time rather than happen overnight, according to the OpenAI chief.
'They always want to do the thing that was cool five years ago'
Altman reserved some of his sharpest comments for MBA students, arguing that many focus on following established career paths rather than exploring emerging opportunities. "My chronic disappointment with MBA students is that they always want to go do the thing that was cool five years ago rather than try something new," Altman said. 
"I think this is a great time to go do the new thing."
The comments come at a time when AI is reshaping industries ranging from software development and customer service to healthcare, finance and education, creating uncertainty over future job roles while simultaneously opening new business opportunities.
Sam Altman: AI creating a new generation of companies
According to Altman, AI is creating conditions for entrepreneurs to build companies that would have been difficult or impossible to launch just a few years ago. "There are many companies that can be built on top of the technology OpenAI has put out into the world that will be much bigger and, I hope, more important than OpenAI," he said. The executive pointed to periods of significant technological change as being among the best times for ambitious individuals to start careers or launch ventures.
"If you're heading into the world right now to work on something, I think you want to start your career at a time of the greatest change, when the playing field is most open," Altman said. He added that people with strong ideas, new skills and unconventional ways of looking at problems often perform best when industries are undergoing major shifts.
A founder’s perspective
Altman has built companies from scratch. He dropped out of Stanford, where he studied computer science, in 2005 to co-found the location-based social networking start-up Loopt, which was later acquired. He then joined the start-up accelerator Y Combinator and served as its president from 2014 to 2019. He now sees AI as a chance for a new generation of founders to tackle problems that once seemed out of reach.
Other tech leaders share similar views
Altman's optimism about AI-driven entrepreneurship is shared by other technology leaders. Alexis Ohanian, co-founder of Reddit, has argued that startups created in the AI era have an inherent advantage because they are designed around the technology from the beginning rather than retrofitting it into existing business models. Meanwhile, billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban has repeatedly urged founders to view AI as a core business capability rather than an optional tool. "If you're not using AI to move faster or make smarter decisions, you're behind," Cuban previously told Fortune.

title: Diljit Dosanjh Delhi Concert: Metro services to run till midnight on October 30, DMRC announces special arrangements
raw_text:
To facilitate the movement of spectators attending the "Aura India Tour 2026" concert by 
Diljit Dosanjh
 at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on October 30, the 
Delhi Metro
 Rail Corporation (DMRC) has decided to extend Metro train services till Friday midnight, an official said.
The Delhi Metro has made special operational arrangements, including the extension of Metro train services beyond normal operating hours, on all Metro Lines - except the Airport Express Line and Rapid Metro, Gurugram, said Anuj Dayal, Principal Executive Director, Corporate Communication, DMRC, in a statement on Thursday.
The DMRC has planned to extend Metro train services on all Lines (except the Airport Express Line) up to 12 midnight on the day of the concert, which is likely to attract over 70,000 spectators, said the statement.
Additional train trips will be operated across the network to facilitate the smooth dispersal of spectators after the event. Standby trains will also be kept ready for deployment, if required, to cater to any unforeseen surge in passenger traffic, it said.
In addition, the timings for QR ticket purchase on the DMRC mobile App (Delhi Metro Sarthi) shall also be increased by an hour owing to extended service timings on the day, it said.
To ensure smooth entry and dispersal of spectators, DMRC has made special arrangements at JLN Stadium Metro Station and other important interchange stations. Additional DMRC staff, customer service personnel and Customer Facilitation Agents (CFAs) shall be deployed to guide commuters and regulate passenger movement, the Delhi Metro said.
Further strengthening passenger convenience and safety measures, additional security personnel will be deployed at JLN Stadium Metro Station. Door Frame Metal Detectors (DFMDs) and enhanced security screening arrangements will be put in place to facilitate orderly passenger movement while ensuring adherence to security protocols, it said.
The concert is expected to attract a large gathering of approximately 70,000 spectators, many of whom are likely to use Delhi Metro services for travelling to and from the venue. The JLN Stadium Metro Station on the Violet Line (Kashmere Gate - Raja Nahar Singh corridor) is the nearest Metro station to the venue, said the Delhi Metro.
The DMRC encourages spectators to use Delhi Metro services for a convenient, safe and environmentally friendly travel experience while attending the concert, while reducing dependence on private vehicles.
Earlier, the 
Delhi Traffic Police
 on Wednesday laid out detailed vehicular diversions and available routes, while advising commuters to use public transport, particularly Delhi Metro.
In a post on 'X', the Delhi Traffic Police said: "In view of the Live Music Concert by Diljit Dosanjh at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on 30.10.2026, traffic restrictions and diversions may be in place from 1:00 PM to 12:00 Midnight."
"Commuters are advised to plan their journeys, avoid affected roads around JLN Stadium and use public transport (Delhi Metro recommended)," it added.

title: Gurdas Maan backs Daler Mehndi, REACTS on singers stepping back from playback singing, remix trend: ‘Artists are human too’ - EXCLUSIVE
raw_text:
Some handful of artists have captured the soul of Punjab and carried its music across generations, and one of those is 
Gurdas Maan
. With a career spanning over four decades, the legendary singer, songwriter, actor, and poet has built an enduring body of work rooted in Punjabi folk, meaningful lyrics, and deeply felt emotions. In an exclusive conversation with ETimes, the legendary singer - composer spoke about the changing face of the music industry, the evolving role of playback singers, the growing popularity of remixes, and the responsibility artists carry towards their craft. Excerpts from the interview:
The recent controversy surrounding Daler Mehndi's performance at an event: how much responsible should an artist be towards their art?
An artist’s journey is often more complex than what we see from the outside. We must remember that artists are human too, with personal circumstances and challenges of their own. An artist will always try and do his best for his fans in spite of health issues, personal loss, injuries, etc. We must approach every situation with compassion, give the benefit of the doubt, and allow due process to take its course.
About the controversy: Daler Mehndi faced controversy after his performance at Uttarakhand’s Kunjapuri Mela on October 18, 2026.  The singer was performing at the event when Subodh Uniyal reportedly questioned his singing and accused him of being intoxicated.Do you think music today is driven more by commercial success and viral trends than by melody, lyrics, and emotion? What do you think of this?
Music has always reflected its times, and every generation has its own way of expressing itself. Today, technology has given artists wonderful opportunities to reach people across the world. But for me, the heart of a song remains the same: melody, meaningful words, and emotion. A song may become popular overnight, but the songs that stay with us for years are the ones that touch the heart. Trends will come and go, but the language of the heart never becomes old.
What is your take on singers stepping back from playback singing, and do you think playback singers today have enough creative freedom in the film industry?
Playback singing is a beautiful part of our musical tradition. It allows a singer to bring life to a character and give a film an emotional voice. At the same time, every artist has a natural desire to explore, experiment, and express their own identity. I believe creativity flourishes when there is mutual respect between singers, composers, lyricists, and filmmakers. When everyone works together with an open heart, the music benefits. Ultimately, the purpose is to create something that connects with people, whether it is for a film or an independent album.
Remixes of old classics are increasingly popular. Do you see this as a way of introducing timeless music to younger audiences, or is the industry running short of original ideas?
Every generation is entitled to rediscover the music it loves. If a new arrangement introduces a young listener to an old classic, that can be a beautiful thing. But we must remember that a great song is not merely a tune; it carries the emotions, poetry, and experiences of the time in which it was created. A remix should honor that original spirit rather than lose it. I would love to see young composers draw inspiration from our musical heritage and create something new from it. Our roots are not meant to hold us back; they are meant to give us the strength to grow.
You have remained relevant across generations. What have you done to stay connected with younger audiences while remaining true to your musical identity?
I have never thought of music as something that belongs to a particular age group. A child, a young person, and an elderly person may understand the same song differently, but all of them can feel its emotion. I have simply tried to remain honest with my music and to keep learning from the world around me. My connection with the younger generation comes from listening to them, understanding their times, and sharing the values that have shaped me. My language, my soil, and my culture are my foundation. If you remain sincere with who you are, you do not have to chase every generation; you can grow alongside it.
With elaborate stage productions and audiences recording everything on their phones, has the focus of live concerts shifted from music to spectacle?
A concert is an experience, and there is nothing wrong with making that experience visually beautiful. Technology and stage production can add a great deal to a performance. But when the lights go out and the music begins, there must be something that reaches the audience beyond what the eyes can see. The real magic happens when thousands of people sing the same words together and feel the same emotion. You can record a performance on your phone, but the feeling of being present in that moment is something else entirely. For me, the voice and the connection with the audience must always remain at the center.
Punjabi music has achieved global popularity, but there are concerns about repetitive lyrics and the loss of folk influences. How can the industry balance commercial success with cultural responsibility?
Punjabi music has travelled far beyond Punjab, and that makes me very happy. Wherever our music goes, a little piece of our soil goes with it. Our folk tradition carries the wisdom of our elders, the beauty of our language, the rhythm of our fields, and the stories of our people. We should never forget that richness. There is room for modern sounds, new ideas, and commercial success, but our lyrics should also have depth, dignity, and variety. We must give young artists the freedom to experiment while encouraging them to understand the treasures they have inherited. If we keep creating with sincerity and pride in our culture, Punjabi music will continue to find new hearts across the world.
What is your advice to young artists navigating an industry driven by streaming numbers, social media trends, and instant fame? What does it take to build a lasting legacy?
My advice to young artists is simple: learn your art, respect your elders, work hard, and be patient. The world may measure a song in views and streams, but an artist’s true worth is measured by the place their work finds in people’s lives. Do not be discouraged if success takes time, and do not allow quick success to make you forget the reason you began. Stay curious, keep improving, and remain connected to your roots. Fame can come through many doors, but a legacy is built through honesty, consistency, and love. If your music can bring comfort to someone, give courage to someone or make someone feel less alone, then you have created something that will outlive you.

title: 'Madhubala and Dilip Kumar are burried close to each other at Juhu Kabrastan, just 5-10 metres apart,' reveals her sister Madhur Bhushan talking about their break-up: 'She died when she turned 36'
raw_text:
Madhubala
 and Dilip Kumar’s relationship remains one of the most remembered romances in Hindi cinema, with their separation continuing to invite speculation decades later. Several accounts have emerged over the years about what led to their breakup. Veteran actress Mumtaz recently suggested that Dilip Kumar ended the relationship after learning about Madhubala’s heart condition and her inability to conceive. However, Madhubala’s sister, Madhur Bhushan, has now disputed the claim, insisting that the actor’s illness was diagnosed much later.
Madhur described the circumstances surrounding the breakup and said Mumtaz’s account was inaccurate. “This is a very big story,” she remarked before clarifying that Madhubala’s heart condition had developed after her relationship with Dilip Kumar had ended. “She got heart problem much later. Dilip Kumar was nowhere in the picture,” she said in an interview with Vickey Lalwani.
Madhur said Madhubala began experiencing heart complications around the time she was shooting for ‘Chalti Ka Naam Gaadi’ (1958). Rejecting Mumtaz’s version of events, she added, “The statement is completely wrong.” She also revealed that Madhubala and Dilip Kumar are buried close to each other at Mumbai’s Juhu Muslim Kabrastan. 
“They are buried very close to each other. Just five to 10 metres apart.”
Madhubala and Dilip Kumar’s relationship reportedly came to an end in 1957, while they were working on ‘Mughal-E-Azam’. Their separation is widely attributed to differences between Dilip Kumar and Madhubala’s father, Ataullah Khan, who opposed their relationship.
In his autobiography, ‘Dilip Kumar: The Substance and the Shadow’, the veteran actor recalled that Ataullah Khan had initially planned to set up a film studio with Dilip Kumar and Madhubala as its leading stars. However, Dilip Kumar was uncomfortable with the proposal, adding to the differences between them. By the time they were working on ‘Mughal-E-Azam’, the former couple were reportedly no longer speaking to each other.
Dilip Kumar also made it clear in his book that Madhubala’s heart condition was not responsible for their separation.
Recalling the onset of her sister’s illness, Madhur said Madhubala fainted while shooting for ‘Bahut Din Huwe’. She also vomited blood for the first time during this period. “When we visited the doctor, they said we feel there is something wrong in the chest,” Madhur recalled.
Her account, however, appeared to differ from her earlier statement that Madhubala’s heart complications began during the filming of ‘Chalti Ka Naam Gaadi’. While the latter was released in 1958, ‘Bahut Din Huwe’ came out in 1954. Madhur acknowledged that she could not recall the film titles accurately, explaining, “I don’t remember these film names as Abba didn’t allow all this.”
Madhubala was shooting in Chennai at the time and returned to Mumbai for further medical examinations on her doctor’s advice. It was then that she learnt she had a hole in her heart.
“No doctor in Bombay was capable to treat her as technology wasn’t so advanced then. It was a complicated surgery. Madhubala and Kishore Kumar were in a romantic relationship by then. They had even starred in multiple movies together,” Madhur said.
According to Madhur, Kishore Kumar decided to marry Madhubala after her diagnosis and later took her to London for medical consultations. Recalling the visit, she said, “When they went to London, the doctor within fifteen minutes of meeting her said she had a hole in her heart and she had another two years to live. There is no cure to this and no doctor would take the risk,” she recalled.
Madhur said several doctors consulted by the family reached similar conclusions, but Madhubala found it difficult to accept the diagnosis. “Madhubala didn’t believe them. She said, ‘Sab bakwas karte hai. There is no hole in my heart. I can run, I can dance.’ However, she fainted during the Mughal-E-Azam song where she is in chains,” Madhur said.
Madhubala’s condition reportedly worsened after the incident, and she lost a considerable amount of weight. Recalling the final years of her sister’s life, Madhur said, “She was critically ill. She struggled breathing. That’s why she died. She was bedridden even before the age of 30. As soon as she turned 36, she died.”
Madhubala died in 1969 at the age of 36 after years of battling her heart condition.
When asked how Kishore Kumar responded to Madhubala’s illness, Madhur declined to discuss her personal experiences with him. “I don’t want to speak about the kind of attitude and behaviour he had. I have been taught to let the dead be in peace. I don’t want to speak about him,” she said.
In an interview with The Illustrated Weekly of India, Kishore Kumar had acknowledged that he knew Madhubala was “very sick” when he married her.

title: Quote of the day by BTS’ RM: ‘Happiness is not something that you have to achieve, If you change your perspective a little bit, this moment could be the most beautiful moment of our lives'
raw_text:
In an era driven by constant hustle and moving goals, BTS’s RM talked about a timely reality check on how we measure peace of mind. Today’s quote from the beloved musician is all about understanding and directly challenging the belief that happiness requires a final stamp of achievement. Instead, he highlighted the power of reframing our current circumstances and changing the perspective of how we live life.
The quote of the day from the BTS leader reads, "Happiness is not something that you have to achieve. You can still be happy during the process of achieving something. So if you change your perspective a little bit, I know many people are going through tough times right now, but this moment could be the most beautiful moment of our lives.”
What does the quote mean?
The BTS leader's quote of the day is all about understanding that you can change your perspective in life and that can help you lead a better life.  (Credit: Instagram)
Today’s quote from RM, whose real name is Kim Namjoon, is from his speech during the BTS 2015 ‘HYYH (The Most Beautiful Moment in Life) On Stage’ concert series, which was held from November 27–29, 2015, at the SK Olympic Handball Gymnasium in Seoul, South Korea.
RM’s quote directly talks about how modern society views success, self-worth, and emotional fulfillment. His speech is about our changing our perspective and taking a different approach to living in the present rather than postponing happiness for a future milestone. 
While most people view happiness as something that can only be awarded at the end of a long journey. The situation can be different; after graduating, securing a promotion, or achieving financial stability, however, the motive stays the same. RM points out that treated this way, happiness becomes a target rather than something that you feel and enjoy in the moment. When one goal is reached, another takes its place, keeping true fulfillment perpetually out of reach.
Youth and personal growth are mostly full of uncertainty, failure, and self-doubt. Along with that, society also often frames these difficult phases as obstacles that delay happiness. RM argues that the process of working through hardship is itself meaningful because the resilience and knowledge gained while striving for a goal contributes directly to personal character. Experiencing solidarity, effort, and growth during tough times holds intrinsic beauty, regardless of the final result.
By sharing this insight, RM offered a comforting reminder to people about how you do not need to wait until you "make it" to deserve peace, joy, and self-acceptance.
About RM’s early life
The rapper started off solo as an underground rapper from 2007 to 2009. Later, he made his debut with BTS  in 2013. (Instagram)
Kim Namjoon (RM) was born on September 12, 1994, in Dongjak-gu, Seoul, South Korea, and spent his childhood in the Ilsan District of Goyang, where his family relocated when he was around four years old. From a young age, RM was heavily involved in his studies and was an exceptionally bright student, scoring in the top 1% nationally on South Korea’s university entrance examinations and holding an IQ of 148. While his parents initially wanted him to pursue a traditional academic career because of his high grades, his interest lay more in the music industry.
He also taught himself how to speak English fluently by regularly watching the American sitcom ‘Friends’ with his mother, as well as spending four months studying abroad in New Zealand when he was 12 years old. His interest in music sparked around the same time he heard the song ‘Fly’ by Epik High. Inspired by the legendary group and later American artists like Eminem, he realized his poetry could be turned into song lyrics and began writing rap tracks.
He started as an underground rapper from 2007 to 2009 and started posting tracks and covers online. His career with BTS started in 2010 when he signed with Big Hit Entertainment. Later, on June 13, 2013, he debuted as the leader and main rapper of BTS under the stage name Rap Monster. Around 2015, the group started gaining traction after the release of their album, ‘The Most Beautiful Moment in Life.' In November 2017, he officially changed his stage name to RM, which stands for "Real Me."
To date, RM and BTS continue to rise to global dominance, and earlier this year, they released their first album in around 3 to 4 years, titled 'ARIRANG.'

title: ‘Worked against the norm, took up a 9-to-5 job after returning to India’: Kim Sharma on her journey from ‘Mohabbatein’ to talent management and now turning producer with 'Hoemonal' - EXCLUSIVE
raw_text:
Kim Sharma, who made a memorable Bollywood debut with 'Mohabbatein', has explored several professional avenues beyond acting over the years. From modelling and films to hospitality, talent management and now producing, her journey has been shaped by the willingness to step out of her comfort zone and start afresh. In an all-heart interview with ETimes, Kim reflects on the experiences that have shaped her career, why she chose to move away from acting, and how her work with comedian Sumukhi Suresh on 'Hoemonal' led her to explore production. She also opens up about the gender disparity in the entertainment industry, the stereotypes surrounding actresses and models, and why she believes women should have more space to find their own voice and more..
How would you describe your journey so far, from starting out as a model at 15 to exploring different avenues professionally?
It's been crazy in the sense of good crazy. I started off very young, and I think when I began, there wasn't a lot of purpose or direction to whatever I did. I got discovered as a model when I was 15, and it meant financial independence. It welcomed me into a world that I had previously had no access to. Advertising back in the 90s was a very potent, creative industry, full of cool people. For me, as a 15-year-old, it was eye-opening. So, we went down that road.
Then films happened, which was a totally different beast to straddle. But nonetheless, it was films, and again, all that recognition and attention at a young age. For a long time, I just went along with whatever was happening.
I also remember feeling that I wasn't 100% ingrained in whatever I was doing at that point. When I was about 30, I stopped doing films and decided to pivot. I'm 46 now, and I'd say the last 15 years have been milestones for me, year on year. I decided to put a lot of what I had already established over 15 years behind me and start from scratch. It's been a journey of immense learning, self-exploration and self-knowledge.
Tell me more about the self-exploration part.
There is an aspect of yourself that you tend to explore when you're personally living your life. 
But I think the amount you learn about yourself through professional endeavour, for me at least, has been huge and had a lot of impact on me.
I've done, experienced and learned so many things in my almost 26-27-year career that I feel very wise. I don't know if I'm qualified to say that, but I feel like I know so much more and have experienced so much. I think life experience is the biggest currency you can carry, and I'm happy to have had so many opportunities to pivot.
What led you to move away from acting and explore the business side of things?
A lot of things that have happened to me in my life, most of them, actually, have been organic opportunities. I'm a person who loves to go with the flow, and I'm also inherently somebody who loves to take on new things. I think I was able to just go with it.
The first step was getting married, moving out of the country and stopping films. That became a natural setting for me to do something else. In that environment, I worked in hospitality for five years. That was the starting point for me to understand that having good looks or being skilled in front of a camera is wonderful, but perhaps my skill set runs much deeper and wider in other spaces.In this space, I think I realised that the way I could use my mind in business, or create value through something tangible, which is money and revenue, was a much more potent skill set than the one I'd been exploring for the last 10-odd years. I felt much more work satisfaction from there. That seed was planted at that point, and even after I came back, I needed to work.
How does one have the gumption though to start from scratch? Didn't it feel like a risk?
Of course, film, cinema and being an actor came up again as something I could explore. But very clearly, the answer for me was no. I feel that's where the word gumption, or courage, comes in. Once you have clarity on what works for you, what you really love doing or enjoy doing, it's easy because it's a choice, and you're not doing it because you lack options. For someone like me, if I choose to do something, I welcome whatever comes with it, the highs and lows alike.
What inspired you to come on board as a producer for a stand-up comedy special like 'Hoemonal', and how did the project come about?
I've lived with this piece for about two and a half years. I met Sumukhi Suresh when I was doing talent management. When I first saw her, I had a very strong instinct that this was a person who would travel the distance. At the time, I had no understanding of stand-up, the industry, the business or everything it encompassed.
I candidly told her that I didn't know anything about this particular business of hers and that perhaps we should outsource it. That was the decision we took because I didn't have the wherewithal. But when I took that to the market, I realised something very early on. As with most things, unfortunately, there was a huge disparity in the way female comedians were received for their voice and their order of business. They were very much a subset of male comedians.
I couldn't understand why because I was concentrating on the piece and the artist. For me, it was gender-neutral. It didn't matter whether it was a boy or a girl; it was great that it was a girl. She spoke in a voice that I felt had a lot of relatability across the board. I couldn't understand the lacklustre response I was receiving from people in the business, the big boys of the business. Then it hit me: this was the boys' club I had encountered. I had a decision to make at that moment. This was the boys' club, and this was how one would have to play the game if we chose to play with them. But how about we started a girls' club? Probably, the only members at the start would be Sumukhi and me, but let's see how it goes. That became my driving force. Initially, the idea was to create a community around her, the piece and the content, which we did. We toured with it for over two years, taking it nationally and internationally and doing all the things people said wouldn't happen with it. The more we performed it, the more I realised its potency. For every comic, a special on a platform is the ultimate goal. This was always part of our plan. Along the way, we achieved many firsts with it, many that even the boys weren't clocking.
So, you wanted to work towards making stand-up comedy gender-neutral?
My point is that I don't think the boys make half this effort. This isn't a boy-girl thing. I'm not trying to segregate or take an opposing side, but I'm making comparisons because they do exist. I don't want to sound anti-boy or anti-girl. I'm not that. But I feel that if Sumukhi's piece does well, as it should and is, it becomes a fire starter for other female comedians. It becomes a moment for this to happen much more normally, much more as a matter of course. It doesn't have to be pegged as the achievement of a lifetime or the year. It should be normal for a piece to have its genesis, journey and end. If a piece is good, whether it's told by a male or a female, it should be able to find its own space. Stand-up comedy could be gender-neutral. It should be. of course, a woman's psyche appeals to a woman's psyche, and that is why our community is largely women. But if you watch the piece and hear her voice, it's not segregated by gender. It talks about things that affect everyone, such as societal expectations and pressure. What does success look like for a human being? It looks like being told that by a certain age, you'll do this, and by another age, you'll do that. If you don't reach those metrics, a large portion of the world finds you unsuccessful. What does it take to be brave in the face of that perceived unsuccess? These are things I really want to push through this piece.
How do you think the industry has evolved in terms of opportunities and acceptance for women?
I think we've come a long way. There are so many wonderful, brave women who have blazed a path, decided to speak up or stood their ground. These are exactly the women we need. But while we've come a long way, I also think we have a very long way to go.
Things become normal when we stop needing to have these conversations and stop reiterating that someone is a female comic. I remember going in for my first meeting with people I wanted to tour with Sumukhi. It was always about her being a female comic, one of the top three female comics. I don't understand why it has to be emphasised so much. A comic is a comic, but she's a female comic.
Did you face any male-female stereotypes when you made your debut in movies? And how have things changed now?
I think we've come a long way. There are so many wonderful, brave women who have blazed a path, decided to speak up or stood their ground. These are exactly the women we need. But while we've come a long way, I also think we have a very long way to go. Things become normal when we stop needing to have these conversations. When these things stop being the norm and conversations revolve around the value of what someone brings to the table, rather than their gender or biology, I think we'll be ushering in a new era.
Having said that, I think our generation is the one that straddles this and carries the burden most heavily. I come from an extremely matriarchal home, so I've always been lucky enough not to experience gender disparity in my own house. But in general, I think the generation before us didn't have as much awareness. Then awareness came into our souls, bodies and blood because it all became too much. The new generation approaches it with a lot more ease, and I would definitely give credit to parents who raise their children this way today. I think the future is bright. The future should definitely be female because it's currently male, and look at the mess we're in.
You spoke about having to deal with perceptions, did you also have to deal with the stereotype that models or actresses may not have skills beyond their appearance?
All this perception and stereotyping, and women being encouraged to be more consumed with their looks than anything else, leads to a very siloed form of growth for a human being. It revolves around your skill sets, how you look, and then how you can run a home, cook or do some bizarre stuff like that. This is all patriarchy. It's subliminal, systemic and something we're fed from the time we're old enough to understand what we're consuming.
I don't really subscribe to it, nor do I give it much importance, because I feel that the more you shine a light on it, the more you're creating polarised views and waking up people's dormant, systemic patriarchal views. I prefer to do the work rather than get into the why or what of it.
But yes, I do face perception as something that really comes in my way. It's something I have to continually battle, but I don't feel tired by it. I feel invigorated because I think, this is who I am, and this is the society I live in. These are the thoughts that exist, and if I have to change them, there will be a certain amount of thought and work I have to put into it. That's just what it is. So we do it happily and with a lot of pleasure.
What do you think is the biggest barrier women face in the entertainment industry today?

What was it like stepping into talent management, especially when you had no formal training in the field?
Karan Johar spotted it in me because he is that person. He gave me the job, and I gladly took it from him. After that, it seemed more instinctive to me because I don't really have a formal education in this field. I definitely haven't trained in any of this. Perhaps years of experience in films were something I could draw from. It put me in a very sweet spot where I could understand both sides of the coin. I could understand the artist's point of view because I had been there, but I could also understand the business point of view because I was there. I think I had a larger view. When you can look at the bigger picture, you can actually create it. So I think this really helped me. This is what I say: nothing in life is a waste. Today, I may have done a feature film when I was 18 years old, but today, that experience comes back to give me the life experience, lessons or whatever else I need to help me in what I could be doing now. Everything is interconnected, and everything adds value. That's why I'm always happy to go out and try new things because you never know what works where and how. Even producing this show has been very instinctive. I don't have any background in production, but it came to me because I suppose it's very instinct-driven for me.
'Mohabbatein' remains one of your most memorable films. How does it feel to still be remembered for it, even after all these years?
I think that's the genius of the film that was made. It really speaks to how impactful cinema can be. I think the newer generation doesn't really know me at all. I'm still in the millennial Gen X bracket, where most people who remember me are now in their 40s, 50s or late 30s. Hopefully, as time goes on, I'm known for other things besides that. But I think it's fascinating to see the power and impact a film can have on so many lives, including yours.
You're absolutely right. Even today, that is my defining moment. I could have done a million other things, but people still go back to that because it's the most memorable thing they connect with me, and I have no problem with that. I love it.
I can't say I always love the attention because I'm quite a private person. Life has really opened itself up these days, and everything about your own self is very accessible. I can't say I like the attention all the time, but I also can't say that if there were no attention, I'd be fine. I'd probably be a little lost. I love it and enjoy it. Sometimes people come up to you and ask for a picture, and they're so sweet and loving. This is love that you never asked for or worked for. It's just there, happily and gratefully, and you take it. Why not?
How did moving abroad and later returning to India change your perspective on life and your career?
Going away was an amazing thing that happened to me. It gave me such a large worldview and introduced me to a whole new side of myself and a whole new side of life. Business was something I had never experienced before, and the life I lived there was huge and plentiful. It gave me so much to learn from. Coming back was also lovely because I missed my country, my friends and home. I was grateful that I had a home to come back to and that I had my roots here. I came back with so much learning that I was able to discern, as you said, whether films were a choice. They were one of the choices. When I came back, I had to work, and there were financial considerations that meant I had to take up a job. Films seemed like the easiest option, but because I had had that experience abroad, knew how much I loved it and believed I could do things with it, I was able to take the harder choice. Because I took the harder choice, I feel life became so much more gratifying for me. I didn't do things people expected me to do. I worked against the norm, struggled and did things I'd never done before. I took up a nine-to-five job when I came back, which was unheard of for me. I'd never imagined myself doing that. It was just amazing. There was so much newness. It was a choice, and I'm glad I made it. I'm so happy that I'm sitting here today doing this interview with you rather than talking about something mundane.

title: England’s grandest historic houses are inviting visitors to lie down on cushions and look up at their ceilings, from gold-leaf stars at Bolsover Castle to intricate plasterwork at Queen Victoria’s seaside retreat on the Isle of Wight
raw_text:
When you visit a historic place, your eyes usually go where you expect them to: the paintings at eye level, the carved doors and the glass cases full of relics. Few people ever think to tilt their heads back and take in what hangs overhead. That is a missed opportunity, because ceilings are where many builders and artists saved their boldest work, far from the crowds and the velvet ropes. Doubt it? Then you must certainly visit one of the sites featured in conservation charity English Heritage’s ‘Lie Down and Look Up’ campaign, which runs until November 1. At five of its sites, the charity has set out cushions so visitors can lie down and stare upwards for as long as they like. “Ceilings are often the crowning glory of a historic building. Designed to inspire awe, they can be wonderfully distinctive, with decoration that survives remarkably well,” Jeremy Ashbee, head curator of properties at English Heritage, said in a statement. “But when visiting a historic place, there’s not always the opportunity to enjoy a splendid ceiling to the fullest. We’re inviting visitors to put formality to one side, make themselves at home, linger, even lie down and enjoy the view up above.”
Here’s what you can expect from the ‘Lie Down and Look Up’ campaign.
Bolsover Castle, Derbyshire
The Star Chamber at Bolsover Castle is unlike anything you have seen. Its blue ceiling is dotted with 254 gold-leaf stars, and once you lie back, the room starts to feel like a clear night sky. That’s not all. Biblical scenes are painted on the walls, panels and tapestries, playing out beneath the constellations. The castle was built for William Cavendish, whom English Heritage describes as a ‘horse-mad Cavalier playboy’.
Belsay Hall, Northumberland
Belsay Hall in Northumberland takes a different route. It is both a medieval castle and a Greek Revival mansion, the conservation charity said. Its New Hall, built in the early 19th century, was inspired by Greek marble temples. Its roof is made of glass, so the courtyard below feels open to the sky. Charlotte Woolley, the hall’s cluster manager, told the BBC that the building’s design was meant to be seen more than its decoration. “Obviously, our weather isn’t as kind as that of the Mediterranean,” she said, which explains the covered space. But looking up from the centre of the hall “creates a truly remarkable view, where the full scale and symmetry of the space can be appreciated”.
Osborne, Isle of Wight
Queen Victoria’s seaside retreat at Osborne has its own showstopper. Its ornate ceiling has nothing to do with stars, but something better. The Durbar Room was designed by Lockwood Kipling, father of the writer Rudyard Kipling, and its ornate plasterwork was shaped by Indian master carver Bhai Ram Singh. The room features intricate Indian-style plasterwork to reflect the Queen’s status as Empress of India. “The ceiling is the room’s pièce de résistance, made up of intricate floral plasterwork and honeycombed muqarnas vaulting,” English Heritage says.
Wrest Park, Bedfordshire
Built in the 1830s, the mansion was inspired by French châteaux. According to the conservation charity, there are “many gems to be found within the intricate wall and ceiling décor of this 19th-century ‘French château’-style mansion”. When you head to the drawing room, pause and look up. Take a moment to admire the ceiling painting of Venus and Cupid flying through the sky.
Eltham Palace, south-east London
Eltham Palace, in south-east London, mixes several centuries in one building. Its Great Hall dates to the 1470s, when Edward IV oversaw its construction, and its oak hammerbeam roof still stretches overhead. In the 1930s, the site was turned into what English Heritage calls an “Art Deco party palace”. Over the years, the hall has served as an indoor tennis court, a banquet room and a music hall.
So, are you convinced to look up? Yes, the floor may be cold and your neck may complain, but the view is well worth it.

title: Psychology says women who choose handloom sarees over luxury labels may be drawn to more than craftsmanship, and their preference could reveal a different way of seeing fashion
raw_text:
Imagine a woman standing in front of two racks of sarees. One carries the unmistakable appeal of a luxury label, its name promising exclusivity before she has even touched the fabric. The other holds a handwoven saree in a slightly uneven shade of indigo, with tiny variations in its weave that reveal the human hands behind it.
She reaches for the second one.
Perhaps she remembers her grandmother wearing something similar. Perhaps she likes the way the fabric falls, or knows the saree will grow softer with use. Or perhaps she simply prefers it. There is no single explanation for her choice, but the decision raises an interesting question: when a woman chooses handloom over a luxury label, is she buying a garment, or choosing what she wants her clothes to say about her?
Psychology offers a way to explore that question, although it cannot tell us someone's personality from her wardrobe alone.
What our clothes say about us
Clothing is rarely just about covering the body. It can communicate taste, social position, cultural identity and the kind of person we would like others to see.
A 2025 study published in 
Fashion, Style & Popular Culture
, based on interviews with seven women, explored how personal clothing style connects with self-perception. The researchers found that participants viewed their style as a way to express their sense of self, the person they hoped to become and their creativity. 
Consistency and comfort also mattered. The small sample does not represent all women, but it offers a useful insight into why clothing choices can feel deeply personal.
For a woman who gravitates towards handloom, the appeal may lie in qualities that a logo cannot communicate on its own. The texture, the weave, the colours and the knowledge that a textile carries a regional tradition may matter as much as how it looks.
That does not mean women who buy designer labels care less about individuality. Luxury fashion can also be a form of self-expression, artistic appreciation and personal identity. The difference lies in what each person values, not in one choice being psychologically superior to another.
The appeal of something made by hand
Handloom has a quality that is easy to miss when fashion is discussed mainly in terms of trends and labels: the process is part of the product.
A handwoven saree may carry the distinctive techniques of a weaving cluster, the knowledge passed between generations and the work of people whose names are rarely as visible as a fashion brand's. India's handloom sector remains an important source of livelihood, with the government's Handloom Mark scheme designed to help identify authentic handwoven products.
Why a saree can feel personal
A handloom saree may also carry memories that have little to do with fashion.
A particular border might recall a mother's wedding photographs. A cotton saree might bring back the image of a grandmother getting ready for an ordinary afternoon. A familiar weave might remind someone of a hometown she no longer lives in.
This is especially relevant to clothing with cultural significance. Sarees are worn across generations and regions, with weaving traditions shaped by local materials, techniques and aesthetics. UNESCO's tentative listing on India's iconic saree-weaving clusters describes saree weaving as a living tradition that continues to connect historical craft with contemporary life.
Of course, not every handloom saree comes with a family memory, and not every buyer has an emotional connection to tradition. Some women simply enjoy the fabric, prefer natural textures or find the colours more appealing than those of mass-produced clothing. Personal taste does not always need a deeper explanation.
Is it about rejecting status?
It is tempting to assume that a woman who prefers handloom is rejecting consumerism or refusing to be impressed by luxury labels. Sometimes, that may be true. But the evidence does not justify turning the preference into a personality diagnosis.
A 2010 paper in the 
Journal of Consumer Psychology
 examined the relationship between luxury fashion, aesthetics and identity. It explored how fashion can operate as wearable art, shape ideas about the self and influence how people think about their appearance. Luxury brands, therefore, can carry meanings beyond their price tags, just as handloom can.
The more useful question is not whether a woman cares about status, but which signals matter to her. One person may enjoy the recognition that comes with a famous label. Another may value the rarity of a particular weave. A third may choose a saree because it feels comfortable, lasts for years or works beautifully with jewellery she already owns.
And these motivations can overlap. A woman can love handloom and luxury fashion, appreciate craftsmanship and enjoy dressing for attention. Human preferences rarely fit into neat categories.
The choice may reveal what she values most
The woman in our imagined shop may leave with the indigo saree because it reminds her of home. She may choose it because she admires the weaver's skill. Or she may simply like the way it looks in daylight.
She does not need to be making a statement about luxury, money or modern life.
Sometimes, the most revealing part of a clothing choice is not what someone refuses to buy. It is what makes her stop, reach out and say, quietly, 
this is the one I want
.

title: World Stroke Day: Stroke symptoms that disappear within minutes may seem harmless, but doctors warn they could signal a mini-stroke (TIA), an urgent red flag that should never be ignored even when speech, vision or strength returns to normal
raw_text:
A sudden episode of slurred speech, blurred vision or weakness in one arm can be frightening. But when everything returns to normal within minutes, the immediate reaction is often relief. Some people sit back, carry on with their day and assume the problem has passed. Neurologists warn that this could be a dangerous mistake. These brief episodes may indicate a transient ischaemic attack (TIA), commonly called a mini-stroke, which can warn of a potentially disabling stroke.
When symptoms disappear, the danger may not
A TIA occurs when blood supply to part of the brain is temporarily interrupted. Symptoms may resolve within minutes, but that does not mean the underlying problem has disappeared.
“Complete recovery of speech, vision or strength does not mean the danger has passed,” said Dr Sahil Kohli, Additional Director of Neurology at FMRI, Gurugram.
The concern is particularly serious during the first 48 hours, when the risk of a subsequent stroke is highest. A scientific review published on PubMed found that nearly half of the strokes occurring within 90 days of a TIA happened within two days.
2Why a mini-stroke should never be ignored
The biggest mistake is assuming that feeling normal means everything is fine. 
A person cannot reliably distinguish a TIA from a stroke at home, particularly when symptoms have already resolved.
Dr Aparna Gupta, Director of Neurology at ISIC Multispeciality Hospital, warned against treating these episodes as harmless.
“The most serious worry is that a TIA may be a first sign of a stroke,” she explained. “It is important to get medical assessment right away, even if a person feels fine after a few minutes.”
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also classifies TIA as a medical emergency. Prompt assessment can help doctors identify the cause and reduce the risk of a subsequent stroke.
Remember BE-FAST, even when symptoms are brief
Stroke symptoms can appear suddenly and affect different parts of the body. The BE-FAST check offers a simple way to recognise warning signs:
B - Balance: Sudden dizziness, loss of balance or difficulty walking.
E - Eyes: Sudden vision loss or changes in eyesight.
F - Face: Drooping on one side of the face.
A - Arms: Sudden weakness or numbness in an arm or leg, especially on one side.
S - Speech: Slurred speech, difficulty speaking or trouble understanding others.
T - Time: Seek emergency medical help immediately.
Dr Aditya Kulkarni, Consultant Neurology at Manipal Hospital, Sarjapur Road, stressed the urgency of recognising these symptoms.
“A stroke happens when blood flow to the brain is blocked or a blood vessel bursts. Brain cells begin to die within minutes, which is why I say ‘time is brain’,” he said.
What should happen after symptoms appear?
Do not wait for symptoms to return or arrange a routine appointment for another day. Call an ambulance immediately. In India, 108 is an emergency ambulance number in many states.
Note when the symptoms began and tell the medical team what happened, even if the person appears completely normal by the time help arrives.
“Don't waste time hunting for a hospital when help can come to you,” Dr Kulkarni advised. He also recommended keeping the person comfortable and avoiding food, water or medicines until medical professionals provide guidance.
What doctors need to investigate
An urgent evaluation helps determine whether the episode was a TIA, a stroke or another condition. Depending on the clinical findings, doctors may recommend brain and blood vessel imaging, heart rhythm monitoring, and checks for high blood pressure, diabetes and high cholesterol.
These investigations matter because treatment must address the cause, not just the symptoms.
People with high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, heart disease or a history of smoking face an increased risk. However, a stroke can affect people without these known risk factors, so sudden symptoms should never be dismissed based on age or apparent fitness.
This World Stroke Day, the message from neurologists is clear: when speech, vision or strength suddenly changes, a return to normal is not an all-clear. Get emergency medical help.

title: Avika Gor celebrates her first Karwa Chauth in Bangkok with husband Milind Chandwani; says 'I love the whole vibe of it, getting dressed up, wearing beautiful ethnic outfits...'
raw_text:
Balika Vadhu fame 
Avika Gor
, who tied the knot with boyfriend Milind Chandwani on reality show, Pati Patni Aur Panga, is celebrating her first 
Karwa Chauth
. The actress shifted base to Bangkok a few months ago and is celebrating the festival in Bangkok with her husband.
In a conversation with IANS, the actress opened up about her plans to celebrate her first Karwa Chauth with husband Milind in Bangkok. Speaking about her excitement about the celebrations, Avika Gor shared, “For me, festivals are all about the emotions, the traditions and of course, dressing up! Karwa Chauth is such a beautiful occasion to celebrate love and togetherness. I love the whole vibe of it, getting dressed up, wearing beautiful ethnic outfits, enjoying the festivities, and spending quality time with your partner.”
“But what I love most is the intention behind the festival. It’s a lovely reminder to pause amidst our busy lives and celebrate the person who makes our world a little more special. We are celebrating in Bangkok this year and this will be very special,” she added.
Talking about what commitment means to her, she explained, “I think love is in the little things, showing up for each other, being each other’s biggest cheerleader, laughing together, and standing by each other through everything. 
For me, commitment isn't just about grand gestures; it’s about choosing each other every single day. Karwa Chauth celebrates that beautiful bond, and I think that’s what makes it so special. The rituals are lovely, but the love, understanding, and friendship behind them are what truly matter. And honestly, having your favourite person to share life’s crazy little moments with is such a blessing!”
She further said that traditions remain relevant for younger generations when they are celebrated in ways that fit into their lives. The actress believes that modern lifestyles and cultural values can go hand in hand, allowing people to stay connected to their roots while interpreting traditions in their own way.
Avika mentioned, “I think it’s super important, but in a way that feels authentic to you! We’re a generation that loves experimenting, expressing ourselves, and doing things our own way, and I think we can do all of that while staying connected to our roots. Traditions don’t have to feel old-school; you can give them your own little twist and make them relevant to your life.”
“Whether it’s wearing a gorgeous traditional outfit, celebrating with family, or understanding the story behind a festival, these little things keep us connected to our culture. For me, it’s all about embracing where we come from while creating our own traditions along the way. You can be modern, independent, and totally rooted in your culture, one doesn’t have to come at the cost of the other,” she added.
Avika Gor and Milind Chandvani tied the knot on 30th September 2025 in the presence of their families and close friends.

title: Rohit Sharma declares Rajpal Yadav and Kiku Sharda’s episode as the best of 'Family Full House': Enacts Rajpal's iconic 'Raha nahi jaata' dialogue with him
raw_text:
On Family Full House with 
Rohit Sharma
, two teams face off in an episode that leaves Rohit Sharma making a big declaration. Featuring 
Rajpal Yadav
, 
Paritosh Tripathi
, Farhad Samji and Hemant Pandey in one team, and Kiku Sharda, Gaurav Gera, Suresh Menon and Vrajesh Hirjee in the other. The episode brings together some of the most recognisable comic acts. Rohit welcomes Rajpal Yadav and reveals how excited he was when he first learnt that the actor would be joining them. What follows is a comedy-packed episode, with Kiku bringing back his iconic Baccha Yadav character and Rajpal taking over with his natural humour and dance moves.
The two comedians keep Rohit thoroughly entertained, leading him to make a rare declaration about the show, Rohit says, “Yeh best episode hai, andar se khushi ho rahi hai.”
Amid the comedy, Rohit also shares a personal memory of how Rajpal Yadav’s films helped him deal with disappointment after a difficult day on the field. Recalling the days, Rohit said, “Jab mai khelta hu, out ho jata hu, hum match haar jaate hai toh jab hotel jata hu dukhi rehta hu toh mai aapki movie dekhta hu, woh movie dekhne ke baad subah jab uthta hu toh mujhe aisa lagta hai ki kal toh kuch hua hi nahi, mai toh jaldi out hua hi nahi.
”
Rohit then decided to share proof of just how much he enjoyed Rajpal’s comedy. Asking the actor if he would like to see it, he said, “Toh proof ki baat, aap dekhna chahoge?" A video was then played, taking everyone back to 2016, when Rohit used an app to create videos featuring Rajpal’s dialogues.
Explaining the video and the memories attached to it, Rohit shared, “Ye 2016 ki baat hai ek app aaya karta tha. Woh app me aap aise video create karte the, toh maine bataya na jab na hum hotel me aate the khelne ke baad, hotel me baithke yehi karte the, toh ye tha proof mera, ye 2016 ki baat hai, 10 saal phle ki baat hai.”
Touched by Rohit’s words and the video, Rajpal Yadav responded with appreciation for the hitman. Praising Rohit’s contribution to Indian cricket, he said, “Ek chiz aapke samman me kehna chahunga, ki aap umar me jaroor hum logo se chhote hai lekin aapne hum logo ki height ek ek haazar feet ki banayi hai pure duniya ke saamne.”
Rajpal went on to speak about the connection between entertainment and sports. He said, “Aur dusri chiz ye entertainment hum log humesha bolte hai na mujhe comedy aati hai na tragedy aati hai, we are all entertainers…” Pointing towards Rohit, he added, “Par aap hum sabke captain hai.. Aapne yuvayon me joh josh bhara, aapne jo prerna di, khel humesha umar badhata hai, aapka blood circulation badhata hai, aapka focus badhata hai aapka vision badhata hai, Rohit Sharma aur Rohit Sharma ke team ne humare desh ka maan badhaya, God bless you brother.”
From Kiku’s iconic Baccha Yadav act and Rajpal’s comedy and dance moves to Rohit’s throwback video and admiration for the actor, the episode features plenty of laughs and personal memories.

This week, as mothers and saasu-maas step into the spotlight, 
Vivek Dahiya
 takes a trip down memory lane to reveal how his mother was initially far from convinced about his decision to marry 
Divyanka Tripathi
!

title: Anand Deverakonda lends support to brother Vijay and Rashmika Mandanna amid ‘Ranabaali’ criticism; shares post praising the period drama
raw_text:
Actor Anand Deverakonda has come out in support of his brother 
Vijay Deverakonda
 and sister-in-law 
Rashmika Mandanna
 amid the criticism surrounding their film ‘Ranabaali’. The period drama, directed by Rahul Sankrityan, was released in theatres on October 16 and received mixed reviews from audiences and critics.
Anand Deverakonda shares post calling ‘Ranabaali’ a blockbuster
Following the couple’s appearance on Karan Johar’s talk show ‘Koffee With Karan’, 
Vijay
 and Rashmika also faced scrutiny over their personal lives. Amid the discussions, Anand shared posts from both actors on his Instagram stories praising ‘Ranabaali’.
The post read, “Ranabaali slaps the negativity in the face, emerges as a profitable blockbuster, and wins something far more valuable than box-office numbers, immense respect.”
The post came amid criticism of the film and discussions surrounding the lead actors.
Vijay Deverakonda and Rashmika Mandanna in ‘Ranabaali’
Directed by Rahul Sankrityan, ‘Ranabaali’ stars Vijay Deverakonda as Singanamala Bobbili Ranabaali, a man who rises against British colonial exploitation and atrocities. The actor appears in a rugged look for the role and underwent horse-riding training for the film.
Rashmika Mandanna plays Jayamma, Ranabaali’s wife, who plays an important role in his personal journey and resistance. 
Hollywood actor Arnold Vosloo, known for ‘The Mummy’, plays the antagonist, Sir Theodore Hector.
The film’s music has been composed by Ajay-Atul.
‘Ranabaali’ box office collection
According to Sacnilk, the film collected an estimated Rs 1.03 crore on Day 13, across 1,488 shows. Its total India net collection reached approximately Rs 56.38 crore, while the India gross collection stood at an estimated Rs 65.45 crore.
Couple’s first film after marriage
‘Ranabaali’ marks Vijay and Rashmika’s first film release together after their wedding in February 2026. The couple previously worked together in ‘Geetha Govindam’ and ‘Dear Comrade’. It is also Vijay’s second collaboration with Rahul Sankrityan after ‘Taxiwaala’.
Meanwhile, Anand Deverakonda was last seen in the romance drama ‘Epic - First Semester’, starring alongside Vaishnavi Chaitanya in the lead.

title: Rajinikanth’s ‘Jailer’ may get black-and-white version like ‘Spider-Noir’; cinematographer says ‘Nelson and I have been dreaming of it’
raw_text:
Rajinikath’s ‘Jailer’ franchise is enjoying a blockbuster success with it becoming Tamil cinema’s highest grosser. Interestingly the prequel which was released in 2023 could get a new version in black and white. Cinematographer Vijay Karthik Kannan has revealed that he and director Nelson Dilipkumar have been discussing the idea of presenting the entire film in monochrome.

title: When Noah Wyle bought his 80-acre Santa Ynez, California, ranch in 1999 for nearly $2.5 million, he was too young and inexperienced to maintain it; today, The Pitt star and Sexiest Man Alive calls it his sanctuary
raw_text:
Noah Wyle
 may be enjoying renewed attention for his performance in The Pitt and the title of PEOPLE’s Sexiest Man Alive, but the actor’s idea of a perfect life is far removed from Hollywood’s red carpets. At his 80-acre ranch in Santa Ynez, California, the 55-year-old actor finds comfort in open landscapes, family time and a menagerie of animals. Purchased in 1999, the property has become his personal sanctuary, a place where he can step away from the demands of his profession and reconnect with a slower pace of life.
“I’m kind of a homebody type,” Wyle told PEOPLE, describing his Santa Ynez property as his “go-to sanctuary”. He also summed up the place with two words: “Laboratory. Oasis.”
Why Noah Wyle bought his 80-acre ranch in 1999
Wyle purchased the sprawling property in 1999 for nearly $2.5 million, when he was starring in the medical drama 'ER'. Although his career required him to remain close to Los Angeles, he wanted to raise his children away from the pace of the city.
In a 2019 interview with Cowboys & Indians, the actor explained that he was looking for a more rural setting where his family could enjoy a quieter lifestyle.
“I needed to be geographically close to Los Angeles just for practical purposes, but I didn’t want to raise my kids in Los Angeles,” he told the publication. “I was raised in Los Angeles. I’m an Angeleno, and I just wanted something a little bit more rural and smaller and slower than city life for my kids. Two hours was about as far as I could drive after work on a Friday night when I was doing ER and not fall asleep at the wheel. That kind of radius brought me up to the Santa Ynez Valley.”
The landscape ultimately helped seal the deal. Recalling his first impressions of the region, Wyle said the view from Highway 154 reminded him of the Italian countryside.
“Once I came down that Highway 154 hill and saw Lake Cachuma and the valley spread out before me, it looked just like Tuscany to me. Then I found this property that just spoke to me,” he recalled.
‘I was way too young to buy it’: The challenges of owning the ranch
The Pitt star bought his ranch in 1999 while still young and inexperienced. (Photo: Facebook)
Buying an 80-acre property was a major decision for Wyle, particularly at a stage when he was still building his career and learning what it took to manage a ranch.
Looking back, the actor admitted that he had taken the plunge before he was entirely prepared for the responsibilities involved.
“I was way too young to buy — didn’t have enough money to buy it, and didn’t know how to maintain it,” he told Cowboys & Indians.
However, the challenges did not diminish his attachment to the property. Nearly two decades after buying it, Wyle described the decision as “one of the best decisions I’ve ever made”.
For the actor, the ranch has become more than a home. With work taking him across the world, it gives him a familiar place to return to and a sense of stability amid a demanding professional life.
“I love being here. Because I work all over the world and I travel so much, it’s really important for me to have a comfortable and anchoring home base,” he said. “And to be able to come back here and recharge my battery and lock my gate and be with my family and enjoy the animals and the things this valley has to offer, the happier I am, and then I can leave again.”
Noah Wyle’s ranch life includes pigs, horses, dogs and rescue animals
Noah Wyle’s ranch is home to his family and a menagerie of animals. (Photo: Facebook)
The sprawling property has also become home to an assortment of animals over the years. In his 2019 interview, Wyle described the ranch as a “menagerie”, listing pigs, chickens, a rescued steer, horses, dogs and cats among its residents.
Although the family is no longer adding animals at the same pace, his affection for those in need remains unchanged.
“It’s still a lot of animals. We’re not acquiring as many animals as we used to, but if I hear a good hard-luck case or a good sob story about an animal in need, I’m still a soft touch, and everybody knows it,” he said.
For Wyle, looking after animals has also brought an understanding of the natural rhythms of life. Ranch living, he explained, involves experiencing everything from birth and caregiving to loss.
“Ranch life is about life cycles. You see things get born, you care for them, and then you bury them. And it goes over and over again,” he said.
His remarks offer a glimpse into a side of the actor that audiences rarely see on screen: someone who values the responsibilities and everyday experiences that come with living close to nature.
Noah Wyle’s life away from the camera: Breakfast, gratitude and family time
Despite his demanding schedule, Wyle tries to maintain a routine when he is at home. Speaking to PEOPLE, he described a day that revolves around family, his dogs and a few personal habits that help him stay grounded.
“I make breakfast at the house. I usually make breakfast for my wife and my daughter. Three dogs. I have a little kind of daily practice, journal practice, gratitude practice I try to do every day. I try to exercise a little bit every day, take the dogs for a walk, at least, try to read a little bit every day. Try not to scroll too much on my phone,” he said.
The actor admitted that genuine days off are rare, but when he gets one, he prefers to keep things simple.
“I rarely get a day off,” Wyle said, adding that he enjoys doing “normal stuff” when he does have time to himself.
That preference for ordinary pleasures helps explain why his ranch remains so important to him. Away from the attention that comes with a successful acting career, he can focus on family meals, walks with his dogs, reading and the responsibilities of caring for his animals.
