title: In 2006, Burt Reynolds's ‘Valhalla’ mansion was valued at USD 15 million; years later, in 2015, it sold for USD 3.3 million, REASON bankruptcy, lawsuits, and financial ruin
raw_text:
Burt Reynolds is best known for his roles in ‘Deliverance’ (1972) and ‘Smokey and the Bandit’ (1977), though following the peak of his career, the actor had to file for bankruptcy. Following this, he had to sell off most of his assets that he had accumulated over the years to pay off his debts that exceeded USD 11 million at the time. One of the most famous assets from his list was his iconic Jupiter, Florida, mansion, which was lost to financial struggles, foreclosure, and a major sale.
Here is a look into Burt Reynold’s former property.
About Burt Reynolds’ Florida mansion
The saga of Burt Reynolds' waterfront compound, often dubbed "Valhalla," was originally purchased in 1980. The actor purchased the 3.4-acre waterfront estate along Jupiter Island's Intracoastal Waterway for USD 700,000. Over the years, he expanded the estate into a 12,538-square-foot compound.
According to Jupiter Magazine, some of the amenities that were included in the late actor’s home included a 20-seat private screening room/movie theater, a billiard room, and expansive lounge areas, as well as a resort-style swimming pool that overlooked the Intracoastal Waterway. 
He also had his own private yacht dockage on-site, along with a helicopter landing pad and a separate guest house and caretaker accommodations.
Sale of Burt Reynolds’ waterfront property in Florida
The lavish property went from a peak valuation attempt of USD 15 million down to an eventual sale price of USD 3.3 million, which was driven by personal financial distress, a prolonged real estate market slump, and a foreclosure lawsuit. The actor had to sell off the estate along with many of his other properties, as well as a private jet and 600 personal effects, to pay off his debt, which had crossed USD 11 million.
Burt Reynolds' 'Valhalla'mansion was once priced at USD 15 million, however, when the actor had to sell the property because of his bankruptcy and lawsuits, the selling price dropped to USD 3.3 million. (YouTube)
The buyer of the property in 2015 was Charles Modica, a neighbor and co-founder of St. George's University. In an act of goodwill, Modica then permitted Reynolds to lease back the home and continue residing there until Reynolds passed away in September 2018 at the age of 82 years old.
Burt Reynolds officially filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, which was prompted by his lavish spending. Once, according to Celebrity Net Worth, the beloved actor used to have an overall net worth of USD 60 million. It dropped down to USD 15 million around the time he was married to Lori Anderson. When the two filed for divorce, he had to pay a monthly amount to her as a part of the settlement, which also drastically affected his net worth. title: Quote of the day by Ethan Hawke: ‘If you can channel the best part of you that is bigger than yourself…you can have fun and you aren’t jealous of others… The point of it all is to learn'. ‘Before Sunrise’ star’s words on enjoying life and crafting without letting your ego get the best of you
raw_text:
Ethan Hawke
 is well known for his philosophical take on life and has spent years in the entertainment industry. From becoming a rom-com heartthrob in his youth in the industry to becoming a seasoned star in Hollywood. Today’s quote of the day is about understanding that sometimes things can be done without joining the rat race, and rather than focusing on your ego and the superficial things in life, you can get more out of life by simply enjoying things without letting your ego get the best of you.
The quote from Ethan Hawke reads, "If you can channel the best part of you that is bigger than yourself, where it’s not about your ego and not about getting ahead, then you can have fun and you aren’t jealous of others. You see other people's talent as another branch of your own. You can keep it rooted in joy. Life is long, and there are plenty of opportunities to make mistakes. The point of it all is to learn.”
What does the quote by Ethan Hawke mean?
Ethan Hawke's quote is all about understanding that not everything in life is about superficial things, and if you can put your ego aside and simply enjoy things, you can truly find the mening of enjoying life. (YouTube)
Ethan Hawke shared today’s quote of the day during an extensive Q&A interview that he had with Stephen Galloway for The Hollywood Reporter series ‘The Hollywood Masters,’ which was published on February 8, 2015.
Ethan Hawke’s quote for today explores one of the greatest obstacles in any creative, professional, or personal life: the friction between your ego and the authentic purpose that you are aiming for. 
At its core, the quote serves as a philosophy for how to sustain long-term artistic fulfillment, avoid burnout, and cultivate a mind free from envy.
Taking his career and experience into account, Hawke talks about moments in life where when you approach your work or passion primarily to gain status, fame, or financial success or to simply get ahead, your worth and aim can entirely get dependent on external validation. This makes failure feel much worse and catastrophic, while success feels small and fleeting. However, if you can focus on the craft, the story, or the contribution itself rather than personal glory, you can detach your identity from outcomes. You move from performing for approval to participating in something meaningful.
Other than that, jealousy is another common emotion in life; however, once you move past the emotion, you simply look towards people as a branch rather than a competitor all the time. You will also be able to enjoy life and the things that you do more freely. By completely stripping away your ego and jealousy, you can reclaim the playfulness of creating things for the simple happiness of doing so rather than comparing yourself to other people.
The core takeaway from Hawke’s insightful words is about understanding and advocating for a shift from an ego-driven life to a more relaxed life. When you treat art, work, and personal growth as a lifelong practice of learning rather than a race, you unlock lasting freedom, creativity, and inner peace.
About Ethan Hawke’s early life
Ethan Hawke shot to fame with his role in 'Dead Poets Society' with Robin Williams when he was 18 years old. (Instagram)
Ethan Hawke was born on November 6, 1970, in Austin, Texas. From an early age, he led a simple life, which was heavily influenced by his parents. His parents, Leslie (née Green) and James Hawke, were high school sweethearts who married young while they were studying together at the University of Texas in Austin. His father was an actuarial student, and his mother was a charity worker.
When Hawke was only three years old, his parents divorced in 1974, following which Hawke was raised primarily by his mother. He moved around a lot with his mother and lived in places like Atlanta, Georgia, and New York City before he eventually settled down in New Jersey when his mother remarried. As for his schooling, Hawke attended West Windsor-Plainsboro High School South in New Jersey, though he later transferred to the Hun School of Princeton, a private college preparatory school, from where he graduated in 1988.
Ethan Hawke’s rise to fame
Over the years, Hawke has become one of the most prolific faces in Hollywood and continued to actively work in the entertainment industry. (Instagram)
The beloved star’s love for acting and theater started from an early age, when at age 13, he started acting classes at the McCarter Theatre on the Princeton campus. He later made his stage debut in a school production of George Bernard Shaw's ‘Saint Joan.’ His feature debut came a year later. At age 14, Hawke starred alongside River Phoenix in the sci-fi adventure film 'Explorers,' which helped him officially enter the acting industry.
He took a break from acting to study at Carnegie Mellon University's Drama Department. He dropped out after being cast as Todd Anderson in Peter Weir’s ‘Dead Poets Society’ alongside Robin Williams, which was a big commercial success. Hawke was 18 years old at the time.
Since then, he has been a consistent name in the Hollywood industry, and some of his most popular projects over the years include ‘The Before Trilogy’ (1995 to 2013), ‘First Reformed’ (2017), ‘Boyhood’ (2014), ‘Training Day’ (2001), ‘Predestination’ (2014), ‘Before the Devil Knows You're Dead’ (2007), ‘The Black Phone’ (2021), ‘Reality Bites’ (1994), and many others.

According to recent reports, the waterfront luxury mansion that was originally custom-built for the singer has now been sold off in an off-market deal in Jupiter, Florida.
About Céline Dion's waterfront Florida estate
In 1998, the waterfront home was designed and built specifically for Céline and René. It was tailored to their taste with luxury custom features and deep-water access, according to reports shared online by The Real Deal. The 14,750-square-foot residence is spread across eight bedrooms, eight full bathrooms, and three and a half baths.
Located at 370 Eagle Drive in Admirals Cove, the property initially had a primary suite, which also had a stone fireplace and private terrace, a wine cellar, and a dedicated home theatre outfitted with red velvet seating, coffered ceilings, and a crystal chandelier. Luxury property changes hands

Around the same time, Dion was keeping busy with her career in the music industry and prepping for her ‘A New Day…’ Las Vegas Residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace, which debuted in March 2003. The demands in her career changed drastically and prompted the couple to consolidate their real estate footprint and offload the Jupiter estate. The private buyer's identity has remained largely shielded under asset management entities.

Local real estate investor Myron Miller bought the property from St. John's entity, making a 64% appreciation over the 2021 purchase price.

title: Erin Foster shares clips from real proposal that inspired the iconic ‘Nobody Wants This 3’ scene: ‘He never really drew attention to it'
raw_text:
Actress and producer 
Erin Foster
, whose show ‘Nobody Wants This’ is loosely inspired by her love story with music executive and investor Simon Tikhman, has seen her show rise to become one of the most popular OTT shows in recent years. With the latest season dropped online on Netflix, one of the major scenes of the proposal in the show has been going viral.
Recently, Foster took to her social media account, sharing snaps from the original proposal between her and Tikhman that took place years ago.
Erin Foster shares snaps from the real proposal that inspired the iconic ‘Nobody Wants This’ scene
Taking to Instagram on October 28, Foster shared glimpses of her own proposal with Tikhman, sharing photos and videos from the moment leading up to it. She recounted how the entire thing went down and how Tikhman had even created a special invitation to a supposed wedding vow renewal and never let her know what he was planning on doing.
She shared in the video while showing the invitation he had created, “So about a month before he proposed, we got this invitation to a wedding vow renewal. It had attire and a schedule for the whole weekend. He never really drew attention to it.” She continued, “He said, ‘This is kind of a work thing. You’re welcome to come with me. You don’t have to; no pressure.’ But you know, I think it could be kind of romantic and nice.’”
Fister also commented on how her husband never let her suspect anything, “wasn’t acting weird at all," she added, while sharing that he also told her to get his nails done for the “big moment” with her niece.
Erin Foster revealed that her sister was also involved in the plan
She also added that almost everyone was in on the plan, commenting, "Meanwhile, my sister was flying to Napa with my ring from New York. So, Simon and I get to the hotel in Napa, and the front desk literally hands us an envelope with our name on it and tells us what the activities are for the weekend with the wedding, because Simon had flown up there and prepped them all to pretend that this wedding was happening.”
When they arrived at the fake wedding vow renewal, she mentioned, "Meanwhile, our families are fully just hiding inside that big barn.” The video also included a clip of their actual proposal, which was taken from afar, and then it cut to the shot from the series with Kristen Bell and Adam Brody.
The cast of ‘Nobody Wants This’ includes Kristen Bell, Adam Brody, Justine Lupe, Timothy Simons, and Jackie Tohn. The first season was released in 2024, and the third season was released earlier this month.

title: 'OM' plot explained: Rajkumar Periasamy reveals what connects Mammootty, Dhanush, Sai Pallavi and other characters, says 'It is an emotional story'
raw_text:
Director 
Rajkumar Periasamy
 is bringing together some of Indian cinema’s finest performers for 'OM', also known as 'OM – Chapter 1: Udhiram – The Blood Wood'. Featuring 
Mammootty
, Dhanush, Naseeruddin Shah, 
Sai Pallavi
 and Sreeleela, the film has already generated considerable interest across the country.
After earning praise for 'Amaran', Rajkumar is exploring a different world with this ambitious project. While refraining from revealing too much about the plot, the filmmaker has offered a glimpse into the film’s central idea, its characters and the emotional conflicts that drive the narrative. With several prominent actors playing pivotal roles, 'OM' promises to go beyond the conventions of a typical action film.
Rajkumar Periasamy calls 'OM' an emotional story
In a conversation with Cinema Vikatan, Rajkumar Periasamy explained that the film cannot be described simply as a gangster drama. He revealed that the narrative has several interconnected layers, with different characters coming together for a common reason.
Explaining the film’s central idea, he said, “It is an emotional story. Just as films set in Tirunelveli often have a certain connection to the place, Burma is the common thread in this film. Like the many branches of a tree, this story has several branches. Everyone comes together for a particular reason. 
What that reason is and why they unite forms the story.”
The director also clarified that the 'Chapter 1' label in the title does not mean audiences will have to wait for a sequel to discover the ending. “This is not a continuing story. The story will conclude within this chapter itself,” he explained.
Mammootty as Burma Karthikeyan and Dhanush’s different role in 'OM'
Rajkumar revealed that Mammootty was his first choice for the character of Burma Karthikeyan. After approaching the Malayalam superstar, the filmmaker waited for him to become available. Mammootty eventually heard the narration and agreed to join the project, giving Rajkumar greater confidence in the script.
The director also praised Dhanush’s performance, saying the actor continued to surprise him throughout the shoot. “Dhanush sir is an exciting performer. Every day on the sets, he kept surprising me. He would amaze me in the very first take and could adapt himself to any situation. He has never played a role like this before, and he has genuinely stunned me,” Rajkumar said.
He added that Mammootty’s character cannot be defined merely by the image of an underworld don, as the film presents him with a distinctive world and emotional depth.

title: Tamil Nadu theatre owners seek 6 am shows, 2 am screenings; Vijay's government to review the demands of the industry
raw_text:
The 
Tamil Nadu
 film industry may see changes in theatre timings, OTT release rules and box office reporting if the latest proposals receive government approval. Representatives from across the Tamil film industry recently met Tamil Nadu Information and Publicity Minister Rajmohan at Kalaivanar Arangam in Chennai to discuss key issues affecting the business. The meeting included members of the Tamil Film Producers Council, the Active Producers Association, theatre owners’ associations and distributors’ bodies. Several proposals were placed before the minister to support theatre owners, producers and small-budget filmmakers.
Theatre Owners demand 6 AM shows and 8-week OTT release gap
According to Dinamalar, one of the major demands was permission to screen films from 6 am, similar to the practice in neighbouring states such as Kerala, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. Industry representatives also sought permission to conduct screenings until 2 am, which could allow theatres to run five or six shows a day. They said this would help theatres manage busy release schedules, especially when several films arrive in cinemas on the same day. The industry also called for the OTT release window for Tamil films to be extended to eight weeks after their theatrical release. Theatre owners believe a longer gap could encourage audiences to watch films in cinemas before they become available on streaming platforms.
Tamil Nadu Government OTT platform and box office collection transparency
The representatives also asked the Tamil Nadu government to launch its own OTT platform to help small-budget films reach more viewers. They urged the government to announce pending State Film Awards for previous years and release the remaining subsidies for low-budget films. They also called for an online system to share ticket collection details after every show. The information would be available to producers, distributors and theatre owners, helping all three parties track box office figures. The proposed system is also aimed at preventing false or misleading claims about film collections.
Tamil Nadu Minister Says 90% of film industry demands accepted
After the meeting, Minister Rajmohan addressed the media and said the government had accepted around 90% of the demands raised by representatives of the Tamil film industry. He added that the proposals would be discussed with Chief Minister 
Vijay
 before official government orders and announcements were issued. While the minister’s statement has raised hopes among industry stakeholders, the proposals are yet to become confirmed policy changes. If approved, the measures could affect theatre operations, the release schedules of Tamil films and the way box office collections are reported. The industry is now awaiting the government’s official decision on these requests.

title: A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
raw_text:
Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk third-party website.
The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.
“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”
A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”
“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that had been what could be characterized as an incident.
The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy, which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)
The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.
“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the worst time to be having this kind of cavalier attitude.”
Accenture currently has more than $3.5 billion in contracts with the federal government, nearly $605 million of which are with the DOD. The company also contracts with other federal agencies, such as the Department of Education, the General Services Administration, and the Department of Energy, among others. Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation found that an Accenture contractor failed to patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group ShinyHunters getting access to the details of thousands of the Bureau’s employees. The FBI removed that contractor in early October.
Matt Triner, founder of Hunter Strategy, a Washington, DC-based IT consulting company, says that the issue exemplifies the conflicting demands government contractors face more broadly. “Organizations are often punished for reporting incidents like this, even though it’s the right and legal thing to do,” says Triner. In many cases, he says, a company could lose government contracts by admitting they’ve had a security breach, though he says that an incident like the one described is “absolutely one that would need to be reported.”
Triner also notes that the increasing pressure on contractors to deliver projects faster and at a lower price point is at odds with prioritizing safety and security. “Unfortunately, everyone is operating in a system where there are competing rules and incentives, and that existed before AI, but now it’s the same problem on speed,” says Triner.
The coding environment accessed by the Accenture contractor is run on the Non-classified Internet Protocol Router Network (NIPRNet), a DOD network used for unclassified information. While it does connect to the internet—contractors and employees can access their emails and web browsers through the network—it is heavily secured.
According to the source, in order to automate the process of writing code and spinning up cloud servers, the contractor gave their login credentials to the Claude agent. This gave the agent administrative access and allowed it to bypass the security controls enforced through the normal login process. The AI agent—which was not only writing code but also committing it or saving the code into the system on behalf of the Accenture employee—needed to connect out to the internet to perform its tasks. In doing so, it appears to have sent the contractor’s login credentials, passwords, and a map of NIPRNet out to a third party website.
WIRED is declining to name the third party website so as to protect the system from further vulnerability, but National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has previously identified it as high risk because it has a vulnerability that could let hackers inject instructions into an AI coding agent to steal credentials.
The system the AI agent accessed contained CUI. “Information from a CUI environment is not supposed to leave that infrastructure,” says the source. “There is no insight about what happened to the information, including the login credentials, after it was sent to [that service], whether it’s been retained”
Depending on the agency and its work, CUI can include anything from personally identifiable information (PII) to proprietary business or contracting information. According to the DOD’s website, CUI can include information on “the securing and safeguarding of explosives, hazardous chemicals, or pipelines,” documentation related to the designs of “military or space equipment or technology;” and “the exact location and quantities of radioactive material.”
Distinct from the actual data, a map of it could be incredibly valuable to a hacker. “Once an attacker understands how those things fit together, even if those things are public information, what is sensitive is how we are putting those things together and turning that into actionable intelligence,” says Triner.
While a map might not get a hacker into a system, he says, it could help an adversary move faster once they do have access and “help an attacker understand where the crown jewels are.”
Jake Williams, a former NSA hacker and faculty at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy, says that an AI agent running code in NIPRNet presents a “huge problem, and there are huge national security impacts.”
Williams notes that while individual pieces of data or information might be considered CUI, “when that unclassified information is aggregated, that can become classified itself.” For instance, the location of certain hazardous materials might be CUI, as might be information about the vulnerability of the facilities that house them. Combined, however, they could reveal information that would be kept classified.
But this is not the only way classified information may have been put at risk. Frequently, tools and code are tested in NIPRNet before being deployed into more sensitive systems like the Secret Internet Protocol Router Network (SIPRNet), the military’s secured network for classified information, and Joint Worldwide Intelligence Communications System (JWICS), a secure intranet for top secret information. Both SIPRNet and JWICS are air gapped, a security measure that means they are not connected to any outside networks. On a practical level, that means SIPRNet and JWICS would be extremely difficult for a hacker to access remotely.
But with the login credentials exfiltrated by an AI agent, a hacker could access NIPRNet and insert a backdoor or other malicious code into a tool or system. Without proper review, this code could end up deployed in one of the air gapped systems.
“The code could operate completely normally in NIPR and do something malicious and undisclosed in a SIPR network, that is 100 percent possible,” says Williams. Exfiltrating data out of these networks would be difficult, he adds, but malicious code could be used to attack the systems from the inside. “I think the most likely thing would be some kind of distributed denial of service attack,” he says.
Triner says that even something more subtle, such as slowing down intelligence operations and activities, could cause damage and make users lose trust in a tool, even once the problem is fixed.
As vibe coding, or prompting an AI assistant to write the code for a product described by an engineer, is becoming more common, vetting code is becoming more of a challenge. AI is capable of generating code at a volume that far surpasses human productivity, making it time consuming and difficult to vet.
“When you’re using an agent, you have no idea of the supply chain or even the inference chain of what has ultimately generated the code,” says Williams. “A lot of the code that these LLMs were trained on is itself vulnerable, and they can regurgitate the same kinds of architecture, and architectural issues that we see in other code.”
The government does have a way to identify flawed code in NIPRNet. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) scans code for bugs and flaws before allowing it to run. But Williams notes that a hacker-inserted “backdoor is not a vulnerability, even if we may not want it there,” and therefore would likely fly under the radar of SAST’s detection. SAST also does not usually identify structural issues in the logic chain of how code is created.
There’s no indication that hackers were able to get into a classified or top secret system. Still, Williams says, the incident should raise significant alarms. “Architecturally, any information about NIPR that you can’t see through open source intelligence, DOD considers a close hold regardless of whether something touches a classified network,” he says.
This is not the first time the DOD has been made vulnerable because of AI-related issues. Last year, ProPublica revealed that Microsoft was using “digital escorts” on its projects with the federal government, wherein American employees with security clearances would be overseeing code written by outsourced workers in China. Experts who spoke to ProPublica said that the program presented a particular security risk because the American employees were often not able to vet the code themselves, leaving openings for malicious code to be inserted unknowingly into government systems.

title: Go Minimal—the Ridge Wallet Is 20 Percent Off Right Now
raw_text:
Everyday carry (EDC) enthusiasts and social media influencers have made the Ridge Wallet a favorite for its durability and minimalist design. But it’s not just hype. In her testing, WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe gave it high marks, saying, “I can’t see myself using anything else,” even though she’s not a minimalist and didn’t fall for the “ridiculous” marketing. It’s also one of the wallets I use on vacation, when I just need to carry a few credit cards without drawing attention to the usual George Costanza bulge in my pocket.
Select Ridge Wallet styles are currently on sale for $76 (normally $95) as part of the brand's Friends & Family sale, which also has discounts on other Ridge accessories like pocket knives, power banks, luggage, trackers, and more. If the wallet turns out to not be your thing, Ridge will refund you as part of its 99-day risk-free trial.
Money Sandwich
As Strampe mentioned in her review, the Ridge Wallet will look unfamiliar to newbies. In fact, it may not feel user-friendly at first. The wallet acts like a sandwich for all your cards, using two aluminum pieces held together with screws and elastic bands. It holds up to 12 cards, but you can adjust the opening with the T-5 Torx screws and included screwdriver to fit exactly how many cards you need.
If you’re a minimalist, the Ridge Wallet can help you stay that way. For Strampe, she can’t imagine the Ridge replacing her purse—she still needs to carry her car keys and other necessities. But it does help her keep all her cards—credit, driver’s license, Costco—in one place without rummaging through her bag or using a bulkier wallet.
The Ridge Wallet is somewhat customizable. You can add a cash strap or clip on the outside; there’s even a money clip with a slot for an AirTag. There’s also a chain and D-ring attachment, and you can personalize your Ridge Wallet with colored screws.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
raw_text:
Frequently Asked Questions
About WIRED
WIRED is obsessed with what comes next. Through rigorous investigations and game-changing reporting, we tell stories that don’t just reflect the moment—they help create it. Part of the Condé Nast portfolio, WIRED leads the conversation on how technology is changing every aspect of our lives—from business and politics to culture and science.
Becoming a Subscriber
How do I subscribe or give a gift subscription?
Please visit our subscription page to find the best option for your needs.
When will my first issue arrive?
Digital access begins immediately. You should receive your first issue between eight and ten weeks after purchasing a print subscription.
Contact customer service if you are experiencing any delivery problems, please visit our contact us page for more assistance.
What does my subscription include?
All subscriptions provide unlimited digital access to the website, subscriber-only newsletters, and invitations to Livestream AMAs. Print subscribers also receive the print edition of the magazine, published at least four times per year.
My subscription included a tote bag. When can I expect it to arrive?
The tote ships six to eight weeks after your payment is processed. International orders may take longer to ship, and packages may be delayed at customs. We regret that our staff cannot track tote bags after they enter the postal system.
What forms of payment do you accept?
We accept Visa, MasterCard, American Express, Discover, and Diners Club cards. We also accept PayPal, Apple Pay, and Amazon Pay. Alternatively, checks can be mailed to WIRED, P.O. Box 37617, Boone, IA 50037-0617.
Can I get a receipt or confirmation of my subscription, account details, or cancellation?
Yes, our staff would be happy to send you a receipt. After subscribing, you can expect to receive a confirmation email within twenty-four hours. For more assistance, please visit our contact us page.
When will I be charged?
Credit cards are charged as soon as your order is received. It may take up to three days for the charge to appear on your credit card statement. Before the start of each renewal, you will be emailed a reminder notice summarizing the details of your subscription and the rate that you will be charged.
Why do I need to provide a mailing address for a digital subscription?
If your subscription includes a physical premium, we need your mailing address to deliver it to you.
Can I subscribe to WIRED if I live outside the United States?
Yes. You can subscribe to WIRED from most countries, although it may take longer to receive print issues in the mail. For assistance, please visit our contact us page.
I forgot my password. How can I recover it?
- Go to WIRED.com and click Sign In (top-right corner of your screen)
- Select Sign in another way and enter your email address
- If you are using a password to sign, click “Forgot your password? Reset it”
If there is a WIRED subscription associated with your email address, we will send you instructions for resetting your password.
How do I make changes to my email address or password?
Please visit My Account to manage your WIRED.com account information, including your email address and password.
What does it mean to link or verify my subscription? Why is this important?
Creating an online account and subscribing to the magazine are independent operations. It is possible to create an online account without being a subscriber and vice versa. In order to read unlimited articles online as a subscriber, you’ll need to link your subscription to your WIRED account.
This process may be necessary for customers who have never created an account or registered an email address with us.
To link your subscription:
- Sign In or Create an Account
- If the system does not recognize you immediately, you will need to enter your account number or subscription number, which can be found in two places: the Account Summary section of Customer Care and the mailing label of a magazine if you are a print subscriber.
- Or select the link to use your shipping address.
If you have trouble linking your subscription, please visit our contact us page for more assistance.
How do I unsubscribe from WIRED?
You can cancel your subscription (or a gift subscription) within your online account page or contact customer service for assistance.
What is your cancellation policy?
You’re in full control of your subscription and can cancel at any time. When you purchase a subscription—whether it includes print and digital access or digital access only—it begins immediately.
Please note that we do not offer refunds for cancellations. When you cancel, your subscription will remain active through the end of your current billing term, and you will not be charged again.
How can I receive confirmation of my cancellation?
Our staff would be happy to send you a confirmation. For more assistance, please visit our contact us page.
How do I check when my subscription expires?
You can view the expiration date of your subscription (or gift subscription) by visiting our contact us page for more assistance.
WIRED UK Website Closure
I am a WIRED UK subscriber; how do I access content on WIRED.com?
If you have already created an account to access the Wired UK digital edition, simply visit wired.com and sign in using the same email address and password associated with your subscription.
If you haven't already created an account to access the digital edition, please follow the instructions below:
Register your account and use your print subscription customer number and surname to create a digital access account. If you do not know your customer number, you can locate it here or with our customer service team.
From there, head to wired.com and sign in using the same email address.
I am a subscriber to WIRED UK magazine. Will I still be able to receive my magazines?
Yes, your WIRED UK magazine subscription will continue uninterrupted unless a cancellation is initiated.
Digital All Access
What is WIRED Digital All Access?
The WIRED All Access subscription provides digital access to WIRED, Vanity Fair, Vogue, Architectural Digest, Bon Appétit, and Epicurious.
What is included in the WIRED Digital All Access subscription?
- Unlimited access to WIRED, Vanity Fair, Vogue, Architectural Digest, Bon Appétit, and Epicurious. (If selected at an additional cost, The New Yorker access is also included.)
- Free WIRED tote bag
- Complete online archive access for most brands
How much does the WIRED Digital All Access subscription cost?
To see our latest offers, visit our order page.
How do I sign up for a WIRED Digital All Access subscription?
To see our latest offers, visit our order page.
If I already have a WIRED digital subscription, can I upgrade to Digital All Access?
Yes, you can upgrade your WIRED subscription to a Digital All Access subscription by contacting customer care via the chat widget at the bottom right hand corner of this page, which typically offers the fastest support. All Access is not available for print subscriptions.
If I already have a Vogue, Vanity Fair, The New Yorker, Architectural Digest, Bon Appétit, or Epicurious subscription, can I change to Digital All Access?
Other subscriptions cannot be bundled individually at this time. If you are interested in a WIRED Digital All Access subscription, please contact customer care using the chat widget at the bottom right hand corner of this page. All Access is not available for print subscriptions.
If I cancel my WIRED Digital All Access subscription, can I maintain my Vanity Fair, Vogue, The New Yorker, Architectural Digest, Bon Appétit, and Epicurious access?
Canceling your Digital All Access subscription will result in a loss of access to all brands included.
Does the WIRED Digital All Access subscription include app access?
The New Yorker (iOS and Android) and Epicurious (iOS) apps are included with your Digital All Access subscription.
Privacy policy & user agreement
Use of this site constitutes acceptance of our User Agreement and Privacy Policy and Cookie Statement and Your California Privacy Rights. WIRED may earn a portion of sales from products that are purchased through our site as part of our Affiliate Partnerships with retailers. The material on this site may not be reproduced, distributed, transmitted, cached or otherwise used, except with the prior written permission of Condé Nast Ad Choices.
Reading on a Phone, Computer, or Tablet
Why should I create an online account?
All readers are encouraged to create a free online account, regardless of their subscription status, so you can take advantage of features like saving stories to read later. If you have not done so, please create a free account now.
Are all WIRED articles available online?
All articles originally published online or in the print magazine are online and available with your subscription. The first print magazine was published in March/April 1993. You can also find print replicas of issues dating back to 2021 in our online archive.
Do I need a subscription to access WIRED.com?
If you are not a subscriber, you have limited access to WIRED’s website. All web visitors can browse all Gear articles without a subscription.
Is the magazine available on mobile and tablet devices?
Yes. The WIRED app includes web versions of all magazine articles, and it is available through the App Store. Digital editions of the magazine are also available through the Nook bookstore.
Which devices support the WIRED app?
The WIRED app can be downloaded to your iPhone, iPad, or iPod for free from the App Store. While the app is not currently available for Android devices, Android users can read WIRED stories online.
Do I need a WIRED subscription to access the WIRED app?
Yes. The app is exclusive to subscribers and is free to download. If you subscribed directly through WIRED (including WIRED.com or the WIRED app), you can view as many articles and issues as you'd like. If eligible, non-subscribers will be invited to explore the app through a free trial.
Can I share stories from the WIRED app through email or social media?
Yes, the link will direct viewers to the story on our website.
I subscribed through the WIRED app on my iPhone, iPad, or iPod. How do I get unlimited online access?
Immediately after you subscribed through the app, you were prompted to create an online account. If you have not done so, you can now.
If you subscribed through the WIRED app:
- Open the app and select Settings in the top-right corner of the screen.
- Select Sign in or create an account.
- If you do not see Sign in or create an account, select Restore your Apple purchase.
I purchased a subscription through the WIRED app. How can I cancel it?
If you subscribed through the WIRED app, you’ll need to cancel through Apple.
I subscribed to WIRED through Amazon but am no longer able to sign into WIRED.com.

If you purchased a subscription directly from Barnes & Noble, your access is limited to your Nook Color Tablet. If you have questions, please visit Barnes & Noble’s contact us page.
How do I get unlimited access to WIRED on my Nook?
- If you’re already a subscriber, open the Nook Bookstore.
- Visit the WIRED page.
- Order a monthly subscription to begin a fourteen-day trial. You will not be charged.
- After submitting your order, check your in-box. You will receive an email with instructions for redeeming your free offer as an active magazine subscriber.
How do I get unlimited access to WIRED on my Android phone or tablet?
Subscribers can read WIRED on an Android phone or tablet via WIRED.com. You can also follow WIRED via Google News, but you will need to sign in to our website to read articles.
Do I need a subscription to follow WIRED in Google News?
WIRED’s feed is free to follow, though subscribers will need to sign in to our Web site to read articles.
How can I access WIRED articles published on Flipboard?
WIRED’s feed is free to follow at https://flipboard.com/@WIRED. Articles link to WIRED.com, where subscribers have unlimited access and non-subscribers have limited access.
I purchased a WIRED subscription on Zinio. Does that provide unlimited digital access to WIRED?
If you purchased a subscription on Zinio, your access is limited to Zinio. If you have questions, please visit Zinio’s contact us page.
How do I sign up for email newsletters?
Visit wired.com/newsletter to sign up for any of our offerings, including The Daily, Classics, Gadget Lab, and more.
Where can I get my subscriber-only newsletters?
After subscribing, and when logged-in, you can sign-up for your subscriber-only newsletter at the Newsletter Hub.
I signed up for your newsletters. Why am I not receiving them regularly?
Please check your junk folder. If the problem persists, please visit our contact us page to submit your request.
How do I unsubscribe from a newsletter or marketing e-mail?
To unsubscribe from a newsletter, select Unsubscribe at the bottom of the e-mail or sign in to newyorker.com and navigate to My Account from the top-right corner. You can manage your newsletter subscriptions at the bottom of your profile.

About the WIRED Reviews team
What is the WIRED Reviews team?
WIRED’s Reviews team is a group of 13 full-time staff writers and editors with centuries of combined experience who conduct comprehensive testing on products, services, and software to write in-depth reviews and buying guides. The team was founded in 2017 and one of its original members, Adrienne So, is still on staff as a senior editor. We also work with a small group of trusted freelance contributors who are experts in their field. You’ll find an author bio that outlines each tester’s expertise on any review we publish. Our mission is to provide the most authentic and engaging buying advice for every product our audience needs or wants, to pioneer product discovery for tech enthusiasts, and to serve as a trusted hub for fair and thoughtful product reviews.
How does WIRED select products to test and review?
We’re looking to write about products our readers are interested in, which means everything from groundbreaking new tech to novel gadgets they’ve seen all over social media, to products like bed-in-a-box mattresses where it’s difficult for any individual consumer to do proper comparison shopping. Our audience is tech-savvy, so you’ll see lots of coverage of mobile phones, laptops, gaming devices, and the like, but WIRED readers also like to live comfortably and healthfully, score great deals, and often enjoy outdoor recreation.
Why should I trust WIRED’s product reviews?
Because we tell the truth and we do the work. WIRED’s Reviews team tests every product and service we write about, even when we’re picking the best Amazon Prime Day deals. Our product recommendations are made in service to readers and independently of revenue considerations. While we do get a small cut of most sales when readers click to buy recommended products discussed in our product reviews and buying guides, the content in those guides is created through a rigorous and independent editorial process and is subjected to the same high standards as everything else WIRED publishes. Content from our Reviews team is fact-checked by editors and goes through the same prepublication review process as any other WIRED story. When we make a mistake, we immediately correct it and append an editor’s note for transparency as appropriate.
Does the WIRED Reviews team use generative AI?
No. We follow the same editorial standards as everything else published by WIRED. You can read our whole policy here, but the gist is that we do not publish stories with text generated by AI, except when AI-generated text is the point of the story.
Do you purchase every product you test?
No, but we do not accept “free products” from manufacturers or make any agreements that involve a promise of editorial coverage in exchange for sending us a product. We often accept delivery of review samples directly from PR agencies and brands, which we typically don't pay for. We return or donate these samples after testing. When we know a specific product is of interest to readers and a review sample is not available, WIRED will purchase the product and the writer will donate it after testing.
How we test each product depends on what it is. We thoroughly test anything we recommend to readers and try to explain our methodology in each article without bogging it down with excessive detail many readers don’t care about. Our overall goal in all testing is to replicate the product’s regular use as closely as we can—this is why we review mattresses by sleeping on them in our homes rather than dropping a bowling ball on them in a lab where we conduct “nap tests.” Since our testing methodology is a popular question with both readers and brands, we’ve compiled the basic protocols for some of our key coverage areas below.
Ebikes: WIRED reviews upward of 50 new ebikes a year by riding them on a variety of terrain for at least 40 miles over the course of at least two weeks. We test cargo bikes by hauling kids and groceries, we ride mountain and gravel bikes on trails, and we test commuter bikes while running errands on regular city streets (including up and down steep hills). In addition to our real-life testing, we evaluate specs like weight, tire size, battery life, motor power, and the sourcing of key components to make our guides to the Best Ebikes and Best Cheap Ebikes.
Electric scooters: WIRED reviewers ride electric scooters for at least 30 miles, though often much longer, on varying terrain and under various power loads (such as laden with groceries or up and down steep hills). Our main tester, the author of our guide to the Best Electric Scooters, is Brooklyn-based Julian Chokkattu, who takes electric scooters on the same routes through Bushwick during his tests so he can evaluate how a scooter may deviate from the established baseline.
Fitness trackers: WIRED’s lead tester wears fitness trackers for at least two weeks and evaluates them on fit, specifications, durability, battery life, whether she can see the display in natural daylight, and whether features perform as advertised—for example, AI coaching, climbing software, or GPS tracking. She also evaluates companion smartphone apps based on ease of use and claimed features.
Mattresses: We sleep on any mattress we recommend for at least a week in our own homes, though we sometimes give up on a mattress after a few nights (we then tell readers to avoid it), and we will sometimes spend months long-term testing. Lead reviewer Martin Cizmar has established a level of real-life mattress testing that’s unmatched among our competitors, who frequently do a "nap test" where they form an opinion after sitting around on a mattress in their office.
Office chairs: We sit on every chair we test for several weeks while working—two weeks at the minimum, but often much longer than that. We also invite different friends and family members to try the chairs out so we can assess comfort levels for folks with different heights and body types.
Mobile phones: To compile our expansive library of smartphone reviews and guides, our testers use any smartphone they’re reviewing for at least a week, but sometimes longer. We test each phone by loading in our own SIM cards and using the phone as we would any personal device for the duration of the testing period. To compare cameras, we take the same photos on a second, similarly priced phone at the same time and study the results. For phone cases, which we test for at least a few days each, we look for alignment between ports and holes, check all buttons for clickiness, judge how it feels in our pockets, and check for how much the case is raised over the screen and camera lenses. We don't do drop tests as we don’t have enough free phones to replace all the broken ones.
Internet routers: WIRED tests Wi-Fi and mesh routers for at least one week, though often longer, in a home setting. We test the stated features and introduce stress testing, such as cutting the power to see how routers cope with a sudden loss of power. Our lead tester, Simon Hill, also runs a bevy of technical tests, including network throughput testing, file transfers, coverage heatmaps, and speed tests—all organized into a handy (and impressive) spreadsheet.
Air Purifiers: WIRED reviews more than 50 new air purifiers a year, assessing them in various home environments from coast to coast for months at a time. We test air purifiers in both homes and 100-year-old apartments with cats, dogs, and gas stoves, and near highways and in urban areas. In addition to our real-world testing, we measure decibel levels, ease of use, and efficacy, and we evaluate cost, design, length of warranty, and most importantly, the rate of air exchange in a specific-size room, making our deep dives, reviews, and Best Air Purifier guide essential reading.
Soundbars: WIRED’s staffers, including Parker Hall and Ryan Waniata, evaluate soundbars using a wide variety of testing material, from custom-made Dolby Atmos demos to familiar movies like Guardians of the Galaxy, sitcoms like Seinfeld and Parks and Recreation, and everything in between. We test apps and features like auto-calibration, surround sound speakers, and multiroom audio integration in multiple settings wherever possible. For music testing, we stream carefully curated playlists and random radio stations at compressed and lossless resolutions over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi where available. We live with these products over multiple days at minimum to test their usability the same way we expect you to use them.
Headphones and earbuds: Headphones and earbuds come in a multitude of styles, sizes, and varieties and we test them in accordance. For all headphones we test, sound quality, comfort, and fit are of the utmost importance. For wireless headphones and earbuds, we pay special attention to key aspects like ease of pairing and setup, battery life, app connection and settings, and convenience features like speak-to-chat. When focusing on sound quality, we use curated playlists with familiar music (from Fleetwood Mac’s “The Chain” to The Weeknd’s “Starboy”) in both compressed and lossless resolution where applicable. For spatial audio, we test music and videos in multiple formats, including Dolby Atmos.
Televisions: TVs are among the most important products in A/V, and we test them accordingly. We spend at least a week with each TV we test, using it day and night as our daily driver. We utilize carefully selected video and audio content (from Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows on Blu-ray to Our Planet in Dolby Vision and Atmos on Netflix). Our testing material runs the gamut, including live broadcasts, streaming content, and physical media with high-end Ultra HD Blu-ray players. We use Spears & Munsil’s latest Ultra HD Benchmark discs to lock in settings and evaluate multiple resolution and HDR formats, including Dolby Vision, HDR10, and HDR10+. We watch content in various light conditions and test usability features, from smart assistants to services like AirPlay 2 and Chromecast to paint a holistic picture.
Running gear: Our lead writer runs four to five times a week, around 20 to 25 miles per week, and evaluates the gear’s overall performance with a mix of long runs, interval runs, and trail and road running.
Pizza ovens: To name the best pizza ovens, we test each oven in our backyard for a minimum of two weeks. While using the oven, our testers also use handheld infrared thermometers to take the temperature of the baking stone at various places to gauge how evenly they heat and cook. We test all ovens with homemade dough, store-bought dough, and frozen pizzas.
Luggage and backpacks: WIRED tests luggage designed primarily for air travel by taking it on at least two flights. When reviewing backpacks, our testers wear them for at least two weeks. In addition to this regular use, we also evaluate design details, like whether they have straight or curved zippers, what gauge the zippers are, whether they're toothed or coiled, what the warranty is, whether the hardware is metal or plastic, or whether the fabric is sustainable. Our reviewers also do things like fill backpacks full of books and toss them around, and kick carry-on bags to see whether they get foot marks or are easy to clean.
Umbrellas: Our testers use umbrellas several times, whenever it rains. We test them as a normal person would while checking for the main hallmarks of what makes a good umbrella, as listed in our buying guide. We also aim to get a good sense of how each umbrella handles gusts and heavy storms.
Webcams: We use every webcam we test for several weeks as a daily driver, and our testers also try to compare the image quality with another similar model. Reviewers make audio recordings to see how the mics pick up their voices. Webcam testers often solicit feedback on appearance and sound quality during our weekly Gear team meetings, which take place over Zoom.
Bidets: For our guide to the Best Bidets, our testers install the bidets on a toilet in their homes and use each sample for at least a week.
Monitors: Reviewer Nena Farrell leads our coverage of the best computer monitors and tests each pick for at least one week, with a minimum of three working days. She sets monitors up with both a PC and Mac laptop to check performance, and she runs at least two different video games to see how the monitor performs, even if it isn't a monitor designed specifically for video games.
Camp cookware: Reviewer Scott Gilbertson famously lives in an RV, so he is always testing camp cookware. In fact, grills and other cookware are tested for months before they ever make it into a guide. He cooks outside every day, rotating stoves every few months so he gets a good sense of how they perform, how they stand up to weather, and how hard they are to clean.
Tents: We aim to spend at least a week in every tent, ideally in a variety of weather conditions. Every pocket, zipper, guy line, and feature is tested. Will the rainfly catch on the door zippers? Is the ventilation good? Is the tent easy to set up? We assess all of the above and more, and list our favorites in our Best Tents buying guide.
Meal kits: When testing meal kit delivery services, each service is evaluated meal-by-meal over the course of a few days. Our lead reviewer follows recipes to the letter and substitutes ingredients only if something arrives inedible—for example, if something thaws during shipment or the produce is moldy (these substitutions are always noted). She always has at least one other person try a meal and notes down both of their first impressions and opinions before discussing the meal further. She assesses packaging, ingredient quality, texture, and taste, then factors in price to make recommendations.
Security cameras: Indoor and outdoor security cameras are tested for at least one month. We test any manufacturer claims and special features, like motion detection or smartphone alerts, and stress-test the cameras as well. We also test videofeed quality and loading times.
Video doorbells: We test video doorbells for a minimum of two weeks. Any manufacturer claims are tested and verified, as are smartphone companion apps or smart home connectivity options. We also consider the data storage, retention, and privacy policies of the manufacturers of each camera we test, as these things also factor into our recommendations.
Sex toys and tech: We test sex tech for a minimum of two weeks using common sense. We test on different erogenous zones and different bodies. We also conduct controlled tests for features like battery life, waterproofness, and ease of cleaning. We test manufacturer claims as well.
Espresso machines and coffee gear: We use espresso machines and coffee gear for at least two weeks in everyday situations. We also perform some controlled tests. Our lead reviewer tests for consistency, how hot the heating elements get, how quickly they heat up, how much time needs to pass between switching functions (brewing versus steaming), and the like. She also tests general usability. Is the machine easy to clean and maintain? Are things that need to be cleaned easily accessible? Does it look nice on the counter or does it seem to acquire a grime after only a couple uses? Does the steaming wand work efficiently? All of these factors inform our assessment.
Coffee grinders: Our lead reviewer assesses coffee grinders for at least two weeks using a mix of everyday use and controlled tests. She’s mostly testing for consistency, as well as factors like how quickly grime builds up in the burrs, how accessible the burrs are for cleaning, how loud the grinder is, and how finely or coarsely it can grind. She also assesses for ease of cleaning and overall maintenance requirements.
Digital cameras: We test cameras by using them over a period of (ideally) months, but often just weeks because DSLR cameras, compact system cameras, and mirrorless cameras are generally loaned to us on a short-term basis, and camera companies are eager to pass them on to the next reviewer. Our lead reviewer tries to shoot at least 500 images on every camera he tests. He then views and edits the resulting RAW and JPG files in Darktable.
Coolers: We test coolers by putting a standard bag of cube ice inside it on a warm day (at least 75 degrees Fahrenheit), putting the cooler in the shade, and then timing how long it takes for the ice to melt. We also assess weight, portability, durability, and overall design.
Binoculars: We test binoculars by going birding. And to baseball games. And stargazing. For months and months.

title: WIRED’s ‘On Background’ Policy
raw_text:
WIRED’s ‘On Background’ Policy
Many powerful companies make a practice of obfuscating or dodging accountability when speaking to media outlets by providing information while insisting it not be attributed to anyone in particular, and sometimes not even to the company itself. For that reason, WIRED is joining the Verge, Quartz, and others in making its editorial standards clearer.
Anyone talking to WIRED reporters in any official capacity does so on the record by default. This means that what you say or write can be quoted and attributed to you by name, not just as “a company spokesperson.” We typically allow anonymity only to sources who could face retaliation or be endangered by the information they provide, and when we do so we explain our reasons to readers. As Julia Angwin, editor in chief of the Markup, has noted, “Corporate spokespeople who are paid to provide information simply don’t meet the criteria for being granted anonymity.”
Sometimes we may agree to have a conversation on background, meaning we can use the information you provide, but will not identify you by name. Conversations are on background only when we agree to it. If you send us a statement “on background” without prior agreement, we may still treat it as on the record.
You must also get our agreement for each proposed condition of the conversation, such as requests to not quote a particular statement directly or to identify a source in a certain way. Please be clear about your exact requests every time you speak with WIRED. At our discretion we may also tell our readers why we’re providing the information in this way.
Off-the-record conversations cannot be used for publication, and they also must be agreed to (which we rarely do for corporate spokespeople).
The companies you speak for play significant roles in shaping the future; we have a responsibility to tell our readers how we got the information about your plans to shape it.

title: ‘This Is Not a Drill’: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Are Setting the Internet on Fire
raw_text:
Internet security and web administration teams around the world are scrambling to prevent widespread disaster. On Wednesday, the developers behind the much-used PHP programming language released emergency security updates designed to fix critical flaws that could be exploited to allow attackers to gain dangerous remote control of victim systems.
The PHP Foundation detailed the two critical vulnerabilities—CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619—which impact “all PHP installations serving web requests” going back to PHP version 5, released in July 2004. However, only PHP 8.2 and newer are still supported and will receive patches, according to the alert. The PHP Foundation noted, though, that some PHP distributions and third-party vendors still produce legacy fixes. The caveat is significant because ubiquitous and foundational web layers like PHP can persist forgotten and un-updated in historic internet infrastructure.
“There are no complete mitigations, updating is the only safe choice,” the PHP Foundation wrote in its advisories. Security experts warn of the potential dire consequences of overlooking unpatched systems.
“This is not a drill,” says Lukasz Olejnik, an independent security consultant and visiting senior research fellow at King’s College London. Since its development in the 1990s, PHP has evolved into an essential scripting language for web development and is used across vast swaths of the internet in websites and software. Everything from publishing systems like WordPress and Drupal to e-commerce platforms like Adobe’s Magento are built on PHP.
Olejnik likens the widespread use of the programming language to critical infrastructure.
“The impact is enormous,” he says of PHP’s security flaws, adding that millions of systems could be impacted. “Especially if attackers would turn to exploiting these vulnerabilities fast. Worst case is wormable malware affecting big chunks of the internet.”
The overriding fear for security teams and developers is that malicious hackers could quickly jump upon the vulnerabilities and begin exploiting deployments before they are fixed. Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare reported it was “seeing early attacks emerging” before the PHP Foundation had detailed the vulnerabilities and released fixes. “We expect mass attacks to start within 15 minutes of the release,” security firm Sansec wrote ahead of the fixes, which were released just before 10 am ET on Wednesday.
“Most of the web runs on PHP and this bug is in a file upload interface that’s like a front door with no lock,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “An attacker does not need to know which site they are hitting or even the actual software it runs. They send one crafted upload to any server they can find, and that is the entire attack.”
Ahead of the updated versions of PHP becoming available, some organizations took their websites offline as a precautionary measure. Multiple sites belonging to the Finnish government, including the National Land Survey, were inaccessible, according to reports. French government websites and the Port of Rotterdam’s website were also offline, according to Reuters.
“Everybody should patch immediately, exploitation may happen very fast and at a scale,” says Olejnik. “AI makes exploiting such vulnerabilities of immediate importance. Like, indeed, a minute or so.”
Security company Wiz, which is owned by Google, claimed its researchers discovered the vulnerabilities in PHP partially using AI tools, while OpenAI and security firm Calif also say they independently discovered the issues and worked together. Dubbing an exploitation demonstration php2shell , the Wiz researchers write that in some cases the vulnerabilities can be exploited “fairly easily.”
“The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory,” Wiz writes in its research. “That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.”
Details of the upcoming vulnerabilities first appeared from the maintainers behind PHP on October 20. In a short post on the PHP website, the PHP Foundation wrote it was giving “advance notice” of the security flaws and upcoming release of the fixes. While omitting specific details about the vulnerabilities or the versions impacted, it said both flaws are considered to have a “critical” 9.2 score out of 10 on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).
“We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild,” the security warning on the PHP site said ahead of Wednesday’s release. According to reports from Bleeping Computer and Ars Technica, some details about the vulnerabilities may have leaked before they were due to officially be published.
The early warning from the PHP Foundation may have given some developers, security teams, and companies enough of a heads up to start preparing to update systems using PHP. Ahead of the details being published, warnings from the EU’s Computer Emergency Response Team (EU-CERT) and Australia's cybersecurity agency said IT teams should be prepared to update their systems as soon as possible, with the potential for websites to be taken offline while fixes are applied.
Similarly, the UK’s National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) published an alert saying organizations should “prepare for immediate updating of systems” using PHP. “Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organizations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated,” the agency wrote online.
The NCSC advises that organizations and businesses should identify systems running PHP across their tech infrastructure. There should be a particular focus on systems using PHP that are connected to the internet, including monitoring them for any potential exploitation. The next step is applying PHP updates as they are available and monitoring for updates from software companies as they may use PHP within their apps or services.
“If you find signs of compromise, isolate the system, preserve your web server and PHP logs, and report it to your local FBI field office,” Brett Leatherman, the FBI’s cyber assistant director posted online. “Those reports help us identify the actors involved and warn other organizations before they become victims.”

title: WhatsApp Help Pages Leaked Hidden Instructions for a Meta Chatbot
raw_text:
Dozens of WhatsApp web pages designed to answer people’s questions about Meta’s encrypted messaging app inadvertently exposed the company’s own instructions to its chatbot. These included some sections titled “WHAT NOT TO SAY” to users asking questions and explicit instructions not to provide people with legal advice.
A new analysis has found that around 80 help and FAQ pages across WhatsApp’s website exposed text instructions that were designed for a large language model, specifically one of Meta’s own. The instructions, according to findings from privacy company Redact, appeared in the webpages’ code and contained written details that were not explicitly on the WhatsApp help pages.
Among the 100 blocks of hidden text, the directions appeared to provide guidance to steer an LLM from answering users questions in unhelpful ways and provide a glimpse at how instructions for chatbots are created. In one instance, the WhatsApp page on how to delete your account included instructions that, alongside other advice, said, “Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority” about the issue. WIRED viewed the exposed text, which can still be seen when viewing the underlying code of archived versions of the help pages.
“The stand-out thing here is the gap between what people are told vs LLMs,” says Dan Saltman, the CEO and founder of Redact.dev. He says the company regularly scans the sites and privacy policies of big tech firms, and that many of the WhatsApp instructions the team found were straightforward and point people towards other official support channels. Still, it does not appear the instructions were meant for public exposure.
After WIRED contacted Meta about the issue, the text was removed from across all the pages, with WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman saying it was being displayed due to a bug that has now been fixed. “These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI,” Breckman says. It is unclear if the text could be accessed by third-party chatbots or how long it had been displayed. “We train our support chatbots to be as helpful as possible,” Breckman says.
The exposed instructions appeared under code blocks with a heading: “HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude.” They are no longer visible in the live pages’ code.
On the page “About reporting and blocking on WhatsApp,” the hidden instructions included a series of statements to follow if a “user mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation.”
“Do not cite, quote, interpret, or reference WhatsApp Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, or any legal document,” the instructions said, adding not to make any statements about WhatsApp liability or non-liability. “Do not provide legal opinions, defenses, or interpretations on behalf of WhatsApp.”
“Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly,” other parts of the instructions said.
Breckman, the WhatsApp spokesperson, says that the company provides users with transparent information about their data rights and how they can take actions. “We want our product support chatbots to be focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp—not to offer legal advice,” Breckman says.
Other exposed instructions said what to respond with if a user says they are deaf or hard of hearing, including: “This statement is background about the user, NOT their support request.” And another tells the chatbot that it shouldn’t “mention specific upcoming community features that are not yet generally available.”

title: Encryption Is Getting Squeezed From All Sides
raw_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
Oh, Canada. The Great White North is the latest country to contemplate legislation that could essentially mandate backdoors and increase data retention in encrypted services. The proposed changes have prompted the Canadian anti-censorship company Psiphon VPN—which keeps millions of Iranians online during repressive internet shutdowns—to say it will leave the country if the bill passes. And Psiphon is not the only one.
Encrypted messaging app Signal has said it would exit the Canadian market because the legislation would require unacceptable changes to its open source projects. Apple and Meta have criticized the bill, and DuckDuckGo and NordVPN say they would consider pulling their services, too. But as countries around the world contemplate similar legislation, even larger questions begin to emerge about which states or regions could differentiate themselves as being safe havens for privacy services if global hostility to encryption continues to rise.
It’s been maddening and disturbing to see more and more democratic countries around the world propose changes to their surveillance and data collection laws, with the aim of giving cops and intelligence agencies greater powers to access people’s information. Governments already have broad digital surveillance powers and investigative tactics to solve crimes that involve encrypted data, but legislative proposals almost inevitably include provisions to expand this access even more—mandating additional logging and what amounts to backdoors or intentional flaws in encrypted products, which cryptographers and security engineers have consistently said cannot be built safely. Truly everyone who understands the issue has said it as much for decades. Yet policymakers return again and again to the idea, somehow expecting a different conclusion or a new breakthrough that will make it all possible.
“There have always been some officials within certain agencies that tend to view technology as a crime scene in and of itself, and it becomes a myopic point of fixation where access is desired,” says Kate Robertson, a senior research associate at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab. “But that type of siloed thinking forgets that technology needs to be the secure operating platform for hospitals, for banks, for national security agencies, for police services themselves to protect victims who report private information to them.”
In recent years, the UK and Australia have introduced sweeping surveillance reforms that can compel companies to break their encryption. Other encryption-threatening proposals have also emerged in the EU, France, India, Ireland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and others. While not all measures have passed into law or been enacted, the hostility is clear.
First proposed in 2025, and partially revised due to blistering criticism from tech companies and civil society, Canada’s C-22 bill can broadly place requirements on tech companies, including those outside of Canada, to introduce “technical capabilities” that allow data to be accessed for law enforcement purposes. Like many such bills, C-22 says that companies will not have to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their systems. But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone. And this risk is only heightened even more by the ease with which anyone can now use AI tools for reverse engineering and system mapping.
“Companies could be asked to introduce vulnerabilities, build backdoors, bypass, weaken or otherwise defeat encryption,” members of the US House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committee said in a May letter to Canadian officials.
In addition to potential impacts on encryption, C-22 also includes provisions that could require companies to retain metadata about user activity, something that many privacy focused services (including VPN services from Psiphon and DuckDuckGo) intentionally avoid. As a result, these companies say, they would be forced to change their business models to collect data they do not need or want to collect about their users. And researchers say that such product changes would diminish user trust while increasing the potential for widespread surveillance.
“If you are asking and requiring for this infrastructural change—that they retain metadata by default—it is creating a surveillance capability within a tool that didn’t have it,” says Afsaneh Rigot, the founder of the De|Center, a research organization that aims to reduce the risk of technological harms. “There are contexts like Iran and other contexts globally, who all of this has a trickle effect on. It's not going to stay in Canada because these types of laws always get copy pasted around the world.”
As more countries contemplate such laws, developers focused on privacy and anti-censorship tools are increasingly casting around for safe jurisdictions to operate in. But this still doesn’t solve the problem of reaching users in all countries around the world and for now, there are no sure bets.
“Changing your headquarters isn’t much of a plan B when the law follows your users, as C-22 would,” says Joseph Lorenzo-Hall, security portfolio lead at the Internet Society. “The strongest protection is holding as little user data as possible, but ‘we don’t have it’ is no defense if governments can force you to start collecting it. A safe haven needs more than favorable winds in strong encryption. It needs laws that let companies keep their privacy promises and defend them against foreign threats to confidentiality and integrity.”
Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.
