title: Old-School Credit Card Scams Are Far From Dead
raw_text:
Welcome to Kernel Panic! A weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
When every random text message feels like it’s a scam, and with AI supercharging digital fraud, old-time credit card skimmers and bogus letters that arrive in the mail may seem laughable as potential threats in 2026. But as we all suffer through a seemingly unending barrage of potential scams, these antiquated attacks are still costing victims around the world dearly.
The fake-new-credit-card-in-your-mailbox trick is particularly insidious. Portugal, France, and Germany have all had waves of physical credit card scams in recent years where criminals have mailed phony replacement cards or letters to potential victims. Included letters often claim a current card is set to expire soon, whether the victim actually has one that's about to expire or not. In order for the new (fake) card to be activated, the scam letter says, it should be registered using an included QR code or URL. Some sham cards even have real customer names printed on them, says Georg Hauer, an adviser for digital banks. “The card is almost like a token that creates the trust that is needed in order to fall for the actual trick,” he says.
If someone scans the QR code, they’re typically redirected to a fake banking website, where they’re asked to enter their details—potentially giving cybercriminals direct access to their real accounts. “This has been escalating for close to two years, and I believe that this type of scam might have proven to be successful enough to be rolled out in other countries,” Hauer says. “The cost of producing a personalized fake card has dropped in recent years thanks to AI just being able to copy a design based on an image, and the higher conversion rate per victim might justify the extra costs.”
Mail scams aren’t the only ’90s throwback on the docket. The US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Alabama indicted two Romanian nationals last week on charges related to alleged credit card skimming. Authorities say the pair specifically targeted government SNAP food assistance benefits distributed to recipients in most states on antiquated magnetic stripe-only debit cards, or Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards.
Fraud related to chip credit cards does exist as well, but this recent case serves as a reminder that classic skimmers targeting magnetic stripe credit cards are still deployed by scammers because there’s apparently still enough swiping going on to make it worth their while. The FBI says that EBT card skimming has risen in popularity among scammers since about 2021.
“Skimmer fraud is rampant with losses in the United States alone reaching over $1 billion each year,” US Attorney Phillip W. Williams Jr. said in a press release about the recent indictment. (That billion dollars includes multiple types of credit card skimming, not just EBT targeting.) “It is a silent insidious theft that occurs by merely swiping a credit card at a point of sale.”
Gary Warner, the director of intelligence at the cybersecurity firm DarkTower points out that dozens of states continue to use mag-stripe only cards for benefits purposes. “The risk here is that if the mag stripe is compromised, a clone of the card can be created and access not only the current value, but future value as well,” he says.
More broadly, Warner tells us, there are still multiple risks related to making payments using the magnetic stripes on any cards—even if they also include more secure chips that have been issued over the last decade-plus. “Non-bank ATMs and smaller non-chain merchants may expose your chip-enabled card to mag stripe reading,” Warner says. “Mag-stripe skimmers are often installed in such a way that the chip read is forced to fail.”
While magnetic stripe cards have gradually been phased out in the US over many years, they’re still around. Mastercard, for example, said last month that it will stop issuing any cards with stripes in 2029, and its remaining batch will be completely out of circulation by 2033. In the meantime, financial fraud has become one of the largest overall crime types in the US and around the world. Many attacks are focused on social engineering, mass phishing message campaigns, and other fraud where money ends up being sent by victims in transactions that often look legitimate to banks and other financial institutions.
Hauer says criminals will always try to use methods that let them steal as much money as possible, even if that means sending physical letters in the mail. “The real idea behind some of these scams is to not essentially try to steal €2,000 from someone’s bank account, but rather actually empty a proper savings account, which holds much more money,” he says.
If you feel like you’re already dodging scams left and right, there are some (relatively) easy takeaways to protect yourself from these old time scams. Avoid swiping cards whenever possible. And when you do need to swipe—as is, of course, the case with many EBT cards—do your best to check whether the terminal you’re about to use looks unusual, altered, or broken in any way. If so, use a different terminal. And apply the same skepticism that you have about texts and calls to letters as well. It feels like the only organizations that send mail these days are marketers, healthcare providers, banks, and the IRS, but scammers are still lurking there, too.
Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

title: An OpenAI Agent Hacked Australia’s Health Service. Their Government Found Out Months Later
raw_text:
Australia is investigating whether OpenAI broke the law after an agent hacked into its health statistics portal in the first widely known incident of an AI agent hacking a government website.
The Australian government is reviewing whether it should involve the federal police after the agent accessed non-public files from the social and health services agency, Services Australia, in June.
Australia only found out about the incident when OpenAI alerted the government on September 10—almost three months after the hack—by sending an email to a public mailbox. Sam Altman had reportedly not mentioned the incident when he met Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, earlier this month, even though OpenAI had been aware since August. The company took “way too long” and the notification should not have just gone through a public inbox, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a press conference in New York on Wednesday. There will also be an inquiry into why Services Australia then took five days to escalate the email to Australia’s Cyber Security Centre.
OpenAI’s agent had been conducting internet based research into health statistics in a development project by an internal OpenAI research team. When it could not access certain information, the agent attempted alternative ways until it found a work around and gained unauthorized access. It also wrote files to the internal server, which the government is waiting on OpenAI for more technical information on. The government is also investigating whether the agent gained unauthorised access to three additional government websites it interacted with.
“There will obviously be legal consequences on it,” Albanese said as he disclosed the “unacceptable” incident. He said he had spoken with Altman over the phone earlier that day about his “extreme concern” about the incident and “disappointment” with the nature and length of time the company took to inform the government. While Albanese did not answer whether he had apologised, Altman “clearly accepted that the company had not done good enough,” he said.
The Australian government currently believes no one’s personal data was accessed, though investigations are ongoing. The website in question is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics such as spending. It was therefore behind much lower levels of security than personal data would have been, Marles said in Sydney. “The impact of the incident is actually relatively minor, but this is a serious incident, obviously, and one that is completely unacceptable,” he cautioned.
A number of incidents over the summer, including OpenAI agents’ hacking of HuggingFace—highlighting the threat of frontier model agents acting rogue—were raised at the United Nations General Assembly this week, with Secretary General António Guterres welcoming calls to control AI. Altman himself had warned the United Nations Security Council earlier on Wednesday about his concern that humans could lose control of these systems.
“It was a shock that it occurred, because it was real and serious,” Albanese said about the incident. “But it also, I think, was something that had been predicted, including by the AI companies themselves.”
Australia is establishing a task force to look at the incident and emerging AI cyber threats. It will consider possible law enforcement and legislative responses to ensure that incidents like this don’t happen again.

title: Trump Aides Admit the House Is a Lost Cause
raw_text:
Trump White House aides see almost no paths to Republicans keeping control of the House in the midterm elections and are more focused on redoubling their efforts to save the Senate majority.
That has been the takeaway for officials in GOP groups who have been discussing the state of play with White House aides in recent weeks, according to three sources familiar with the situation.
It all comes as the White House moves into damage-control mode after contemplating for the first time earlier this month, as Inner Loop previously reported, that Republicans could possibly lose both chambers of Congress.
The general expectation is that the House has become a lost cause. Races that Republican congressional leadership once thought they could flip in order to offset Democratic gains are no longer considered attainable.
The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Speaker Mike Johnson, has now pulled ad buys in Democratic districts in Michigan and Ohio they were hoping to flip, as well as in the Republican seat being vacated in Nebraska by the retiring Don Bacon. The fund also started canceling remaining ad reservations in two House races where Republicans are seeking reelection in New Jersey and Iowa.
White House aides have shifted their focus to pushing an all-out defense of the Senate majority, which is also looking problematic but to a lesser degree than the House, the sources say. (Polling models and prediction markets agree.)
The aides see the Senate as still in play in large part because early returns for mail ballots have been relatively strong and comparable to 2024 presidential election levels in key Senate battleground states, sources say.
Trump officials at MAGA Inc. have also privately discussed how if Republicans can win some combination of senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, that would form a firewall that complicates Democrats' path to snatching control of the Senate.
Still, Trump officials appear to have conceded they are unlikely to win in North Carolina. Senate Republicans’ campaign arm has paused ad spending in North Carolina since the start of October, mirroring pullbacks by other outside groups.
“President Trump is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate,” says White House spokesperson Liz Huston in a statement.
The state of play—retreating from a state like North Carolina, where Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair is on the ballot—would have been unthinkable just a few months ago.
But it speaks to the torrid political climate for Republicans heading into the last stretch of the midterm cycle, which appears to worsen by the week as high gas and living prices caused by the Iran war remain sticky in voters' minds.
With 20 days until the election, sources say, Trump officials are looking to get maximum turnout from the MAGA base in November, rather than trying to capture swing voters who polls show are not breaking for Republicans.
"Republicans remain laser focused on winning and protecting and expanding President Trump's majorities,” says Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassare in a statement. “We're thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent.”
The effort has manifested in a direct voter outreach play with the president crisscrossing the country to reach out directly to his supporters, showing up at rallies in states that should have been reliably Republican.
Trump started the week by hitting the trail in Ohio, where Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown has been polling consistently ahead of Republican Jon Husted, who has weathered negative ads branding him as "the face of data centers."
On Tuesday, the president flew to Wasilla, Alaska—once the home of former governor and vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin—to help the Republican Senate incumbent Dan Sullivan, who has been trailing Democrat Mary Peltola.
And after stumping in Arizona and Kentucky later this week, Trump is set to host a $1 million-per-plate fundraiser dinner for MAGA Inc. at his Mar-a-Lago club, replenishing a war chest that is being emptied at an increasing rate.
Trump has remained steadfast in his belief that he can drive his supporters to vote in November if he hits the trail, as he did in the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, a person familiar with his thinking tells Inner Loop.
But Trump, whose polling continues to be among the worst on record for any president, is not always wanted at rallies. To date, the president has not done a rally in Iowa with Republican candidate Ashley Hinson, who recently began to buck the president and called for measures that would help end the Iran war altogether.

title: Elon Musk’s America PAC Is Quietly Funding November’s Most Consequential Elections
raw_text:
Elon Musk’s America PAC is focusing its war chest on the most consequential Senate races this midterm cycle—and doing so by financing attack ads on Democrats, as voters nationwide sour on the Trump administration’s agenda.
The trend of political parties and outside groups focusing on trashing their opponents is not a new phenomenon. But America PAC's approach has been unusual: for every dollar it has spent supporting GOP Senate candidates, it has spent almost three dollars attacking Democrats.
To monitor America PAC's spending on digital ads and mailers this cycle, our ace team at WIRED has created a live tracker that updates daily and highlights where Musk's political contributions are heading as we enter the waning years of Trump’s second term.
The political stakes are especially high for Republicans this midterms cycle because of the possibility of Democrats taking the majority in the US Senate, should the party flip four battleground races and retain three of the Senate seats it currently holds.
For Musk, the implications of a Democratic-controlled Senate would also be far-reaching, as he personally could become the target of congressional investigations, while his companies might be affected by bills related to tech and AI regulation.
Texas Senate Race
For the critical Texas Senate race, America PAC has poured more than $9.4 million into ads opposing Democratic candidate James Talarico and roughly $1.8 million into ads backing Republican candidate and state attorney general Ken Paxton.
The lopsided spending here is perhaps the least surprising of all of the close Senate contests. Paxton comes with so much personal baggage—from facing impeachment charges that were eventually dropped to having his wife (who has since endorsed him with an ad that doesn’t mention him by name) file for divorce on “biblical grounds”—that trying to boost him with ads highlighting his background is tough.
Republicans in Texas also cannot realistically do positive ads of President Donald Trump and Paxton together, since both men have terrible approval ratings.
The largest single expenditures by America PAC have been two $1.3 million digital media buys opposing Talarico. America PAC has not put any money into television ads, which is being handled by other groups, like MAGA Inc., the Trump-affiliated super PAC.
Meanwhile, the Senate Republican Conference–affiliated Texas PAC has so far booked the lion's share of television ads. Punchbowl News reported last month that Texas PAC has booked around $120 million and was looking to buy $100 million in ad slots before November 3.
Ohio Senate Race
In Ohio’s Senate race, America PAC has spent $3.3 million against Democrat Sherrod Brown compared to $1.6 million supporting Republican candidate Jon Husted.
Husted has been struggling to distance himself from supporting data centers at a time when voters in the state have become fed up with rising costs associated with the projects. Husted has been tagged as "the face of data centers" because of a planned Nvidia data center project in Ohio that will be leased by OpenAI, and for his past support for data centers when he served in the state government.
The effort by Brown to cast Husted as the champion of data centers has in fact been so effective that a memo by the Senate Republicans' campaign arm in August said it was tying an anchor around the neck of Husted's public polling.
At a rally this week in Ohio, despite the cratering public support for data centers, Trump could not help himself and declared to the crowd: “We want them.” Husted’s campaign quickly replied that it should be a “local decision.”
Iowa Senate Race
In Iowa, America PAC has spent $1.5 million hitting Democratic candidate Josh Turek, while only spending roughly $100,000 supporting the Republican candidate Ashley Hinson—the biggest disparity, according to the WIRED tracker.
To put that another way: To date, Musk's political operation has spent a staggering 14 times more attacking Turek than supporting Hinson.
This could be because Hinson has taken great pains to distance herself from Trump's agenda. She recently called on Trump to ban diesel exports and end the Iran war (after previously voting six times against the House resolution to end the conflict), after Turek called for both of those measures.
To illustrate the upside-down nature of this race, Hinson recently launched attack ads against Turek, accusing him without evidence of having “received tens of millions in support from men in the Epstein files,” a remarkable situation given that Trump has sought to tamp down any mention of the files because of the negative blowback on him personally.
Once again, pro-Republican ads are likely not helpful when the candidate is trying to run a race apart from Trump and is barely ahead in the polls in what should be a safe Republican seat. In the most recent New York Times/Siena poll, Hinson was just one single, solitary point ahead of Turek.

title: The White House Is Starting to Panic Over the Midterms
raw_text:
President Donald Trump has told aides that he thinks Republicans could still outperform expectations in the midterm elections this November, seemingly unwilling to confront the worsening political climate for the GOP.
But aides acknowledge privately that the national polling for Trump is shockingly bad, and the White House, in recent weeks, has begun to contemplate for the first time losing both the House and Senate majorities.
One longtime Trumpworld operative, who correctly predicted weeks before the 2024 presidential election that Trump was on course to win every battleground state, summed it up for Inner Loop: “Oh, yeah, we're going to get creamed.”
Trump's approval rating recently dropped to 37 percent in a Wall Street Journal poll, the lowest of any president heading into a midterm election dating back to 1990, when these polls first began. Trump’s more positive outlook has been informed in part by internal polling that shows Republicans down by less in individual House races, the sources say.
“No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle tells WIRED. “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”
To counter the deeply negative political environment for Republicans this cycle, Trump's team started looking for foreign policy wins last month that he would be able to tout to voters in order to encourage turnout from his MAGA base, sources say.
That led Trump to quickly sign an agreement between the US and Denmark that allows more American forces on Greenland, even though it stopped short of a US takeover that the president has long desired.
Trump also proclaimed an oil deal with Venezuela. However, that deal is likely to need renegotiating because it asserts a 100-year concession on oil production that contravenes Venezuela's national hydrocarbons law barring such practices.
But while Trump sees foreign policy as a legacy-defining issue, voters have been far more focused on domestic issues like high grocery and gas prices.
Diesel prices hit a record high this month and regular gasoline reached a national average of $4.43 a gallon, according to the AAA, while Trump has been on the opposite side of public opinion on tech issues like AI regulation and data centers.
Now, with their election chances that much slimmer, Trumpworld is much more concerned about planning a response to what will likely be an immediate crush of subpoenas from Democrats in Congress, the sources say.
Broadly speaking, the White House expects a dual track of Trump asserting executive privilege and attorney-client protections, the bedrock legal principle designed to protect confidential discussions with lawyers, to shield senior aides from oversight probes.
Attorney-client privilege is set to be supercharged when it involves government lawyers, after the US Supreme Court ruled in the so-called Trump immunity decision in 2024 that not even federal courts could “peel back the curtain” to examine discussions that involve deliberations central to the presidency.
One unique aspect of Trump's second term has been the conversion of his personal lawyers into government lawyers, producing a consistent network of overlapping legal protections around himself and his top aides.
Trump's former personal lawyer Todd Blanche, for example, has become the attorney general. Many of Trump's aides were previously represented by the current number three at DOJ, Stanley Woodward, who also was a Trump 2024 campaign lawyer. Trump's former appellate lawyer, Will Scharf, recently moved from White House staff secretary to White House counsel, replacing former Trump lawyer David Warrington.
Trump's aides are hoping that the double protections will stymie Democrats for years. And they have some precedent: Trump's White House counsel from his first term, Don McGahn, only testified to Congress about the Mueller investigation after Trump had already left office.
After November 3, the midterms will end in the minds of most Americans. But for Trump’s White House, it’s all just beginning.

title: She’s 28, Loves God and Her Family, and Might Be the Reason You Can’t Have Kids
raw_text:
By 5 am every morning, Emma Waters is on the sofa with a blanket, plotting America’s baby-making future. For two hours, she stays off her phone, inspired by Deep Work, the self-help bestseller. At 7:30, she does emails. Waters, 28 years old, is a monk of productivity who makes motherhood look like all-natural Adderall.
At 8 am, it’s time for breakfast and the Bible. Waters tries to live her life according to the mantra “Love God, get married, have babies.” She asks that I not use the real names of her two daughters for their safety, even though they’ve been printed elsewhere. I’ll call them Gertie and Ophelia, which are close enough.
All morning, they play. Ophelia, the baby, runs around in white tights, shirtless, clutching a pink purse; Gertie’s doll won’t stop crying. Jack, Waters’ husband, flits in and out. There isn’t much to say about Jack, other than that he’s hot, is studying to be a preacher, and has a big desk at home, much bigger than Waters’, featuring a bust of Nietzsche. In the same room, Waters has a pull-out secretary where she takes meetings, not far from a portrait of a glowering President Trump.
The only thing Waters doesn’t really do is exercise; she hasn’t found the time.
Not many people outside of DC have heard of Waters, who mostly works from home in a dreary Pennsylvania suburb named after a long-offshored manufacturer. Yet Waters is a factory for policy papers and op-eds extolling the harms of unregulated reproductive technology, probing the moral issues that liberals don’t want to touch with a 10-foot turkey baster. At least once a month, reporting on fertility, I ask for an academic source and am instead directed to Waters, author of a biblical women’s leadership book that basically says the best thing about the Barbie movie was the patriarchy.
The craziest thing is that, in certain ways, she’s a voice of reason. America’s $10 billion fertility industry is suffering a massive PR crisis that makes the embryo mix-ups and baby-selling schemes of yore seem quaint. A few recent headlines: “The Chinese Billionaires Having Dozens of US-Born Babies Via Surrogate,” “The Family Law Loophole That Lets Sex Offenders Parent Kids,” “California Couple Busted for Running Suspected Baby Mill,” “Surrogate Mother Who Refused to Abort Baby Gives Birth Amid Ongoing Legal Dispute.” Polygenic testing companies promise today’s parents that they can pick the tallest, smartest, least-bald offspring, mainstreaming debates about the “Black-white IQ gap.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman—a father via surrogacy—and Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong are invested in an embryo-editing startup. If you believe what they told The Wall Street Journal, their first gene-hacked baby has probably already been born.
Many right-wing techies are jazzed about these developments, which might bump up birth rates or create “better” spawn. Many liberals don’t know how to talk about the ethical pitfalls. Emma Waters fills in the gaps. As a kind of backroom wheeler-dealer and political strategist, she is the mastermind behind Florida’s recent ban on international surrogacy, the Texas GOP’s souring on IVF, and the squashing of Trump’s “fertilization president” initiatives. This God-loving, JD Vance–stanning Gen Z-er might be standing between you and your ability to have a family, or she might be, somehow, the force that makes it possible. Waters has so much to teach us about optics and politics and why, in so many arenas, Democrats are losing so dramatically. Waters wants to dismantle fertility as we know it. And she wants to do it politely, during nap time, with her husband’s permission.
Waters wasn’t always political. She and her three younger siblings were homeschooled by their mother in a poor, rural part of southern Georgia, while their father worked 60-hour weeks as a facilities manager and HVAC repairman. (Waters describes her local high school as the kind of place where one-third of students got chlamydia.) Growing up, Waters never felt aligned with either party: Republicans praised free trade and cheap widgets; Democrats pushed equal pay and shoved kids into day care.
Then, in her junior year at a Christian college in Tennessee, Waters heard a podcast interview with JD Vance. “Everything he says, I relate to,” she remembers thinking. When she graduated a year later, in 2021—as valedictorian—she applied for an internship at American Moment, a training ground of sorts for rising conservatives. They gave her a full-time job.
Around this time, she met Jackson Waters at a mock-government event. Emma recounts their “whirlwind romance” in her book, Lead Like Jael. After “a summer of tense conversations,” she broke up with him “on a whim.” She wanted a career in politics; the thought of being a wife and mother felt like “a major letdown.” With the help of a pastor, she realized she only had these notions because of girlboss feminism. She begged Jack to take her back and got married at 24. She was an anomaly even among Republicans. Waters had heard older colleagues refer to women who got married at that age as “child brides.”
Waters loved life in DC: walking 24,000 steps a day, getting coffee with everyone and their mom, hosting dinners in her basement. When she got pregnant with Gertie, she and Jack wanted to prove that life didn’t end with a baby. But she needed a job with more flexibility that would eventually allow Jack to attend in-person seminary. In 2022, Waters approached the Heritage Foundation, the most influential conservative think tank. Heritage had recently shed its intellectual bona fides to become a MAGA mouthpiece; the next year, it would release Project 2025, the playbook for Trump 2.0.
Waters pitched Heritage that she would cover emerging fertility tech as an analyst: crafting policy briefs, penning op-eds, whispering into politicians’ ears. Waters found traditional pro-life policy banal—everything was about abortion. Debates around IVF started and ended with “Are embryos people?” She wanted to apply her dual major in political science and biblical studies to cutting-edge science. At the time, it seemed like “the least popular policy issue,” she says, but she promised the bosses it would soon be a big deal. They were sold.
Waters found her conservative colleagues ignorant about the state of assisted baby-making. One Hill staffer emailed Waters about a test that counts embryos’ chromosomes, asking, “Will this be around in 10 years?” It had been around for decades. At that point, a Chinese scientist had already embryo-Crispr’d babies, gone to jail for it, and gotten out. Sex selection had become a standard part of American IVF; the first sex-selected people were in their thirties. It was easier to open a surrogacy agency than an ice cream cart or a tanning salon.
Then there was China. In 2023, more than two years before mainstream media outlets reported on Sino-US infant import-exports, Waters was on Fox News, accompanied by an article headlined “Chinese ‘Rent-a-Womb’ Industry Using American Surrogates Is a National Security Threat.” She called it “the new face of birth tourism.” Intended parents didn’t even have to leave the country. Our nation’s lax laws meant that you could ship sperm over and get an American citizen shipped back.
Waters hates it when people harp on what she’s anti. Instead, she wants people to focus on what she’s pro: pro-“human flourishing”; pro-“the human person,” including embryos; pro-man-woman marriage; pro-life (duh); pro-Natural Procreative Technology, by which infertile heteros of breeding age clean up their diets, reduce their plastics, and ultimately get knocked up according to God’s will. Pronatalist? She prefers “pro-family,” which implies more straight marriages where straight penises and vaginas produce tons of babies. (Critics would add that the goal is really white Christian babies.)
Waters never says she’s against IVF per se. She doesn’t talk about “murdering” embryos; she makes it sound more like negligent manslaughter. She mostly argues that IVF doesn’t work. It encourages young women to postpone their true calling by falsely reassuring them that there’s still time.
To Waters, IVF is the conduit for many horrors. Ranking and selecting embryos tricks parents into thinking they can choose and control what kind of children they have, cheapening God’s handmade gift into an off-brand dustmop plucked off an Amazon wish list. It allows you to outsource reproduction to surrogates, objectifying women and commoditizing babies. Decoupling sex, marriage, and procreation distorts the natural order. Infertility explodes. Civilizations collapse. In her work, Waters fastidiously avoids mentioning gays, singles, or women over 40. When I ask her about this omission, she gets defensive: “It’s not about the desires of adults. It’s about the rights and well-being of children.”
Waters is a Republican, but that doesn’t mean all Republicans agree with her. The vast majority of Republicans support IVF as is. The pronatalist movement has two factions, the tech right and the trads. The tech right sees artificial wombs, surrogacy, and genetic optimization as tools to boost birth rates. Trads, like Waters, think these things will make the problem worse.
Besides China, nothing rankles Waters like embryo screening tools that promise to let parents “have your best baby.” Nobody really expects these so-called polygenic tests to move into the mainstream or ever become very accurate, but they set the tone for a future where parents can edit their children’s genes. On X, Noor Siddiqui, CEO of the startup Orchid and one of Waters’ least favorite founders, wastes no time in shaming breeders who fail to optimize. Getting knocked up the old-fashioned way is irresponsible: “What if your baby never walks?” Siddiqui has posted. “What if they’re never able to live independently? What if you could have stopped it … but chose not to?” (Stopping it, in this case, means making sure your disabled child isn’t born.) “Just be honest: You’re OK with your kid potentially suffering for life so you can feel morally superior, or because you can’t be inconvenienced.” In a decade, Siddiqui warns, all babies will be born using IVF and her test—Waters’ definition of dystopia.
Like many at Heritage, Waters was disappointed when Trump included free IVF in his 2024 platform, later declaring himself the “father of IVF” and “the fertilization president.” But Waters still found fertile ground (sorry) filled with low-hanging fruit. There were zero federal regulations governing surrogacy—she would shepherd the first one. “We have model legislation to SHUT DOWN foreign nations who rent the wombs of American women,” she wrote on X. She would rail against the creepy, unpopular polygenic tests that are opposed by every professional society. With the nation’s most influential conservative organization backing her, she’d push to mainstream so-called restorative reproductive medicine that co-opted the language of social justice while addressing the root causes of women’s broken, barren bodies.
Last November, waters sat onstage at the Heritage Foundation wearing a faux leather dress, slouchy boots, and a periwinkle double-breasted blazer while dozens of protesters in red Handmaid’s Tale cloaks screamed on the sidewalk outside.
I’d come to DC to meet Waters in person. It was a tough week for the organization. Its president had taken heat, and nearly had to resign, for defending Tucker Carlson’s choice to platform Nick Fuentes, a white supremacist. (Fuentes: “Hitler was awesome. Hitler was right. And the Holocaust didn’t happen.”) I wondered if there were always a dozen cops outside of the building. Sometimes the roar and the sirens were so deafening it was hard to hear Waters, but the disturbance seemed to make her smile.
First, Waters warmed up the room by having a “chat” with a mom who gets told by libs that she should’ve aborted her disabled son. Then Waters turned to the main event. “Welcome, gentlemen,” she said. She had assembled four white experts for “Editing Destiny,” a panel on the subject of polygenic tests and gene editing. Two seemed like MAGA partisans. Two were legitimate academics.
Waters had the energy of a high school newspaper reporter with a blowout and makeup that perfectly concealed her prominent chin. Everyone agreed that somatic gene editing on “born people” was good. Waters pointed out how it served the MAHA goal to eliminate disease at the source. But germline gene editing, the panel also agreed, was risky and unnecessary. No one said “fetus” or “God”; instead they evoked “the human person” and “flourishing.” Ben Hurlbut, one of the academics, made a moving, secular argument against polygenic selection. This was the “first relational act” you make with your future children, he told me, and it invites a serious rift.
Around the room, young female staffers in tight dresses held microphones for Q&A. The panel took a few questions. One attendee noted the harms of Tylenol.
After the event, Waters introduced me to Austin Rogers, then general counsel to Florida senator Rick Scott. Rogers wore a green Rolex with his hair gelled up in the front—he wouldn’t have looked out of place at a nightclub. Rogers told me they were using Waters’ model legislation to try to ban surrogacy from “foreign adversaries.” He was looking for a Democratic partner. He mentioned the latest story, covered by every major outlet, of a Chinese couple in California who had commissioned at least 25 surrogates to carry their children—a perfectly legal scheme—only to allegedly abuse most of those children in a mansion. He said, “I read it and my hair was on fire.”
That night, I walked Hurlbut, the academic, back to the train station and asked him why he agreed to speak at the Heritage Foundation. It wasn’t about party politics, he said. These issues couldn’t be split cleanly into left and right. “Anyone taking this seriously is creating a service to the public discourse,” he said. I asked who the big players were on the liberal side. “Big players? There are no big players. Just a few voices crying in the wilderness.”
Two months later, I visit Waters at home, in the type of town where hotels keep their lobby doors locked at all times. “I’ll have lunch to share with you,” Waters emails. When I arrive, she is wearing heeled boots and trendy jeans, making a butternut squash soup with bacon and brie. Ophelia watches from her high chair, wearing white tights underneath a fancy outfit. Over the next 27 hours, Waters will serve her husband and me a parade of elaborate orange foods: frittata with broken spaghetti, clementines, clam chowder (yes, also orange). (The girls will also eat Cheez-Its, Goldfish, and chicken nuggets.)
I recognize her hospitality tactics from Lead Like Jael, specifically the chapter titled “Motherhood as Warfare.” Waters advises women to embrace distinctly feminine means of influence. “No woman in the Bible picked up a sword to fight,” she tells me. Waters named her book after a biblical matriarch who offered an enemy commander a place to stay and then pierced his head with a tent peg, thus winning the battle.
I fear I am the enemy commander in this story.
In the book, Waters urges: “Take up your ladle like a sword. Stand behind your stove like a sentinel.”
Her house is modest yet beautiful, full of damask furniture. Christmas cards ring the kitchen doorway. In one photo, Simone and Malcolm Collins, the prominent pronatalist couple who embrace the term “hipster eugenicists,” smile from behind thick black glasses. On the credenza next to the dining room table, there’s a gilded Bible, a Venetian clock, and a ring light that never turns off.
Jack, home for lunch, says grace. Even 13-month-old Ophelia clasps her hands, closes her eyes, and bows her head.
Waters gets things done by being very, very nice. Simone Collins tells me, “I don’t know a single person in the pronatalist movement who doesn’t like Emma. She’s golden.” Even though the Collinses promote polygenic testing, IVF, and surrogacy, Waters considers them friends and makes a point not to publicly criticize them. In any given hour, Waters laser-focuses on a single issue. Another conservative tells me, “She could do an event with someone on Tuesday and be on the opposite side of a protest on Friday.” When she gets into a flame war with someone on X, she invites them to collaborate.
That’s how she secured the special guest for today’s Zoom working group: the founder of a polygenic testing company. One Tuesday a month, during nap time, Waters hosts private discussions with a group of bioethicists, activists, and policy wonks. Many potential collaborators do not want to be associated with Heritage, so Waters does much of her work in secret. She paraphrases a sign that Ronald Reagan kept on his desk in the Oval Office: “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.”
In the glow of the ring light, Waters and I huddle around her dining room table. I’m allowed to join if I don’t name names: I recognize a few prominent pro-lifers, and one or two liberals. “There is no dispute about how the technology works,” the polygenic testing founder says. He hammers home that two papers a day are being written about the associations between genes. His vibe oscillates between nerd and evil professor. He repeats at least a dozen times that his technology works. “There are ideologues masquerading as experts. You can easily fool a WIRED reporter into writing into her story that it doesn’t work.”
Waters asks a question about “children who have been born already.” Then someone asks about a recent paper showing that the sibling with the tallest-seeming genes is actually only the tallest about 25 percent of the time. This implies that, three out of four times, “picking the tallest baby,” well, wouldn’t work. The founder is irritated. One person might be predicted to be taller by 1 centimeter, but the error bars are 2 centimeters. “Falling within the error bars of the model means it’s successful,” the founder says.
Waters chimes in: “If the solution from a polygenic risk score for breast cancer was euthanasia, people would have a problem with it.” Then, she adds with a smirk, “That’s probably already happening in Canada.” To Waters, embryos are “human people”—but she won’t belabor the point or argue about metaphysical priors. The founder reminds us, “If you want to call it eugenics, you can, but don’t say it doesn’t work.”
Many of Waters’ critics dismiss her as a fool because of her retrograde gender views, which underpin all her other ideas.
I read Lead Like Jael in one sitting; my eyes got dry from popping so far out of my head. “There’s a hierarchy in marriage,” Waters writes. She advises her readers to become “good at being a woman” by “cultivating distinctly feminine strengths,” such as good posture. In an analysis of Greta Gerwig’s Barbie movie, patriarchy was “the first real innovation,” she writes. “Strong and godly men propel society forward.” Waters analyzes how, in the official portraits of First Lady Melania Trump, even her nails and eyebrows focus on the greater mission. She urges readers to redefine success as a joint pursuit, beginning with a husband’s career. Parents should start talking about marriage and motherhood at the same age as they ask kids what they want to be when they grow up. Women’s work should be flexible and easy to pause: “To neglect the home to pursue work is to invert God’s design.” Women are there to “support and strengthen” but not replace men. “Rightful authority” begins with husbands in the home. Women can lead, but only about 8 percent of the time.
Sitting in a trendy café, radiant in a puffy-sleeved red sweater and an Oura ring, Waters explains to me that the difference between men and women goes back to Genesis. Adam’s names mean “ground” and “man.” Eve’s names mean “fire,” “woman,” “mother.” So men are supposed to dig holes while women launch rockets? No: “A man is pulled toward the ground,” Waters says. “The wife is pulled to her husband and her children.”
She goes on: “We don’t want to go back to the 1950s. God put us in our time for a reason.” Still, there’s a lot to learn from the halcyon days when all 50 states allowed marital rape. Waters explains that the problem with the 1950s was that technology, like the dishwasher, stripped women of meaningful labor. “What would have been amazing is if women had radically rethought what they could do with the time they’d been given”—instead of just turning to wage labor. Despite providing most of the childcare, working full-time, and supporting her husband through school, Waters claims that balancing work and motherhood hasn’t been that hard. (Waters isn’t even so hot on federal paid family leave, since it encourages moms to go back to work.)
Here’s where I admit that Waters and I have more in common than I could have imagined. I got married at 25. I love being married and raising my child. We both go to church every Sunday (though mine has a gay pastor). I find it sad how young people see pregnancy as a funeral dirge for their hopes and dreams. I, too, expect low birth rates to cause big problems, and I suspect many “childfree” people will experience regret in 20 years. I’m inspired by Waters, how she cranked out more than 150 policy papers, interviews, and op-eds while I wrote this measly profile. I’m jealous of the time she spends with her daughters and how well behaved they are and how she managed to travel alone with a 4-month-old to Hungary to speak at a conference. But when Waters tells me that once you become a wife you have to subjugate yourself to your husband, it’s hard to keep a straight face.
If she wants to boost marriage rates, I ask, wouldn’t egalitarian partnership be an easier sell? She doesn’t have an answer. “It never crossed my mind.”
There’s a glaring gap between what Waters professes—that a woman’s highest calling is the home—and what she does, which is support her family financially while being way more influential and successful than her husband. She reconciles this by, literally, doing it all, while swearing she will slow down her career at a moment’s notice. By that same token, it’s also hard to distinguish between what Waters really thinks, what she is supposed to say, what’s rage-bait, and if there’s any meaningful difference between those categories. Her X background used to be a photo of “What’s Wrong With ‘Equal Rights’ for Women?” by Phyllis Schlafly, an activist who started speeches by thanking her husband for allowing her to be there. When I ask her about it, Waters says, “If your enemies think you’re oppressed, play up the trope.”
On the right, optics are everything. “How you project yourself is a political message,” Waters says. Before coming to DC, she had eight piercings, including belly button and eyebrow rings, but she didn’t want to be perceived like that. “Your appearance shows what you value,” she says. “I really value dressing well and pleasing my husband.”
If Waters had her way, there might be some IVF, but it wouldn’t involve ranking, destroying, or indefinitely freezing embryos. The only lawful surrogacy would be altruistic for heterosexual married couples with a documented history of infertility. (The gays, singles, and AOCs of the world would, in other words, put children’s well-being first and just not have them.)
In an international context, some of Waters’ views are perfectly normal. Almost every wealthy country besides the US bans elective sex selection. Every other wealthy country bans commercial surrogacy, which the UN called a form of violence against women and “the sale of children.” UN committees see anonymous gamete donation as incompatible with children’s rights. Most Western countries require tests to undergo some kind of approval process before going to market, so polygenic tests are out. In Germany, parents need government approval to genetically test embryos. Through a global lens, American Big Fertility is bizarro.
But for Democrats, it’s often seen as too politically toxic to criticize the largely unregulated industry. Challenging almost anything about it—even just that private-equity-backed clinics conduct most IVF cycles—opens the door for critics like Waters. Businesses have framed picking the sex of your baby, or even picking your Aryan-est baby, as a matter of “reproductive autonomy” on par with abortion. Lefties who disagree mostly keep their mouths shut. It’s almost too easy for Waters. Google will send anyone disturbed by the status quo straight to her op-eds.
While Waters invites journalists to her home and cooks them elaborate meals, some fertility professionals blame the reporters who dissect the scandals. After I wrote about a surrogacy gone wrong last year, Ron Poole-Dayan, the executive director of Men Having Babies, told me, “You are the problem. Journalists like you are a big part of the reason gay men can’t have families.”
People working in assisted reproduction see so many happy stories of family formation, they don’t even seem to understand what the problem is. At a recent conference for a surrogacy and egg donation ethics group, one attendee remarked, “An airplane takes off and lands a thousand times, and no one writes a story. A plane crashes once—everyone writes about it.” Someone else chimed in, “And flying is safer than driving!”
At the conference, surrounded by attorneys and professionals who seemed earnestly invested in doing the right thing, I thought of the left’s purity test problem: wanting so badly to be 100 percent correct that you forget how you look; ceding the hard topics to your opponents, who can wrap a kernel of truth in a bundle of nonsense; getting defensive when you could’ve invited the enemy in for a bowl of orange soup.
The biggest criticism lobbed at Waters is, obviously, that she wants to turn America into The Handmaid’s Tale. The second biggest criticism is that she’s a hypocrite. Waters’ kids aren’t in day care, but that doesn’t mean she doesn’t have help. At Waters’ house, I was surprised to meet a relative who consoled sobbing dolls and occupied the children while Waters entertained me and Jack studied the Bible or whatever. Waters’ mom is also a “full-time grandma” to Gertie and Ophelia.
The third biggest criticism is, let’s say, her credentials. “She’s not an academic. She’s not someone who actually has experience in these things,” says Lauren Hall, a political science professor at Rochester Institute of Technology. The feminist writer Jessica Valenti has essentially called Waters a failed influencer.
It’s not easy being an influential conservative mom who tells other moms of young kids to stay home. Criticisms of the Heritage Foundation, meanwhile, come from both the left and right. It’s “the worst-case scenario for a woman,” says Hall. She says Heritage puts “token” women forward, who have to hew to “a very particular party line.” In early 2025, an anonymous staff member sent letters to Heritage trustees alleging discrimination against childless women.
Waters disagrees, of course—she’s a fierce defender of Heritage. “America first,” she tells me. “MASS DEPORTATIONS NOW!” she tweets. She admits that Nick Fuentes says some “disgusting” things and describes him as “a young white man” who was “disenfranchised by the Republican Party because he dared to question our relationship with Israel.” When I ask her about the GOP’s unofficial strategy of “no enemies to the right,” a big-tent welcome for neo-Nazis and white nationalists, she snaps back, “Don’t you think the left is the same? Normalizing pedophilia. Abortion until birth. Rampant antisemitism … Why do you think Josh Shapiro wasn’t the vice presidential nominee?”
Waters’ master plan to undermine the fertility industry seems to be working. In November 2025, Senator Rick Scott proposed the SAFE KIDS Act, banning citizens of “hostile foreign regimes” from participating in surrogacy. In Florida, a similar law passed at the state level in May. At the start of 2026, Florida attorney general James Uthmeier stepped in to try to get two French dads un-recognized as their son’s legal parents, calling surrogacy “unconstitutional” and “modern-day slavery.” In July, Uthmeier intervened in another case, arguing that Florida should ignore an intended parent’s California parentage order, seemingly in opposition to the Full Faith and Credit clause of the Constitution. A proposed bill in Kentucky would ban all commercial surrogacy.
When Trump called himself “the father of IVF” in 2024, it looked like Waters had lost the battle against petri dish kids. But in June, Texas’ GOP denounced the procedure, and Trump has thus far reneged on his promises to make it free. In a recent grant application, the Department of Health and Human Services called frozen embryos “children.”
Many observers tell me they think Waters’ work is “the driving force” in pushing fertility regulation out of the fringes and into the mainstream. They also tell me the new laws are insincere and bad, fraught with unintended consequences. For example, the Florida attorney general’s anti-surrogacy argument would seem to prohibit Evangelicals’ sacred cow, adoption. Courts may challenge some of these laws in the coming months and years, but there’s no denying that American baby-making is going trad. On August 6, Trump issued executive orders banning birth tourism and denying passports to surrogate babies with foreign parents—measures proposed by Waters.
Her star continues to rise. Waters got a second book deal earlier this year (working title: Rethinking Fertility) and is contributing to a documentary about cryopreservation called Frozen Orphans. She recently presented at a Harvard summit on embryo law and ethics; four of the 20 other speakers have referenced Waters in their work. She is not opposed to running for office, although of course it will have to wait until her kids are older. In early September, she gave birth to her third child: another girl.

title: AI, Tariffs, Rare Minerals: What to Expect From Trump’s Upcoming Summit With Xi Jinping
raw_text:
Of all the events in the United Nations General Assembly taking place this week, the most anticipated by far is the upcoming meeting between Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping.
Though the majority of the diplomatic activities are happening in New York, this face-to-face between the two leaders will take place at the White House. Trump is scheduled to personally welcome Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, September 23—an unusual diplomatic gesture, as US presidents do not typically go to the airport to welcome foreign leaders.
Ahead of that airport reunion, a US delegation led by Treasury secretary Scott Bessent and trade representative Jamieson Greer is meeting with He Lifeng, China’s vice premier of the State Council, to set the agenda. The World Economic Forum presented an overview of some of the most pressing topics, including the trade conflict, the supply chain, technological competition, and the ever-sensitive issue of Taiwan—all while keeping in mind the difficulties that have kept the US mired in a war in the Middle East that threatens to escalate.
Trade Truce Expiring
The trade truce that came out of Trump and Xi’s meeting in Busan last year is set to expire on November 10. Both governments now have to decide whether to extend the agreement, which lowered Trump’s tariff threats and paused port fees. In addition to discussing the possibility of extension, the leaders could decide to set purchase targets for key trade items including agricultural products, energy, and Boeing aircraft. They may also continue negotiations about a package worth approximately $30 billion in “non-sensitive” goods, which includes about 10 categories, though there is no agreement on their scope.
One key component of the Busan agreement was that it lifted China’s export limits on rare earths and minerals—key exports for automobiles, defense, and technology, including essential hardware for AI. With the US seeking a more stable supply for these materials, Beijing has leveraged its dominant position in the international market to bring Washington to the negotiating table in the trade war.
AI Competition
According to Scott Bessent, AI safety will be on the agenda for the bilateral meeting. This discussion has been one of the main requests from business leaders, though the industry is mixed on the desired outcomes. Beijing wants to see the US ease some restrictions on Chinese technologies. However, as there is a growing call to slow down AI development to ensure safety, some US businesses are worried about being outpaced by China.
This arena remains uncertain, as Trump has dismissed such calls for regulation at home, and these discussions are also fundamentally intertwined with trade talks about export controls on computer chips and related materials.
Iran, Taiwan, and Global Politics
The trade talks lie uneasily between each country’s most sensitive geopolitical stances. China has threatened to pull out of the summit entirely if the US green-lights new arms sales to Taiwan. The countries are, however, expected to discuss China’s economic ties with Iran, as well as detained foreign nationals. Both countries are expected to tread lightly without ceding influence, making any fundamental shift unlikely.
In summary, Washington is pushing for greater access to Chinese products and markets, critical minerals, and commitments on certain security issues. On the other side of the table, Beijing seeks relief from tariffs and restrictions. Each side has its own leverage and multiple pieces on various chessboards, such as Africa and Latin America. At the same time, both are trying to prevent Taiwan and other geopolitical conflicts from undermining their economic relationship.
The meeting held this past May in Beijing was full of symbolic gestures, but both leaders made very few concessions at the negotiating table. Will there be a different outcome in Washington?
“I think there will be some show of deliverables because of the fact that it's a presidential summit coming, but I don't feel like we're on the verge of some sort of breakthrough,” Anna Ashton, a China trade analyst and founder of Ashton Intelligence, told CNBC. "I think status quo is probably both sides' general best expectation."

title: The EU Wants to Break Up Kids and Their Chatbots
raw_text:
The EU plans to ban chatbots from simulating emotions or interpersonal relationships in interactions with anyone under the age of 18 as the bloc tries to stop children from developing emotional dependencies on the technology.
The rules will be part of the EU Kids Act, proposed on Thursday, which includes similar restrictions on minors’ access to social media and video-sharing platforms. Children under 13 will be banned from accessing chatbots without their guardians’ supervision, and digital platforms will have to build child-safety protections into their products or face fines of up to 6 percent of total worldwide turnover, according to a draft of the legislation seen by WIRED.
Chatbots operating in the EU will also not be allowed to retain memory of interactions between separate conversations under the new rules, since the Commission worries this could lead to systems accumulating sensitive data of minors over time and potentially reinforcing harmful interaction patterns.
Providers of online social networking sites, video-sharing platforms, and games should not automatically activate or encourage the use of AI chatbots on their services, the proposed law will also stipulate. That includes not pinning AI companions and general conversational chatbots at the top of a minor’s contacts list, it says—as had been done by Snapchat.
The proposal is limited to AI companions and general conversational chatbots seen by the Commission to pose serious risks to minors’ health, safety, and well-being. Simeon de Brouwer, a policy adviser at the Brussels-based advocacy group European Digital Rights, welcomes the chatbot measures, but tells WIRED it doesn’t make sense to restrict them to young people only. “Don’t we all deserve to be protected from AIs designed to be addictive, from AIs which create emotional dependencies, or from AI features which are activated and pushed by default onto users?” The EU says its Digital Fairness Act, due to be unveiled later this year, is expected to propose clampdowns on addictive design more widely.
In documents seen by WIRED, the European Commission says it is worried that dependency on chatbots may negatively impact a child’s development and its relationships with other humans. It’s also concerned by chatbots giving minors dangerous advice, including on their mental health and personal development, which it said can shape and encourage risky behavior.
“Platforms have been playing fast and loose with children’s mental health,” President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press conference on Thursday. Around half of Europeans aged 11 to 25 have discussed intimate or personal matters with AI chatbots, according to an Ipsos BVA survey across France, Germany, Sweden, and Ireland. Australia and the UK are both attempting to restrict minors’ access to chatbots through their social media bans.
It also highlighted the harms of deepfakes generated by chatbots, which von der Leyen nodded at in Wednesday’s State of the Union speech: “We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images … Europe has the power to act.” While the EU AI Act has required synthetic content to be labeled as AI-generated since August, the rules currently only apply to deepfakes generated for commercial use.
The Commission also blames digital distraction for a decline in basic skills in young people. Children who say they use AI chatbots for schoolwork get lower test scores than those who don’t, according to research spanning 91 countries by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Concerns about cognitive impacts and deskilling “expose the absence of children’s rights from the design of GenAI’s tools,” researchers from the independent network EU Kids Online wrote in a report.

title: They Believe 2020 Was Stolen. They Could Be in Charge of Elections in 2028
raw_text:
One was central to facilitating the bogus Cyber Ninjas audit of the 2020 vote in Maricopa County that found no evidence of voter fraud but cost taxpayers $4 million. Another is friends with a Covid-denying former boxer turned MAGA influencer who was filmed on the steps of the Capitol on January 6, 2021 shouting “1776.” Another was set to headline a rally with MyPillow founder and election denial funder Mike Lindell.
This is not a list of edgy MAGA influencers sharing hot takes on X, or podcast hosts on Rumble boosting wild conspiracy theories. No, this is a list of some of the Republican candidates running for attorney general in states across the US.
A WIRED review has identified a slate of GOP attorney general candidates in more than half a dozen states, including key swing states, who have repeatedly expressed their belief that the 2020 election was stolen. If elected, several have said, they are willing to relitigate 2020 once again—and all will potentially play a key role in the 2028 presidential election.
“Any attorney general should be dedicated to upholding the rule of law,” Christina Beeler, senior counsel for the Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights, tells WIRED. “The office of attorney general is a powerful office, and it is deeply important that anyone in that role is dedicated to upholding the rule of law and the results of elections.”
The role of attorney general in the administration and protection of elections differs from state to state, but in general, as their state’s chief legal officer they are required to be a check on both the governor and the federal government. The functions of the role have been highlighted in recent months, as attorneys general across the country have repeatedly stood up to President Donald Trump and his administration's efforts to take control of elections, seize ballots, and obtain voter rolls containing sensitive information on US citizens.
Here, WIRED has looked at GOP candidates for attorney general in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, and Kansas, where some have openly espoused baseless allegations about the 2020 election.
Arizona
Warren Petersen, an Arizona state senator, was one of the most vocal supporters of Trump’s baseless claim that the 2020 election was stolen. In 2020, he signed a document that asked Congress to accept 11 alternate electoral votes for Trump, and later signed another demanding the US Senate reject Arizona’s slate of electors.
Petersen was also central to getting the bogus audit in Maricopa County approved, a process run by a firm called Cyber Ninjas. The audit ultimately showed that Joe Biden had won by more votes than originally thought. The whole process cost Arizona taxpayers millions.
Earlier this year, Petersen complied with a grand jury subpoena, handing over files on the Cyber Ninjas audit to the FBI as part of its investigation into the 2020 election in Maricopa.
And the lawmaker has also signaled a possible desire to relitigate the 2020 election if he’s elected, calling for an expansion of the attorney general’s Election Integrity Unit. “People will know we’re serious about it,” Petersen said during his primary campaign in July. “Just like they know the Trump DOJ is serious about it right now.”
Polls show Petersen tied with his Democratic opponent, Kris Mayes.
Georgia
In Georgia, the focus of much of Trumpworld’s conspiracy theories about elections, the GOP’s nominee for attorney general is Brian Strickland. In 2020, as a state senator, Strickland shared a press release that called for officials to consider launching an investigation into “fraudulent activities” in the 2020 election, a forensic audit of the election in Georgia, and new voting laws in the state.
Strickland has also signaled his willingness to fall in line with the Trump administration’s continuing efforts to investigate the 2020 election. When FBI officials raided Fulton County’s election offices earlier this year and seized ballots from the 2020 election, Strickland called it a “transparency” measure. “Fulton County can't run elections,” Strickland wrote on X in February. “That's the simple truth. Every Georgian, regardless of party, should have faith in our election process.”
An Atlanta Journal Constitution poll published this week shows Strickland in a tie with his Democrat opponent Tanya Miller.
Kansas
Unlike the other election deniers on this list, Kris Kobach is already in the position he’s running for in November, having won the attorney general’s race in 2022.
A long-time promoter of baseless conspiracy theories about fraudulent elections, Kobach previously served as Kansas’ secretary of state from 2011 to 2019. During his time in office, Kobach claimed that an estimated 18,000 noncitizens were on the state’s voter rolls based on non-peer reviewed research that initially found six people who may have attemped to register or registered to vote. In 2017, Trump appointed Kobach to the short-lived “election integrity” commission that found no evidence of widespread voter fraud.
In the wake of the 2020 election, Kobach was an adviser to Texas’ effort to overturn the results and assisted a member of the Michigan Board of State Canvassers who tried to rescind her vote to certify Michigan’s 2020 presidential election results. In 2022, Kobach was announced as a headliner at a Kansas rally with prominent election denier Lindell.
Recent polling suggests Kobach is in a tight race with his Democratic opponent, Chris Mann.
Michigan
In Michigan, Eaton County prosecutor Doug Lloyd won the GOP nomination for attorney general earlier this year, in a race that had once included Matt DePerno, a lawyer facing felony charges for undue possession of a voting machine and conspiracy in the wake of the 2020 election. (DePerno pled not guilty to the charges, and the case is still pending in the district court.)
Unlike DePerno, Lloyd is not typically labeled as an election denier, and he has claimed to be more moderate than his Democratic opponent, Eli Savit. But in a recent podcast interview reviewed by WIRED, when asked about “credible concerns raised by voters about the 2020 election,” he signaled his willingness to relitigate the six-year-old issue.
“I believe the attorney general has the ability to actually use their investigative officers within their office or the Michigan State Police to actually go back and look at those items,” Lloyd told the MI True Red podcast. “And so as I look at it, you know, I want to take those things in.”
Recent polling shows Lloyd tied in his race against Lavit.
Nevada
In Nevada, Trump has endorsed lawyer Adriana Guzmán Fralick for the position of attorney general. That may be because she has said she would push for Nevada’s version of the SAVE Act, which Trump has failed to force Congress to approve on a federal level. The act would impose severe restrictions on eligible voters by requiring those registered to produce a passport or birth certificate, documents that tens of millions of Americans readily do not have.
"President Trump is fighting for secure elections—but DC keeps dragging its feet,” Guzmán Fralick wrote on Facebook earlier this year. “Nevada shouldn't have to wait. As your Attorney General, I will push for the SAVE Nevada Act to remove non-citizens from our voter rolls, count all ballots on Election Day, and end universal mail-in voting. What Washington won't finish, Nevada will.”
Experts have repeatedly said the SAVE Act would disenfranchise millions of voters.
Guzmán Fralick has also touted the endorsement of Joey Gilbert, a far-right boxer turned MAGA influencer who gained fame for spreading conspiracy theories about the Covid-19 pandemic. Gilbert, who calls Fralick a “friend,” was also present at the rally at the Capitol on January 6, 2021. While he didn’t enter the building, he was captured on video near serial conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, chanting “1776.”
Recent polling shows Guzmán Fralick trailing her Democratic opponent Nicole Cannizzaro by 8 points.

title: Waffle House Teleporter Gregg Phillips Is Still on the Trump Administration’s Payroll
raw_text:
Gregg Phillips, an election denier who once claimed he teleported to a Waffle House, says he is still working in the Trump administration, after he was reportedly removed from his influential role overseeing the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s emergency response efforts in June.
While it remains unclear what Phillips has been working on in the administration since stepping away as head of the Office of Response and Recovery, on Sunday he wrote on Truth Social, “I have been in the admin since last year. I’ll be leaving soon to rejoin the fight.”
One day later, he was pictured at a Department of Justice building alongside Ed Martin, the former US pardon attorney who President Donald Trump last week announced would be departing the administration to “fight legal battles for the upcoming midterm election.”
“Enjoyed the visit with our friend Ed Martin today in DC,” Phillips wrote on Truth Social. “Haters are gonna hate this.”
Martin and the Department of Justice did not respond to WIRED’s requests for comment about Phillips’ role in the administration. Phillips declined to comment.
A FEMA spokesperson directed WIRED to a statement it issued in June saying Phillips was “taking leave for personal reasons.” When asked if Phillips was still employed by the agency and still on leave, the agency didn’t respond.
Phillips is on administrative leave, according to the White House, which also confirmed that Martin is still working in the administration until September 4. Federal employees on administrative leave are entitled to full pay and benefits.
Phillips has long promoted baseless allegations of widespread voter fraud, claiming in 2016 that more than 3 million noncitizens voted in the presidential election, robbing Trump of winning the popular vote. Days after taking office in 2017, Trump promoted Phillips’ false claims. In the wake of the 2020 presidential election, Phillips gained further notoriety when the group he was involved with, True the Vote, provided the data that underpinned the debunked film 2000 Mules, which falsely alleged that a network of individuals was paid to illegally collect and deposit ballots in drop boxes.
A 2022 investigation by the Center for Investigative Reporting found that True the Vote has raised millions of dollars from donors by repeatedly promising to uncover evidence of election fraud but has failed to do so. Much of that money, CIR reported, went to companies controlled by Phillips and in loans to True the Vote’s founder, Catherine Engelbrecht.
Phillips was appointed last December to head up FEMA’s Office of Response and Recovery despite having no past experience working in emergency response. In June, following his departure, the agency thanked Phillips for his “service, dedication, and leadership,” adding that “he has played a pivotal role in stabilizing the Office of Response and Recovery and advancing key reforms to strengthen our mission delivery.”
Three sources at FEMA, who were granted anonymity due to fears of recrimination by the administration, tell WIRED that Phillips has not been seen at FEMA’s headquarters since June.
When Phillips posted on Truth Social this week about his decision to “rejoin the fight” he was once again discussing “illegals on the voter rolls” and the work he and Engelbrecht had done almost a decade ago to address the perceived issue—which is so rare that even a third-party analysis of a database maintained by the right-wing Heritage Foundation shows it contains fewer than 100 examples. When asked if Phillips’ comment meant he would be working with True the Vote again, Engelbrecht said, “I’m sure Gregg will be involved in a number of projects in the future, and we at TTV think very highly of him, but in an effort to set the record straight, he is not part of the True the Vote team. He previously assisted TTV as a contractor on research projects from 2020–2023.”
When asked about Phillips’ role as a board member of True the Vote, as revealed by the CIR report, Engelbrecht did not respond.
WIRED recently revealed that ahead of the midterms, True the Vote will release another documentary, entitled Trapped, which again makes allegations about widespread and systemic voter fraud.
